en: Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle One.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
The Omniscient One extinguishes all darkness and pulls sentient beings out of the mire of birth and death;
I shall now expound the Abhidharmakośa in honor of that Great Teacher who teaches according to reality.
The commentary states:

If one wishes to correctly compose a treatise, one should first cause others to know the unique qualities of the Great Master; therefore, having first described his manifold virtues, one subsequently pays homage to the Great Master.
This verse is spoken solely based on the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The verse says:
"The one with all-encompassing wisdom extinguishes all darkness."
The commentary states:
"The extinction of all darkness is by means of the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Regarding 'ignorance concerning all phenomena' (*sarvadharma-avidyā*): because it can obstruct the vision of the true meaning, it is called 'darkness'."

Regarding this ignorance, because the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has attained the ultimate antidote and because it is of a nature such that it will never arise again in any way with respect to all phenomena, it is called "extinguished."
Although Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas have eliminated ignorance regarding all phenomena, because they do not give rise to the most subtle defiled ignorance, this is not by way of every aspect.

Why is this? Because all other noble ones possess non-afflicted ignorance regarding the unique qualities of the Tathāgata, as well as regarding other objects characterized by infinite distinctions across the most remote times and places.
Having praised the Buddha by way of the perfection of his practice for self-benefit,
he next praises the World-Honored One by way of the fulfillment of his practice for the benefit of others.
The verse says:
"To pull sentient beings out from the mud of birth and death.
The commentary states:
Because birth and death are the place where the world sinks and clings, and because they are difficult to cross, they are likened to mud.

When sentient beings are submerged therein without anyone to rescue them, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, out of compassion desires to deliver them; extending the hand of the True Dharma, he ransoms these people in accordance with reason, acting in harmony with practices that benefit both self and others.
The verse says:
Homage to the Great Teacher who teaches according to reality.
The commentary says:
Placing one's head at the Teacher's feet is called "prostration.
One who establishes the teaching without falsehood is called a "Great Master" (Śāstr).
One who is without error is called "consistent with reality" (yoniśas).
Having attained excellence and being free from evil speech, one’s words accord with the teaching.
To speak such reasoned instruction is the skillful means for benefiting others.
It is by means of this reasoned instruction that one rescues sentient beings from the mire of saṃsāra, and not through supernatural powers, the granting of boons, or majestic authority.
Having prostrated to the Teacher who teaches according to reality, what is it that one intends to do?
The verse says:
"I shall expound the Abhidharmakośa."
The commentary states:
This dharma is generally termed the "Teaching of Extinction and Salvation.
What are its specific names?
Abhidharmakośa. What dharma is called "Abhidharma"?
The verse says:
"Abhidharma is the pure wisdom along with its attendants.
The commentary explains:

"Wisdom" refers to the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*); "pure" means stainless, referring to untainted (*anāsrava*) wisdom; "along with its attendants" refers to its causes, conditions, and provisions.
If that is so, then the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) are said to be the Abhidharma; this is the true Abhidharma.
If one speaks of the nominal Abhidharma, [it refers to the treatises].
The verse says:
"The various treatises on wisdom that can attain this Dharma.
The commentary says:

That is to say, it consists of the outflowing wisdoms of reflection, hearing, and innate wisdom, along with their associated mental factors and the treatises; because they can transmit and produce uncontaminated knowledge and serve as the provisions for that uncontaminated knowledge, they are also called Abhidharma.
For what reason is this name established?
It is called *dharma* because it can maintain its own essential characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Alternatively, it is called *dharma* because among all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), the true dharma—nirvāṇa—is its characteristic.
Because this wisdom confronts all phenomena and brings them directly before one, it is called Abhidharma.
Why, then, is this treatise named the *Abhidharmakośa* (Treasury of Abhidharma)?
The verse says:
By virtue of its meaning, the Abhidharma is included herein.
The commentary says:

Those words and phrases are called Abhidharma; because they accord with the ultimate meaning and are subsumed within this treatise, this treatise may be called a "Piṭaka" (Basket) in relation to them.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The treatise relies upon the Abhidharma; thus it is named Abhidharmakośa."
The commentary states:
The Abhidharma is the basis of this treatise. Why is this so?

Because this treatise is derived from that Dharma, the latter also receives the name "Treasury" (*piṭaka*) with respect to this work. For this reason, this treatise is called the *Abhidharmakośa* (The Treasury of Abhidharma).
Furthermore, what is the function of this Dharma?
Who first taught this Dharma, such that the Dharma Master respectfully desires to explain it?
The verse says:

Apart from the discernment of phenomena, there is nothing else; it is the specific means for pacifying the afflictions. Since the world revolves through the ocean of existence by means of these afflictions, for this reason the Buddha transmitted the Abhidharma.
The commentary states:

If one is separated from the factor of enlightenment that is the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), there is no other means capable of eliminating the various afflictions (*kleśa*). These afflictions are able to cause one to revolve within the world, wandering in the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
For this very reason, desiring that his disciples attain the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), the Great Teacher, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, first taught the Abhidharma.
For apart from these correct teachings, disciples would be unable to discern the true Dharma in accordance with reality.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught this Dharma in various places and at various times; the Venerable Kātyāyanīputra and other disciples compiled and arranged it.
This is just as the Venerable Dharmatrāta compiled the Udāna and Gāthā sections, as the Vaibhāṣika masters have transmitted.
What are those phenomena that are to be investigated?
It is for the sake of enabling others to investigate those phenomena that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught the Abhidharma.
The verse says:
Regarding "defiled and undefiled phenomena," the commentary states:
Briefly stated, all phenomena are categorized as either defiled or undefiled.
Among these, what are those with outflows?
The verse says:
Conditioned phenomena, excluding the Noble Path, are with outflows.
The commentary says:
With the exception of the Noble Truth of the Path, all remaining conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Why is this?
The verse says:
"In the intermediate state, [afflictions persist] because they increase through latent tendencies.
The commentary says:

If such were the case, the outflows would arise taking the two truths of cessation and the path as their objects; however, since they do not "sleep" therein nor increase in accordance with those objects, one cannot establish that the outflows exist within them.
This is a counter-objection regarding the meaning of "non-sleeping" (asampramoṣa), which shall be explained in detail later in the Chapter on the Analysis of Defilements (Anuśaya-nirdeśa).
Having explained the contaminated dharmas (sāsrava-dharma), what are the uncontaminated dharmas (anāsrava-dharma)?
The verse says:
"The untainted dharmas are the noble path and the three kinds of unconditioned [phenomena].
The commentary says:
What are the three unconditioned phenomena?
The verse says:
Space and the two types of cessation.
The commentary says:
What are the two types of cessation?
They are analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Thus, these three unconditioned phenomena—beginning with space—as well as the noble path, are called untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas.
Why is this? Because within them, the various outflows (*āsrava*) cannot lie dormant; this is stated in brief.
Among the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), which one is space?
The verse says:
"In this context, space is non-obstruction."
The commentary states:
Because space has the nature of being unobstructed and non-resistant, form moves within it.
The verse says:
"Pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha (cessation through deliberation) refers to eternal separation.
The commentary states:
It is called pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha because it is the eternal dissociation from dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*) of each of the Noble Truths, such as suffering and so forth, is called "discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā*), which is the preeminent cause of wisdom (*jñāna*).
That which is attained through this [discernment] for one's own benefit is termed "cessation through discernment" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

Although it should properly be expressed as "the cessation obtained through discernment," it is referred to simply as "cessation through discernment" due to brevity, just as a vehicle associated with oxen is called an "ox-cart."
Are all contaminated phenomena (sāsrava-dharma) one single analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), or are they not one?
They are not one.
Why is this so?
The verse says:
Each corresponds to its respective fetter.
The commentary says:
The number of analytical cessations (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) is equal to the number of fetters (saṃyojana).

If this were not the case, then by realizing the analytical cessation of the afflictions abandoned through the vision of suffering, one would simultaneously realize the analytical cessation of all afflictions; if that were so, the cultivation of other remedial paths would be empty and fruitless.
The Buddhist sūtras state:
"Cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) has no similar type (sabhāga).
What is the meaning of this statement?
Cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) has no homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), nor is it the homogeneous cause of anything else.
This is the meaning of the Sūtra; it does not mean that there is nothing similar to it.
Having explained cessation through deliberation, [the discussion continues].
The verse says:
There is a distinct non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) which eternally obstructs the arising of that which is to arise.
The commentary says:

That which can eternally obstruct the arising of future dharmas, distinct from analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), because it is not obtained through discernment.
How is it that [they] do not arise?
Because the necessary conditions are not complete.

For example, when a person’s mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) arise in relation to a single visual object (*rūpa-viṣaya*), at that time all other objects—visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles—have already ceased. Consequently, the collection of the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) cannot take them as objects and arise again.

Why is this? The five consciousnesses lack the functional capacity to take past objects as their spheres; therefore, these consciousnesses possess non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), due to the incompleteness of their causes and conditions.
Based on the two types of cessation (*nirodha*), four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) can be established.
There are certain phenomena that possess only analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); these are all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena of the past and present that are destined to arise.
There are certain dharmas that possess only non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), namely those dharmas that are unarisen and are untainted conditioned (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*) phenomena.
There are certain dharmas that possess both types of cessation, namely those tainted (*sāsrava*) phenomena that are definitively not destined to arise.
There are certain phenomena that do not have two types of cessation; namely, those that are past, present, or destined to arise, and which are all untainted (*anāsrava*).

Having explained the three unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, it was previously stated that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), with the exception of the Noble Path, are called tainted (*sāsrava*).
What are conditioned phenomena?
The verse says:
Furthermore, all conditioned phenomena refer to the five aggregates, such as form and so forth.
The commentary states:

The aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*)—these five aggregates encompass all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Because they have already reached a state of accumulation and are produced by causes and conditions, they are called "conditioned."
Why is this? Because there is no dharma that arises without conditions or from only a single condition, as it belongs to that same category.
There is no contradiction regarding the future, just as in the case of the *dhuta* [ascetic practices].
The verse says:
It is taught that the paths of the world, the verbal bases, existence, detachment, and the categories [of phenomena] exist.
The commentary explains:
These conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) exist, have existed, and will exist; therefore, they are called "paths of the world" (*adhvan*).
Furthermore, because they are consumed by impermanence (*anityatā*), they are so termed.
"Speech" (*vāk*) refers to regional dialects (*deśabhāṣā*).
That which is the object expressed by speech is called the "basis of speech" (*nāma-adhiṣṭhāna*), because speech is apprehended as having an object.
The Buddha’s sūtras state that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are the basis of speech.
If it were otherwise, it would contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
That treatise states:
"The term 'basis' (āśraya) is subsumed within the eighteen elements (dhātu). To emerge forever from this is called 'detachment' (niḥsaraṇa), namely, nirvāṇa.
This is because nirvāṇa is the eternal emergence from all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta)."
Conditioned phenomena have detachment, whereas nirvāṇa has no detachment;
therefore, conditioned phenomena are called "with detachment. They are called "with categories" (sabhāga) because they possess causes;
"category" (bhāga) here signifies the meaning of cause.
The Vaibhāṣika masters state this:
such terms as these are alternative names for conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, regarding these conditioned dharmas, the verse says:
"Those with outflows are called the aggregates of grasping.
The commentary asks:
What is being revealed by this?
That which is associated with grasping (*upādāna*) can be called an "aggregate of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*).

However, not all aggregates are associated with grasping; this refers to untainted conditioned phenomena (*anāsrava-saṃskṛta*). In this context, "grasping" refers to the afflictions (*kleśa*); because the aggregates arise from grasping, they are called "aggregates of grasping," just as fire is named after its fuel, such as grass, wood, or chaff.
Furthermore, because they follow and adhere [to them], they are called "grasping," just as one speaks of a king’s servant.
Furthermore, because all graspings arise from those [aggregates], they are called "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*), just as one speaks of a flower-tree or a fruit-tree.
These are the dharmas associated with outflows (*sāsrava*). The verse says:
"Some say they are characterized by strife.
The commentary explains:
The various afflictions (*kleśa*) are called "strife" because they can disturb all wholesome dharmas and cause harm to oneself and others.
Because they lie latent (*anuśaya*) within this strife, it is said that there is "strife."
It is like that which possesses outflows.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The world is the truth of suffering and the truth of origination."
The commentary states:
It is called suffering (*duḥkha*) because it contradicts the intent of the Noble Ones.
It is called origination (*samudaya*) because suffering arises from various views.
It is called the "world" (*loka*) because it is subject to destruction, as there exists its antidote.
The verse says:
It is the locus of views and the three realms of existence (*bhava*).
The commentary states:
The various views abide within these [three], for they accord with and increase therein; therefore, they are the "bases of views" (*diṭṭhāyatana*).
They are called "existence" (*bhava*) simply because they cause existence to come into being.
Thus, the contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas have been explained according to their specific names as previously stated.
Regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth, the verse here says:
"The aggregate of form consists of the five faculties, the five objects, and the unmanifest (*avijñapti*)."
The commentary states:
The five faculties refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body;
the five objects are the domains of these five faculties, namely form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility.
And including the unmanifest (avijñapti), this much is called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
Among these, the five objects previously mentioned—form and so forth—are as follows.
The verse says:
This consciousness relies upon pure matter (*rūpa-prasāda*), which is designated as the sense organs, such as the eye.
The commentary states:

the five types of pure matter that serve as the bases for the consciousnesses of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch should be understood, respectively, as the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
As the Blessed One said:
"O Bhikṣus!
The eye is an internal sense-base (āyatana), composed of the four great elements; it is of the nature of translucent matter (rūpa-prasāda). Thus it is explained in detail.

Furthermore, it has already been stated previously that the five faculties, such as the eye, are so named because these consciousnesses rely upon translucent matter (rūpaprasāda) to be called the "eye faculty" and so forth.
Such is the meaning of the eye faculty and the others being the supports for their respective consciousnesses.
If this principle is established, it accords with the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
That treatise asks:
"What is the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*)?"
That is to say, visual consciousness relies upon pure matter (*rūpa*).
Having explained the five sense faculties, one should next explain the five objects.
Here, the verse says:
"Form is twofold.
The commentary states:
first, visible color (varṇa-rūpa); second, shape (saṃsthāna-rūpa).
Visible color (*varṇa*) is of four kinds, namely blue, yellow, red, and white; other colors are merely variations of these four.
Shape (*saṃsthāna*) is of eight kinds, namely long and so forth.
Regarding this, the *rūpāyatana* (visible form base) is explained again;
the verse says: "Or twenty.
The commentary says:
That is to say: blue, yellow, red, white; long, short, square, round; high, low, upright, slanting; cloud, smoke, dust, mist; shadow, glare, light, and darkness.
Other masters say that space constitutes one type of form; thus, there are twenty-one types of form.
Among these, the view that shape is the primary [criterion] is correct.
Imbalance is termed "perversion" (mithyā).
The vapor of the earth is termed "mist" (nīhāra).
The radiance of the sun is termed "light" (prabhā).
The moon, stars, fire, medicinal herbs, precious gems, and lightning flames are called "luminosity.
Among these, that which appears as a colored form is called "shadow" (chāyā), while the opposite is called "darkness" (andhakāra).
Other forms are easy to understand and are therefore not explained here.
There are material bases (*rūpāyatana*) that possess color but lack shape, namely: blue, yellow, red, white, shadow, light, brilliance, and darkness.
There are material bases that possess shape but lack color, namely: one part of length and so forth, which has the informative bodily action (*vijñapti-kāya-karman*) as its characteristic.
There are material bases (*rūpāyatana*) that possess both manifest color (*varṇa*) and shape (*saṃsthāna*), namely all other types of matter.
Other masters say:
there are material bases that possess neither shape nor manifest color, namely unmanifest matter (*avijñaptirūpa*).
Other masters say:
Only light and brightness possess color (varṇa) but lack shape (saṃsthāna). Why is this?
One constantly perceives various colors such as blue, etc., with distinctions such as length, etc.
How can two cognitions have a single object as their focal point?
Because these two colors appear within a single atom.
This interpretation is incorrect,
because it would result in a counter-argument regarding informative bodily action (*vijñapti-kāyakarman*).
Having thus explained the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), [the text continues:]
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of sound-objects.
The commentary says:

There are sounds produced with the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their cause, whether they are based on sentient beings (*sattva-nikāya-saṃgṛhīta*) or not based on sentient beings; these are called the four types of sound.
These sounds become eightfold through the distinction between those that are agreeable and those that are disagreeable.
Among these, those that have grasping as their cause refer to sounds such as "hand" and so forth.
Those that do not have grasping as their cause refer to sounds such as wind, trees, and waves.
Those designated as belonging to sentient beings refer to vocal sounds that possess meaning; other than these are those not belonging to sentient beings.
Other masters say:

There are certain sounds that have as their cause the four great elements (mahābhūta), both those based on grasping (upātta) and those not based on grasping; these are said to arise from the conjunction of the hand and a drum.
For example, just as it is not admitted that a single atom of visible form (varṇa-paramāṇu) arises based on two sets of the four great elements, so too should this sound be understood.
Having finished explaining sound,
the verse says:
Taste is sixfold.
The commentary states:
This refers to the distinctions between sweet, sour, salty, pungent, bitter, and bland.
The verse says:
There are four types of odor.
The commentary states:
they are distinguished as fragrant, foul, balanced, and unbalanced.
In the Abhidharma, it is taught that there are three kinds of odor: fragrant, foul, and neutral.
The verse says:
The object of touch consists of eleven kinds.
The commentary states:
It should be understood that there are eleven kinds of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya*), namely: the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), smoothness, roughness, heaviness, lightness, cold, hunger, and thirst.
Among these, the four great elements will be explained later.
Softness is called "smoothness" (ślakṣṇatva).
Roughness and dryness constitute "roughness" (karkaśatva).
That which can be weighed is called "heavy" (gurutva); the opposite of this is "light" (laghutva).
Craving for warmth is cold;
craving for food is hunger;
craving for drink is thirst.
The name of the effect is established upon the cause; therefore, it is said thus.
As the Buddha stated in a verse:
"The birth of all Buddhas is blissful; the teaching of the True Dharma is also blissful."
"The harmony of the great assembly is blissful; gathering as renunciants is blissful.
Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no contact of hunger or thirst, though other contacts do exist.
Among these, if that garment cannot be weighed individually, it can nevertheless be weighed because it is produced by the aggregation of the four great elements.
Within it, there is no cold-tangible quality that causes harm, but there is a cold-tangible quality that provides benefit.
Thus he spoke.

It has already been stated that matter (*rūpa*) is of many kinds; herein, at times visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises by means of a single object, provided that at that time one is discerning a single category.
Sometimes visual consciousness arises from many objects; at such times, there is no conceptual discrimination.
This should be understood as being like an army consisting of immeasurable colors and shapes, or like seeing a collection of jewels from a distance.
The same applies to the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth.

As for body-consciousness, at most it arises from five types of tangibles, namely the four great elements and one among the various tangibles such as smoothness; this is the position held by some masters.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"The body-consciousness arises fully endowed with eleven types of contact.
If this were so, then it would be taking the objects collectively as its objective support.

If the universal object were taken as the sensory field (*viṣaya*), the five consciousnesses would necessarily be established as such; for they do not merely perceive individual objects, but take the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sense bases as their objects.

If it is granted that these [consciousnesses] take specific characteristics as their objects, yet this does not mean they face the specific characteristics of the actual thing itself, what fault is there in this?
One should reflect on this meaning:
when the objects of both the body and tongue faculties arrive simultaneously, which consciousness arises first?
That which corresponds to the stronger object gives rise to its consciousness first.
If the object is equally present [to both],
why does gustatory consciousness arise first?
Because the mental continuum is drawn forth by the desire for food.
Having thus explained the five faculties, the five objects, and the manner of apprehending those objects,
we shall now explain non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
The verse says:

"Is it a distracted mind or a mindless state? Flowing along with the pure and the impure, and depending upon the four great elements—why then is there no mention of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*)?
The commentary explains:

A "distracted mind" refers to a mind directed toward a different object. Entering the meditative attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) and the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) is termed a "mindless state. The word "or" (*ye*) is used to indicate that this is neither a distracted mind nor a state of having a mind.
Because these resemble a continuum—whether occurring simultaneously or subsequently—they are called "flowing along" (*anugata*).
"Wholesome" is termed "pure," while "unwholesome" is termed "impure"; this applies equally to their acquisition and their continuity.
To distinguish these from others, it is said that they "depend upon the four great elements."
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"To rely upon" has the meaning of "cause," because the four great elements serve as the five causes— namely, arising and so forth— for the unmanifest [form].
In order to clarify the reason for establishing this name, it is asked:

"What? Although this phenomenon has material action as its nature, because it cannot be made known to others like informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*), it is therefore called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*).
This is stated as the teaching of other masters (ācārya).
To speak briefly, informative matter (vijñapti-rūpa) and the wholesome or unwholesome nature of matter produced by meditative concentration (samādhi) are called non-informative matter (avijñapti).
It was previously stated that it depends upon the four great elements (mahābhūta); what, then, are these four great elements?
The verse says:
"The great elements are the earth element, as well as the water, fire, and wind elements.
The commentary says:
These four great elements are called *dhātus* (elements) because they can sustain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as well as the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
Why are these four elements called "great"?
Because all other forms depend upon them and because they are coarse (*audārika*) in comparison to them; therefore, they are called "great."
Furthermore, they are called "great" because they arise as extremely pervasive, having a vast magnitude within the aggregates of earth, water, fire, and air.
Furthermore, they are called "great" because they can cause all material things to expand and grow, and because they are capable of performing great functions within the world.
Furthermore, in what kind of karma are these elements such as earth established,
and what is their intrinsic nature?
The verse says:
"Accomplished through the functions of upholding and so forth.
The commentary explains:

Upholding (*dhṛti*), cohesion (*saṃgraha*), maturation (*pakti*), and expansion (*vyūhana*) are successively accomplished among the four functions. Because the elements of earth, water, fire, and wind respectively transfer and augment [these qualities], they are called "expansion. This is the sequence of the intrinsic natures of the functions of the four great elements.
The verse says:
"The natures of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion.
The commentary says:
The earth element has solidity as its nature; the water element has moisture as its nature; the fire element has heat as its nature; and the wind element has motion as its nature.
To draw the continuity of the great elements to another location, like blowing a lamp’s flame, is called motion.
The *Vibhaṅga-prakaraṇa* states:
"What is the wind element? It is that which has the quality of lightness as its tactile sensation."

The Sūtras state this as well; some describe light touch as derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), because this phenomenon has motion as its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), motion is described as the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*).
Thus, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of wind is revealed through its activity.
Furthermore, what is the difference between "earth" (*pṛthivī*) and so forth, and the "earth element" (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) and so forth?
The verse says:
"Earth is said to be manifest color and shape; its name and concept are established by worldly convention."
The same applies to water and fire as well.
The commentary states:
When worldly people manifest the earth-element to others, they merely manifest its color and shape.
Just as the great element of earth is manifested, so too are the great elements of water and fire manifested.

Since they merely manifest color and shape, they are designated by conventional worldly names and concepts, and thus the sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is spoken of as the three great elements, such as earth and the rest.
The verse says:
Only the wind element.
The commentary says:
This wind element is what people in the world call "wind.
The verse says:
It is likewise.
The commentary says:
Just as worldly people metaphorically designate color and shape as "earth," they do the same for "wind," speaking of it as either "black wind" or "circular wind.
Why, then, is non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) designated as the last of these aggregates, called "matter" (*rūpa*)?
Because it appears and undergoes transformation,
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"O Bhikṣus!"
Because this dharma undergoes transformation and decay, it is called the aggregate of form-attachment (*rūpôpādānaskandha*).
What is it that can cause transformation and decay?
It is through contact with the hands and so forth; as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Because it possesses resistance and obstruction, it is subject to transformation and decay.
Furthermore, the Arthavargīya Sūtra states:
"The person who seeks after sensual objects is defiled and attached by the thirst of craving."
"If what is sought is not attained, one rejoices as if being pierced by a thorn.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"This form arises from transformation within the desire realm; it is called 'form' (rūpa) because it is characterized by resistance (pratigha)."
If that were so, then the color of an atom (*paramāṇu*) would not constitute "form" (*rūpa*), because it cannot be transformed or impaired.
This statement does not constitute a valid objection;
for the color of an atom does not exist in isolation, as it does not occur apart from aggregation.
If it exists as a composite, then it is subject to transformation and decay.

If that were so, past and future matter would not qualify as matter; for they too have undergone transformation and decay, or are destined to undergo it, because they belong to the same category of being subject to transformation and decay, just like firewood that is being burned.

If that were so, unmanifest form (*avijñapti*) would not be established as matter; however, this too is subject to transformation and decay because it follows from manifest form (*vijñapti*), just as when a tree moves, its shadow moves.
This argument is not tenable, because there is no informative intimation (*vijñapti*) and no transformation or decay.
If that were so, when informative intimation ceases, non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*) should likewise cease, just as a shadow vanishes when a tree disappears.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"Because its basis undergoes transformation and decay, non-informative form (*avijñapti*) also undergoes transformation and decay.
This interpretation is not correct.
If that were so, visual consciousness and the others would also have to be considered matter (*rūpa*) because they undergo transformation based on their supports.
Therefore, your position is inconsistent.
Nevertheless, there is a distinction.
Why is this? Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) arises dependent upon the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), just as a shadow arises dependent on a tree or light arises dependent on a jewel.

The visual and other consciousnesses are not like this; they arise dependent upon the visual and other faculties (*indriya*). These faculties serve exclusively as the generative causes (*janakahetu*) for the visual and other consciousnesses.
This position is not the tenet of the *Vibhāṣā*, namely that shadows arise depending on trees and light arises depending on jewels.
Those masters assert that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the visible colors of shadows and so forth each depend upon their own respective four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If this were truly the case—that shadows and light arise in dependence upon trees and jewels—then the unmanifest (avijñapti) should not be similar in its dependence.
Why? Because the four great elements (mahābhūta) upon which the unmanifest depends have already ceased.
That teacher does not accept that non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) perishes along with its support; therefore, this position fails to provide a valid defense.
Furthermore, another teacher offers a different defense, stating:

"The supports of the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness and others, each have their own distinctions. Some supports undergo transformation and decay, such as the eye and so forth; others do not undergo transformation and decay, such as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and so forth."

Since the basis for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is not like that, this objection is unequal; therefore, this principle must hold: it is called the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) because it is subject to transformation and decay (*rūpaṇa*).
This dharma has already been explained previously; its nature is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The verse says:
These faculties and objects are further described as the ten bases (*āyatana*) and the ten elements (*dhātu*).
The commentary states:
If established according to the system of bases (*āyatana*), they belong to eighteen bases, namely the eye base and the form base, up to the body base and the tangible base.
If established according to the system of elements (*dhātu*), they belong to ten elements, namely the eye element and the form element, up to the body element and the tangible element.
Having explained the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the establishment of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), the other aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*) shall now be explained.
Here, the verse says:
"The aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*) is the experience of contact."
The commentary says:
There are three kinds of experience that follow contact, which are designated as the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha). What are these three?
That which is able to experience contact that is pleasant, painful, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant is called the three feelings (*trivedanā*).

Furthermore, if these feelings are further analyzed, they constitute the six groups of feeling (*ṣaḍvedanākāya*), namely: feeling born of eye-contact, up to and including feeling born of mind-contact.
The verse says:
The aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is the distinct grasping of characteristics (nimitta).
The commentary says:

The grasping at the distinctions between characteristics—such as blue and yellow, long and short, male and female, friend and enemy, pleasure and pain, and so forth—is called the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
Furthermore, if one analyzes this perception, there are six types, just as there are for feeling (*vedanā*).
The verse says:
The four [aggregates] other than form are the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha).
The commentary says:
Excluding the four aggregates of form, feeling, perception, and consciousness, all other conditioned phenomena are called the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
In the Sūtras, the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, stated:
"The collection of six volitions is called the aggregate of grasping at formations (*saṃskāra-upādāna-skandha*)."
This is stated because it is preeminent.
This collection of volition is of the nature of karma and is the most preeminent among all formations;
thus the Blessed One said:
Because they function to produce conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), these are called the aggregate of formations with mental activity (*sābhisaṃskāropādānaskandha*).

If it were otherwise, and the remaining mental factors (*caitasika*) and dissociated factors (*viprayuktadharma*) were not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), then they could not be established as the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) or the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*); nor could they be established as that which is to be known (*parijñeya*) and that which is to be abandoned (*prahātavya*).
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:

"I do not say that there is even a single dharma which, if not seen and not fully realized, leads definitively to the end of suffering; the same applies to that which has not been abandoned and not extinguished.
Therefore, one should believe this principle: all conditioned phenomena are subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
The verse says:
These are the three aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*).
The commentary says:
This refers to the three aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations. When these are established as bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*), the verse says:
"Or they are called the base and element of phenomena (*dharmāyatana-dhātu*), together with the unmanifest (*avijñapti*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
The commentary states:
These seven types of phenomena are designated as the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of mental objects (*dharmadhātu*).
The verse says:
"The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is that which cognizes each respective object.
The commentary states:
"The mental consciousness (manovijñāna-citta) that cognizes each respective sense-object is called the aggregate of consciousness."
Furthermore, if this consciousness is analyzed, it constitutes the aggregate of the six consciousnesses, namely, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
This aforementioned aggregate of consciousness, when established as an *āyatana*, is stated in verse as:
"Or it is called the mind-base (*manāyatana*)."
The commentary says:
If one establishes the realms (dhātu),
the verse states:
Alternatively, they are said to be seven elements.
The commentary asks: what are these seven?
The verse says:
"That is to say, the six consciousnesses and the mind-faculty.
The commentary says:

The visual-consciousness element up to the mental-consciousness element, as well as the mind element—among these, the five aggregates have already been explained as the twelve bases and eighteen elements.

With the exception of non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*), the aggregate of form is established as ten bases and ten elements; the aggregates of feeling, perception, and formations, along with non-informative matter and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), are established as the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).

Is it not the case that this aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) consists of the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), the six elements of consciousness (ṣadvijñānadhātu), and the element of mind (manodhātu)?
Previously, it was stated that only the six consciousnesses constitute the aggregate of consciousness.
If that is so, what dharma other than these six consciousnesses is called the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
There is no separate mind-element apart from the six consciousnesses.
Nevertheless, among these various consciousnesses, the verse says:
"Among the six, that which has ceased without interval is called the mind-faculty (manas-indriya).
The commentary explains:
"Whichever one among the six consciousnesses has just ceased, this consciousness is designated as the mind-element (manodhātu)."
For example, it is like one person who is first a son and later becomes a father, or like that which is first a fruit and later becomes a seed.
Consciousness is also like this: it is first the six consciousnesses and later becomes the mental element (*manodhātu*).
If that is so, then in terms of substantial entities, there would be only seventeen elements or twelve elements. Why?
Because the six consciousness-elements and the mind-element mutually subsume one another.
If that is so, how are they established as eighteen elements?
Nevertheless, the verse says:
"In order to establish a basis for the sixth [consciousness], the elements are established as eighteen."
The commentary states:
These five consciousness-elements take the five elements of the eye and so forth as their bases.
Since the sixth mental consciousness-element has no distinct base, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) is taught in order to establish this basis.
Since the bases (*āśraya*), the supported (*āśrita*), and the objects (*viṣaya*) are thus established as three sets of six, the elements (*dhātu*) become eighteen.
If that were so, the final mind of an Arhat would not be the mind-element (*manodhātu*), because no consciousness would arise subsequently.
Is it because this [consciousness] has ceased without interval that it constitutes the mind-element (*manodhātu*)?
This interpretation is not correct. Why is that?
Because this [consciousness] has already abided within the nature of the mind and because the necessary causes and conditions are not complete, subsequent consciousness does not arise.

Herein, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are subsumed by the aggregates (*skandha*); all that is subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) is subsumed by the appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*); and all phenomena (*dharma*) without exception are subsumed by the sense bases (*āyatana*) and the elements (*dhātu*).
One should know that there is further a brief summary of all phenomena.
The verse says:
All phenomena are briefly summarized by means of one aggregate, one sense-base, and one element.
The commentary states:

Among the aggregates (*skandha*), it is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*); among the bases (*āyatana*), it is the mind base (*manāyatana*); and among the elements (*dhātu*), it is the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). One should know that these encompass all phenomena without exception.
Wherever the Tathāgata speaks of "encompassing," its meaning should be understood in this way.
The verse says:
Because they are of the same nature and category.
The commentary says:
This inclusion is due to correspondence through the same category, not through different categories. Why is this?
The verse says:
"Separated from the nature and category of other phenomena.
The commentary explains:
Since all phenomena are separated from the nature of others, that nature is not associated with them; therefore, one cannot encompass others by means of that nature.
For example, the eye-faculty is subsumed under the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣurāyatana*), and the element of the eye (*cakṣurdhātu*),
as well as within the two truths of suffering and origin, because it shares the same nature (*sabhāgatva*).
It is not subsumed under other aggregates and so forth, because its nature is incompatible with them.
If that is so, there are passages stating that one gathers others through another, such as when all sentient beings are gathered by means of the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
One should understand that such gathering is not constant and is therefore merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*).
Why are they not established as twenty-one elements?
For what reason?
Because the eyes, ears, and noses each exist in pairs; it should not be so.
Why is this? The verse says:
Because the category, the object, and the consciousness are identical, although there are two, they constitute a single realm.
The commentary states:
Herein, "of the same kind" means that these two share the same nature as the eye.
"Of the same object" means that these two both take visible form as their objective condition.
Regarding "identical consciousness," it is because these two together serve as the support for a single visual consciousness.
Therefore, although the eye-faculties are two, they collectively constitute a single element (*dhātu*); one should know that the same applies to the ears and nose.
The verse says:
If that is so, how can there be two?
They arise as two for the sake of adornment.
The commentary states:
If this were truly so, how could a single element such as the eye arise as two?
It is for the sake of adorning the basis.
If it were otherwise, and if only one eye and one ear were produced in a single location, or only one nostril were produced, this body would be extremely ugly.
This argument is not tenable.
If it were originally thus, then what adornment would there be in the birth of two eyes, ears, or noses in cats, raccoons, starlings, and the like?
If that were so, what purpose would there be in their being born with two?
This is for the purpose of assisting the formation of consciousness.
For example, if a person closes one eye while opening the other, or opens one eye while half-closing the other, their perception of forms will not be clear.
In order to adorn consciousness and bring it to fulfillment, each of the three faculties must have two locations.
Having already explained the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), this meaning should now be explained:
what is the significance of the aggregates, bases, and elements?
The verse says:
"Aggregation, arrival, gate, and nature—these are the meanings of the three names: aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
The commentary says:

Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; base or excellent; far or near—all such forms, gathered together in one place, are called the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
From this scriptural statement, the meaning that the aggregates (*skandha*) signify a "collection" is established.

Herein, past form (*rūpa*) is that which has already ceased through impermanence; future [form] is that which has not yet arisen; and present [form] is that which has already arisen but not yet ceased.
That which belongs to one's own continuum is internal; anything other than this is called external. Alternatively, internal and external are distinguished by way of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
That which is obstructive is coarse; that which is non-obstructive is subtle. Alternatively, coarseness and subtlety are distinguished by way of mutual dependence.
If you say: "The distinction between coarse and subtle is not established because they exist in mutual dependence," this argument is incorrect,
because the objects of dependence are different.

If something is established as coarse in dependence upon another, there is no means by which it could be established as subtle in dependence upon that same thing; it is like the case of father and son.
That which is defiled is base, while that which is undefiled is beautiful.
The past and future are distant, while the present is near.
This applies even up to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).
Furthermore, there is another distinction: that which relies upon the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) is coarse, while that which relies upon the mind (*manas*) is subtle.
The Vaibhāṣika masters determine coarseness and subtlety based on the [sensory] bases (*āyatana*).
A Bhadanta says:
that which is the object of the five sense faculties is coarse; other than this, it is called subtle.
That which is unlovely is called "vile" (*hīna*); that which is lovely is called "excellent" (*praṇīta*).
That which is in an invisible location is "distant" (*dūra*); that which is in a visible location is "near" (*antika*).
The past and so forth are made manifest by their own names and require no further explanation.
One should know that feeling and the other [aggregates] are likewise.
Their distance or proximity is determined by their respective bases;
the meaning of "coarse" and "subtle" is as previously explained.

"Entry" (*āyatana*) has the sense of a gateway through which the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) enter; alternatively, it is said to have the sense of "increase," as it can cause the arrival and growth of the mind and mental factors.
"Element" (*dhātu*) has the sense of "distinction," just as a single mountain location contains various distinctions such as iron, copper, gold, and silver; therefore, it is called an element.
Thus, within a single basis or a single continuum, there are eighteen types of distinctions which are called the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).
Herein, "basis" is used in its primary sense; "basis" refers to the homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*).
These eighteen dharmas constitute similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu) through their homogeneous continuity; therefore, they are said to be distinct.
If that were so, then the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) would not be a realm (dhātu).
This is not the case, because these [eighteen] are the similar-causes for the mind and mental factors.
Furthermore, other masters state:
"Dhātu" has the meaning of "category.
There are eighteen categories of phenomena; because they are defined by their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are called *dhātus*.

If the *skandhas* were defined by the sense of "aggregation," then the *skandhas* would have to be mere designations (*prajñapti*), because they consist of a collection of many things, just like a heap or a person.
This interpretation is not correct, because a single substance, such as an atom (*paramāṇu*), can receive the name *skandha*.
If that is so, one should not say that the aggregates (skandha) have the meaning of a collection. Why?
Because a single entity lacks the meaning of a collection.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"The meaning of 'aggregate' (skandha) is that which can bear a burden.
Still other masters say:
Each part has the meaning of an aggregate (skandha). Why is this?
For instance, as some say: "I should transform the things of the three aggregates."
This interpretation is inconsistent with the sūtras. Why?
Because the sūtras state that the meaning of "aggregate" (skandha) is merely a collection, as the sūtra says:
Regarding all forms—whether past, future, present, and so forth—as explained at length in the Sūtra:

if you say that the meaning of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) applies to each individual instance of past form and so on, it should be understood from the Sūtra that for this reason every single instance of past form and so forth is individually called the aggregate of form.
One should not hold such a view; rather, when all these forms are gathered together in one place, they are called a "skandha.
Because it is said thus, the skandhas are merely designated as existing, like a heap.
If that were so, then for you, the material sense-bases (*rūpīny āyatanāni*) would have to exist only as designations (*prajñaptisat*).
Why? Because they are composed of many atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the eye and other [senses] that function as gateways for the arrival [of objects].
This interpretation is incorrect, because each individual constituent within the aggregate acts as a cause.
Furthermore, since the sense organ functions in conjunction with its object, it cannot be classified as one of the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Therefore, the *Vibhāṣā* states:

If the Abhidharma masters speak while considering the aggregates (*skandha*) as mere designations (*prajñapti*), they say that such an atom (*paramāṇu*) is a portion of one element (*dhātu*), one base (*āyatana*), and one aggregate.
If they speak without such consideration, they say that such an atom is one element, one base, and one aggregate.
In this context, a partial [set] is metaphorically designated as "complete," just as when one part of a garment is burned, it is said that "the garment is burned.
Furthermore, why does the Blessed One provide three types of formal descriptions of the community of disciples by way of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth?
The verse says:
Because of delusion, faculties, and the three types of pleasure, the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) are taught.
The commentary says:

The Abhidharma masters explain it thus: there are three kinds of delusion among sentient beings. There are those sentient beings who, being unclear regarding mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*), grasp at the collection [of aggregates] as a self; there are those sentient beings who are unclear regarding form (*rūpa*); and there are those sentient beings who are unclear regarding both form and mind.
The faculties are also of three types: sharp, medium, and dull.
The inclinations are also of three types: extensive, concise, and intermediate.
For these three types of persons, the detailed text explains the three [categories] in sequence: namely, the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus).

Furthermore, for what reason did the Blessed One place all other mental factors within the single aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), while separately establishing the two factors of feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) as distinct aggregates?
The verse says:

Because they are the root of contention, the cause of birth and death, and established as sequential causes, feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) among mental factors are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*).
The commentary says:
There are two roots of contention: first, attachment to the objects of desire; second, attachment to various views.

The two factors of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) serve, respectively, as the primary causes for these two types of contention. Because sentient beings cling to the flavor of sensation, they become attached to the objects of desire; because they follow inverted perceptions, they become attached to various views.
The two dharmas of sensation (vedanā) and perception (saṃjñā) are the primary causes of birth and death. Why is this?
Because sentient beings, through their craving attachment to sensation and the arising of inverted perceptions, transmigrate through birth and death.
Furthermore, there is a reason for establishing the sequence, which will be explained in the subsequent text.
It should be understood that herein, based on this sequential reason, the two dharmas of sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established separately as distinct aggregates (*skandha*).
This will be explained in the section establishing the sequence [of the aggregates].
Furthermore, why is it that the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is mentioned among the elements (*dhātu*) and bases (*āyatana*), but not among the aggregates (*skandha*)?
The verse says:
The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is excluded from among the aggregates (*skandha*), because their meanings are incompatible.
The commentary states:
If one were to speak of the three unconditioned phenomena within the five aggregates, they could not be established in a way that conforms to the nature of the aggregates.
Why is this? Because the meaning is inconsistent.
In what way is it inconsistent?
This unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) state within the category of form is neither form nor, up to, neither consciousness; it cannot be described as a sixth aggregate (skandha).
Why? Because it does not conform to the definition of an aggregate.
The meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) as a collection has already been explained previously.

Since unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) lack distinctions such as past, future, and present—unlike form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates—it would be impossible to establish them as an "unconditioned aggregate" by collecting all such distinct factors into a single unit.

The "appropriative aggregates" (upādānaskandha) are taught to reveal the basis of defilement, while the "aggregates" (skandha) are taught to reveal the basis for both defilement and purification. Since these two meanings do not apply to unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta)—as they are incompatible with its nature—unconditioned phenomena are not established among the aggregates.
Just as a jar, once broken, is no longer a jar, so too when these aggregates (skandhas) are destroyed, they cannot be established as aggregates; this is what other masters say.
If one holds such a position, it results in a logical contradiction regarding the elements (dhātus) and the sense-bases (āyatanas).
Having explained the distinct meanings of the aggregates (skandha),
the verse says: Furthermore, in order, according to their coarseness, defilement, vessel-like quality, and so forth, are the meanings of the elements (dhātu).
The commentary states:

Form (*rūpa*) is characterized by resistance and is the coarsest among all [phenomena]; among the formless (*arūpa*), it is the sensation (*vedanā*) that possesses a coarse mode of activity (*ākāra*).
Regarding this, there is a saying in the world:
"My hand hurts; my foot hurts.
Perception is coarse compared to these two because its distinctions, such as male and female, are easily discerned.
Mental formations are coarse compared to consciousness because their characteristics, such as desire and hatred, are easily discerned.
Among these, consciousness is the most subtle because its intrinsic nature is difficult to discern;
therefore, it is described last, while the most coarse is mentioned first.

Furthermore, from beginningless saṃsāra, men and women have mutually delighted in form; this delight arises from attachment to the flavor of craving, this craving arises from the inversion of perception, and this inversion arises from the afflictions.
These afflictions arise from a defiled mind;
thus, their sequence is established according to their defilement.

Furthermore, their sequence is established by way of the analogy of vessels and so forth: just as there are vessels, food, side dishes, a cook, and an eater, so too are the five aggregates, beginning with form.

Furthermore, the sequence may be established by way of the realms (*dhātu*): the desire realm is manifested by sensual objects and forms; the various meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) are manifested by feeling; the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*) are manifested by perception (*saṃjñā*); and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is manifested solely by formations (*saṃskāra*). These four are the stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), wherein consciousness is able to rely and abide within them.
This sequence of the aggregates (skandhas) is intended to reveal the sequential meaning of the field and the seed;
therefore, only five aggregates are established, neither more nor less, based on this cause for establishing their order.

Within the [five] formations (*saṃskāra*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*). This is because feeling and perception are the most coarse, serving as the causes for the sequence of defilements.
Furthermore, like food and its condiments, they are established as separate aggregates because they manifest the two realms.
Among the elements (*dhātu*), the order of the six [faculties], beginning with the eye, should be explained. Why?
Because the order of these objects and their corresponding consciousnesses is easily understood; therefore, these six, beginning with the eye, [are arranged in this sequence].
The verse says:
Because the first five manifest their objects.
The commentary says:
The five faculties, such as the eye, take present objects as their conditions; therefore, they are mentioned first.

The objective sphere of the mental faculty (*manas*) is indeterminate: there are instances where the mental faculty takes a present object as its condition, and instances where it takes objects from the three periods of time or from that which is neither past, present, nor future.
The verse says:
Because there are four derived objects.
The commentary says:
The preceding discussion has reached this point among the five [objects]. Four of these were explained previously because they consist of derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) as their objective field.
The body-object (*kāya-viṣaya*) is indeterminate: sometimes the body takes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as its object, sometimes it takes derived matter, and sometimes it takes both.
The verse says:
"Other [objects] are distant, rapid, or clear.
The commentary says:
The "others" refer to the first four faculties, which were explained in their respective order previously.
Because they perceive distant objects due to distance, speed, and clarity, the eye and ear faculties are explained before the latter two.
Between the former two [faculties], the function of the eye is the most distant; for one sees a river from afar yet does not hear its sound. Therefore, the eye comes first.
Subsequently, there is the matter of urgency and slowness, as when one first sees a person beating a drum and only afterwards hears the sound.
The nose and the tongue do not perceive distant objects.
The nose is mentioned first because its function is more urgent; for example, even before food reaches the tongue, the nose already perceives its fragrance.
Furthermore, the function of the nose is more distinct, as it can apprehend subtle fragrances within tastes, whereas the tongue does not.
The verse says:
Furthermore, according to the sequence of their respective locations.
The commentary says:

Furthermore, within the body, the eye faculty is situated at the top; the ear faculty is below it; the nose is below the ears; the tongue is below the nose; and the body faculty is mostly below the tongue. The mind faculty has no fixed location upon which it depends. Therefore, their sequence is established according to their physical positions.
Furthermore, for what reason are all ten bases (āyatana) subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), yet among them only one base is called the "base of form" (rūpāyatana)?
And why, when all bases have the dharma as their intrinsic nature (svabhāva), is only one among them called the "base of dharmas" (dharmāyatana)?
The verse says:
"In order to distinguish their excellence, and because they encompass many excellent dharmas, only one base is named 'form' (rūpa) and only one base is named 'dharmas' (dharma).
The commentary explains:
What is the purpose of this distinction?

It is intended to make known that these ten factors each individually receive the designation of "entry" (āyatana), because they are established as faculties and objects; thus, they need not be gathered together.
Furthermore, although it is distinguished by the eye and other [faculties], this visible form does not receive the names "eye" and so forth; it is nonetheless the nature of form (*rūpa*).
One should know that because it is included within the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*), no separate name is established for it.
Furthermore, the sense-sphere of form (rūpāyatana) is predominant therein.
Why? Because it possesses resistance (sapratigha) with greater strength.
If objects such as the hand touch it, it immediately undergoes transformation and decay.
Furthermore, its essential characteristics manifest here and there, because they are easily pointed out and because they resemble shadows.
Furthermore, it is commonly known in the world that this base is called "form" (rūpa), whereas the other bases are not so known.
In order to distinguish it from them, one base is designated as the "base of phenomena" (dharmāyatana), while the others are not so designated.
Furthermore, within the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana), many factors such as apprehension and so forth are subsumed; because it teaches these many factors, it is given a general name.
Moreover, nirvāṇa is the supreme dharma and is subsumed within this [sphere], not within any other sphere; therefore, it specifically receives the name "dharma."
Furthermore, other masters say:

[The aggregate of form consists of] twenty types because it comprises many varieties of matter, and because it is the object of the three eyes—the fleshly eye, the divine eye, and the noble wisdom eye.
There are also other phenomena that share the same names as the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), which have already been explained in other sūtras.
Are all those [factors] fully encompassed by these three categories, or are they not?
They are fully encompassed without exception.
Regarding this, the verse says:

The Tathāgata taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*); these are merely words and names, and are thus subsumed within the aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
The commentary states:
There are certain masters who maintain that the Buddha’s true teaching has vocal sound as its intrinsic nature; according to those masters, it is included within the aggregate of form.

Furthermore, there are other masters who maintain that the nature [of the *dharmaskandha*] consists of words and phrases; according to those masters, it would be subsumed within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
As for the numerical quantity of these *dharmaskandhas*, the verse says:
Regarding the measurement of the aggregates (skandha) according to the Dharma,
the commentary states: Some masters say:

There is a portion of the Abhidharma called the *Dharmaskandha*, which consists of six thousand verses; each of the eighty thousand *dharmaskandhas* within the eighty-thousand-fold canon is of that same measure.
Furthermore, there are other masters who say, as the verse states:
"The aggregates and so forth are each taught [separately].
The commentary explains:

The aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), truths (*satya*), nutriments (*āhāra*), meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), formless attainments (*ārūpya*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), aids to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣika*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), vows (*praṇidhāna*), knowledges (*jñāna*), and the absence of contention (*araṇā*)—the correct teachings concerning each of these are individually termed "aggregates of dharma" (*dharmaskandha*).
The verse says:
"In reality, they are determined as the antidotes to the [defilements] that are to be abandoned; they correspond accordingly to the categories of the Dharma-aggregates.
The commentary says:
The various masters have indeed judged it thus:
sentient beings possess eighty thousand types of afflictive conduct, due to the distinctions among desire, hatred, delusion, pride, and so forth.
To counteract this tendency, the Blessed One correctly taught eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma (*dharmaskandha*).
Just as these eighty thousand aggregates of Dharma are included within the five aggregates, they are subsumed under the two aggregates of form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*).
The verse says:

"In this same way, other categories that are logically appropriate—such as the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus)—are included within what has been previously explained; one should reflect deeply upon their essential natures.
The commentary says:

If there are other aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), or elements (*dhātu*) mentioned in other sūtras, they should be properly discerned and included within the aggregates, bases, and elements as previously explained in this treatise, according to their respective natures and categories.

Within this, there are five distinct aggregates (skandhas), namely: the aggregate of ethical discipline (śīla-skandha), concentration (samādhi), wisdom (prajñā), liberation (vimukti), and the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha).
The aggregate of ethical discipline is subsumed within the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha); the remaining four are subsumed within the aggregate of mental formations (saṃskāra-skandha).

Furthermore, there are ten spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*). Because the first eight spheres of totality have non-attachment as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

If they are considered together with their associated factors (*sānucara*), they have the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as their nature and are therefore subsumed under the two spheres of mind (*manāyatana*) and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
The same applies to the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Because the sphere of universal emptiness (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*), the sphere of universal consciousness (*vijñānakṛtsnāyatana*), and the four spheres of the formless (*ārūpyāyatana*)—namely, space and so forth—have the four aggregates as their intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the two spheres of mind (*manāyatana*) and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Furthermore, there are five liberations (vimokṣa-mukha); because they have wisdom as their intrinsic nature, they are subsumed under the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana).
If they include their associated factors, they are subsumed under three spheres: sound, mind, and mental objects.

Furthermore, there are two spheres of entry (āyatana), namely the sphere of non-perception (asaṃjñi-āyatana) and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñā-āyatana). The first sphere is the Heaven of Non-perception (asaṃjñisattva-deva), which is comprised of ten spheres, excluding the spheres of odor and taste.
The second [sense-field], the mind-base (*manāyatana*), is subsumed within the two bases of mind and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
Thus, in the *Bahudhātuka-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke of sixty-two elements (*dhātu*);
these various elements should be understood, according to reason, as being subsumed within the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*).
Among those, six elements are taught, namely: the earth element, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
Of these six, the characteristics of two elements have not yet been explained.
Should this unconditioned emptiness be understood as being identical to the element of space?
Should all consciousness be understood as being identical to the element of consciousness? He said: No.
What are the exceptions?
They are the openings of the gates, the apertures, and the interior of the nose and mouth.
The verse says:
"Apertures are called the space element.
The commentary states:
If one speaks of apertures, it should be understood what kind of phenomenon this is.
The verse says:
"They say it is light and darkness.
The commentary says:
Why is this? Because there is no cavity that can be perceived apart from light and darkness.
Therefore, that which is called the space element (*ākāśadhātu*) has only light and darkness as its nature, and day and night as its states.
This space element is called "proximate-to-obstruction matter" (*pratigha-sāmantaka-rūpa*).
Those who speak of "obstruction matter" refer to that which is most easily subject to transformation within a mass of matter.
Because light and darkness are proximate to obstruction matter, they are termed "proximate-to-obstruction matter."
Furthermore, other masters explain:
This [space] also obstructs others, yet because it is unobstructed by them, it abuts other forms.
The verse says:
The consciousness element is itself consciousness and is with-outflow (*sāsrava*).
The commentary asks:
Why is it not said to be without-outflow (*anāsrava*)?
Because the Buddha authorized six elements,
the verse says:
"The basis for birth."
The commentary states:

These six elements serve as the basis for the mind from the initial moment of conception until the mind at the time of death and falling; however, untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) cannot function in this manner.

Thus, among these six elements, the first four are subsumed under the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavyadhātu*), the fifth is subsumed under the element of visible form (*rūpadhātu*), and the sixth is subsumed under the seven elements of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*).
The meaning of subsumption has now been explained.
Regarding the eighteen elements previously mentioned, how many among them are manifest (*sanidarśana*) and how many are non-manifest (*anidarśana*)?
The verse says:
Among them, one is manifest, namely, visible form (*rūpa*).
The commentary states:
This visible form is easily manifested, as when one says "this form" or "that form.
By virtue of this statement, it should be understood that the implication is that all else is non-manifest.
How many are obstructive and how many are non-obstructive?
The verse says:
Ten are obstructive and possess form.
The commentary states:
These ten elements (dhātus), being subsumed under the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha), are characterized by resistance (sapratigha).
What is this phenomenon of resistance?
It is called "obstruction" (āvaraṇa) because it acts as a hindrance.
This obstruction is of three kinds:
first, spatial obstruction; second, objective-field obstruction; and third, object-of-cognition obstruction.

Among these, "obstruction by resistance" (*pratighāta*) refers to that which, within its own location, obstructs the arising of another; for example, a hand obstructs another hand when they face each other, and the same applies to a stone and another stone.
"Obstruction by object" (*viṣayapratighāta*) refers to the sense faculties, such as the eye, with respect to their objects, such as visible forms. As stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"There is an eye that has obstruction in water but not on land, such as the eyes of fish."
There are eyes that encounter resistance on land but not in water, such as the eyes of humans and most other beings.
There are eyes that encounter resistance in both places—namely, on land and in water—such as the eyes of turtles, crocodiles, frogs, and those who catch fish with nets.
There are eyes that are unimpeded in two locations; this excludes the previous three cases.
There are eyes that are impeded at night but not during the day, such as the eyes of bats, owls, and the like.
There are eyes that are obstructed during the day but not at night, such as the eyes of humans and others for the most part;
there are eyes that are obstructed both by day and by night, such as the eyes of dogs, jackals, horses, leopards, cats, and wildcats.
There is an eye that is unimpeded at two times; this excludes the three preceding cases.
Such is the nature of obstruction regarding the object-field (*viṣaya*).
As for obstruction regarding the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the mind and mental factors are obstructed with respect to their own object-conditions.
What is the difference between the obstruction of the object-field (*viṣayāvaraṇa*) and the obstruction of the objective condition (*ālambanāvaraṇa*)?
When a phenomenon possesses efficacy within a particular obstructed location, that location is said to be the object-field of that phenomenon; this is termed the "obstruction of the object-field."
The objects apprehended by the mind and mental factors are called "obstruction as object-condition" (*ālambanapratighāta*).

Why are these faculties said to have obstruction with respect to their own objects, and why is consciousness said to have obstruction with respect to its object-condition? It is because they arise in a continuous succession regarding their respective objects. Thus, they are termed "possessing obstruction."
Because beyond this [point], it does not arise in that [object].
Furthermore, "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) here has the sense of "reaching," meaning that it arises toward its own object; herein, there is obstruction by way of reaching.
One should know that the ten elements possess resistance (*sapratigha*), because they mutually obstruct one another.
If a dharma possesses resistance by virtue of being obstructed by an object (*viṣaya*), does it also possess resistance by virtue of being obstructed by an obstacle (*āvaraṇa*)?
There are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first phrase refers to the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and that portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) consisting of associated mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
The second phrase refers to the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
The third phrase refers to the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*).
The fourth phrase refers to a portion of the dharma-realm consisting of factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktadharma*).
If a factor is obstructive by way of obstruction through its object (*viṣayāvaraṇa*), is it also obstructive by way of obstruction through its objective condition (*ālambanāvaraṇa*)?
