Excluding the latter two cases, if a phenomenon possesses resistance due to resistance toward its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it necessarily possesses resistance due to resistance toward its sensory field (*viṣaya*).

There are phenomena that possess resistance due to resistance toward their sensory field but do not possess resistance due to resistance toward their object-condition, such as the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*).
The Venerable Kumāralāta said:
"Where the mind intends to arise, But another obstructs it so that it does not do so, One should know that this is 'obstructive'; Anything other than this is not obstructive."
Having explained that which is obstructive, [the author asks]:
Among the eighteen elements (dhātus), how many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
The verse says:
Eight are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The commentary asks: which eight?
Among the ten types of obstructive [dharmas] previously mentioned, the verse says:
"All of these, with the exception of visible form and sound.
The commentary explains:

The five faculties, as well as the elements of odor, taste, and tangibility—these eight are called "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because they cannot be defined in terms of the distinction between wholesome and unwholesome.
Other masters say:
they are called indeterminate because they cannot be defined in terms of their karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
If that were so, it would result in a counter-objection regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*).
The verse says:
"The others are of the three natures."
The commentary states:
The remaining ten elements possess the natures of wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral.

Among these, the seven consciousness elements are wholesome when associated with non-attachment and so forth; they are unwholesome when associated with attachment and so forth; and the remainder are neutral.

The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is of a wholesome nature when it is associated with or originates from wholesome states such as non-attachment, and is the cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha); it is of an unwholesome nature when it is associated with or originates from unwholesome states such as attachment; and the remainder is of an indeterminate nature.

The elements of form and sound, when initiated by wholesome or unwholesome minds, possess a wholesome or unwholesome nature because they are subsumed under bodily and vocal karma; otherwise, they are of an indeterminate nature.
Having explained the virtuous and other natures of the various elements (*dhātu*),
how many among the eighteen elements are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*),
and how many are associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)?
The verse says:
"All exist in the desire realm.
The commentary says:
"Associated" (saṃprayukta) means "having the same object" and "not being dissociated.
Within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), all eighteen [mental factors] are fully present.
The verse says:
"Fourteen in the realm of form.
The commentary states:
Within the realm of form, they are not complete; there are only fourteen.
What are these fourteen?
The verse says:
Because odors, tastes, and the consciousnesses of the nose and tongue are excluded.
The commentary states:
Within the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are no odors or tastes, because these two belong to the category of edible food (kavaḍīkārāhāra).
This is because birth is taken there by those who have become detached from edible food.
Because these objects do not exist, the two consciousnesses of the nose and tongue cannot arise either, as they lack an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
If that were so, one should not establish the existence of the element of tangibles (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*) there, since tangibles are also a category of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).
It is indeed so; if touch were not of the nature of edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*), it could exist there.
If that were the case, then odor and taste would also be so.
But this is not the meaning.
Why is this? Apart from nutriment, smell and taste have no distinct function such as that of the tangible.
The tangible has a distinct function, namely, it can form the sense organs, serve as their support, and produce clothing and so forth.
The sentient beings there are free from desire for edible food; therefore, odor and taste are useless to them, whereas touch is not so.
Other masters say:

based on meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), they may see forms or hear sounds associated with pliancy (*praśrabdhi*), and there exists a superior category of touch that can benefit their bodies.
Therefore, these three [faculties] arise concomitantly in the places where meditative concentration is born, whereas odor and taste do not.
If that is so, then the two faculties of nose and tongue should not exist there.
This interpretation is not correct. Why?
Because these two have utility.
If one were devoid of these two, the body would be unsightly due to the absence of the two organs;
furthermore, speech would not be possible.

If such were the case, one would require only the physical bases of the nose and tongue for the sake of bodily adornment and speech, but the two faculties of nose and tongue themselves would be unnecessary.
This interpretation is not correct; there is no support that is not a sense faculty (*indriya*).
Just as the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) depends upon it, it would be reasonable for this [support] not to arise, because it would serve no purpose.
The nose and tongue have utility in dependence upon that [womb]; therefore, it is logical that they arise there even if separated from their [respective] faculties.
If the various faculties were to arise without utility—as occurs with beings destined to die in the womb—their arising would still be possible; yet, they cannot arise without a cause.
From what cause do these faculties arise?
They arise from craving for the faculties.
Regarding all superior karma, if a person is free from desire, they will certainly be free from desire for both objects and the faculties.
If that person has already become detached from the two objects of fragrance and taste, the two faculties of nose and tongue should not arise in them.
If the two faculties of nose and tongue do arise, why would the male faculty not also arise?
Because it would result in ugliness.
If the organs were concealed like the private parts of an elephant king, how could they be considered ugly?
Furthermore, their arising does not necessarily depend upon their utility.
How does it arise?
It necessarily arises by means of causes.
Although it may be ugly, if there is a cause, it must necessarily arise.
Since the cause does not exist, this [effect] is not produced; how then could that [other effect] be produced?
This interpretation is incorrect, as it contradicts the sūtra.
The sūtra says:
The claim that such a person possesses their faculties without deficiency is not correct;
for it is said that they possess no deficiency in respect to whatever faculties they actually have—what contradiction is there in this?
If it were otherwise, then the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) would also have to exist in them.
They explain it thus:
there, the two faculties of nose and tongue exist, but odors and tastes do not.
There, craving arises toward the six faculties by way of their internal bases, not by way of external objects.
Love for the male organ necessarily arises through the gateway of sexual contact.
Therefore, this point is established, and there are fourteen elements in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
The verse says:
Those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
The commentary states:

Having already abandoned desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), one is reborn there; since ten elements have matter as their nature, and the five consciousness-elements take those [elements] as their bases and objects, they cannot exist in the formless realm.
How many elements (dhātu) are with-outflow (sāsrava), and how many are without-outflow (anāsrava)?
The three elements of mind (manas), mental objects (dharma), and mental consciousness (vijñāna) have been previously explained.
The verse says:
"All those that are with-outflows (sāsrava) and without-outflows (anāsrava)—these are the three.
The commentary states:
If, within the three realms, they are subsumed under the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) or the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), they are without-outflows; other than these, they are with-outflows.
The verse says:
"The rest are with outflows.
The commentary says:
The remaining fifteen elements are invariably associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).
How many elements possess both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*)?
How many elements are without applied thought but possess sustained thought?
How many elements (dhātus) are without vitarka and without vicāra?
The verse says:
Those that possess both vitarka and vicāra are necessarily the five consciousness-elements (vijñāna-dhātu).
The commentary states:
These five consciousness-elements are said to be "concentrated" because they are always associated with vitarka and vicāra; this is intended to distinguish them from other elements.
The verse says:
Regarding the three final elements, there are three meanings.
The commentary states:

because the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental-object element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are the last among the eighteen [elements], they are called "final."

This comprises three categories: the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) associated with the mind, excluding applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*). In the desire realm and the first dhyāna, there is both applied and sustained thought; in the intermediate dhyāna, there is no applied thought, but only sustained thought.

From the second dhyāna upwards, including the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), which is without vitarka and vicāra, all factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), as well as the vicāra of the intermediate dhyāna, constitute *vitarka*. These are always without *vitarka* and possess only *vicāra*, because there is no second *vitarka* and they are associated exclusively with *vicāra*.

Regarding the contemplations (*vitarka*) in the desire realm and the first dhyāna, they are not included within the three categories [of *vitarka*, *vicāra*, and *avikalpa*]. What should their designation be?
They are "without *vicāra* and possessing only *vitarka*," because there is no second *vicāra* and because they are associated with *vitarka*; therefore, it is stated thus.
In the stage characterized by vitarka and vicāra, there are four categories of dharmas:
first, those with both vitarka and vicāra, which refers to all mental factors associated with the mind (citta-saṃprayukta-dharma) excluding vitarka and vicāra themselves;
second, those without vitarka but with vicāra, which refers exclusively to vitarka.
Third, those without vitarka and without vicāra, namely the factors dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktadharma).
Fourth, those without vicāra but with vitarka, namely vicāra alone.
The verse says:
"The remaining realms are devoid of both.
The commentary states:
The ten material realms are termed "the remainder"; these ten realms are always devoid of vitarka and vicāra because they are dissociated from the mind.
If the five groups of consciousness possess vitarka and vicāra, why is it said that they are without conceptualization?
The verse says:
Because of manifestation and recollection, they are non-conceptual by virtue of these two.

The commentary states: That [text] explains that there are three kinds of conceptualization (*vikalpa*): first, conceptualization of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*); second, conceptualization of manifestation (*abhinirūpaṇa-vikalpa*); and third, conceptualization of recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*).

The five consciousnesses possess only conceptualization of intrinsic nature and lack the other two types of conceptualization; therefore, they are said to be "without conceptualization" (*avikalpaka*), just as a horse with only one leg is said to be "legless."
Among these, the discrimination of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vikalpa*) is precisely vitarka and vicāra; this will be explained later in the section clarifying the mental factors (*caitasika*).
As for the characteristics and sequence of the latter two types of discrimination, what are they?
The verse says:
"Two are the minds of distraction; all mindfulnesses belong only to the mental ground.
The commentary says:

This wisdom is called "mental wisdom" because it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it is called "distracted" because it is not in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This wisdom is precisely the manifestation of conceptualization (*vikalpa*); all recollections associated with the mental consciousness—whether in a state of concentration or distraction—are termed "recollection-conceptualization."
How many elements (dhātu) have an object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya)?
How many elements lack an object-condition?
The verse says:
"Seven consciousnesses have an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The commentary explains:

namely, the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, as well as the mind-faculty (*manas*) and mental consciousness; these seven consciousness-elements possess an object-condition because they are able to apprehend objects.
The verse says:
"Within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), there is one half.
The commentary says:
This [dharma] also possesses an object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), because its essence consists of mental factors (*caitta*).

One should know that the remaining ten material elements (*rūpa-dhātu*) and that portion of the dharma-element (*dharma-dhātu*) consisting of factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*) lack an object-condition.
How many are with grasping and how many are without grasping?
The verse says:
Nine elements are not objects of grasping.
The commentary says:
Which are the nine?
They are the seven realms that have objects as their objects (*sālambana-dhātu*), together with half of the eighth.
The verse says:
Eight sounds.
The commentary says:
These nine are not objects of grasping (anupāttaka), namely: the seven consciousness-elements (vijñānadhātu), the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), and the sound-element (śabdadhātu).
The verse says:
"The remainder are of two kinds."
The commentary states:
There are two remaining [categories], namely, those with grasping (*sopādāna*) and those without grasping (*anupādāna*).
Among these, the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body are "with grasping" when they are present.

Regarding present form, odor, taste, and tangibility, those that are not separated from the sense faculties are also characterized by grasping (*sopādāna*); the remainder are without grasping (*anupādāna*).

For example, among things such as the sense faculties, hair, body hair, nails, teeth, feces, urine, mucus, saliva, and blood, as well as within earth, water, and so forth, there are both those with grasping and those without grasping.
What is the meaning of this statement?
It refers to the mind and mental factors; they take that [matter] as their own support because they mutually follow one another in terms of impairment or benefit.
This is what the world calls "possessing cognition," and it is termed "possessing grasping" (sopādāna).
That which is characterized by the meaning of "grasping" (upādāna) is called "with-grasping" (sopādāna); the remainder is called "without-grasping" (anupādāna).
How many elements (dhātu) have the four great elements (mahābhūta) as their intrinsic nature?
How many elements have as their nature being derived from the four great elements?
The verse says:
The element of tangibility is of two kinds.
The commentary states:

Tangibility consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements. The four tangibles, such as solidity and so forth, are the four great elements; the seven tangibles, such as softness, smoothness, and so forth, are derived from the four great elements.
Because they arise based on the four great elements, they are called "derived.
The verse says:
Nine material [dharmas] are derived.
The commentary states:
The five sense-faculty elements (*indriya-dhātu*) and the four object elements (*viṣaya-dhātu*), these nine are exclusively derived (*upādāya*).
The verse says:
And a portion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
The commentary states:
Within the dharma-realm there is no non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*); that which is spoken of [as such] is also derived (*upādāya*).
Among the remaining seven consciousness-elements within the dharma-element, excluding the non-informative (avijñapti), they do not belong to either of the two types.
Buddhadeva states:
"The ten bases consist solely of the four great elements."

This position is incorrect. For in the sūtras, the four great elements and the four characteristics such as solidity are definitively taught; furthermore, these four great elements are exclusively tangibles.

These four characteristics, such as solidity, are not objects perceived by the eye and other [faculties], nor are the four objects such as visible form perceived by the body-faculty. Therefore, this position is untenable.
In the Sūtra, the Blessed One said:
"O Bhikṣus!

The eye-faculty is an internal sense-base; it is derived from the four great elements, consisting of translucent matter produced by those four great elements; it possesses form, is non-manifesting, and is obstructive. This applies likewise up to the body-faculty."
"Monks! Form is an external sense-sphere; it is derived from the four great elements, produced by those four great elements, possessing form, possessing visibility, and possessing resistance. Monks!"
Sound is an external sense-base (āyatana); it depends on the four great elements (mahābhūta) and is produced by them; it possesses form, lacks visible manifestation, and is resistant.
This applies even to taste, and so forth. Monks!

Tangibility (*spraṣṭavya*) is an external sense base (*bāhyāyatana*); it consists of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), or that which is derived from the four great elements; it is material (*rūpin*), invisible (*anidarśana*), and resistant (*sapratigha*).

According to this sūtra, since the four great elements are entirely subsumed within the single category of tangibility, it is clearly understood that all remaining [objects] are not the four great elements.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtras:
"The eye refers to the fleshy orb; that which is solid within it and its like [is the eye].
Such sūtras merely state that the fleshy orb is inseparable from the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*), but they do not speak of the visual faculty itself.
In the *Gabbhāvakanti Sutta*, it is said:
"O Bhikkhus,
that which enters [the womb] consists of nothing but the six elements."
This is taught to reveal the fundamental basis for the maturation of sentient beings; furthermore, it is because the Buddha has spoken of six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatana*) therein.
Otherwise, even for you, mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) would likewise not exist.

If you claim that mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) are identical to the mind (*citta*), this is not correct. Perception (*saṃjñā*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are mental factors that arise dependent upon the mind.
Because of this scriptural statement and because the mind is taught to be the basis, this position is untenable.

Because it is taught that the mind is associated with desire, the previously stated point—that the various elements consist of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements—is thereby established.
How many elements (dhātu) are composed of atomic aggregates?
How many elements are not composed of atomic aggregates?
The verse says:
The ten material atomic clusters (*paramāṇu-saṃcaya*).
The commentary states:

These are the five sense-faculty elements (*indriya-dhātu*) and the five object elements (*viṣaya-dhātu*), which are constituted by atomic clusters because they are composed of a multitude of atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle One;
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Two.
Composed by Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Elements (Dhātuvibhaṅga), Part Two. Among the eighteen elements, which phenomena are capable of cutting, and which phenomena are that which is cut?
What phenomena can burn, and what phenomena are burned?
What phenomena can weigh, and what phenomena are weighed?
The verse says:
"That which can cut and that which is cut refer to the four external elements.
The commentary explains:
"Color, odor, taste, and tangibility are termed 'axe' and 'fuel'; these are precisely that which can cut and that which is cut."
What dharma is called "cutting"?
When a collection or a stream is in association and arising, the severance that interrupts its arising is called cutting.
The body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and so forth are not subject to cutting; for if they were cut, nothing would remain, as it is impossible to produce two [distinct] entities from one.
Why is this? If the sense faculties were divided into many parts, they would no longer constitute faculties, because the severed parts are not faculties.
Nor are they capable of cutting, for they are as pure as the radiance of jewels.
Just as that which cuts and that which is cut consist only of the four external elements,
the verse says:
"That which is burned and that which is weighed are likewise."
The commentary states:
Only the four external elements are that which is burned and that which is weighed; the sense organs are not. Why is this so?
Because it is subtly pure, it is like radiance.
Sound is also thus, because its intrinsic nature is severed.
The verse says:
"Disputing the capacity to burn what is weighed.
The commentary states:
There are certain masters who say:
The four external elements are that which burns and that which is weighed.
Some masters say:
among these, only the fire element can burn, and only the tangible quality of heaviness is what is weighed.
How many elements arise from maturation?
How many elements arise from accumulation?
How many elements arise from outflow?
How many elements possess substantial reality?
How many elements arise for only a single moment?
The verse says:
"Retribution and development produce the five internal [elements].
The commentary states:

The five internal elements refer to the five faculties, such as the eye and so forth; they arise from retribution (*vipāka*) and development (*aupacayika*), but do not arise from outflow (*naiṣyandika*). This is because there is no distinct outflow apart from retribution and development.
In this context, that which arises from a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is called "retribution-born" (*vipākaja*), because the intermediate term [cause] is omitted, just as one says "ox-cart.
Furthermore, when this karma reaches the time of the ripening of its retribution, it is designated as "retribution."
Because it is that which can bring [the cause] to fruition and because it arises from this [cause], the fruit produced by retribution is said to be "ripening.
Furthermore, the name of the fruit may be applied to the cause, just as the name of the cause may be applied to the fruit.
As the Sūtra says:
"These six bases of contact (ṣaḍ-spraṣṭavyāyatana) should be known as being [the result of] past karma.
That which is nourished by the excellent conditions of food and drink, maintenance, sleep, and meditative concentration (samādhi), etc., is called 'growth-born' (aupacayika)."
Other masters say:
"It increases by means of the holy life (brahmacarya).
This statement is not correct.
Why is this? The holy life (*brahmacarya*) merely prevents harm; it does not possess the sense of providing benefit.
It is able to provide protection for the continuity of the fruit and the continuity of growth, just as an outer city wall defends the inner city.
The sound-element arises either through accumulation or as a result of outflow.
The verse says:
Sound is not a retribution.
The commentary says:
Why is it not born from karmic retribution?
Because it arises according to one's will.
If that is so, how is it stated in the *Prajñapti-śāstra*:
"By being forever free from harsh speech and by having properly cultivated the precept against harsh speech, one attains the mark of a Great Man known as the Brahma-like voice"?
Other masters say:
Sound belongs to the third transmission; from karma arise the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of *śaṅkha*, and from these four great elements of *śaṅkha* sound is produced.
Furthermore, other masters say:

Sound belongs to the fifth transmission: from the great elements born of karmic fruition (*vipākaja*) arise the great elements of growth (*aupacayika*); from the great elements of growth arise the great elements of outflow (*naiṣyandika*); and from the great elements of outflow arises sound.
If that were so, bodily sensation (*kāyika-vedanā*), being produced from the four great elements born of karma, would not constitute a karmic fruition (*vipāka*).
If sensation were like sound, it would contradict reason.
The verse says:
The eight kinds of unimpeded elements (*anāvaraṇa-dhātu*) are those born of outflow (*nairmāṇika*) and those born of retribution (*vipākaja*).
The commentary asks: What are these eight?
The seven consciousness elements and the dharma element are produced as outflows (*niṣyanda*), because they arise from homogeneous causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) and pervasive causes (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
That which is born of retribution (*vipākaja*) refers to that which arises from a retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
These eight elements do not arise through increase, because unobstructed phenomena do not increase.
The verse says:
"The remaining three."
The commentary states:
The remaining four elements—namely, visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility—are either born of maturation (*vipākaja*), born of accumulation (*aupacayika*), or born of outflow (*naiṣyandika*).
The verse says:
"One is the 'existent thing' (*vastu*).
The commentary explains:

Because this unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) possesses substantial reality, it constitutes an existent thing; since it exists within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), only the single dharma-realm is the existent thing.
The verse says:
"The last three are for one moment.
The commentary says:

The mind-element (*manodhātu*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) are called the "last three" according to the sequence of the textual phrasing.

These three do not arise as a result of outflow (*niṣyanda*) within the first moment of the untainted (*anāsrava*), namely during the single moment of the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*); therefore, they are said to be "of one moment."

In this context, the mind associated with the receptivity to the dharma of suffering refers to the mental faculty (manodhātu) and the mental consciousness faculty (manovijñānadhātu), as well as the factors that arise together with and are associated with them.
This meaning should be carefully examined.
If a person is not associated with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and later attains such association, will they also be associated with the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
And if a person is associated with the eye-consciousness-element, will they also be associated with the eye-element?
The verse says:
The eye-faculty and the consciousness-element may be acquired either separately or together.
The commentary says:

Regarding "attained alone": there are cases where it is associated with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) but not associated with eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). For example, when a person in the desire realm successively attains the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), or when one falls from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to be born in the second dhyāna or similar states.

There are cases where one is associated with eye-consciousness but not associated with the eye-element; for example, when a person who has already been born in the second dhyāna brings eye-consciousness into manifestation, and subsequently falls from that state to be reborn in a lower realm.

Regarding those who obtain both simultaneously: there are cases where one is endowed with both the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*) at the same time, such as when a person falls from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or is born in the first dhyāna.
Regarding those who obtain neither: this excludes the first three cases.
If a person is associated with the eye-element (*cakṣurdhātu*), are they also associated with the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*)?
There are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Regarding the first phrase: it refers to a person who has already been born in the second dhyāna or higher levels and does not bring eye-consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) into manifestation. Regarding the second phrase:
it refers to a person in the desire realm who has not yet obtained the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*), or one who has already lost it.

The third case refers to when a person has already acquired the eye faculty in the desire realm and does not lose it, or when they perceive visible forms while born in the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, or similar states.
The fourth case consists of those remaining after excluding the previous three cases.

Regarding the phrase "the acquisition" (*prāpti*) of the eye-element and the form-element, as well as the eye-consciousness-element and the form-element, one should reflect in this manner; it is for the purpose of inducing such reflection that this is stated.
Furthermore, how many elements serve as the basis for the self,
and how many elements are external to the basis for the self?
The verse says:
"The twelve elements are my basis.
The commentary asks:
Which are the twelve?
The verse says:
"Excluding form and so forth.
The commentary says:
The six consciousnesses and the six sense organs—these twelve elements (dhātus) are called the "basis of the self," while the six objects such as form are called "external.
Since the self is non-existent, how can one speak of a basis of the self or what is external to the basis of the self?
Because it is the basis for the conceit of "I," the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self.
As a verse says:
"The self is the self's excellent support; Apart from this, what support could be superior?"
"If I am well-tamed, the wise will attain liberation.
Elsewhere, the Blessed One said:
"Only the mind is to be tamed."
As a verse says:
"The taming of the mind is supreme, for by taming the mind one brings forth happiness.

This mind is what the world calls the "self" (*ātman*); because the eyes and other faculties serve as its support and are closely associated with it, the eyes and so forth are designated as the "self," while form and other objects are called "external" because they serve as its objective spheres.
If that were so, the six consciousness elements would not constitute the support of the self.
Why? Because as long as the six consciousnesses have not yet reached the state of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), they cannot serve as the support for the mind.

At that time, if one takes the mind-element (*manodhātu*) as the basis, it is precisely the six consciousnesses that constitute it and nothing else; therefore, the six consciousnesses are not separate from the essence of the mind-element.
Were it otherwise, the mind-element would exist only in the past and not in the future or present, yet that school maintains that the eighteen elements encompass all three time periods.
If future and present consciousness lacked the essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the mental element (*manodhātu*), it could not be established as the mental element even within the past.
Why? Because the characteristic does not possess the quality of being indeterminate across the three periods of time.
How many elements (dhātus) are with-partnered (sabhāga)?
How many elements are not with-partnered (tatsabhāga)?
Which ones are exclusively with-partnered?
The verse says:
"The dharmadhātu is equal.
The commentary says:
These objects are certainly the objective spheres (*viṣaya*) for consciousness.
If consciousness has already arisen with respect to them, or is destined to arise as a matter of course, these objects are termed "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).
There is not a single element of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in which an infinite mental consciousness has not already arisen or is not destined to arise.

Why is this? Because for all noble ones, when the mind takes the dharma-realm as its object, it necessarily arises in this way: namely, that all phenomena are without self, and this mind is free from both intrinsic nature and associated dharmas.
All other phenomena are entirely objects of cognition; this first momentary mind becomes an object for the second momentary mind.
Within these two moments, all phenomena become objects of cognition; therefore, the dharma-realm is eternally homogeneous.
The verse says:
"The non-homogeneous and the rest.
The commentary says:
Excluding the dharma-element, the remaining elements are both non-homogeneous and homogeneous.
What dharma is called "non-homogeneous"?
The verse says:
"Not performing its own function.
The commentary states:
This meaning has already been explained.
If it performs its own function, it is called "having an objective counterpart" (sabhāga).
If the eye-element has already seen a form, is currently seeing a form, or will see a form, it is said to have an objective counterpart; this applies likewise up to the mind-element.
The term "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) is established based on the capacity of the object itself.
The Master of Kaśmīr says:

There are four types of non-homogeneous eyes (*asabhāga-cakṣus*): those that do not see visible forms, those that have already ceased, those that are currently ceasing, and those that are about to cease and are destined never to arise.
The masters of the West state that there are five kinds of non-arising phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma*), which are divided into two categories:
those associated with consciousness (*citta-samprayukta*) and those dissociated from consciousness (*citta-viprayukta*).
The same applies even to the body.
As for the mental faculty (*manas*), it is called "non-homogeneous" (*apratisaṃkhyā*) when it is of a nature that does not arise.
Regarding visible form (*rūpa*), if it has been seen, is being seen, or will be seen, it is called "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*).

There are four kinds of non-homogeneous [elements]: if a form is not being seen, has already ceased, is currently ceasing, or will cease, and is of a nature not to arise, it is called non-homogeneous.
The same applies up to the sense of touch.

One should understand that visible forms and the other objects have the status of being "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) according to the function of their respective faculties.
An eye that is homogeneous for one person is non-homogeneous for all others; this applies likewise up to the mind.

Visible form is not like this; depending on whether it can be seen by a person, for that person it constitutes "homogeneous" (sabhāga), whereas if it cannot be seen, for that person it is "non-homogeneous" (tatsabhāga).
Why is this? Because there is such a principle:
this form may be seen by one person and yet also be seen by many people, as in the case of forms such as the moon, dancers, or a gathering of people seen during a performance.

There is no such principle that two people could see a form with a single visual faculty; therefore, because the faculties are not shared, they are distinguished as "functioning" (*sabhāga*) or "non-functioning" (*tatsabhāga*) with respect to a single continuum.
Because form is shared, it is not established as functioning or non-functioning with respect to a single continuum.
As it is with the realm of visible form (*rūpa-dhātu*), so should the realms of sound, odor, taste,
and tangibility (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dhātu*) be understood.
While the realm of sound may be admitted to be thus [common], the three realms beginning with odor are such that what is perceived by one individual is not perceived by another.

Why is this? Because these three all reach their respective sense bases (*indriya*), they are not obtained in common; therefore, it would be logical to establish them separately as being like the eye and so forth.
Although they are not obtained in common, there is such a principle that allows for their establishment as being obtained in common.
Why is this? Because there is this principle:

these [objects] such as odors can produce the nose-consciousness and so forth of one person, and they can likewise produce the nose-consciousness and so forth of other persons; the eye and other [faculties] are not like this. Therefore, odors and so forth may be cited as examples for explaining the concepts of "homogeneous" (*sabhāga*) and "non-homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*) regarding the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth, because they are respectively determined to be produced or not produced, just like the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
What is the meaning of "equal participation" (*sabhāga*)?
It refers to the mutual correspondence between the sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness;
furthermore, they collectively perform all functions and share the same objective, which is contact (*sparśa*).

The "non-homogeneous" (asabhāga) refers to that which is of the same class as the homogeneous (sabhāga); although it resembles the latter, it is not actually it, and is therefore called non-homogeneous.
How many elements (dhātus) are abandoned by the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya)?
How many elements (*dhātu*) are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*)?
How many elements are not to be abandoned?
The verse says:
"Ten realms are abandoned through the path of cultivation; five are also [abandoned through the path of cultivation].
The commentary states:
The ten realms, such as form (*rūpa*), along with the five consciousness realms, are exclusively abandoned through the path of cultivation.
The verse says:
"The last three have three [each].
The commentary says:
The mind-element (manodhātu), the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), and the mental-consciousness-element (manovijñānadhātu)—these three each have three types.

The eighty-eight underlying tendencies (anuśaya) and the factors coexistent with them are their acquisitions (prāpti); together with their associated attendants, all are abandoned through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya).
All remaining contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava*) are not to be abandoned.
Is there any other distinct phenomenon that is abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*)? No, there is not.
What are the distinct dharmas?

The nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) can induce rebirth in the evil realms; because the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are contrary to the Noble Path, these are not abandoned through the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
Herein, the characteristics of what is abandoned through the vision of the truths are briefly explained.
The verse says:
Not defiled, not abandoned by vision, not form, and not produced from the six [consciousnesses].
The commentary states:
Among those things abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*), there is not a single dharma that is not afflicted (*kliṣṭa*).
Furthermore, matter (*rūpa*) is not abandoned through the vision of the truths; the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is neutral (*avyākṛta*) and non-afflicted.

Because ordinary persons who have severed the roots of goodness and those who are free from desire are associated with this [state], and because the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are material form (*rūpa*), they are therefore not abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*).
Why is this? Because it cannot contradict the principle of the Four Noble Truths.

If that were so, then at the moment the Dharma-patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) arises, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) would still exist; this would then constitute the difficulty of contradicting one's own tenet.

The sixth refers to the mind-base (*manāyatana*). If it arises elsewhere apart from this, it is called "not born from the six," meaning it arises from the five sense-faculties; such phenomena are also not abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are vision (*darśana*) and how many are not vision?
The verse says:
"A portion of the eye and the dharma-element is called 'seeing'.
The commentary asks:
"What constitutes this portion?"
The verse says:
There are eight kinds.
The commentary says:

The five views, beginning with the view of a self-entity (satkāyadṛṣṭi), along with mundane right view, the right view of those in training (śaikṣa), and the right view of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)—these eight are a portion of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) that are called "view" (dṛṣṭi); the remainder of the dharma-element is not "view."

Among these, the five views, beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), will be explained in detail when the time comes in the section on the discrimination of afflictions (*vibhāṣā*).
Worldly right view (*laukikī samyagdṛṣṭi*) is wholesome, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The right view of those in training refers to the untainted wisdom (*anāsravaprajñā*) of those in training;
it is the same for those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

These four types of vision—like seeing forms at night or by day when there are clouds or no clouds—are likewise applied to the observation of all phenomena by those with defiled and undefiled mundane views, as well as by those in training and those beyond training.
Why is it said that mundane right view is associated exclusively with the mental consciousness?
For this reason,
the verse says:
The wisdom co-arising with the five consciousnesses is not "view" (*darśana*), because it does not involve deliberation (*pariccheda*).
The commentary states:
"View" has the nature of decisive determination (*niścaya*), for it is capable of initiating the discernment (*vivecana*) of what is right and what is wrong.
The wisdom associated with the five consciousnesses is not so, because it is non-conceptual; therefore, it is not "view" (*dṛṣṭi*).
Whether that [wisdom] is defiled or undefiled, it is in all cases not a view.
If that is so, the eye faculty also lacks deliberative judgment; why then is it called "seeing"?
Because it is capable of observing and beholding visible forms.
How is this known?
The verse says:
"The eye sees forms.
The commentary explains:
If the eye sees forms while associated with another consciousness, the person should be able to see those forms.
If it is not the case that the eye sees forms in all instances, then what is it that can see?
The verse says:
"Equal parts.
The commentary explains:
At the time when this eye possesses consciousness, it is then able to see;
otherwise, it cannot see.
If that is so, one must admit that it is consciousness, relying upon the eye faculty, that sees.
The verse says:
It is not the visual consciousness that depends [on it].
The commentary says:
It is not possible to establish that visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) is capable of seeing. Why?
The verse says:
"Because form is not visible, it is held to be so when obstructed.
The commentary states:
When this form is obstructed by walls and the like, it cannot be seen.
If consciousness were able to see, then because consciousness is unimpeded, walls and other such obstructions would not hinder it; therefore, it should see objects obstructed by barriers.
Since consciousness does not arise with respect to obstructed objects, how could it see them?
How is it that [consciousness] does not arise?

If one maintains that only the eye sees visible form, then for such a person, because the eye is obstructed, it lacks the capacity regarding the obscured form; thus consciousness cannot arise, since it must arise with its support (the sense organ) directed toward the same object. This principle must be so.
If that is so, why is it that the eye does not reach its object, just like the body-faculty? It is because it does not see obstructed forms, owing to its resistance.
If that is so, how can forms obstructed by mica, lapis lazuli, crystal, or clear water be seen?
Therefore, it is not because of physical obstruction that the eye cannot see forms that are concealed.
If this is so, why is it not seen?
It is because in those places where light can pass through without interruption, visual consciousness arises with respect to the concealed form.
If light is obstructed and cannot pass through a certain place, visual consciousness does not arise therein.
Because it does not arise, one is unable to see the obscured form.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra say:
"By means of the eye one sees forms.
In this context, the meaning of the sutra is that seeing is achieved by relying [upon the faculty].
It is as when it is said: "By means of the mental faculty (manas), consciousness cognizes phenomena (dharma)"; yet the mind itself cannot cognize phenomena, because it has already passed away.
What is it that cognizes?
It is exclusively the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The Sūtra’s statement that "one sees by means of the eye" is likewise [figurative].
Furthermore, the basis is sometimes spoken of as the dependent entity, just as in the expression "the tower cries.
Furthermore, as stated in other sūtras:
"Those forms cognizable by the eye that are lovely, desirable, and pleasing to the mind—these forms are not cognizable by the eye."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"O Brahmin! The eye is merely a gateway for the purpose of seeing various forms."
By virtue of these proofs, it is known that one sees forms by means of consciousness, with the eye serving as the gateway.
This principle is revealed by such evidence: the eye, which is the seer, functions as the gateway.
Why is this? If it were the case that the eye itself constitutes seeing in order to see various forms,
this principle would not be correct.
If consciousness is able to see, what phenomenon is able to cognize?
What is the difference between these two? Why is this so?
This consciousness of form is itself the vision of form; it is like liberation, which is called either "vision" or "knowledge.
In the same way, this consciousness is called either "vision" or "consciousness."
Furthermore, other masters say:
"If the eye were able to see, the eye would then become the agent; what dharma, then, would constitute the distinct act of seeing?
Such is the fault."

This statement is not difficult to refute; just as you admit that consciousness can cognize while not establishing a distinction between an agent and an action therein, so it is with the eye’s ability to see visible forms.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"Visual consciousness is called 'seeing. Because it is the basis for seeing, it is said that the eye can see.
This is like saying a bell produces sound because it is the basis for striking it."
If that is so, since consciousness depends upon [the sense organs], it would follow that one should say "the eye cognizes," which is not tenable. Why?
Because in the world, this visual consciousness is established by convention as "seeing."
How is this known?
When this consciousness arises, it is said that form is "that which is seen," not "that which is cognized.
The *Vibhāṣā* itself states as much:
If it is reached by the eye and experienced by visual consciousness, it is then said to be "seen"; thus one says "the eye sees" and not "visual consciousness sees.
It is merely because consciousness is present that it is called "able to cognize," just as one says "the sun makes the day."
The Sautrāntika school asks:
Why do you gather together to refute emptiness?
For what reason?
Depending on the eye and conditioned by visible forms, visual consciousness arises.
In this process, what is it that sees?
And what is it that is seen?
All things are without substantiality; there is only phenomena, namely cause and effect.

Within this, for the sake of mutual understanding, conventional designations are employed according to one's inclination—such as saying "the eye sees" or "consciousness cognizes"—yet one should not cling to these expressions as being ultimately real.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"Do not cling to local dialects, and do not follow after the names established by worldly convention.
The *Siddhānta* (doctrinal tenets) of the Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra is determined as follows:
The eye can see, the ear can hear, the nose can smell, the tongue can taste, the body can touch, and the mind can cognize.
Does one see forms using only a single eye?
Is it by means of both eyes that one sees forms?
There is no fixed rule on this matter.
The verse says:
Alternatively, it is seen by means of both eyes, because color is perceived with clarity.
The commentary states:
Color is also seen by means of the two visual faculties (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The Abhidharma masters say this. Why?
Because when both eyes are open, vision is most clear.
If one opens one eye and half-closes the other, one sees two moons.

Because the vision is not clear due to the alteration of either one, consciousness cannot be divided into two on the basis of a difference in its location, for consciousness has no abiding place and thus differs from material form (*rūpa*).
If the eye can see, the ear can hear, and so on up to the mind being able to cognize, do those objects reach [the sense organs] or not?
The verse says:
The sense organs of the eye, the ear, and the mind do not reach their objects.
The commentary says: Why is this so?
The eye can see distant forms, yet if one applies medicinal ointment to the eye, it cannot see them.
The ear is able to hear distant sounds.

If the eye and ear were to perceive objects only when they reach them, then practitioners cultivating meditative observation would not be able to achieve the divine eye or divine ear, just as is the case with the nose and other such faculties.
If that is so, why is it that [the eye] cannot see all objects that do not reach it— namely, those that are extremely distant as well as those that are obstructed?
If that is so, why does a magnet not attract all iron that does not reach it?
If it were the case that [the eye] could perceive objects through direct contact, this objection would be equal.
Why is it that one cannot see all objects with which it comes into contact—such as eye-salve or the applicator stick—just as the nose and other [senses] perceive objects through direct contact?
Because it does not take as its object all things that do not reach it, since [the sense organ] cannot apprehend odors and so forth when they are not in contact.
Thus, although the visual object (*cakṣurviṣaya*) does not reach [the eye], it is not the case that everything which does not reach [the sense organ] constitutes a visual object.
Because the mental faculty (*manas*) is formless, it lacks the capacity for physical contact; therefore, it does not take a proximate object as its condition.
Other masters say:
the auditory faculty takes both proximate and non-proximate objects as its conditions, because one hears sounds within the ear.
Regarding the remaining [faculties]—nose, tongue, and body—the verse says:
"Three are different.
The commentary says:
This extends even to the point of reaching the object.
How is it known that the nose reaches the object?
If the breath is cut off, one does not smell odors.
What is "contact" (*prāpti*)?
It is the immediate arising [of one thing] after another.
Do atoms (*paramāṇu*) touch one another, or do they not touch?
The Master of Kaśmīra says:
they do not touch. Why is this?
If they were to touch by way of their entire substance, all things would necessarily intermingle.
If they were to touch by way of a single part of their substance, then atoms would possess spatial dimensions; however, atoms have no spatial dimensions.
If that is so, how is sound produced?
It is due to their being in immediate proximity (*nairantarya*).
If you claim they come into contact, then when two hands clap together, they should adhere to one another; the same would apply when one stone is thrown against another.
If that is so, how is it that the atoms of the aggregate do not disperse when they strike one another?
Because they are sustained by the wind element (*vāyu-dhātu*). Why is this?
There is a wind-element capable of dispersing and breaking apart, as at the end of an eon;
there is a wind-element capable of gathering and supporting, as at the formation of an eon.
Why, then, are three sense-bases and their objects mentioned here?

Reaching [the object] by way of being immediate, it takes as its object that which is reached; this meaning of "immediacy" is designated as "reaching," which means that there is no other substance intervening between them.
Furthermore, because aggregated matter possesses spatial dimensions (*digbhāga*), there is no fault if they do touch one another.
If one maintains this position, this scriptural passage from the *Vibhāṣā* is established.
Does this contact arise with contact as its cause,
or does it arise with non-contact as its cause?
By posing such a question, the answer is given in terms of its cause.
Sometimes non-contact arises with contact as its cause, as when an object disintegrates.
Sometimes contact arises with non-contact as its cause, as when an object grows.
Sometimes contact arises with contact as its cause, as when one aggregate meets another aggregate.
Sometimes non-contact arises with non-contact as its cause, such as the motes of dust within a crevice.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
"If atoms were to touch one another, they would have to persist into the subsequent moment.
The Venerable [Vasumitra] says:
Atoms do not touch one another; it is within the absence of an interval that the world conventionally designates the term "contact.
This is acceptable to the Venerable One’s intention.
If it were otherwise, atoms would have intervals between them.
Since the interior is empty, what dharma could obstruct its movement such that one could say it possesses resistance?
This aggregate is not different from its constituent atoms; if the aggregate were to touch, it would be the atoms themselves that touch, just as they are subject to transformation and destruction.
If you claim that atoms possess spatial dimensions, then whether they are in contact or not, they all incur the fault of having parts.
If they lack spatial dimensions, you cannot admit them to be matter (*rūpa*).
If there were actual contact, this objection could be raised.
However, the sense organs such as the eye perceive their objects by conforming to their own dimensions; because of the extreme rapidity of the action, it is like a whirling firebrand.

Up to the point where one perceives great mountains and the like, color is taken as an object of perception that may be equal or unequal in size to the sense organ; this refers to the previously mentioned "reaching" (prāptaviṣaya) objects of perception.
The verse says:
The three organs—namely, the nose and the others—are held to perceive objects of their own dimension.
The commentary states:

Just as the atoms of the sense organs are minute, so too are the atoms of the objects; these combine to produce the consciousnesses of the nose and other senses. However, for the eyes and ears, there is no fixed rule.
At times they apprehend the smallest objects, such as when one sees the tip of a hair.
Sometimes one perceives particles of equal size, as when seeing a grape;
sometimes one perceives the largest particles, as when seeing a great mountain.
It is the same with hearing at that time: the ear may hear the sound of a mosquito, or it may hear the sound of thunder.
Since the mind has no substance, its shape and magnitude cannot be described.
How, then, can the shape and characteristics of the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the various faculties, such as the eye, be known?
The atoms of the eye faculty reside within the pupil of the eye, covered by a blue tint like that of the *utpala* flower; for this reason, they do not scatter.
Other schools say:
Like a mass of objects piled one upon another, they abide without obstructing one another, being as transparent as crystal (*sphāṭika*).
The atoms of the auditory faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) abide within the ear like *bhūrja* bark.
The atoms of the nose-faculty reside within the nasal cavity.
The first three faculties are arranged horizontally, without any variation in height.
The atoms of the tongue-faculty are shaped like a half-moon; it is said that at the center of the tongue, an area the size of a hair-tip is not covered by the atoms of the tongue-faculty.
The atoms of the body-faculty (kāyendriya) are shaped according to the form of the body;
those of the female-faculty (strīndriya) are like the head of a drum;
and those of the male-faculty (puruṣendriya) are like a thumb.

Among these, the atoms of the eye-faculty are at times all homogeneous (sabhāga), at times all non-homogeneous (tatsabhāga), and at times some are homogeneous while others are non-homogeneous; this applies likewise up to the atoms of the tongue-faculty.
The atoms of the body-faculty (kāyendriya-paramāṇu) do not all possess the quality of being "homogeneous" (sabhāga).

For instance, in the case of sentient beings who are held fast within the Reviving Hell (saṃjīva-naraka), although there are immeasurable atoms of the body-faculty, they likewise do not all possess the quality of being homogeneous.
Why is this? If all [atoms] were to give rise to body-consciousness simultaneously, the body would disintegrate.

There is no single atom of a sense organ (*indriya-paramāṇu*) nor a single atom of an object (*viṣaya-paramāṇu*) capable of producing consciousness, because the five consciousnesses take subtle aggregations as their bases and objects.
Therefore, atoms have no manifest form, because they cannot be seen.
These six consciousness-elements are as previously described, namely, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
Among these, the objects of the five consciousnesses exist only in the present, while the object of the final consciousness exists in all three time periods.
Is that basis as such? It is said: it is not so. Why is it not so?
The verse says:
"The final realm depends on the past.
The commentary says:
The consciousness element takes the immediately preceding ceased consciousness as its support.
The verse says:
"The supports of the five elements are also common."
The commentary states:
The word "also" indicates the past; herein, the eye-consciousness relies upon [the eye-organ] because they are co-existent and belong to the same time-period.
This applies likewise up to the body-consciousness; its past support refers to the mind-faculty (*manas*).
Thus, because these five groups of consciousness arise based on two faculties, it is stated in this way.
If a dharma can serve as the basis (*āśraya*) for visual consciousness, can it also function as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
In this context, there are four propositions.
The first proposition refers to the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The second proposition refers to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*) that have already ceased in succession.
The third phrase refers to the mind that has already ceased in successive order.
The fourth phrase excludes the preceding three phrases.
This should be stated in the same way even for body-consciousness and its own faculty.

Regarding mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), there is only the absence of the first phrase, because whatever dharma serves as its support (*āśraya*) necessarily functions as its immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*).

If there is a dharma that is an immediately preceding condition but not a support, it refers to the mind and mental factors (*cittacaitta*) that have just ceased; the arising of consciousness depends upon these two conditions.
Furthermore, for what reason are only the eyes and so forth said to be their supports, while form and so forth are not?
The verse says:
Because consciousness varies according to the variation of the faculties, the eyes and so forth constitute the supports.
The commentary states:
Because there are distinctions among the sense organs such as the eye, there are likewise distinctions among the various consciousnesses.
If the sense organs such as the eye undergo increase or decrease, the consciousnesses accordingly become clear or dim.

It is not because of the variations of the various consciousnesses due to distinctions such as form that the eye and so forth are established as the supports of consciousness among the two conditions of consciousness; rather, the eye and so forth are so designated because they are predominant, whereas form and so forth are not mentioned because they are merely the objects cognized by consciousness.
Furthermore, for what reason are they called "eye-consciousness" up to "mind-consciousness," rather than being called "form-consciousness" up to "dharma-consciousness"?
Because the eye and so forth are their bases, consciousness is designated according to the sense faculties.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because of their unique causes, consciousnesses are designated according to the faculties.
The commentary explains:
What is the uncommon cause?

This eye-faculty cannot serve as a support for other consciousnesses; whereas visible form can serve as the object-condition for mental consciousness and as the objective domain for other eye-consciousnesses.
This applies even to the body.

Because consciousness relies upon them and because they are its specific causes, consciousness is designated according to the sense faculties (*indriya*) and not according to the objects such as visible form, just as one speaks of "the sound of a drum" or "a sprout of barley."
If a person within this body sees forms with the eye, are the body, the eye, the form, and the consciousness of the same level (*bhūmi*), or are they of different levels?
All of them are distinct.
If a person is born in the desire realm and sees forms of their own level with eyes of their own level, these four factors all belong to their own level.

If this person sees forms of their own level with eyes belonging to the first dhyāna, the body and the forms both belong to their own level, while the eyes and the consciousness belong to the first dhyāna.
If one sees the forms of the first dhyāna, then three factors belong to the first dhyāna.

If one sees the forms of one's own level with the eye of the second dhyāna, the body and the forms reside on their own level, the eye belongs to the second dhyāna, and the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.

If one sees the forms (*rūpa*) of the first dhyāna, the form and the consciousness (*vijñāna*) belong to the first dhyāna; the body belongs to its own level (the desire realm), while the eye belongs to the second dhyāna.
If one sees the forms of the second dhyāna, the eye and the form belong to the second dhyāna; the body belongs to its own level, while the consciousness belongs to the first dhyāna.
In this manner, one should apply the same logical reasoning as appropriate when the eye of the third or fourth dhyāna perceives visible forms of its own level or lower levels.
If a person is born in the level of the first dhyāna and perceives visible forms of that same level with an eye belonging to that same level, then these four factors all belong to their own level.
If one sees the forms of a lower stage, then the three types [of consciousness] belong to one's own stage.
If one sees the forms of one's own stage with the eye of the second dhyāna, then the three types belong to one's own stage.

If one sees the forms (*rūpa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the body and consciousness (*vijñāna*) belong to their own level (*svabhūmi*), the forms belong to a lower realm, and the eye belongs to the two dhyānas.
If one sees the forms of the second dhyāna, the eye and the forms belong to the second dhyāna, while the other two [consciousness and body] belong to their own level.
The same principle should be applied by analogy to the eyes of those in the third dhyāna and so forth.
If one is born in a level such as the second dhyāna, when seeing forms of one’s own level or other levels with the eye of that very level, it should likewise be applied by analogy.
This is the definitive determination therein.
The verse says:
"The eye does not have the sense objects of lower stages."
The commentary states:
The body, the eye, and visible forms belong to five levels, namely, from the level of the desire realm up to the level of the fourth dhyāna.

Eye-consciousness belongs to two levels, namely, the desire realm and the first dhyāna. Within this context, according to the level of the body, the eye faculty may be of the same level or of a higher level.

There is certainly no [visual object] belonging to a lower stage; rather, according to the stage of the eye faculty, the visual form belongs either to its own stage or to a lower stage, and this constitutes the objective domain of the eye.
The verse says:
"Visual forms of a higher stage are not the objects of a lower [eye]."
The commentary states:
It has never occurred that matter (rūpa) of a higher stage can be seen by an eye belonging to a lower stage.
The verse says:
Consciousness.
The commentary states:
Consciousness cannot reside in the eye, just as form [cannot].
The verse says:
Regarding this pervasion of form, there are two types of "all" with respect to the body.
The commentary says:

Regarding this, it is said that for the aforementioned visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), all visible forms (*rūpa*) constitute its objective sphere (*gocara*), whether superior, inferior, or equal.
Second, both consciousness and form exist in their entirety within the body.
As has been explained in detail regarding the eye faculty, it should be understood that the same applies here.
The verse says:
"The ear is likewise."
The commentary states:
The ear does not have the lower body as its object, and a sound from a higher realm is not the domain of a lower [sense].

Regarding consciousness, it is pervasive throughout both the body and the two [realms] in relation to this sound; as explained at length according to principle, it should be understood to be like the eye.
The verse says:
The remaining three belong entirely to their own level.
The commentary says:
The nose, tongue, and body elements:
the body itself, its objects, and their consciousnesses all belong to their own respective levels (*svabhūmi*). Thus, they have already been established generally without distinction.
Subsequently, in order to differentiate them, further specific statements are established.
The verse says:
"Body-consciousness belongs to its own level or a lower one.
The commentary says:
When one is situated in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the body and the tangible objects are likewise; these three always belong to their own level (*svabhūmi*).
As for the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), it sometimes belongs to its own level, as when a person is born in the desire realm or the first dhyāna (*prathamadhyāna*).
There are cases where [a faculty] belongs to a lower stage, such as when a person is born in the second dhyāna.
The verse says:
The sphere of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*) is indeterminate.
The commentary states:
Sometimes the mental faculty (*manas*), the body, the mental consciousness, and mental objects belong to the same level; sometimes they belong to different levels, such as higher or lower.
Regarding the five levels, the body, mind, and so forth may belong to any level—namely, at the time of entering meditative absorption and at the time of taking birth.
This principle shall be explained in detail in the chapter on the Analysis of Meditative Attainments (*samāpatti-vibhaṅga*).
To avoid excessive prolixity, it is not discussed here.
Why is this? Because the effort expended is great while the result is meager.

Having concluded the preceding discussion regarding what is spoken according to one's wishes, we should now deliberate upon this meaning: among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) and the six consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*), which element is that which is known?
Which consciousnesses are able to cognize them?
The verse says:
"The five external [objects] are known by two."
The commentary states:

The realms of visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects are, respectively, cognized by the consciousnesses of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body, and are further known by the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Furthermore, external objects are known by one or two consciousnesses; since the remaining thirteen elements are not the objects of the five sensory consciousnesses, they are known solely by the element of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-dhātu*).
This is what is revealed through the principle of implication (*arthāpatti*).
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are permanent and how many are impermanent?
Not a single element is entirely permanent.
Nevertheless, the verse says:
"The permanently abiding dharma is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The commentary states:
"The unconditioned is one portion of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) which is permanently abiding; all other realms are impermanent."
How many elements (dhātu) are faculties (indriya), and how many are not?
The verse says:
Half of the dharma-element is called a faculty, as are the twelve bases of the self (ātmāśraya).
The commentary states:
The sūtras teach that there are twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). Which are they?

The eye faculty, ear faculty, nose faculty, tongue faculty, body faculty, and mind faculty; the female faculty, male faculty, and life faculty; the faculty of pleasure, faculty of pain, faculty of joy, faculty of grief, and faculty of equanimity; the faculty of faith, faculty of vigor, faculty of mindfulness, faculty of concentration, and faculty of wisdom; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of knowing, and the faculty of one who has already known.

The Abhidharma masters refute the established order of the six internal bases by placing the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*) immediately after the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because it is capable of taking objects as its cognitive domain.

Within this context, "half of the dharma-sphere" (*dharmadhātu*) refers to the eleven faculties beginning with the life-faculty, because these constitute one portion of the dharma-sphere, which is itself a part of the three [final] faculties.
Regarding the twelve bases of the self (*ātma-āśraya*): the five faculties, beginning with the eye, are as described by their respective names.
The seven mind-elements (*citta-dhātu*) are called the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).
The female faculty and male faculty are portions of the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*), which will be explained later.
The remaining five elements (*dhātu*) and a portion of the element of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) are established as non-faculties (*anindriya*).
Chapter Two: Analysis of the Faculties (*Indriyaviniścaya*), Part One. Having thus explained the twenty-two faculties within the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, [the analysis of the faculties begins].
What is the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*)?
Its meaning is "supreme sovereignty," because it possesses dominant mastery over its own respective functions.
Furthermore, its meaning is "ornamentation," because it is most clearly manifest within the body.
Therefore, its meaning is that of supreme mastery and adornment.
Among these, which faculty exercises mastery over which sphere?
The verse says:
Regarding the four meanings, the five faculties possess predominance.
The commentary states:
Each of the two faculties, eye and ear, possesses predominance with respect to four meanings.
First, it has predominance regarding the adornment of one’s own person, for if a person is blind or deaf, their physical appearance is unsightly.
Second, it has predominance regarding the protection of one’s own person, for through seeing or hearing, one is able to avoid places that are unsafe or inauspicious.

Third, it exercises sovereignty over the arising of eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness, as well as their associated mental factors (saṃprayuktadharma), because consciousness and its associated factors become clear or dim according to the increase or decrease [of the sense organs].
Fourth, they serve as the uncommon dominant causes for seeing forms and hearing sounds, because they are not the causes for mental consciousness or other types of consciousness.
As for the nose, tongue, and body faculties, they adorn the self-body, just like the first two faculties;
second, they exercise dominance in attracting and protecting the self-body, because these three are capable of consuming edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*).
Third, it exercises sovereignty over the arising of the three consciousnesses—nose-consciousness and the others—as well as their associated mental factors;
fourth, it exercises sovereignty as the specific cause for smelling odors, tasting flavors, and feeling tangibles.
The verse says:
"Regarding two, two, and four faculties.
The commentary says:
The female faculty, the male faculty, the life faculty, and the mental faculty each possess predominance in two respects.
The female and male faculties possess predominance with respect to the differentiation of sentient beings and the distinction of their physical characteristics.

The distinction refers to differentiation; that is, the male and female characteristics differ, meaning their physical forms—such as the shape of the breasts—and their voices and deportment are each distinct.
Furthermore, other masters state that it exercises sovereignty over defilement and purification.
Why is this so? Because those who are congenitally eunuchs, as well as those with dual sexual organs, do not possess the restraint [of the precepts];

they lack the protection against the immediate karmic offenses (ānantarya-karma) and the severance of the roots of virtue (kuśala-mūla), and thus they lack such protection even when reaching the fruits [of the path] or attaining freedom from desire (vairāgya).
These two [faculties] exist only in males and females.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exercises predominance over the integration of the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), its association, and its maintenance. The mind-faculty (*manaindriya*) exercises predominance over the linking to a subsequent existence, its association, and its sovereign following.
Regarding the association with future existence (*punarbhava*) herein, as the Sūtra says:
"At that time, for the gandharva, one of two mental states manifests—either associated with desire (*rāga*) or associated with hatred (*dveṣa*)."
The attendant says in verse:
"The mind leads the world; the mind causes it to transform.
This single dharma of the mental faculty—every dharma follows its lead."
What is the predominance of the five faculties beginning with pleasant feeling and the eight faculties beginning with faith?
The verse says:
"The five and the eight [predominate] in regard to defilement and purification."
The commentary states:
It should be understood that their predominance follows this sequence.
The five faculties, beginning with the faculty of pleasure, possess predominance over defilement.
Because the various afflictions, such as desire, follow after them;
and because the eight faculties, beginning with faith, are predominant over purification. Why is this so?
Because all forms of purity are accomplished through them.
Other masters state that pleasant feelings and so forth also exercise predominance over purity; for through bliss, the mind attains concentration.
The Buddha said:
"Faith has suffering as its requisite.
Furthermore, there are six types of feelings, such as joy, which serve as the basis for renunciation.
The Vaibhāṣika masters state this. Furthermore, other teachers say:
it is not by means of the two faculties of eye and ear that one protects oneself, because one has already previously known how to avoid places that are inauspicious.

These two [faculties] exercise sovereignty only with respect to consciousness; there is no seeing of forms or hearing of sounds that is distinct from consciousness. Therefore, the two faculties of eye and ear should not be further established as sovereign within their own uncommon causes. Consequently, the eye and other faculties should not possess such sovereignty.
If that is so, what is their predominance?
The verse says:
They obtain predominance over their own respective objects; all six faculties obtain [predominance] over everything.
The commentary states:

The five faculties, beginning with the eye, possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) in the acquisition of their respective objects; the mental faculty (*manas*) possesses predominance in the acquisition of all objects. Therefore, each of these six is established as a faculty (*indriya*).
If that is so, since the various objects (viṣaya) possess predominance (ādhipatya) over this [consciousness], why are they not established as such?
Because the sense organs (indriya) do not possess predominance. Why is this?
It is called "predominant" (*adhipati*) because it is the most excellent sovereign.
Among the acquisition of visible forms, the eye is the sovereign and most excellent, for it is the common cause for the apprehension of all visible forms.
It is due to the increase or decrease of the eye that consciousness becomes clear or dim; visible forms do not act in this way.
Because these two meanings are reversed.
In this manner, it should be understood that the same applies up to the mental faculty (*manas*) and mental objects (*dharma*).
The verse says:
"Femininity and masculinity are predominant; from the body, two faculties are established.
The commentary explains:
Furthermore, from the body faculty, the two faculties of female and male are additionally established.
