These two are not distinct from the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*); rather, they are a specific portion within the body-faculty that, in the lower gate, sequentially receives the names "female-faculty" and "male-faculty," because they exercise predominance over the female and male natures.
The female sex refers to the female physical marks, voice, conduct, and desires; this is called the female sex.
The male physical marks, voice, conduct, and desires are called the male sex.
Because these bodily parts bring about the accomplishment and discernment of the two sexes, and because they exercise predominance over these two sexes, they are established as faculties (*indriya*).
The verse says:

Abiding in the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), being defiled, and exercising sovereignty over purification; life-force, the five sensations, and faith and the others are established as faculties (*indriya*).
The commentary says:
Within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*), life-span is predominant; with respect to the five defiled feelings (*vedanā*), they are predominant.

Why is this so? Because the latent tendency of desire (*kāma-anuśaya*) resides in pleasant feeling, aversion (*pratigha*) in painful feeling, and ignorance (*avidyā*) in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra.
Regarding the five [faculties] beginning with pure faith (*śraddhā*) as predominant, how is this so?
The various afflictions are suppressed by them and cannot arise again; since the Noble Path is induced by them, each of these is therefore admitted to be established as a faculty (*indriya*).
The verse says:

"The 'faculty of desiring to know the unknown,' 'knowing,' and 'having known' are established as faculties in this way; they serve as the predominant conditions for attaining successive paths, nirvāṇa, and so forth."
The commentary states:
Among these three, each should be established as a faculty (*indriya*). To clarify this meaning, it is said thus:
"The faculty of 'desiring to know what is not yet known' (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is established as a faculty because it exercises sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) over the attainment of knowledge."
Knowledge has predominance over the attainment [of the fruit], and having known, there is predominance over the attainment of nirvāṇa; therefore, it is established as a faculty (*indriya*).
Why is this? If a person’s mind is not yet liberated, there is no sense of attaining nirvāṇa.
The word "etc. (ādi) is used to indicate the meaning of distinct categories.
What is this distinct meaning?

Among the cessations of the afflictions that are to be abandoned through the vision of the truths, the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) serves as the predominant condition.
Regarding the abandonment of afflictions and the cessation [of suffering] during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is predominant;
regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life, the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is predominant, because it is able to realize and experience the joy and bliss of liberation.
If the status of being a faculty (*indriya*) were established on the basis of predominance (*ādhipatya*), then afflictions such as ignorance (*avidyā*) should also be established as faculties. Why?

Because these factors, such as ignorance, also possess predominance over [their respective] formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth; therefore, ignorance and the others should be established as faculties.

The same applies to those capable of speech and so forth; that is to say, the tongue, hands, feet, anus, and the male and female sexual organs should all be established as faculties (*indriya*), because they possess predominance (*ādhipatya*) over speaking, grasping, moving away, excreting, and sexual pleasure, respectively. Therefore, they ought to be established as faculties.
It cannot be established as a faculty (*indriya*). Why?
Because the function of a faculty is such.
The verse says:
Based on these distinctions of the mind—its abiding, its defilement, its equipment, and its purification—the faculties are established in this measure.
The commentary says:
Among these, the basis of mind refers to the six faculties, such as the eye, because sentient beings take the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as their fundamental root.

These six types of bases are differentiated by the two faculties of female and male; their persistence throughout a single lifetime is due to the life faculty (*jīvitendriya*); their defilement is due to the five feeling faculties (*pañca-vedanendriya*); and the provisions for purification are due to the five faculties beginning with faith (*pañca-śraddhādīndriya*).
True purity arises from the three untainted faculties; therefore, ignorance and the like are not admitted as faculties.
The verse says:

Furthermore, there are the basis for birth and birth itself, the abiding of birth, the arising of birth, and the enjoyment [of birth]; fourteen are established [as faculties], while the latter eight are established as faculties with respect to liberation.
The commentary states:
The repetition of the word "again" is intended to reveal the distinct tenets of various schools.
Other schools say:
The basis of birth and death consists of what are called the six sense faculties (ṣaḍāyatana).
By what dharma does this basis arise?
It arises by means of the two faculties of female and male.
This abiding is due to the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), because it continues in accordance with the succession of that life-faculty.
Its experience is due to the five feelings (*vedanā*).
To clarify this meaning, fourteen faculties are established.
Based on these four meanings, the remaining factors related to liberation are also established as faculties (*indriya*).

The five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) are the basis for liberation; the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is its arising; the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) is its abiding; and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) is its enjoyment. Therefore, the number of faculties is thus—neither more nor less—and their sequence is likewise fixed and cannot be inverted.
The tongue cannot be established as a faculty (*indriya*) within the context of verbal expression.
Why? Because it is observed that its superior capacity pertains to training (*śikṣā*).
The hands and feet should not be established as faculties (indriya) with respect to grasping and moving away, because there is no difference [between them].
This entity arises in another place by way of a different characteristic; it is designated as "grasping" and "moving away" when it is separated from the hand and separated from the foot.
Since snakes and other such creatures are also capable of grasping and can turn away from objects,
the hands and feet cannot be established as faculties in these two respects. Furthermore,
the anus cannot be established as a faculty with respect to the act of excretion.
Heavy objects fall everywhere in mid-air and are also brought forth by the wind.

Furthermore, the female and male sexual organs cannot be established as faculties (*indriya*) based on sexual pleasure, because female and male sexual pleasure is not accomplished by their own respective organs, but rather arises through mutual arousal.

The throat, teeth, eyes, and eyelids should be established as faculties (*indriya*) because they exercise predominance (*ādhipatya*) over the actions of swallowing, chewing, opening and closing, and contracting and extending.
Furthermore, all causes and conditions should be established as faculties, as they each exercise predominance over their own respective functions.
If the meaning of the sense organs, such as the tongue and so forth, were not accepted in this way, then this [system] would also not be established.
Herein, beginning with the eye organ and ending with the male organ, they have already been explained in detail.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is a dissociated formation (*viprayuktasaṃskāra*); it shall be explained in detail among the dissociated phenomena.
The five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*) shall be explained in detail among the mental factors (*caitasika*).
The pleasant feelings and so forth, as well as "that which is to be known by one who has not yet known" and so forth, shall now be explained.
They are explained according to their respective order.
The verse says:
The faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) is that which is not desired; it is experienced by the body.
The commentary explains:
"That which is not desired" refers to that which is capable of causing harm and affliction because of its painful nature.
The verse says:
"The faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya) is that which is beloved.
The commentary says:
The faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) refers to the bodily sensation that is agreeable, because it is capable of providing benefit.
The verse says:
In the third dhyāna, mental sensation is called the faculty of pleasure.
The commentary states:
In the third dhyāna, there is a pleasant feeling (*vedanā*) that arises based on the mind-ground; this is termed the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). Why is this so?
In the third dhyāna, there is no bodily sensation because the five sensory consciousnesses are absent.
The verse says:
"This bliss, in other places, is the faculty of joy."
The commentary states:

Excluding the third dhyāna, in other locations—namely, within the desire realm and in the first and second dhyānas—if it occurs within the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is designated by the name *saumanasyendriya* (the faculty of joy).
In the third dhyāna, because of the departure from desire for joy (*prīti*), one possesses only the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) and not the faculty of joy. Why is this?
Because joy is coarse and turbid, it receives only the name of the "faculty of joy."
The verse says:
"In the mental ground, there are the faculties of suffering and grief.
The commentary says:
That which is not a pleasant feeling, if it resides in the mental ground, is called the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The verse says:
"The faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*)."
[In the] middle.
The commentary states:

That which is neither agreeable nor disagreeable refers to sensations that are neither pleasant nor painful; therefore, it is established as the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) within the neutral category.
Is this bodily sensation or mental sensation?
The verse says: Both.
The commentary says:
There is bodily sensation (*kāyikī vedanā*) or mental sensation (*caitasikī vedanā*).
For what reason are these two sensations combined and established as a single faculty?
The verse says:
"Because there is no distinction.
The commentary says:

Mental pleasure and pain arise mostly from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), whereas physical sensation does not; it arises solely in accordance with sensory objects (*viṣaya*). This is also the case for an Arhat. Therefore, there is a distinction between these two as faculties (*indriya*).

Regarding the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*): because it arises by its own nature without discrimination—whether in the body or in the mental ground—it is combined with the other two [faculties] to constitute a single faculty.
There is a distinction between bodily pleasure and its benefit; the same applies to mental pleasure. The same holds true for suffering.
There is a distinction between bodily pain and its harm; the same applies to mental pain.
However, within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), there is no such opposition; because this distinction is absent, it is therefore not divided into two separate faculties (*indriya*).
The verse says:
"In the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning, there are nine [types of] three.
The commentary says:

The five faculties of intention, joy, equanimity, faith, and so forth—these nine faculties are designated as three faculties within the three paths: they are called the faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) in the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) in the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Why is this so? In the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one practices in order to know the true reality that has never been known before.

In the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), there is no object that was previously unknown which must now be known for the first time; rather, it is what was already known that is known again, for the purpose of eliminating the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*).
Within the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*), one has already known thus;
furthermore, because one is able to guard what has been known, it is called "guarding what is known" (*ājñātāvīnāman*). Why is this?
Because one has already attained the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), [one realizes]:
"Suffering has been abandoned by me; it need not be abandoned again.
The faculties (*indriya*) obtained by a person in this stage are called either the faculty of "having known" (*ājñātāvīndriya*) or the faculty of "having known and guarding" (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
Having explained the essential nature [of the faculties], the distinctions among their types shall now be discussed.
How many faculties are with-outflow (*sāsrava*) and how many are without-outflow (*anāsrava*), and so forth?
Among these, the faculties have just been explained immediately prior, namely, the "faculty of one who intends to know the unknown" (*anājñātamājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others.
The verse says:
Three are stainless.
The commentary says:
"Untainted" (*anāsrava*) has the meaning of being "stainless," because "taints" (*āsrava*) is a specific name for the outflows (*āsrava*).
The verse says:
The two types of suffering associated with form and life are tainted.
The commentary states:
The seven material faculties, the life faculty, the faculty of suffering, and the faculty of grief are invariably with-outflows (*sāsrava*). Why is this?
The seven faculties that possess form, such as the eye and so forth, are associated with outflows because they are subsumed within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
The verse says:
"Nine are of two kinds."
The commentary states:

The faculties of mental pleasure (*saumanasya*), joy (*sukha*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*)—these nine faculties are either with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*).
Other masters say:
Faith and the other [faculties] are exclusively untainted (anāsrava). Why is this?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said:

If a person lacks, in every respect, the five faculties such as faith and so forth, I declare that this person stands outside the True Dharma and dwells among the ranks of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
This sūtra is insufficient as proof, for it speaks in reference to the untainted (*anāsrava*).
How is it known that this sutra was spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, only after he had established the noble ones? It says:
"If a person lacks, in every respect, the five faculties such as faith," as explained at length in the sutra.
There are two kinds of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*):
first, those within the True Dharma who have not severed their roots of goodness; second, those outside the True Dharma who have severed their roots of goodness.
It is with reference to these people that the Buddha spoke these words.
That is to say, I declare that such a person dwells outside the True Dharma among the class of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
As the Buddha said in a sutra:

"There are sentient beings who are born into the world and grow up in the world—whether of sharp faculties, middling faculties, or dull faculties—at a time before the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma has been turned."
Therefore, it is known that there exist the five faculties, beginning with faith, which are associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*).
Furthermore, the Buddha said in a sutra:

"As long as I had not, according to reality, known the five faculties—faith and the rest—their origination and cessation, their gratification, their peril, and the escape from them, I was unable to claim that I had transcended this world with its gods and Brahmās," as explained at length in the sutra.
If all phenomena are untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no such analytical categorization as:
"How many faculties (*indriya*) are retribution (*vipāka*);
how many faculties are not retribution?"
Regarding that which is exclusively a result of maturation (*vipāka*), the verse says:
"Life is a result of maturation.
The commentary says:
If that is so, when an Arhat bhikṣu draws forth the life-force (jīvitasaṃskāra) and causes this life-force to endure, this too is the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
Of what dharma is it the fruition (vipākaphala)?
It is stated in the Abhidharmapiṭaka:
What is the prolongation of the life-faculties?

It refers to an Arhat bhikṣu who possesses the noble supernormal power of *ṛddhi-vidyā*, having attained mastery over the mind, who—whether before a great assembly or a single individual—bestows either a bowl, a robe, or any other requisite for the sustenance of a śramaṇa’s life.
Therefore, he made this vow and entered the fourth dhyāna, the samādhi of the ultimate limit (*atyantakoṭika*).
Emerging from this concentration, he formed this thought and spoke these words:
"Whatever karma of mine is destined to ripen as wealth and happiness, may that karma instead ripen to produce my life-span."
At that time, this Arhat’s karma, which was destined to result in wealth and happiness, instead ripened as a lifespan.
Furthermore, other masters maintain that it was the residual karmic retribution that transformed and matured.
He explains that regarding the karma performed in previous lives, there remains residual karmic fruition which is drawn forth and experienced through the power of cultivation.
How, then, does he relinquish the formations of life?
In this manner, having made offerings and formulated aspirations, he enters the fourth dhyāna and contemplates the samādhi of the ultimate limit.
Emerging from this meditative absorption, he forms such a thought and speaks these words:
"Whatever karma of mine is destined to ripen as a lifespan, may that karma instead ripen to produce for me wealth and pleasure, just like those sensual pleasures."
As it thus becomes increasingly refined,
the Venerable Ghoṣaka says: within one's own basis (āśraya),

through the power of meditative concentration (samādhi), one causes the great elements (mahābhūta) of the form realm to manifest— either those that are conducive to life-span or those that are contrary to it.
By such means, the life-constituents (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) are drawn forth to remain or are relinquished; it should be understood that this is accomplished in this way.

Arhats possess such mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā*), by which power they can entirely redirect the duration for which the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the great elements (*mahābhūta*) produced by past karma would otherwise have remained.
Previously, there was no duration of time for the sustained presence of samādhi; now, however, such a duration is induced. Therefore, this kind of lifespan is not a karmic maturation (*vipāka*).
That which differs from this is called a karmic maturation.
From this question, another distinct inquiry arises:
For what reason does an Arhat make a vow to sustain the life-force,
and is it for the sake of benefiting others?
Or was it to cause the True Dharma to endure for a long time?
These Arhats have already perceived that their own lifespans are nearing their end; between these two [tasks], they do not see in others the capacity to accomplish them.
Furthermore, for what reason does one relinquish the life-force?
While still possessing life, one perceives that there is little benefit to be gained for others and is oppressed by the suffering of one's own illness, as the verse says:
"The practice of the holy life is complete; The Noble Path has been well cultivated."
"Because he rejoices at the relinquishing of life, it is like a person whose illness has been cured.
If this is so, one should understand where and by whom these activities—prolonging the life-faculty (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*) and its relinquishment—are performed.

Within the human realm, among those in the three continents, and among men and women who are non-time-liberated (*akāla-vimukta*) Arhats and both-way-liberated (*ubhayatobhāga-vimukta*) Arhats, one attains the concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*). Why is this?
This person possesses mastery over all meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), and their mental continuum is not permeated by afflictions (*kleśa*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"The Blessed One willed to retain his life-faculties (*jīvitasaṃskāra*) and relinquished his vitality-faculties (*āyuḥsaṃskāra*)."
What is the distinction between the two formations of life-force (*jīvita*) and longevity (*āyus*)?
Other masters say:
there is no distinction.
How is this known?
It is stated in the Sūtra:
"What is the life-faculty (jīvitendriya)?"
This refers to the life-span within the three realms.
Furthermore, other masters state:
the fruit of past karma is called the "formations of life" (*āyusaṃskāra*), while the fruit of present karma is called the "formations of vitality" (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
Furthermore, another teacher says:

"That by which one abides within a homogeneous class of beings (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is called the life-force (*āyus-saṃskāra*); that by which one abides for a temporary period is called the vitality-force (*jīvita-saṃskāra*).
The plural [in the term 'life-forces'] is used because many life-force forces arise through the intentional retention of life."
Why is this? Because it possesses the capacity to arise in a single moment without any desire to remain.
Furthermore, other masters say:
There is not a single thing called "life-force" (*jīvitendriya*) that can abide even for a moment; it is to clarify this meaning that various statements have been made.
Furthermore, other masters say:
the designation "life-force" is established conventionally (*prajñapti*) upon a plurality of formations (*saṃskāra*); there is no separate, singular entity named "life-force."
If this were not so, the Buddha would not have spoken of "formations" (*saṃskāra*).
Question:
How is it that the World-Honored One relinquished the formations of vitality (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*) while wishing to retain the formations of life (*jīvita-saṃskāra*)?
He relinquished [his life] to demonstrate his mastery over the state of death (cyuti-bhava), and he vowed to remain to demonstrate his mastery over the lifespan (āyus).
Why did he do so for exactly three months and no more?
Because the task of benefiting the disciples who have been converted has been brought to completion.

Furthermore, the Blessed One established this doctrinal statement: "If a bhikṣu cultivates and practices the four bases of psychic power (*catvāra ṛddhipādāḥ*), should he so desire, he can remain for an eon (*kalpa*) or even beyond an eon."
In order to manifest the meaning of what has been established, he retained his life-force while relinquishing his vitality.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:

regarding the five aggregates and death, in order to manifest his own supreme capability, he had already previously defeated the Māra of Defilements and the Māra of the Deva at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
Let this incidental discussion cease; the fundamental meaning upon which it relies shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"The twelve are of two kinds."
The commentary asks:
What are these twelve?
The verse says:
Excluding the last eight [faculties] and the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
The commentary states:
Furthermore, excluding the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the remaining twelve are of two kinds: some are retribution (*vipāka*), and some are not retribution.
Among these, the seven faculties beginning with the eye, if they are the fruit of growth (*aupacayika*), are not retribution (*vipāka*);

all others are retribution. As for the faculties of mind, suffering, pleasure, joy, and equanimity: if they are wholesome or defiled, they are not retribution; if they are associated with deportment (*airyāpathika*), craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), or supernormal transformations (*nairmāṇika*), they are also not retribution; all others are retribution.
Excluding the life-faculty and the twelve faculties such as the eye, the remaining ones are not retribution; this point is thus established.
If the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is not retribution, how is this sūtra to be interpreted?
The Sūtra states:
"There is karma that is favorable to pleasant feeling; there is karma that is favorable to painful feeling; there is karma that is favorable to neutral feeling.
This statement is made based on the favorability [of the karma] through association (*saṃprayoga*).
If karma is associated with the feeling of mental unease (*daurmanasya-vedanā*), it is said to be "favorable toward the feeling of mental unease.
This is just as when contact (*sparśa*) is associated with the feeling of pleasure (*sukha-vedanā*), it is said that contact is favorable toward the feeling of pleasure.
If that is so, then karma that is favorable toward the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*) or the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā*) should also be established in this same way.
We grant your point as you desire; there is no fault regarding its association (*samprayoga*), nor is there any fault regarding its maturation (*vipāka*).

If that is so, since all [mental factors] are admitted to be thus by virtue of their lack of functional capacity, what other principle is there to establish that *daurmanasya* (sorrow) is not a karmic maturation (*vipāka*)?
The sensation of sorrow arises from the differentiation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and ceases through conceptual construction; however, a karmic maturation is not like this.
If that were so, the same would apply to the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*); one should not establish joy as a karmic maturation (*vipāka*).

If sorrow (*daurmanasya*) were a maturation, then for a person who has committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*), because sorrow arises from that immediate transgression, this karma would have to ripen [as that sorrow].

Joy (*prīti*) should also be understood in this way. If joy were a karmic maturation (*vipāka*), then for a person who performs meritorious deeds, because they experience the feeling of joy arising from those meritorious deeds, that merit would have to be considered already matured.
This argument is not tenable.
Furthermore, there is another proof: because those who have abandoned desire possess no feeling of sorrow (*daurmanasya*), their karmic fruition is not otherwise [characterized by it].
Nor do those who have abandoned desire possess the indeterminate faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*).
If that is so, what are the characteristics of retribution (*vipāka*)?
It corresponds to its own characteristics; if there is past karma, it must correspond to its proper stage.

Even though this is the case, while the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) may have residual retribution, the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) does not, because in all other modes it does not arise or function.
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣika masters state:

"Sorrow (*daurmanasya*) is not a karmic maturation (*vipāka*). With the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as the eighth, there is the maturation of wholesome karma in the happy realms and the maturation of unwholesome karma in the miserable realms; the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*), however, is the maturation of both types of karma in both realms."
The three faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity are the retributive fruits of wholesome karma; the faculty of suffering is the retributive fruit of unwholesome karma.
In the happy realms, these two faculties are acquired by persons through unwholesome karma.
Thus far this treatise has explained these stages; what remains should now be discussed.
How many faculties have retribution (*vipāka*), and how many faculties are without retribution?
Among these, the faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) has already been explained immediately prior.
The verse states:
"It necessarily possesses retribution (*vipāka*)."
The commentary states:
This single faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) possesses retribution (*vipāka*).
The word "certainly" (*niyata*) is used for the sake of determination.

The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) differs from other dharmas; this faculty is neither indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nor untainted (*anāsrava*), because it belongs to the stage of distraction (*vikṣepabhūmi*). Therefore, the faculty of sorrow has no maturation (*vipāka*).
The verse says:
Ten; two kinds.
The commentary says:
There are two kinds, namely: with retribution and without retribution.
What are the ten?
The verse says:
"Mind, the remaining [faculties], feeling, faith, and so forth.
The commentary explains:
"The remaining feelings" should be understood as being distinct from the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculties of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Among these, the mental factors of intention (*cetanā*), joy (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) have a karmic maturation (*vipāka*) if they are either unwholesome or wholesome and associated with outflows (*sāsrava*); the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) has a maturation if it is either wholesome or unwholesome, but has no maturation if it is neutral (*avyākṛta*).
If the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā) are with-outflow (sāsrava), they possess retribution (vipāka);
if they are without-outflow (anāsrava), they lack retribution. It follows by implication that the remaining faculties lack retribution.
How many faculties are wholesome (kuśala)?
How many faculties are unwholesome?
How many are indeterminate?
Among these, those that are exclusively wholesome are stated in the verse:
Eight faculties are wholesome.
The commentary states:
the five beginning with faith, and the three beginning with "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown.'"
The verse says:
There are two kinds of sorrow.
The commentary says:
They may be either wholesome or unwholesome.
The verse says:
"The mental [consciousness] and the other sensations are of three kinds."
The commentary states:
These five faculties are of three kinds—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The verse says:
"Another kind.
The commentary asks: What is this "other"?
The eye faculty is the first, and the life faculty is the eighth; these eight are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
With which faculties and which realms are they associated?
Among the twenty-two faculties, the verse says:
"In the desire realm, there are [roots] excluding the pure.
The commentary states:

It should be understood that this refers to those associated with the desire realm, excluding the three roots that are exclusively untainted, such as "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown'" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*).
Why is this? Because these three determinations do not correspond to the three realms.
The verse says:
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), with the exception of the female and male faculties, there are two types of suffering.
The commentary explains:

as previously stated, excluding the untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties, the "two sufferings" refer to the two faculties of physical pain (*duḥkha*) and mental grief (*daurmanasya*). Because those in the realm of form have abandoned the dharma of sexual desire and because their physical bases (*āśraya*) are not characterized by attractiveness, they lack the two faculties of female and male.
If that is so, how can they be described as "persons" (puruṣa)?
Where is this stated?
As it says in the Sūtra:
There is no place or principle by which a woman could become Brahmā; there is only a place and a principle by which a man may become Brahmā.
Furthermore, he possesses the distinct characteristics of a male, and such a state is attainable as a male only within the desire realm.
In that state, there is no faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*) because its basis is pure and sublime;
furthermore, there is no faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) because there is no unwholesome karma and because the continuity of *śamatha* is supple and smooth.
Furthermore, because its objects are infinite categories,
the verse says:
"The formless realm exists, excluding the two types of pleasure and form."
The commentary states:
Excluding the two faculties of female and male, excluding the two faculties of suffering, and excluding the untainted (anāsrava) faculties, how many remaining faculties are there?
They are the faculty of mind (manas), the life faculty (jīvita), the faculty of equanimity (upekṣā), and the five faculties beginning with faith (śraddhā).
It should be understood that these many faculties are associated with the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), and no other faculties are present there.
How many faculties are abandoned through the vision of the truths (darśana-heya)?
How many faculties are abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya)?
How many faculties are not to be abandoned?
The verse says:
The mental faculty, the three feelings, and the three kinds [of faculties].
The commentary says:
What are the three feelings?
They are the faculties of pleasure, joy, and equanimity.
The verse says:
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is abandoned through seeing and cultivation (*darśana-bhāvanā-heya*).
The commentary says:
The faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) is abandoned by two paths, because it is abandoned by both the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The verse says:
Nine are abandoned by the path of cultivation.
The commentary states:
The eye faculty is the first, and the life faculty is the eighth; these, along with the faculty of suffering, are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The verse says:
"Five are either abandoned through cultivation or not abandoned.
The commentary states:

The five faculties beginning with faith are either abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) or are not to be abandoned, because they include both those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
The verse says:
Three are non-existent.
The commentary says:

The three faculties, beginning with "the faculty of 'I shall come to know the unknown,'" are not eliminated by either the path of seeing or the path of cultivation, because they are untainted (*anāsrava*).
Furthermore, as they are faultless phenomena (*anavadyadharma*), they cannot be discarded.
Having explained the distinctions among the categories of the faculties,
the acquisition of the faculties shall now be discussed.
How many faculties are acquired first as the fruit of retribution in which realm?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, one first attains two fruits of retribution.
The commentary says:
Because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) and the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) are results of maturation (*vipāka*), these two are first acquired at the very moment of entering the womb.
The verse says:
"Not by apparitional birth (*upapāduka*)."
The commentary states:

Among the four modes of birth (*yoni*), by excluding the apparitional (*upapāduka*), it should be understood that the womb-born (*jarāyu-ja*), egg-born (*aṇḍa-ja*), and moisture-born (*saṃsveda-ja*) have already been admitted.
Why, then, are the mental faculty (*manas*) and the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) not mentioned?
Because at the moment of taking birth, these two faculties are necessarily defiled.
If one is born by transformation (*upapāduka*), how many faculties does one initially obtain as a result of maturation (*vipākaja*)?
The verse says:
"He obtains six.
The commentary states:
"If he lacks the female or male faculty, as in the case of those born at the beginning of the kalpa."
What are the six?
They are the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and life.
The verse says:
7. The commentary states:
If one produces a single faculty, it is as when one is born among the gods and so forth.
The verse says:
Eight. The commentary says:
If those beings possess two sexual organs,
can beings born by transformation (upapāduka) possess two organs?
If they may exist in the evil realms, and if this is how they are first acquired in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), what is the case for the form realm (rūpadhātu) and the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
The verse says:
Six within form.
The commentary says:
Because desire is predominant, it is called the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), or simply "desire.
Because form is predominant, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), or simply "form.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
This tranquil liberation transcends both form and non-form.

Within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the first fruit of retribution obtained possesses six faculties; these faculties are the same as those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), with the exception that the two faculties [of male and female] are not obtained through miraculous birth (*upapāduka*).
The verse says:
"The remainder is one.
The commentary says:

The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is called "the remainder" because it differs from the realm of form (rūpadhātu), due to the difference in meditative attainments (samāpatti) and the superiority of its rebirth.
In this [formless realm], at the initial acquisition of retribution, there is only the life-faculty (jīvitendriya); the other faculties are not present.
Having explained acquisition (*prāpti*), the abandonment (*tyāga*) shall now be discussed.
Regarding which realm one dies in, how many faculties (*indriya*) are abandoned?
The verse says:
"One who is dying in the formless realm abandons the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), and the equanimity-faculty (*upekṣendriya*).
The commentary states:
If a person is in the process of dying in the formless realm, they abandon these three faculties—life, mind, and equanimity—at the final moment of consciousness.
The verse says:
"In the case of form, there are eight.
The commentary says:

If a person is in the process of dying in the form realm (rūpadhātu), they relinquish eight faculties at the final moment of consciousness: three as previously mentioned, plus the five faculties beginning with the eye. Why is this?
All beings born by transformation are born with their sense faculties complete and die with their sense faculties complete.
The verse says:
"In the desire realm, nineteen, eight."
The commentary states:

If a person in the desire realm is in the process of dying, at the final moment of consciousness, one who possesses both sexual organs abandons ten faculties—eight as previously mentioned, plus the female and male organs.
If one dies with one faculty remaining, then nine faculties are relinquished;
if one dies without any faculties remaining, then only eight faculties are relinquished.
Such is the principle for simultaneous death.
The verse says:
"In the case of successive death, one relinquishes four.
The commentary says:
If a person dies gradually, at the final moment of consciousness they simultaneously relinquish four faculties: namely, the faculties of body, life, mind, and equanimity. Why is this so?
Because these four are inseparable until their exhaustion.
One should understand that this principle applies when death occurs with a defiled or neutral mind.
However, when a person dies with a wholesome mind, at that time the verse says:
Regarding the five [faculties] in wholesome states:

the commentary states that if a person dies with a wholesome mind, in all cases as previously explained, when they relinquish the life-faculty, they also relinquish the five faculties beginning with faith.
Why is this? Because these five faculties, beginning with faith, necessarily arise together within a wholesome mind.
Thus, eight faculties are abandoned in the formless realm, and thirteen faculties are abandoned in the form realm.
In this manner, following the previous sequence, one should further enumerate [the faculties] extensively.
Within the *Mūla-āgama*, all phenomena pertaining to the faculties (*indriya-dharma*) are to be discerned; they should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, what are the fruits of the śramaṇa,
and by how many faculties are they attained?
The verse says:
"Nine [roots] attain the two extreme fruits.
The commentary states:
By means of nine faculties, one attains the fruits of śrāmaṇya at the prior and subsequent limits.
What constitutes the two extremes?
They are the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpanna-phala) and the fruit of arhatship (arhat-phala), because they are attained at the prior and posterior limits [of the path].
How many fruits are found in the middle limit?
The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin and the fruit of the Anāgāmin.

Among these, the fruit of the Srotāpanna consists of the faculties of faith and so forth, excluding the faculty of "having known" (ājñātāvīndriya) as well as the mental faculty (manas-indriya) and the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya); by means of these nine faculties, one attains the fruit of the prior limit.

The faculty of "desiring to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) resides in the path of sequential application (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the faculty of "knowing" (*ājñendriya*) resides in the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); it is by means of these two faculties that one attains the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), because they are respectively able to induce the acquisition of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and serve as its basis.

Furthermore, there are the faculties of faith and so forth pertaining to the fruit of arhatship, excluding the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the mental faculty, and any one among the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity; by means of these nine faculties, one attains the fruit of the future limit.
The verse says:
"Seven, eight, nine, and two in the middle.
The commentary says:
The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin and the fruit of the Anāgāmin are termed "middle" because they are observed in relation to what precedes and follows them.
Each of these two fruits is attained through seven, eight, or nine faculties.
Why is this so? The fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin is attained only if a person practices the stages in succession.

If one relies on the worldly path (*laukikamārga*), this fruit is obtained by means of seven faculties (*indriya*): the five faculties beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), along with the two faculties of equanimity (*upekṣā*) and mind (*manas*).
If one relies on the supramundane path, this fruit is attained by means of eight faculties: seven as previously stated, with the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*) as the eighth.
If one who has already largely abandoned desire attains this fruit, it is attained by means of nine faculties.
Just as with the attainment of the fruit of *srotāpanna*, the fruit of *anāgāmin* is attained by a person who practices the stages in succession.
If one relies on the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), this fruit is obtained through seven faculties, as previously explained.

Regarding the attainment of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*: if it is attained by means of the supramundane path (*lokottaramārga*), this fruit is obtained through eight faculties, as previously explained.
Regarding the attainment of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*: if one who has already been detached from desire attains this fruit, it is obtained through nine faculties, as previously explained.

One attains the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. This fruit differs from the preceding fruits in that it is associated with either pleasure (*sukha*), joy (*saumanasya*), or equanimity (*upekṣā*) according to the specific faculty involved, due to the distinction in its basis.
If a person practicing by way of gradual cultivation enters the fundamental dhyāna during the ninth path of liberation via the mundane path,
at that time they attain the fruit of Anāgāmin by means of eight faculties.

Why is this? In the ninth path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*) serves as the eighth; in the subsequent path (*anantaryamārga*), however, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*) is definitely employed. It is by means of these two faculties that one attains the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

If a person relies on the supramundane path and enters the ninth path of liberation, that person attains the fruit of *anāgāmin* by means of nine faculties, among which the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*) serves as the ninth.
If that is so, how is it stated in the Abhidharma-piṭaka? That Piṭaka asks:
"By means of how many faculties (indriya) can one attain the fruit of arhatship?"
In that [text], it was answered by means of eleven faculties.
Why, then, is it said here that one attains [the fruit] by means of nine faculties?
It is necessarily by means of nine faculties.
The verse says:
"Eleven attain arhatship; it is taught that this is accomplished based on a single person.
The commentary says:

There is this principle: when one person has already fallen away, having fallen away, they again attain the fruit of arhatship through the faculties of pleasure, joy, or equanimity; therefore, it is said that [this attainment occurs] by means of eleven faculties.
It is impossible for the three faculties, such as the faculty of pleasant feeling, to arise simultaneously.
Why, then, is this principle not discussed regarding the person who has attained the stage of Anāgāmin?
This is not the case for the Anāgāmin.
Why? Because there is no instance where one who has previously fallen away later realizes the original fruit again by means of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*).
Furthermore, for one who has previously abandoned desire, there is no possibility of falling back, because this person’s abandonment of desire is realized through both paths.
This point should be carefully considered:
with which faculty (*indriya*) is it associated?
How many faculties are necessarily associated with one another?
Regarding this, the verse says:
The faculty of equanimity, life, and mind are necessarily associated with three [other faculties].
The commentary states:
If a person is associated with any one of the faculties such as equanimity (*upekṣā*), that person is necessarily associated with three faculties.
These three faculties are equanimity, life, and mind (*manas*).
Why is this? Because these three are mutually inseparable from their association.
Their association with other faculties, however, is not fixed; they may be associated or dissociated.
Among these, those born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are not endowed with the faculties of eye, ear, nose, or tongue; the same applies to those in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
That is to say, persons who have not yet acquired them or have already lost them, as well as those born in the formless realm, are not endowed with the body faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Those born in the realms of form and formlessness are not endowed with the female faculty;
the same applies to those in the desire realm who have not yet acquired it or have already lost it. The same is true for the male faculty.
If an ordinary person is born in the second dhyāna level of the fourth dhyāna or in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), they are not associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
If an ordinary person is born in the third dhyāna, the fourth dhyāna, or the formless realm, they are not associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
If an ordinary person is born into the realm of form or the formless realm, they are not associated with the faculty of suffering (*duḥkhendriya*).
If one is free from desire, they are not associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*).
If one has severed the roots of goodness, they are not associated with the faculties of faith and so forth.
Ordinary persons and those who have attained the fruits [of the path] are not associated with the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown.
Ordinary persons, those on the path of vision, and those beyond training (aśaikṣas) are not associated with the faculty of "knowing."
Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) are not associated with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātāvīndriya*).
In cases where there is no exclusion, as previously described, it should be understood that they are associated with the remaining faculties.
The verse says:
"Endowed with the four, possessing a blissful body.
The commentary says:

If a person is endowed with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), that person is necessarily endowed with four faculties: namely, the three beginning with equanimity (*upekṣā*) and the faculty of pleasure itself.
If a person is endowed with the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*), that person is necessarily endowed with four faculties: the three as previously mentioned, together with the faculty of the body.
The verse says:
"Together with the five, there are those with eyes, etc.
The commentary says:

If a person is endowed with the eye faculty, that person is necessarily endowed with five faculties: namely, the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣā*), the mental faculty (*manas*), the body faculty (*kāya*), and the eye faculty itself.
It should be understood that the same applies to those endowed with the ear, nose, or tongue faculties.
The verse says:
"There is also [a state] accompanied by joy.
The commentary explains:

If a person is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), that person is necessarily associated with five faculties: namely, equanimity (*upekṣā*), life (*jīvita*), mind (*manas*), and the faculty of joy.
If a person is born in the second dhyāna but has not yet attained the third dhyāna, with which faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) are they associated?
It is associated with the defiled faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) of the third dhyāna. The verse says:
"There is suffering, and it is associated with seven.
The commentary explains:

If a person is associated with the faculty of suffering (duḥkhendriya), that person is necessarily associated with seven faculties: namely, the body, life, mind, and the other four faculties of sensation (vedanā).
The verse says:
"There are those, such as women, who are associated with eight."
The commentary states:
If a person is endowed with the female faculty (*strī-indriya*), that person is necessarily endowed with eight faculties: the seven as previously mentioned, plus the female faculty.
The phrase "and so forth" regarding the seven includes the male faculty (*puruṣa-indriya*).

Regarding the faculty of sorrow (*daurmanasyendriya*) and the faculties of faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth: if a person attains such a faculty, each one is associated with eight faculties. Seven are as previously described, with the male faculty (*puruṣendriya*) as the eighth.
If a person is associated with the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*), there are seven as previously described, with the faculty of grief as the eighth.

If a person is associated with the faculties of faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, that person is necessarily associated with these five faculties—faith and the rest—as well as with the faculties of equanimity (*upekṣā*), life (*jīvita*), and mind (*manas*).
The verse says:
It is associated with eleven [faculties], including the faculty of knowledge and the faculty of one who has known.
The commentary says:

If a person is endowed with the faculty of knowledge (*ājñendriya*), that person is necessarily endowed with eleven faculties: namely, the five faculties of pleasure, joy, equanimity, life, and mind; the five faculties beginning with faith; and the faculty of knowledge as the eleventh.

The same applies to its association with the faculty of one who has already known (*ājñātendriya*). The ten faculties are as previously stated, with the faculty of one who has already known as the eleventh.
The verse says:
The faculty of one who desires to know the unknown (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) is associated with thirteen.
The commentary asks:
What are these thirteen? They are:

any one of the faculties of mind, life, body, female, or male; the three faculties of sensation; the five faculties beginning with faith; and the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" as the thirteenth.
Furthermore, if a person is endowed with the minimum number of faculties, with how many faculties are they endowed?
The verse says:
"The minimum, when there is no wholesome [faculty], consists of eight: feeling, mind, body, and life."
The commentary states:

If a person has severed their roots of goodness, they are said to be "without goodness. At the very minimum, they are associated with eight faculties: namely, the five feeling faculties, as well as the faculties of body, mind, and life.
Just as a person who has severed the roots of goodness possesses only the most minimal faculties,
the verse says:
"So it is for ordinary beings in the formless realm."
The commentary states:
If an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are endowed with eight faculties (*indriya*).
The verse says:
"Abandoning life, mind, faith, and so forth.
The commentary explains:
one abandons the three faculties of life, mind, and equanimity, as well as the five faculties beginning with faith, because those beginning with faith are invariably wholesome.
With the exception of those who have severed their roots of goodness (*samucchinna-kuśalamūla*), [these faculties] are present in all places.
If that were so, then the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīndriya*) and the others should also be established for them.
This objection is not valid, because [the faculties] are established as eight and because they pertain to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If a person possesses the maximum number of faculties (*indriya*), with how many are they associated?
The verse says:
At most, nineteen; excluding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) and two faculties.
The commentary states:
Excluding the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*), if a person possesses both the female and male faculties as well as other faculties, they are endowed with nineteen faculties.
Furthermore, what other kind of person is endowed with the maximum number of faculties?
The verse says:
"There is the noble one with desire.
The commentary explains:
If a noble person in training (śaikṣa) who has not yet abandoned desire possesses the maximum number of faculties, they likewise possess nineteen faculties.
The verse says:
"One faculty [is added], excluding two pure [faculties]."
The commentary states:
Excluding one faculty and excluding two untainted faculties—that is, excluding the faculty of one who has already known (ājñātāvīndriya)—the preceding two [categories] each exclude one faculty.
The manner in which the various faculties are brought forth based on the distinctions of their respective realms, and the detailed analysis of their meanings, have already been explained.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Two (Fascicle Three) Composed by Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India.
Commentary on the Analysis of the Bases (Indriya-vibhāga), Part Two. Furthermore, this matter should be considered:

just as these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) differ from one another according to their respective intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), is it likewise the case that their arising is also different, or are there certain phenomena that necessarily arise together?

Why is this? All phenomena consist of five categories: first, matter; second, mind; third, mental factors; fourth, non-associated formations; and fifth, unconditioned phenomena. Among these, unconditioned phenomena are without arising; as for those material phenomena, they shall now be definitively analyzed.
The verse says:
In the desire realm, there are eight substances; sound and the sense-faculties are absent from the atoms.
The commentary says:
The most subtle aggregation of matter is called an atom (*paramāṇu*), intended to make it known that there is no other substance subtler than it.
If this atom exists in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and is devoid of sound as well as sense organs, then eight substances arise together, with none of them lacking.
The eight substances refer to the four great elements, such as earth and so forth, and the derived matter of color, odor, taste, and tangibility.
If there is a sense-faculty atom that is without sound, then nine substances arise together, or ten substances arise together.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"The body faculty consists of nine substances.
The commentary explains:
If the atom of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is present, there are nine substances therein.
Eight are as previously described, with the body-faculty as the ninth.
The verse says:
"Ten substances when there are additional faculties.
The commentary explains:
if there are additional faculties within this atom (paramāṇu), then it consists of ten substances.
The first nine are as previously described, with one of the five faculties, such as the eye, serving as the tenth.
If these atoms arise together with sound, they arise as nine, ten, or eleven substances respectively.
Why is this? There is sound that is not separate from the sense-faculties, namely, sound whose cause is the grasping of the four great elements as its basis.
If the four great elements are not separate [from one another], how can there be an aggregation?
One may see only solidity, or only fluidity, or only heat, or only mobility.
Because one or another of these qualities predominates within this aggregate, or because its power is most preeminent, one perceives that single quality with clarity.
It is like the touch of a needle point and cotton, or like the taste of flour and salt powder. If this is so, how is it?
One should know that the remaining [elements] are also present therein; this can be known by their functions. These functions are: supporting, cohering, maturing, and propelling.
Furthermore, other masters say:
If one encounters distinct conditions, solidity and so forth may become softness, moisture, and so forth;

for instance, within water, due to extreme cold, one may perceive the sensation of heat. Although these qualities are not separate from one another, there exists a preeminent distinct quality of cold, just as sound and feeling possess preeminent distinct qualities.
Furthermore, other masters say:
within the aggregate, that [existence] exists by virtue of its seeds, not by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
As the Sūtra says:
Within a heap of wood there are various elements (*dhātu*).
From this statement, it is known that they exist by way of seeds.
If that is so, how is it known that visible form (*varṇa*) exists within wind?
This meaning can only be accepted through faith; it cannot be inferred.
Why? Because the fragrance is sustained by being intermingled [with the air].
Because the four [other] elements are not fixed in relation to wind, fragrance and taste do not exist in the form realm; this point has already been explained previously.
Therefore, by this statement, it is established that there are distinct atoms (*paramāṇu*) in the form realm.
Furthermore, it has already been explained that by this [definition], a paramāṇu consists of six, seven, or eight substances;
thus, there is no need to state it again.
In this context, is "substance" (dravya) spoken of in reference to the substance itself, or is it spoken of in reference to the sense-sphere (āyatana)?
If that is so, what is the purpose?
If one speaks of things by way of their substantial entities, this explanation is limited, namely to eight, nine, or ten entities. Why is this?
Within this [aggregate], there must necessarily be shape and form, because it is an accumulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

There is either the tactile sensation of lightness or heaviness, or the tactile sensation of smoothness or roughness; in some places there is the tactile sensation of cold, and in some places there are the tactile sensations of hunger and thirst.
If one speaks of entities (dravya) in terms of the sense bases (āyatana), this explanation becomes manifold, namely the eight entities and so forth.
Why is this? One should speak of only four entities, for the four great elements (mahābhūta) are also included within the base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana).
This interpretation is not correct.
In this context, there are instances where "substance" (*vastu*) is spoken of in reference to the object itself, namely the supporting substance;
and there are instances where "substance" is spoken of in reference to the sense-sphere (*āyatana*), namely the supported substance.
Even so, although the four great elements (mahābhūta) transform into many derivative entities, each dependent entity possesses all four great elements as its basis.

Furthermore, in this context, there are those who maintain that the category of "derived matter" (upādāyarūpa) constitutes a distinct entity; yet, despite being of a different class [from the primary elements], it does not transcend their own nature. Why, then, is such an effort expended to provide this analytical explanation?
Since these meanings and expressions arise according to intention, one should contemplate only the meaning.
Having explained that matter is necessarily co-arising, the arising of the remaining categories shall now be discussed.
A verse here says:
"Mind and mental factors necessarily coexist.
The commentary explains:
Why is this? Because this mind and its mental factors cannot arise if they are mutually separated from one another.
The verse says:
"All function together as their characteristic.
The commentary states:
the word "necessarily" carries over; it is not only the mind and mental factors that necessarily arise together.

Among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), whatever is subject to arising—whether it be matter (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), or the like—is termed "all"; if it arises, it necessarily arises together with the common characteristics of the conditioned (*sādhāraṇa-saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
The verse says:
"And with attainment.
The commentary says:

If a phenomenon is designated as "sentient being," it necessarily arises together with acquisition (*prāpti*); other phenomena are not so. For this reason, this distinct phenomenon is established and designated as a "mental factor" (*caitasika*).
What are they? The verse says:
"The mental factors are fivefold, due to the distinctions of the universal ground and so forth."
The commentary states:

There are five categories of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*): first, the universal ground; second, the virtuous universal ground; third, the defiled universal ground; fourth, the unwholesome universal ground; and fifth, the limited defilement ground.
What dharma is called "ground" (*bhūmi*)?
It is the sphere of activity.
If a dharma is the sphere of activity for another dharma, that [latter] dharma is said to have that [former] dharma as its ground.
Among these, those factors are called "universal mental factors" (*mahābhūmika*) because they constitute the great ground; that is, those factors which exist in all states of mind.
Which factors exist in all states of mind?
The verse says:

Feeling, conceptualization, intention, contact, discernment, mindfulness, attention, resolve, concentration, and equanimity—these ten factors, whose characteristics are clearly defined, are present throughout all states of mind.
The commentary explains:
these ten factors are said to arise together, assembled within every single moment of mind.
In this context, feeling (*vedanā*) refers to three types: the experiencing of pleasure, pain, and that which is neither pleasure nor pain.
Attention (*manasikāra*) refers to the mind taking an object as its task.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) refers to the mind grasping the specific characteristics of an object.
Desire (*chanda*) refers to the seeking to act.
Contact (*sparśa*) refers to a distinct dharma produced by the conjunction of the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) refers to discernment (*dharmapravicaya*).
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) means not forgetting the object of focus.
Volition (*manasikāra*) means the mental turning toward [an object].
Clarity of characteristics (*nimittapratyavekṣaṇā*) refers to that factor which, regarding the characteristics of the object, enables the mind to be clearly aware.
Concentration (*samādhi*) refers to one-pointedness of mind.

The distinctions among mental factors (*caitta*) are so subtle that they are difficult to discern; they are hard to know even within a continuous stream (*saṃtāna*), let alone within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).

There are medicinal herbs with form that possess many kinds of tastes; among them, there are medicines whose distinct flavors are difficult to differentiate even when they can be verified by the sense organs, let alone this Dharma, which is formless and realized only through wisdom.

These dharmas are the excellent foundation for all wholesome states; they are called the "wholesome universal mental factors" (kuśalamahābhūmika) because these dharmas always arise within a wholesome mind.
What are these dharmas?
The verse says:
Faith, heedfulness, serenity, equanimity, shame, and dread; the two faculties, non-affliction, and diligence are always directed toward the wholesome.
The commentary says:
Such dharmas as these always arise within a virtuous mind.
Here, "faith" (śraddhā) refers to the clarity and purity of the mind.
Other masters say:
Faith (*śraddhā*) is so called because it is a firm conviction regarding the truths, karma, and its fruits.
Heedfulness (*apramāda*) refers to the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
What kind of cultivation is there that is distinct from wholesome dharmas?
To constantly abide in wholesome dharmas is called non-heedlessness (*apramāda*).
In the sūtras of other schools,
it is said that the guarding of the mind is called non-heedlessness.
"Tranquility" (praśrabdhi) refers to the mind’s capacity for its object.
This meaning need not be understood in this way;
for it is stated in another sutra:
The body is called "peaceful" (kṣema) because it is capable of its function; it is not that this is not said of the body as feeling. One should know that this is also the case here.
If so, why are they established as factors (aṅga) of enlightenment?
Why is this? Because within this state, the body possesses efficacy regarding its function; this is what should be understood as "bodily pliancy" (*kāyapraśrabdhi*).
If that is so, why is it described as a factor of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*)?
It receives the name "factor of enlightenment" because it accords with the factors of enlightenment.
Why is this? Because this physical pliancy is able to induce mental pliancy, thereby causing the factors of enlightenment to arise.
It has been seen elsewhere that such a statement has never existed before.
It is just as the Sūtra says:
"Joy and the factors conducive to joy—these the Blessed One calls the factor of enlightenment of joy."
There is another explanation:
hatred and its causes are called the hindrance of ill-will (*vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa*).

Furthermore, right view, right intention, and right effort—these three are called the factors of wisdom (*prajñā-aṅga*). These provisions receive that name because they are conducive to it; just as physical pliancy receives the name of the factor of mental pliancy and the factor of awakening because it is conducive to them.
Equanimity (*upekṣā*) means the mind is impartial and free from partiality or opposition.
How does this statement correspond [to that definition]? What is it?

It was previously stated that *cetanā* (volition) has the nature of mental dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), whereas it is now stated that *tyāga* (renunciation) has the nature of non-dedication in the mind.
How are these two statements consistent?
Was it not already explained previously?

This means that the meaning and principles of the mental factors (*cittadharma*) are difficult to understand; there are things that can only be understood after they have been difficult to understand, and this is the most difficult to comprehend.

That is to say, establishing non-contradiction where there is contradiction: in some instances there is dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), while in others there is no dedication. What contradiction is there in this?
If that were so, all associated dharmas would not share a single object; other dharmas of this same category should also be included here.
You must certainly understand this principle of dharmas.
Shame (*hrī*) and modesty (*apatrāpya*) will be explained later.
The two roots refer to the two types of wholesome roots: non-attachment (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adveṣa*).

Non-delusion (*amoha*) is also a wholesome root; however, since this wholesome root has wisdom (*prajñā*) as its essence and was already established among the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) previously, it is not mentioned again here among the wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*).
Non-affliction means not wishing to harm or oppose others.
Diligence means valor.
Having explained the ten universal wholesome mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), they are called "universal" because these factors are present in all [wholesome] levels of mind.
Because delusion (*moha*) is their universal ground (*mahābhūmi*), they are called the "universal ground of delusion" (*moha-mahābhūmika*); these factors always arise in a defiled mind.
Which factors are these?
The verse says:
Delusion, negligence, laziness, lack of faith, lack of tranquility, and restlessness are always present in the defiled.
The commentary says:
In this context, delusion refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), which is a lack of knowledge and a lack of clarity.
Heedlessness refers to the non-cultivation of wholesome dharmas; it is the antithesis of the cultivation of wholesome dharmas.
Laziness refers to the mind lacking superior capability.
Lack of faith refers to the mind lacking clarity and purity; this is the counteractive factor to faith.
Lack of tranquility refers to heaviness of body and heaviness of mind, whereby the body and mind lack capacity for their respective tasks.
The Abhidharma-piṭaka states:
"There are two kinds of non-pliancy (asthāna): namely, non-pliancy of body and non-pliancy of mind.
How can a mental factor be designated as a bodily factor?
As it is said, "feeling" refers to bodily feeling;
"restlessness" refers to the lack of tranquility of the mind.
These six factors are called the universal defiled mental states (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
Is it not stated in the Abhidharma-piṭaka that ten dharmas constitute the universal ground of afflictions (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*)?
Furthermore, non-tranquility (*asamprasāda*) is not mentioned therein either. What are these ten?
Lack of faith, laziness, forgetfulness, mental distraction, ignorance, lack of discernment, improper reflection, perception of false signs, restlessness, and heedlessness.
Devānampiya!
You know the destination, but you do not know the method.
What, in this context, constitutes the method?

Forgetfulness, mental distraction, lack of discernment, improper attention, and the perception of false signs—since these factors already belong to the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*), they cannot be established again as belonging to the ground of afflictions (*kleśamahābhūmika*).
Just as non-delusion is among the great wholesome ground factors, so too is this [non-remembrance].
If mindfulness is defiled, it is called forgetfulness;
if concentration is defiled, it is called mental distraction.
The same applies to the remaining [mental factors]; therefore, this was stated in such a manner.
Could these universal mental factors (*mahābhūmikadharma*) be established as the universal factors of defilement (*kleśamahābhūmika*)?
Regarding this, there are four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first category refers to sensation, perception, attention, volition, and contact.
The second category refers to lack of faith, laziness, ignorance, restlessness, and heedlessness.
The third phrase refers to the five factors beginning with mindfulness (*smṛti*).
The fourth phrase refers to all other dharmas remaining after excluding those mentioned in the first three phrases.

Furthermore, there are other masters who, regarding desire (*chanda*), mental distraction (*citta-vikṣepa*), and erroneous concentration (*mithyā-samādhi*), formulate their fourfold classification differently from this.
Other masters maintain that *styāna* (sloth) is associated with all afflictions, yet it is not mentioned among the "universal mental factors of affliction" (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
What fault is there in this?
They should reply: It is not mentioned because it conforms to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, it is not stated.
Why is this? If a person has laxity (*laya*) as their predominant mode of conduct, they can quickly attain concentration (*samādhi*) through the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*);
this is not the case for one whose conduct is characterized by agitation (*auddhatya*). What are the characteristics of such a person who has laxity as their conduct rather than agitation?
If one acts with restlessness as one's mode of behavior rather than acting without agitation, what are the characteristics of such a person? Why is this?
Because these two factors do not abandon each other but arise together as a single event.

Nevertheless, although these two factors may become predominant in a person and thereby define that person's conduct, the six factors are nevertheless established as the universal mental factors of affliction (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*). Why is this?
These six factors always arise in a defiled mind and do not arise elsewhere.
The verse says:
"If it is unwholesome, as well as shamelessness and lack of dread."
The commentary states:

Because shamelessness (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) constantly arise in all unwholesome minds, these two factors are established as the universal ground of the unwholesome (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*).
The characteristics of these two factors will be explained later.
The verse says:
Enmity, resentment, deceit, jealousy, stubbornness, concealment, as well as avarice, deception, intoxication, and affliction—these are the ten minor defilements (*upakleśa-bhūmi*).
The commentary says:
Because minor afflictions constitute its ground, it is called the "ground of minor afflictions.
This is because it is associated only with ignorance that arises based on the mental faculty and is to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
These ten afflictions will be explained among the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Having finished explaining the five categories of mental factors (*caitasika*), there remain other indeterminate mental factors, namely vitarka, vicāra, kaukṛtya, middha, and so forth; among these, it should now be stated which mental factors necessarily arise together with which types of consciousness.
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are five types of consciousness (*citta*): one wholesome consciousness;
two unwholesome consciousnesses, namely that which occurs independently and that which is associated with other afflictions (*kleśa*);
and two neutral (*avyākṛta*) consciousnesses, namely the obscured (*nivṛta*) and the unobscured (*anivṛta*).
In this context, the mind of the desire realm necessarily possesses both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought). Therefore, regarding it, the verse says:
Because it possesses both vitarka and vicāra, in the wholesome mind of the desire realm, there are twenty-two mental factors.
The commentary states:
They necessarily arise together. Which twenty-two?
The ten universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), the ten wholesome universal factors (*kuśalamahābhūmika*), along with *vitarka* (applied thought) and *vicāra* (sustained thought).
The verse says:
"In some cases, it persists for a long time.
The commentary explains:
It is not the case that remorse (kaukṛtya) is present in all virtuous minds.
Where it does exist, it is added as an additional factor, such that there are twenty-three mental factors in that state.
What dharma is termed "remorse"?

Regarding the remorse that arises in the mind after having committed an evil deed, this mental factor is called "evil-doing" (*kaukṛtya*) because it arises by taking evil-doing as its object; this factor is itself remorse (*paścāttāpa*).
It is, for example, like the gate of liberation which takes emptiness as its object and is thus called the "emptiness gate of liberation."
Furthermore, just as non-attachment arises by observing the sign of impurity and is thus called the "contemplation of impurity," we also see such a thing in the world:
where one speaks of a location based on what is situated therein, as when one says, "all the counties have arrived" or "all the lands have arrived."

This remorse (*kaukṛtya*) is the locus of subsequent burning (*paritāpana*). Alternatively, the name of the cause is metaphorically applied to the effect, as when the six bases of contact (*ṣaḍ-spraṣṭavyāyatana*) are called "past karma.
If that is so, how can this remorse be called "remorse" if it takes as its object something not yet done?
To designate as "made" that which has not yet been made is a conceptual construction,
as the Sūtra says:
"If I do not perform it, it is not well-performed by me."

What is this? "Subsequent remorse" (*paścāttāpa*) is called "wholesome" because one feels remorse later due to not having performed wholesome deeds and having performed unwholesome ones; this is wholesome subsequent remorse.
The opposite of this is called "unwholesome subsequent remorse."
These two each arise taking two objects as their conditions.
The verse says:
"In the case of an independent unwholesome mind, there are twenty associated with views."
The commentary states:

In an independent unwholesome mind of the desire realm, twenty mental factors arise simultaneously; namely, the ten universal ground factors (*mahābhūmika*), the six universal defilement ground factors (*kleśamahābhūmika*), the two universal unwholesome ground factors (*akuśalamahābhūmika*), as well as vitarka and vicāra.
Regarding "solitary minds": herein, there is only solitary ignorance (*avidyā*) without other afflictions such as desire (*rāga*).

Not only in solitary unwholesome minds, but also in unwholesome minds associated with views (*dṛṣṭi*), there are twenty mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*), just as in the various factors found in solitary unwholesome minds.
If that is so, why is it not established as twenty-one based on the predominance of "view"? It is not so;
for it is because the specific distinctions of wisdom included within the universal mental factors (mahābhūmika) that are designated by the term "view."
