"Prajñā has the functional capacity to ensure that latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) do not arise again; this alone is called analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Herein, the non-arising of future suffering results from the destruction of the latent afflictions and the absence of the conditions for their arising."

If this phenomenon were established independently of that [analysis], then wisdom would have no efficacy therein; such cessation is termed "cessation not through deliberation" (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
However, if this phenomenon cannot be established apart from analytical discernment, then this cessation is precisely "cessation through deliberation" (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha).
Other masters say:
"If a dharma has already arisen and subsequently ceases, that cessation by its own nature is called non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
According to this position, non-analytical cessation would necessarily be impermanent, because as long as a dharma has not yet ceased, non-analytical cessation does not yet exist.

Is it not so? Your argument regarding *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation) is no different from the previous difficulty, because you hold that it is preceded by deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā*).
As for us, we do not maintain that *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* exists subsequent to deliberation.
Why is this? It is not that after first performing discernment, those dharmas that have not yet arisen subsequently fail to arise.
What is your position?

Previously, all phenomena were already non-arising; yet, if one were apart from analytical discernment (*pravicaya*), these phenomena would have arisen. When analytical discernment arises, they never arise again thereafter.
In this context, it is the function of analytical discernment that, whereas previously there was no obstacle to arising, it now acts as an obstacle to arising.
If you maintain that nirvāṇa is merely non-arising, how do you interpret this scriptural passage?
The Sūtra says:

"If the five faculties, such as faith and so forth, are cultivated, developed, and repeatedly practiced, they lead to the abandonment and cessation of all suffering—past, future, and present; the arising of this abandonment and cessation is itself nirvāṇa."
Non-arising pertains only to the future; there is no sense of non-arising regarding the past or the present, for they truly exist.
Nevertheless, because the afflictions that take the three times as their objects are extinguished, the Blessed One designated it as the cessation of suffering.
How is this determined?
As another sutra states:
"O bhikṣus, you should eliminate craving for form."
If craving has already ceased, then for you, this form is ceased and abandoned; as explained at length in the Sūtra, this applies even up to consciousness.
If that is so, then regarding the suffering of the three periods of time, abandonment and cessation are likewise.

If such a view is held, this sutra was taught in order to eliminate the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the past, future, and present; the principles of its interpretation should all be understood in this way.
If such a view is held, then past afflictions belong to past births, and present afflictions belong to the present birth.
For example, among the eighteen modes of craving (*tṛṣṇā-carita*), it is taught that with reference to the past—meaning with reference to past births—and so on, up to the present, it is likewise.

Because the afflictions of these two periods have already established their seeds within the present continuum for the purpose of producing future afflictions, it is said that those [afflictions] are also extinguished when the seeds are extinguished;
this is just as it is said that karma is exhausted when its retribution is exhausted.
Because future suffering and future afflictions lack seeds, they will never arise again; this is what is called "separation through cessation.
If one holds a view contrary to this, what could possibly be ceased in the past or the present?
Regarding that which has already ceased and that which is tending toward cessation, what further fruit is there for the function of cessation?
If the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) were truly no entity at all, how would one account for the Sūtra spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, which says:
"Of all dharmas, whether conditioned or unconditioned, among them the dharma of detachment is said to be peerless"?
How can one speak of "non-existence" regarding that which is non-existent?
If we do not say that "non-existence" is itself non-existent, I would say that such a thing exists.

According to what I have said, just as it is said that sound exists prior to its arising and does not exist after its cessation, although there is the word "existence," it is not a substantial entity; ultimately, it does not constitute existence.

One should know that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are likewise: there is a non-existence that is most worthy of praise, namely, that all calamities and misfortunes shall never again exist. This non-existence is superior to other forms of non-existence because it is peerless, and thus it is worthy of praise; it is intended to cause those disciples who are ready for conversion to joyfully seek this Dharma.
If the unconditioned were merely non-existence, then cessation and detachment would not be noble truths. Why?
Because they would be nothing at all.
If that is so, what is the meaning of "truth" (*satya*)? Is it not thus:
that its meaning is "non-erroneousness," and these two [the truths] are also non-erroneous?
Just as the Noble Ones perceive suffering as suffering, so too does suffering not exist; it is as if it were non-existent.
If this is so, what contradiction is there with regard to the Noble Truths?
How is it that "nothing whatsoever exists" constitutes the third noble truth?
The meaning of the noble truths has already been explained; because it is seen and taught by the Noble Ones immediately following the second [truth], it constitutes the third.
If you maintain that there is no activity and nothing at all exists, then the consciousness that takes space and nirvana as its objects would necessarily be without an objective referent.
This point shall be definitively resolved within the investigation into the real existence of the past and the future.
If you grant that unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are indeed distinct entities, what would they possess?
And what further would they possess?
In that case, the original doctrine of the *Vibhāṣā* would be protected, and the gods should protect it.
If one were to know this, it would necessarily be something that could be protected.
This attachment is not real. Why is it not real?

This unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be realized through its own nature in the way that form (*rūpa*), sensation (*vedanā*), and so forth can; nor can it be established through objective evidence in the way that the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth can.
How can this establishment—that this cessation (*nirodha*) is the cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*) and suffering (*duḥkha*)—be valid?

Why is this so? Because this disjunction from cessation is unrelated to the afflictions and the like, as the principles of cause and effect do not apply; it is therefore logical that its meaning consists solely in the negation of their denial.

This means that such-and-such [defilements] do not exist; if one were to grasp them as being substantially existent entities, then because their acquisition (*prāpti*) has been severed and this dissociation (*visamyoga*) has been attained, it is said that these defilements have been dissociated and extinguished.
Furthermore, what cause can definitively establish the attainment of this dharma?
A sūtra states:
"The bhikṣu has already attained nirvāṇa in the present life."
If there is nothing that exists, how can there be attainment?
Because it is the antidote to attainment, and because it serves as a basis that is eternally incompatible with both the afflictions and future rebirth, one speaks of "attaining nirvāṇa."
The various *Āgamas* reveal that this dharma has only "non-existence" as its meaning.
The *Āgama* says: "This is the remainderless cessation of all suffering;

it is relinquishment, the limitless, exhaustion, dispassion, fading away, tranquility, abandonment, and disappearance. It is the non-continuation of further suffering, non-grasping, and non-arising. This dharma is tranquil and sublime; namely, the relinquishing of all craving, its exhaustion, dispassion, fading away, and cessation—this is called *nirvāṇa*."
Why is it not accepted that [things] are called "unborn" (ajāta) simply because they do not arise therein?
We see that this interpretation is inconsistent with both the meaning and the logic.
What, then, does this passage intend to reveal?
If it were associated with what already exists, it would logically never have arisen, because nirvāṇa is eternally abiding.

If it were associated with what has already been attained, then from that attainment one could distinguish this dharma as "already possessed" or "already obtained"; you must therefore admit that it does not arise.
This analogy is most consistent with reason.
Just as light is, so too is the liberation of the mind in *nirvāṇa*.
As light is, so too is *nirvāṇa* not a substantial entity; the Blessed One’s liberation of the mind is likewise.
The Abhidharma-piṭaka also speaks in this way.
That Piṭaka asks:
"What are the dharmas that lack counterparts?"
Answer: Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
"Lack of category" means lack of essence; this statement reveals the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"The meaning of the words is not like this.
If so, what then is the meaning?"
There are five kinds of categories (*jāti*):
first, the category of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-jāti*), as the Sūtra says:
"If one has already attained this category, that person will necessarily be endowed with it."
Second, the category of objects (*ālambana-vastu*), as the Sūtra says:
"All phenomena are to be known by wisdom according to their categories.
Third, the category of fetters (*saṃyojana-vastu*), as the Sūtra says:
If, within this category, one is associated with the fetter of desire (*rāga-saṃyojana*), is one also associated with the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*)?
Regarding the four types of categories, as the Sūtra says:
"What are the dharmas belonging to the category of existence (*bhava-gati*)?"
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are comprised within five categories, as the Sūtra says:
"the category of fields, the category of houses," and so forth.

In this passage, [the author] indicates [the nature of unconditioned phenomena] by means of their generic name; therefore, all unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma) are substantially existent distinct entities.
This is the position of the Vaibhāṣika masters, who maintain that unconditioned phenomena have neither cause nor fruit.
Having explained the three unconditioned phenomena,
there are five kinds of results; among these, which result belongs to which cause,
and which cause belongs to which result?
The verse says:
"Subsequently, there are the fruit of cause and the fruit of retribution.
The commentary says:
Because the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is explained last, it is called "subsequent"; this cause takes the retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*) as its result.
The verse says:
"The preceding causes have the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*)."
The commentary states:
Because it is mentioned first among the causes of production, it is called "prior. This cause takes the sovereign fruit (*adhipatiphala*) as its result.
Since this cause is characterized solely by non-obstruction, what kind of sovereignty does it possess?
This itself is the predominant cause (*adhipati-hetu*).

Furthermore, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) possesses an auxiliary function; for example, the ten bases (*āyatana*) have a meritorious function with respect to the five consciousnesses, and various karmas have a functional capacity with respect to the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
The various faculties, such as the ear, possess indirect predominance (*adhipatya*) over the arising of visual consciousness, because the desire to see arises from hearing.
Such matters should be reflected upon.
The verse says:
"Of the same class and the pervasive [causes], [the result] is an outflowing [result].
The commentary states:
Since the results of these two causes both resemble their respective causes, they both take the outflowing result as their fruit.
The verse says:
"The power of two.
The commentary says:
The second refers to the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), both of which take the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) as their result.
It is called "human effort" because it is capable of accomplishing something; this very effort is itself the result.
What dharma is called "efficacy" (*puruṣakāra*)?
This dharma possesses a functional capacity toward other dharmas; because this efficacy is like the ability of a man (*puruṣa*), it is called "efficacy.
It is as worldly expressions go: "the crow-foot herb," "the intoxicated elephant," or "the general."
Do other causes also have a dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), or is it only these two? Other causes also have it;
for other ripening causes (*vipākahetu*), there is a dominant fruit that arises either simultaneously or immediately after [the cause], whereas the ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*) is not like this.
This cause of retribution also has a distant efficient fruit (*puruṣakāra-phala*), such as the rice that a farmer is destined to obtain.
What dharma is called the fruit of retribution (*vipāka-phala*)?
And what dharma is called the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*)?
The verse says:
"Retribution is an indeterminate dharma.
The commentary says:
This is an unobscured-neutral dharma.
Is this retribution not termed "non-sentient"?
The verse says:
"Sentient beings.
The commentary states:
These dharmas belong exclusively to the internal [self], and because they are not shared with others, they are designated by the name "sentient beings."
Is this dharma an increase (*upacaya*) or a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*)?
The verse says:
It is born of the determinate (*vijñapti*).
The commentary states:
The two dharmas of good and evil are designated as "determinate" (vyākṛta) because they can be defined in terms of their retribution;
since this arises at a later time rather than arising immediately after [the cause], it is called "retribution" (vipāka).
Such is the nature of the retribution.
Since dharmas that are not named "sentient beings" also arise from karma, why are they not called retribution?
Because they are obtained in common; these dharmas can be shared in this same way by other people as well.
The retribution of karmic fruit cannot be shared. Why is this?
It is impossible for the retribution of the karma performed by one person to be experienced in common with another.
The dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*) is also produced by karma; how then can it be shared?
Because it arises from collective karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*).
The verse says:
"The outflow resembles its own cause.
The commentary states:
If the fruit resembles its cause, it is called an outflowing fruit (*niṣyandaphala*), such as the causes and effects of similar types (*sabhāga*) and universal application (*sarvatraga*).
If the causes and effects of the similar-class and universal [factors] are all of the same class, why do you not allow that they are all similar-cause factors (*sabhāga-hetu*)?
For this reason, these effects share their original cause with respect to their level (*bhūmi*) and their defiled nature, but not by way of every category.
If a dharma is accepted as a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) because it resembles its fruit in all respects,
for this purpose four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) are established:
if a dharma is a homogeneous cause of another dharma, is it also a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) of that same dharma?
There are four propositions.
The first proposition refers to that which is not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*), but is merely a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*).
The second proposition refers to the pervasive cause belonging to a different category (*nikāya-antara-sarvatraga-hetu*).
The third phrase refers to the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) within a single category.
The fourth phrase excludes the preceding three phrases.
The verse says:
"Separation through cessation occurs by means of knowledge.
The commentary explains:

"Cessation" refers to permanent separation; "knowledge" refers to the three faculties within the Three Paths. Because suffering and its origin are exhausted in succession by means of this knowledge, it is termed "permanent separation and cessation," which is to say *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment), and is designated as the fruit of separation.
The verse says:
If it arises through the power of a dharma, that fruit is called "efficacy.
The commentary says:
If a phenomenon arises through the functional power of another phenomenon, that phenomenon is the *puruṣakāra-phala* (fruit of human effort) of the former.

For example, the preparatory mind of a lower stage [is the cause] for the samādhis of a higher stage, for outflowing and non-outflowing meditative minds, for transformation minds, and so forth. As for *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation), it should be said to be merely attained (*prāpti*) through the functional power of the Path.
The verse says:
Prior to its existence, there was no conditioned phenomenon; [the result] is the dominant fruit of the conditioned.
The commentary says:
When conditioned phenomena arise separately from previously arisen conditioned phenomena, this is called the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
What is the difference between the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit?

The fruit obtained by the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu) is called the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala); the fruit obtained by causes other than the efficient cause is called the sovereign fruit (adhipati-phala).
For example, that which is obtained by a craftsman is both the fruit of human effort and the sovereign fruit; however, that which is obtained by others is merely the sovereign fruit.
Furthermore, among these six causes, which cause at what time can take an effect and which can give an effect?
The verse says:
Five [causes] in the present take an effect.
The commentary states:

Excluding the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes can grasp their own results in the present; this is because past [causes] have already grasped their results, and future [causes] lack functional efficacy.
The same applies to the act of creation.
Since this cause does not necessarily possess a fruit, it is not mentioned.
The verse says:
The second is "giving fruit at the same time.
The commentary states:
The two causes—the co-existent cause and the associated cause—also give their fruit while existing in the present.
Why is this? Because these two causes—the grasping of the fruit and the giving of the fruit—occur at the same time.
The verse says:
"Two [factors] in the present and past.
The commentary explains:
these are the two causes that are similar in kind to their fruit and the universal cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).
If these two causes give rise to their fruit in the past, that principle is acceptable.
But how do these two causes give rise to their outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) in the present?
It is because they arise in succession.
If the fruit has already arisen, these two causes have already passed away; once they have given their fruit, they do not give it again.
Is there a homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that can only take up a fruit but does not actually give it?
In this regard, there are four propositions. The first proposition is:
when a person severs the roots of goodness, it refers to the final acquisition (*prāpti*) that is severed.

The second proposition is: when a person reconnects the roots of goodness, it refers to the initial acquisition obtained; one should explain it thus: for such a person, it is the reconnection with the previous acquisition.
The third phrase refers to virtuous persons in their remaining stages who do not sever the roots of goodness.
The fourth phrase excludes those of the three preceding cases.

If it concerns the homogeneous cause of unwholesome states, the first phrase refers to a person who is currently attaining detachment from desire, specifically the acquisition (*prāpti*) of that which is abandoned at the very end of the realm of desire.

Regarding the second phrase: if a person falls away from the detachment from desire of the desire realm, the first acquisition (prāpti) obtained should be described as such—the prior acquisition of one who has fallen away.
The third phrase refers to those who have not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm, during their remaining states.
The fourth phrase excludes the three preceding cases.

In this manner, one should reflect accordingly upon the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) factors, from the attainment of the fruit of Arhatship until its regression.
The "unobscured-neutral" (anivṛtāvyākṛta) has no subsequent category.

If a cause is capable of giving its fruit, it must necessarily be capable of taking its fruit; however, there are cases where it is capable of taking its fruit but not capable of giving it, such as the final aggregate (skandha) of an Arhat.
If one considers the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that possesses an object, it is determined according to each moment.
Regarding whether there is a wholesome homogeneous cause that only takes up a fruit but does not give one,
there are four possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Regarding the first phrase: if, following a wholesome mind, a defiled or neutral mind arises and manifests.
Regarding the second phrase: the reverse of the former.
Regarding the third phrase: a wholesome mind arises in succession to a wholesome mind.
The fourth phrase consists of those cases excluded by the preceding three phrases.
Just as with the fourfold set of wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth, one should likewise reflect according to reason.
The verse says:
First, "the past gives the fruit.
The commentary states:
the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), being in the past, is able to give its fruit.
Why is this? Because there is no simultaneous arising of karmic fruition, nor is there any arising without an interval.
Other masters say:
There are four kinds of fruits:
first, the fruit of dependence (*āśraya-phala*), such as the water-circle being the fruit of the wind-circle, up to grass and so forth being the fruit of the earth.
Second, the fruit of application (*prayoga-phala*), such as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) being the fruit of the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).
Third is the fruit of collection, such as the visual consciousness and so forth in relation to the eye and so forth.
Fourth is the fruit of cultivation, such as the transformation produced by the path of the form realm serving as the fruit.
These four kinds of fruits are subsumed under the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*).
Having explained the causes and their effects,
what is the phenomenon (dharma),
and by what cause does it arise?
By how many causes do they arise?
To state it briefly, there are four kinds of phenomena:
first, defiled phenomena; second, phenomena born of retribution; third, initial untainted phenomena; and fourth, the remaining phenomena other than the first two.
What are the residual dharmas?

They are the indeterminate (avyākṛta) dharmas remaining after excluding those that are retribution (vipāka), and the wholesome (kuśala) dharmas remaining after excluding the first moment of the untainted (anāsrava).
Regarding these four kinds of dharmas, the verse says:

Defiled [dharmas], retributive [dharmas], and the remainder arise in sequence from the first, the untainted, excluding the retributive and the universal causes; two arise from the similar cause, and the remainder from the producing cause.
The commentary states:
Defiled dharmas, with the exception of the single retributive cause, arise from the remaining five causes.
Dharmas that arise as maturation (vipāka) are produced from five causes, excluding the universal cause (sarvatraga-hetu).
All remaining dharmas are produced from four causes, excluding both the maturation cause and the universal cause.

Regarding the first category, the untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas—excluding the two causes of fruition (*vipāka*) and universal (*sarvatraga*), as well as excluding the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*)—arise from the remaining three causes.
What kind of dharmas are these four?
The verse says:
"Mind and mental factors.
The commentary says:
These four dharmas arise from other causes and are exclusively mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).
If that is so, what about those dharmas that are not associated (*viprayukta*) and those that are material (*rūpa*)?
The verse says:
"Excluding other associated causes.
The commentary explains:

with the exception of one associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*), other dharmas such as those that are defiled (*kliṣṭa*) arise in this manner, just as mind and mental factors do. Among these, defiled dharmas arise from four causes; dharmas born of maturation (*vipākaja*) arise from four causes; and all remaining dharmas arise from three causes.
Initially, uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas arise from two causes; there is not a single dharma that arises from only one cause.
The detailed explanation of causes is hereby concluded.
What, then, is the condition (*pratyaya*)?
How many kinds are there?
The verse says:
It is taught that there are four kinds of conditions.
The commentary says:
Where is this stated?
It is stated in the sūtras.
The Sūtra states: There are four types of conditions: first, the condition as cause; second, the condition as immediate antecedent; third, the condition as object; and fourth, the dominant condition.
In this context, "homogeneity" (sabhāgatā) refers to the nature of its object.
Regarding the causal condition (hetu-pratyaya), the verse says:
"The causal condition consists of five causes."
The commentary states:
With the exception of one efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), the remaining five causes are designated as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The verse says:
"Mind and mental factors that are not subsequent are the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for those already arisen.
The commentary explains:
With the exception of the final mind and mental factors of an Arhat, all other already-arisen mind and mental factors are called the equal-and-immediate condition.
What is called the "successive condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Because these dharmas constitute an equal and immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), they are termed the successive condition.
Therefore, matter (*rūpa*) is not a successive condition, because its arising is not equal [to that of mind and mental factors].

Why is this? From the form of the desire realm, at a subsequent time, there arises in succession the non-informative form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) of both the desire realm and the form realm; at a later time, the untainted form (*anāsrava-rūpa*) of the desire realm arises; and at a further time, all three types of form arise.
This form arises from the cause of the fault of present distraction; the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) is not subject to such faults or distractions.
This is the meaning of dependent origination, as stated by the Venerable Vasumitra:
"Because the two [subsequent moments] arise after having increased within a single, non-contradictory continuum."
The Venerable One says:
Because the subsequent arises from the cause as either minimal or maximal, at a later time, great form arises from small form.

For example, chaff produces ash. Or, great form arises from small form; for example, from within the seed of a *piṭaka* tree, a person [of the tree] grows stage by stage until the branches hang down in profusion, eventually transforming into a *nyagrodha* tree.

Is it not thus? Mental states and mental factors sometimes arise in great numbers and sometimes in small numbers—namely, in the states of the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate; in states with vitarka and vicāra; and in the three dhyānas. This occurs according to different categories [of dharmas], but within their own category, there is never a time when they arise in multiple instances simultaneously.
The same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*) and the other [mental factors].
Is the status of the equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) established in reference to its own category?
No, such a principle does not exist.

Why is this? A complete aggregate serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for another complete aggregate; it is not the case that many sensations and other factors arise from fewer sensations and other factors.
This meaning has already been explained previously.
The Saṃtānāntaravādin school maintains this position:

that which belongs to its own category is the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and not that which belongs to another category; for example, a mind is the immediately preceding condition for a [subsequent] mind.
The same applies to sensation (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates, as should be understood in detail.

If a defiled dharma arises immediately after a non-defiled one, the previously ceased defiled state serves as the immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) for the present defiled state, just as the mind entering the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) serves as the condition for the mind emerging from them.

If one does not now uphold this tenet, then even those factors that are not associated with mental states would fail to constitute an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), because they too would arise from the fault of being disturbed by present conditions;
furthermore, factors belonging to the three realms as well as those that are unconditioned (*apratisaṃyukta*) would all arise simultaneously in the present.
Why is it not admitted that future dharmas serve as the *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition)?
Because the *samanantarapratyaya* would otherwise be disordered; for in the future world, there is no distinction of priority or sequence.

If this were so, how could the Blessed One attain such knowledge—knowing, with respect to all sentient beings until the very end of saṃsāra, the sequence that "this future dharma should arise first" and "subsequently, this other dharma should arise"?

Because it is known through inference based on the past and the present, he [the Buddha] said: "The Blessed One has seen that from such a type of karma, such a type of retribution has arisen; likewise, from a phenomenon (dharma), a phenomenon arises."

In this present life, there are likewise such types of karma; from such types of karma, such types of retribution arise, and in future lives they shall likewise be born. It is the same for the arising of phenomena from phenomena.

Knowing it to be thus and so, this is the Tathāgata’s wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), not inferential wisdom (*anumānajñāna*). By means of inference from the past and the present, the Blessed One, having directly perceived the disordered and intermingled states of things in future lives, gives rise to such knowledge:
"Having performed such karma, this person will necessarily experience such and such results in the future."
If that were so, the Blessed One, not having seen the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), would be unable to know the subsequent limit (*aparānta*).
Other masters say:
Within the continuum (*saṃtati*) of all sentient beings, there exists a conditioned particularity (*saṃskṛta-viśeṣa*) associated with the mind that serves as the mark of the future fruit.
The World-Honored One, observing this, knows future fruits—that is, those meditative concentrations and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) that have not yet manifested.
If this were so, the Tathāgata would be knowing by means of observing signs, and thus would be unable to realize them anew.
Therefore, the Sautrāntikas say that the Blessed One possesses correct and universal knowledge regarding all objects according to his will. Why is this so?
The World-Honored One has said:
"The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable.

If future dharmas do not arise in a sequential order, how is it that immediately after the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering (*duḥkhe dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises, and no other dharma arises?
Up until the moment when the mind is like a diamond, immediately thereafter the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, and no other dharma arises.

If a dharma can obstruct the arising of another dharma, then from the cessation of that dharma, the subsequent dharma may arise; for example, there is no immediate condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) for sprouts and the like to arise from seeds and the like.
Why is the final mind of an Arhat not a condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*)?
Because it does not associate with any subsequent mind.
If that is so, then the mind that has just ceased without interval constitutes the mental faculty (*manas*)?

No. Why? Because no subsequent consciousness arises after the [death] moment of uninterrupted succession; if it were not established as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), then the final mind should likewise not be established as the mental faculty (*manas*).
The nature of the mental faculty (*manas*) is manifested by way of its being a support, not by way of its functional capacity; therefore, it possesses the sense of "support.
Is it not the case that other consciousnesses do not arise because other conditions are incomplete?
Because it does not serve as a basis, consciousness does not arise.

The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is manifested by its functional capacity; if there is a phenomenon that is grasped by this condition as its fruit, no other phenomena or sentient beings whatsoever can obstruct or hinder it so as to prevent it from arising.
If a phenomenon follows the mind in succession, can it be said to be immediate (*anantara*) to that mind?
Regarding this, there are four possibilities (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The first possibility consists of the mind emerging from a mindless meditative attainment (*acittaka-samāpatti*), as well as the moments of the second *samāpatti* and so forth.
The second phrase refers to the first moment of the *samāpatti*, as well as the subsequent mental states and [factors] such as birth (*jāti*).
The third phrase refers to the first moment of the *samāpatti* and the states possessing mind (*sacittaka*).

Regarding the fourth phrase: [it refers to] the second moment of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and so forth, as well as birth and so forth, in relation to the mind emerging from meditative attainment.
If a phenomenon is sequential to the mind, is it also sequential to the meditative attainment?
In this context there are four propositions.
The former third and fourth propositions are identical to the first and second propositions here;
the former first and second propositions are identical to the third and fourth propositions here.

When the mind emerges from the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is an extremely long interval of time during which the preceding mind has been severed; how, then, can it be said that the present mind arises in immediate succession (*anantara*) from that preceding mind?
It is because there is no intervening consciousness to separate them.
Having explained the condition as immediate antecedent (*samanantara-pratyaya*),
what is the characteristic of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
The verse says:
"Object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) refers to all dharmas.
The commentary states:
"All dharmas consist of the five aggregates; herein, one should understand the characteristics of the object-condition as they appropriately apply."

For example, visual consciousness and its associated mental factors take visible form as their object; likewise, auditory consciousness takes sound, olfactory consciousness takes fragrance, gustatory consciousness takes flavor, tactile consciousness takes tangibles, and mental consciousness takes all phenomena as its objects.
If a phenomenon is the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) for another phenomenon, there is no time when it is not that phenomenon's object-condition.
Even if it is not [currently] being taken as an object, it remains an object-condition, because its essential nature (svabhāva) and characteristic (lakṣaṇa) are one and the same.
For example, fuel is called "fuel" even when it is not currently burning, because its essential nature and characteristics remain one and the same.

Regarding the mind and mental factors, which enter into an object through concentration for a single moment and are fixed upon their respective objects of perception: is this fixation due to the stability of the support (the body), or is it independent of such stability?
When that concentration has arisen, it is necessarily associated with its basis; when it has not yet arisen or has already passed away, it is dissociated from its basis.
Other masters say:
even when past, it is established as being based upon its basis.
Having explained the object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya),
the verse says:
"The efficient condition (adhipati-pratyaya) follows from the creative condition (kāraṇa-hetu)."
The commentary states:
Since the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) is identical to the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the dominant condition is therefore the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*). Why is this so?
Because all phenomena are conditions by way of being objects (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
Of these two conditions, which one is more extensive?
It is impossible for co-existent phenomena (*sahabhū-dharma*) to function as a condition by way of being an object.
There is such a possibility; because it can function as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), the dominant condition is extensive.
It is called "dominant" because its scope as a condition is broad.
With respect to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), excluding their own nature (*svabhāva*), everything serves as a dominant condition.
Is there a phenomenon that constitutes a condition for another phenomenon by way of the four conditions?
Yes; namely, when a self-nature is a condition for itself, an other-nature for another-nature, the unconditioned for the conditioned, and the unconditioned for the unconditioned.
If these four conditions exercise their functional efficacy, in what state of phenomena do they exercise it?
Regarding the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), five types have already been explained.
The verse says:
It exercises its functional efficacy upon the two causes at the moment they are in the process of ceasing.
The commentary states:
"In the process of ceasing" refers to dharmas of the present.
Why is this? Because the dharmas of the present have already arisen and are now tending toward cessation.
Within this stage, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*) and the associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*) exercise their functional efficacy.
Why is this? Because this cause possesses efficacy with respect to its co-nascent fruit.
The verse says:
The three causes [operate] with respect to that which is presently arising.
The commentary states:
"Presently arising" refers to future dharmas.
Why is this? Because future dharmas have not yet arisen, but are now tending toward arising.
Within this stage, the similar-cause (sabhāga-hetu), the pervasive-cause (sarvatraga-hetu), and the retributive-cause (vipāka-hetu) exercise their functional efficacy.
The functional capacity of causes and conditions is thus.
The verse says:
Regarding the two conditions, their functional capacities are the reverse of those mentioned above.
The commentary states:
By way of the principle of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*), the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is divided into two.
One should understand that the reversal of this functional capacity constitutes the positions of the sequential condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) exerts its function upon that which is in the process of arising, because it provides the state for that [arising].

The object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) exerts its function upon that which is in the process of ceasing, because it is that which is apprehended by the mind and mental factors of the present moment.
The dominant condition (adhipati-pratyaya) functions as a condition in all stages by virtue of its non-obstruction; this is precisely its function.
Having explained the conditions and their functions, what next is the "dharma"?
By how many conditions do they arise?
The verse says:
Mental factors arise by way of four conditions.
The commentary states:
Regarding the causes and conditions for this mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*), there are five types of causes.
As for the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), it consists of the preceding moments of mind and mental factors, uninterrupted by any other moments of mind or mental factors.
The object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) consists of the five sense objects, such as visible forms, as appropriate, and all phenomena.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) consists of all other phenomena excluding its own nature.
The verse says:
The two attainments arise from three conditions.
The commentary states:
the attainment of cessation and the attainment of non-conception lack objective conditions (*ālambana*), because these two attainments do not arise by taking an object as their support.
Regarding the causal conditions herein, there are two causes: namely, the coexistent cause, which refers to [the factors] such as birth;
and the homogeneous cause, which refers to previously arisen wholesome dharmas of the same stage.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to the mind of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) together with its associated mental factors (*saṃprayukta-dharma*).
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) is as previously described.
Since these two types of meditative absorption arise through the functional activity of the mind, the mind serves as their immediately preceding condition.
Because they can obstruct the arising of the mind, external factors are not equivalent conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).
The verse states:
"Other dharmas arise from two [conditions]."
The commentary states:

"Other dharmas" refers to those dharmas dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) and those possessing form (*rūpin*). These arise through the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
All conditioned dharmas that possess birth arise from the six causes and four conditions established as previously described.
The entire world does not have a single cause such as a self, a supreme being, or a primal nature.
What evidence is there for this? If you maintain that all established things are produced by causes and conditions, [then how can a single cause account for them]?
Is it not so? By holding this view, you contradict and abandon your original position, namely, that a single Īśvara and so forth are the cause of the entire world.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because it is not the sequence of the Sovereign (Īśvara).
The commentary explains:
The world does not arise from a creator god (Īśvara) or similar causes, because it arises sequentially.
If you maintain that a single Īśvara is the cause of the arising of the entire world, or if you maintain any other such cause, then the entire world ought to arise all at once.
The sequential arising of all things is clearly perceptible.

If you maintain that this sequence is established according to the will of Īśvara, then let it be: "May this dharma arise now; may this dharma cease now; may this dharma arise or cease later. Since there would be a difference in his will, this [sequence] could be established—namely, that the cause is not one because the will differs. However, [if the cause were one], they should all arise simultaneously.
Desire has sovereignty because it is not distinct [from itself].
If its establishment were due to the differentiation of other causes, then desire would not be the cause; rather, it would be the sequence of arising within that [process].
If one examines distinct causes, there is the fault of infinite regress;
if one does not examine distinct causes, there is no sense of sequential order.

These successive causes have boundless variations, yet because this person believes in a beginningless [process], their fondness for clinging to Īśvara as the cause does not exceed the principles revealed by the disciples of Śākyamuni.
If you say:
"Although the desires of Īśvara arise simultaneously, the world does not arise simultaneously because it arises in accordance with [his] will," this argument is incorrect;
for there would be no basis for such a desire of Īśvara in a future existence.
If the world is produced through such great effort and transformation, what benefit does the Īśvara obtain?
If you say that his function is constant joy and pleasure:
This argument is not tenable, because this pleasure cannot be obtained unless one possesses mastery over the means [for its attainment].
One lacks mastery over pleasure, and the same applies to other things as well.
Furthermore, if the Lord [Īśvara] were to experience joy because he sees that the world, including the hells and other realms, is for the most part oppressed by wrongful suffering—alas!
how lamentable!
Of what use is this crude and wicked Īśvara?
If one relies upon the god Īśvara, then the world (*loka*) would become a *sugata*.
"Because he can burn, is sharp and fierce, Is terrifying, and constantly afflicts others,"
"Delighting in the consumption of flesh, blood, and marrow, you cause [others] to weep while you chant 'dharmāḥ'.
If you accept that independent factors such as Īśvara are the sole cause of the world, then any other factor that is observed to have human effort as its cause is abandoned.
If you conceptually cling to the idea that Īśvara, together with other causes,
acts as a cause, this clinging is spoken of merely for the sake of affection and reverence. Why is that?
Because an autonomous capacity cannot be perceived apart from various causes;
since all causes must combine with other causes to exercise autonomy, if that were so, they would not be autonomous.
Furthermore, if the initial creation were caused by Īśvara, then because this [creation] does not depend on any other cause, it would follow that, like Īśvara himself, it has no beginning.
The same applies to the establishment and refutation regarding the self (*ātman*) and the supreme nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, there is no such thing as a single cause for the world.
This is karma created by oneself, which, through the path and its manifold conditions, is able to produce the world.

It is truly lamentable that those who do not study wisdom experience their own retributive fruits and their own fruits of efficacy, yet give rise to false discrimination, claiming that a creator god (*īśvara*) or other such entities are the cause.
This point has already been addressed.
Previously it was stated that "other dharmas arise from two [causes]"; what does this statement mean?
It means that for the great elements (mahābhūta), the great elements serve as their cause-condition (hetu-pratyaya).
The verse says:
"The two kinds are the great causes.
The commentary says:

If the four great elements (mahābhūta) are established as causes for the four great elements, there are two kinds of causes: namely, the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) and the co-existent cause (sahabhū-hetu).
The verse says:
"Regarding the five types of derived matter (upādāya-rūpa)."
The commentary states:
If the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), they constitute five kinds of causes.
How are they so constituted?

First, because it can produce; second, because it can serve as a basis; third, because it can sustain; fourth, because it causes [the result] to abide; and fifth, because it causes [the result] to increase.
This is the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), which is divided into five types according to these meanings: first, the producing cause, because [the result] arises from this;
second, the basis cause, because once produced, [the result] follows along with this.
Third is the cause of support (*dhṛti-hetu*), because it supports that which is supported, like a painting and its wall;
fourth is the cause of abiding (*sthiti-hetu*), because it causes that [which is supported] to continue without interruption;
fifth is the cause of growth (*vṛddhi-hetu*), because it causes that [which is supported] to reach fulfillment.
Thus, these four great elements serve as the causes for the arising, transformation, support, maintenance, and growth of derived matter; in this way, five meanings are made manifest.
The verse says:
Derived matter [arises] from three types of mutual [causes].
The commentary states:

If derived matter produces derived matter, it does so by way of three kinds of causes, namely: the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*), and the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*).
Because they arise equally as concomitant causes (*kāraṇa-hetu*), they are not always counted [separately].

Herein, regarding the mutual cause (*anyonya-hetu*) among the co-existent factors: it refers to the two types of action—body and speech—which transform according to the mind, and not to other derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
As for the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu), all preceding [dharmas] are [the cause] of subsequent homogeneous [dharmas].
As for the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu), if there are the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—they induce the sense organs such as the eye as their retribution.
The verse says:
"The great cause of the derived [elements] is one.
The commentary says:
If derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) takes the four great elements (mahābhūta) as its cause, it has only one type of cause, namely, the retributive cause (vipāka-hetu).

It has already been stated in general that bodily and vocal karma take the four great elements as their retribution; however, regarding the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta), they act as the equal-and-immediate condition (samanantara-pratyaya). It has not yet been specified which particular mind acts as the equal-and-immediate condition.
Which minds arise from the condition of immediate succession?
This meaning shall now be explained.
Herein, if stated briefly, there are twelve types of mind.
What are the twelve?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, there are wholesome, unwholesome, obscured, and unobscured minds.
The commentary states:
Within the desire realm, there are four types of mind, namely: wholesome, unwholesome, obscured-neutral, and unobscured-neutral.
The verse says:
"In the two realms, excluding the unwholesome, there is the remainder.
The commentary explains:
In the form realm (rūpadhātu), there is no unwholesomeness; there is the remainder of the other three [kinds of action].
The same applies to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Thus, these ten types of mind are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).
The verse says:
"Two are outflow-free.
The commentary states:
namely, the outflow-free of those in training (śaikṣa) and the outflow-free of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Thus, these minds together constitute twelve. Regarding this, the verse says:
"In the desire realm, nine [minds] arise from the wholesome.
The commentary explains:
Regarding the statement on "succession," it should be explained last.

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all wholesome minds (*kuśalacitta*) arise in succession from nine minds: four minds of its own level (*svabhūmi*), and two minds each from the form (*rūpadhātu*) and formless (*ārūpyadhātu*) realms.

If one is correctly entering meditative absorption, it is a wholesome mind; if one is taking rebirth, it is an obscured-unspecified mind. In the formless realm, there is only the obscured-unspecified mind; because the moment of taking rebirth is the furthest [from the wholesome], there is no wholesome mind there.

The formless realm is the most distant from the desire realm by way of four types of distance: namely, distance of support (*āśraya*), distance of grasping signs (*nimitta*), distance of object (*viṣaya*), and distance of antidote (*pratipakṣa*).
Furthermore, regarding the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the verse says:
"This wholesome [mind] arises from eight."
The commentary states:
Furthermore, this wholesome mind of the desire realm arises in succession from eight minds: the four minds of its own level and the two wholesome minds of the form realm.
This refers to the obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) at the time of emerging from meditative absorption;
that is, being pressured by a defiled state of absorption, one returns to rely upon a wholesome mind of a lower stage.
It also refers to the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) at the time of emerging from contemplation.
The verse says:
"It arises from the ten unwholesome minds.
The commentary says:
Excluding the minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa). Why is this?

If a person takes rebirth in the desire realm (kāmadhātu), an unwholesome mind can arise immediately after any mind belonging to the desire realm, the form realm (rūpadhātu), or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
The verse says:
From this, four.
The commentary says:
From an unwholesome mind of the desire realm, only four minds of its own level arise in immediate succession.
As it was said regarding the unwholesome mind in the desire realm, the verse states:
"The same applies to the obscured [neutral mind]."
The commentary states:
The obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm also arises in succession from ten minds of the three realms.
From the obscured-unspecified mind of the desire realm, only the four minds of its own level arise in succession.
The verse says:
From the five non-obscured minds.
The commentary says:

Regarding all non-obscured neutral minds (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they arise in succession from five types of mind: the four minds of its own level and the wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), namely, the transformative mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) produced when one is born in the desire realm.
The verse says:
Furthermore, from these seven minds.
The commentary says:

From an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm, seven minds arise in succession: four minds of its own level, two minds of the form realm, and the wholesome mind—namely, the defiled mind that arises in succession from a mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) at the time of taking rebirth.
The defiled mind of the formless realm refers to the moment of rebirth.
The verse says:
From the wholesome [mind] of the form realm, eleven [minds arise].
The commentary states:

From any wholesome mind belonging to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), eleven minds arise in immediate succession, excluding the non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The verse says:
"From nine, these are further produced.
The commentary states:

A wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) arises immediately after nine minds, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the non-obscured neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The verse says:
"It arises from the eight obscured [minds].
The commentary says:

The obscured-unspecified mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the form realm arises in immediate succession from eight minds, excluding the two defiled minds of the desire realm and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The verse says:
"These six."
The commentary states:

From a defiled-neutral mind (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), six minds arise in succession: three minds of its own level and three minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the undefiled-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The verse says:
Three are non-obscured.
The commentary says:
The unobscured-neutral mind of the form realm arises in succession only from three minds of its own level.
The verse says:
"These six."
The commentary states:

From an unobscured-neutral mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), six minds arise in immediate succession: three minds of its own level, two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and one defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
As it was stated regarding the unobscured-neutral mind in the form realm, the same principle applies to the formless realm.
The verse says:
"The principle for the formless is likewise."
The commentary states:
The unobscured-neutral mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) also arises in succession from only three minds within its own level.
From these six minds, there arise in succession three minds of its own level and three defiled minds of the lower levels.
The verse says:
"From the wholesome, nine.
The commentary says:

From a wholesome mind of the formless realm, nine minds arise in immediate succession; with the exception of the wholesome mind of the desire realm and the non-obscured neutral minds of the desire and form realms, all remaining minds may arise.
The verse says:
"This arises from six.
The commentary says:

A wholesome mind of the formless realm arises in immediate succession from six minds: the three minds of its own level, the wholesome mind of the form realm, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The verse says:
"The obscured [mind] arises from seven."
The commentary states:

From a mind that is obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), seven minds arise in succession: three minds of its own level, the wholesome mind and the defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and two defiled minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The verse says:
"This is so. The commentary says:

This obscured-unspecified mind of the formless realm arises in succession from seven minds—excluding the defiled minds of the desire and form realms, as well as the minds of those in training and those beyond training—and arises from all remaining minds.
The verse says:
From these four, there is the learner (*śaikṣa*).
The commentary says:
This mind of one in training (śaikṣa) arises in immediate succession from four minds: the wholesome minds of the three realms and the mind of one in training.
The verse says:
From this, five arise.
The commentary states:
From this mind of one in training (śaikṣa), five minds arise in succession, namely the four preceding ones and the mind of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The verse says:
The mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) also arises from five.
The commentary states:
this mind of one beyond training arises in succession from the five minds previously described.
The verse says:
"From the four minds of one beyond training.
The commentary says:
From the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*), four minds arise in immediate succession: the wholesome minds of the three realms and the mind of one beyond training.
Having thus explained the twelve minds, a verse is now composed:
"The twelve become twenty."
The commentary says:
How is it performed?
The verse states:
"Preparatory and innate; the wholesome [minds] of the three realms are divided into two.
The commentary states:

Within the three realms, each wholesome mind is further divided into two types of minds: first, that acquired through preparatory effort (*prāyogika*), and second, that acquired by birth (*upapattilābhika*).
The verse says:
Retribution, deportment, craftsmanship, and transformation—these four types of neutral [states] exist in the desire realm.
The commentary says:

The unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) of the desire realm is divided into four types: first, the mind born of retribution (*vipākaja-citta*); second, the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika-citta*); third, the mind of the arts and crafts (*śailpasthānika-citta*); and fourth, the mind of transformation (*nairmāṇika-citta*).
The verse says:
In the realm of form, the artistry [knowledge] is excluded.
The commentary says:

Within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the unobscured-neutral mind (*anivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*) is divided into three types, excluding the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika-citta*), because craftsmanship does not exist there.
Thus, these twelve minds are further divided into twenty minds:
six wholesome minds (*kuśala*) and eight unobscured-neutral minds.
The mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*) and others do not exist within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), because there are no objects such as deportment there.

The four sensory objects—visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects—are the spheres of these three minds; the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*) also takes sound as its object. These four minds are exclusively mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); as for the five sensory consciousnesses, they are also induced by the mind of application (*prayogacitta*) in the spheres of deportment and craftsmanship.
Other masters say:
there is a mental consciousness induced by deportment (*airyāpathika*) that takes the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as its object.
Among these twenty types of mind, which mind serves as the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*)?
From which minds do they arise in succession?
From the eight minds of the desire realm, ten minds arise in succession from the mind of application (*prayoga-citta*).
Within its own level, seven minds arise, excluding the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*).

The preparatory mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-prayoga-citta*), as well as the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), arise in succession from eight types of minds: from the wholesome and defiled minds of its own level; from the defiled minds of the preparatory stage of the form realm; and from the minds of those in training and those beyond training.
From the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-citta*), nine minds arise in succession: seven minds of its own level, excluding the fruition-of-communication mind (*abhiññā-phala-citta*);

the defiled minds of the form and formless realms; and this mind arises in succession from eleven minds: from the seven minds of its own level as previously stated, and from the preparatory mind of the form realm, the defiled minds [of the form and formless realms], and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

From an unwholesome mind (*akuśala-citta*) and a mind obscured by defilements (*nivṛtāvyākṛta-citta*), seven minds arise in immediate succession; that is to say, the minds of their own level (*svabhūmi*) as previously stated.

These two types of mind arise in succession from fourteen minds: the seven minds of their own level, and four minds of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), excluding the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) and the mind resulting from supernormal powers (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
Regarding the three minds of the formless realm, excluding the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*):

from the deportment mind (*airyāpathika-citta*) and the resultant mind (*vipāka-citta*), eight minds arise in succession—namely, the six minds of their own level, excluding the preparatory mind and the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*).
Regarding the two defiled minds of the form and formless realms, these two minds arise in succession from seven minds—namely, the seven minds of their own respective levels as previously stated.

From the mind of craftsmanship (*śailpasthānika*), six minds arise in succession—namely, the six minds of their own level, excluding the mind of application (*prāyogika*) and the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala*). This [mind of craftsmanship] arises in succession from seven minds—namely, the seven minds of its own level, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition.

From the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇacitta*), two minds arise in immediate succession: namely, the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*) of its own stage and the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). This mind also arises in immediate succession from two minds, which are precisely those two aforementioned minds.
Now, we shall explain the sequence of the six minds with reference to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

From the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*) of the form realm, twelve minds arise in succession: two from the desire realm—the wholesome mind and the mind of supernormal power (*abhijñā-phala-citta*); six minds of its own level; the preparatory mind of the formless realm; and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This mind arises in succession from ten minds: the preparatory mind and the supernormal fruit mind of the desire realm; four minds of its own level—excluding the functional mind of deportment and the resultant mind; the preparatory mind of the formless realm; and the defiled mind.

The minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), arising from a mind acquired at birth, give rise in succession to eight minds: two from the desire realm, five minds of their own level excluding the mind of supernormal fruition (abhijñā-phala-citta), and the defiled mind of the formless realm.
This mind arises in succession from five minds, namely the five minds of its own level, excluding the fruition-of-communication mind.

From a defiled mind, nine minds arise in succession: four minds of the desire realm (the wholesome mind and the defiled mind), and the five minds of its own level, excluding the fruition-of-communication mind.

This mind arises in succession from eleven minds: the acquired minds of the desire realm, the functional minds of deportment, the resultant minds, and the five minds of its own plane, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition.
Regarding the three minds of the formless realm, excluding the preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*):

from a mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*), seven minds arise in succession—namely, two defiled minds of the desire realm, four minds of its own level (excluding the preparatory mind), the mind of supernormal fruition (*abhijñā-phala-citta*), and the defiled mind of the formless realm. This [formless] mind arises in succession from five minds: the five minds of its own level, excluding the mind of supernormal fruition.
The fruition-result mind is also like this.

From the fruition-result mind, two minds arise in succession: namely, the preparatory mind of its own stage and the fruition-result mind itself; this mind also arises in succession from two minds, as previously stated.
Now, the sequence of the four types of consciousness shall be explained in relation to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

From the preparatory consciousness (*prayogika-citta*) of the formless realm, seven types of consciousness arise in succession: the preparatory consciousness of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), the four types of consciousness of its own level, and the consciousnesses of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

This mind arises in succession from six minds: the preparatory mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-prāyogika-citta*), three minds of its own level—excluding the resultant mind (*vipākaja-citta*)—and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
From a mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*), seven minds arise in succession: the four minds of its own level and the defiled minds of the lower levels.
This mind, in turn, arises in succession from four minds, namely, the four minds of its own level.

From a defiled mind, eight minds arise in immediate succession: four minds of its own level, the preparatory mind and the defiled mind of the form realm, and the two defiled minds of the desire realm.
This mind arises in succession from ten minds: the four minds of its own level, and the acquired, functional, and retributive minds of the desire and form realms.
From a retributive mind, six minds arise in succession: three minds of its own level—excluding the preparatory mind—and the defiled minds of the lower levels.
This mind arises in succession from four minds, namely the four minds of its own level.

From a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*), six minds arise in succession: the preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*) of the three realms, the acquired minds (*upapatti-lābhika-citta*) of the desire realm, and the minds of those in training and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
This mind arises in succession from four minds: the preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*) of the three realms and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa-citta*).
From the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*), five minds arise in succession, just as with the five minds of one in training, except for the mind of one in training itself.

This mind arises in succession from five types of minds: the preparatory minds (*prayoga-citta*) of the three realms, and the minds of those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

Furthermore, for what reason do the retributive (*vipāka*), deportment (*airyāpathika*), and craft (*śailpasthānika*) minds arise in succession from the preparatory mind, while these [latter] minds do not arise from them?
Because the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*) is able to induce deportment (*iryāpatha*) and craftsmanship (*śilpa*),
whereas a weak mental continuum cannot induce such preparatory application, it therefore does not follow the mind of preparatory application.
The mind emerging from meditative observation does not arise through effort; this may be so in the case of its arising after a preparatory mind (*prayoga-citta*).
If that were the case, however, a preparatory mind should not be able to arise from a defiled mind, because the latter lacks such qualities.
Nevertheless, because if a person becomes utterly weary, or if the mind of preparatory application (*prayoga-citta*) is forced upon them, it can cause [the defiled state] to cease;
therefore, after a defiled mind, a mind of preparatory application may arise. This is because the mind acquired at birth (*upapatti-labdha*) in the desire realm is characterized by clarity.

The minds of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), as well as the preparatory minds (prayoga-citta) of the form realm (rūpadhātu), can arise in succession [from the desire realm mind]; however, because they do not arise through effort, those [desire realm] minds cannot arise from them.
From a defiled mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), a mind acquired at birth (*upapattilābhika*) of the desire realm can arise, because it is clear.
From a defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), a mind acquired at birth of the form realm cannot arise, because it is not clear.
There are three kinds of contemplation (*manasikāra*):

first, contemplation of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-manasikāra*). For example, form has transformation and decay as its characteristic, up to consciousness having discernment as its characteristic; such instances are called contemplation of specific characteristics.
Second is contemplation of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), which refers to contemplation associated with the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths.

Third is contemplation of specific desires (*chanda-ruci*), which refers to contemplations such as the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

From the three types of contemplation (*vitarka*), one can successively give rise to the Noble Path (*āryamārga*) so that it becomes manifest; likewise, from the Noble Path, one gives rise to contemplation.

If this is so, these statements are consistent and not contradictory: namely, when a practitioner cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness (*smṛti-saṃbodhyaṅga*), it is associated with the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Other masters say:
The manifestation of general mental attention (*sāmānyamanasikāra*) is itself the noble path (*āryamārga*), and from this, the three types of mental attention arise in succession.
If a person has already subdued the mind through the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), the noble path arises in succession from general mental attention.

This statement is made based on the successive transmission of this tradition: that one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness in conjunction with the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Other masters say:
following the sequence of the Noble Path, there arises only the general mental application (*sāmānya-manaskāra*).

This principle may also apply: if one enters the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*) based on the three stages beginning with the *anāgamya*, the universal mental application (*mārga-sāmānya-manasikāra*) of the desire realm arises sequentially from the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) of those three stages; likewise, if one enters the stage of right determination based on the second dhyāna and so forth.
What is the meaning of this? Why is that?
Because the mind of this desire realm is incapable of responding to this path, as its level is too far removed.

The pervasive mental application (vitarka-vicāra) of the desire realm is not obtained in the stage of the second dhyāna, except for the capacity of the stages leading to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya).
Furthermore, it is impossible for a noble one (ārya) to again give rise to the capacity of the stages leading to penetration so as to bring it into manifestation.

Why is this? If a person has already attained the fruit, it would be inconsistent with reason to further cause the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) or the stage directed toward the fruit (*phalābhimukha*) to manifest.
If that is so, how then is this statement to be understood as consistent?

There is another general mental contemplation (*saṃjñā-manasikāra*) that is of the same category as those [previously mentioned], which is cultivated after the Noble Eightfold Path; namely, the contemplation that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent," "all phenomena are selfless," and "nirvāṇa is tranquility. One must certainly cause this to manifest before one.
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not maintain this position.

If a person attains the fruit of arhatship by relying on the stage of *anāgamya* (the threshold concentration), their subsequent mind emerging from meditative absorption may take either *anāgamya* as its basis or the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as its basis.

If one attains the fruit of arhatship based on the sphere of nothingness as the ground, the mind that emerges from meditative absorption may take either the sphere of nothingness or the peak of existence as its ground.
Upon emerging from meditative absorption in the remaining stages, one relies solely upon the stage itself.

Within the desire realm, there are three types of reflection: first, reflection based on the wisdom of hearing; second, reflection based on the wisdom of contemplation; and third, reflection based on innate wisdom.

In the realm of form (rūpadhātu), there are likewise three kinds of reflection—namely, those acquired through hearing (śrutamaya), cultivation (bhāvanāmaya), and birth (upapattilābhika)—but there is no wisdom consisting of reflection (cintāmayī prajñā). Why is this?
Because if a person there applies effortful reflection, they immediately enter meditative absorption (samādhi).
In the formless realm, there are two kinds of contemplation: that acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*) and that acquired through birth (*upapatti-labdha*).

Among these, one attains the noble path (*ārya-mārga*) from five types of contemplation, which arise in succession and cause it to manifest; the three types acquired through birth are excluded because the noble path belongs to the category of preparatory application (*prayoga*).
From the noble path, only those minds that arise in immediate succession are acquired; these are the "acquired-through-birth" minds of the desire realm, because they are clear and distinct.
Among the twelve types of mind previously mentioned, which of them manifest?
How many minds should one obtain?
The verse says:
Within the defiled minds of the three realms, one obtains six, six, and two minds respectively.
The commentary states:

When a defiled mind of the desire realm arises and manifests, one should obtain six minds, because although they were previously non-associated with those six minds, they are subsequently obtained again.

Having previously become separated from the wholesome mind of the desire realm, because one reconnects with the wholesome roots through doubt and because one falls back to the lower realm, one again acquires unwholesome minds and obscured-unspecified minds.
Furthermore, one acquires a defiled mind of the form realm due to falling back;

again, due to falling from meditative absorption, one acquires a defiled mind of the formless realm; and again, due to falling from meditative absorption, one acquires a mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
When a defiled mind of the form realm arises and manifests, one also acquires six minds: one acquires three minds of the form realm, as well as an unobscured-neutral mind of the desire realm.
Because of falling back to a lower realm, one acquires the defiled mind of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and the mind of one in training (*śaikṣa*).
Because of falling away from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), when the defiled mind of the formless realm arises and manifests, one acquires two minds.
Due to falling away from meditative absorption, one acquires a defiled mind and a mind of one in training (śaikṣa).
The verse says:
"In the realm of form, there are three wholesome [minds]."
The commentary states:

When a wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) arises and manifests, three minds are acquired: one acquires the wholesome mind of its own level, as well as the unobscured-unspecified (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*) minds of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm.
The verse says:
"Four for those in training.
The commentary says:
