"If you establish the thesis that sentient beings pass from one world to another, then our original position is proven—namely, that a real self exists."
Now this argument is refuted.
The verse says:
There is no self.
The commentary says:
What are the characteristics of this self?
It is that which can abandon these aggregates and take up those aggregates.
As it is conceptually constructed, this self does not truly exist—that is, an internal agent or person.
Why? Because it is not an object of the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the sense-object of form and the eye-faculty, etc.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has also said: "There is karma and there is its retribution, but an agent cannot be found.
Because such an agent does not exist, it cannot be spoken of.
This 'I' which abandons these aggregates and takes up those aggregates exists only as a conventional designation apart from dharmas."
In this context, the "designation of phenomena" refers to the detailed exposition of the twelvefold dependent origination: "When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises.
What, then, are the characteristics of this self?
That is to say, it is not that which is to be refuted.
The verse says:
"Only the aggregates."
The commentary states:
If it is merely a conventional designation that the aggregates (*skandha*) alone are called "self," then this self is not what is being refuted.
If that were so, then when the aggregates pass from this world to another world, the logical consequence would be that the aggregates themselves do not transmigrate to another world.
What are these aggregates?
The verse says:
Arising from afflictions and karma, through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), they enter the mother’s womb like a lamp.
The commentary states:
The aggregates (*skandha*) perish moment by moment; they lack the capacity for transition because they are comprised of afflictions (*kleśa*) and transformed by karma.
There are only the aggregates that, through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), proceed and enter the mother’s womb.
For example, although a lamp is extinguished moment by moment, it reaches another location through its continuity; the aggregates (*skandha*) are likewise.

Therefore, there is no logical error. In reality, there is no self (*ātman*); rather, it is established that the continuity of the aggregates, impelled by afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, enters the mother’s womb. This principle is thus proven.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Six.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Seven.
Composed by Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
Commentary on the *Madhyāntavibhāga*, Chapter Two: Analysis of the World. Furthermore, the verse says:
"Just as [a body] grows gradually through successive stages, so too does the continuity [of existence], driven by afflictions and karma, enter again into another world."
The commentary states:

Because there are differences in the karma that induces the lifespan, all the aggregates (*skandha*) are drawn forth in an unequal succession; this succession increases according to the force of what draws it forth, following such a sequence.
What is the sequence?
As the verse says:
"The first is named kalala; next, arbuda is produced."
From this, pesī is produced; from pesī, ghana is produced;
from ghana, peśī (the flesh) is produced, along with hair, body hair, nails, and so forth, as well as the various material sense faculties, such that the parts of the body are produced in succession.
These five stages are all within the womb, namely: kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā.
This fetal thorn grows through the succession of stages until it reaches maturity.

Within the mother’s womb, driven by winds born of karmic retribution, these winds turn the fetal thorn and position it toward the opening of the mother’s body. This fetus is like a mass of potent excrement, excessive and unbearable.
Next, when one falls from this state, at that time the two types of suffering are beyond all analogy.
Furthermore, sometimes due to the mother’s excessive indulgence in food, drink, postures, or manual labor, or due to the faults of past karma, the fetus dies within the womb.

At that time, there were women skilled in expedient means and physicians who understood how to care for infants. They first warmed ghee and the smooth juices of *śyāmāka* grain and used them to coat their hands. Holding small, sharp blades in their hands, they entered the womb—which is like a pit of excrement, a vessel of extreme stench, darkness, and impurity; a dwelling place for immeasurable thousands of types of worms where foul fluids constantly flow and require perpetual treatment; defiled by filth, blood, grime, grease, mucus, and fluids; soaked, rotted, stinking, and slippery; loathsome and hideous to behold; covered only by a thin, leaking skin; and a great wound upon the body produced by past karma—and inserted their hands within it to cut and sever the fetus piece by piece and pull it out.
This child within the womb is led by the ripening of past karma toward another realm of existence, its destination being difficult to discern.
Furthermore, if birth occurs without difficulty, at that time either the mother or another woman will be able to attend to the child.
This child’s body is like a fresh sore; touching it is as if one were struck by a weapon or harsh lye.

Out of love for the child’s body, he washes and wipes it, then gives it a mouthful of clarified butter and feeds it breast milk. Gradually, he provides fine and coarse foods to allow the child to become accustomed to them; thus, this child grows through these successive stages.
Due to the maturation of the faculties, various afflictions arise again; various karmas are further produced and further increased.
Because of these afflictions and karmas, after the abandonment of life, one enters another world once more through the continuity of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), as previously described.
The verse says:
Therefore, the wheel of existence has no beginning.
The commentary says:

By this principle, birth has afflictions and karma as its cause; afflictions and karma have birth as their cause; and birth, in turn, has afflictions and karma as its cause. In this way, one should understand that the wheel of saṃsāra has no beginning.
Why is this? If one discriminatively clings to the existence of a beginning, then this beginning would have to be established without a cause.
If the beginning were truly without a cause, then everything else would likewise arise spontaneously, and all things would be without a cause.

We observe this directly: seeds and other such things possess functional capacities within sprouts and the like, because their location and timing are fixed; the same applies to causes such as fire regarding effects such as ripening. Therefore, there is no arising without a cause.
The assertion that an eternal entity serves as the cause has already been refuted; therefore, saṃsāra is necessarily without beginning.
While it may be possible for this saṃsāra to have an end through the exhaustion of its causes, this is because birth is dependent upon those causes.
For example, just as a sprout belongs to its seed and ceases when the seed perishes,
so too is this described as the continuity of the aggregates (*skandha-saṃtāna*), with three births constituting its stages.
The verse says:
Regarding these dependently originated phenomena, they consist of twelve factors divided into three sections.
The commentary states:

Among these twelve factors, they are: (1) ignorance, (2) volitional formations, (3) consciousness, (4) name-and-form, (5) the six sense bases, (6) contact, (7) feeling, (8) craving, (9) clinging, (10) existence, (11) birth, and (12) aging and death.
Regarding the three periods: first, the prior limit; second, the posterior limit; and third, the middle limit—namely, the past, the future, and the present.
How are the twelve factors established within these three periods?
The verse says:
Two each at the prior and posterior limits, and eight in the middle.
The commentary says:
Ignorance and formations belong to the prior limit; birth, old age, and death belong to the posterior limit; the remaining eight factors belong to the intermediate limit.
Do all sentient beings possess these eight factors in their entirety during this lifetime?
Answer: No.
If that is so, which sentient beings possess all eight?
The verse says:
"Possessing birth.
The commentary says:

If sentient beings experience all stages [of existence], they are said to be "fully born" (upapanna); this does not refer to those who die in the intermediate state (antarābhava), nor to those who take birth in the form or formless realms. Why is this?
In the *Mahānidāna-sūtra*, this is explained solely with reference to sentient beings of the desire realm.
The sutra says:
"Ānanda!"
"If consciousness were not to rely upon the red and white elements in the mother's womb, would it be able to undergo transformation and become the *kalala*? It could not,
World-Honored One."
The detailed explanation is as set forth in the sūtra.
At times it is said that dependent origination is of two kinds: that which is subsumed under the prior limit and that which is subsumed under the subsequent limit.

Within this, seven members are designated as the prior limit (*pūrvānta*), namely from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to feeling (*vedanā*); the remaining five members are designated as the posterior limit (*aparānta*), because the causes and effects of the prior and posterior limits are combined into these two divisions.
What phenomena are designated as "ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth?
The verse states:
Ignorance is the state of past afflictions.
The commentary states:

Regarding all stages of the afflictions in past lives, they are termed "ignorance" (avidyā) in the present because they function in conjunction with ignorance and because the remaining [afflictions] arise through the power of ignorance.
For example, when describing the king’s journey, the journey of his attendants is also called the king’s journey.
The verse says:
"And past karma is also called 'volitional formations' (*saṃskāra*)."
The commentary states:
The term "state" (*avasthā*) refers to a sequential flow.
That which was the state of karma—such as merit—in a previous life is called "formations" (*saṃskāra*) in the present; if it exists now, it is the maturation (*vipāka*) of that [past karma].
The verse says:
"That which appropriates the aggregates at birth is called consciousness.
The commentary says:
At the very first moment of conception within the mother’s womb, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are termed consciousness (vijñāna).
The verse says:
"Thereafter, it is called name-and-form (nāmarūpa), which arises prior to the six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana)."
The commentary states:
From the moment of the mind of rebirth until the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have not yet arisen, this stage is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).
One should say that the four sense bases arise first; why then speak of "six"?
Sixth, because entry is established according to this measure, at which time the four modes of birth and the six perfections [of the faculties] are present.
The verse says:
"This is preceded by the triad of conjunctions."
The commentary says:

When the six sense bases have already arisen, this stage is called the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*), up until the point when the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness has not yet come together.
The verse says:
"Contact [precedes] pleasure, pain, and equanimity; it is the wisdom that can discern their causes.
The commentary states:
"Contact is defined by the conjunction of the three."
As long as this person has not yet been able to discern the differences between the causes of the three types of sensation, this stage is called "contact" (sparśa).
Once they have become able to discern the causes of the three types of sensation, the verse says:
"Sensation is preceded by the craving for sexual desire."
The commentary states:
That which "possesses the state" has as its essence the discernment of the causes of the three types of sensation, up until the point when sensual desire has not yet arisen.
The verse says:
"Craving for the means of sensual pleasure.
The commentary states:

The stage at which desire arises toward the objects of the senses (*kāmaguṇa*) and the forms of sentient beings (*rūpa*), prior to actually seeking out the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), is called craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
The verse says:
The four graspings refer to the requisites for existence; one seeks them everywhere in order to obtain them.
The commentary says:
If, within this stage, one’s mind becomes attached and seeks out the five sense objects, running about everywhere in pursuit of them so as to obtain them, this stage is called *upādāna* (clinging).
Regarding such frantic pursuit, the verse says:
"The karma capable of producing future existence is called *bhava* (becoming)."
The commentary states:

Because this person seeks and pursues objects of desire with a restless mind, they are able to produce and grow karma that brings about retribution for future existence; this stage is called *bhava* (existence).
By virtue of this karma, one passes away from the present life and enters the state of actual conception in a future world.
The verse says:
Rebirth is that which is further connected and possesses a name.
The commentary says:
This stage is called "re-connection" (pratisaṃdhi). Why?
Because that which is the factor of consciousness in this present life is called "birth" (jāti) in the future.
From this point onward, the verse says:
"Old age and death, down to sensation.
The commentary says:
From the moment after birth until sensation, this stage is called old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
These four factors—namely name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and sensation (*vedanā*)—are designated as "old age and death" in the future.
The classification of the twelve links is thus.
Regarding this dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is explained elsewhere as being of four kinds:
first, in terms of a single moment (*kṣaṇika*); second, in terms of multiple periods of time (*adhvika*); third, in terms of association (*sāmbandhika*); and fourth, in terms of stages (*āvasthika*).
How is it explained in terms of moments?
Within a single moment, all twelve factors are present.
For example, when a person, driven by the defilement of craving and attachment, takes the life of a living being, that person possesses all twelve factors within a single moment.

Among these, delusion and confusion are called ignorance (*avidyā*); the formation of the intention to kill is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); the discernment of the categories of objects is called consciousness (*vijñāna*); the four aggregates that arise simultaneously with consciousness are called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the pure faculties categorized by name-and-form are called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); the meeting and conjunction of the six sense bases with their respective objects is called contact (*sparśa*); the experiencing of contact is called feeling (*vedanā*); craving for this is called thirst (*tṛṣṇā*); the remaining afflictions of the active mind associated with thirst are called grasping (*upādāna*); the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—produced by those are called becoming (*bhava*); the arising of such factors as these is called birth (*jāti*); their transformation is called aging (*jarā*); and their cessation is called death (*maraṇa*).
Furthermore, it is explained in terms of moments (*kṣaṇa*) and in terms of association (*saṃprayoga*), as stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.

As for the explanation in terms of stages (*avasthā*), all twelve links possess the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); the continuous succession of arising without interval is termed "a long duration."
Among these four, which cause of arising is being discussed now?
The verse says:
This is now explained in terms of stages.
The commentary states:
If each constituent part possesses the five aggregates, why are only ignorance and the others designated as "parts" (aṅga) while the rest are not?
The verse says:
"Because it is predominant, it is designated as that [member].
The commentary states:

If within a particular state ignorance is predominant, that state is called "ignorance"; if within that same state formations are predominant, it is called "formations," and so on, up to when old age and death are predominant, it is called "old age and death. Therefore, there is no fault.
Furthermore, why is it that while the Sūtras speak of dependent origination as having twelve factors, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* speaks of it differently?
That treatise asks:
"What is dependent origination?"
That is to say, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
They are spoken of as twelve in the Sūtras because of a specific underlying intention; in the Abhidharma, they are explained according to the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there is another explanation:

Dependent origination is of six kinds: namely, that explained in terms of stages, that explained in terms of moments, that explained in terms of extended time, that explained in terms of association, that explained in terms of names for sentient beings, and that explained in terms of names for both sentient and non-sentient beings.
Why is it that in the sūtras only the name "sentient beings" (sattva) is mentioned?
The verse says:
It is for the sake of removing the ignorance of others regarding the past, future, and middle [limits].
The commentary states:
For this reason, three sections are taught.
Among these, regarding ignorance concerning the past (*pūrvānta-avidyā*), doubt arises from this:
Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist?
What was I that existed in the past?
In what manner did I exist in the past?
Regarding ignorance concerning the future limit (*aparānta-avidyā*), doubt arises from this:
"Will I exist further in the future, or will I not exist?
The detailed explanation is as before.
Regarding ignorance concerning the middle limit, doubt arises from this:
"What is this phenomenon?
How is this phenomenon?"
"What am I now?
What shall I be in the future?
It is to eliminate these three kinds of ignorance that [the Buddha] spoke in terms of "sentient beings."
The three sections are explained as the twelvefold dependent origination, as set forth in sequence in the sūtras, namely: ignorance, formations, and so on, up to birth, old age, and death.
How is this known?
As the Sūtra says:
"O Bhikṣus!

If a bhikṣu, by means of the wisdom of reality as it is (yathābhūta-prajñā), thoroughly penetrates conditions and the phenomena produced from conditions, that bhikṣu does not, out of doubt or reflection, speculate about the past, saying: 'Did I exist in the past, or did I not exist? as explained at length above."
Furthermore, other masters say:
craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) constitute ignorance regarding the past (*pūrvānta*) and the future (*aparānta*). Why is this?
Because these three are the causes for future fruits, one should understand that this twelvefold dependent origination has three natures:
first, afflictions; second, karma; and third, the categories [of existence].
A verse here says:
"The three delusions.
The commentary states:
Three parts have delusion as their nature, namely ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*).
The verse says:
two parts are karma.
The commentary states:
Two parts have karma as their nature, namely *saṃskāra* and *bhava*.
The verse says:
The seven factors are classified as the result.
The commentary states:

These seven factors have "category" (*nikāya*) as their intrinsic nature; namely, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, birth, and old age and death, because they are the basis for afflictions and karma.

This category is sometimes called "fruit"; these seven members are designated as "fruit" in other contexts, while the remaining members are designated as "causes," because their nature consists of afflictions and karma.
For what reason is the fruit and cause explained extensively regarding the middle period?
Because there are five kinds of distinctions in their types, and because they are divided into two parts by way of being free from afflictions.
Regarding the subsequent period, the fruit is explained concisely, because it is divided into two parts.
Regarding the past limit (*pūrvānta*), the causes are stated briefly because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are explained by way of a single door.
The verse says:
"The results and the causes are stated briefly; from the middle [limit], both can be inferred."
The commentary states:

Since the intermediate period has been explained in detail, the extensive causes and extensive results of the prior and subsequent periods can be understood by analogy with this; therefore, the prior and subsequent periods are not explained in detail again.
Furthermore, if this were explained in detail, such statements would be useless.

If dependent origination consisted of only twelve links, then because the cause of ignorance is not mentioned, saṃsāra would have a beginning; and because the fruit of old age and death is not mentioned, saṃsāra would have an end.
If one posits ignorance as the cause and old age and death as the effect, one should further explain a distinct division [of the members].
If one explains these two as having distinct divisions, there is the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
If one does not explain them as having distinct divisions, one cannot avoid the aforementioned difficulty.
It should not be established separately, because this meaning has already been revealed herein by the Blessed One, the Buddha.
The verse says:

From afflictions arise further afflictions and karma; from karma arises further categories of fruit; from these categories arise further afflictions; such is the principle of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*).
The commentary states:
"From affliction, affliction arises" means that from craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*) arises.
"From affliction, karma arises" means that from grasping, existence (*bhava*) arises, and from ignorance (*avidyā*), formations (*saṃskāra*) arise.
Regarding "arising from the category of karma and its fruit": this refers to arising from formations (saṃskāra) to consciousness (vijñāna), and from existence (bhava) to birth (jāti).

Regarding "arising from the category of types": this refers to arising from consciousness to name-and-form (nāmarūpa), and so on up to arising from contact (sparśa) to feeling (vedanā), and from birth to old age and death (jarāmaraṇa).
Regarding "arising from the category of defilements," this refers to arising from sensation (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Because the Blessed One established the principle of the factors of existence (*bhavāṅga*) in this manner, and because ignorance (*avidyā*) is by nature a defilement, it is self-evident that defilements arise from categories and defilements arise from defilements; for the category of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) has sensation as its limit.

From this, further delusion arises; therefore, within this [formula], nothing can be added or subtracted. This is because of the statement: "Thus this entire great mass of suffering arises through the conjunction of conditions.
If it were otherwise, what would be the relevance of this passage?
Other masters say:
In another sutra it is stated that ignorance has improper mental attention as its cause, and improper mental attention has ignorance as its cause.
In this sutra, improper attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is also taught as being subsumed under the four types of clinging (*upādāna*).
What is improper attention?
It is that which is subsumed within the four clingings.

If it is argued that [the latent dispositions] are included because of association (*samprayoga*), then one must also say that they are included within craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), since they are associated with them.
If they are indeed included therein, how can they be proven to exist here?
That is to say, ignorance has improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*) as its cause.

If the relationship between cause and effect were established solely by way of inclusion within a category (*avasthā-saṃgraha*), then craving and ignorance should not be established as separate members [of the dependent origination formula], since they are already included within clinging (*upādāna*), just like improper mental attention.
Other masters say:

In another sutra, it is stated that improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) is the cause of ignorance (*avidyā*); this improper mental attention is said to exist at the time of contact (*sparśa*).
As the sutra says:
Depending on the eye-faculty and taking visible forms as its object, defiled and turbid reflection arises, which is capable of giving rise to ignorance.
At the time of feeling, ignorance necessarily arises.
As the Sūtra says:
Because feeling arises conditioned by contact born of ignorance, craving is able to arise.
From this separate sutra, it is known that improper mental attention arises at the time of contact and serves as the causal condition for the ignorance that arises at the time of feeling.
Therefore, ignorance does not lack a cause; thus, there is no need to establish it as a separate category, nor is there the fault of infinite regress.

This improper mental attention arises again from ignorance, for it is said that "defiled thought arises from delusion. This statement from the sutra serves as proof, and this same principle is not absent in other sutras as well.
If you intend to establish such a meaning, it should be further explained here;
those words should not have been spoken.
If they were not spoken, how could one know that [the object] exists?
It is known through reasoning that [ignorance] exists. What is this reasoning?
If there were no ignorance, it could not serve as the causal condition for craving.
For example, in the case of an arhat, if contact is not inverted, it cannot serve as the cause for defiled feeling.
How, then, is it known that improper mental attention arises from ignorance?
Because Arhats are free from ignorance (*avidyā*), their contact (*sparśa*) is non-perverted.
If one were not to speak further on this principle, it would result in the fault of excessive brevity.
If this meaning can be seen through reasoning, there is no need for a separate explanation, as it can be understood of itself.
Not only would improper reflection be so, but the remaining factors could likewise be understood even without being mentioned; thus, there would be no need to state them at all.
This adherence fails to provide a valid defense, and the objection previously raised likewise fails as an objection.

That is to say, because [the Buddha] taught the transition from ignorance to old age and death without mentioning anything else, it follows that birth and death have a beginning and an end; thus, the direct teaching is not incomplete.

Why is this? Sentient beings who are to be transformed are deluded regarding existence; they do not understand how [existence] arises from the past life to the present life, nor how it arises again from the present life to the future life.
This sequential correspondence of the three periods of time is intended by the Tathāgata to convey only this much meaning, a point already explained previously.
As the verse says:
"Regarding the prior, posterior, and middle limits, it is for the sake of removing the ignorance of others."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"O bhikṣus!
I shall now, for your sake, explain dependent origination and those phenomena that arise conditioned by it."
What is the difference in meaning between these two phrases?
According to the doctrine of the Abhidharma, there is no distinction between them. Why is this so?
These two are all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*).
How so? Future phenomena have not yet arisen, yet they are designated as "that which is to arise."
If that is so, how can that which is future and not yet produced be called "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*)?
It is called conditioned because it is capable of being produced and because it is brought forth by the mind.
If that is so, how is it with the outflow-free (anāsrava)?
That too is induced by a wholesome volition (kuśala-cetanā).
If that is so, then regarding the attainment (prāpti) of nirvāṇa, this same principle should also apply.
Because this conditioned phenomenon belongs to the category of that which is produced, it is designated as "produced" even though it has not yet arisen;
just as matter (*rūpa*) is designated as "matter" even when it has not yet undergone transformation, because it belongs to the category of that which undergoes transformation.
Therefore, there is no fault.
Now, the true intent of the sūtra shall be explained.
The verse says:
"Among these, that which is the cause of dependent origination is called the 'result' once it has been produced.
The commentary explains:
This very factor is the cause, and is termed "dependently originated" because other phenomena arise from it.
These parts are precisely the fruit; they are designated as "that which is produced.
In this way, all these parts are established in two ways, because they constitute cause and effect.
If it were established in such a manner, this meaning would not be tenable.

Otherwise, because there would be a distinction between what is observed, if one observes this factor, that factor becomes the condition for dependent origination; it does not mean that observing this very same factor further constitutes that which is produced.
It is like cause and effect, or father and son.
As that [teacher] said:
"The Venerable Pūraṇa Kassapa declared:"
There are phenomena that are dependently originated, yet not produced by dependent origination.
This consists of four propositions.
The first proposition refers to all future phenomena.
The second phrase refers to the final moments of consciousness of Arhats in the past and present.
The third phrase refers to all other dharmas in the past and present.
The fourth phrase refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
Regarding this, the Sautrāntika masters ask:
"Is this [position] a mere technical device, or is it the actual meaning of the sūtra?"
This is the meaning of this sutra.
If one speaks of the meaning of this sutra, it is not the meaning of the sutra. Why is it not so?
Regarding the dependent origination previously explained, which establishes twelve links based on stages,
the claim that each individual stage possesses all five aggregates is inconsistent with the sūtras. Why is this so?
In the sūtras, the twelve divisions [of the scriptures] are distinguished because they have distinct meanings.
A sūtra asks:
"What is ignorance?"
This refers to ignorance regarding the past, ignorance regarding the future, and ignorance regarding both the past and the future, as explained at length in the sūtra.

Since a sūtra of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) cannot be cited and subsumed under the category of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), this interpretation does not accord with the meaning of the sūtra.
Not all sūtras become definitive (nītārtha) merely by virtue of being analytical; sometimes various sūtras establish their meaning through superior analysis, as stated in the *Hastipadopama-sūtra*:
"What is the earth element?"
This refers to hair, body hair, and so forth; yet within hair and body hair, there are also other things such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest.
It is the same in this sutra: the meaning is distinguished according to what is predominant.
Therefore, this sutra cannot be cited as proof.
Why is this? Because therein, the earth element is not established as a complete exposition by means of a distinction from hair, body hair, and so forth.

Rather, it is by means of hair, body hair, and so forth that the earth element is distinguished; there is no earth element existing apart from hair, body hair, and so forth. Therefore, this statement is a complete exposition.
Is it not the case that this sutra explains ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth in their entirety, with nothing remaining?

Beyond hair, body hair, and the like, there is also the earth element (*pṛthivī-dhātu*) in other substances such as tears, mucus, saliva, and so on; yet these [others], such as tears, are all already included in what has been explained.
As the Sūtra says:
"Whatever else remains within the body is likewise called the earth element.
I now also grant that such remaining factors [as those mentioned] are [the result of] ignorance.
If that is so, one might argue that other categories of phenomena could be manifested and introduced as being subsumed under ignorance; what, then, would be the meaning of such a subsumption?

If, within this state, the five aggregates must necessarily exist, and if the presence or absence of one phenomenon necessarily entails the presence or absence of another, then that phenomenon may be established as a constituent part (*aṅga*).

If the five aggregates exist, it does not necessarily follow that the various formations (saṃskāra) exist, nor consciousness, nor meritorious, non-meritorious, or imperturbable formations, nor even craving and so forth; therefore, as distinguished in the sutra, this is indeed the meaning of the sutra.
Regarding the four propositions previously stated, if one were to maintain that future phenomena are not produced by dependent origination, this position contradicts this sūtra.
The sūtra asks:
"What are the phenomena produced by dependent origination?"
This refers to [the links] from ignorance up to old age and death.
Furthermore, if one were not to admit that the two parts—birth and old age and death—are subsumed within the future life, then the establishment of the three sections would also have to be refuted.
Other schools state:
"Dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is an unconditioned dharma (asaṃskṛtadharma). How is this known?"
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, this dharma remains eternally as it is.
Based on this statement from the Sūtra, this [interpretation] may be accepted if it is judged according to such an intention; otherwise, it is not so.
How is it that it is "thus" and not "not thus"? If one judges according to this intention:

whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear in the world, [the dharmas] always arise conditioned by ignorance and so forth, and by formations and so forth; there is never a time when they do not have these as conditions or when they take other dharmas as conditions. Therefore, they are eternally abiding and truly so.
This position may be accepted.
However, if one holds such a view— that there is a distinct dharma called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) which is eternal—
this position must be rejected, for it does not exist in that way.

Why is this? Because arising (*jāti*) is a characteristic of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Never before has another eternally abiding phenomenon been seen to possess the characteristic of a non-eternal phenomenon.

Arising is the characteristic of a phenomenon that was previously non-existent moving toward existence; how could this be associated with ignorance (*avidyā*) and the other factors such that they are said to be the conditions for arising?
The meaning of the phrase is also inconsistent.
This dharma is both permanent and produced by conditions; yet the original statement says it "arises through the arrival of formations" (*saṃskāra-samudaya*). What is the meaning of this phrase?

If one synthesizes the meaning revealed by this phrase, it means that when all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-dharma*) reach their causes and conditions, they come into being from non-existence through their aggregation; this is the meaning revealed by the expression "arising through the arrival and accumulation of formations."
The meaning of this statement is inconsistent. Why?

If there is a single agent performing two actions, one purpose is accomplished regarding the first action and a second purpose is accomplished regarding the subsequent action, just as, for example, one bathes before eating.
If a phenomenon does not exist prior to its arising, what phenomenon could arise later?
For no thing is established without depending upon an agent.
Regarding this, he states a verse:
It is not the case that [the cause] can exist prior to [the arising of the effect], because it would then be non-existent;
nor is it the case that they exist simultaneously. Since the matter is considered in terms of temporal sequence, there is no such fault.
Regarding this point, one should question those who study the science of grammar (śabdavidyā): In what state does this phenomenon arise?
Is it in the present, or is it in the future?
If that were so, what would be the consequence?
If you say that arising occurs in the present life, how can it exist in the present life?
If it has not yet arisen, what need is there for it to arise again?
If that which has already arisen were to arise again, there would be the fault of infinite regress.
If you say that arising occurs in the future state, how can a dharma that does not yet exist become an agent?
If there is no agent, how can the action be accomplished?
Therefore, if it arises in this state, it must also depart in this state.
At what stage does it arise?
It arises in the future as that which is currently tending toward birth.
Within this stage, upon reaching its conditions, the Grammarians (Śabdavādins) establish the agent and the action.
This position is not established.

That which has the capacity [to act] is called the agent (*kartṛ*), and that which possesses the name is called the action (*karma*). I do not now perceive any distinct entity named "existence" (*bhāva*) apart from the dharma that possesses the capacity for existence; therefore, regarding conventional designations (*vyavahāra*), there is no further room for objection.
The names established previously shall now have their meanings further clarified.
That is to say: "When this exists, that exists; with the arising of this, that arises.
The meaning of these two phrases is precisely the definition of the terms *pratītya*, *samudaya*, and *utpāda*.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"Just as that which does not exist can arise, so it is with respect to conditions;
if that which has already arisen were to arise again, there would be no end, because it already exists."

In your treatise, you have established a definitive judgment: regarding a single agent performing two actions, one meaning is established for the former action, and a second meaning is established for the latter action.
This judgment is not definitive.
For one may observe that two things are accomplished by a single agent, such as when a lamp reaches a place and darkness is extinguished simultaneously.

Or, for example, when one sleeps with the mouth open: if you claim that the eye [perceives] later, why does it not perceive at the time of closing, or at some other time? Why would it act [only] at a different moment?
Other masters offer a detailed rebuttal to this objection:
*pratī* has the sense of "repeatedly"; *tya* signifies a state of non-abiding, meaning impermanence; *tri* has the sense of "accumulation"; and *udapāda* has the sense of "arising."
This phrase expresses the following meaning: in relation to various causes and conditions, impermanent phenomena arise through aggregation; therefore, they are called *pratītyasamutpāda*.
Such a distinction is established within this sutra; how, however, is it established in other places?
As the sutra says:
"When there is the eye and when there are forms, visual consciousness arises."
How does the Blessed One explain these two phrases by way of dependent origination? That is to say:

"If this dharma exists, that dharma necessarily exists; from the arising of this dharma, that dharma necessarily arises. This is for the sake of certainty, so as to cause the knowledge that "this arises from that" to occur.
If there is ignorance, there must be volitional formations and nothing else; therefore, volitional formations arise with ignorance as their condition.

Furthermore, two phrases are spoken in order to demonstrate the successive transmission of the members: if this member exists, that member must exist; because this member arises, that member must arise.

Furthermore, two phrases are spoken in order to reveal the successive transmission of arising: if there is a middle limit when there is a prior limit, then by virtue of the middle limit, a subsequent limit also arises.
Furthermore, two phrases are stated in order to demonstrate both the immediate cause (*hetu*) and the transmitted cause (*paramparā-hetu*). Why is this?

Sometimes the various formations (*saṃskāra*) arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) in immediate succession; at other times, the various formations arise from ignorance through a series of successive transmissions.
Other masters say:

The two phrases were spoken in order to eliminate the attachment to causelessness and the attachment to an eternal cause; for if all existents were without cause, they would not exist, nor would they arise from non-existence.

Regarding their conception of permanence—namely, [the notions of] self-nature (*svabhāva*), the self (*ātman*), and so forth—if one were to hold such views, establishing the preceding phrase would be useless; rather, it is because the phrase "from the arising of this, that arises" refutes these two extreme attachments and establishes the teaching.
Furthermore, there is another way of analyzing it as follows: if I exist as a basis, then the various factors such as volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) must necessarily exist;
because they arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, the volitional formations and the rest come into being.

To refute this attachment, the Blessed One definitively established this meaning: "If this arises, that necessarily arises; if this dharma exists, that necessarily exists, and not otherwise. That is to say, conditioned by ignorance, the various formations arise, and so on, until it is said: "In this way, this entire great mass of suffering comes into being."
Furthermore, other masters say:

Two phrases are spoken in order to reveal non-extinction and arising; that is, if ignorance does not cease, the formative forces do not cease, and because ignorance arises, the formative forces arise.
Furthermore, other masters say:

two phrases are spoken in order to manifest abiding and arising; as long as the continuity of causes and conditions exists, the continuity of the phenomenon must necessarily follow; and because of the arising of causes and conditions, the phenomenon must necessarily attain birth.
The Blessed One intends to explain birth; what relevance does the explanation of abiding have?
Why does the Blessed One disrupt the sequence and present them in reverse order, first explaining abiding and subsequently [explaining] taking birth?
Furthermore, other masters say:
"If this exists, that exists" means that if a thing exists, it must necessarily exist once its conditions have ceased.
If that were so, then this thing would not arise from causes.
This interpretation is not correct, for there is no such thing as causelessness. Why?
Because the arising of this brings about the arising of that.
If the meaning of the sutra were such as this, one should have stated only the preceding phrase: "When this exists, that exists.
Furthermore, one should first state the arising of phenomena, and only afterwards state, "When this exists, that exists."
If one explains it in this way, the phrasing remains consistent.
Otherwise, if one were to ask what it is that is dependently originated and then explain its cessation, it would not follow the proper sequence.
Therefore, such interpretations do not reflect the intended meaning of the sūtra.
How is it that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have ignorance (*avidyā*) as their condition, up to and including old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) having birth (*jāti*) as their condition?
In this regard, we should clarify the meaning of mere association (*samyoga*).
Among those infants and ordinary worldlings in the world, they do not know that what arises through causes and conditions is merely the conditioned and that there is no other phenomenon besides it.

Because of this ignorance, their minds are defiled by the view of self and the conceit of "I am. For the sake of obtaining pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure for themselves, they perform three kinds of karma through the body and so forth: they perform meritorious actions to obtain future pleasure; they cultivate immovable actions to obtain the experience of pleasure and neither-pain-nor-pleasure; and they perform non-meritorious actions to obtain pleasure in the present life.
These three types of karma are called "formations arising conditioned by ignorance.
Driven by these karmas, the continuity of consciousness proceeds, corresponding with the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) to undergo various destinies, just like the light of a lamp.
The statement "conditioned by formations,
consciousness arises" implies that this consciousness has already arisen.
This should be understood from the section on the analysis of consciousness, which says:
What is consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.
With consciousness as the precursor, name-and-form subsequently arises, fully endowed with the five aggregates.
Since it is stated thus within the *Vibhaṅga*, the remaining words are as explained previously.
Following the maturation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) arise.

Next, when a distracted mind arises toward objects due to the production of consciousness, contact (*sparśa*) arises from the conjunction of the three; that is, it is predominant in relation to pleasant feeling and so forth. Following this, the three types of feeling (*vedanā*) arise from it; following these feelings, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) arises.

If a person is oppressed by suffering, they give rise to craving for pleasant feeling; toward pleasure, they give rise to craving for the realm of form (*rūpa-tṛṣṇā*); and toward neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, they give rise to craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya-tṛṣṇā*).
Next, because of craving for pleasant feelings (*vedanā*), one grasps the four things, beginning with desire (*kāma*).
Here, "desire" refers to the five objects of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*).
"Views" refer to the sixty-two views, as explained in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
"Precept" (śīla) refers to being free from immoral conduct.
"Adherence" (parāmarśa) refers to the mind's firm grasping, such as adhering to the practices of dogs, oxen, and so forth, or like the practices of the Nirgranthas.
As the Sūtra says:
This person goes naked and does not keep or wear clothes, as explained at length in the sutra.

Furthermore, there are those such as the Brahmins, the Pāśupatas, the Pāṣaṇḍas, and other non-Buddhist ascetics, who carry staffs, black antelope skins, matted hair, bags of ash, three staffs, or shave their heads.
What I call "the utterance of 'I'" refers to the body; because within this [body] there is the verbal expression "this is I," the body is therefore called the "utterance of 'I'.
Other masters say:
because within the body there exist both the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the conceit of "I am" (*asmimāna*), these two are called the "utterance of 'I'."
How do these two establish the statement "I"?
Because it is by means of these two that one speaks of the existence of a self (*ātman*).
Other masters say:
Because the "self" does not exist, there is only verbal expression without any real referent; thus, one uses the word "self.
As a sutra says:
"O Bhikṣus!"

Ignorant infantile ordinary beings follow after worldly conventional designations and fall into the grasping at a self; yet therein, in reality, there is neither a self nor anything belonging to a self.
Furthermore, "desire" refers to all other phenomena apart from the latter three [categories].
The clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are explained as before.

Although the term "self" (*ātman*) applies generally to all three realms, it exists here only in the form and formless realms, where all phenomena are devoid of the aforementioned two [types of clinging].
Among these four, what dharma constitutes "clinging" (upādāna)?
Within this context, craving (rāga) is called clinging. Why is that?
In all instances, the Blessed One provides this very explanation.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is grasping?"
Within that state, craving arises;
next, with grasping as its condition, it is able to project future existence. This growth of karma is called "becoming" (*bhava*).
As the Sūtra says:
Ānanda! This karma is able to project a future existence; herein it is called "existence" (bhava).
Next, with existence as a condition, consciousness again takes rebirth; this future birth is called "birth" (jāti), which possesses the five aggregates.
Furthermore, once [birth] has arisen, one should know that there is aging, death, and so forth.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Such a purely [conditioned aggregate]" refers to its being devoid of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman* and *ātmīya*).
"Great" means it is without beginning and without end.
"A mass of suffering" means it is an accumulation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) associated with the outflows (*āsrava*).
"Arising from the conjunction of conditions" means there is no [independent] fruit, as it is produced solely by causes and conditions.
This principle is elucidated by the Vaibhāṣika masters; therefore, it was explained first.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "ignorance" (avidyā)?
It is that which is not knowledge (vidyā); this is called ignorance.
If that were so, there would be the fault of over-extension; the eyes and other faculties would also have to be considered ignorance (*avidyā*).
If that were so, then the absence of knowledge (*vidyā*) would be ignorance.
If that were so, one must conclude that the non-existence of something constitutes ignorance, because these two positions are mutually inconsistent.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) should be understood as a distinct dharma.
Regarding this distinct dharma, the verse says:
Ignorance is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*), just as "non-friend" or "untruth" are opposites [of friend and truth].
The commentary states:
A person distinct from a relative is called "non-relative" as the antidote to a relative; it does not mean merely following others, nor is it the absence of relatives.

Regarding "unreal," just as with speech and non-falsity, there exists a verbal expression that serves as an antidote, which is termed "unreal. This applies to what is not the Dharma, not the beneficial, not the purposeful, and so forth.
Those dharmas that are the antidotes to dharmas such as "dharma" are called "non-dharma" and so forth; they are neither something other than those nor non-existent.
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is likewise.
There exists a distinct dharma that serves as the antidote to knowledge (*vidyā*), which is named ignorance. How is this meaning to be known?
Because they are taught as causes and conditions.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because they are taught as fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth."
The commentary states:
Other sūtras say that ignorance constitutes a fetter (saṃyojana), a bond (bandhana), a latent tendency (anuśaya), a flux (āsrava), and an association (saṃprayoga).

If it were merely the absence of anything at all, one should not speak of such meanings as these, nor could it be established as the eye and so forth; therefore, there must be a real, distinct dharma named ignorance (*avidyā*).
If that is so, then just as people in the world say "no wife" when referring to a bad wife, or "no son" when referring to a bad son,
so too should it be with ignorance (*avidyā*):
a bad understanding is called ignorance.
The verse says:
Because it is not non-virtuous and is clearly seen.
The commentary says:
If you say it is not so, then that which is censurable would indeed be censurable.
To claim that what the wise call ignorance (avidyā) is actually non-ignorance—that is not correct. Why is this?
If this cognition were censurable, it would necessarily be defiled; since its nature is that of a [wrong] view, it should not constitute ignorance (*avidyā*).
If that were so, this cognition would simply be ignorance itself.
This wisdom cannot be established as ignorance. Why?
The verse says:
"Because views are associated with it.
The commentary explains:

If ignorance were of the nature of unwholesome wisdom (*duṣprajñā*), then various views would not be associated with ignorance, because two types of wisdom cannot arise in association at one and the same time.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because it is taught that [ignorance] defiles cognition.
The commentary explains:
The Sūtra states:
"Due to the defilement of desire, the mind is not liberated; due to the defilement of ignorance, wisdom is not purified.
If this [ignorance] were wisdom, it could not constitute a defilement of wisdom."
Just as there are distinct defilements of the mind that differ from the nature of the mind—namely, desire and ignorance—the same applies to wisdom (*prajñā*). Why, then, do you not accept this?
Because wholesome wisdom is intermingled with defiled wisdom, it is not pure; therefore, this [defiled wisdom] is said to be the defilement of that [wholesome wisdom].
This mind, when defiled by desire, is said to be "not liberated.
Is it transformed by a fixed desire?
Because it is harmed by desire, liberation is not attained; however, if a person applies the antidote and cultivates the transformation of desire, they will attain liberation.
In this way, we distinguish that wisdom is not pure because it is defiled by ignorance; that is, wisdom is not pure due to the affliction caused by ignorance.
If one wishes to make such a distinction, who can prevent it?
The various masters state that ignorance (*avidyā*) is of a different category from knowledge (*jñāna*), just as desire (*rāga*) is distinct from the mind (*citta*).
If anyone were to maintain that all afflictions (*kleśa*) are termed ignorance, this position should be refuted by the aforementioned reasoning.
Why is this? If ignorance were the essential nature of all afflictions, it should not be established as a distinct affliction within the categories of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
If it were identical to view (*dṛṣṭi*), it should not be said to be associated with view, because other afflictions and views do not mutually subsume one another.
One should also say that the mind is defiled by ignorance, and therefore it is not liberated.
If you claim that this statement is made for the sake of distinguishing specific categories, then one should likewise distinguish specific categories of ignorance with respect to wisdom as well.
I allow that ignorance (*avidyā*) is a distinct affliction; what is the nature of this ignorance?
Its nature is the failure to discern the reality of the truths and the results of karma.
This is unintelligible: what phenomenon is called "non-discernment"?
Is it that non-apprehension (*avijñapti*) exists because there is no apprehension (*vijñapti*)?
If this were so, both positions would be flawed.
For instance, if there were a distinct dharma called "non-apprehension" that serves as the antidote to apprehension, such a thing could not be explained either.
Therefore, there is no lack of such categories as that which discriminates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is the eye-faculty?"
This refers to pure matter (*rūpa*), which is the basis for visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Furthermore, there are phenomena that cannot be conceptually distinguished, yet it cannot be said that they do not exist.

For example, within the meditation on loving-kindness (*maitrībhāvanā*), there is the nature of non-attachment (*alobha*); within the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), there is the nature of non-hatred (*adveṣa*), and so forth.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta says:
"I have such a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) which is called ignorance (*avidyā*).
Apart from the conceit of self (*asmimāna*), what other distinct dharma is there that could be called a "conceptualization" as described in this sutra?
The Sūtra says:

"Because I now know thus and see thus, all craving, all views, all categories, all clinging to 'I' and 'mine,' and the underlying tendencies of the conceit 'I am'—having been extinguished and not arising again—I have entered nirvāṇa without shadow."
Regarding such categories as these, how can it be definitively determined that this is ignorance (*avidyā*)?

For one cannot say that this category is distinct from other afflictions; might it not rather be of the same nature as the remaining afflictions, such as pride (*māna*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and so forth?
If one were to further deliberate upon this matter, there would be much to be said; therefore, let us cease this discussion.
Furthermore, what is the meaning of "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*)?
As for "form" (*rūpa*), it has already been explained at length above.
The verse says:
"Name (nāma) refers to the formless aggregates (arūpaskandha).
The commentary says:
Why is it called "name" (nāma)?
Because it conforms to names and depends upon the sense faculties and their objects, transforming with respect to their meanings, it is called "name.
To what specific names does it conform?
This is what is conventionally understood by the world as that which can designate various objects, namely: oxen, horses, persons, forms, sounds, and so forth.
Why is this capacity to designate objects called "name" (*nāman*)?
It is called "name" (*nāman*) because it undergoes transformation (*pariṇāma*) according to its function with respect to various objects.
Other masters say:
within this path, having cast off the body, that which is able to transform and produce another birth is called "name," namely the formless aggregates (*arūpiṇaḥ skandhāḥ*).
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have already been explained previously; contact (*sparśa*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"Contact is sixfold."
The commentary states:
This refers to visual contact through to mental contact.
What kind of phenomena are these six types of contact?
The verse says:
"Arising through conjunction.
The commentary says:
It is said that [cognition] arises from the conjunction of three factors—namely, the sense faculty (*indriya*), the object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
This principle is plausible, because the five sense faculties, their objects, and consciousness arise simultaneously in mutual conjunction.
Once the mental faculty (*manas*) has ceased, how can it harmonize with future or present mental objects (*dharmas*) and mental consciousness?

This very harmony of the three—meaning that cause and effect constitute the sense of harmony, or that they accomplish a single function—is because these three possess the most preeminent capacity for the arising of contact (*sparśa*).
Regarding this, the wisdom of various masters arises in diverse ways.
Some masters maintain that contact is merely the name given to a conjunction; they also cite a sutra as proof for this position.
The Sūtra states:
"The coming together, conjunction, and aggregation of these three factors is called contact (sparśa).
Other masters say:
There is a distinct dharma associated with the mind called contact (*sparśa*), and they likewise cite a sutra as proof.
The sutra says:
"The sixfold set of six dharmas."
What constitutes the Dharma-gates?
There are six internal bases, six external bases, six groups of consciousness, six groups of contact, six groups of sensation, and six groups of craving.
Why is this? Because in this sūtra, contact (*sparśa*) is explained as a distinct aggregate from the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Regarding this, if certain masters assert that contact is merely the conjunction [of these three], their defense of this position is as follows.

It is not the case that because you speak of them separately, the dharmas possess distinct categories; otherwise, the dharmas such as feeling (*vedanā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) would constitute separate categories within the *dharmāyatana*.
There is no such fault, for there exists a *dharmāyatana* distinct from the dharmas of feeling, craving, and so forth, from which contact arises through the coming together of the three.
There is no such separate third [category] among these in which one could maintain that something else exists.

If, within this context, there were a sense faculty and an object without consciousness as the "remainder," or a separate consciousness without a sense faculty and an object as the "remainder," then it would not be so; however, since none of these exist, if contact is mentioned again after the three have already been stated, it would serve no further purpose.
Other masters say:
Not all eyes and forms are causes of visual consciousness, nor is every visual consciousness the effect of eyes and forms.
Therefore, those instances within this relationship where the cause and the effect are established as being present are what constitute contact (*sparśa*).
If various masters claim that contact (*sparśa*) is distinct from conjunction (*saṃnipāta*), how do they avoid this sūtra?
The sūtra states:
"The coming together, conjunction, and assembly of these three factors is called contact."
Their recitation of the sūtras differs.
Furthermore, the name of the effect is spoken by way of the cause, as for example "the bliss of heaven" or "the suffering of hell.
Since this discussion involves numerous distinctions regarding establishment and refutation, it would become a digression; therefore, let us cease this discourse.
The Abhidharma masters state that contact (*sparśa*) is indeed a distinct dharma.
Regarding the six types of contact, the verse says:
Five are contacts with resistance (*pratigha-saṃsparśa*), and the sixth is contact based on designation (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*).
The commentary states:
the contacts of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—these five are called contacts with resistance because they depend upon sense faculties that possess resistance.
The sixth, mental contact, is called "contact based on verbal expression" (*adhivacana-saṃsparśa*). Why is this?
"Verbal expression" refers to names (*nāman*); these names are the predominant objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Mental consciousness can be designated by means of words; therefore, mental contact is called "designation-based" (*adhivacana*).
As the Sūtra says:
"By means of visual consciousness, one merely cognizes blue, but cannot cognize that 'this is blue.'"
If one cognizes blue by means of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), one can also cognize that "this is blue.
The first type of contact is manifested by its basis (*āśraya*); the second type of contact is manifested by its object (*ālambana*).
Other masters say:

"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in dependence upon words regarding its object, whereas the five [sensory] consciousnesses do not; therefore, only this one is called 'dependent on words' (*nirukti-saṃsparśa*).
The contact associated with it is called 'contact dependent on words' (*nirukti-saṃsparśa*)."
Therefore, the first is manifested by way of its basis, and the second is manifested by way of its association.
Furthermore, these six contacts are further established as three types of contact.
The verse says:
Regarding "contact with knowledge, contact with ignorance, and other contacts," the commentary states:

there is contact with knowledge (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*), there is contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), and there is a contact distinct from these two, namely contact that is neither knowledge nor ignorance (*naivavidyā-nāvidyā-saṃsparśa*). These contacts should be understood in this sequence.
The verse says:
"The untainted, the defiled, and the remainder.
The commentary says:
If it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called contact with clarity (*vidyā-saṃsparśa*);
if it is defiled (*kliṣṭa*), it is called contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśa*), because it is associated with either clarity or ignorance;
the remainder is contact that is neither with clarity nor with ignorance (*na-vidyā-nāvidyā-saṃsparśa*), because it is not associated with either of the two.
What are the remaining ones?
They are the wholesome states associated with outflows (*sāsrava-kuśala*) and the non-obscured neutral states (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Furthermore, because the contact of ignorance (*avidyā-sparśa*) arises repeatedly, it is taken as a single category and thus constitutes two types of contact.
The verse says:
Contact associated with hatred and greed.
The commentary says:
Because they are associated with hatred and desire, and furthermore because they encompass all [feelings].
The verse says:
"There are three: the experiences of pleasure, pain, and equanimity."
The commentary states:

Furthermore, there are three types of contact, namely: contact experienced as pleasant feeling, contact experienced as painful feeling, and contact experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Because it is favorable toward pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and so forth; furthermore, because it experiences and is easily experienced, it is called "feeling" (*vedanā*).
Since this feeling exists therein, it is termed "contact associated with pleasant feeling" (*sukha-vedanīya-sparśa*).
It should be understood that the contact associated with painful feeling and the contact associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling are likewise so.
If this were the case, these contacts would amount to sixteen.
Having explained contact, feeling shall now be explained.
Among these, the six types of contact have already been explained previously.
The verse says:
From this, the six feelings arise.
The commentary states:
Regarding the six feelings, these are the feeling produced by eye-contact, and the feelings produced by ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
Within this context, the verse says:
"Five belong to the body; the rest belong to the mind.
The commentary explains:

These five types of sensation, arising from visual contact through to tactile contact, are called "bodily sensations" (*kāyikī vedanā*) because they depend upon the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*).
Feeling arises from mind-contact; this is called mental feeling because it relies solely upon the mind.
Furthermore, when feeling arises, does it occur after contact or simultaneously with contact?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
They arise simultaneously, because they serve as simultaneous causes for one another.
How, then, can the distinction between the producer and the produced be established among two dharmas that are co-nascent?
Why is it not established?
Because there is no capacity; regarding a dharma that has already arisen, other dharmas have no further capacity [to produce it].
This proof is no different from the thesis being established.
Why is this? At that time, how could the distinction between the producer and the produced be established among two dharmas that arise simultaneously?
At this point, that same principle is stated: once a dharma has already arisen, no other dharma has further capacity [to produce it].
If that were so, there would be the fault of mutual production.
Since this is what is accepted [by us], what fault is there?
That simultaneous causes (*sahabhū-hetu*) are mutually effects is indeed what we accept.
In this sutra, it is not accepted that contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) are mutually cause and effect.
For it has been heard that "conditioned by eye-contact, the feeling produced by eye-contact arises";
however, it has never been heard that "conditioned by the feeling produced by eye-contact, eye-contact arises."
Furthermore, this argument is untenable because it contradicts the principle that a cause must precede its effect.
If a phenomenon is capable of producing another phenomenon, they necessarily occur at different times and cannot be simultaneous.

For example, the seed exists first and the sprout arises later; milk exists first and curd follows; the striking occurs first and the sound follows; and the mental faculty exists first and consciousness arises later.
In this way, it is not that cause and effect lack the distinction of temporal sequence; simultaneous cause and effect are also established.

For example, regarding visual consciousness and its counterparts with respect to the eye, visible forms, the four great elements, and the derivative matter produced by them: herein, the sense organs and objects exist first, and only subsequently does consciousness arise.
If one maintains that the four great elements and the matter derived from them exist first, and subsequently the derived matter arises,
what difficulty is there in this? If that were so,
then contact and sensation would be like a sprout and its shadow.
Other masters say:
Feeling arises after contact. Why is this?

First there are the sense faculties and their objects, followed by consciousness; the conjunction of these three constitutes contact (*sparśa*). With contact as a condition, feeling (*vedanā*) arises in the third moment.
If this were so, it would follow that feeling does not necessarily exist in every instance of consciousness, nor does contact exist in every instance of consciousness.
There is no such fault.
Why? Because feeling arises within the subsequent contact, taking the preceding contact as its cause.
All contact is accompanied by feeling; it is not logical for [feeling] to arise again [at that point].
Why is this illogical?
Within each of the two contacts there is its own respective object; with the prior contact as the cause, the feeling arises in relation to the subsequent contact.
If feeling produced by contact with an object of a distinct category must arise by taking that distinct object as its condition, how can this principle be tenable?
Furthermore, since this mind is associated with feeling, and yet this feeling has a different object from the mind, how can this principle be established?

If that were so, this principle should be established: at that time, consciousness constitutes contact, yet this consciousness lacks feeling; from that point onward, subsequent consciousnesses possess feeling but lack contact, because the causal conditions would be inconsistent.
What is the fault in this position?
If that were so, the definition of the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) would be undermined—namely, that the ten universal factors must necessarily coexist with every state of mind.
Where, then, is this definition of the universal factors established?
It is established in the Abhidharma.
However, we rely upon the Sūtras, not upon the Abhidharma.
For the Blessed One has said:
You all should rely upon the sūtras for practice;
the meaning of "the great earth" is not like that,
for it must exist within every mind.
If that is so, what is the meaning of "universal ground" (mahābhūmi)?
There are three grounds: the ground with vitarka and vicāra, the ground without vitarka but with vicāra, and the ground without vitarka and without vicāra.
Furthermore, there are three levels: namely, the wholesome level, the unwholesome level, and the indeterminate level.

Furthermore, there are three levels: namely, the level of those in training (śaikṣa), the level of those beyond training (aśaikṣa), and the level of those who are neither in training nor beyond training.
Therefore, among the aforementioned three categories, those that exist in the first category are called "universal mental factors" (mahābhūmika).
If a dharma is fixed as existing only within wholesome stages, that dharma is termed a "wholesome universal mental factor" (kuśalamahābhūmika).
If a dharma is established as existing within the defiled stages (kliṣṭabhūmi), that dharma is called a great ground of evil (akuśalamahābhūmika).
These dharmas arise in mutual alternation as appropriate; they do not all arise simultaneously at all times.
Other masters say:
"The phrase 'such as the wholesome universal mental factors' is cited here because it conforms to the wording [of the sūtra].
Now we shall explain what was not previously stated: if feeling arises after contact, you must defend this sūtra."
The Sūtra states:
"Depending on the eye and conditioned by visible forms, eye-consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three there is contact, and feeling and perception arise simultaneously with it.
While the *Manobhūmi* and other sūtras speak of their simultaneous arising, they do not specify that they arise simultaneously with contact.
What does this save?
If they were simultaneous, they would necessarily touch; yet this term "simultaneous" is also seen used in reference to sequential [processes], as in the Sūtra:
How is it that one cultivates the awakening factor of mindfulness arising together with loving-kindness?
Therefore, the claim that the word "together" (saha) does not constitute proof is incorrect. Why is this so?

In the Sūtras it is said that feeling is this, perception is this, volition is this, and consciousness is this; these dharmas are mutually mixed and not separate from one another. Therefore, there is no consciousness that is not mixed with feeling.
This point should be considered: what is the meaning of "intermingled"?
In this very sutra it is also stated thus: "That which is felt is that which is thought; that which is thought is that which is perceived; that which is perceived is that which is cognized."

This meaning is not yet clear: does it resolve the objective sphere (*viṣaya*) of the four dharmas, or does it resolve the momentariness (*kṣaṇika*) of the four dharmas? Within the context of the simultaneous arising of lifespan (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), because the term "intermingled" (*saṃsṛṣṭa*) is employed, their momentariness is established as certain.
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"The conjunction of the three is called contact.
How could there be consciousness that is not a conjunction of the three, or a conjunction of the three that is not contact?
Therefore, this principle must necessarily be so: that within all consciousnesses, there exist contact, sensation, and so forth, which arise simultaneously with contact.
The various debates presented thus far have sufficiently established this matter.
The meaning of their fundamental basis shall now be explained.
Regarding the mind and feelings previously mentioned briefly, the verse says:
"These further become eighteen, through the mental differentiation of formations."
The commentary states:
This mental feeling is further divided into eighteen types, due to the differentiation of the eighteen mental explorations (*manopavicāra*).
What are these eighteen mental explorations?

There are six modes of mental application associated with joy (*saumanasya-vitarka*), six modes associated with grief (*daurmanasya-vitarka*), and six modes associated with equanimity (*upekṣā-vitarka*).
How are these established?
If they were established by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), there would be only three: namely, the mental applications of joy, grief, and equanimity.
If [the mental consciousness] were established by way of association, it would be one, because it is associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
If it were established by way of its object, it would be sixfold, because it takes the six objects, such as visible forms, as its conditions.

If established as eighteen, they necessarily depend upon three [categories]. Among them, fifteen are called "discriminative mental applications regarding form and so forth" (*rūpādi-vikalpa-manopavicāra*); they do not have mixed objects, because they arise determinedly by taking form and so forth as their conditions.
Three are called "discriminative mental applications regarding phenomena" (*dharma-vikalpa-manopavicāra*); these consist of two types of discriminative mental applications regarding the mind.
What is the meaning of this phrase?
It is said that it refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discerning objects such as joy and so forth.

Other masters say it refers to causing the mind to engage in discernment regarding the six sense-objects; because it follows after feeling (*vedanā*), the mind repeatedly engages in discernment within those objects.
Why are bodily sensations not said to be mental conceptualizations?

These sensations do not rely on the mind and cannot be conceptually differentiated, because the five consciousnesses are non-conceptual; therefore, they should not be regarded as conceptual activities.
Why is the bliss of the third dhyāna not included within the category of "discriminative formations"?

Because from the outset, in the desire realm, there is no faculty of bliss (*sukhendriya*) belonging to the mindless states (*acittaka-bhūmi*), and because there is no discriminative formation that can counteract this suffering.
If those [mental factors] arise solely based on the mind-ground, how is this principle to be understood?
A sutra states:
"Having seen a form with the eye, that which is capable of serving as a basis for joy is then engaged in conceptualization."
Such statements as these are made on the basis of the mental consciousness induced by the five sensory consciousnesses.
If one were to categorize them according to their actual nature, all eighteen elements would have the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) as their ground.
This is, for example, like the meditation on impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*), which, though induced by visual consciousness, resides in the ground of the mind.
Furthermore, regarding the sequence from "having seen" up to "having touched," because these are conventional expressions, they cannot be used as a basis for objection.
If one gives rise to discursive mental activity (*vikalpa-cāra*) without having seen, up to without having touched, this too is a discursive mental activity of the mind (*manas*).

If it were not so, then within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there would be no discursive investigation (*vikalpa-cāra*) regarding the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) or its constituent factors such as form;

likewise, discursive investigation regarding the odors, tastes, and tangibles of the desire realm would also not be established within the form realm, according to the principle of clear manifestation.

To speak thus: if a person perceives a form and then engages in conceptualization regarding sound, this too is a conceptualization; it is spoken of in this way because they do not overlap, as the sense faculties and their respective objects are definitively determined.
Is it the case that such form is invariably a basis for joy, and so on, up to being invariably a basis for equanimity?
