Yes; this is determined with respect to the continuity [of the mind], not with respect to the object.
Among the modes of conceptualization (*vikalpa-pracāra*), how many are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)?
How many types are there therein?
And what phenomena serve as their objects (*ālambana*)?
This should be asked in the same way even regarding the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
The verse says:
"All have the desire realm as their object."
The commentary states:
Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all eighteen [mental applications] are present; these five have all things as their objects.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"There are twelve objects of the realm of form.
The commentary states:
The realm of form consists of twelve objects of mental application (*manopavicāra*). Six—the applications of smell and taste—are excluded, because these two do not exist there.
The verse says:
"Three follow.
The commentary says:

Regarding the objects of experience (*ālambana*), they flow from above; if one is in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there are only three types of mental application (*manasikāra*) as their objects, because form and so forth do not exist there.
Having already explained those associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), I shall now explain those associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The verse says:
"In the two meditative attainments, there are twelve.
The commentary says:
Excluding the six modes of afflicted mental application (*paryavasthāna*), the remaining twelve are associated with the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*). Why is this so?
The verse says:
"Practicing in the desire realm.
The commentary says:
"If they take the desire realm as their object."
The verse says:
"Eight objects for itself.
The commentary says:

If this form realm (*rūpadhātu*) serves as the object for one's own mental applications (*vikalpa*), it consists of only eight objects of mental application, because the four mental applications related to odor and taste have been excluded.
The verse says:
"In the formless [realm], two."
The commentary states:
The formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is the objective domain for the mental application of discernment regarding two phenomena.
The verse says:
"In the two meditative absorptions, there are six.
The commentary states:
"In the third and fourth meditative absorptions, there are only six modes of mental application (vitarka-vicāra) consisting of equanimity, and no others."
Regarding these six objects, the verse says:
"In the desire realm, there are six.
The commentary explains:
If they take the desire realm as their object, these constitute six types of equanimity-based mental applications (upekṣā-vicāra) as their sphere.
The verse says:
"Four of its own."
The commentary states:
If one takes one’s own realm as an object, there are only four types of equanimity (*upekṣā*) among the mental applications (*vitarka*), because odors and tastes do not exist therein.
The verse says:
"The other realm has one object.
The commentary explains:
The Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) is called "other" because it differs from the two lower realms; this [realm] has only the single dharma of mental application (dharmavikalpācāra) as its object.
Having explained those associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those associated with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"There are four at the limit of form."
The commentary states:
Regarding the path of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), this is termed the "limit of form" (*rūpānta*).
Within it, there are four types of mental application (*vitarka*), namely: mental application regarding form, sound, touch, and phenomena (*dharma*).
The verse says:
"The practice of form.
The commentary explains:
These four conditions take the fourth dhyāna as their object.
If one maintains this view, then they are distinct from the fourth dhyāna as their objects.

If one maintains that they are combined with the fourth dhyāna as their object, then within that there is only a single collective object, namely, the mental application to the dharma-sphere (dharmāyatana-vicāra).
The verse says:
"One practice leads upward.
The commentary says:

If one speaks of the mental applications of discrimination (*vikalpa-manasikāra*), there is only one that arises with the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as its object; namely, the mental application of discrimination regarding mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya-vikalpamanasikāra*).
The verse says:
"One is in the fundamental [realm]."
The commentary states:
If, within the fundamental formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is only the mental application (*manopavicāra*) directed toward a single object-field (*dharmaviṣaya*) without remainder,
this application is described in the verse as follows:
"Regarding its own object":
the commentary explains that it takes only the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) as its object.
Why is this? Because the fundamental concentrations of the formless realm cannot take the lower realms as their objects; this point shall be explained in detail later.
Regarding such mental activities of conceptualization, the verse says:
Regarding the phrase "all eighteen [factors] with outflows" (*sāsrava*),
the commentary states:
because among them there is not even a single factor of discursive activity that is without outflow (*anāsrava*), they are called "all with outflows."
Which person, moreover, is associated with how many types of *vitarka-vicāra* (discursive thought)?

If a person is born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and has not yet attained the wholesome mind of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they are associated with all *vitarka-vicāra* of the desire realm; they are associated with the eight types of *vitarka-vicāra* belonging to the stages of the first and second dhyānas; and they are associated with the four types of *vitarka-vicāra* belonging to the third and fourth dhyānas—all of which are defiled (*kliṣṭa*), except for those taking fragrance and taste as their objects. In the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they are associated with one type of defiled *vitarka-vicāra*.

If a person has attained a mind of the form realm but has not yet attained freedom from desire, they are associated with all types of discursive mental activities (*vikalpa-caryā*) of the desire realm; they are associated with ten types of discursive mental activities of the first dhyāna; they possess four types of afflicted joy-based discursive mental activities—excluding those that take odors and tastes as objects—and six types of equanimity-based discursive mental activities, which have the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*) as their basis.
The second, third, and fourth dhyānas, as well as the formless realms, should be understood to correspond to the application of discursive thought (*vitarka*) as previously explained.
By this principle, the remaining cases should be judged accordingly on one's own.

If a person has already been born into the realm of meditative concentration (dhyāna-bhūmi), they possess one type of mental application associated with equanimity within the desire realm, namely, the mind of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta) of the desire realm.
Other masters say:
there is such a meaning of mental application as established by the Vaibhāṣikas.
In the Sūtras, the meaning of "discursive mental activity" (*vitarka*) is seen to differ from this. Why?

Because if a person has become detached from a particular stage [of existence], that person cannot give rise to discursive mental activity directed toward that stage as an object. Therefore, although they may still be associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), not all instances of joy (*prīti*) and so forth constitute discursive mental activity of the mind.
If that is so, what constitutes "discursive investigation" (vikalpa-gati)?
It is either that which is afflicted or the mind; because it is by means of these that one can engage in discursive investigation regarding objects, they are called "discursive investigation."
What is the practice of discrimination?

It consists of either attachment to objects, aversion toward objects, or indifferent equanimity toward objects without discernment. To counteract these three, the Tathāgata taught the Dharma-gate of the six constant abidings.
As the Sūtra says:

"When seeing forms with the eye, one gives rise neither to a mind of joy nor to a mind of sorrow, but dwells in equanimity, possessing mindfulness and clear comprehension; and so it is, even up to the point where one cognizes all phenomena with the mind."
How is this known?

All Arhats do not lack the faculty of joy (*prīti-indriya*) arising from the worldly wholesome conditions of the Dharma; however, if there is defilement involved in their conceptual engagement, one should know that this Dharma-gate serves as the remedy for it.

Furthermore, there are thirty-six bases of serenity (śamatha-pāda) such as joy and so forth, distinguished by the differences between attachment and renunciation; this distinction is that which is taught in the Abhidharma.
In this context, that which relies on attachment is entirely defiled, while that which relies on renunciation is entirely wholesome.
Such factors of existence are termed "feeling" (*vedanā*); one should know that there are immeasurable distinctions among them. The remaining factors will not be explained further.
Why is it not so stated? For this reason,
the verse says:
"Because it has been explained and will be explained.
The commentary states:
Among these, some "possessors of parts" (avayavin) have already been explained previously, while others will be explained later.
Regarding the consciousness within this context, it has already been explained as stated in the verse:
"The aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is the act of cognizing each respective object;
it is sometimes called the sense-base of mind (manāyatana), or it is said to be the seven elements (dhātus), namely, the six consciousnesses and the mind-faculty (manas)."
The six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) have been explained previously, as the verse says:
"This consciousness, depending on translucent matter, is called the eye and other faculties.
Regarding formations and existence (*saṃskāra* and *bhava*), they shall be explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Craving and grasping among the afflictions will be explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Seven. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Eight.
Regarding the existence of action (*karma*) within conditioned existence (*bhava*), this shall be explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*. *Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.* *Middle Section: Analysis of the World, Part Three.*
Craving and grasping are among the afflictions; this will be explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.
Such dependent origination, if stated briefly, consists of only three categories: namely, afflictions, karma, and fruits.
These three meanings have already been explained previously.
The verse says:
Regarding these, the various afflictions are described as being like seeds and dragons, like roots, trees, and husks.
The commentary states:
In what way are these afflictions similar to seeds and so forth?
Just as sprouts, leaves, and other parts arise from a seed, so too do the categories of affliction and karma arise from affliction.
Furthermore, just as a pond where a nāga dwells is never exhausted, so too the stream of birth, wherein the nāga of afflictions dwells, continues without interruption.

Moreover, just as a tree whose roots have not been uprooted grows back again and again despite being cut down, so too the various paths of existence, whose roots of affliction have not been eradicated, arise again and again despite their cessation.
Furthermore, just as a tree produces flowers and seeds from time to time, so too do these afflictions repeatedly give rise to further afflictions and categories of karma.

Again, just as rice enclosed by its husk possesses the capacity for germination whereas the rice alone does not, so too karma enclosed by the husk of the acquisition (*prāpti*) of afflictions possesses the capacity for producing rebirth (*punarbhava*), whereas karma alone does not.
These various afflictions should be understood as being like seeds and so forth.
The verse says:
They are like rice with its husks, and like karma; they are also like paddy and flowers.
The commentary states:
It has already been explained above that afflictions (*kleśa*) are like husks; now it is explained that karma is like rice with its husk.
Furthermore, just as rice, plantains, and the like have their limit at the stage when the fruit has ripened, so too these various karmas, having already ripened, do not produce further retribution.
Furthermore, just as a flower is the proximate cause for the production of a seed, so too is karma the most proximate cause for the production of a karmic retribution.
As the verse says:
"Like cooked food and the like."
The commentary states:

Just as food and drink that have already been consumed are solely for the purpose of being experienced and cannot be transformed again into something else for the sake of production, so too is it with this category of retribution (*vipāka*):
it cannot further draw forth another retribution within a subsequent birth. If it were to draw forth further retribution, there would be no possibility of attaining liberation.

In this way, the continuity of birth arises depending on causes and depending on conditions; it does not exceed the four types of existence, namely: intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), existence at birth (*upapattibhava*), existence prior to death (*pūrvakālabhava*), and existence at death (*maraṇabhava*).
These four have already been explained previously.
The verse says:
Among the four types of existence, the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) is necessarily defiled.
The commentary states:
Among these, how many are determinate or indeterminate, and how many are defiled?
If they are exclusively defiled, they are solely *upapatti-bhava* (existence at birth).
By which afflictions?
The verse says:
By the various afflictions of its own level.
The commentary states:

If birth-existence (*upapattibhava*) occurs in this stage, all afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to that same stage constitute its defilement; there is not a single affliction within the three realms by which this sentient being does not undergo rebirth.
The Abhidharma masters explain it thus:
this defilement arises from the great afflictions (kleśa) and not from the secondary afflictions (upakleśa), because of their sovereignty.

If at this stage [of existence] one is most dull and obtuse, whichever affliction has previously arisen repeatedly or is most proximate will arise within this stage as defilement, due to its prior swiftness and sharpness.
When one encounters the conditioned within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), should one necessarily know it to be thus defiled?
The verse says:
"The other three."
The commentary states:
Regarding the remaining three types of existence—namely, intermediate existence (*antarābhava*) and so forth—each has three varieties, namely: wholesome, defiled, and indeterminate.
Among these various existences, how many are associated with which realm?
The verse says:
"Three in the formless realm.
The commentary says:
Excluding the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), what remains? Why is this so?

Because the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not a spatially distinct location, one does not arise in an intermediate state to reach it; whereas in the desire and form realms (*kāmadhātu* and *rūpadhātu*), it is not excluded. Thus, one knows that all possess the four states of existence (*catasro bhavas*).
The manner in which sentient beings arise based on causes and conditions has already been explained at length.
If sentient beings have already arisen, how do they abide?
The verse says:
"The world subsists by means of food.
The commentary explains:
There is one dharma that the Blessed One, having personally realized and known for himself, has correctly taught to others—namely, that all sentient beings subsist by means of food.
The Sūtra says this.
How many kinds of food are there?
There are four kinds.
The verse says:
"Edible food.
The commentary says:

Edible food is of two kinds: coarse and subtle. The subtle kind is the food of sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), who feed on fragrance; it also includes the food of the gods and of sentient beings at the beginning of a kalpa, because it does not undergo transformation into impure excretions.
This food entirely enters their bodies, like oil into sand.
Furthermore, if the sentient beings are minute, their food is also minute, such as the case with hair-mites and similar creatures.
The second is the nutriment of contact; the third is the nutriment of mental volition; the fourth is the nutriment of consciousness.
Regarding these, as for the nutriment of edible food, the verse says:
"In the desire realm."
The commentary states:
This nutriment does not exist in the form and formless realms, because birth occurs there through the abandonment of desire for them.
The verse says:
It has the three bases as its substance.
The commentary states:
Within the desire realm, all [objects] of the bases of odor, taste, and touch are called "edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*), because they are swallowed in morsels.
Because one first holds it in the mouth and nose, and subsequently swallows it bit by bit.
As for shadow, light, flame, and radiance, how could these constitute food?
Such a statement is made because they consist mostly [of such elements].

If these things, though not being eaten, can cause the continuity [of the body] to persist, they too would be included in the category of subtle nutriment (*sūkṣmāhāra*), such as bathing and ointments.
Why, then, is the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) not considered nutriment?
If one partakes of edible food, it must necessarily involve the sense-sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*).
The verse says:
Because it is not the sense-sphere of form, it does not benefit its own faculty, nor does it lead to liberation.
The commentary says:
What is this phenomenon called "nutriment"?
It is that which can benefit one's own sense faculties and the four great elements.

When the visual faculty (rūpāyatana) is engaged during the act of eating, it cannot benefit its own sense organ or the four great elements (mahābhūta), let alone benefit other organs or the four great elements;
for it is not its own objective domain.
Sometimes, upon seeing a form, pleasure and joy arise; yet this form itself is not nutriment.
Rather, by taking it as an object, it can produce contact that gives rise to pleasant feelings and so forth; it is this [contact] that serves as nutriment, not the form.
Furthermore, for those who have already attained liberation—namely, the *anāgāmins* and *arhats*—they perceive that even pleasant food and drink are of no benefit.
As the verse says:
"Contact, mental attention, and consciousness—these three flow through both [realms]."
The commentary states:
Contact arises from the conjunction of the three; attention is the activity of the mind; and consciousness is the mental consciousness.
If these three are with outflows (*sāsrava*), they are necessarily nutriments (*āhāra*); these three pervade the existence of all three realms.
Why is the untainted (*anāsrava*) not established as nutriment?

Because nutriment is established on the basis of the meaning of being able to nourish and increase all forms of existence (*bhava*), whereas the arising of the untainted leads to the total extinction of all existence; such is the position held by the Vaibhāṣika masters.

Furthermore, regarding the meaning of "nutriment" as taught in the sūtras, there are four kinds of nutriment. They serve to enable sentient beings who have already been born to subsist and to sustain their continuity, and they also serve to benefit sentient beings who are seeking birth.
Untainted phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) are not like this; therefore, they are not nutriment (*āhāra*).
Regarding "those already born," this refers to sentient beings who have already been born within the path; this meaning is easy to understand.
What, then, are those "seeking birth"?
The verse says:
"Mind-born, seeking birth, gandharva, intermediate existence, and that which faces existence.
The commentary says:
The World-Honored One uses these five names to describe beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Why is this?
Because these beings are born from the mind, they are called "mind-born" (*manomaya*); they do not take external impurities, blood, or any other such things as the basis for their birth.
Seeking birth means that because one desires to be born but has not yet attained it, one seeks birth everywhere.
As for the gandharva, it is so called because it feeds on fragrance; by means of this fragrance, its body is sustained as it proceeds toward the path of rebirth.
Regarding "facing existence" (*bhava-abhimukha*): it arises directed toward the place of birth.
As the Sūtra says:
"Facing [existence], one gives rise to that which obstructs and harms one's own self; one gives rise to that which obstructs and harms the world."
On account of this scriptural statement, there exists an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) that is a "being-in-existence" (*bhava*).
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"There are sentient beings for whom the fetter of being-in-existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*) has been exhausted, but not the fetter of birth (*upapattisaṃyojana*)."
In this sutra there are four phrases.
Furthermore, "those already born" refers to arhats;
"those seeking birth" refers to sentient beings possessed of craving.
Furthermore, how many kinds of nutriment cause already-born sentient beings to endure?
How many kinds of nutriment can nourish and benefit those seeking birth as sentient beings?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
All forms of nutriment are capable of performing two functions. Why is this?
Even edible food causes sentient beings who possess craving for existence to obtain future existence.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"There are four nutriments that serve as the root of disease, the sting of an ulcer, and the conditions for old age, death, and so forth.
It has also been observed that the nutriment of mental volition (*manasikāra-āhāra*) causes the present life to endure; thus say the ancient masters.
There was a father who, encountering the hardship of famine, hung a sack filled with ashes on a wall and consoled his two sons, telling them it was flour.
The two sons thought of the sack of flour repeatedly, and thus remained settled for a long time.
Later, when someone opens it for him, he realizes it is ashes; having lost his previous mental focus, he immediately passes away.
Furthermore, there were many people at sea whose ship was wrecked; seeing a great mass of foam, they thought it was land and headed toward it.
Upon arriving and touching it, he realizes it is a wave; losing his prior mental focus, he immediately passes away.
In another recension it is said:
There is a large-bodied sentient being in the ocean who comes ashore from the water, lays its eggs upon the sand, covers them with sand, and returns to the sea.
If the mother does not forget to attend to this egg, the egg will not perish;
if she loses mindfulness regarding it, the egg will perish.
The Sautrāntikas explain that this is not so, lest one’s own food become [the food] of another simply by virtue of another eating it.
If one explains it thus:
therein, if the egg is mindful of the mother and does not forget her, the egg will not perish;
if it forgets, it perishes.
Other masters say:
"This recollection occurs during the stage of contact (*sparśa*).
If so, why is it said that there are only four nutriments?
Is it not so? All contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are necessarily able to nourish existence (*bhava*); nevertheless, they are spoken of [as such] by virtue of their predominance.
The verse says:
For the sake of benefiting both this supported [consciousness] and its support [the body], two further distinct existences are drawn forth; these are explained in sequence as the latter two.
The commentary states:
"The support" refers to the body endowed with sense faculties; for the nourishment of this body, edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) is preeminent.
The "supported" refers to the mind and mental factors; for the nourishment of these factors, the nutriment of contact is preeminent.
Thus, these two nutriments are superior to others in nourishing the existence already arisen in the present life.

Furthermore, regarding the establishment of attention (*manasikāra*) as nutriment: it is preeminent for projecting future existence (*punarbhava*). This projected existence arises from the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) perfumed by karma.
Thus, these latter two [nutriments] are preeminent for projecting and generating unarisen existence.
The first two types of nutriment are like a wet nurse, for they are able to nourish that which has already been born;
the latter two are like a biological mother, for they are able to give birth to that which is yet unborn.
Because they are superior to the others, only four are established.
Are all portions that are swallowed considered edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?
There are portions that are swallowed but are not edible food; regarding this, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*). As for the first permutation:
if one swallows such a portion, it causes the sense faculties (*indriya*) to deteriorate and harms the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
The second phrase refers to the remaining three nutriments.
The third phrase refers to that which is swallowed in morsels, which can nourish the sense faculties and increase the four great elements.
The fourth case consists of those instances excluded by the preceding three cases.
In this same manner, for contact and the other [nutriments], four cases should each be established according to reason.
Is there that which, having contact and so forth as its object, brings nourishment to the sense faculties and growth to the four great elements, yet is not itself nutriment?
There is [such food], namely that which belongs to other stages and that which is untainted (*anāsrava*).
The remaining phrases should be considered as follows:

if a person eats this food and it diminishes the faculties (*indriya*) and the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) of the eater, this substance is also food, because it is grasped as being "present" (*pratyutpanna*).
Why is this? Edible food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra) serves as sustenance during two periods:
when it is being consumed, it counteracts the primary illness; when it is being digested, it increases the physical mass. Thus say the Vaibhāṣika masters.
In which realms are there how many types of nutriment?
In all realms, all four types of nutriment exist; it is the same regarding birth.
How can there be edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) in the hells?
There are those who take glowing red iron fragments as food and molten red iron as drink.
If anything that can cause harm were also considered "food," it would contradict the preceding four propositions and also contradict the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
That treatise states:
"What is edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?

It is that which, when taken as a morsel, nourishes the sense faculties, increases the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and causes their continuity to flourish; it is the same for consciousness (*vijñāna*). The detailed explanation is as in the treatise."
Because this is stated in reference to food that provides nourishment (*upacaya*), there is no contradiction.
Food that causes harm (*apacaya*) also possesses the characteristic of being food within the hells. Why is this so?
This food is capable of temporarily warding off the afflictions of hunger, thirst, and so forth.

Furthermore, there are other places within the hells where, just as in the human realm, there is substantial food (kavaḍīkāra-āhāra); therefore, it is logical that substantial food exists throughout all five destinies. This principle should be accepted as such.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:

"If someone were to give food to a hundred sages who are free from desire and beyond the realm of desire, and another person were to give food to a single ordinary person (pṛthagjana), the latter person walking in the Jambū Grove would have merit hundreds of thousands of times greater than the former gift."
What ordinary person is walking in the Jambū-vana grove?
Other masters say:
it is one who dwells in Jambudvīpa.
Some say: "This is a meritorious ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
This adherence is incorrect, because it is stated to be "one."

In this regard, what is the reason that the merit of giving food to a single ordinary person is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who are free from desire? It would be logical for the merit of giving food to many ordinary persons to surpass that of giving to a single ordinary person. However, [the former] is superior. Why is this so? Because the recipient is more distinguished. Just as the merit of giving to one who is free from desire surpasses that of giving to one who is not free from desire, so too does the merit of giving to one who has attained the fruit of stream-entry surpass that of giving to one who is merely free from desire. Therefore, it is established that the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has attained the fruit of stream-entry is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who are free from desire. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has entered the path of cultivation is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have attained the fruit of stream-entry. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has entered the path of cultivation is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have attained the fruit of stream-entry. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has attained the fruit of once-returning is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have entered the path of cultivation. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has attained the fruit of once-returning is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have entered the path of cultivation. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has attained the fruit of non-returning is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have attained the fruit of once-returning. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has attained the fruit of non-returning is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have attained the fruit of once-returning. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single ordinary person who has entered the path of arhatship is greater than that of giving to many ordinary persons who have attained the fruit of non-returning. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is greater than that of giving to many noble disciples who are beyond training. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha is greater than that of giving to many Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha is greater than that of giving to many Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single Buddha, the World-Honored One, is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single Buddha, the World-Honored One, is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas. This is because the recipient is most distinguished. As it is said in a sutra: "If a person were to fill the great trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and offer them to the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, their merit would still be inferior to that of a person who, having heard the Dharma from a Buddha, World-Honored One, gives rise to a mind of faith, even if only for a moment. This is because the recipient is most distinguished. Therefore, it is established that the merit of giving to a single Buddha, the World-Honored One, is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha is greater than that of giving to many Buddhas, World-Honored Ones. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha who has entered the path of cultivation is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas who have attained the fruit of arhatship. This is because the recipient is even more distinguished. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha who has entered the path of cultivation is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas who have attained the fruit of arhatship. Furthermore, the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha who has attained the fruit of arhatship is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas who have entered the path of cultivation. Thus, it is established that the merit of giving to a single Pratyekabuddha who has attained the fruit of arhatship is greater than that of giving to many Pratyekabuddhas who have entered the path of cultivation. Other masters say:
"This refers to a bodhisattva who is close to the stage of Buddhahood.
Other masters do not accept this interpretation.
Why is this? If one gives to this bodhisattva, the merit is greatest and incalculable.
The merit obtained from giving to such a person is such that even giving to a hundred koṭis of arhats would not equal it.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:

there are ordinary persons who have already attained the capacity for the analytical discernment (*viniścaya*) of the contemplation of the Four Truths; these are here said to be "wandering in the dense grove of Jambū."

This name does not correspond to its meaning, nor has it ever been established as such elsewhere; for in the Sūtras and the Abhidharma-piṭaka, it is taught that by walking in the Jambūvana grove, one necessarily attains the capacity for the stage of "discrimination" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) regarding the contemplation of the Four Truths. Therefore, this [assertion] is merely your own fabrication.
If that is so, how is it? This statement must be understood as referring specifically to the time when the Bodhisattva was walking within the dense grove of Jambūvana. Why is this?

At this time, because this bodhisattva accords with both the state of an ordinary person and the state of one who has abandoned desire for the realm of desire, he is distinguished from other sages; compared to them, he is infinitely and immeasurably superior.
As for the reward of a hundredfold, it follows what was previously established; this principle must necessarily be so.
Why? Because, setting aside this person, one must evaluate an external seer (ṛṣi) by the standard of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna).
If it were not so, one would have to measure the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) by the pace of walking through the Jambūvan grove.
Having thus explained the meaning of how sentient beings arise based on causes and conditions, and how sentient beings abide.
The meaning of the death and falling of sentient beings has already been explained—that it occurs through the exhaustion of merit, not through the exhaustion of the life-span, and so forth.
This point shall now be discussed:
at the precise moment when which consciousness arises do sentient beings undergo death and take rebirth?
The verse says:
The severance and reconnection of roots of goodness, the departure from desire, falling back, death, and rebirth—these matters occur within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The commentary says:

The severance of the roots of goodness, the reconnection of the roots of goodness, the departure from desire in the lower realms, and the falling away from or rebirth in the higher realms—these six dharmas are accomplished within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and not in any other consciousness.
Since birth is mentioned, the sense of "relying upon" the intermediate state (antarābhava) is also implied.
How does this apply to the experience of death and birth?
The verse says:
Regarding death and birth occurring within the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*),
the commentary states:

both the mind at the moment of casting off life and the mind at the moment of taking birth exist within the feeling that is neither painful nor pleasant (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*), because this feeling is dull and indistinct.
Other sensations are clear; death and birth do not occur within a consciousness that is clear.
Regarding this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the verse says:
"Not one, nor two, nor mindless."
The commentary states:
Although death and birth occur within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), they do not occur in a single moment of mind nor in a state devoid of mind. Why is this?

If a person is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita-citta*), there is no possibility of death or rebirth, because the stage [of concentration] is not of the same category [as the realm of birth], because it is produced through effort, and because it is capable of providing benefit.
One cannot die while in a state of mindlessness. Why is this?
Because for one who is without mind, there can be no untimely harm.

At that time, if a transformation of the basis is about to arise, then at that moment the mind belonging to that basis will necessarily arise and manifest; only thereafter does one relinquish life, and not otherwise.
If it were the case that there is no mind at the moment of rebirth, that too would not be possible, because the cause for the cessation of the mind would not exist;
furthermore, one cannot undergo rebirth apart from the afflictions of the higher realms.
Therefore, it is not logical for there to be no mind therein.
There are three types of death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*), as previously explained.
The verse says:
Nirvana is of two kinds of neutral (avyākṛta).
The commentary states:
Within the mind of deportment and the mind of maturation (vipāka), if within the desire realm (kāmadhātu), that which is called maturation is termed "equanimity" (upekṣā).
If it were absent, one would attain parinirvāṇa within the mind of deportment (*airyāpathika*).
Why does this occur only in the neutral (*avyākṛta*) mind and not in other minds?
It is because this neutral state is conducive to the cessation of the mind, owing to its weak power.
When a person is dying, in which part of the body does the mental consciousness cease?
If death occurs instantaneously, the body faculty and the mental consciousness perish simultaneously.
Regarding the sequential death of a person, a verse here states:
"In sequential death, [the faculties cease] at the feet, the navel, and the heart; consciousness is severed. One is not reborn among the lower realms, humans, or gods.
The commentary explains:

If a person is destined to be reborn in the evil realms, or in the human or celestial realms, for such a person, the cessation occurs sequentially at the feet, the navel, and the heart-mind consciousness.
Not undergoing further rebirth is called "non-arising," referring to the Arhat; for such a person, the mind, intellect, and consciousness have been severed.
Other schools state that this occurs at the crown of the head.
Why is this? Because the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) perishes together with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in these locations.
When a person is dying, this body-faculty gradually diminishes like water on a hot stone, ceasing successively in the feet and other parts of the body.
Furthermore, if sentient beings die according to this sequence, among them many are only able to die after being oppressed by the painful sensations resulting from the severing of the *marmans*.
What is meant by the "severing of the *marmans*"?
The verse says:
"The *marmans*, water, and so forth.
The commentary explains:
The *marmans* (vital points) are specific locations within the body.
As a verse says:
"There are certain locations in the body, by being touched at which one dies."
"If an *utpala* flower is touched by even a single mote of dust on its filaments.
Thus we know that there are specific locations within the body; if these are damaged or touched, they can induce death, and these parts of the body are called the *marmans*.

Regarding these vital points (*marmāṇi*), if even one of the three elements—water, wind, or fire—arises in a state of mutual opposition, it is as if they were being struck by a sharp blade; they are immediately destroyed.

This is unlike firewood or similar objects which, when cut, are simply severed; rather, like something that has been cut, they no longer possess movement or sensation, and for this reason they are said to be "cut."
Why is it not caused by the earth element?
Because the fourth type of disease does not exist.

The three diseases of wind, heat, and phlegm have the elements of wind, fire, and water as their respective primary causes, respectively; because they resemble the three calamities of the external vessel-world, there are thus three calamities within the internal body.

Regarding those who die from the painful sensation of having their vital points (*marmans*) severed, this [retribution] arises most frequently for such a person; that is to say, because they repeatedly performed the act of severing the vital points of others, this person will necessarily die from the painful sensation of having their own vital points severed.
Among the gods, there is no death accompanied by the suffering of the vital points (*marmans*).
Nevertheless, when a son of the gods is destined to fall from his celestial realm, five minor signs of transformation first appear:

first, his garments and ornaments emit unpleasant sounds; second, the radiance of his body becomes dim; third, when bathing, drops of water remain clinging to his body; fourth, his mind, which formerly roamed among sensory objects, now dwells fixed upon a single object; and fifth, his eyes blink.
These five signs may sometimes be uncertain;
however, there are another five kinds of great signs of transformation that appear when death is inevitably unavoidable:

first, one's clothing becomes stained with dust and filth; second, flower garlands wither and dry out; third, sweat breaks out from under the armpits; fourth, a foul odor enters the body; and fifth, one is unable to sit comfortably in one's own seat.
Such is the world of sentient beings, with such arising, abiding, and passing away.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, establishes and categorizes sentient beings into three groups.
There are three kinds of groups:
First, the group of those fixed in the right; second, the group of those fixed in the wrong; third, the group of those who are not fixed.
Regarding this, a verse says:
"The groups fixed in the right and fixed in the wrong [are characterized by] the noble ones and the uninterrupted [karmas]."
The commentary states:
What constitutes "correct"?

It is the exhaustion of desire without remainder, the exhaustion of hatred without remainder, and the exhaustion of delusion without remainder; because all afflictions are exhausted without remainder, it is called "correct."
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra.
Regarding "Noble One" (ārya): if the untainted path (anāsrava-mārga) has already arisen within this person's continuum, they are therefore called a Noble One.
Why are they called "Noble"?
They are called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*) because they are able to emerge far from the states that lead to evil; this is due to their attainment of the fruit of cessation, which is certain and eternal.
Such persons are called "rightly established" (*samyaktva-niyata*) because they are fixed by the exhaustion of their afflictions (*kleśa*).

If a person has already attained the capacity for the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and their roots of goodness are destined for *nirvāṇa* as their nature, why is such a person not established as being of right determination (*samyaktvaniyata*)?
For this person may later fall into wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyata*).
This person does not attain certainty through fixed time, but attains certainty precisely at midday,
like the seven victors and others.
What constitutes the heterodox?
The realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts are called "wrong" (*mithyā*).
Because those who commit the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*) are certain to be reborn within the realm of hell, they are said to be "fixed in the wrong" (*mithyātva-niyata*).
If it is distinct from the two types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), then the remainder is not concentration; this meaning is established by itself.
These three aggregates are observed as being subject to causes and conditions, and they belong either to the two [realms] or do not belong to the two.
Having already explained the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Within this, the receptacle world is said to rest upon a lower foundation; it is sixteen *lakṣas* deep, and the wind-circle is immeasurable in breadth.
The commentary says:
In the trichiliocosm, the Buddhas have taught that it rests upon a wind-circle at the very bottom, which abides in emptiness and is produced by the predominant karma of sentient beings.
This wind-circle is sixteen *lakṣa* yojanas in thickness, while its length and breadth are incalculable; it is as solid and firm as this.
Even if a person with the strength of Mahānagna were to strike and hurl a vajra-pestle at it, the vajra would shatter and break, yet the wind-circle would suffer no damage.
Upon the wind-circle, the verse says:
"The water-circle is eleven [yojanas] deep, plus twenty thousand.
The commentary says:
Upon the wind-circle, through the predominant influence of the karma of sentient beings, clouds gather and rain down drops as large as great pillars.
This water-circle is thus formed, with a depth of eleven lakṣas and twenty thousand yojanas.
Why does the water wheel not flow out sideways within it?
It is due to the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings.
For example, just as when food and drink have not yet been digested, they do not fall into the receptacle for digested food (*pakvāśaya*); so say other teachers.
Alternatively, according to the Sautrāntika school, it does not flow away because it is sustained by wind, as is the principle for food.

Furthermore, this water is produced by the superior power of the karma of sentient beings; a distinct wind-element blows and turns this water so that gold forms upon its surface, like the cream that rises on top of boiled milk.
The verse says:
The water is eight *lakṣas* thick; the remainder is all gold.
The commentary says:
How much remains? Three *lakṣas* and twenty thousand *yojanas* constitute the Golden Wheel (*kāñcanamaṇḍala*), which rests upon the Water Wheel (*apmaṇḍala*).
The thickness of both the Water Wheel and the Golden Wheel has already been explained.
The verse says:
The diameter is three thousand, plus four hundred and a half, and twelve *lakṣas*; such is the extent of the water and gold wheels.
The commentary says:
The diameters of these two wheels are equal.
The verse says:
"If the circumference is threefold."
The commentary states:
If calculated by its perimeter, the number becomes threefold, totaling thirty-six *lakṣas*, ten thousand three hundred and fifty *yojanas*.
The wheel of golden earth rests upon the waters.
Within this earth, the verse says:
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains; Mount Yugandhara; Mount Īṣādhara; Mount Khadiraka; Mount Sudarśana; Mount Aśvakarṇa; Mount Vinataka; and Mount Nimindhara.
The commentary states: These mountains rest upon the golden wheel of earth.

At the center of the eight great mountains is Mount Sumeru; the remaining mountains surround Mount Sumeru, namely: first, Yugandhara; second, Īṣādhara; third, Kailāsa; fourth, Sudarśana; fifth, Aśvakarṇa; sixth, Vinataka; and seventh, Nimindhara.
This Mount Sumeru is surrounded by seven mountain ranges; the outermost mountain range is named Nimindhara.
A verse says:
Outside the four great continents, there is further the Cakravāḍa mountain.
The commentary states:
Beyond the seventh mountain range lie the four great continents; beyond these four great continents lies the Iron Rim Mountain (*Cakravāḍa*).
Because of this mountain, the world is circular in shape like a wheel.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"Seven are of gold; this one is of iron.
The commentary explains:
The seven mountains, beginning with Cakravāḍa, are all composed of gold; this outermost mountain is composed solely of iron.
The verse says:
"Sumeru consists of four jewels."
The commentary states:
In terms of its four sides, it is composed, respectively, of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Because the light of each side corresponds to the nature of the jewel that constitutes it, the empty space in all directions manifests colors that resemble those original jewels.
On the side of Mount Sumeru facing Jambudvīpa, there is a region composed of lapis lazuli; because it is illuminated by the radiance of this gem, the sky appears blue, resembling lapis lazuli.
Furthermore, how do such jewels come into being?

Upon the golden ground, there arise clouds that rain down drops as large as axle-trees; this water serves as the womb for various seeds and possesses diverse distinctions of majestic power. The wind blows upon and transforms this water, turning it into various kinds of precious jewels.

Such a transformation constitutes the production of distinct categories of phenomena, both general and particular; this is possible through the principle that causes and conditions function neither by pre-existence nor by simultaneous existence, and thus differs from the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*) established by the non-Buddhist Sāṃkhya school.
Regarding the Sāṃkhya theory of transformation (*pariṇāma*): this entity already exists previously and then transforms into a different dharma.
If that were so, what fault would there be? This existing dharma [of yours] is unintelligible.
This dharma already exists; it is because of the conceptual differentiation of other dharmas within it that one speaks thus.
A dharma is distinct from its own existence, yet this nature of the dharma is not different; it is merely the manifestation of a distinct characteristic that is termed "transformation."
If that were so, it would likewise not be logical.
Why is it not logical?
Because this very thing is that, yet that very thing is not this; such a state has never existed before.
This explains the underlying principle.

Through such a process, once gold and other various treasures have already been produced and accumulated, a distinct wind arises through the power of karma; this wind draws these treasures together into one place, thereby forming mountains and continents.
The locations where these are taken form the inner and outer oceans, Mount Sumeru and the other mountains, ending with the Iron Rim Mountains (*Cakravāḍa*).
The verse says:
"Entering the water by eighty thousand [yojanas]."
The commentary states:
Upon the golden ground there is water eight thousand *yojanas* deep, into which the various mountains gradually sink.
The verse says:
This mountain rises above the water for eighty thousand yojanas.
The commentary states:
Thus, Mount Sumeru is sixteen thousand yojanas in height.
The verse says:
"The eight mountains decrease by half each.
The commentary says:
From the Gandhamādana Mountain, it rises forty thousand yojanas above the water and extends halfway down toward Mount Sumeru.
Mount Īṣādhara extends halfway down from Mount Gandhamādana.
In this manner, it should be understood that for all the mountains, the height successively decreases by half.
Down to the Cakravāḍa Iron Rim Mountains, the height is half that of Mount Nimindhara, being three hundred and twelve and a half yojanas.
The verse says:
"Its height and breadth are equal.
The commentary says:
Just as the height of the mountains above the water, their breadth is likewise.
The verse says:
"Between them are the seven seas."
The commentary states:
Nimiṃdhara is the last [of the mountain ranges], and between them lie seven seas filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
This water is cool, delicious, light, soft, and fragrant; when drunk, it does not irritate the throat, and once consumed, it benefits the internal elements without harming the stomach.
Regarding these seven seas, the verse says:
"The first sea is eighty thousand [yojanas].
The commentary says:
Within Mount Cakravāḍa, the first ocean is eighty thousand yojanas wide.
The verse says:
This is called the Inner Ocean.
The commentary states:
There are two kinds of oceans, the first being internal and the second external.
Regarding this internal ocean within these two mountains, the verse says:
"Each side is threefold.
The commentary explains:

It has already been stated that this ocean is eighty thousand *yojanas* wide; if one calculates from the inner edge of Mount Gandhamādana, each side is threefold, and thus its total width amounts to two *lakṣas* and forty thousand *yojanas*.
The verse says:
"The remaining oceans decrease by half and half.
The commentary says:
Between these two mountains, Gandhamādana and Isadhara, lies the second sea; it is half as narrow as the first sea and forty thousand yojanas in breadth.

The second is half as wide as the first, and the third is half as wide as that; by this successive halving of the width, one should know the measurements of the remaining [rings], up to the seventh, which is twelve hundred and fifty yojanas wide.
The great dimension is not mentioned because it arises from many distinct dimensions.
The verse says:
"The remainder is called the outer ocean."
The commentary says:
What is meant by "the rest"?
The area between Mount Nimindhara and Mount Cakravāḍa is called the Outer Great Ocean. This ocean is filled with salt water of an intensely salty taste, and its breadth is measured in yojanas.
The verse says:
Three *lakṣas*, twenty thousand, and two thousand.
The commentary says:
The measure of the great ocean is thus.
The verse says:
"Within it."
The commentary states:
There are four great continents situated on the four sides of Mount Sumeru.
The verse says:
Jambudvīpa is two thousand [yojanas] in extent; its three sides are shaped like a chariot.
The commentary states:
Within this ocean, one side of Jambudvīpa is two thousand yojanas, while its other three sides are equal in measure, resembling the shape of a chariot.
In the center of this continent, a diamond throne (*vajrāsana*) rises from the golden ground, penetrating through the earth of Jambudvīpa and reaching level with its upper limit.
All bodhisattvas sit within it and cultivate the diamond-like samādhi (*vajrasamādhi*).
Why is this? Because there is no other basis or locus capable of sustaining this samādhi.
The verse says:
"One and a half yojanas.
The commentary states:
The width of this fourth side is three and a half yojanas; therefore, this continent has the appearance of a chariot.
The verse says:
"The Eastern Continent is like a half-moon.
The commentary says:
From this continent, proceeding toward the east, opposite the side of Mount Sumeru, there is a continent named Pūrvavideha that emerges from the sea; its shape is like a half-moon.
Regarding the measurement of its sides, the verse says:
"Three sides are equal."
The commentary states:
The three sides of this continent are like the three sides of Jambudvīpa, each measuring two thousand yojanas.
The verse says:
"Each of the other three sides is three hundred and fifty yojanas.
The commentary states:
"This refers to the fourth side, which is three hundred and fifty yojanas wide."
The verse says:
Aparagoyānī is circular, measuring seven thousand five hundred yojanas.
The commentary says:

To the west of this continent, directly opposite the side of Mount Sumeru, there is a continent named Aparagoyānī; it measures seven thousand five hundred yojanas in circumference, and its shape is circular like the full moon.
The verse says:
Its diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas].
The commentary says:
Its center is two thousand five hundred yojanas wide.
The verse says:
"Kuru is eight thousand, etc."
The commentary states:

To the north of this continent, directly opposite the side of Mount Sumeru, there is a continent named Uttarakuru. It measures eight thousand yojanas in circumference and is square in shape with four equal sides. Its dimensions are comparable to those of Videha; each side is exactly two thousand yojanas, and the other sides are likewise identical, without the slightest increase or decrease.
In accordance with the characteristics of each continent, the facial features of the sentient beings dwelling therein are likewise.
Between these four continents, there arise various other islands; what are the names and locations of these islands?
The verse says:
"The two Dehas and Kuru, Cāmara and Śāṭhā; in between there are eight islands, including Śaṅkha and Uttaramantriṇa. The commentary says: [These are the names of the subcontinents.]
Within this [continent], there are two subcontinents: first, Deha, and second, Videha; these belong to Pūrvavideha because they are of its same category.
Furthermore, there are two other subcontinents: first, Kuru, and second, Kaurava; these belong to Uttarakuru because they are of its same category.
Furthermore, there are two other continents: first, Śāṭhāha, and second, Uttarakuru; these belong to Aparagoyānī, as they are of its kind.
Furthermore, there are two other continents: first, Camara, and second, Aparacamara; these belong to Jambudvīpa, as they are of its kind.
All these continents are inhabited by humans; only the single continent of Aparacāmara is inhabited by rākṣasas.
The verse says:
In this region to the north, at the edge of the nine mountains, lies the Snowy Mountain (Himavat).
The commentary states:

Within this continent of Jambudvīpa, there are three Black Mountains to the north; beyond these three Black Mountains, there are another three Black Mountains; and beyond those three Black Mountains, there are yet another three Black Mountains. Because all these mountains are low, they are called the Ant Mountains (Valāhakaparvata).
To the north of the nine mountains lies the Snowy Mountain (Himavat); from the Snowy Mountain toward the northern lands, the verse says:
"Between the Fragrant Mountain and the Snowy Mountain, there is a lake fifty yojanas wide."
The commentary states:
On the northern side of the Snowy Mountains and the southern side of the Fragrant Mountain, this location is most excellent.
Therein lies a lake named Anavatapta, from which four great rivers flow: first, the Gaṅgā; second, the Sindhu; third, the Sītā; and fourth, the Vakṣu.

This pond is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, filled everywhere with water possessing the eight virtues; it is not a place frequented by humans, and can only be traversed by those possessed of supernormal powers.
The mountain on the southern side of this lake is twenty-five yojanas high, while the mountain on the northern side is fifty yojanas high; these two mountains are composed of various materials.

From the most excellent location on the northern side of Gandhamādana Mountain, there is a rock named Nanda, composed of the seven precious gems, measuring fifty yojanas in both length and breadth, which serves exclusively as the dwelling place of the Elephant King.

From here, one traverses six lands and crosses seven layers of forests and seven layers of rivers; beyond the seventh river are two more forests shaped like half-moons. To the north of these forests grows the Jambu tree, which is one hundred yojanas high; when its fruit ripens, its flavor is incomparably delicious.
Because the fruit of this tree is the highest in stature and the most exquisite in flavor, the continent is named Jambudvīpa after it.
Where are the hells located,
and what is their number?
The verse says:
Twenty thousand [yojanas] downward, the Avīci hell is as wide.
The commentary says:
Twenty thousand yojanas beneath this Jambudvīpa lies a hell named Avīci, twenty thousand yojanas in both depth and breadth.
From its floor to its top it extends forty thousand yojanas; because within it there is uninterrupted suffering, it is called Avīci.
Why is this? Because in other hells, there are intervals between the experiences of suffering.

For instance, in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell, when the bodies of sentient beings have been cut, split, or pounded, a cold wind blows upon them and they are restored to life; therefore, it is called the Saṃjīva Hell.
In the *Abhidharma*, there is no such matter.
Other masters say:
because there is no pleasure interspersed with suffering therein, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*).
Why is this? Because although there is no pleasant retribution (*vipāka-phala*) in other hells, it does not preclude the presence of the concordant result (*niṣyanda-phala*).
The verse says:
"Above there are seven hells. The commentary states:

Above this Avīci Hell, there are seven kinds of hells arranged in successive layers: first, Mahāraurava (Great Screaming); second, Raurava (Screaming); third, Mahāraurava (Great Screaming); fourth, Raurava (Screaming); fifth, Saṃghāta (Crushing); sixth, Kālasūtra (Black Line); and seventh, Sañjīva (Reviving).
Other schools state:
These seven hells are located on the four sides of the Avīci hell.
Regarding these eight hells, the verse says:
Eighty-six parks.
The commentary states:
Each of these hells has sixteen parks.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"These eight hells, which I declare are difficult to cross, are filled with those who have committed the most heinous deeds; each possesses sixteen gardens."
On its four sides are four gates, equal in size and equipped with all manner of instruments of harm.
Encircled by an iron city, the six directions are all of iron plates;
the iron ground is entirely scorched and hot, with fierce fires constantly blazing through it.
"Extending for countless hundreds of yojanas, it is filled everywhere with intersecting flames.
What are the sixteen gardens?
The verse says:
"Heat Ashes," "Corpse," "The Path of Blades," and so forth, as well as the "Fierce River"—these are situated at the four directions [of each hell].
The commentary states:
At the four sides of these eight hells, there are four types of groves facing each respective gate.

First is the Garden of Hot Ashes, which is knee-deep; when sentient beings set foot within it, their flesh and blood immediately rot away entirely, like drops of wax falling onto red-hot iron, yet when they lift their feet, the flesh and blood grow back again.

Second is the Śmaśāna (Cemetery) Garden; this garden is filled everywhere with corpses, and the ground is entirely composed of excrement. Within it there is an insect named Khañjāda, white-bodied and black-headed, with a mouth as sharp as a needle; it pierces the skin, flesh, and bones of those sentient beings and devours their marrow.

In the third, the Garden of the Path of Razor Blades, there is a great road densely covered with sharp razor blades; when sentient beings set foot upon it, their flesh and blood are all sliced and destroyed, yet as soon as they lift their feet, the flesh and blood grow back again.

Furthermore, there is the Sword-Leaf Forest Garden (*Asipattravana*), wherein weapons such as red-hot swords fall when blown by the wind, hacking and piercing the bodies and limbs of those sentient beings.

Furthermore, there is the Iron Śālmali Forest, where the sharp thorns are sixteen inches long. Within it, sentient beings move either upward or downward; if they go up, the thorns point their heads downward, and if they go down, the thorns point their heads upward, piercing the bodies of those sentient beings until their flesh and blood are completely exhausted.
Within that place, there are also dogs of black and brindled color, each seizing those sentient beings to devour them.
Furthermore, there are iron-beaked crows that peck at and eat the hearts and eyes of those sentient beings.
Because these three types of sentient beings—the Path of Sword Blades and the others—are all equally harmed by weapons, they are combined into a single garden.

Fourth is the Garden of the River of Fierce Ash-Lye; the river is named Vaitaraṇī and is filled with intensely burning water of ash-lye. If sentient beings enter it, there are people on both banks holding swords, spears, tridents, and other weapons, who block them and prevent them from reaching the surface.
The sentient beings therein either leap upward or sink downward, or revolve horizontally as they are steamed and cooked.
It is like a great cauldron filled with water over a fierce fire, wherein rice, beans, sesame, wheat, and the like are steamed and cooked; so too it is with those sentient beings.

This River Garden is like the moat of the Great Hell; because these four gardens differ according to their directions, they constitute sixteen. They are called "gardens" (ārāma) because they are places of extreme slaughter, affliction, and suffering.
Other masters say:
Because one enters and exits from within the hells and further sinks into suffering there, it is called a "garden" (udyāna).
From this question, another question arises: Are these hell-wardens sentient beings or non-sentient beings?
It is said that they are not sentient beings.
If that is so, how do they move?
It is by means of the karma of sentient beings, just as, for example, the winds that form the world-system [arise].
If that is so, how should one interpret the verse spoken by the Venerable Dharmasubhūti:
"Those who are constantly angry, whose most coarse karma is malice, Who take delight in evil,
and who find joy in seeing the suffering of others, Will surely become the henchmen of Yama."

These hell-wardens, because they cast sentient beings into the hells by the command of the King, are called the Rākṣasas of King Yama; it is not the former [the wardens] who, having performed the act of killing, are established as sentient beings.
Other schools say:
"They are all sentient beings.
If that is so, where else would this karma receive its retribution?
One shall experience retribution in this very place. Why is this?
Because one is born in this place due to the retribution of past evil karma, and having further committed evil karma therein, one experiences the retribution right there.

If that is so, regarding the place where beings who have committed an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*) undergo their retribution: what dharma exists therein to obstruct them from receiving this retribution?
And how is it that they are not burned while remaining within the fire?
Do you think in this way?
Since karma belongs to fire, it is not burned.
Being born within this [realm], how could one be different from others; why then would one be a "sudden" (or "violent") death?
These eight types are called the hot hells.
The verse says:
"The eight cold hells are Arbuda and so forth."
The commentary states:
Furthermore, there are eight other cold hells: first, Arbuda; second, Nirarbuda; third, Aṭaṭa; fourth, Apapa; fifth, Huhuva; sixth, Utpala; seventh, Padma; and eighth, Puṇḍarīka.
Among these eight, sentient beings are oppressed by extreme cold; they are thus named according to the transformations of their bodies, voices, and sores.
These eight are situated beneath Jambudvīpa, adjacent to the great hells.
Since Jambudvīpa is of such vast extent, how can it accommodate the locations of the hells, such as Avīci?
The continents widen toward the bottom, like a heap of grain; therefore, the great ocean gradually deepens in succession.
These sixteen hells are produced by the predominant karma of all sentient beings.
There are also separate locations of hell produced by the individual karma of sentient beings, where many people may gather together, or two, or even one.

These various distinct hells differ in many ways and their locations are not fixed; they may be situated by a river, on a mountain slope, in a wilderness, or in other places. While the primary location of the hell-realm is always below, these specific sites vary.
The realms of animals are threefold: namely, on land, in water, and in the air. The great ocean is their primary abode; from the ocean, they travel to other places.

For ghosts and spirits, the realm of King Yama is the primary abode. This king’s domain lies five hundred *yojanas* deep beneath Jambudvīpa; there is a great kingdom there, measuring five hundred *yojanas* in length and breadth, which is the original dwelling place of these ghosts and spirits. From this primary abode, they disperse to other locations.

Within the realm of ghosts and spirits, there are those with great merit, karma, and supernormal powers who enjoy wealth and pleasure as if they were in the heavens; other ghosts and spirits are as described in the *Ghosts and Spirits’ Fundamental Karma Sūtra*.
Furthermore, where do the moon and the sun reside?
They abide within the wind. Why is this so?

This wind arises in the sky through the dominant influence of the collective karma of sentient beings; it revolves around Mount Sumeru like a swirling eddy, and is able to sustain and govern the sun, the moon, and the stars.
How many yojanas above this continent do the sun and moon travel?
The verse says:
"The sun and moon [are at] half the height of Mount Meru."
The commentary says:
It is level with the summit of Mount Yugandhara; such is its course.
What are the dimensions of the moon and the sun?
The verse says:
Fifty-one yojanas.
The commentary says:

The diameter of the lunar disk is fifty yojanas; the diameter of the solar disk is fifty-one yojanas; as for the dimensions of the various stellar disks, the smallest is one krośa in diameter, while the largest is sixteen yojanas.
The outer edge of the lower surface of the solar disc is composed of *sphaṭika* (crystal) gems; these are all fire-pearls, and this gem is capable of both heating and illuminating.
The outer edge of the lower surface of the lunar disc is composed of *candrakānta* (moon-loved) gems; these are all water-pearls, and this gem is capable of both cooling and illuminating.

Through the karma of sentient beings, the moon possesses the capacity to bring about benefit or harm, as appropriate, regarding the eyes, bodies, fruits, flowers, grains, sprouts, and medicinal herbs.
Within the four continents, a single moon alone is able to perform these acts of benefit and harm; the same applies to the sun.
Does this single sun perform the functions of the sun simultaneously for all four continents? No. Why is it not so?
Regarding this, a verse says:
"Midnight, sunset, midday, and sunrise occur at the same time.
The commentary says:
When it is exactly midnight in Uttarakuru, at that time the sun is setting in Pūrvavideha, it is midday in Jambudvīpa, and it is rising in Aparagoyānī.
In other instances, the principle is the same throughout.
Within this continent, due to the variations in the movement of the sun, the moments (*kṣaṇa*) of night sometimes increase and sometimes decrease; the moments of day are likewise.
Regarding this, a verse states:
"During the second half of the two months of the rainy season, the nights gradually lengthen.
The commentary explains:
On the ninth day of the second half of the second month during the rainy season, from this point on, the nights gradually lengthen.
The verse says:
During the fourth month of the cold season, the nights are short.
The commentary states:
On the ninth day of the second half of the fourth month of winter, from this point on, the nights gradually shorten.
The verse says:
The Japanese version translates this as follows.
The commentary states:
"At a time when the night increases, at that same time the day decreases; [at a time when the night decreases, at that same time the day increases]."
When the nights decrease, the days increase accordingly.
By how much do they increase and by how much do they decrease?
The verse says:
"Day and night, *kalāpas* increase.
The commentary states:
"If the nights increase, they increase by one *kalāpa*; the same applies to the increase of the days."
The sequence of this increase should be understood as follows.
The verse says:
"When the sun moves north and south."
The commentary states:
If the sun travels along the southern edge of Jambudvīpa, the nights are long; if the sun travels along the northern edge of Jambudvīpa, the days are long.
At the beginning of the waxing moon (śuklapakṣa), why is the lunar disc seen as not being full?
What is the cause for this?
The verse says:
Because its own shadow approaches the sun, the moon appears not full.
The commentary states:

When the lunar palace moves near the solar palace, the sunlight then strikes and illuminates the lunar palace; because of this, the shadow of the sun covers the other side of the moon, and it is this shadow that makes the lunar disc appear incomplete.
The *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra* speaks thus.
The former masters say:
the movements of the sun and moon must correspond to this, such that at times they are seen as incomplete or as mere halves.
Furthermore, it is said that the palaces are equal [in number] to those of the sun; what sentient beings dwell within them?
They are the devas belonging to the retinue of the Four Great Kings.
Do these devas dwell only within these [palaces], or are there other locations as well?
If they dwell in palaces, they dwell only in these places;
if they dwell upon the earth, they dwell within the various tiers of Mount Sumeru.
How many tiers does this mountain have?
What are the dimensions of each individual terrace?
The verse says:
The mountain king has four terraces, each separated from the next by ten thousand [yojanas].
The commentary states:
From the water’s edge to the first terrace of Mount Sumeru, the distance between them is ten thousand yojanas; the same distance applies up to the fourth terrace.
These four tiers of mountain kings are surrounded by successive layers that are half their height; these four tiers emerge in succession.
Furthermore, what is their extent?
The verse says:
It extends sixteen, eight, four, and two thousand *yojanas* outward.
The commentary states:
the first tier extends sixteen thousand *yojanas* outward from Mount Sumeru; the second, eight thousand; the third, four thousand; and the fourth, two thousand *yojanas*.
What sentient beings dwell within this?
The verse says:
The Kuru, the Utpala, the Mālādharas, the Sadāmattas, and the gods of the Four Great Kings.
The commentary states:

There is a yakṣa deity named Kūṭadapāṇi who dwells on the first terrace; furthermore, there are various celestial deities named Mālādharas who dwell on the second terrace; and there are celestial deities named Sadāmattas who dwell on the third terrace. All such beings as these constitute the military hosts of the Four Great Kings, while the Four Great Kings themselves, along with their other retinues, dwell on the fourth terrace.
Just as the retinues of the Four Great Kings dwell within the four tiers, the verse says:
"It is likewise on the other mountains.
The commentary explains:

In the small and large territories of the seven mountain ranges, such as Yugandhara and the others, the remaining retinues of the Four Great Kings dwell, filling them entirely; therefore, the hosts of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings all dwell upon the earth.
The Heaven of the Thirty-three dwells upon the summit of Mount Sumeru.
The verse says:
"The Thirty-three dwell on the summit; its length and breadth are twenty thousand [yojanas]."
The commentary states:
On Mount Sumeru, Śakra and the gods of the Thirty-three reside in this most excellent place.
What are its dimensions in length and breadth?
Other masters say:
each side is eighty thousand yojanas, as at the lower limit; this is called the "Supreme Place.
Still other masters say:

At the center of the summit of Mount Sumeru, each side measures twenty thousand yojanas and the circumference is eighty thousand yojanas; this most excellent place is where the Trāyastriṃśa gods dwell.
The verse says:
At the four corners are four peaks, where the Vajra-devas dwell.
The commentary says:
On each of the four intermediate directions of Mount Sumeru there is a peak; each of these peaks is five hundred yojanas in diameter, and its height is likewise the same.
There dwells a yakṣa deity named Vajrapāṇi, who resides therein to protect the devas.
Regarding this summit of Mount Sumeru, the verse says:
In the center, it is two thousand and a half [yojanas] wide, and one and a half yojanas high; there is a city named Sudarśana, made of gold, soft, and possessing many desirable qualities.
The commentary states:

At the summit of Sumeru, the king of mountains, there is a great city in the center named Sudarśana. It is two thousand five hundred yojanas in length and breadth, and one and a half yojanas in height. It is composed entirely of gold and adorned with one hundred and one varieties of jewels; the ground of the city is likewise so adorned.
The ground is soft and supple like a mass of cotton; when one steps down, it sinks, and when the foot is lifted, it fills back up.
This city is the capital where Śakra resides.
The verse says:
Each side is two hundred and fifty [yojanas]; this is the Vaijayanta Palace.
The commentary states:
The palace where Śakra, Lord of the Devas, resides is in the center of the great city and is named Vaijayanta, because it is adorned with various kinds of precious substances.
This place is most excellent, able to eclipse the lovely appearances of all the celestial palaces.
This palace measures two hundred and fifty yojanas in both length and breadth.
Within this great city, there are such supreme and lovely features as these.
The verse says:
Bāhyā, Nandana, Cūta, and Pāruṣyaka adorn the gardens.
The commentary says:

On the four sides outside the city, in the most excellent and lovely places, there are four kinds of gardens where the devas sport: first, the Saṃtarpita Garden; second, the Pāruṣyaka Garden; third, the Miśraka Garden; and fourth, the Nandana Garden. These gardens adorn the great city from the outside.
The verse says:
Twenty yojanas in the center, with four excellent lands in the four directions.
The commentary says:

In each of the four directions of the gardens such as Saṃtarpaka, there is a distinct location called Sudarśana; they are twenty yojanas apart from one another, serving as the most excellent and rare places for the gods' recreation.
Just as they feel mutual envy and conceive thoughts of endearment toward one another, such as no other garden can surpass.
