Outside the great city, the verse says:
"To the northeast is the Pāriṣadya Garden; to the southwest is the Sudharmā Hall."
The commentary states:
In the heavens there is a tree named Pārijāta, which is the most excellent place for the play of sensual desires among the Thirty-three Gods (*Trāyastriṃśa*).

The trunk of the tree is five *yojanas* in diameter and one hundred *yojanas* in height; its branches and leaves extend fifty *yojanas* outward on each of the four sides to their tips, covering an area of three hundred *yojanas* in circumference.
When the flowers of this tree bloom, their fragrance wafts with the wind to fill a hundred yojanas, and against the wind it wafts to fill fifty yojanas, provided it is wafting with the wind.
This may indeed be so.
But as for the statement that [the fragrance] wafts against the wind, how can it be believed?
Other masters say:
It is because [the fragrance] does not transcend the realm of the tree that this statement was made. Why is this?
Because there is no fragrance capable of wafting against the wind.
Other masters say:
This single tree possesses such power of fragrance that even when celestial blended perfumes are obstructed by the wind, this fragrance continues without interruption.
As for other fragrances, if they are blown by the wind, they gradually fade and diminish until they are completely exhausted; therefore, such fragrances cannot travel far.
It is said this because, when compared with other trees, its fragrance is superior.

Regarding the continuity of floral fragrance: does it rely upon its own four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to perfume other locations, or does it merely perfume the wind without reaching other locations?
There is no fixed rule on this point; various masters maintain that both cases occur.
If that is so, why did the Blessed One speak this verse?
"The fragrance of flowers cannot be wafted against the wind, Nor can the scents of roots and fruits do so;
But the fragrance of the precepts of a virtuous person wafts against the wind, The sweet aroma of their right conduct pervading the entire realm."
This verse was spoken based on the fragrance of human beings.
Why is this? Because this fragrance is commonly known in the world, yet none possesses such power as this.
The Mahīśāsaka school states:
This fragrance perfumes a hundred *yojanas* with the wind and fifty *yojanas* against the wind.

There is a hall for the assembly of devas named Sudharmā, located at the southwest corner of the Great City; there the devas sit and deliberate upon matters concerning what should and should not be done in the world.
The manner in which the four great kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three establish the receptacle world is thus.
The verse says:
Above this, the palaces of the devas are situated.
The commentary states:
On each of the thirty-three heavens there are palaces, and the remaining devas dwell within them.
Who are these "remaining" ones?
These are the Yāma, Tuṣita, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, and Brahmakāyika heavens, and so forth.
As previously stated, there are sixteen such abodes in total.
Thus, to speak briefly, there are twenty-two classes of gods in total.
Each of these possesses its own distinct world-system (*bhājanaloka*).
As the verse says:
"Six [classes] experience sensual pleasures.
The commentary explains:

Among the twenty-two [divisions], there are six devas of the desire realm who are able to enjoy sensory objects, and no others; namely, from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations.
Regarding these six heavens, the verse says:
"Sexual union, embracing, holding hands, smiling, and looking at one another constitute lust.
The commentary explains:

Because they dwell in accordance with the stage [of existence], all engage in sexual intercourse with their two bodies joined; that is to say, the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings and the Heaven of the Thirty-three are no different from the human realm. These gods, because they emerge from wind, have their mental heat extinguished immediately, as they possess no impurity.
In the Yāma Heaven, sexual union consists of embracing; the fever of desire subsides immediately. In the Tuṣita Heaven, it consists of holding hands;

in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, it consists of laughing together; in the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, it consists of gazing at one another. All the heavens of the Desire Realm likewise engage in sexual union through the physical intermingling of two bodies.
The four [levels] beginning with "later embracing" (paścād-āliṅgana) are named according to the duration of their respective similes;
this is as stated in the *Lokaprajñapti-sūtra*.
For the higher heavens, as the objects of desire become progressively more excellent, so too do the pleasures of desire increase in intensity as one ascends.
If a boy or girl deva is born upon the lap of a male deva or a female deva, this boy or girl deva is the child of those two deities.
What is the body size at birth?
The verse says:
It is like that of a five-year-old, up to like that of a ten-year-old, at the time of birth. Among those born [in the various realms], it is thus.
The commentary states:

In sequence, among the abodes of the six heavens of the desire realm, a newly born son of a deity in the first heaven is like a five-year-old child among humans; likewise, up to the newly born son of a deity in the sixth heaven, he is like a ten-year-old child among humans.
This newly born deva-son quickly attains the full perfection of his physical stature.
The verse says:
"All possess their faculties; they have clothing, as it is in the Form Realm."
The commentary states:
The gods of the form realm possess complete physical stature, and their garments and clothing are naturally draped upon their bodies because they are deeply possessed of a sense of shame.
All these gods speak the same language as those of the central region, using the speech of the brahmins; this principle should be understood to apply within the desire realm as well.
The verse says:
There are three types of birth within the realm of desire: the gods and humans of the desire realm.
The commentary says:
What is it that beings within the three realms of existence naturally obtain the objects of desire?
It is the exercise of sovereign mastery over those naturally obtained objects of desire, as is the case with humans and other classes of devas.
As for the other devas, this refers to the first four classes of devas.
There are beings who manifest objects of sensual desire and exercise sovereign mastery over these manifested objects; these are the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (Nirmāṇarati).

There are sentient beings who, regarding the objects of desire created by others, exercise sovereign mastery over those created objects of desire; these are known as the gods of the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Creations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin).

This birth is so called because it is able to experience objects that arise spontaneously, because it is able to experience objects emanated by oneself at will, and because it is able to experience objects emanated by others; it is defined in terms of these sensual objects.
There are three types of birth in the desire realm.
Regarding the form realm, the verse says:
There are likewise three types of pleasant birth, within the nine stages of the three dhyānas.
The commentary states:
Within the three dhyānas there are nine stages; these are called the three types of rebirths of bliss. Why is this?

These devas, by virtue of the bliss born of seclusion, the bliss born of meditative concentration, and the bliss born of the fading away of joy, dwell in long-term peace and happiness; because they are free from suffering and experience long-term bliss, they are called "Born of Bliss."
Because joy and bliss do not arise in the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna, it should be considered whether this bliss arises [there].
These deities consist of twenty-two abodes, as previously described.
How far apart are they from bottom to top?
Although it is impossible to measure their distance everywhere in terms of *yojanas*,
the verse says:
"In this manner, up to that measurement, the same applies to all instances above.
The commentary states:

From Jambudvīpa and so forth toward the regions above, and from those regions back toward Jambudvīpa and so forth, whatever the distance between them may be, the distance from those regions upward is likewise the same.

Just as the fourth layer, where the Four Great Kings reside, is forty thousand yojanas [in extent], so too is the distance from here to Jambudvīpa equal to the distance from here to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The distance from the Heaven of the Thirty-three to Jambudvīpa is the same as the distance from there to the Yāma Heaven.
The distance from the Yāma Heaven to Jambudvīpa is likewise the same as the distance from there to the Tuṣita Heaven.
In this manner, all such extensive examples are likewise;
even the distance from Sudarśana toward Jambudvīpa is equal to the distance from here to Akaniṣṭha.
Above the Akaniṣṭha heaven there is no further realm; for this reason, this place is superior to all others, and no other place is superior to it, hence it is named Akaniṣṭha.
Other masters say:
This place is called Akaniṣṭha; "agha" refers to the accumulation of matter abiding there, and "niṣṭha" means that this is the ultimate limit.
Furthermore, other masters say:
This place is named Akaniṣṭha, meaning "the ultimate limit of what is traversed.
Do sentient beings born in lower realms obtain the ability to ascend to higher planes and behold the palaces of those higher planes?
The verse says:
Those in the lower heavens cannot ascend, unless they possess supernormal powers or rely on another.
The commentary says:

One may reach the Heaven of the Thirty-three either through supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) or by relying on others—namely, being escorted by those possessing supernormal knowledge or being escorted by deities from the higher heavens.
The same applies to all other devas.
If devas born in a higher realm descend to a lower realm, those in the lower realm can see those in the higher realm;
however, if they ascend to a higher realm, they see nothing, because it is not within their sensory domain.
Just as one cannot perceive the tactile objects (*spraṣṭavya*) of a higher stage, it is the same regarding the seeing of forms (*rūpa*); therefore, those [forms] do not come from their own bodies.
Nevertheless, because a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of a lower stage is manifested, it comes to the lower stage; thus, the beings of the lower stage are able to see it at will.
Those in higher stages can see those in lower stages at will;
other schools explain it in this way. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Volume Eight. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Volume Nine.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
Chapter Four: The Detailed Exposition of the World. Furthermore, what are the dimensions of the celestial palaces of the Yāma and other heavens?
The four upper heavens are equal in size to Mount Sumeru; this is how other schools explain it.
Furthermore, other masters state that they double in width as one ascends.
Furthermore, other masters say:

the extent of the first dhyāna stage is equal to a world system of four continents; the extent of the second dhyāna stage is equal to a small thousandfold world system; the extent of the third dhyāna stage is equal to a medium two-thousandfold world system; and the extent of the fourth dhyāna stage is equal to a great three-thousandfold world system.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"The extent of the first three dhyānas—such as the First Dhyāna and so forth—is equal to one thousandfold worlds and so on, while the Fourth Dhyāna has no further limit.
Furthermore, in what sense are they called a small thousandfold world, a two-thousandfold world, and a three-thousandfold world?
The verse says:
Four continents, the moon and sun, Mount Sumeru, the desire realm, and the Brahma abodes—each of these one thousand is called a small chiliocosm.
The commentary says:

One thousand Jambudvīpas, up to one thousand Uttarakurus; one thousand moons and suns; one thousand Sumeru mountains; one thousand Cāturmahārājakāyika heavens, up to one thousand Paranirmita-vaśavartin heavens; and one thousand Brahmā realms—this is called a small chiliocosm.
The verse says:
A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a second-order intermediate world system (*dvisāhasro madhyamo lokadhātuḥ*).
The commentary says:
A thousand times a small chiliocosm is called a medium dichiliocosm.
The verse says:
A thousand times a trichiliocosm.
The commentary states:
A thousandfold multiplication of two-thousandfold intermediate worlds is called a trichiliocosm (three-thousand great thousandfold world system).
Regarding all such [worlds], the verse says:
"Shared destruction and formation.
The commentary states:
These worlds likewise share the minor, medium, and great calamities; this great trichiliocosm undergoes destruction and formation simultaneously. This point shall be explained in detail later.
Just as the dimensions of the vessel-world (bhājanaloka) differ, do the dimensions of the bodies of the sentient beings dwelling therein also differ?
They do. Regarding this, the verse says:
"The stature of the people of Jambudvīpa is four cubits and three and a half cubits."
The commentary states:
Generally, the people of Jambudvīpa are three and a half cubits tall, though some individuals may reach four cubits.
The verse says:
They increase twofold successively for the inhabitants of the eastern, western, and northern continents.
The commentary states:
the people of Pūrvavideha in the east are eight cubits tall; the people of Aparagodānīya in the west are sixteen cubits tall; and the people of Uttarakuru in the north are thirty-two cubits tall.
As for the gods,
the verse says:
"The size of their bodies increases by one-quarter [of a krośa] up to half a *kośa* in the Desire Realm."

The commentary states: The height of the gods of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is one-quarter of a krośa; the height of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is two-quarters (one-half) of a krośa; the height of the gods of the Yāma Heaven is three-quarters of a krośa; the height of the gods of the Tuṣita Heaven is four-quarters (one whole) of a krośa; the height of the gods of the Nirmāṇarati Heaven is five-quarters of a krośa; and the height of the gods of the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven is one and a half krośas.
The verse says:
"In the realm of form, it begins at half a yojana and increases sequentially.
The commentary says:
Among the gods of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), those in the first station, the Heaven of the Retinue of Brahmā (*brahmapārṣadya*), have a body height of half a *yojana*.
From this point onward, the verse says:
"Increasing by half [a *yojana*] in succession."

The commentary states: in these three places, the height increases by half a yojana at each stage. The gods of the Brahmakāyika heaven are one yojana in height; the Mahābrahmā gods are one and a half yojanas in height; and the Parīttābha gods are two yojanas in height.
The verse says:
From the Śubhakṛtsna heaven upward, the height of the body doubles at each stage, except for the Anabhraka heaven, which is three yojanas [less].
The commentary says:

The gods of the Immeasurable Light Heaven are four yojanas in height; the gods of the Pervasive Light Heaven are eight yojanas in height; doubling the yojanas in this manner, up to the gods of the Universal Purity Heaven, who are sixty-four yojanas in height.
In the Anabhraka Heaven, [the height] increases by three yojanas less than double; their body length is one hundred and twenty-five yojanas.
From this point onward, the heavens such as Puṇyaprasava increase further by doubling, up until the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where the body length is sixteen thousand yojanas.
Since there is such a difference in physical stature as one proceeds further [in the realms], is there also a difference in lifespan? Yes.
The verse says:
In Uttarakuru it is one thousand years; in the two [other continents] it is halved by half.
The commentary states:

The fixed lifespan of the people of Uttarakuru is one thousand years; in the two continents of the West and East, the lifespan is reduced by half each, such that the lifespan in Aparagoyānī in the West is five hundred years, and in Pūrvavideha in the East it is two hundred and fifty years.
The verse says:
This is indeterminate.
The commentary says:
In Jambudvīpa, the lifespan is indefinite; at times it is extremely long, and at times it is extremely short.
How long and how short?
The verse says:
"Finally, ten years.
The commentary states:
This lifespan gradually decreases until, at the end, it is only ten years.
The verse says:
"At first, it is immeasurable.
The commentary says:
At the beginning of the eon, the lifespan of sentient beings was immeasurable, for it could not be calculated by numbers such as thousands.
Having explained the human lifespan, I shall now explain the lifespan of the devas.
If one first establishes the day and night [of the gods], only then can the lifespan of the various devas be calculated.
What are the days and nights of the devas?
The verse says:
"Fifty years among humans is one day and night for that lower heaven.
The commentary states:
Fifty years among humans constitutes one day and night for the lowest heaven in the desire realm, namely the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājakāyika).
The verse says:
"By this, their lifespan is five hundred years.
The commentary says:
Thirty such days and nights constitute one month, and twelve such months constitute one year; five hundred such years constitute the lifespan of those devas.
The verse says:
"Above this, they increase twofold.
The commentary explains:
In the higher realms, the days and nights increase twofold; the lifespan of those gods is calculated by means of these days and nights.
What is their lifespan?
One hundred years among humans constitute one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa gods; by this reckoning of days and nights, one thousand years constitutes the lifespan of those gods.
One should know that the sequence for the Yāma Heaven and the others is as follows:

two hundred, four hundred, eight hundred, and sixteen hundred human years constitute one day and night for those [heavens] respectively. Based on these days and nights, two thousand, four thousand, eight thousand, and sixteen thousand celestial years constitute the life spans of the higher heavens in succession.
From the region of Gandhamādana upward, there are neither sun nor moon; how do the various devas establish day and night?
By what means is the function of light and radiance accomplished?
How is this brought about?
Day and night are determined by the blooming and closing of flowers— such as the kumuda and padma—
and by whether various birds sing or remain silent, and whether they come or go to sleep.
Regarding the matter of radiance: their bodies are naturally luminous and do not require external light.
Having explained the lifespan of the gods of the desire realm, the verse says:
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there are no suns or moons; their lifespan is determined by *kalpas*, and the number of *kalpas* corresponds to the measurement of their bodies.
The commentary states:
Within the realm of form, if the gods have a body size of half a *yojana*, their lifespan is then half a *kalpa*.
If the body measures one *yojana*, the lifespan is then one *kalpa*.
In this manner, for those beings, the number of *kalpas* constituting their lifespan corresponds exactly to the number of *yojanas* in their body size.
Up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, the lifespan is sixteen thousand great kalpas.
The verse says:
In the formless realms, it is twenty thousand; thereafter, it increases by two for each.
The commentary states:
In the Sphere of Infinite Space, the lifespan is twenty thousand kalpas;
in the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, it is increased by another twenty thousand kalpas.
In the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), the lifespan increases by another twenty thousand *kalpas*.
In the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), it increases by another twenty thousand *kalpas*.
It should be understood that within these realms, the lifespans are respectively twenty, forty, sixty, and eighty thousand *kalpas*.
What is meant by a kalpa?
Is it an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*), a kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*), a kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*), or a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*)?
The verse says:
"From the Parīttābha [Heaven] for a great kalpa; from this point downward, it is half a kalpa.
The commentary states:

From the Brahma-loka of the Parīttābha Heaven upward, one should know that the lifespan is measured by a *mahākalpa* (great kalpa); from this point downward, half of a great kalpa is designated as a "kalpa," in order to distinguish the lifespans of Mahābrahmā and the others.

Why is this so? At that time, twenty intermediate kalpas are spent in formation, twenty intermediate kalpas in remaining after formation, and twenty intermediate kalpas in dissolution; these sixty intermediate kalpas are designated as one and a half kalpas in the realm of Mahābrahmā. Such is the analysis.
Half a kalpa has already passed; that is to say, forty intermediate kalpas (antarakalpa) are established as one kalpa, and this is how their lifespan is described.
Having finished describing the lifespans in the happy realms, the lifespans in the miserable realms shall now be explained.
The verse says:
The life spans of the six [hells], beginning with Saṃjīva, are equal in sequence to the days and nights of the gods of the desire realm; their lifespans are like those of the desire-realm gods.
The commentary says:
It should be understood that the lifespans of the six classes of desire-realm devas, as previously described, are respectively equal to one day and night in each of the six hells.
These six are: Saṃjīva (Reviving), Kālasūtra (Black String), Saṃghāta (Crushing), Raurava (Crying), Mahāraurava (Great Crying), and Tapana (Scorching).
Regarding those yojanas, days and nights, and so forth, one should know that the lifespan there is likewise equal to the lifespans of the six classes of gods of the desire realm.
How is it that this is said?

The lifespan of the Four Great Kings constitutes one day and night in the Saṃjīva hell; based on these days and nights, months and years are established, and five hundred such years constitute their lifespan.
The lifespan of the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-three is one day and night in the Black Rope Hell; by this reckoning of days and nights, their lifespan therein is a full thousand years.

In this manner, one should understand the sequence for other places as well, up until the lifespan of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, which constitutes one day and night in the Tapana Hell; by this reckoning of days and nights, the lifespan therein is sixteen thousand years.
The verse says:
"In the Great Burning Hell, it is half an eon; in Avīci, it is a distinct eon.
The commentary says:
In the Great Burning Hell, the lifespan is half an intermediate kalpa; in the Avīci Hell, the lifespan is a full intermediate kalpa.
As for the lifespan in the animal realm, there is no fixed duration.
The verse says:
Animals [endure] for at most an intermediate kalpa.
The commentary says:
Among animals, the maximum lifespan is but one intermediate kalpa, namely that of the nāgas such as Nanda, Upananda, and Aśvatara.
For what reason?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"O Bhikṣus!"
There are eight classes of nāgas called the Great Nāgas, all of whom remain to sustain the earth-wheel for one kalpa; this is explained at length as in the sūtra.
The verse says:
"The ghosts, sun, and moon [last] five hundred [kalpas]."
The commentary states:
One month among humans is one day and night for the hungry ghosts (*preta*s); with this day and night, their lifespan is five hundred years.
What is the lifespan in the cold hells?
The verse says:

"From a *vaha* of sesame seeds, removing one seed every hundred years until they are exhausted constitutes the lifespan of [the first hell]; for the *Arbuda*, it is twenty times that, and for each subsequent [hell], the lifespan doubles. The commentary explains: [The lifespan of the first hell, Samjīva, is equivalent to the time it would take to exhaust a *vaha* of sesame seeds if one seed were removed every hundred years. For the Arbuda hell, the lifespan is twenty times that amount; for each of the remaining hells, the lifespan increases by doubling.
By means of an analogy, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke of the lifespan in the cold hells.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus!"

Suppose, for example, that there were twenty *kharī*—measured according to the standard of Magadha—of *vaha* of sesame seeds filling [a container] to overflowing; and suppose that from this, a person were to remove a single sesame seed once every hundred years.
"Monks! Suppose there were twenty khāris of a single vāha of sesame seeds; by this method, I say they could be quickly exhausted.
Yet, I have not said that the lifespan of beings born in the Arbuda hell can be so easily exhausted."
"Monks! As is the lifespan in the Arbuda hell, twenty times that is the lifespan in the Nirarbuda hell.
And so on, monks!"
Twenty times the lifespan of a *pātumā* is the lifespan of a *puṇḍarīka*.
Regarding such lifespans as these, is there anyone who dies prematurely before their full term has been reached?
They exist in all places.
The verse says:
"Except for those who die prematurely in Kuru."
The commentary states:
In the northern continent of Uttarakuru, the lifespan of all people is fixed; they must exhaust their full allotted lifespan before they can pass away. In other places, the lifespan is not fixed.

If we consider specific individuals, it is generally impossible for them to die during that interval. These include Bodhisattvas in their final birth who dwell in the Tuṣita Heaven, Bodhisattvas in their last birth before enlightenment, those prophesied by a Buddha, those sent by a Buddha, those practicing through faith (*śraddhānusārin*), those practicing through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), the mother of a Bodhisattva, and the mother of a Wheel-Turning King while she is pregnant. For such persons, the location and body size are described in terms of *yojana* measurements.
The measure of lifespan has already been explained by way of its annual quantity; however, the simultaneous measure of these two has not yet been stated.
Thus, all these applications have been analyzed through their names; this limit of nomenclature should also be clearly explained.
Because these three are explained, the preliminary establishment of the means (*upāya*) is set forth.
The verse says:
"The atom (*paramāṇu*), the syllable (*akṣara*), and the moment (*kṣaṇa*) are the ultimate limits of matter (*rūpa*), name (*nāman*), and time (*kāla*)."
The commentary states:
If matter is analyzed part by part until it reaches the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), then the ultimate atom is the minimal measure of matter.
The same applies to the measure of time; its minimum is the moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The same applies to the measure of names: it is limited to the shortest syllable, such as the short vowel *i*.
Furthermore, what is the measure of a *kṣaṇa*?
When the causes and conditions are fully assembled and a phenomenon arises for a single moment, that duration is called a *kṣaṇa*.
Furthermore, when this dharma moves across the distance of a single atom (*paramāṇu*), that duration is called a *kṣaṇa*.
Moreover, according to the Abhidharma masters, sixty-five *kṣaṇas* elapse during the time it takes for a strong man to snap his fingers.
Regarding this, a verse says:

One should know that seven *paramāṇus* make a *aṇu*, and from *aṇu* to *loharaja*, *ab-raja*, *śaśaraja*, *aviraja*, *goraja*, *chidraraja*, *likṣā*, *yūka*, *yava*, and *aṅguliparvan*, each subsequent unit is seven times the size of the preceding one.

The commentary states: Taking the atom (*paramāṇu*) as the starting point, one should know that each subsequent unit increases sevenfold. Seven atoms make one *aṇu*; seven *aṇus* make one iron-dust particle (*loharaja*);

seven iron-dust particles make one water-dust particle (*ab-raja*); seven water-dust particles make one rabbit-hair dust particle (*śaśaraja*); seven rabbit-hair dust particles make one sheep-hair dust particle (*aurabhra-raja*); seven sheep-hair dust particles make one cow-hair dust particle (*goraja*); seven cow-hair dust particles make one dust particle in a sunbeam (*chidraraja*); seven sunbeam dust particles make one nit (*likṣā*); seven nits make one louse (*yūka*); seven lice make one barley grain (*yava*); seven barley grains make one finger-joint (*aṅguliparvan*); and three joints make one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*).
Because this is already understood by the world, it is not mentioned in the verse.
If the fingers are laid side-by-side horizontally, the verse says:
twenty-four finger-breadths make one cubit (*hasta*); four cubits make one bow (*dhanus*); five hundred bows make one *krośa*; this is called "forest-dwelling" (*āraṇyaka*).
The commentary states:

Twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) constitute one *vitasti*; twenty-four finger-breadths constitute one *hasta* (cubit); four *hasta* are called one *vyāma*, which is also called one *dhanus* (bow-length). Five hundred *dhanus* constitute one *krośa*, which is also called a village (*grāma*) or an *araṇya* (wilderness).
The verse says:
These eight [yojanas] make one yojana.
The commentary says:
These eight *krośas* constitute one *yojana*.
Having explained the measure of the *yojana*, the measure of the year shall now be explained.
The verse says:
One hundred and twenty kṣaṇas constitute one tatkṣaṇa.
The commentary states:
one hundred and twenty kṣaṇas make up one tatkṣaṇa.
The verse says:
Sixty [kṣaṇas] are called one lava.
The commentary says:
Sixty *tatkṣaṇas* are said to constitute one *lava*.
The verse says:
"The latter three [units] increase by thirty each; these are one *muhūrta*, as well as a day-and-night, and a month."
The commentary states:

Thirty *lava*s constitute one *muhūrta*; thirty *muhūrta*s constitute one day and night. This [day and night] is sometimes long, sometimes short, and sometimes equal; thirty such days and nights constitute one month.
The verse says:
Twelve months constitute one year; in one year, there is a reduction of nights.
The commentary says:
There are four months of the cold season, four months of the hot season, and four months of the rainy season.
These twelve months constitute one year, together with the omitted nights.
Why is this? Because there are six *ūnarātra* (intercalary nights) included within a year. How is this so?
"In the three seasons of cold, heat, and rain, when half of the middle month has already passed,
during the remaining half-month, the wise know that nights decrease.
Having explained the measure of the year, the measure of the eon (kalpa) shall now be explained.
The verse says:
It is said that there are many kinds of kalpas.
The commentary says:
There are the intermediate kalpas, the kalpa of destruction, the kalpa of formation, and the great kalpa.
Regarding these, the verse says:
"The kalpa of destruction begins with the exhaustion of beings in hell and ends with the destruction of the receptacle world."
The commentary states:
Within the various hells, from the point when no sentient beings remain until the destruction of the receptacle world, this is called the kalpa of dissolution. Why is this so?
There are two kinds of destruction:
first, the destruction of the path; second, the destruction of the world-system.
Furthermore, there are two other kinds of destruction:
First is the destruction of sentient beings; second is the destruction of the receptacle world.
There comes a time when, during that period, the sentient beings in the hells only die and are no longer reborn there; this is the beginning of the kalpa of destruction.
At that time, twenty intermediate kalpas of the world’s formation and its abiding have already passed; it should be known that this kalpa of abiding has been completed.
Furthermore, in another twenty intermediate kalpas, the world shall undergo destruction.
This is the period of destruction; it should be understood that at this time, the sequence returns once more.
When not a single sentient being remains in the hells, by this measure of time the world has already been destroyed, due to the destruction of the hells.

During this time, if there are sentient beings with fixed karma who must necessarily undergo retribution in hell, their unexhausted karma will draw these beings to undergo retribution in the hells of other worlds.
The destruction of the animal realm and the destruction of the realm of hungry ghosts (preta) should also be explained in this same way.
Those animals dwelling in the great ocean perish first; those animals that coexist with humans perish later.
Furthermore, at such a time, among those in the human realm, there may be a certain person who, without a teacher and by the very nature of things, attains and enters the first dhyāna.
Emerging from that first dhyāna, this person speaks these words:
"O virtuous ones!"
The joy and bliss born of seclusion are most sublime,
good friend!
The joy and bliss born of seclusion are subtle and tranquil.
Hearing these words, other people likewise each practiced and cultivated this meditative absorption.
After such individuals passed away, they were all reborn in the Brahma realm.
When not a single sentient being remained in Jambudvīpa, by that measure of time the world was considered destroyed, due to the destruction of Jambudvīpa.
In the same way, one should also speak thus regarding the destruction of Pūrvavideha in the east, Aparagoyānī in the west, and Uttarakuru in the north.
When not a single person remains in the human realm, at that time the world is said to be destroyed, because the human realm has been destroyed.
When a person from Uttarakuru passes away, they are reborn among the gods of the desire realm, because within their own level there is no detachment from desire.
Likewise, having cultivated the first dhyāna while in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, one is born in the Brahma realm.
When not a single deva remains in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, by that measure of time the world has already been destroyed, because of the destruction of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings.
In this manner, one should likewise speak until the destruction of the Paranirmita-vaśavartin deities.
When, at that time, not a single deity remains in the heavens of the desire realm, by that measure of time the world has already been destroyed, due to the destruction of the desire realm.
Among the Brahmā realms, a certain being, by the very nature of things, enters the second dhyāna; emerging from this meditative absorption, he speaks these words:
"This bliss is most excellent—namely, the joy and bliss born of concentration."
This bliss is most tranquil, namely the joy and bliss born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Upon hearing these words, other beings likewise practiced and cultivated this concentration.
After such devas pass away, they are all reborn in the realm of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When not a single sentient being remains in the Brahma realm, by that measure of time the world has already been destroyed.
Because sentient beings have perished, at that time the receptacle world becomes entirely empty.
From this point, the karma that gives rise to the world-receptacle (*bhājana-loka*) and enables its perception has entirely ceased and perished.
Seven suns appear in succession, burning away the great earth and all the Mount Sumerus until nothing remains. From there, fierce winds blow the flames upward, burning as far as the Brahma realms.
One should know that such flames belong to the same category as those of the first dhyāna stage.
Why is this? If a calamity were not of the same category, it could not cause destruction; because they arise through mutual correspondence, it is said that this fire is capable of burning.
Why is this? Because the fire of the desire realm can connect with the fire of the form realm.
This principle should be understood to apply similarly to the other calamities as well, according to reason.

From the time when beings die within the hells and no more are reborn there, until the destruction of the receptacle world, the passage of such a duration is called a *saṃvarta-kalpa* (aeon of dissolution).
The verse says:
The *vivarta-kalpa* (aeon of formation) begins first with the wind, and continues until the existence of the hells.
The commentary states:
From the initial arising of the wind until there are sentient beings in the hells, this is called the kalpa of formation (*vivartakalpa*). Why is this so?
When the world has thus been destroyed and only space remains, it persists for a long period of time.

Eventually, through the predominant power of the karma of sentient beings, the preliminary signs of the receptacle-worlds first arise; that is to say, a subtle wind begins to stir gradually within the void. At that time, the world has remained in its state of destruction for twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*).
It should be known that this kalpa of destruction has already passed; after another twenty intermediate kalpas, the world should be formed.
Regarding this formation, it should be known that the sequence will arrive once again at this time.

From that time onward, the winds gradually increased in magnitude until they had fully formed the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) as previously described. All the successive events as previously explained were accomplished: namely, the water-circle, the great earth, the golden wheel, and the earth-wheel, up to the various continents, Mount Sumeru, and so forth; first the palace of Mahābrahmā was formed, followed in succession by the palaces of the Yāma devas.
From this point onward, the wind-circle arises; by this measure of time, one should know that the world has been formed, due to the formation of the receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*).

At that time, whichever sentient being was destined to become the Great Brahmā King fell from the Ābhāsvara Heaven to take birth in the palace of Mahābrahmā. Other sentient beings followed in succession from there, some taking birth in the realm of the Brahma-purohitas, some in the realm of the Brahmapārṣadyas, and some in the realm of the Paranirmita-vaśavartins.
In this sequence, they are born successively even in Uttarakuru, Aparagoyānī, Pūrvavideha, Jambudvīpa, the realm of hungry ghosts, the realm of animals, and the realm of hell-beings.
This is the natural law: namely, that the world is destroyed later and formed earlier.

At this time, if even a single sentient being were to be born in the place of the hells, by that measure of time, twenty intermediate kalpas of the world’s formation would already have been completed.
It should be understood that this kalpa of formation has already passed; for another twenty intermediate kalpas, the world should remain.
This period of abiding is the time that should be known as arriving in succession.
The verse says:
A distinct kalpa ranges from an immeasurable [age] down to ten years.
The commentary says:
From the initial formation of the world, nineteen intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*) have already passed within the period of immeasurable lifespan.
During this time of immeasurable lifespan for sentient beings, their life expectancy gradually decreased until it reached ten years.
The world having been formed and abiding constitutes the first intermediate kalpa of that duration.
The verse says:
"First, one intermediate kalpa of descent; next, eighteen of ascent and descent."
The commentary states:
From this first stage (*vihāra*), there are eighteen "upper" and eighteen "lower" periods that constitute eighteen intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*). Why is this so?

From this point, when the lifespan of sentient beings increases from ten years up to eighty thousand years, and then decreases again down to ten years, this constitutes the second intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).
In this manner, it continues up to eighteen.
The verse says:
"The final ascent is one intermediate kalpa."
The commentary states:
The final upper intermediate kalpa is the twentieth intermediate kalpa of the *sthiti-kalpa* (abiding kalpa); in this manner, [the lifespan] decreases from eighty thousand years down to ten years.
If that is so, to what extent does this increase reach its culmination?
The verse says:
Up until a lifespan of eighty thousand [years].
The commentary states:
Beyond this, there is nothing higher.

Within the eighteen kalpas, the duration of one cycle of ascending and descending is equal to the duration of the initial descending kalpa, and likewise equal to the duration of the final ascending kalpa; therefore, all these durations are equal.
The verse says:
"The world is thus formed and remains for twenty kalpas.
The commentary says:
By this principle of the intermediate kalpas, the world remains for twenty intermediate kalpas after it has been formed.
Just as the duration of its formation and its abiding are equal, so too, the verse says:
"The kalpa of formation and that of destruction, and the periods of destruction and abiding, are all equal."
The commentary states:

Twenty intermediate kalpas constitute the formation of the world, twenty intermediate kalpas the destruction of the world, and twenty intermediate kalpas the period of emptiness following destruction.
Although there is no variation in the duration of these three periods, the measure of these kalpas is equal, as their calculation is uniform.

In this context, the receptacle world is formed during one intermediate kalpa; it remains inhabited for nineteen intermediate kalpas; it is dismantled during one intermediate kalpa; and the receptacle world remains empty, devoid of sentient beings, for nineteen intermediate kalpas.
Thus, these distinct intermediate kalpas consist of four sets of twenty, totaling eighty.
The verse says:
Eighty [intermediate kalpas] are called a great kalpa (mahākalpa).
The commentary says:
If the measure of a great kalpa (*mahākalpa*) is thus,
what dharma constitutes its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
The five aggregates constitute its intrinsic nature.
It is stated in the sūtras that,
over the course of three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, the Buddhas attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
Among the four types of kalpas, to which category do these three asaṃkhyeyas belong?
Those spoken of here are *mahākalpas*.
As this verse says:
"Three *asaṃkhyeya* great kalpas.
The commentary states:
"It is through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas that the sought-after fruit of Buddhahood is finally accomplished."
Since an *asaṃkhyeya* is already without numerical limit, how can the three numbers be established?
One should not understand it in this way. If so, how then?
Although there are sixty numerical places, they are called one asaṃkhyeya.
This is stated in other sūtras.
What are these sixty?
There is the number one, but no number two; this position is called "one.
Ten times this one is called the second position.
Ten times the second position is called a hundred; ten hundreds are called a thousand; ten thousands are called ten thousand; and one hundred thousand is called...
Ten *lakṣa* is called an *atilakṣa*; ten *atilakṣa* is called a *koṭi*;
ten *koṭi* is called a *madhya*; ten *madhya* is called an *ayuta*;
ten *ayuta* is called a *mahāyuta*; ten *mahāyuta* is called a *nayuta*; ten *nayuta*...
Ten *mahā-nayuta* are called a *prayuta*; ten *prayuta* are called a *mahā-prayuta*; ten *mahā-prayuta* are called a *utsaṅga*;
ten *utsaṅga* are called a *mahotsaṅga*; ten *mahotsaṅga* are called a *vahana*.
Ten *po-ha* (bhaṅga) are called one *mo-ha-po-ha* (mahābhaṅga); ten *mo-ha-po-ha* are called one *chih-chih-po* (kambha);
ten *chih-chih-po* are called one *mo-ha-chih-chih-po* (mahākambha); ten *mo-ha-chih-chih-po* are called one *he-tou* (hetu);
ten *he-tou* are called one *mo-ha-he-tou* (mahāhetu); ten *mo-ha-he-tou* are called one...
Ten *karoṣa* are called a *mahākaroṣa*; ten *mahākaroṣa* are called an *indra*;
ten *indra* are called a *māthava*; ten *māthava* are called a *vartanī*;
ten *vartanī* are called a *mahāvartanī*; ten *mahāvartanī* are called...
Ten *gaṇanā* are called a *mahāgaṇanā*; ten *mahāgaṇanā* are called a *nimba*;
ten *nimba* are called a *mahānimba*; ten *mahānimba* are called a *vibhūta*;
ten *vibhūta* are called a *mahāvibhūta*; ten *mahāvibhūta* are called a *bala*; ten *bala*...
One *mahābala* is called a *śana*; ten *śanas* are called a *mahāśana*;
ten *mahāśanas* are called a *viśvada*; ten *viśvadas* are called a *mahāviśvada*;
ten *mahāviśvadas* are called a *balakṣa*; ten *balakṣas*—
One *mahā-bhavaśa* is called one [unit], and ten *mahā-bhavaśas* are called an *asaṃkhyeya*.
In the interim, eight places were lost.
Counting these great eons (*mahākalpas*) in succession up to the sixtieth place is termed one *asaṃkhyeya*.
Counting one *kalpa* in this manner constitutes the second; the third is likewise. Thus, it is said that there are three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
It is called *asaṃkhyeya* because it cannot be calculated by any means of calculation.
Sentient beings have already made their vows; why must they further undergo this most protracted period of cultivation before attaining unsurpassed bodhi?
How could such a thing not be possible?

Why is this? Because it is only through the practice of the vast accumulations of merit and wisdom, and by means of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) on a path of a million difficult practices over three great incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), that Bodhisattvas finally attain the fruit of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
If liberation were possible through some other means, why would one need to practice this path of great difficulty for so long?
It is for the sake of others that such great effort must be exerted.
"How can we, having emerged from the great flood of suffering, be able to deliver others?
It is with this intention that I have practiced for many eons.
What benefit to myself is there in benefiting others?"
What is for one’s own benefit is called the benefit of others, because it is what one delights in oneself.
O Lord, who can believe this now?
This matter is truly difficult to believe.
If a person regards their own self as a heavy burden and lacks compassion for others, it is difficult for them to believe in this [teaching].
However, for one who possesses wisdom and compassion, this is easily believed.

For example, there are other people in the world who constantly habituate themselves to evil faults; although they derive no personal benefit from them, they take delight in causing harm and distress to others—a fact commonly witnessed by all.

Furthermore, there are others who constantly practice great compassion; within this state, they have no self-interest but instead delight in performing deeds that benefit others. Therefore, this matter may be compared to that.

Furthermore, for example, just as ordinary worldlings, due to long-term habituation, are unable to discern the essential nature and characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*)—which in reality are not the self—and consequently give rise to self-love toward those conditioned phenomena, thereby constantly bearing manifold sufferings because of this self-love.

Furthermore, there are others who, through long-term cultivation of wisdom, abandon self-attachment toward their own mental continuum and increase self-attachment toward others; because of this attachment, they take upon themselves all manner of suffering for the sake of others.
Therefore, one should know that this meaning is not different.

Furthermore, there is a distinct nature that arises in such a manner: it experiences suffering because of the suffering of others and happiness because of the happiness of others, rather than through its own self; for it does not perceive the welfare of others as being distinct from its own welfare.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"Inferior persons seek their own pleasure, employing various means;
Middle persons seek the cessation of suffering, for pleasure is not the basis of suffering."

"Because the Superior One [the Buddha] undergoes suffering for himself, he delights in others attaining peace and happiness, and in the eternal extinction of their suffering; this is because the suffering of others is his own suffering.
Do the Buddhas appear in the world during the upward phase of a kalpa, or do they appear during the downward phase of a kalpa?
The verse says:
Buddhas attain enlightenment during the period when the lifespan decreases from eighty thousand to one hundred years.
The commentary says:

When the lifespan of people in the world is eighty thousand years, as it begins to decrease down to a lifespan of one hundred years, during this interval, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world.
Why does he not appear during the period of increase?
Because at that time, sentient beings are difficult to instruct in the practice of wearying detachment.
Why does he not appear during the period below one hundred [years]? Because at that time, sentient beings are too degenerate to be capable of receiving the teaching.
During this period, the five corruptions (pañca-kaṣāya) are in full blaze.
What are these five corruptions? First, the corruption of lifespan;
second, the corruption of the eon; third, the corruption of afflictions; fourth, the corruption of views; and fifth, the corruption of sentient beings.
At the end of a kalpa, because the five [factors] beginning with lifespan have become the coarsest and lowest, like dregs, they are called "corruptions" (kaṣāya).
Due to the first two corruptions, lifespan is successively diminished, as are the requisites for happiness.
Furthermore, two other corruptions diminish the aids to virtue. Why is this?

Because of these two corruptions, there are sentient beings who extensively practice the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the practice of self-mortification, which can damage the aids to virtue for both householders and renunciants.

Due to the latter corruption (kalpa-kaṣāya), one's own physical stature is diminished, as these qualities—complexion, freedom from disease, strength, wisdom, mindfulness, right exertion, and imperturbability—are destroyed.
At what time do Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world?
The verse says:
"Pratyekabuddhas [appear] in the upper and lower periods.
The commentary says:
Pratyekabuddhas appear in the world during both the increasing and the decreasing phases of a kalpa. Why is this?
Because there are two types of pratyekabuddhas:
First, those who practice in a group; second, those who are like a rhinoceros horn.
Regarding these, those who practice in a group were formerly śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
Other masters say:
There are those who were formerly ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and later became *pratyekabuddhas* of the "group-practitioner" type (*vargacārin*).

If such a person had already cultivated the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya kuśalamūla*) in a previous life, they will spontaneously awaken to the Noble Path in this present life.
How is this known?
It is stated in the *Mūlapravṛtti-sūtra*:
"In a certain mountain region, there were five hundred non-Buddhist seers (bāhiraka-ṛṣi) practicing difficult and arduous austerities."
Eventually, there was a monkey who lived together with a pratyekabuddha.

Later, it went to the abode of some non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) and manifested the majestic deportment and adornments of a pratyekabuddha; consequently, all five hundred non-Buddhist practitioners became pratyekabuddhas.
If he were previously an *arhat*, he would not have had to practice difficult and painful austerities.
Regarding the "rhinoceros-horn" simile, it refers to dwelling alone.
Among the two types of *pratyekabuddhas*, the verse says:
"The rhinoceros-horn simile refers to a hundred kalpas.
The commentary explains:
Only after completing one hundred great kalpas of practicing the provisions for enlightenment does one become a rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddha.
What is meant by "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer)?
Because they awaken to the truth through correct reasoning within themselves alone, apart from the formal teachings of a teacher, they are called Pratyekabuddhas. Why is this?
Because the various Pratyekabuddhas discipline only their own single person and do not discipline others,
how is it that they are called "rhinoceros-horn" analogies?
It is because, within the most excellent class among the realms of humans and gods, they are steadfast, authentic, and peerless.
For what reason do they not awaken others?
It is not that the Pratyekabuddhas lack the capacity to teach the Dharma to others, for they have attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
They also possess the ability to retain the authentic teachings spoken by past Buddhas and to expound them to others.
He is not devoid of compassion either, for he constantly manifests supernormal powers and wisdom for the benefit of others.
However, because sentient beings do not elicit the fruit of sainthood [from him], he does not preach for them.

Why is this? At that time, there were also sages who had cultivated worldly paths to transcend desire; nevertheless, because they had practiced in previous lives and because they delighted in few desires, they were unable to preach the true teaching to enable others to receive the profound Dharma.

Why is this? Because it is difficult to lead those who follow the flow of craving through the world to turn against that current; because one seeks to remain free from miscellaneous conduct while gathering a community of followers; and because of the fear of distraction and idle chatter.
Furthermore, at which of the two periods does a Wheel-turning King appear in the world?
The verse says:
During the period when the lifespan is less than eighty thousand years, no Wheel-turning King is born.
The commentary states:
Universal Monarchs (cakravartin) appear in the world when the human lifespan is immeasurable up to eighty thousand years, but not when it is less than eighty thousand. Why is this?
If human lifespan decreases below eighty thousand years, such persons are not vessels for this auspicious prosperity and happiness;
because he attains the rank of kingship by means of the wheel as his dharma, he is called a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin).
There are four kinds of such kings.
The verse says:
Those with wheels of gold, silver, copper, and iron.
The commentary states:

If a person possesses a wheel made of gold, that person is of the highest of the high grade; if the wheel is made of silver, they are of the high grade; if the wheel is made of copper, they are of the middle grade; and if the wheel is made of iron, they are of the low grade.
The verse says:
"The four follow the order of the continents, numbering one, two, three, and four.
The commentary explains:

If a person possesses a wheel made of iron, he becomes the king of one continent; if his wheel is made of copper, he becomes the king of two continents; if his wheel is made of silver, he becomes the king of three continents; and if his wheel is made of gold, he becomes the king of four continents.
Such is explained in the *Vibhaṅga* regarding the world.
In the Sūtras, however, because they emphasize what is preeminent, only the gold wheel is mentioned.
As the Sūtra says:

If a king is born of the Kṣatriya caste and has already received the consecration, on the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight during the Poṣadha, having bathed from head to foot and observed the eight precepts, he ascends a high tower for the Poṣadha ceremony while surrounded by his assembled ministers. Then, in the eastern direction, a wheel-treasure appears, complete with a thousand spokes, a hub, and a rim; it is perfectly adorned and fully equipped, as if fashioned by a skilled craftsman, entirely made of gold, and arrives at the king’s location.
One should know that this king must be a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin).
It is the same for any other wheel-turning monarch who is born.
The verse says:
"It is not the case that two appear simultaneously like Buddhas.
The commentary explains:
The sūtras state that there is no place and no occasion where two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, appear in the world, neither before nor after one another.
Regarding place and status: it is held that there may be one Tathāgata or two Tathāgatas, and the same applies to two Cakravartin kings.
Herein, this point should be considered:
does the "place" in question refer to a single great trichiliocosm, or to all worlds?
Other schools state:
The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear only in a single location and not in other places. Why is this?
One must not allow for the possibility that the powers and functions of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are deficient, for a single World-Honored One possesses these capacities in all places.
If, in a particular place, one Buddha were unable to sustain all disciples to be converted, then other Buddhas would likewise lack such capacity therein.
In a sutra it is said: "Śāriputra,
suppose a person were to come to you and ask you:..."
"Venerable sir!
At this present time, are there any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are equal, even to the point of being identical with the śramaṇa Gautama, regarding unsurpassed enlightenment?
If you were asked this, how would you answer?"
"Bhagavān!
If someone were to come to me and ask such a question, being thus questioned, I would answer in this way:
'At this present time, there is no śramaṇa or brāhmaṇa who is equal to my Bhagavān regarding unsurpassed enlightenment.'"
For what reason?
World-Honored One!
I have personally heard these words from the auspicious mouth of the World-Honored One; I have personally received and upheld these words.
There is no place and no occasion for two Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas to appear in the world simultaneously, neither before nor after one another.
There is, however, a place and an occasion for one.
If that is so, how is the meaning of what the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said in the *Brahmā-sūtra* to be understood?
The Sūtra says:
"O Brahmā!"
Regarding the statement, "I have attained mastery within the trichiliocosm," this is an intentional teaching (*ābhiprāyika-vacana*) whose meaning is not explicitly literal.
What is the meaning that is not explicit?

If the Tathāgata, with respect to his natural mind (*svabhāva-citta*), does not form a separate volitional effort but simply speaks for the sake of benefiting others and so forth, then all such activities are spontaneously accomplished within this sphere of experience.
If the Tathāgata were to exercise his intentional sphere separately, it would be boundless according to his will.
Another school asserts:
"In other worlds, there are likewise various Buddhas and Tathāgatas."
Why is this? Because one sees many people practicing the provisions for enlightenment together;
it is impossible for many Buddha-Bhagavāns to appear in a single place at the same time.
If he were to appear in other places, there would be no obstruction.
Therefore, he must attain perfect enlightenment in other worlds and so forth.
If that is so, then regarding this point, the previously cited sūtra states:
There is no place or time—meaning there is neither before nor after—in which two Tathāgatas appear in the world.
How is this meaning to be understood?
This point should now be considered:
Does this sūtra speak with reference to a single world-system, or with reference to all world-systems?

If it speaks with reference to all world-systems, then a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) should not appear in other world-systems, because their simultaneous birth is precluded, just as in the case of the Tathāgata.
If you accept this as it is, why do you not accept this point?
The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is a source of great auspiciousness and merit.
There is no fault in many Buddhas appearing in many worlds; rather, it allows immeasurable sentient beings in the world to attain their own benefit, which is conjoined with great merit.
If that is so, why do two Tathāgatas not appear simultaneously in a single Buddha-field?
It is because it would be purposeless and because it accords with their original vows. Thus, Bodhisattvas make this vow:
"In this blind world, which has no leader, no protector, and no refuge, may I become a Buddha therein to serve as eyes and a refuge, so that beings may show reverence and proceed swiftly."
Why is this? Because if there were only one Buddha, it would give rise to extremely profound reverence in others.
Furthermore, it would cause others to reflect in this way:
Other Buddhas are most difficult to encounter.
Therefore, practice swiftly according to the teachings established; do not let it be that after the Great Teacher has departed and entered parinirvāṇa, we shall be left without a refuge.
Furthermore, regarding these four types of wheel-turning kings who subjugate the world by means of the golden wheel and so forth:
what is the sequence of their subjugation?
The verse says:
"Others come to welcome him; he goes to them; they all submit to his superiority.
The commentary explains:
If a king obtains the golden wheel as his regalia, the kings of Jambudvīpa each come in person to welcome and attend upon him, each saying:

"Our lands are wealthy, peaceful, secure, and fertile, and are filled with vast multitudes; all these belong to the World-Honored One. We pray that the World-Honored One will grant us instructions, for we are all your followers."
If a king possesses a silver wheel as his regalia, he goes to those lands in person, and all the kings there humble themselves and submit.

If a king possesses a copper wheel as his regalia, he approaches those lands and sends an envoy back and forth to engage in conflict with them; only after that do the kings humble themselves and submit.

If a king obtains an iron wheel as his regalia, he himself goes to those lands, donning armor and grasping weapons to display the signs of an attack; only then do the various kings humble their hearts and submit.
Regarding all wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*), the verse says:
"They are non-harming.
The commentary explains:
If he subdues other lands by wielding his weapons, there is still no killing, let alone as in the case of other kings.

Having brought the whole world under his control, all sentient beings dwelling within the king’s realm are instructed by him to uphold the ten wholesome paths of action; therefore, such kings are certain to be reborn in heaven after death.
The Sūtra states:
"With the appearance of a Wheel-Turning Sage King in the world, seven treasures manifest in the world.
What are these seven?"

First, the wheel-treasure; second, the elephant-treasure; third, the horse-treasure; fourth, the mani-jewel treasure; fifth, the woman-treasure; sixth, the householder-treasure; and seventh, the minister-treasure.
Since elephants and other such treasures belong to the category of sentient beings, how could they be produced by the karma of another?

If not even a single sentient being is produced by the karma of another, then this person must have previously performed various karmas together with others that can bring about their mutual corresponding retributions.
When this person is reborn, other sentient beings are born through their own past karma and become associated with this person.
Regarding this wheel-turning monarch and other kings, is there a distinction between them solely in terms of the seven jewels, or are there further distinctions?
There is another distinction: namely, these four wheel-turning kings possess the thirty-two marks of a great man, whereas other kings do not, just as with the Buddhas.
If this is so, what is the difference between a king and a Buddha?
Regarding this, a verse says:
"Abiding in the correct [state], clear, and perfect; the Buddha’s marks are peerless.
The commentary states:
The Buddha’s thirty-two marks possess three virtues that distinguish them from those of a wheel-turning king. These three virtues are:
first, they are perfectly positioned and not biased; second, they are extremely clear and not obscure; third, they are perfectly complete and without deficiency.
At the beginning of the kalpa, did humans have a king or not?
Although there was no king, the verse says:
"At first, they were like those in the realm of form."
The commentary states:
At the beginning of the kalpa, humans were born like the sentient beings of the form realm (rūpadhātu), each dwelling in their own abode.
As it is said in the Sūtra:

At the beginning of the eon, humans were born with form and mind-born; they possessed complete bodies and limbs, with all sense faculties unimpaired. Their physical forms were lovely, they possessed natural radiance, and they were able to fly through the air. With joy as their food, they dwelt for a long time sustained by that joy.
The verse says:
Sentient beings gradually craved flavors; out of laziness they began to store up goods, and for this reason they hired guards with wealth to protect their fields.
The commentary says:
Once sentient beings had thus come into being, the flavor of the earth (*pṛthivī-rasa*) gradually emerged; its taste was sweet and exquisite, surpassing even that of fine honey.

Among them, there was one person whose nature was characterized by craving; upon smelling the fragrance of the earth-flavor, he tested it by tasting it and subsequently began to eat it. The others followed suit, imitating him one after another.
It was at this time that the first stage of solid food appeared.

Because the people of that time habitually consumed this food, two sensations—hardness and heaviness—arose within their bodies; they lost their former radiance, and from that point on, darkness arose, whereupon the sun and moon appeared.
Due to their craving for the taste, that earth-essence gradually vanished; the surface of the earth became parched and cracked, and they took this as their food.
Becoming attached to it, they lost even this sustenance.
Next, forest creepers grew, which they took as food.
Becoming greedy for them, they again lost this food.
Next, śāli rice grew spontaneously without being cultivated, which they took as food.
This food is the coarsest; it undergoes transformation and leaves a residue. To eliminate this residue, the passages for excrement and urine arise.
These passages arise together with the male and female organs, and their characteristics also differ.

At that time, those people gaze at one another; following the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of their former delusions, they give rise to perverse thoughts (*vitarka*). Seized by these perverse thoughts, as if swallowed by a rākṣasa, the transformation of lust becomes violently intense within their minds, and they immediately commit the transgression. It is at this moment that the demon of lust first enters and takes hold of the mind.
At that time, those people would gather śāli rice for their evening meal at dusk and for their daytime meal at dawn, agreeing together to collect it in this manner.
Among them was one man whose nature was indolent; he would collect śāli rice over long periods and store it up for his meals. The others, imitating him, each began to store up their own provisions.
At that time, the notion of "mine" arose within them.

Because of this sense of "mine," they later gathered the grain-essence (śāli), and once it was taken, it was exhausted and did not grow again. Thereupon, those people divided the fields among themselves.
When they developed intense greed and attachment toward their own fields and committed acts of encroachment and damage against what others had obtained, it was at that time that theft first arose.

To eliminate this fault, everyone gathered together and each contributed one-sixth of their harvest to collectively employ a superior person as the guardian of the fields; they called such a person a *kṣatriya* (from the root *kṣi*, meaning "to protect").

Because he was born from the *kṣatra* (ruling power) and the *śūmi* (soma), he received the name Kṣatriya; he was approved by the great multitude of beings and was able to captivate the hearts of the world. Therefore, upon his birth, he was named King Mahāsammata.
All kings have transmitted this tradition, and this king was the first among them.
Among them, if there were anyone whose mind turned toward renunciation and left the household life, that person received the name "Brahmin.
Later, there was a certain king who, out of greed and stinginess for wealth and possessions, did not practice the act of distributing gifts or bestowing favors upon his subjects.
Due to their poverty, people frequently committed acts of theft.
The King, being fond of using the sword and staff against such offenders, initiated the practice of punishment; it was at this time that killing first came into being.
At that time, the offender concealed his actions and said, "I did not do this.
It was at this moment that the first instance of lying occurred.
The verse says:
Subsequently, due to the increase of the ten non-virtues, the lifespan decreases until it reaches ten years.
The commentary says:

Successively, through these karmic paths of action, [unwholesome deeds] increase; consequently, their lifespan gradually diminishes until, at the final stage, all people have a lifespan of only ten years.
Therefore, all calamities and misfortunes have two factors as their root: namely, attachment to sensory flavors and indolence.
At that time, the human lifespan is ten years; this marks the conclusion of the intermediate kalpa.
How does it come to an end?
The verse says:
This kalpa comes to an end by means of weapons, disease, and the calamity of famine.
The commentary states:
A minor kalpa (antarakalpa) comes to an end due to three causes: first, weapons; second, pestilence; and third, famine.

When a minor kalpa is ending, people with a lifespan of ten years are defiled by unrighteous desire, oppressed by unequal greed, and pervaded by false teachings. Their poisonous hatred increases further; if they see one another, they immediately give rise to a mind of extreme, heavy malice and the intent to kill, just as a deer hunter sees wild deer in the present day.
At that time, whatever each person grasped—whether wood or grass—it all became for them an extremely sharp blade or weapon.
Those people thought to themselves:
"I must certainly go first."
Therefore, they kill one another, and by this means they all die.

Furthermore, at the time when another intermediate kalpa comes to an end, because those people with a lifespan of ten years have accumulated excessive transgressions, malevolent spirits give rise to feelings of hatred and inflict various calamities upon them; consequently, they encounter the *asādha* disease everywhere, and by this means they all die.

Furthermore, at the time when another intermediate kalpa is coming to an end, because those people of ten years of age have accumulated excessive transgressions, the devas and nāgas give rise to feelings of aversion and no longer send down rain. Consequently, there is famine and destitution everywhere, and as a result, they all die.
At that time, there were three kinds of food:
first, *cañca*-food; second, white-bone-food; and third, tally-food.
Regarding what is called *cañca*-food, there are two reasons for its name: it is called *cañca* because people gathered [the grain] at that time, and also because a small basket is called *cañca*.
At that time, driven by hunger and emaciation, people gathered together in great numbers and all died of starvation.

Furthermore, out of a desire to preserve their provisions for the coming year and out of compassion for their families, they stored away small amounts of grain and seeds in wooden boxes (*piṭaka*) for future use; therefore, it is called *cañcā-anna* (the "box-grain").
Regarding the "white-bone provisions," there are also two causes: first, because that person's body has long been parched and withered, the bones turn white shortly after death;
second, due to foodlessness and starvation, they take these white bones, boil them, and drink the broth.
Regarding the rationing of grain, there were also two reasons for it: at that time, people took turns distributing the grain from house to house by passing out counting sticks (*śalākā*).
Today the head of the household ate, and tomorrow the wife ate; such was the sequence.

Furthermore, in former times there was a place where grain had been stored; when it had cracked open, people would probe it with tally-sticks to retrieve the grains, and as they obtained them, they would boil many portions of water with them and drink this as their sustenance.
It is thus transmitted in the Sūtras:

if a person can observe the precept against taking life for even a single day, or can give a single *harītakī* fruit, or can give a single meal with a heart of reverence toward the great assembly, that person will not be born during the kalpas of swords and staves, pestilence, or famine.
Regarding the three calamities of swords and staves, pestilence, and famine, for how long does each arise?
The verse says:
Seven days, seven months, and seven years; they end in this successive order.
The commentary states:

The calamity of killing sentient beings with clubs arises within seven days; the calamity of pestilence arises within seven months and seven days; and the calamity of famine arises within seven years, seven months, and seven days.

At that time, among the inhabitants of the two continents, events resembling the three calamities also arise: there, malice increases until it becomes heavy, dark, emaciated, and ugly in appearance; physical weakness also arises there, as do hunger and thirst.
One should know that within all the various calamities, each of those three types of destruction mentioned above occurs in succession.
The verse says:
There are three aeons of dissolution and accumulation, arising from fire, water, and wind.
The commentary states:
Within each fixed realm, sentient beings disperse from below and gather at the top; therefore, it is called a kalpa of dispersal and gathering (*vivyasaṃvarta*).
Due to the rising of seven suns, there is a calamity of fire; due to great rains, there is a calamity of water; and due to the opposing forces of great winds, there is a calamity of wind.
By means of these three calamities, every most subtle part of the receptacle world is utterly exhausted without remainder.
Regarding this, certain non-Buddhist teachers maintain the following position:
"Such atoms (paramāṇu) are eternal; at this time, they remain as the residue."
How can they maintain that this meaning is established?
Is it not the case that when other great elements arise subsequently,
their arising would otherwise be without a seed?
The wind produced by the power of the karma of sentient beings is designated as the "seed" because its functional capacity is preeminent.
Furthermore, the wind at the head of the calamity is also a cause that serves as a seed.
The *Mahīśāsaka* school’s sūtras state:
"The wind draws those seeds from other currently existing worlds and carries them here.
Nevertheless, the teachers of the non-Buddhist schools do not admit that sprouts and so forth arise from seeds.
If that is so, what is their position?
[They hold that] things arise from themselves, and so on, up to the fact that a part arises from its own atom (*paramāṇu*).
If this is the case, what function do seeds and the like have with respect to sprouts and the like?
Apart from the established atoms (*paramāṇu*), there is no other functional capacity, because the atoms of the sprout arise from the seed.
For what reason do they maintain this?
Because it would be illogical for [the sprout] to arise from a cause that is not of a similar class (*asabhāga*).
Why is this not reasonable?

If that were so, the arising of all things would be indeterminate; however, this is not the case, because their functional capacities (*śakti*) are fixed, and thus there is no sense of indeterminacy, as for example with the ripening of grain and the like.
If this principle were not so, why would it be?
Because the various *guṇa*-dharmas differ from one another, whereas the *tālavya* [dental] dharmas are not like that.
If a thing is to arise, it must necessarily arise from a thing of its own kind, just as a bamboo mat arises from bamboo strips or a cloth arises from threads.
Now, however, the principle of non-correspondence arises.
In this context, what meaning is inconsistent?
You cite the meaning of non-attainment to prove the meaning of non-attainment.
In this context, what meaning is "non-attainment"?
That a mat is distinct from the bamboo and a garment is distinct from the threads—this argument is not established. Why?
Because it is these bamboos and these threads that, through such an aggregation, receive a distinct name, just like a line of ants.
How is this known?
Because a garment is not perceived within the combination of a single thread. Why is this so?
In this regard, if the garment truly exists as a whole, what phenomenon could obstruct it so that it does not appear?
If it does not exist as a whole but consists only of parts of the garment, then these are not the garment.
Why is this? Because it is merely a collection that constitutes the garment; furthermore, what part of the garment could there be that is distinct from these threads?
If the garment is established through the observation of a combination of many bases, then the garment should already be perceived within the mere combination of the threads.

At that time, one does not perceive this "cloth" as a whole, because its beginning, middle, and end do not simultaneously confront the sense faculties. Therefore, we know that there is no distinct cloth apart from the threads.

If the parts of the cloth were to confront the sense faculties in succession, one could not say that it is perceived as a whole by means of the eye or the body; for it is only through successive determination that a "whole" is established.
Therefore, the cognition of a cloth arises merely by depending on its parts, like a fire-wheel (*alātacakra*).
If the threads possessed distinct colors and other qualities, yet the cloth lacked those colors and so forth, then the cloth could not be apprehended.

If the cloth possesses various distinct categories such as colors, yet no distinct category arises, this principle is not established; for one would either not perceive the cloth at those parts where there are no various colors and so forth, or one would perceive those various colors precisely at those very parts.
Since the threads of a garment possess various properties, the garment itself should not have various differences; therefore, one knows that the garment is not a distinct entity from its parts.
