In this way, there are four permutations regarding the existence of untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) that is not the restraint of cessation (*nirodha-saṃvara*); these should be understood according to reason.
If so, how do we account for the verse spoken by the Blessed One, the Buddha:
“Excellent is restraint of the body; Excellent also is restraint of speech;”
"It is well to guard the mind; it is well to guard everything.
Furthermore, there is another explanation:
"O Bhikṣus!"
The faculty of the eye is well-guarded and abides in being protected.
What is the intrinsic nature of this guarding of the mind and guarding of the faculties?
These two are not of the nature of non-informative (avijñapti) discipline.
How so? The verse says:
"Combined with wholesome wisdom and right mindfulness, each is said to be the protection of the mental faculty."
The commentary states:
In order to show that each of the two types of restraint possesses two natures, they are explained both collectively and separately.
To clarify their sequence: mental restraint has virtuous wisdom and right mindfulness as its nature; the same applies to the restraint of the faculties.
This point should now be considered:
with what kind of informative and non-informative [karma] is which person associated, and for how long?
Regarding this, the verse says:
"If one abides in the *prātimokṣa*, one is endowed with the present and that which will arise until its relinquishment, and is endowed with the non-informative (*avijñapti*).
The commentary explains:

"If a person abides in the protection of the *prātimokṣa*, as long as they have not yet relinquished the non-informative, throughout that interval they are constantly endowed with the present non-informative."
The verse says:
"The preceding thought gives rise to the subsequent and the past.
The commentary says:
From the moment after the first instant, one is also endowed with the past non-informative [action] until it is relinquished.
This principle should be understood to apply in all cases, as in the description of a person abiding in the restraint of the *prātimokṣa*.
The verse says:
"The same applies to one who dwells in non-restraint.
The commentary says:
If a person abides in non-restraint, until they have abandoned that non-restraint, they are at all times associated with the present non-restraint non-informative action (*avijñapti*).
From the second moment onward, they are also associated with the past [non-restraint].
The verse says:
There is that which is associated with the restraint of meditative concentration (dhyānasaṃvara), [which exists] in the past and the future.
The commentary says:

If one attains the restraint born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ja-saṃvara*), one is always associated with the past and future non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), until it is abandoned. Why is this?
Because even if one has abandoned the past restraint born of meditative concentration during previous lives, it is acquired at the very first moment [of its attainment].
The verse says:
"For the Noble One, there is no past [karma] at the beginning.
The commentary explains:
The same applies to the noble ones (ārya) regarding the outflow-free restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).

This is the distinction of the noble ones: namely, when first attaining the outflow-free restraint, it is not associated with the past, because the outflow-free path had never been attained in previous lives.
The verse says:
Abiding in meditative concentration and the noble path is associated with the present life.
The commentary says:

If a person is endowed with the restraint of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*) or the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*), and enters into the contemplation of meditative absorption or the contemplation of the Noble Path, that person is successively endowed with the unmanifest action (*avijñapti*) of the present; however, this is not the case when they emerge from such contemplation.
The case of one who abides in either restraint or non-restraint has already been explained.
As for one who abides in the intermediate state, how is it?
The verse says:
Regarding the two types of those who abide in the intermediate state—the initial and the subsequent—the commentary states:

If a person does not abide in either restraint (*saṃvara*) or non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), they are called one who abides in the intermediate state; such a person does not necessarily possess non-informative action (*avijñapti*).

If there is non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) subsumed under either bad discipline or a portion of discipline, it is associated with the "middle" at its inception; this is called "middle" because it exists in the present within the context of the past and future.
The verse says:
"In the latter two periods.
The commentary says:
From the moment after the first instant, it is associated with the past and also associated with the present, until it is relinquished.
If a person abides in non-restraint, is there ever a time when they are associated with wholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*)?
If a person abides in restraint (*saṃvara*), is there ever a time when they are associated with unwholesome non-informative action (*akuśalā-avijñapti*)? If so, for how long?
The verse says:

"One who abides in non-restraint may possess the wholesome; one who abides in restraint may possess the unwholesome. These are associated with non-informative action (*avijñapti*), extending even to the pure, the defiled, and the swift.
Commentary:
If a person abides in non-restraint but, through the power of a strong and wholesome faith, performs acts such as prostrating before a stūpa, then wholesome non-informative action arises.
If a person abiding in restraint commits acts such as striking or binding others with a mind of intense affliction, then unwholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*) arises.
As long as these two [the restraint and the affliction] continue without being severed, this non-informative action will perpetually arise in succession during that time.
This person is associated with the present non-informative [matter] (*avijñapti*) at the first moment, and in subsequent moments, they are also associated with the past [non-informative matter].
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Ten; *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Eleven.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Tripitaka Master Paramārtha of India.
Part Two of the "Analysis of the Chapter on Karma," following the detailed explanation of non-informative action (avijñapti).
The verse says:
Furthermore, all [actions] together with the instruction, and those being performed, correspond to the intermediate [state].
The commentary says:

For all persons—whether abiding in the state of restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state—as long as the performance of informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) has not yet ceased, they remain associated with present informative action during that interval.
The verse says:
"After the first moment, it is associated with the past until its relinquishment.
The commentary says:
From the moment immediately following the first instant until its relinquishment, one is associated with past informative action (*vijñapti*).
The verse says:
"It is not associated with the future."
The commentary states:
No person is associated with a future informative act (*vijñapti*).
The verse says:
Regarding the obscured-unobscured [neutral] and the unobscured [neutral], they do not correspond with the past.
The commentary states:
If there is informative action (vijñapti) that is either obscured or unobscured, it does not correspond with the past; the same applies to the future.
If the power of a phenomenon is weak, its acquisition (prāpti) is also weak and cannot continue in succession.
By what is this weakness of power produced?
It is produced by the mind.
If that were so, one might argue that the obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) karma produced by the mind would lack potency.
This is not the case; for bodily and vocal karma are dull and obtuse, and are established in dependence upon others, whereas mental karma is not so.
This unobscured informative [action] is also originated by a weak intentional impulse; therefore, its power is the weakest.
It has already been stated previously that there are persons who abide in non-restraint (*avirati*).
What dharma is called non-restraint?
The verse says:
Non-restraint, evil conduct, bad morality, or the paths of action.
The commentary states:
These and others are various names for non-restraint (*asaṃvara*).
In this context, it is called "non-restraint" because one is unable to restrain the misconduct of body and speech.
They are called "misconduct" because they are censured by the wise and because they result in undesirable retribution;
they are called "immoral conduct" because they are the opposite of virtuous discipline.
It is called "karma" (action) because it is produced by body and speech;
it is called a "path of karma" (karmapatha) because it is subsumed under its fundamental [intention].
There are those who possess informative intimation (*vijñapti*) but do not possess non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*); regarding this meaning, there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*).
The verse here says:
"Only that which accords with the teaching, abiding in the middle, and performed by one of inferior resolve.
The commentary explains:

If one performs a good or an evil action with a weak intention, this person abides in a state that is neither restraint nor non-restraint; they possess only informative action (*vijñapti*) and not non-informative action (*avijñapti*). This is even more so when performing an indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) action, except in the case of meritorious actions involving material things (*aupadhika-puṇya-kriyā-vastu*) and remote actions (*dūra-karma*).
The verse says:
One who has abandoned [the path] possesses the non-informative [action] that has not yet arisen; others, the noble ones, possess the remaining non-informative [actions].
The commentary says:

Regarding those who are associated only with non-informative action (*avijñapti*) and not with informative action (*vijñapti*): this refers to noble ones (*ārya*) who have already changed their state of existence, or who have not yet performed bodily or vocal actions, or who have already relinquished such bodily or vocal actions.

Regarding association with two [courses of action]: if a person abiding in the restraint of the *prātimokṣa* initiates bodily or vocal karma, or if they abide in neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint, they perform either a wholesome or an unwholesome deed by means of an extremely superior volition.
Regarding those who do not correspond with either [the state of restraint or non-restraint], these are excluded from the first three cases.

Having explained the establishment of one who abides in restraint, non-restraint, or the intermediate state—including the meaning of the acquisition of informative and non-informative [action]—how is it that one is able to obtain this restraint?
The verse says:
"That which arises from meditative concentration is obtained through the stages of meditative concentration.
The commentary says:

At that time, if one attains a mind belonging to the dhyāna stage that is associated with outflows—whether it be the fundamental dhyāna or the preparatory stage—one simultaneously attains the restraint born of meditative concentration, because they arise together at that very moment.
The verse says:
"Because the noble ones rely on this, it is untainted.
The commentary says:
If one attains this support of the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) meditative state (*samāpatti-bhūmi*), one immediately attains the uncontaminated restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).

Within this, there are six meditative states which may all be uncontaminated—namely, the four dhyānas, the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*)—the meaning of which shall be explained later.
The verse says:
"Prātimokṣa [is so called] because it mutually causes others [to restrain themselves].
The commentary says:
The Prātimokṣa restraint is obtained from others; if one person causes another to obtain it, that other person may likewise cause others to obtain it.
This is obtained either from a great assembly or from a single individual.
Those obtained from the assembly refer to the precepts of the bhikṣu, bhikṣuṇī, and śikṣamāṇā.
Those obtained from a single person refer to all the remaining precepts.
Regarding the Vinaya, the Vaibhāṣika masters state that there are ten ways of receiving the full ordination (*upasampadā*); it is for the sake of including these that the word "etc.
is used. What are these ten?
First, one obtains the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*) by natural spontaneity, as in the case of the Buddha Bhagavān and the Pratyekabuddhas.

Second, one obtains the full precepts by entering the stage of those destined for rightness (*samyaktva-niyāma*), as when the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya, attained the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Third, one obtains the full precepts by being addressed with "Come, Bhikṣu," as was the case with Yaśas and others.
Fourth, one obtains the full precepts through faith and acceptance of the Great Teacher, as was the case with Mahākāśyapa.
Fifth, one obtains the full ordination by answering difficult questions, as in the case of Sudāyin.
Sixth, one obtains the full ordination by accepting the eight rules of respect, as in the case of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī.
Seventh, one receives the full precepts through delegation, as in the case of the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā.
Eighth, one receives the full precepts in a borderland country by having a competent holder of the Vinaya serve as the fifth member of the assembly.
Ninth, receiving the full precepts (*upasampadā*) in the Middle Kingdom by means of the ten groups;
tenth, receiving the full precepts through the three recitations of the Three Refuges, as was the case when the sixty virtuous groups gathered together to receive the precepts.
This Prātimokṣa restraint of these individuals does not necessarily follow from an explicit instruction.
If one wishes to receive this Prātimokṣa restraint, for how long should it be received?
The verse says:
One properly undertakes the vows for as long as life lasts, or for a day and a night.
The commentary says:
The Prātimokṣa restraint maintained by the seven classes of practitioners should be observed for as long as life lasts;
the Upavāsa restraint, however, lasts for one day and one night, and the time of its reception is fixed.
When observing this [vow], there are two limits: the limit of one's lifespan and the limit of a day and night.
Because it is specifically taught in relation to the day and night, it constitutes the half-month observance (*pakṣa-śīla*).
What dharma is designated as "time"?
This term reveals the meaning of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*). Within the four continents, the state of light is called "day," and the state of darkness is called "night.

This interpretation is plausible: after death, although one may still possess the observance of vows (*saṃvara*), one cannot obtain a basis for rebirth because it is not of the same class (*asabhāga*); consequently, one cannot initiate application (*prayoga*) based upon that [intermediate] state, nor can one cause the recollection of previous conduct.
If a person, after one day and night, or five days, or ten days, receives the *upavāsa* restraint, what factor could obstruct the arising of many instances of the *upavāsa* restraint?
There must be a factor capable of obstructing [the observance],
because the Tathāgata stated in the sūtras that the *upavāsa* restraint lasts for only one day and night.
This point should now be considered:
Is it because the Tathāgata perceives that the *upavāsa* restraint cannot arise after one day and night has passed, that he speaks only of the *upavāsa* restraint as lasting for one day and night?
Is it for the sake of establishing those beings with difficult-to-tame faculties that one correctly undertakes the *upavāsa* restraint for a period of one day and one night?
How can such a matter be conceived?
If one were to attain birth by protecting [the precepts] at this time, what contradiction would there be with reason?
Since we have never seen the Tathāgata speak of such a thing for a single individual, the Vaibhāṣika masters do not dare to speak of it unless it was taught by the Tathāgata.
What is the determination of the time for non-restraint?
The verse says:
There is no non-restraint by day or night.
The commentary states:

Because this person delights in performing evil deeds for the duration of a single lifetime, they do not maintain restraint; they cannot observe it for even a single day and night, unlike the *upavāsa* (fasting) vow.
Why is this? It is because they hold such a view.
The verse says:
Because it is not accepted in this way;
the commentary states:
no one accepts non-restraint (asaṃvara) in the manner that one accepts the upavāsa restraint, by wishing, "May I observe non-restraint for one day and one night."
Because this action is censured by the wise, if that were the case, there would likewise be no such undertaking as:
"I vow to undertake non-restraint for the duration of one lifetime."
Therefore, one does not obtain non-restraint for a single period [of life] merely by failing to undertake it.

Although one does not formally accept it, because one consistently opposes what is wholesome and intentionally commits these unwholesome acts, one obtains non-restraint; it is not obtained through a temporary opposition to the wholesome intention. For this reason, all obtain non-restraint for the duration of a lifetime.

Although the upavāsa restraint does not involve a single-minded state of mind, because it is obtained through the power of the intentional resolve to undertake it, one acquires it for one day and one night, according to the duration requested.
If someone seeks to obtain non-restraint and receives it for a brief period, they will necessarily obtain that non-restraint.
This principle has never been observed before; therefore, such a position cannot be established.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
Just as non-informative restraint (*avijñapti*) does not exist as a substantial entity,
so too non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) does not exist as a substantial entity.
This non-restraint (*arakṣā*) has as its essence the intentional pursuit of evil matters, and it continues to follow along with those matters.
For this reason, even if a person gives rise to a virtuous mind, they are still said to possess non-restraint, because they have not abandoned it.
Furthermore, regarding this *upavāsa* restraint (*saṃvara*), if a person wishes to receive it for one day and one night, what is the method of reception?
The verse says:

"In the morning, receive it from another; sitting in a lower position, recite the words after them. This is the *poṣadha* restraint with all its parts: abstaining from adornments for a day and a night."
The commentary states:
"At dawn" refers to the time when the sun first rises; this period of protection is the briefest, lasting for only one day and night.
If a person has previously formed the intention to seek and receive it—thinking, "I must certainly observe the *upoṣadha* restraint on the eighth day and so forth"; [then...]

If one has already finished eating, one may still receive [the food], but it must be received from another; one may not receive it for oneself. This is because one observes others, so that in the event of circumstances that would constitute an offense, one remains free from offense.
The junior monk should either squat or kneel with his mind lowered and palms joined, except when he is ill.
If a person lacks a heart of reverence, no wholesome protections will arise.
One should speak after the donor has spoken regarding the precepts; one must not speak before or simultaneously.
If this is done, it can be said that the precepts are received from another;
if not, the reception of the precepts is entirely invalid.
If one accepts [the precepts], they must be accepted in their entirety; they cannot be diminished.
Regarding "separation from adornments," this refers to separating from those that are not traditional adornments. Why is this so?
If one uses ornaments that are worn constantly, they do not give rise to a state of extreme intoxication or distraction as new ornaments would.

If one undertakes the vow, it must last for a full day and night until the following morning; if one undertakes it in a manner other than this rule, it merely produces wholesome conduct, but the *upavāsa* protection is not obtained.
This wholesome conduct can induce a desirable retribution.

If one maintains this view, then even a person who hunts or engages in sexual misconduct would certainly receive the fruit of retribution for observing the *upavāsa* restraint by day or by night; this does not contradict reason.
What is the meaning of *upavāsa*?

By means of this protection, a person dwells near the vicinity of an Arhat because they train in accordance with the Dharma of an Arhat, and furthermore, because they dwell near the vicinity of the protection that lasts as long as life.
It is also called *poṣadha*. Because it causes those sentient beings whose roots of goodness are meager to grow, and further purifies their roots of goodness, it is named *poṣadha*.
As a verse says:
"By this, one is able to nurture the pure and wholesome minds of both oneself and others."
Therefore, the Buddha, the Tathāgata, said: "This is called the *poṣadha*.
Why must one receive this protection by means of the eight branches?
For this reason, the verse says:

The factors of morality (*śīla-bhāga*), the factor of non-negligence (*apramāda-bhāga*), and the factors of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhāga*) follow in sequence: four in the former, one in the middle, and three in the latter.
The commentary states:

the first four are called the factors of morality, ranging from abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from false speech; these four constitute the abandonment of natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Next is the section on non-negligence, which refers to abstaining from drinking alcohol.

If a person has properly received the full precepts, yet becomes intoxicated and deranged by drinking alcohol, they will be able to disturb the ocean of all training rules (*śikṣāpada*) due to such negligence.

The final three items constitute the section on cultivation (*bhāvanā-aṅga*), up to the abstention from eating at improper times, because they serve as meritorious aids that can follow and support the mind of wearying detachment (*nirveda*).
If one does not undertake the section on non-negligence (*apramāda-aṅga*) and the section on cultivation, what fault is there?
The verse says:
"By this, one loses mindfulness and becomes intoxicated.
The commentary explains:
If a person drinks alcohol, they immediately lose mindfulness regarding what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
If a person indulges in high and luxurious beds, or in dancing, singing, music, and the like, mental intoxication and confusion will arise.
In either of these two cases, one is not far from breaking the precepts.
If a person eats only at the proper time, by abandoning their previous habit of eating at improper times and maintaining the upavāsa restraint, a sense of renunciation will arise.
If the eighth [precept] did not exist, these two would not exist either. Others say:
among these eight, it is specifically the abstention from eating at improper times that is designated as *upavāsa*.
The remaining eight [unwholesome courses of action] are divided for this purpose; specifically, viewing dancing and singing and wearing perfumes and flowers are each divided into two.
If one maintains such a position, it contradicts the Sūtra.
The Sūtra states:
"Abstaining from eating at improper times is the eighth limb; I now follow and practice this as all the noble Arhats do.
If that is so, what distinct dharma is called *upoṣadha*?
Taking these eight as its components (*aṅga*), this collection is designated by the name "components" according to each individual factor.
Just as one speaks of the components of a chariot, the fourfold army, or the fivefold dispersal, it should be understood that the eightfold *upavāsa* is likewise.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
abstaining from eating at improper times is both the upavāsa (fast-day observance) itself and a constituent part of the upavāsa.

For example, right view is both the noble path itself and a constituent of the noble path; the factor of awakening consisting of the investigation of dharmas is both awakening itself and a constituent of awakening; and samādhi is both concentration itself and a constituent of concentration.
The former masters say:
It is not possible to establish right view and the others as being its factors.
If right view and the others produced in a prior life were to become factors for what is produced later, then the Noble Path arising at the first moment would not constitute eight factors.
Is the *upavāsa* restraint possessed only by laymen (*upāsaka*), or is it also possessed by others?
It is also possessed by others.
The verse says:
Regarding the statement that others have the *poṣadha*, yet it does not exist for those who lack the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*):

the commentary explains that if a person who is not yet a lay follower (*upāsaka*) takes refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha for a single day and night, and subsequently receives the *upoṣadhasaṃvara* (the fast-day restraint), this person then obtains this restraint.
Otherwise, it cannot be attained, except in the case of ignorance.
As stated in the Sūtra, the Buddha said to Mahānāma:
"If a layman, a white-robed man endowed with male organs, takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Saṃgha, and also utters these words:"
"Venerable sir, please bear this in mind: I am now the upāsaka Mahānāma.
Is it by this alone that one becomes an upāsaka?
Or does one become an upāsaka simply by receiving the three refuges, or not?"
The masters of foreign lands say this is not so;
the masters of Kaśmīra say that apart from the five precepts, one does not become an upāsaka.
If that is so, how is there no contradiction with what is stated in the Sūtra?
This is because it says therein that the five precepts are "produced" (*utpādita*).
Therefore, the verse says:
"By virtue of being called an upāsaka through protection.
The commentary explains:
By accepting [the precepts] and declaring oneself to be an upāsaka, this person then generates the upāsaka restraint (*upāsaka-saṃvara*).
At that time, having accepted them, one declares:
"Venerable sir, please remember me as an upāsaka."

From this time forth, for as long as life lasts, I shall abstain from taking life and from acts such as depriving others of life; because the intermediate words have been omitted, it is simply said that one "abstains from life.
Once the precepts have been received, the subsequent recitation of the precepts is performed so that the practitioner may recognize what is permissible to observe and what is not.
The verse says:
It is said to be like the protection of a bhikṣu.
The commentary says:
Once full ordination has been obtained, one is further instructed to receive the training rules; the same applies to a śrāmaṇera.
This is done so that he may recognize the characteristics of the precepts: "From this and from that, you must now protect yourself."
The same applies to the upāsaka: apart from the fivefold restraint, there is no distinct upāsaka.
The verse says:
"If all [upāsakas] possess the restraint, how can there be distinctions such as 'one place' and so forth?"
The commentary states:
If all upāsakas abide in the upāsaka vows, why did the Buddha Bhagavat speak of four kinds of upāsakas: first, those who observe one part;
second, those who observe a few parts; [third, those who observe most parts; and fourth, those who observe all parts]?
3. Retaining many locations;
4. Retaining complete locations.
The verse says:
"It is said so because of being able to maintain [the vows].
The commentary explains:

If a person is able to maintain whatever is to be maintained, it is with reference to such a person that he is said to be "able to maintain"; therefore, it is said that all *upāsakas* inherently possess the protection [of the precepts].
This current position contradicts the sūtras.
How does it contradict the sūtras?
It is because they accept and proclaim that the five precepts are obtained immediately upon [the act of] taking life—that is, by saying, "I abstain from killing."
How does this statement contradict the sūtra?
The sūtra does not say so.
How does the sūtra speak?
As stated in the *Mahānāma-sūtra*:
"In this [sūtra], the characteristics of an upāsaka are clarified, whereas they do not exist elsewhere.
In that place, the following passage is spoken:
"As long as life remains, until the end of my life, I now place my sole faith in you; may the Venerable One bear this in mind.
In this passage, one who has seen the Four Truths demonstrates the nature of their realization and knowledge by receiving the True Dharma through the duration of their lifespan.
Even for the sake of saving one's life, I would have no reason to further abandon the True Dharma.
This passage does not intend to define the characteristics of an upāsaka.
As for the phrasing you claim refers to "renouncing life," such a reading has never been seen elsewhere.
Who could possibly explain these passages that are not clearly understood, such as the passage on "maintaining one place," if they were spoken by one who violates the precepts?
Even a question regarding them would be inappropriate, let alone an answer.
Why is this? Who among people has understood the protection of the upāsaka?
Since they do not understand it in this way, if a person does not break these precepts, that person maintains them.

If a person does not know the measure of the *upāsaka* vows, yet asks based on their understanding of the measure of those who can maintain such vows, that question is indeed reasonable. The question is as follows:
"Bhagavān, what is the measure for an *upāsaka* who maintains [the vows] in one place?"
To what extent does one become an upāsaka who maintains the complete precepts?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:

One becomes an upāsaka even apart from the formal undertaking of protection; likewise, one should also become a bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera even if one does not fully undertake the protection, just as in the case of the upāsaka.
What is the definitive extent of the protection [afforded] by upāsakas and others?

You must also admit that the distinctions among upāsakas and so forth are established according to the specific classifications and determinations set forth by the Great Teacher, for these distinctions are established in accordance with the Great Teacher’s own classifications.

Why is this? If there were no such thing as "protection" (saṃvara), then the way the World-Honored One established the upāsaka would not be the same as the way he established the śrāmaṇera and the bhikṣu.
The masters of Kaśmīra do not accept this view that all forms of protection [arise simultaneously].
The verse says:
"Inferior, middling, and superior, according to one's wish.
The commentary says:
The protective restraints (*saṃvara*) maintained by the eight classes of beings are categorized as inferior, middling, and superior; how are these established?
They are distinguished by differences in the volition (*cetanā*) regarding the intent to undertake them.
If one holds such a view, then the Prātimokṣa restraint of an Arhat would be the most inferior, while that of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) would be the most superior.
If one only undertakes the precepts but does not take the three refuges, can one become an upāsaka?
No, except in the case of ignorance.
When a person takes refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, in what dharmas does this person take refuge?
The verse says:

"The dharmas that can bring about the Buddha and the Saṃgha—namely, the Aśaikṣa and the two kinds [of Śaikṣa], as well as refuge and Nirvāṇa—constitute taking refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṃgha.
The commentary explains:
If a person takes refuge in the Buddha, they necessarily take refuge in those dharmas of the stage beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) that constitute Buddhahood.
What are these constitutive dharmas?
It is because of the excellence of those dharmas that this body is designated as "Buddha."
Alternatively, because one has attained those dharmas and thus possesses superior capacity for all-encompassing awakening, such a person is called a Buddha.
What are the characteristics of these dharmas?

They consist of the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and its associated factors; they are so designated because there is no distinction between the physical body (*rūpakāya*) before and after [attainment].
If one takes refuge in the Buddha, does one take refuge in a single Buddha or in all Buddhas?
According to reason, one takes refuge in all Buddhas, because the characteristics of the Path do not differ.
If a person takes refuge in the Saṃgha, that person takes refuge in those dharmas of the Śaikṣas and Aśaikṣas that constitute the Saṃgha;
for by attaining those dharmas, the persons who have attained the fruits of the Eightfold Path become the Saṃgha, which is indestructible.
If one takes refuge in the Sangha, does one take refuge in a single monk or in the entire Sangha?
According to the principle of reasoning, one takes refuge in the entire Sangha, because the characteristic of the Path is not different [in all members].
The Sūtra states:
"In a future age, there shall be monks who are named [as such]; these individuals also take refuge in this Sangha.
These words are intended to manifest the most supreme qualities of the present Sangha Jewel.

If a person takes refuge in the Dharma, that person takes refuge in nirvāṇa, which is to say, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); for the afflictions and suffering within the continuums of oneself and others are of a single characteristic in their state of tranquility.

If one were to maintain that the Buddha consists solely of the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma), how could one who conceives an evil thought toward the Tathāgata and draws blood from the Buddha’s body incur an immediate retributive offense (ānantarya-karma)?
The Vaibhāṣikas explain it thus: because the physical basis [the body] is harmed, those dharmas are also harmed.
The Abhidharma-piṭaka does not state this; rather, it says that only the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called "the Buddha's teaching.
How, then, can the dharmas by which one becomes a Buddha be called "the Buddha"?
Since this does not preclude the basis [of those dharmas] from being the Buddha, this objection is not a valid objection.
If it were not so, the Buddha would not be established as a Buddha while in the world, and the same would apply to the Saṃgha;
only the precepts can establish one as a bhikṣu. Therefore, the precepts are the bhikṣu.
Just as when a person makes offerings to a bhikṣu, they are making offerings to that which enables the bhikṣu-precepts to be accomplished;
so too, when a person takes refuge in the Buddha, they take refuge solely in those dharmas of the Aśaikṣa which enable one to become a Buddha.
Other masters say:
"If a person takes refuge in the Buddha, that person takes refuge in the eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma).
What is the essential nature of this refuge?"
The teaching has speech as its nature.
What is the meaning of "taking refuge"?
Its meaning is "to provide rescue and protection."
Because by relying on these three, one is forever liberated from all suffering.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said in verse:
"Many people seek refuge In mountains and dense forests..."
The groves, the trees, and the shrines—when one is oppressed by fear, these refuges are not supreme; these refuges are not the highest.
By resorting to these refuges, one is not liberated from all suffering.
If a person takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma and the Saṅgha,
and constantly observes the meaning of the Four Noble Truths with wisdom—
the truth of suffering, the origin that gives rise to suffering, and the path that leads exclusively to the transcendence of suffering— [they shall attain liberation].
Possessing the Noble Eightfold Path, one proceeds toward the tranquility of suffering;
this refuge is most excellent, this refuge is supreme.
If one reaches this refuge, one is liberated from all suffering.
Therefore, the practice of faith, acceptance, and taking refuge serves as the gateway to all forms of undertaking the precepts.

Furthermore, for what reason does the Buddha establish the abstention from sexual desire as a training rule within other types of vows, yet establish the abstention from sexual misconduct as the training rule specifically within the vows of a lay follower (*upāsaka*)?
The verse says:
Sexual misconduct is most censurable; it is easy to commit, yet one can achieve its non-commission.
The commentary says:
Sexual misconduct is the most censurable act in the world, for it involves violating and destroying another’s wife and can lead to karma that drags one toward the evil realms;
sexual desire is not like this.
For a householder, it is easy to abstain from sexual misconduct, but it is difficult to abstain from sexual desire altogether.
Because they are unable to perform difficult deeds, they do not go forth into homelessness.
The noble ones attain the restraint of non-action regarding the nature of sexual misconduct, because by their very nature they would not commit it in future lives.

This is not the case regarding sexual desire; therefore, among the precepts for upāsakas, abstaining from sexual misconduct is established as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*), so that an ārya who has been reborn elsewhere might not be considered to have violated a portion of the upāsaka vows.
Why is this? That which is definitively not to be done is called "non-action protection" (*akaraṇa-saṃvara*).
If a person has already become an upāsaka and only then marries a wife or concubines, does this person obtain that protection with respect to them?
It can be said that one does not obtain the restraint in a single location.
How is it that the restraint is not destroyed therein?
The verse says:
Just as one obtains the restraint through the intention to undertake it, it is not obtained within the continuum itself.
The commentary says:
Just as one receives the restraint [of the precepts], so too does one obtain the restraint through intentional resolve (*cetanā*).
What is this intentional resolve for receiving the restraint? It means:
"I shall now forever abstain from sexual misconduct"; it does not refer to the continuity of that [act] itself, but rather: "I shall not engage in sexual desire from this time forth."

Therefore, a person who has received the five precepts obtains protection regarding the abstention from sexual misconduct by relying on that [precept], rather than obtaining it through the abstention from all sexual desire. Consequently, engaging in sexual intercourse with one's own wife does not constitute a violation or breach of that protection.
Why is it that only the abstention from false speech is established as a training rule for the upāsaka’s vows, while the abstention from divisive speech and so forth are not?
This is due to the three preceding proofs: namely, that false speech is most censurable, it is easy to commit, and it is possible to attain the state of not committing it.
The verse says:
Because it involves the utterance of false speech, it transgresses all rules of training (*śikṣāpada*).
The commentary says:
Regarding all transgressions of the training rules, if one is questioned and immediately utters a falsehood, saying,
"I did not do it," then by means of that lie, a downfall (āpatti) arises that is pervasive and cannot be remedied.
Therefore, the Great Master, based on this meaning, asked: "What is a person who has violated the precepts? He replied:
"Because one must reveal and disclose one's own failure as it truly is, the abstention from false speech is established as a protection."
Furthermore, for what reason is one not established as a lay follower (upāsaka) by observing the offenses of conventional prohibition?
They say: it is indeed so established.
The verse says:
Among the offenses of conventional prohibition, one must abstain only from alcohol.
The commentary says:
For what reason is it that one observes the precept of abstaining from intoxicants alone, rather than abstaining from others?
The verse says:
"In order to protect the rest."
The commentary states: Why is this?
If a person drinks alcohol, they will be unable to maintain the other components of their restraint.
How is it known that drinking alcohol is a *prajñapti-āpatti* (an offense of conventional designation)?
Because it lacks the characteristics of an *intrinsic offense* (*svabhāva-āpatti*).
An intrinsic offense is defined as follows: if one commits this offense only when giving rise to a defiled mind, it is called an intrinsic offense.
Sometimes one may drink alcohol in measured amounts with the sole intention of treating an illness so as not to become intoxicated.
If this were the case, such a mind would already be defiled (*kliṣṭa*), for one drinks intentionally while knowing that it can cause intoxication.
It is not an affliction, for one drinks knowing the proper measure so as not to become intoxicated.
All masters of the Vinaya-piṭaka state that drinking alcohol is a natural transgression (prakṛti-sāvadya).
As stated in the Vinaya:
"World-Honored One,
how should one treat a sick person?"
The Buddha said:
"Upāli! With the exception of natural offenses."
What constitutes a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)?
It is that which I have established as a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for the upāsakas.
Furthermore, when Śākya was ill, the Blessed One did not permit the drinking of alcohol.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says:
"O Bhikṣus!
If a person declares me to be their teacher, they should not drink even as much alcohol as would wet the tip of a blade of grass."
Therefore, one should know that drinking alcohol is a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
Furthermore, since the noble ones (*ārya*), having transformed their specific dispositions, do not by nature commit this— just as they do not commit killing and so forth—
it is because it is taught to be an unwholesome bodily action (*kāya-duścarita*).
The Abhidharma masters say: It is not so. Why is this?
At times, for the sake of the sick, a temporary allowance is made for certain prohibited offenses;
yet, the drinking of alcohol is strictly forbidden.

Why is this so? Because it leads to the occurrence of what is not permitted, and because the amount required to cause intoxication is indeterminate; therefore, even drinking from the tip of a blade of grass is not allowed.
That which is not transgressed by the Noble Ones is due to the fact that the Noble Ones possess a sense of shame regarding the loss of mindfulness.
Because of this loss of mindfulness, even a single drop is not permitted to be drunk.
Because its scope is not fixed, it is like a potent poison.
Regarding the description of bodily misconduct as a basis for heedlessness:
for this reason, the designation "basis for heedlessness" is established for it, but not for others, because those other cases constitute natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*).
If one practices this excessively, the Blessed One has stated that by means of this, one enters the evil destinies.
What is the meaning of this?

Because through the habituation of craving, these unwholesome actions arise in continuous succession, they are able to induce karma that leads to rebirth in the evil destinies; thus, one is born there.
"Alcohol is the basis for intoxication and heedlessness.
What is the meaning of this statement?
"Alcohol" refers to the drinking of liquor.
"Alcoholic beverages" refers to other types of liquor.
These two [categories] may, at times, not have reached or may have already passed the stage of intoxication and thus are not termed "intoxicants.
To exclude such cases, it is said that even betel nuts and *kūṭava* grains can cause intoxication.
To eliminate this, alcohol and its derivatives are taught.

Although these are offenses established by convention (*prajñapti-āpatti*), they are described as the basis of negligence because they are the foundation for all unwholesome conduct; thus, they are taught so that one may recognize their causal conditions and remove them with earnest urgency.

Regarding these three types of precepts—namely, the prātimokṣa, those born of meditative concentration, and the outflow-free—if one obtains one precept from this cause, does one thereby obtain the other two?
This is incorrect. If so, how is it?
The verse says:
"One who desires [to leave] both [the desire realm and the form realm] obtains the prātimokṣa restraint in the present.
The commentary states:
"The precepts of the desire realm refer to the prātimokṣa restraint."
"From all" refers to the preliminary, the fundamental, and the subsequent phases.

"From two" refers to those involving sentient beings and those not involving sentient beings, as well as those involving natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and those involving conventional prohibitions (*prajñapti-sāvadya*).

Regarding "from the present," this refers to the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) of the present world; from these, one obtains the *prātimokṣa* precepts. Why is this so?

Because it arises with sentient beings as its object, it does not derive from the past or the future; this is because the two periods of past and future do not constitute the category of sentient beings.
The verse says:
"From the root and at all times, one obtains the restraint of meditative absorption and the outflow-free [restraint]."
The commentary states:

One obtains the restraint born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ja-saṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) from the fundamental paths of action (*maula-karmapatha*), not from the preliminary (*pūrvāṅga*) or subsequent (*paścāṅga*) stages; how much less could they arise from the restraints of proscribed offenses (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*)?
This is obtained from all times—namely, the past, present, and future—within the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu).
For this reason, four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are established.

There are instances where one obtains the prātimokṣa precepts from these [aggregates, bases, and elements], but does not obtain the precepts born of meditative concentration (dhyānaja) or the outflow-free precepts (anāsrava); this should be explained in detail accordingly.
The first phrase refers to the preliminary and concluding phases of the present life, as well as those arising from offenses of formal prohibition (*prajñapti-āpatti*).
The second phrase refers to the fundamental paths of action (*mūla-karmapatha*) of the past and future.
The third phrase refers to [non-restraint] arising from the fundamental paths of action in the present life.
The fourth phrase refers to [restraint or non-restraint] arising from the preliminary (sāmantaka) and subsequent (pṛṣṭha) stages of actions in the past or future.
Regarding this restraint and non-restraint, are they all acquired with respect to all objects, all factors, and all causes, or are there differences?
Regarding the definitive attainment, the verse says:
"The protection is attained with respect to sentient beings; it is indefinite due to its parts and causes.
The commentary says:
Protection is obtained from all sentient beings, not from only a portion of them.
Since the portions [of beings] are indefinite, there are those who obtain protection from all portions, namely, those who receive the bhikṣu precepts.
There are those who obtain restraint from four parts, namely by undertaking the remaining precepts; for the courses of action constitute all parts of restraint.
Due to this causal principle, there is a sense in which one obtains it from all [parts], and a sense in which one does not obtain it from all.
If non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion are established as the causes for protecting living beings, then they are obtained from all [minds], because they are not mutually exclusive.

If, however, lower, middling, or superior intentions are established as the causes for protecting living beings, then they are not obtained from all [minds], because these three grades do not arise simultaneously.
Now, it must be discussed that the subsequent cause is established as the cause of arising.

There is a person who maintains the restraint (*saṃvara*) and possesses restraint toward all sentient beings, yet not by means of all parts and not by means of all causes; this refers to a person who, through a weak, middling, or superior intention, undertakes the restraint of an upāsaka or a śrāmaṇera.

There is a person who possesses restraint toward all sentient beings by way of all aspects, but not by way of all causes; this refers to a person who receives the bhikṣu precepts through an inferior, middling, or superior degree of volition.
There is one who obtains restraint toward all sentient beings, in all aspects, and by all causes; this refers to one who receives the three types of restraint through the three grades of volition.

There is also one who obtains restraint toward all sentient beings by all causes, but not in all aspects; this refers to one who receives the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts through the three grades of volition.
If one does not [take it] from all sentient beings, such a protection does not exist. Why is this?
Because only by abiding in a virtuous intention toward every single sentient being can one obtain this protection; otherwise, it cannot be obtained.
Why is this so? Because evil intentions have not been severed.
If a person does not engage in the five kinds of fixed discrimination, they obtain the prātimokṣa restraint.
The fivefold determination of restriction refers to the restrictions concerning sentient beings, parts, places, times, and conditions.
To resolve, "I shall abstain from killing and so forth regarding a certain sentient being," is called the restriction of sentient beings.
"I maintain [this restraint] for a certain portion" is called the classification of determination by portion.
"I maintain [this restraint] in a certain place" is called the classification of determination by location.
"I maintain this protection for as long as one month, etc. is called the classification of determination by time.
Excluding matters of combat, this is called the distinction of the conditioned restraint (*pratyayika-saṃvara*).
If a person undertakes such an undertaking, they obtain only good conduct (*kuśala-caryā*) but do not obtain restraint (*saṃvara*).
How could one obtain restraint with respect to an object that is beyond one's capacity?
Because it is acquired through a virtuous intention that does not harm the lives of any sentient beings.

If this restraint were acquired from objects that are capable [of being harmed], then this restraint would be subject to increase and decrease, because the capable and the incapable would mutually interchange.

If that were so, then the acquisition of restraint or the relinquishment of restraint would occur independently of the causes and conditions for acquiring or relinquishing it; this point is self-evident, as the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain.
Other teachers, however, say:
"This point should not be understood in such a way."
Why is this? For example, when grass and the like do not yet exist, or at times wither and perish, there is no sense of increase or decrease in their protection.
Likewise, when sentient beings—whether capable or incapable—are transformed into one another, there is likewise no sense of increase or decrease.
This interpretation is not correct, because sentient beings exist throughout the past and future, whereas grass and such things do not.
If sentient beings were to enter parinirvāṇa and never exist again, how could the principle of the protection of increase and decrease not be established?
Therefore, this defense is logically untenable;
the previous explanation is correct.

If that were the case, then for all sentient beings who had already attained parinirvāṇa under a former Buddha, the Buddhas appearing later in the world would not obtain the prātimokṣa restraint from them.
How could the precepts of a later Buddha be inferior to those of a former Buddha?
This proposition is untenable, because [the precepts] are obtained from all sentient beings.
If those sentient beings were still present, one would likewise have to obtain them from them.
Having explained the meaning of the causes that enable one to obtain restraint,
how is it that non-restraint is obtained?
The verse says:
"Non-restraint arises from all [beings], but not from all factors as its cause.
The commentary states:
"Non-restraint" is acquired with respect to all sentient beings and with respect to all courses of action.

Why is this? There is no such thing as a person who is not protected [by non-restraint]; one becomes unprotected by possessing non-restraint, rather than through all causes, because factors such as the inferior grade do not arise simultaneously.
If a person acquires non-restraint through a weak state of mind, that same person may also take the life of a sentient being through a strong state of mind.

Such a person is endowed with the weak non-restraint, yet is also endowed with the strong unmanifest karma (*avijñapti*) of killing; the same applies to those who act through middling or strong states of mind.
Among these, such a person is called one who lacks restraint (*arakṣaka*).

This refers to those who slaughter sheep, slaughter chickens, slaughter pigs, catch birds, catch fish, hunt deer, commit theft, execute criminals, act as jailers, bind elephants, cook dogs, set nets, serve as generals, or act as judges.
Such persons, in terms of their meaning, are all those who do not observe restraint (*asaṃvṛta*), because they abide in non-restraint.
They are called "persons who do not observe restraint" because they possess this non-restraint; thus they are termed "persons who do not observe restraint."
This point may be so; that is to say, all forms of restraint (*saṃvara*) are obtained from all sentient beings, because they are undertaken with the intention of seeking their welfare and benefit.

However, how can it be said that those who slaughter sheep obtain restraint from all sentient beings, given that they harbor no intent to harm their own mothers, fathers, wives, children, and so forth, and do not even wish to cause them injury even to save their own lives?
Even if one's close relatives were to be reborn as sheep or other such animals, one would still be able to kill them. Why is this?
Because one knows that they have not yet become those [animals], one does not kill them.
It is impossible for those who are close relatives to become noble ones (ārya) and yet again become animals;
from such a state, how could non-restraint (avirati) arise?
If it were the case that non-restraint arises from the present continuum by observing future events, then sheep and other animals would necessarily become children and so forth in the future.
If one has consistently refrained from killing, how could one fail to obtain non-restraint (*arakṣā*) in the present life?
If a person constantly harbors harmful intentions toward sentient beings, they will inevitably incur non-restraint on that account.
What is the meaning of this adherence?
This principle applies equally to one's closest relatives and others.
Although this person has no intention to harm them, they nevertheless obtain non-restraint from them.
What is the meaning of this?

If there are those who, for instance, kill sheep and so forth, yet throughout their entire lives refrain from taking what is not given, are content with their own wives, and are mute regarding false speech, how can they be said to possess non-restraint (avirati) in all its aspects?
Because it is destroyed by a wholesome intention (*kuśalacetana*).
If a meaning ought to be manifested through speech, he is able to manifest it with the body.
If that were so, there might be someone who receives the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) either two or three at a time.
What is the meaning of this?
There is never such a thing as a non-restraint that is incomplete or a non-restraint that pertains to only one part.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
In this way, according to the intention with which one undertakes [the vows], one obtains non-restraint (arakṣa) even if it is incomplete or pertains to only one part;
the same applies to the undertaking of restraint (rakṣa), with the exception of the eightfold restraint (aṣṭāṅga-rakṣa).
The Sautrāntikas say this:
because it serves as a restraint against both virtuous and non-virtuous conduct by means of such a measure, they state that non-restraint is acquired from this. But how is non-restraint acquired?
This meaning has not yet been explained; it shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"The acquisition of non-restraint arises from two causes: through one's own action and through formal undertaking."
The commentary states:
Non-restraint is acquired through two causes: if one is born into such a family, it is by personally committing acts such as killing;
if one is born into another family, it is by seeking to undertake this occupation, thinking, "We should perform this work in order to establish our livelihood."
Due to these two causes, non-restraint arises.
The verse says:
One acquires the remaining types of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) through the field, formal undertaking, or intense practice.
The commentary states:

There exists such a field characterized by these features, within which the mere gift of a monastery (*ārama*) and so forth gives rise to wholesome non-informative action (*avijñapti*), as explained in the section on meritorious deeds involving acquisition (*parigraha*).
Furthermore, there is the vow to undertake virtuous conduct:
"If I have not yet paid homage to the Buddha, I vow not to eat nor to sleep.
On fast days, as well as during the half-month and the month-long periods, I shall constantly give food to others."

It is as follows: because of this, the non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) of virtuous conduct flows continuously; since it exists in this way, when one performs various wholesome or unwholesome deeds with a resolute mind, further non-informative matter arises from that.
Having explained how one acquires restraint and non-restraint, the relinquishing of restraint and non-restraint shall now be discussed.
Regarding this, the verse says:

The relinquishing of the Prātimokṣa discipline occurs through the abandonment of the precepts, through death, through the transformation of the sexual organs, and through the severance of the faculties.
The commentary states:
"Discipline of liberation" (*vinaya-vinīta*) refers to the restraint of the *prātimokṣa*, for it is able to subdue the actions of body and speech.
There are four causes by which one may relinquish the *prātimokṣa* restraint, with the exception of the *upavāsa* (fasting) restraint:
First, by intentionally relinquishing the training before a person capable of understanding;
second, by relinquishing it through the abandonment of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*);
and third, by the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs.
Fourth, it is abandoned through the severance of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

The *upavāsa* restraint is abandoned by the aforementioned four causes and, furthermore, by the completion of the night; thus, combining these, there are five causes for its abandonment. Therefore, it is said that there are five causes for abandonment.
For what reason is it abandoned on account of these five?

Because the manifest action (*vijñapti*) produced is contrary to the volition (*cetanā*) of seeking to receive [the precepts]; because the basis (*āśraya*) no longer remains; because the basis undergoes transformation; because the causal conditions (*pratyaya*) are severed; and because it has induced only this much [of the result].
The verse says:
"The others are prophesied to experience the Great Burning.
The commentary says:

Other schools state that there are four types of offenses involving great burning torment (*mahāparidāha*); by committing any one of these, one immediately abandons the vows of a bhikṣu or a śrāmaṇera.
The verse says:
"Or, [the vows are lost] when the True Dharma comes to an end."
The commentary states:
Other masters say that when the True Dharma is extinguished, all rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), ordination platforms (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), and formal procedures (*karmavācanā*) are entirely abandoned.
The verse says:
The masters of Kaśmīra say that there are two types of transgressions, like being in debt for wealth.
The commentary says:
The Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīr maintain this position: if a person commits a root offense, they do not lose the bhikṣu precepts. Why?
Because by corrupting a single point, one abandons the entire protection.
This cannot be so. There is no such principle that the violation of one training rule entails the severance of all other training rules.
Nevertheless, this person possesses two aspects: they possess both morality and the breaking of morality, just as a person may possess wealth while simultaneously owing another a debt.

Having confessed and revealed this transgression, one regains the full purity of the precepts and is no longer subject to their violation; it is like a person who, having repaid a debt to another, once again possesses wealth.
If that is so, why did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, say:
"This person is not a bhikṣu, not a śramaṇa, not a son of the Śākya"?

Because he has severed, fallen from, and regressed from the protection of the bhikṣu and the meaning of being a śramaṇa, he is called one who has committed a pārājika offense; this statement was made with reference to a bhikṣu in the ultimate sense.
Now, by disregarding your own life, a great transgression has arisen.
What is this great transgression of disregarding one's life?
It is that which the Buddha, the World-Honored One, established as definitive (nītārtha), which you instead invert and treat as non-definitive (neyārtha).
Regarding the conditions for breaking the precepts, one creates the conditions for transgression by associating with persons of many afflictions.
How is it known that this statement is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*)?
Because this statement is a decisive pronouncement within the Vinaya.
The Vinaya states: "There are four kinds of bhikṣus:
first, the nominal bhikṣu; second, the self-proclaimed bhikṣu; third, the bhikṣu by begging; and fourth, the bhikṣu who has destroyed the afflictions."
Regarding this matter, it is taught that one who receives the precepts through the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* is called a bhikṣu.
There is no such principle as this person being a true bhikṣu at first and subsequently becoming a non-bhikṣu.
Regarding what you have said—that by violating one point, the remainder is not lost—on this matter the Great Master has already rendered a definitive judgment:
it is like a *tāla* tree whose head has been cut off; it will no longer produce new shoots, and it shall not reach maturity, nor grow tall, nor attain greatness.
What meaning does the Blessed One intend to reveal by making this analogy?
It is that because one part of the root has been destroyed, the remaining restraint can no longer arise.

If a person commits a root offense that is most grave, capable of destroying all the practices of a bhikṣu, because it is associated with the most extreme lack of shame and remorse, this person immediately severs the roots of all protection; therefore, they abandon all protection.
This principle must be so. Why?

Because regarding the communal meal and the dwelling place, the Buddha did not permit this person to eat even a single morsel of food or to set even one heel upon the ground; this person has been expelled by the Great Teacher from all the affairs and functions of the great assembly.
With reference to this person, the Buddha further said:
"You should eradicate the sugarcane shoots, uproot the hollow trees, and winnow away the grain without kernels; you must now bring them to an end."
If one who is not a bhikṣu claims to be a bhikṣu, what characteristics would the dharma of a bhikṣu have in such a person?
It would have the same characteristics as those [of a true bhikṣu].
Nevertheless, it is not that the dharma of a bhikṣu does not exist.
Why is this? The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said:
"Cunda, there are only four types of śramaṇas; there is no fifth."
The fourth [category] consists of: first, those born into the path; second, those who preach the path; third, those who live by the path; and fourth, those who defile the path.
Regarding this teaching, is such a person a śramaṇa merely by outward appearance, or is it for other reasons that they are called a śramaṇa?
For example, it is like burnt wood, a dried-up pond, a parrot’s beak, a spoiled seed, a fire-wheel, or a deceased being.
If one becomes a non-monk (*abhikṣu*) due to the breaking of precepts, one should not become a monk who is under training (*śaikṣa*).
We do not say that all persons who violate the precepts become *pārājika* immediately upon the act of violation;
nor do we say that one who is *pārājika* is necessarily no longer a bhikṣu.

There are others who, due to the excellence of their mental continuum, do not commit a *pārājika* offense even when they have transgressed, because they do not dare to conceal it with a single thought of intent.
This is how the Lord of Dharma established the principles of the Vinaya.
If one who has committed a *pārājika* offense is no longer a bhikṣu, why is he not permitted to go forth again?

It is because his mental continuum has been destroyed by the most extreme lack of shame and dread, and thus he is incapable of producing the state of protection; he is like a burnt seed. This is not because one observes that he still possesses the qualities of a bhikṣu.
Why is this? Because if such a person has already renounced the precepts, they are not permitted to go forth again.
What benefit would there be in the effort expended toward such a corrupted state?
If a person has already become such, can they still be called a bhikṣu? Not so;

this is the meaning of "bhikṣu. Because the True Dharma has been extinguished and the Vinaya and karmavācanā no longer exist, one does not obtain new vows; however, if one has already obtained them, they are not lost.
Furthermore, regarding the abandonment of the restraint born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-ja-saṃvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*):
the verse says:
"By transcending a stage and by falling away, one abandons the wholesome [restraint] obtained through concentration."
The commentary states:
All wholesome dharmas acquired through meditative concentration (samāpatti) are abandoned due to two causes and conditions:

either by being reborn in a higher realm and thus transcending the current level, or by falling from a higher concentration and descending to a lower level, or by relinquishing the homogeneous class of beings (nikāyasabhāga).
Furthermore, just as in the form realm one acquires the wholesome through the attainment of a higher stage, and loses it through falling back or relinquishing that stage,
the verse says:
"The same applies to the formless realm."
The commentary states:
In the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), one acquires the wholesome [roots] through the transition to other stages and likewise through falling away;
however, there is no discipline of meditative concentration (*dhyānasaṃvara*). As the verse says:
"A noble one who has attained the fruit, one who refines their faculties, and one who falls away.
The commentary states:
undefiled wholesome states are relinquished due to three causes and conditions:
One abandons the preceding path by attaining a fruit; one abandons the path of inferior faculties by refining the faculties; and one abandons the superior path by falling away.
Whether it be the fruit or the path superior to the fruit, the various dharmas that protect the fruit are abandoned in this manner.
The verse says:
One abandons non-restraint and acquires restraint because of death and the arising of the two faculties.
The commentary says:
There are three causes and conditions by which non-restraint can be abandoned:
first, through the attainment of restraint, meaning the undertaking and maintaining of restraint;
or through the attainment of restraint born of meditative concentration, which is attained through the power of past causes and conditions.
All non-restraint is severed because the power of its antidote is great.
Second, one abandons non-restraint through death, because the physical basis (āśraya) has perished.
Third, one abandons non-restraint through the simultaneous arising of both sexual organs, because the physical basis has undergone transformation.

If a person discards weapons, nets, and the like due to the mental resolve of non-intentionality, although they have abandoned the conditions for [harmful] arising, if they do not receive the protective restraint that serves as an antidote, there is no sense of being "unprotected" or "without interruption."
For example, if one is separated from the conditions for recovery and does not take good medicine, a serious illness will not be cured;
the previous principle is likewise so.

Regarding a person who is not restrained (*asaṃvṛta*), if they undertake the *upoṣadha* restraint, do they pass from restraint back into non-restraint, or do they pass from restraint into that which is neither restraint nor non-restraint?
Other masters say:
"One returns to non-restraint because the intention to relinquish it is not fixed, just as red-hot iron returns to its dark blue color.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:

This interpretation is not correct. If a person again performs the same actions as before, they would return to the state of non-restraint (*avirati*), because the acquisition (*prāpti*) resulting from this is dependent upon informative action (*vijñapti*).
Furthermore, how could one abandon non-informative action (*avijñapti*) that is distinct from both restraint and non-restraint?
The verse says:
"One quickly takes up and practices objects within the state of abandoning when the life-faculty is severed.
The commentary says:
Whether by the forceful intensity of a wholesome mind or by the inevitable forcefulness of an affliction, one can induce the arising of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*).

If this mind is severed, the non-informative matter is likewise severed; it is like the movement of a potter’s wheel or a released arrow, which ceases when the impelling mind is cut off—the same applies to non-informative matter.
If a person abandons the intention to receive [something], thinking, "Let me not receive it in this way," then by the cessation of that activity, this [intention] is also abandoned.
Just as when an action previously performed is no longer carried out, by the cessation of the requisite material conditions, this [action] is also abandoned.
What are the objects possessed?

They refer to items such as shrines (caityas), gardens, bedding and seating, and canopies; these are also severed either by the termination of one's lifespan or by the severance of one's roots of virtue.
If a person undertakes the means to sever the roots of goodness, they abandon them immediately through these six causes.
Regarding the non-informative [matter] therein, the verse says:
"In the desire realm, the roots of goodness are severed; by being born in the formless [realm], one abandons them."
The commentary states:
If all non-material (arūpa) wholesome factors within the desire realm are abandoned due to two causes—namely, the severance of the roots of goodness and rebirth in the form or formless realms.
The verse says:
Because the antidote arises, one abandons the defilements of the formless realm.
The commentary says:

All non-material (arūpa) defilements are abandoned through their antidotes; these categories of afflictions are to be eliminated, and these categories of antidotes are capable of extinguishing them. Thus, as soon as the antidote arises, they are abandoned.
The defilements and their associates do not arise through any other means.
Furthermore, among which sentient beings is there non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) and which have restraint (*saṃvara*)?
The verse says:
The non-restraint excludes those in the human realm who are exempt from it: the two types of eunuchs, the hermaphrodites, and the inhabitants of Kuru.
The commentary states:
Only within the human realm does non-restraint exist; it is absent in other realms.

Within the human realm, this excludes those born as eunuchs (*śaṇḍha*), those who become eunuchs through external causes (*paṇḍaka*), those with both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*), and those of Uttarakuru.
The verse says:
"The same applies to the restraints (*saṃvara*), and likewise for the gods."
The commentary states:
There is protection regarding the human realm, excluding those previously excluded.
There is also protection regarding the celestial realm; therefore, there is protection in both realms.
How is it known that eunuchs and others lack the restraint?
It is known through the Sūtras and the Vinaya.
The Sūtra says:
Mahānāma! If a layman, a white-robed man endowed with male organs, takes refuge in the Buddha, takes refuge in the Dharma, and takes refuge in the Saṅgha.
He also spoke these words:
"May the Venerable One remember me; I am now a lay follower (*upāsaka*), Mahānāma!"
It is solely by this measure that a person becomes an upāsaka.
There is also a textual passage in the Vinaya; the Vinaya states:
"O monks, you must certainly exclude persons with such characteristics."
Furthermore, for what reasons is there no restraint (*saṃvara*) therein?

It is because the afflictions (*kleśa*) based on the two [bodies] are excessive; because the mental continuum lacks the capacity for correct reflection and discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*); and because even the lowest degree of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*) are absent. For these reasons, there is no restraint.
If that is so, why is there no non-restraint?
Because within the unwholesome, the basis is not fixed or real.
Wherever there is restraint, there must also be non-restraint, for the two are mutually opposed as antidotes.

Because the inhabitants of Uttarakuru lack the seeking for [the precepts] and a concentrated mind, and because they have no intentional desire to commit evil, they possess neither restraint nor non-restraint.
How is it that there is neither restraint nor non-restraint in the evil realms?
It is because they lack the most profound sense of shame and dread of blame (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*).
It is only through being endowed with these two, or their destruction, that one attains restraint or non-restraint.
Furthermore, that basis possesses such defects that it becomes a barren field, namely: the two types of eunuchs and those with both sexual organs.
Regarding this basis, the beings of the evil realms neither produce restraint nor non-restraint; it is like a salty, alkaline, and barren field where neither fine seedlings nor even weeds will grow.
How is it stated in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus!
There are dragons born from eggs who, on the eighth day of the half-month, emerge from their palaces and observe the eightfold *upoṣadha* vows."
This practice is merely wholesome conduct; because there is no restraint (*saṃvara*) therein, restraint exists only in the realms of humans and gods.
Furthermore, regarding this, a verse states:
"Humans possess all three."
The commentary states:
Within the human realm, all three types of restraint are fully present; that is, the three restraints beginning with the *prātimokṣa*.
The verse says:
"Those born in the heavens of the desire and form realms possess the protection born of meditative concentration (*samādhi-saṃvara*).
Commentary:
If various devas are born in the desire or form realms, they possess the protection born of meditative concentration; however, this does not exist in the higher realms.
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are no outflows [in the realms] excluding the intermediate dhyāna, the realm of non-perception, and the formless realm.
The commentary says:

The untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara) exists among the gods of the desire and form realms, excluding those in the intermediate dhyāna, the non-conceptual heaven (asaṃjñi-sattva), and the formless realm.

If one is born among the gods of the formless realm, one possesses both the dhyāna restraint and the untainted restraint by way of acquisition (prāpti), but not by way of actual presence (sammukhībhāva).
From this point onward, because karma will be explained through detailed analysis,
I shall now provide a comprehensive analysis of karma, which was only briefly mentioned in the sūtras.
There are three kinds of karma:
That is to say: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"Even and uneven karma are distinct; the wholesome and unwholesome are distinct from those two."
The commentary states:
This refers to the characteristics of the wholesome (*kuśala*) and so forth. If an action is peaceful (*kṣema*), it is established as wholesome.
If its maturation (*vipāka*) is desirable, or if it can lead to nirvāṇa, it is called "peaceful," because it is able to provide relief from suffering both temporarily and eternally.
If it is not peaceful, it is called unwholesome (*akuśala*), as it is the opposite of peace.

If the karmic fruition is undesirable and capable of obstructing liberation—being distinct from the two aforementioned types of karma—it is neither peaceful nor non-peaceful; therefore, one should know that it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome.
What is the meaning of this statement?
Its meaning is that it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
Meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable; furthermore, there are three [types of feeling], such as painful feeling.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, there are three types of karma, namely meritorious karma (*puṇya-karman*), non-meritorious karma (*apuṇya-karman*), and immovable karma (*āniñjya-karman*).
Furthermore, there are three types of karma: namely, karma that results in pleasant feeling, karma that results in painful feeling, and karma that results in neither-pleasant-nor-painful feeling.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"Wholesome karma in the desire realm is merit."
The commentary states:
Within the wholesome karma of the desire realm, it is called "merit" because it is capable of purification and because it frequently induces desirable retribution.
The verse says:
"Wholesome karma of the upper realms is immovable.
The commentary states:
