Wholesome karma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*).
Is it not so? The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"In the three dhyānas there is movement; therein, vitarka and vicāra, as well as all other remaining formations, are called 'movement' by the Noble Ones," as explained at length in the sūtra.
Because there are faults associated with those [lower] concentrations, it is stated thus.
These three concentrations and so forth are called "unshakable" (*āniñjya*) in the *Aniñjya-sūtra* because they constitute the path of wholesome conditions that can bring about the unshakable state.
Furthermore, for what reason is this meditative absorption (dhyāna) actually subject to movement, yet at times described as "unmoving"?
The verse says:
Because of karma within its own stage, it is immovable with respect to its maturation (vipāka).
The commentary states:
If it concerns karma of the desire realm, it possesses the sense of "mobility" with respect to its retribution.
What is meant by "mobile retribution"?
Because there is no fixed location [for its ripening],
karma that has already brought about maturation in one realm may also ripen in another realm.

Furthermore, there is karma that has already brought about maturation in the generic similarity (*nikāyasabhāga*) of one class of devas, which may also ripen in the generic similarity of another class of devas.
Why is this? This karma is capable of producing power, physical form, pleasure, and sensory objects, which ought to ripen in the heavenly realms.
However, at times, due to specific conditions, this karma ripens within the realms of humans, animals, or hungry ghosts.

If karma belonging to the realm of form or the formless realm cannot ripen in any other stage due to the absence of causal conditions—because its retribution is fixed to a specific location—it is therefore called "immovable" (*āniñjya*).
Non-meritorious karma is clearly understood in the world as that which is not wholesome.
If this meaning is already established by worldly convention, why is it necessary to apply effort [to define it] therein?
Having already explained karma such as merit (*puṇya*) in detail, the karma associated with pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya*) and so forth shall now be explained.
The verse says:
"Pleasant [karma] is wholesome up to the third dhyāna."
The commentary states:
If karma is wholesome, it is said to be favorable for pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanīya*).
This karma extends up to the third dhyāna.
Why is this? Because the stage of pleasant feeling (sukha-vedanā-bhūmi) reaches its limit at this point; therefore, the desire realm (kāmadhātu) and the three dhyānas constitute that stage.
Beyond this, the verse says:
"Upward wholesome [karma] is not twofold.
The commentary explains:
All wholesome karma from the third dhyāna upward is favorable toward neither-pain-nor-pleasure, because within that state there is no retribution of pain or pleasure.
The verse says:
Regarding unwholesome karma in the desire realm, it is designated as having painful sensation.
The commentary says:
The mention of the "desire realm" (kāmadhātu) is intended to show that these exist only in the desire realm and definitely do not exist elsewhere.
These karmas do not have feeling alone as their retribution; the requisites for feeling are also retribution.
The verse says:
Others say there is a middling [intention] below.
The commentary says:

Some masters say that among these, there is karma capable of inducing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (aduḥkhāsukhavedanīya-karma), which exists from the fourth dhyāna upward and also exists in the lower stages.
By what reason is its existence known?
The verse says:
Because it is the retribution of the intermediate meditative absorption (*dhyānāntara*).
The commentary says:
If it were not so, karma belonging to the intermediate meditative absorptions would have no ripened fruit;
or else, there would have to be a distinct class of karma within those intermediate absorptions, because therein neither suffering nor pleasure exists.
Regarding karma of the intermediate dhyāna, it is the faculty of meditative pleasure (*samādhi-sukhendriya*) that constitutes its retribution; thus say other masters.
Furthermore, there are other masters who say:
"This karma certainly does not have a fixed retribution."
This position contradicts the Abhidharma-piṭaka. Why?
Because there is such a passage in that Piṭaka.
The text says:
Is it thus? Does this karma take mental factors as its substance for experiencing [the result]?
Is this the ripened fruit-retribution of that karma?
There is; namely, wholesome karma that is without vitarka.
The verse says:
There is no ripening of results before or after [the action], because the Buddha taught three types of karma.
The commentary states: In the Sūtra, it is asked:
"Is there not a case where the three types of karmic results ripen neither before nor after one another?"

There is karma of pleasant feeling whose maturation is the fruit of bodily form; there is karma of painful feeling whose maturation is the fruit of mind and mental factors; and there is karma of neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling whose maturation is the fruit of factors dissociated from mind.
Therefore, there is karma that is neither painful nor pleasant in the lower realms.
Apart from the desire realm, these three types of karma do not ripen simultaneously in other places.
Is this karma wholesome or unwholesome?
This is wholesome, yet its substance is weak.

If that is so, it contradicts the previous statement that wholesome pleasure extends up to the third dhyāna, as well as the subsequent statement that what is called "wholesome" is that which has desirable maturation or that which can lead to nirvāṇa.
This would contradict that statement.
One should understand that this explanation is made from the perspective of the majority.
Since this karma does not have feeling as its intrinsic nature, how can it be said to possess pleasant feeling and so forth?
Because it is favorable toward pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) and so forth, it is said that there is pleasant feeling and so forth.
Furthermore, this karma is pleasant and must necessarily be experienced.
What kind of phenomenon (*dharma*) is this experience (*vedanā*) that is experienced?
This is because this pleasant retribution is to be experienced, as pleasure exists within this karma.

Furthermore, because one must experience a pleasant retribution due to this karma, it is said that this karma possesses pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), just as there is karma involving painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*) within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).
It should be understood that the same applies to karma that results in neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
The verse says:
"By way of intrinsic nature, association, object, retribution, or by way of manifestation, there are five meanings of 'feeling' (vedanā)."
The commentary states:
Regarding the meaning of sensation (*vedanā*), there are five types:
first, sensation by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vedanā*), which refers to suffering, pleasure, and so forth.
The second is that which is associated with feeling, namely contact (*sparśa*).
As the Sūtra says:
"One should experience pleasant contact."
The third is the feeling of the objective sphere, which refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).
As the Sūtra says:
"When one sees forms with the eye, this person experiences the form, but does not experience desire for the form."
Such is the case.
Why? Because one experiences this object by means of sensation (*vedanā*), it is said that one "experiences this object."
Fourth is the experience of fruition, which refers to the experience of karma.
As the Sūtra says:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life, karma to be experienced upon rebirth, karma to be experienced in subsequent lives, and karma of indefinite timing."
Fifth is "manifest experience," which means being associated with one [of the feelings] at a time.
As the Sūtra says:
"At that time one experiences a pleasant feeling; at that time, the other two feelings are both extinguished and absent."
Why is this? At that time, when a pleasant feeling arises, other feelings cannot arise.
Because one is destined to experience that particular feeling, it can be said that one is able to experience it only when it is present before one.
Therefore, based on the fact that its retribution is to be experienced, it is called "karma to be experienced as pleasure"; the same applies to [karma to be experienced as] suffering and so forth.
The verse says:
This may be either determinate or indeterminate.
The commentary states:

These three types of karma—namely, that which is to be experienced as pleasure and so forth—should be understood as each having both determinate and indeterminate aspects, because it is not necessarily the case that they must be experienced.
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are three types of determinate karma (*niyata-karman*), because their retribution is experienced in the present life and so forth.
The commentary explains:

determinate karma is of three kinds, namely: that to be experienced in the present life (*drstadharma-vedanīya*), that to be experienced in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), and that to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
These three types of determinate karma, together with karma of indefinite experience,
thus constitute four types. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 11 [and] Fascicle 12.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
From the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Chapter Three: "Discrimination of Karma," the third verse states:
Furthermore, there are five kinds of karma.
The commentary states:
Other masters further assert that there are five types of karma.
Indeterminate karma is divided into two types: that which is determinate regarding its retribution, and that which is indeterminate regarding its retribution.
Among these, karma to be experienced in the present life refers to karma created in this very birth that ripens in this very birth.
Karma to be experienced in the present life is that which is performed in this life and ripens in the second life.
Karma to be experienced in subsequent lives is that which is performed in this life and ripens from the third life onward.
Other masters say:
"Karma to be experienced in the present life may also have its retribution in other lives, as it is designated by name according to its functional power.
However, the Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this view, lest karma of the strongest force should have weak or inferior retribution.
Why is this? It is said that there are karmas whose retribution is immediate while their proximate retribution is not superior, and there are karmas which are the opposite.
This is like external seeds: the *kalāya* bean bears fruit in three and a half months, whereas wheat and other grains bear fruit in six months.
The verse says:
Other masters explain it as four propositions.
The commentary says:

The masters of the Dārṣṭāntika school state that there are four possibilities: there is karma that is determinate in its timing but indeterminate in its retribution; there is karma that is determinate in its retribution but indeterminate in its timing; and there is karma that is determinate in both respects. As for karma that is to be experienced in the present life, it is indeterminate in its retribution. There is also karma that is determinate in its retribution but indeterminate in its timing; and there is karma that is determinate in both respects.
If it is of the type to be experienced in the present life and so forth, it is also determinate with respect to its retribution.
There are actions that are indeterminate in both respects; if an action is not necessarily to be experienced, it is also indeterminate with respect to its retribution.
For such a person, these karmas constitute eight types:

there are two types of karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), namely the determinate (*niyata*) and the indeterminate (*aniyata*); this applies likewise up to the determinate and indeterminate [karma to be experienced in future lives].

They explain that the [first] three, beginning with karma to be experienced in the present life, are determinate, while the fourth is indeterminate. Within a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), one may project four types of karma, but they cannot arise simultaneously.
How is it obtained?
When one commits sexual misconduct through another in three ways while practicing it oneself, these four are completed simultaneously.
Regarding these four karmas, the verse says:
"Three [types of karma] project the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*).
The commentary asks:
For what reason is this karma of immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*) unable to project the homogeneous class?
Because homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) currently exists.
In which realm and in which path of existence can how many types of karma project [rebirth]?
The verse says:
"Four [types of karma] have the power of projection in all places.
The commentary states:
Within the three realms and across all paths, all four types of karma possess the sense of "projection" (ākṣepa).
These four are either wholesome or unwholesome; they are drawn forth according to their corresponding [causes].
Having opened this up, we now further establish a restriction.
The verse says:
"Three types of wholesome karma can project [rebirth] in hell.
The commentary explains:

Among the three kinds of wholesome karma, there is projection within hell; however, there is no projection for karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*), because there is no desirable retribution therein.
The verse says:
In all cases of detachment from desire, one firmly does not project rebirth as a result of maturation (*vipāka*).
The commentary says:

If an ordinary person has already attained detachment from this stage and remains firmly established therein without falling away, they cannot produce karma that results in rebirth in a lower stage, though they can produce the other three types of karma.
The verse says:
"The Noble Ones do not create further retribution.
The commentary explains:
The statement of Vasumitra extends to this point:

if a noble one has already attained detachment from desire at this stage, they will never again fall back and cannot create two types of karma—namely, karma to be experienced in the next life (upapadyavedanīya) or karma to be experienced in subsequent lives (aparaparyāyavedanīya).

Why is this? Because such a person can no longer bring about rebirth in the lower realms; they can only create karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and karma with indefinite timing (*aniyata-vedanīya-karman*), which will ripen in whichever place they happen to be born in the present life.
The verse says:
One who has fallen from the Peak of Existence does not create [new karma].
The commentary says:

If a noble one were subject to falling back, having already become detached from the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), they would not be able to create karma that results in rebirth or subsequent rebirth within these two realms. Why is this?
This person has already fallen away from the fruit; there is no possibility of relinquishing their life-span.
This point shall be explained in detail later.
Furthermore, does the intermediate state (antarābhava) possess the nature of projecting karma?
There are. A verse says:
Twenty-two kinds of karma project [rebirth] within the intermediate state of the desire realm.
The commentary states:
If it is the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it can project twenty-two kinds of karma. How is this so?
There are five stages of the embryo: namely, kalala, arbuda, peśī, ghana, and praśākhā.
There are five stages of those already born: namely, infancy, childhood, youth, middle age, and old age.

Within this stage, the intermediate state being may sometimes project karma for the experience of the *kalala* stage—whether indeterminate or determinate—to be experienced up through the stage of old age, as well as to be experienced within the intermediate state itself.
The verse says:
This karma results only in retribution in the present life.
The commentary says:

The karma projected by this intermediate state (antarābhava) is definitively of eleven kinds; one should know that it must necessarily be of the "to-be-experienced-in-this-life" (dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya) category. Why is this?
The verse says:
"That is one fruit of retribution.
The commentary explains:
This homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga) is led by only a single karma.

In this context, the intermediate state (antarābhava) belongs to the same homogeneous class (nikāya-sabhāga), and the ten subsequent stages following the intermediate state likewise do; therefore, it is not said that the intermediate state is produced by distinct karma, because both are projected by the karma of retribution in the same birth (sahaja-vedanīya-karma).
Furthermore, by what association can one know that this karma is determinate?
The verse says:
Through intense affliction or a pure mind, or through habitual practice, it is determinate with respect to the field of merit; it is also determinate when it harms one's own father or mother.
The commentary states:

It should be understood that this karma is determinate when it is produced by intense afflictions, or produced by an intense wholesome mind, or performed habitually, or generated toward a field of merit.
Within this, there is the field of merit, namely the Three Jewels or the distinction of persons.
Regarding the distinction of persons: it refers to a person who has attained a superior category of fruition or a superior category of meditative concentration.

In this context, if there is neither a mind of intense affliction nor a mind of intense virtue, this karma—whether wholesome or unwholesome—will necessarily become determinate karma; the same applies to that which is habitually practiced.

Furthermore, if one commits an act of violation or harm against one's own parents with a sudden, impulsive mind, this karma will also necessarily result in retribution; other types of karma, however, are not necessarily so.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of karma to be experienced in the present life?
The verse says:
This karma results in retribution in the present life due to the excellence of the field and the intention.
The commentary states:
Karma to be experienced in the present life may be established by the excellence of the field.

As it is traditionally told, there was once a bhikṣu who, while in the midst of the great assembly, spoke words befitting a woman; consequently, in that very body, his gender was transformed and he became a woman.
There is a scriptural passage for this.

Regarding the superiority of intentional resolve, as it is told in tradition: there was a certain eunuch who, by virtue of resolving to liberate another from the state of being a eunuch, manifested in his present body a transformation of his sexual organs into those of a male.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Because of being eternally separated from the stage of desire.
The commentary explains:

If an action, whether wholesome or unwholesome, arises in dependence upon a particular stage, then by virtue of being permanently free from desire for that stage, that action becomes an action with immediate retribution (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya*).
What are the characteristics of such an action?
The verse says:
"If karma is fixed regarding its retribution.
The commentary says:
If karma is certain regarding its retribution but indefinite regarding its timing, this is what is called "karma to be experienced in the present life.
If karma is certain regarding other timings, this karma will certainly yield its retribution in those other timings; such a person has not yet abandoned desire.
What is meant by "indeterminate"?
This karma has no retribution because one has attained permanent freedom from desire.
What are the characteristics of this field?
Karma created therein will certainly result in retribution in the present life.
To speak generally, the great assembly of bhikṣus has the Buddha as their presiding leader; yet, when distinguished by the individuals involved, there are five [categories].
The verse says:

Regarding the attainment of cessation, the absence of strife, and loving-kindness, which arise upon seeing the fruit of arhatship—the karma that brings benefit or harm toward them bears its fruit in the present life. The commentary says: [This refers to] the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the state of being without strife (*araṇā*), and the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*). These three arise when one has attained the fruit of arhatship. Any action—whether beneficial or harmful—that is directed toward those who have entered these states will yield its result in the present lifetime.
When a person emerges from the meditative absorption of the mindless state, they immediately attain the ultimate tranquility of mind, because this absorption resembles nirvāṇa.
By means of this absorption, such a person is as if going to and returning from nirvāṇa.

When a person emerges from the *araṇā-samādhi* and contemplates immeasurable sentient beings, their mental continuum—accompanied by the most intense and virtuous intentions for the benefit of others through non-contention—is correctly activated, transformed by the cultivation of immeasurable merit.

If a person emerges from the contemplation of immeasurable loving-kindness, their mental continuum—accompanied by the most intense and virtuous intention for the peace and happiness of immeasurable sentient beings—is correctly activated as it is transformed through the cultivation of immeasurable merit.

If a person emerges from the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths are extinguished without remainder; therefore, a new transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) is attained, and a pure continuum immediately arises.

When a person emerges from the contemplation of the fruit of arhatship, the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation are extinguished without remainder; therefore, the newly attained transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) and its pure continuum immediately arise.

Therefore, regarding these five types of persons, whether one performs deeds that bring them benefit or deeds that cause them harm and distress, the karmic retribution for such actions will certainly be experienced in this very life.

Because the path cultivated by others has not yet reached its ultimate consummation, if they emerge from a contemplation of the fruit of their own nature that is not yet perfected, their newly attained transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and purity are not so; therefore, they do not equal the former person as a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
If the experience of retribution (*vipākavedanā*) is considered supreme, then this point should be reflected upon:
Is there karma that has only mental experience as its retribution and not bodily experience?
And is there karma that has only bodily experience as its retribution and not mental experience?
It is said that [feeling] exists.
The verse states:
If it is admitted that feeling is the maturation of wholesome karma that is without vitarka, then this feeling is a mental factor (caitta).
The commentary states:
Regarding "karma without vitarka," from the intermediate dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this wholesome karma without vitarka has only mental sensation as its retribution.
Why is it not a bodily sensation?
Because this bodily sensation necessarily arises together with vitarka and vicāra.
The verse says:
"If evil is experienced only by the body.
The commentary explains:
"If it is an evil karma, it is certain that its retribution will be experienced as bodily sensation."
What is meant by mental feeling that is not the retribution of that [action]?
This karma has painful feeling as its retribution.
If this painful feeling resides in the mental ground, it constitutes the faculty of grief (*daurmanasyendriya*); this faculty of grief is not a karmic fruition, as was already explained previously.
If that is so, when sentient beings experience insanity, in what kind of mind does this insanity reside,
and by what cause does it arise?
The verse says:
"Mind is deranged by mind.
The commentary states:
"Mind and mind" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Why is this? If a person is engaged in the five sensory consciousnesses, there is no occurrence of derangement, because the five consciousnesses lack conceptual discrimination.
The verse says:
"This arises from karmic retribution.
The commentary states:
"This mental derangement arises from the karmic retribution of sentient beings."

If a person uses spells or substances, or performs acts of augmentation to scatter and destroy the minds of others; or causes sentient beings who do not seek such things to drink poison or alcohol; or terrifies sentient beings; or sets fires in hunting grounds, wildernesses, and similar places; or traps sentient beings in pits and ditches; or, through other karmic actions, causes sentient beings to lose their mindfulness.
Due to this karmic retribution, the minds of these sentient beings will become deranged in future lives.
Furthermore, there is another cause, as the verse says:
"Fear, beating, injustice, and grief."
The commentary states:
Regarding "frightening," various spirits and deities (*bhūta-graha*) assume terrifying forms and approach to oppress; upon seeing them, this person becomes struck with fear.
Regarding "beating," various spirits and deities give rise to a mind of hatred and malice due to the person's evil conduct, and they inflict blows upon the person's vital points (*marmāṇi*).
"Disequilibrium" refers to the mutual conflict of wind, heat, and phlegm, which causes the four great elements of the body to become entirely unbalanced.
"Sorrow" refers to conditions such as those caused by *vāsiṣṭhī* and the like, or when the mental consciousness becomes deranged.
This deranged mind arises from karmic retribution; how then can you say that the mind's experience is not a fruit of retribution?
We do not claim that this mind itself is the fruit of retribution.
Why then is it said that the impairment of the four great elements constitutes the fruit of retribution?
Because it arises from this mind, it is said that the mind is born from retribution.
Due to the inequality of the four great elements produced by karma, the mind becomes deranged, lacks self-mastery, and loses mindfulness; thus, this mind is called "insane."
If it is understood in this way, the four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are established.
There is a state where the mind is deranged due to insanity but not distracted due to agitation; this should be understood in detail.
Regarding "derangement due to insanity but not distraction," it refers to a lack of mental autonomy that is non-defiled.
Those who are distracted but not deranged have minds that are autonomous yet afflicted.
Those who are both deranged and distracted have minds that are non-autonomous and afflicted.
Those who are neither deranged nor distracted have minds that are autonomous and unafflicted.
Which sentient beings possess a deranged mind?
The verse says:
In the desire realm, excluding the Kurus.
The commentary says:
Among those existing in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), this excludes only the northern continent of Kuru. Why is this?
If there are even mad gods among the celestial beings, how much more so among humans, animals, and spirits?

The sentient beings in the hells are perpetually deranged; they are afflicted by ten thousand kinds of injuries, vexations, anger, and harm. Because their *marmans* (vital points) are struck with such intensity that they are difficult to endure, they are overwhelmed by painful sensations. They cannot even discern their own bodies, let alone recognize matters such as right and wrong.
With what kind of mind and for what reason do they weep in the hells? This should be explained here.
Even among noble ones (*ārya*), there can be mental derangement due to the imbalance of the four great elements, with the exception of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
If one considers fixed karma (*niyata-karma*), the retribution has already been fully experienced; if one considers unfixed karma (*aniyata-karma*), there is no fruit of retribution.
This is not due to fear, for they have already transcended the five fears.
It is not due to harm, for there is never any evil conduct capable of giving rise to the mind of hatred or resentment in spirits and deities;
it is not due to distress, for one has realized and witnessed the true nature of phenomena as they really are.
Furthermore, it is stated in the sūtras that there are three crookednesses:
crookedness of body, crookedness of speech, and crookedness of mind.
There are also three coarsenesses:
Coarseness of body, coarseness of speech, and coarseness of mind.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of harshness:
harshness of body, harshness of speech, and harshness of mind.
The sequence herein should be understood as follows.
The verse says:
"Crooked, coarse, and harsh karma are said to arise from guile, hatred, and desire."
The commentary states:

If bodily action arises from guile (*śāṭhya*), it is called "crooked bodily action" (*kāya-kuṭila-karman*), because its nature is that of being crooked and devious; the same applies to crooked verbal and mental actions.
If bodily action arises from hatred, it is called coarse bodily action, because its nature is that of anger; the same applies to coarse verbal and mental actions.
If bodily action arises from greed, it is called harsh bodily action, because its nature is that of defilement; the same applies to harsh verbal and mental actions.
The verse says:
"Black, white, and so forth—distinguished; furthermore, karma is said to be of four kinds.
The commentary says:
There is black karma with black fruition;
there is white karma with white fruition;
there is black-and-white karma with black-and-white fruition;
There is karma that is neither black nor white, with a retribution that is neither black nor white, because it arises capable of extinguishing all other karmas.
The verse says:

It is not wholesome in the desire or form realms; one should know that wholesome [karma] follows in sequence. There are two types of black-and-white karma, which can extinguish those [other karmas] through the outflow-free [karma].
The commentary states:
Non-virtuous karma is exclusively termed "black" because its intrinsic nature is black.
Its maturation is also black because its maturation is not desirable.
This karma belongs exclusively to the desire realm.
Wholesome karma in the form realm is entirely white, as it is not mixed with black;
its retribution is also white, because its retribution is desirable.
Why is it that the karma of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is not mentioned?
Because in that realm there are two kinds of retribution— namely, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of rebirth (*upapattibhava*)—
and three kinds of karma— namely, those of body, speech, and mind.
In this context, black and white karma are explained, whereas they are not explained elsewhere.
Other masters say:
"This is also taught in other sūtras."
Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called "black-and-white" karma because it is interspersed with non-wholesome states.
Its retribution is likewise black-and-white because its retributive results are intermingled.
If one were to analyze this karma, it must be done in terms of the continuity of the stream [of consciousness], and not in terms of its intrinsic nature.
Why is this? There is no single karma of such a nature and retribution wherein karma is both black and white.
Such a principle does not exist, because the two are mutually contradictory.
If that were so, because unwholesome karma would be mixed with wholesome karma, it should become "white-and-black" karma.
However, the principle that the unwholesome is mixed with the wholesome does not hold, because within the desire realm the power of the unwholesome is strong;
only the wholesome can be mixed [with the unwholesome], due to its weak power.
As for untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*), it is that which, when arising, can extinguish these three.
Why is this? Because this karma is not black, as it is free from defilement (*saṃkleśa*).
It is not white, because there is no white karmic fruit.
This statement that it is "not white" is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), for it possesses a specific underlying intent.
In the *Mahāśūnyatā-sūtra*, the Blessed One spoke with reference to the dharmas of one beyond training (*aśaikṣadharma*).
Ānanda! Such a teaching is entirely white, entirely wholesome, and entirely beyond reproach.
As it is said in the Abhidharma Piṭaka:
What constitutes white dharmas?
They are wholesome dharmas and non-obscured neutral dharmas.
They are without karmic fruition because they do not fall within the realms of existence and because they are contrary to birth and death.
Can all untainted (anāsrava) karma completely extinguish the three types of karma, such as the white and so forth? No. Why is this so?
The verse says:
Through patience regarding the Dharma and detachment from desire, during the eight successive paths, twelve types of volition are able to extinguish black karma.
The commentary says:

Within the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga), there are four dharmakṣāntis; within the eight successive paths of detachment from the desire realm (kāmadhātu), there are twelve types of volition (cetanā). This karma is exclusively capable of extinguishing black karma (kṛṣṇakarma).
The verse says:
By means of the ninth volition, one is able to extinguish both black and white karma.
The commentary says:
At the ninth stage of detachment from the desire realm, through the volition of the successive path (*ānantarya-mārga*), one is able to extinguish both black-and-white karma and black karma.
The verse says:
"The white karma of the dhyāna of detachment arises subsequently in the successive path."
The commentary states:
If a person definitively practices the path of detachment, this is the ninth successive path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Within this, there are four types of volition that are exclusively capable of extinguishing white karma (*śukla-karma*).
Why is it that only the ninth successive path (*ānantarya-mārga*) can extinguish white karma, and not others?
This wholesome [karma] is not extinguished by its own nature, because once it has been extinguished, it may manifest again.
Nevertheless, because the afflictions that take those [objects] as their objective conditions are extinguished, it is said that they are extinguished.
Therefore, as long as even a single grade of affliction still takes them as its objective condition and has not been extinguished, it cannot be said that they have already been extinguished.
The verse says:
Others say that there are two [types of karma]: those with retribution in hell, and those whose retribution is to be experienced in the desire realm.
The commentary says:

According to the view of other masters, one should understand that karma to be experienced as retribution in hell, and karma to be experienced as retribution in other paths within the desire realm apart from hell, are respectively black karma and black-and-white karma.
Why is this? Because only the hells are definitely the retribution for evil karma, the karma that results in retribution in the hells is called "black karma.

Apart from the hells, within the other realms of the desire realm, there exist both good and evil karmic retributions; therefore, the karma that results in such retribution is called "black-and-white karma."
The verse says:
Others say that [the path] which sees cessation is black.
The commentary says:
Other masters say:
"Karma that is to be abandoned by the vision of the truths is called black karma, because it is not intermingled with the wholesome.
The verse says:
"Other karma of the desire realm is black-and-white.
The commentary explains:
Karma of the desire realm that is distinct from karma abandoned through the vision of the truths is called black-and-white karma.
What is this difference?
It refers to that which is abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). Why is this so?
This karma is both wholesome and unwholesome.
In the Sūtras it is said:
there are three forms of mauna, namely, bodily mauna, verbal mauna, and mental mauna.
The verse here says:
"The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training, and the mind—these should be known as the three *maunas* in their respective order.
The commentary explains:
The bodily and vocal actions of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) are called bodily and vocal mauna;
the mind of one beyond training is called mental mauna, but it is not a mental action. Why is this?
The mind is the true noble one; this can be definitively inferred by means of body and speech.

Furthermore, these two types of action—body and speech—have the nature of abstaining from evil, whereas mental action consists merely of volition (*cetanā*). Because it lacks informative expression (*vijñapti*), it cannot be inferred as being characterized by abstention; therefore, it is called *mauna* (silence).
Therefore, because the mind alone is capable of detachment, it is called *mauna*.
Why is it said that this applies to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and not to others?
Because the Arhat is a truly noble one (*ārya*).
All [are pure], or it is said that they are so because of the cessation of conceptual construction.
The verse says:
"The three are pure."
The commentary states:
It is taught in the sūtras that there are three kinds of purity, namely, purity of body, purity of speech, and purity of mind.
Regarding these three kinds of purity, the verse says:
"All three types of wholesome conduct.
The commentary explains:
All wholesome conduct of the body is called purity of body;
all wholesome conduct of speech and mind is called purity of speech and mind.
This is because it can eliminate and obstruct unwholesome conduct and the defilement of afflictions, either temporarily or permanently.
What is being correctly explained here?
It is for the sake of causing sentient beings who take pleasure in wrong *mauna* (silence) and wrong purification to reflect upon them so that they may distance themselves from them.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtra that there are three kinds of misconduct.
The verse says:
Unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind are called the three types of unwholesome conduct (*akuśala-carita*).
The commentary says:
If the actions of body, speech, and mind are unwholesome, they should be known respectively as the misdeeds of body, speech, and mind.
The verse says:
Greed, hatred, and so forth, though not themselves karma, are said to be the three types of mental misdeeds.
The commentary states:
There are also unwholesome actions that do not possess the nature of karma, namely those distinct categories of the three mental unwholesome actions, because they are not intentional.
The Dārṣṭāntika school says:
Greed and the others are called mental karma (*manas-karman*), as they are performed with intentional mind.
A sutra states:
"If one maintains this view, then afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma would become of a single nature."
If that were so, how could there be karma produced by afflictions?
Such a principle does not exist.
The Vaibhāṣikas say: "In the Sūtras, because volition arises through this gateway, the Master [the Buddha] indicates volition by means of it."
If it were not so, afflictions and karma would become a single entity, and thus the twelve links of dependent origination would fail to be established.

Since this is not accepted—because [such actions] result in undesirable retribution and are censured by the wise—the activities of body, speech, and mind are termed "unwholesome conduct" (akuśala-karma).
The verse says:
The opposite of this is called "virtuous conduct" (*kuśalacaryā*).
The commentary says:

By reversing unwholesome conduct, one should admit the existence of wholesome conduct; that is, wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view, because they do not involve harming or injuring others.
How are right view and wrong view established?
Because the natures of good and evil are the roots of benefit and harm, they are what are described as unwholesome conduct and wholesome conduct.
Regarding this, a verse says:
Because they subsume the coarse categories [of conduct], ten courses of action (*karmapatha*) are taught; this refers appropriately to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
The commentary states:

Among the previously mentioned unwholesome and wholesome conducts, because they subsume the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—which are clear and easy to understand, the ten courses of action are taught in the Sūtra. This should be understood accordingly: the wholesome arises from wholesome conduct, and the unwholesome arises from unwholesome conduct.
Among these, what misdeeds and virtuous deeds are not included?

Within the paths of unwholesome action (*akuśala-karmapatha*), a portion of bodily misdeed is not included—namely, its preliminary (*pūrvāṅga*) and subsequent (*paścāṅga*) stages; the same applies to other defiled actions, as these are not coarse or manifest.

If bodily misconduct can cause others to lose their life, property, or spouse, it is termed a "path of action" (*karmapatha*), because one wishes to cause others to distinguish themselves from such conduct.
Within the unwholesome courses of action, a portion of what is designated as mental misconduct is called "intentionality.

Within the wholesome paths of action, there is a portion of bodily wholesome conduct that is not included [in the primary paths], namely: the preliminary and concluding phases, as well as abstaining from intoxicants, giving, making offerings, and so forth.
Virtuous conduct of speech includes such things as loving speech; virtuous conduct of mind includes such things as intentional action.
Regarding these paths of action, the verse says:
"Six unwholesome ones possess non-informative [action]."
The commentary states:
Only the six unwholesome courses of action are necessarily of the nature of non-informative (avijñapti) karma; namely, killing, stealing, lying, divisive speech, harsh speech, and idle chatter.
If one instructs another to perform [an action], there is no fundamental informative act (*vijñapti*).
The verse says:
"There are two kinds."
The commentary states:
Sexual misconduct always has both informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) action as its nature. Why is this?
Because this is accomplished by oneself;
for causing another to act joyfully is not as effective as acting for it oneself.
The verse says:
"Performed by oneself.
The commentary states:
These six types of paths of action, when performed by oneself, also each have two kinds, namely, informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti).
If one dies at the very moment an informative action (*vijñapti*) arises, then one possesses both the informative and the non-informative (*avijñapti*);
if one dies only after the informative action has arisen, then one possesses only the non-informative.
Regarding the wholesome paths of action, the verse says:
"Seven are of two kinds; only [the last] three are exclusively wholesome.
The commentary says:

The seven wholesome courses of action involving form are necessarily of two kinds, namely informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*), because the precepts obtained through undertaking depend upon the informative.
The verse says:
Non-informative [action] arises from meditative concentration.
The commentary states:

Those restraints (saṃvara) produced by meditative concentration (dhyāna) and comprised within the outflow-free (anāsrava) states are called "born of concentration" (dhyānaja). They consist exclusively of non-informative matter (avijñapti), because they depend solely upon the mind.
The verse says:
"The preparatory stage possesses informative action.
The commentary says:
The preliminary stage of the path of action must necessarily have informative intimation (*vijñapti*) as its nature.
The verse says:
Non-informative intimation (*avijñapti*) may or may not exist.
The commentary states:

If the mind is defiled by the most heavy and intense afflictions—like honeyed poison—and one then applies the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of purification as a means, then there is non-informative action (*avijñapti*);
if it is otherwise, there is none.
The verse says:
"The subsequent part is the reverse of this; the preceding part arises from three roots.
The commentary says:

Reversing the meaning of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the preceding section, it should be understood that the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) of the paths of action (*karmapatha*) is likewise. Why is this?
This subsequent stage is necessarily of the nature of non-informative matter (*avijñapti*); informative matter (*vijñapti*), however, may or may not be present.
If a person has already performed a course of action and subsequently gives rise to a similar dharma, then there is informative intimation (*vijñapti*);
otherwise, there is none at all.
Furthermore, from what point can the preliminary (*prayoga*), the fundamental (*maula*), and the concluding (*pṛṣṭha*) stages of this course of action be established?

For example, suppose there is a person who wishes to kill a bird or beast. Rising from his bed, he takes it up and goes directly to its location; he feels its body, purchases it, and leads it back. Bringing it into the slaughterhouse with the intent to kill it, he then takes up a weapon and strikes once or twice, until the life has not yet been severed—this is called the preliminary stage of killing (*pūrvāṅga*).

This matter is capable of severing life; herein, the informative and non-informative bodily karma arise together in a single moment, which is called the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*). Why is this so?

By two kinds of causes and conditions, this person is touched by the offense of killing: because of the performance of the preliminary effort (*prayoga*) and the completion of the result (*phala-parisamāpti*).
From that moment onward, all moments of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) constitute the subsequent portion (*pṛṣṭha*) of the course of action (*karmapatha*).
Even down to washing, selling, cooking for oneself, and praising its excellence—all such moments of informative action (*vijñapti*) constitute the subsequent portion (*pṛṣṭha*).
In this same manner, the meanings of the preliminary, fundamental, and subsequent portions should be understood accordingly within the remaining six courses of action (*karmapatha*).
The three [unwholesome roots], such as covetousness and the rest, have no prior or subsequent stages; they constitute a course of action (*karmapatha*) precisely upon their manifestation.

You must now state: does this constitute a course of action when a sentient being is currently in the state of death-existence (*cyuti-bhava*), involving both informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*) action, or does it constitute a course of action once they have already died?
If that were so, what would follow?

If the sentient being being killed is in the state of death-existence (cyuti-bhava), and the killer or the one who incites the killing dies at the same time, there should be an offense of taking life.

The meaning of *siddhānta* (established tenet) is not thus: if it were the case that an action becomes a course of action (*karmapatha*) only after death, this would be what is taught in the *siddhānta*. That is to say, if by means of this act of harming one can cause another to be separated from life, there is a manifest bodily action (*vijñapti-kāyakarman*);
and the non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) arising simultaneously with it is called a course of action. This statement [of yours] should not be made.
Furthermore, it is said in the Abhidharma-piṭaka:
"Is there such a case where a sentient being has already been killed, yet this person has not yet ceased the act of killing?"

There is; for example, when one has already caused this sentient being to be separated from the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), yet the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) of killing has not been relinquished or ceased—in such a case, the subsequent stage (*pṛṣṭha*) is designated by the name of the preceding stage (*maula*).
This passage contradicts the meaning of the *Vibhāṣā*.
Since the root [defilement] has not yet been extinguished at this time, one should accept it as such, in accordance with the principle that there is no fault.
How is there no fault?
In this context, the name of the preliminary stage (*pūrvāṅga*) is used to designate the fundamental [action] (*maula*);
thus, there is no fault. If that is so, how can an informative act (*vijñapti*) characterized in this way constitute a fundamental course of action (*karmapatha*)?
Why is it not established?
Because it lacks efficacy.
If that is so, how can non-informative action (avijñapti) be established as a course of action (karmapatha)?
Therefore, when the fruit of the preparatory application is accomplished, these two constitute the path of action (*karmapatha*).
A path of action may sometimes be the preliminary stage (*pūrvāṅga*) of another path of action, or it may be the subsequent stage (*paścādaṅga*) of another path of action.
Regarding the stage of the act of killing, it sometimes constitutes the full course of action (*karmapatha*) and sometimes constitutes the preliminary stage (*prayoga*).

For example, suppose a person wishes to kill an enemy; they employ malevolent arts to kill birds and beasts as an offering to spirits, or perhaps they steal another's property, or commit sexual misconduct with that person's wife in order to kill the enemy together with them; or they utter false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, or even gentle words to destroy the friends and relatives who might provide protection for the enemy to whatever extent possible; or they give rise to unjust greed toward the enemy, or produce hatred toward them, or increase their wrong views in order to kill them.
In this same manner, one should reflect accordingly regarding the other paths of action (*karmapatha*): greed and the others cannot constitute the preliminary stage (*sāmantaka*). Why is this?
It is because there is no such principle that a person would be performing the preliminary stage by means of the mere arousal of the mind alone.
If one sets aside the actual practice, the Sūtra states:
"O Bhikṣus!
There are three kinds of taking life:"
First, arising from greed; second, arising from hatred; third, arising from ignorance—and so it is even for wrong views.
Within this sutra, what are the characteristics of such killing?

Killing born of greed refers to causing another to lose their life for the sake of obtaining their body parts, for the sake of acquiring wealth, for the sake of amusement and pleasure, or for the purpose of protecting oneself and one's own kin.
That which arises from hatred is, for example, [killing] in order to take revenge.
That which arises from delusion is, for example, when a person performing a great sacrifice (*mahāyajña*) gives away [a living being], because their intention is to practice wholesome dharmas;
or as with kings who, in accordance with the measure of legal texts, inflict heavy punishments upon enemies and evildoers, whereby those kings generate great merit and virtue.
Furthermore, the karmic actions of killing among the people of Pāśī also arise from delusion.
Why is this? They speak as follows:
If one's parents are aged and infirm, or afflicted by a serious illness, one must certainly sacrifice one's life for them.
There are the Pīṇākī heretics who say:
"Snakes, centipedes, and venomous bites can constantly harm people; these must certainly be killed."
Deer, sheep, birds, oxen, and the like take birth for the sake of providing sustenance for human kitchens; thus, there is no fault in killing them.
If the act of killing arises from wrong view, it likewise arises from delusion.

Stealing that arises from greed consists of taking what is not given according to one's desires; or it is for the sake of obtaining other gains, honor, and a good reputation, or for the purpose of providing relief for oneself and one’s own kin.
That which arises from hatred is, for example, [killing] in order to take revenge.
That which arises from delusion is, for example, when kings, in accordance with the measure of legal texts and phrases, confiscate the property of evildoers for the purpose of punishing them.
Furthermore, it is as the Brahmins say:
"All things have already been relinquished by Brahmā and given to the Brahmins; yet because the power of the Brahmins is weak, various barbarians have taken them up and enjoy them at their own will."
Therefore, if a brahmin takes [something], he takes his own property;
if he eats, he eats his own property;
if he wears clothing, he wears his own property.
If one gives, giving away one's own property, there is no perception of it as another's wealth.
If theft arises from wrong view, it likewise arises from delusion.

As for sexual misconduct arising from greed: one first conceives a greedy attachment toward another’s wife or concubine before committing the act; or it is done for the sake of gaining profit and honor, or to provide relief for oneself and one’s own kin.
That which arises from hatred is, for example, like seeking revenge against an enemy.
That which arises from delusion is, for example, the practice among the people of Pārasīka of marrying their mothers and so forth;

or as in the Gosava sacrifice, where there are other women who sip water and chew grass, and a man becomes attached to his own kin, such as his paternal aunt, maternal aunt, sister, or those of the same clan.
Furthermore, as the non-Buddhist Pīṇāka says:
"Women are like mortars, flowers, fruits, cooked food, riverbanks, and roads.
False speech and other such acts arise from greed and hatred, as previously explained.
Regarding lying arising from delusion, as stated in the *Veda*:
"In jest, with women, when taking a wife, and for the sake of saving one's life or wealth—
lying in these cases, the Brahma King says, is harmless."
If false speech arises from wrong view, it also arises from delusion.
If divisive speech and so forth arise from wrong view, they also arise from delusion.
All the heterodox doctrines derived from the four Vedas are merely meaningless speech.
Since [the Vedas] are not characterized by greed and so forth, how could they have arisen from greed and so forth?
The verse says:
"From those, they arise in succession; they arise from the three roots such as greed.
The commentary says:
Because they arise in succession from greed, it is said that they arise from greed.
Because they arise in succession from hatred, it is said that they arise from hatred.
Because they arise in succession from delusion, it is said that they arise from delusion.
Having explained the paths of unwholesome karma, what are the paths of wholesome karma?
The verse says:
The wholesome paths of karma arise before and after non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion.
The commentary states:
Together with their preliminary and concluding phases, all wholesome courses of action arise from non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion, because they are produced by a wholesome volition.
This wholesome volition is necessarily associated with the three wholesome roots, such as non-attachment.
What are the characteristics of the three stages—the preliminary, the main, and the concluding?

In this context, if one abstains from the preliminary stage of an unwholesome course of action, that is the preliminary stage of a wholesome course of action; if one abstains from the fundamental stage, that is the fundamental stage; and if one abstains from the concluding stage, that is the concluding stage.

For example, when a śrāmaṇera wishes to receive the full ordination (upasampadā), he enters into communal residence, pays homage to the bhikṣus, and requests an upādhyāya; this continues until the first and second karmavācanās are recited—this is called the preliminary stage (pūrvabhāga).

At the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, the informative action (*vijñapti-karman*) together with a single moment of non-informative action (*avijñapti*) constitutes the fundamental path of action (*maula-karmapatha*).

From that point until the four reliances (*catur-śaraṇa*) are proclaimed, all informative and non-informative actions based upon this fundamental path, as long as their continuity has not been severed, are termed the subsequent portion (*pṛṣṭha*).
Regarding what has been said— that not all courses of action (karmapatha) are brought to completion by greed and the other [afflictions]—
which course of action among them is brought to completion by which unwholesome root?
The verse says:
Killing, malice, and harsh speech—these are all accomplished through hatred.
The commentary says:
Killing, malice, and harsh speech necessarily reach their culmination through hatred (*dveṣa*).
This is because these three are accomplished when a mind of abandonment and a mind of harshness manifest.
The verse says:
Sexual misconduct, covetousness, and stealing reach completion through greed.
The commentary states:
Because covetous desire is present, sexual misconduct, covetousness, and theft are accomplished.
The verse says:
"Wrong view arises from ignorance.
The commentary explains:
If a person gives rise to the most intense degree of delusion, they are able to accomplish wrong view.
The verse says:
It is admitted that the remaining [afflictions] arise from all three.
The commentary states:
What are the remaining [actions]?
They are false speech, divisive speech, and frivolous speech. These three are accomplished through any one of the three unwholesome roots—either by greed, or by hatred, or by delusion.
These paths of action are explained according to four sections, namely three, one, three, and one; they should be understood in this order.
The verse says:
"The basis for sentient beings' enjoyment consists of name-and-form and the collection of names."
The commentary states:

Killing and so forth arise based on sentient beings; sexual misconduct and so forth arise based on objects of enjoyment; wrong view arises based on name-and-form (nāmarūpa); and lying and so forth arise based on the collection of names (nāmakāya).

If a person, having aroused a concentrated mind with the intent to kill another, dies either simultaneously with that person or prior to them, does the fundamental path of action (maula-karmapatha) exist?
The verse says:
"If both die together, or if [the other] dies first, there is no root.
The commentary explains:
Therefore, this question is raised:
Is there such a principle that if a person performs the act of killing and the result is completed,
yet he does not incur the offense of killing?
There is [such a case]: if one is able to kill another, whether the victim dies before [the killer] or dies at the same time.
If that is so, what is the reason?
If the person killed is still alive and has not yet died, the killer is not associated with the offense of taking life.
If the killer and the victim die at the same time, this too is inconsistent.
Why is it inconsistent?
The verse says:
"Arising from a different basis.
The commentary explains:
"By means of this basis, one carries out the act of killing with respect to that [other basis]."
This basis has already been severed and extinguished, and a different basis arises, distinct from the previous homogeneous group (*nikāya-sabhāga*).
Since this [new] basis does not perform the act of killing, there is therefore no sense in which it is associated with a course of action (*karmapatha*).
Furthermore, if for the purpose of killing another, one gathers a multitude as an army, or digs pits, or hunts, or commits robbery—
where many people assemble together for this same purpose— if among them one person performs the act of taking life, who incurs the offense of killing?
The verse says:
Because they share a common purpose, those in an army and so forth all obtain [the result] as if they were the actual doer.
The commentary says:
Just as the perpetrator commits a crime, so too do all these people commit the same offense together, because they share in a single undertaking.
From this perspective, each of them kills the other in turn.
If a person is coerced by the power of others and led into [the act], that person is also associated with this offense.
If a person departs based on this vow, saying: "As long as I live, even to save my own life, I shall not kill."
Excluding only this person,
if one personally commits the act of killing, to what extent does this action constitute a full course of karma (*karmapatha*)? And so on,
up to how much must wrong view be present for it to constitute a full course of karma?
This is explained in the corresponding verse:
"Killing occurs when there is an intentional mind, [the victim is] another person, and there is no error in the identification."
The commentary states:

If a person possesses the intentional thought, "I must kill that one," perceives that specific individual as such, and kills only that person without killing others by mistake—by virtue of these three factors, the act of killing constitutes a full karmic path (*karmapatha*).
If that were so, suppose there is a person whose mind is undecided by doubt when killing a living being, wondering: "Is this a sentient being or not?
Is it that specific individual or not?"
This person, having already resolved upon killing— thinking, "Whether it be this one or that one, I must kill"—
and having already formed the intention to relinquish [the life], incurs the offense of killing if he actually kills a living being.
Within the five aggregates that perish moment by moment, how does one sever *prāṇa*?
What is the meaning of this term?
It has the meaning of "wind," and this wind arises dependent upon the body and the mind.
If a person cuts off this wind—just as wind extinguishes a lamp’s light or a hand silences the sound of a bell—the cutting off of this wind is likewise; this is called *prāṇāyāma*.

Alternatively, it may have the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as its referent: if one obstructs a life-faculty that is currently about to arise in a single moment, one commits the offense of taking life;
otherwise, one does not commit the offense.
To whom does this life belong?
Since that person dies when the life is severed, it is said that this life belongs to that person.
What is that person?
This point shall be considered together when refuting the doctrine of a self.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"The life-faculty, warmth, and consciousness— when these three abandon the body, [it perishes]."
"When that [life-faculty] is abandoned, it is eternal sleep; like a withered tree, there is no awareness.
Therefore, a body possessing the life-faculty is called "alive," while a body lacking the life-faculty is called "dead."
The Nirgrantha said:
"If one kills a living being even without prior knowledge, the killer still incurs guilt; it is just as one is burned by touching fire even without prior knowledge."
If one were to encounter another’s wife there and touch her, the same principle would apply.

Furthermore, if one plucks out the hair of a Nirgrantha and instructs him to practice asceticism, and he dies from abdominal distension, the donor should incur guilt; for both the mother and the fetus are mutual causes of suffering and distress.
Because the offender is associated with the act of killing, he is consumed by it, just as fire consumes its own support.
If a person instructs another to kill, they should not incur the offense;
for example, if one instructs another to touch fire, one is not burned oneself because of that instruction.
Even those who are unintentional regarding earth, wood, and so forth, should incur guilt, just as one incurs guilt when a house collapses and kills living beings.
Furthermore, in the principle concerning the commission of a mortal offense, it should not be established merely by means of establishing an analogy.
Having explained the offense of taking life,
the verse says:
Stealing another's property means taking it for oneself by force or through deception.
The commentary states:
This refers to a continuous flow of non-confused speech.

If a person, through force or through stealth, takes another's property as their own, provided there is an intention to take among the objects belonging to another, then by virtue of that force or stealth—excluding cases of confused taking—the full measure of the path of action of stealing is established.
If one steals the property of a *saṃghārāma*, one incurs an offense against the Buddha. Why is this?
Because at the time of his parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored Buddha accepted all objects of offering.
Other masters say:
"If one can protect this object, the offense is incurred against that person.
If one digs up a pit and finds ownerless property, the offense is incurred against the sovereign."

If a person steals or misappropriates an object that has already undergone the formal ritual (karmavācanā), they incur an offense from the point at which they reach those who do not live in communal harmony;
if the ritual has not yet been performed, they incur an offense from all disciples of the Buddha.
The verse says:
"Engaging in sexual misconduct with those who should not be approached—this is said to be of four kinds.
The commentary explains:
There are four types of conduct that should not be practiced, which are termed sexual misconduct (*kāmamithyācāra*):
first, practicing what should not be practiced, namely with those who are under the protection of others, such as one's mother, daughter, or paternal or maternal relatives;
second, practicing what should not be practiced, namely inappropriately, such as with one’s own wife via the lower orifice or the mouth.

There are three types of places where one should not engage in sexual conduct: improper locations, namely, an open space, a shrine (*caitya*), or a place where the holy life (*brahmacarya*) is practiced.

There are four times when one should not engage in sexual conduct: improper times, namely, when one’s own wife is pregnant, when she is nursing her child, or when she is observing a vow of abstinence.
If one obtains the vow through the husband’s permission, this constitutes an improper time; so say the other schools (*nikāya*).
This follows the context of the discussion on non-confusion.
If one goes to another woman’s place while perceiving her as one’s own wife, the full course of action (*karmapatha*) is not established.

If one perceives another as one's own wife yet approaches a different woman, other masters state that the distinction between the courses of action (karmapatha) is established by the act of approaching another's wife and the actual enjoyment of her.
Because one intends to act in one place but carries it out in another, there is no offense of a *karmapatha*; this is the opinion of other masters, such as in the case of killing.
If one commits this act with a bhikṣuṇī, from what source does the offense arise?
One incurs an offense against the sovereign.
Why is this? Because such a matter is not something the sovereign can tolerate or permit.
If one cannot even act toward one's own wife when she observes the precepts, how much less so toward a bhikṣuṇī?
If one commits this act with a maiden, one incurs an offense against her parents, even if she has been given in marriage by them.
If one has not granted permission to others, one incurs an offense against those who guard [the property], and even against the king.
The verse says:
To speak these words with a different intention, while the meaning is understood, constitutes a lie.
The commentary states:

Regarding the meaning expressed therein, if one utters words based on a conception of that meaning as being otherwise, and the person to whom these words are addressed understands the meaning of those words, then these words constitute false speech.
If the person upon whom this speech depends does not understand the meaning of these words, what are these words?
These words then become meaningless speech.
Regarding the speech that is spoken, sometimes many syllables constitute a word; within such speech, which syllable constitutes the path of action (*karmapatha*)?
The path of action is completed with the final syllable together with the non-informative [action] (avijñapti).
Alternatively, it occurs at the point where the person has understood the meaning; the preceding syllables are merely the preliminary stage (prayoga) of the preparatory effort.
Regarding the explanation of "understanding the meaning": does this refer to having already understood the meaning upon hearing it, or to being able to understand the meaning upon hearing it?
If so, what difference does it make?

If it refers to having already understood the meaning, then since the meaning of speech is an object of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and because speech and auditory consciousness perish simultaneously, the path of action (*karmapatha*) should consist solely of the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
If one can understand the meaning, then this fault does not arise.
How is it that one becomes capable of understanding?
The person who understands the words exists within the auditory consciousness; such a person is the one capable of understanding.
If there is no fault in such an adherence, this may be granted.
However, it is stated in the Sūtra:
"There are sixteen kinds of verbal expression: speaking of what has not been seen as seen, and so on, up to speaking of what has not been known as known."
To say one has not seen when one has seen, up to saying one does not know when one knows—these eight are non-noble utterances.
To say one has not seen when one has not seen, up to saying one does not know when one does not know; these are noble utterances.
Having seen, one speaks of having seen; likewise, up to having known, one speaks of having known—these eight are the noble modes of expression.
In this context, what are the characteristics of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing?
The verse says:

That which is realized by the eye, the ear, and the mental consciousness, as well as the other three [consciousnesses], is termed "seen," "heard," and "known," respectively; or it is said to be "cognized. The commentary states:

that which is realized by the visual consciousness is the "seen"; that realized by the auditory consciousness is the "heard"; that realized by the mental consciousness is the "known"; and that realized by the olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses is the "cognized."

Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of odor, taste, and touch is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), like a corpse; therefore, the consciousness that takes them as its objects is called "sensation" (*vitarka*). This is the explanation of the Vaibhāṣika masters.
What serves as proof for this?
There are two kinds of proof: namely, scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*). Scripture states:
Mālukyīputra! What do you think?

Regarding this form that has not been seen by your eye in the past, is not being seen by it now, and which you have not formed the intention to see—could desire arise, could craving arise, could joy arise, could attachment arise, could fetters arise, or could greed arise on account of such a form?
"No, Bhāradvāja!
This sound has not been heard by your ear before; even so, this phenomenon has not been known by your mind before," and so on, as explained at length.
"No, Bhāradvāja! No, Māluṅkyāputta!"
What do you think?

In this regard, does seeing arise only with respect to what is seen, hearing only with respect to what is heard, sensing only with respect to what is sensed, and knowing only with respect to what is known?
It is stated thus in the Sūtra.
Since seeing, hearing, and cognizing are spoken of with respect to the three [external] objects, we know that the term "cognition" (*buddhi*) is likewise established for the remaining three objects.

If this were not admitted, then because these three would exist outside of the triad of seeing and so forth, there would be no verbal designation for odors and the rest; such is the logical principle (*yukti*).
This sutra is not a proof, because it has a different meaning. Why is this?
Because within this sutra, the Blessed One did not intend to define the characteristics of the four types of verbal expression.
"For what purpose was this statement spoken?
The Buddha said:
"Māluṅkyāputra!"

Regarding the six sense objects and the four types of verbal expressions such as "seeing" and so forth, do these verbal expressions alone arise, or do they further augment causes such as the pleasant and the unpleasant?
Within this teaching, the meaning of the sūtra is seen as follows.
If that is so, what are the characteristics of "seeing," and so forth, up to what are the characteristics of "knowing"?
Other masters say:

That which is realized by the five faculties is "seeing"; that which is obtained through transmission from others is "hearing"; that which is deliberated upon at that time and accepted by one's own mind is "cognition"; and that which is personally realized by one's own mind is "knowledge."
Because these five objects of the senses are perceived according to what each individual sees, the term "seen" (dṛṣṭa) is established on this basis.
If a matter is not personally realized but is obtained solely through transmission from another, this is called "heard" (śruta).
If a matter concerns the five sensory objects, it is called "perception" (*buddhi*) because it is established through one's own deliberation and is what one personally accepts.
Since the sixth object is distinct from these five, it is realized solely by the mental consciousness; therefore, this is called "cognition" (*jñāna*).
Therefore, there is no absence of verbal expression regarding odors and so forth;
thus, the principle you have established does not constitute a valid principle.
The former masters have explained it in this way:

That which is realized by the eye-faculty is called "seen"; that which is obtained through transmission from others is called "heard"; that which is personally reflected upon is called "cognized"; and that which is experienced or attained within oneself is called "known."
Let us not discuss this at length, but further explain this treatise.
If a person expresses a different meaning through their body, does that constitute lying? It does.
Therefore, the Abhidharma-piṭaka states:
"Is there one who commits the offense of killing without performing the act of killing through bodily action? There is."
If it is by means of speech and action, is there an instance where one commits the offense of lying without acting through speech and action?
Yes. If it is by means of bodily action, is there an instance where one commits the offenses of killing or lying without performing these acts through body and speech? Yes.
There is. For example, it is as when one is rebuked by the indignation of a rishi; herein, the analogy of the *poṣadha* is cited as proof.

If [non-informative action] arises from not performing [an act] through body or speech, there is no non-informative action of the desire realm, because it does not have informative action (*vijñapti*) as its precursor.
How does this non-informative [action] (avijñapti) constitute a path of action (karmapatha)?
You should now apply effort toward this point.
The explanation of false speech (mṛṣāvāda) is concluded.
The verse says:
Divisive speech is that which, spoken with a defiled mind, destroys the affection between others.
The commentary says:
The explanation of the meaning states that "unconfused" refers to the flow [of speech].
If one possesses a defiled mind and, for the purpose of destroying the harmony of others or their mutual affection, speaks such words, this is called divisive speech (*paiśunya*).
The verse says:
"Harsh speech is not beloved by others.
The commentary states:
When there is a defiled mind, and one understands the meaning without confusion—these three factors constitute the flow of [harsh] speech.
What is the meaning of these three?
If a person with a defiled mind speaks to someone who understands the meaning, at the place where they wish to speak, and in the words they wish to speak, this is called harsh speech (*pāruṣya*).
The verse says:
"All defiled [speech] is improper speech.
The commentary explains:
All defiled speech is called "inappropriate speech" (asambhinna-pralāpa) because it is inconsistent with the meaning;
it is also called "distracted speech" (pralāpa) because it is not subsumed within the meaning.
The verse says:
Others say it is different from the three defilements.
The commentary says:
Other masters say:
Among the verbal karmas such as lying, those that are defiled are verbal karma;
distinct from those, they are called frivolous speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
The verse says:
Flattery, lamentation, song, dance, and music, and false doctrines.
The commentary says:

For example, there is the bhikṣu of wrong livelihood who utters flattery for the sake of gain and offerings; there is another person who utters words of lamentation when oppressed by the sorrow of separation; there is another who sings due to a mind stained by desire; there is a dancer who composes various lyrics and melodies during a performance to defile others; and there is another who, adhering to false doctrines, gives rise to views and extensively proclaims them, even including common worldly talk and the like. All such defiled speech, distinct from the three types of lying and so forth, is called improper speech (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*).
When there is a wheel-turning monarch, there is song; how then is it not improper speech?
At that time, whatever that person sings is entirely consistent with the meaning of renunciation and is not associated with wrong flavors.
At that time, there may be speech such as "seeking a wife" or "welcoming a bride"; although this is improper speech, it is not a path of action (*karmapatha*). Other masters explain it in this way.
The verse says:
Covetousness (*abhidhyā*) is the unjust desire for another's wealth.
The commentary states:
Regarding the wealth and property of others, one seeks it through improper and unjust means in order to make it one's own, forming this aspiration:
"May all such things as these belong entirely to me."
Whether by force or by delusion, this covetousness is called a path of action (*karmapatha*).
Other masters say:
all sensual desires within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are paths of covetous action.
Why is this? In the *Pañcanīvaraṇa-sūtra*, with reference to sensual desire, there is this statement:
"This person abandons the hindrance of worldly sensual desire."
