If all craving were indeed covetousness, it would not follow that all of it constitutes a course of action (karmapatha), because only those instances that are categorized as grave evils are so designated.
Otherwise, there would be no covetousness as a course of action for universal monarchs (cakravartin) or for the inhabitants of Uttarakuru; thus say other masters.
The verse says:
"Hatred abandons sentient beings.
The commentary explains:

The path of action is established because, due to the faults of sentient beings, one gives rise to a harmful mind of equanimity (*upekṣā-citta*), and because of the intensity of the mind regarding acts that injure others.
The verse says:
"Lack of vision regarding good and evil is wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)."
The commentary states:
To deny the existence of both wholesome and unwholesome karma by asserting that "there is no karma" is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
As the Sūtra says:
There is no giving, no offering, no sacrifice, no wholesome conduct, and no unwholesome conduct; in this world, there are no śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who are arhats.
This constitutes the full complement of wrong view, namely: the denial of karma, the denial of its results, and the denial of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Although there are many scriptural passages on this subject, this verse merely highlights the most significant points; these constitute the essential characteristics of the ten paths of action (*karmapatha*).
What is the meaning of these paths of action?
The verse says:
Of these, the last three are paths alone; the seven are both actions and paths of action.
The commentary states:
Greed and the other two are the paths for karma; thus they are called "paths of karma" (*karmapatha*), because the volition that initiates action arises in dependence upon them.

The first seven are both karma and paths, because they can manifest the original intention and because they belong to its category; therefore they are called "karma. The paths of karma are as previously explained.
It should be understood that non-greed and so forth, as well as abstaining from killing and so forth, are likewise [to be understood].
Why are the preceding and succeeding parts not considered paths of action (*karmapatha*)?

Because they arise for the sake of accomplishing this [principal act] and serve as its basis; since this [principal act] is the root, it is like a coarse summary being designated as the path of action.
This is as previously explained.

Furthermore, because it causes the manifestation of superiority and inferiority among all internal and external things in the world through its increase or decrease, it is established as a course of action (*karmapatha*).

If that is so, since the Dārṣṭāntika masters maintain that only craving and so forth constitute mental action (*manas-karman*), how can these three [unwholesome roots] constitute paths of action (*karmapatha*) for them?
You should ask that teacher.
This may also be answered: because they are both karma and the paths to the miserable destinies, they are called "paths of action" (*karmapatha*).
Furthermore, because they mutually serve as mounts for one another, they are all termed "paths of action."
These ten paths of unwholesome action that have been described are all called "unwholesome" because they are contrary to the practice of wholesome dharmas.
The verse says:
The severing of the roots [of merit] occurs through wrong view.
The commentary states:
Among the ten non-virtuous actions, by which evil is the root of virtue severed?
It is by the most superior and intense degree of perfect wrong view.
If that is so, how is it stated in the Abhidharma-piṭaka:
"What are the most superior and intense unwholesome roots?
They are those capable of severing the wholesome roots"?

When a person reaches the stage of being correctly detached from the desire realm, that which is eliminated first is false view; because it is incited by the unwholesome roots, false view is established as one of the unwholesome roots.
For example, although it is fire that burns the land, because the kalpa draws forth the fire and causes it to arise, one says that the land is burned by the kalpa.
What, then, are the roots of goodness that are extinguished?
The verse says:
The innate wholesome [roots] of the desire realm.
The commentary says:
Only the roots of goodness within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are severed, because they are not associated with the roots of goodness of the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
If this is so, how do you interpret the *Prajñaptiśāstra*?
That treatise states:
"It is solely by this measure that one has already severed the roots of goodness of the three realms; [it refers to] the acquisition (*prāpti*) of the roots of goodness of the higher realms.
This statement is made based on the sense of being most remote and separated, because it renders the mental continuum no longer a fit vessel for them.
Only the innate roots of goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśalamūla*) are severed, because all roots of goodness acquired through application (*prāyogika-kuśalamūla*) have already been lost.
Regarding this wrong view that severs the roots of goodness, what is its objective referent?
The verse says:
"That is to say, the denial of cause and effect.
The commentary says:
If this wrong view negates the cause— meaning it asserts that there are no wholesome or unwholesome actions—
or if it negates the fruit— meaning it asserts that there is no retribution resulting from wholesome or unwholesome karmic actions—
these two types of wrong view resemble, respectively, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The masters of other schools say:

"In this way, they take contaminated phenomena as their objects but do not take uncontaminated phenomena as their objects; they take objects within their own sphere (*dhātu*) but do not take objects outside their sphere. Because they function solely through association (*saṃprayoga*), their power is weak."
The verse says:
"All [arise] in succession.
The commentary says:
The various masters explain:
all such false views can sever the nine grades of wholesome roots simultaneously, just as the afflictions are eliminated through the realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*).
Furthermore, other masters say:
They are severed successively: by means of the nine grades of false views, the nine grades of wholesome roots are severed.
Just as defilements are eliminated through the path of cultivation, even the highest-of-the-high grade of false view severs the lowest-of-the-low grade of wholesome root.
If one maintains this position, the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* is thereby upheld.
The *Śāstra* asks:
"What are the roots of goodness?"
The most subtle [root] is constantly present;
it is the last to be severed by one who has cut off the roots of goodness.
Because it is extinguished, such a person receives the designation of "one who has cut off the roots of goodness."
If that is so, how should the meaning of this treatise (śāstra) be understood?
The treatise asks:
"What are the most superior and intense unwholesome roots?"
If the roots of evil are capable of extinguishing the roots of goodness, this is termed the "highest of the high" grade.
This statement is made with reference to the completion of the causal process. Why is this so?
Because these have been extinguished without remainder, not even a single category remains that could serve as a productive cause for them.
This is just as one does not emerge from meditative absorption during the path of seeing the truths; the severing of the roots of goodness is likewise.
Furthermore, other masters say:
"This matter is of two kinds.
Again, other masters say:
First one severs the wholesome roots that consist of restraint, and subsequently one severs the wholesome roots that are intrinsic.
Furthermore, other masters say:
if restraint is the fruit of the mind, then by abandoning this mind, the restraint is also abandoned.
In what place can the roots of goodness be severed?
The verse says:
In the human realm.
The commentary states:

This occurs within the human realm and not in the miserable destinies (*durgati*), because the wisdom—whether defiled or undefiled—is not firm there; nor does it occur in the heavenly realms, because one directly perceives the retribution of karma there.
It occurs in the three continents, but not in Uttarakuru, because the inhabitants there are naturally devoid of malicious intent.
Other masters say:
it occurs only among the people of Jambudvīpa.
If one maintains this position, it contradicts the *Śāstra*.
The *Śāstra* states:
"The inhabitants of Jambudvīpa, if they possess the minimum number of faculties, possess only eight faculties."
The same applies to Pūrvavideha in the east and Aparagoyānī in the west.
Regarding these roots of goodness, the verse says:
"Only men and women can sever them."
The commentary states:
If one severs the roots of goodness, only men and women can do so.
Other masters say:
Because the faculty of wisdom and the faculty of diligence are dull and weak, women do not sever [the fetters].
If this is so, this position contradicts the *Gāndhārī* (or *Gāndharva*).
The *Gāndhārī* states:
If a person is endowed with the female faculty (*strīndriya*), that person is necessarily endowed with eight faculties.

This is because, among those who possess the male or female faculties, their conduct is driven by craving and they are unable to sever the roots of goodness, as the mental ground is weak and unstable.
If that is so, what kind of practitioner is able to abandon them?
The verse says:
"Those who act through views."
The commentary states:
Because this person’s malicious intent is extremely deep and firm, those such as eunuchs cannot sever it;
for it belongs to the category of craving (*rāga*), just like the evil realms.
What is the essential nature and characteristic of this severance of the roots of goodness?
The verse says:
It is non-possession (*aprāpti*).
The commentary states:
At that time, the possession (*prāpti*) of the roots of goodness reaches cessation and does not arise again, while their non-possession (*aprāpti*) arises.
When this non-possession arises, it is said that the roots of goodness have already been severed.
Since these roots of goodness have already been severed, how can they be reconnected?
The verse says:
"The reconnection of goodness occurs through doubt or views."
The commentary states:
If this person conceives doubt regarding cause and effect, or conceives the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*), this is called right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).
At that time, because this right view reaches the point where it can arise once more, it is said that they reconnect their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

In the past, the nine grades [of defilements] were severed separately; now they are reconnected all at once, appearing in succession, just as one attains both freedom from illness and physical strength.
This person reconnects their roots of goodness; the verse says:
"Now, it is not the case that they commit the immediate transgressions."
The commentary states:
For other persons who have severed their roots of goodness, there is the possibility of reconnecting those roots within this very life.
However, for a person who has committed an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), there is no possibility of reconnecting the roots of goodness within this life.
Based on this person, it is said in the sūtra:
"This person should not be able to reconnect with their roots of goodness in this present life.
This person may be either in the process of passing away from hell or in the process of being reborn there; at that time, they should reconnect with their roots of goodness.
"Correctly arising" refers to abiding in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*); "correctly declining" refers to being on the verge of death.
In this context, if one severs the roots of goodness through the power of causes, it is at the time of decline that the roots of goodness are reconnected.
If the roots of goodness are severed through the power of conditions, they are reconnected at the very moment of their arising.
The same applies when they are severed through one's own power or through the power of another.
Furthermore, if a person severs the roots of goodness by means of their own intention, that person will reconnect them in this very life.

If a person severs the roots of goodness through corruption by their own mind or through the instruction of another, that person will reconnect with the roots of goodness after the body has been cast off.
It is the same for one who severs them through corruption by views, or through corruption by both views and precepts.
There are those who have severed their roots of goodness yet do not fall into the group of those fixed in error; this principle consists of four propositions.
The first proposition refers to those such as Pūrṇa and others.
The second proposition refers to those such as King Ajātaśatru and others.
The third phrase refers to those such as Devadatta and others.
The fourth phrase excludes the preceding three phrases.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 12.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Thirteen.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.
In the fourth section of the Analysis of Karma within the Middle [Treatise], concerning the analysis and establishment of the paths of karma, this meaning should now be explained:
how many types of karmic paths arise simultaneously with the volition that corresponds to them?
The verse says:
"From being conjoined with volition up to [being conjoined with] the eight paths of unwholesome karma.
The commentary says:

Sometimes it arises intentionally together with one unwholesome course of action while being separated from the others; this occurs when greed and so forth arise and manifest, or when a person, though lacking a defiled mind, has previously instructed another to perform a material course of action and that [action] is accomplished.

Regarding those that arise together with two [mental factors]: when a person, while giving rise to a mind of hatred, commits killing; or while their mind is defiled by greed, engages in stealing or sexual misconduct; or utters improper speech.

Regarding those that arise together with three [mental factors]: if a person gives rise to a mind of malice and simultaneously commits killing and stealing against other sentient beings, then at that time, the act of stealing is accomplished not by way of greed.
If a person’s mind does not change at the time the course of action (*karmapatha*) is accomplished, one should understand that the previous determination applies.
This refers to when a person, being defiled by covetousness and so forth, accomplishes two material courses of action through instructing another.

Regarding those that arise together with three or four [paths of action]: if a person, with the intention to break the harmony of others, utters false speech or harsh speech, then in this case there is one path of action of the mind and three paths of action of speech.
Sometimes, when one is defiled by greed and other afflictions, it occurs at the moment of accomplishing three distinct acts through instructing others.
It should be understood that the remaining [cases of] five, six, and seven follow this same principle.
Regarding those arising together with eight: when one instructs others in six [acts] while personally committing sexual misconduct, they are all accomplished simultaneously.
The meaning of the unwholesome paths of action is exhausted at this point.
The verse says:
"If wholesome, up to ten."
The commentary states:
Regarding whether volition (cetanā) is associated with or dissociated from the wholesome paths of action (karmapatha), it may even be associated with all ten paths of action.
Having thus provided this general explanation, [the specific cases follow].
In order to discern this, another specific explanation is provided.
The verse says:
"Not shared: one, eight, and five."
The commentary states:
There is no sense in which volition (cetanā) is associated with one, eight, or five courses of action (karmapatha).

Among these, that which is associated with two occurs at the time when the five wholesome sensory consciousnesses arise, at the time of entering the formless attainments (ārūpyasamāpatti), and at the time when the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) and the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) arise.
Regarding those associated with three [factors]: when consciousness arises in association with right view.
Regarding those associated with four [factors]: when an unwholesome or neutral mind arises while one is correctly undertaking the upāsaka precepts or the śrāmaṇera precepts.
Regarding those associated with six [mental factors]: when the five wholesome consciousnesses arise, one undertakes the first two vows.
Regarding those associated with seven [mental factors]: when the wholesome mental consciousness arises, one undertakes the first two vows.
When an unwholesome mind or an indeterminate mind arises, one undertakes the bhikṣu-prātimokṣa restraint.
Regarding its association with nine [mental factors]: when the five wholesome consciousnesses arise, one undertakes the bhikṣu-prātimokṣa restraint.

If the mental consciousness is associated with the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), this mind associated with the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising is also associated with meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Regarding that which is associated with ten [factors], it is otherwise: when a wholesome mental consciousness arises in other circumstances, one undertakes the bhikṣu restraint (*bhikṣusaṃvara*).

The volition associated with all forms of meditative restraint (*samvara*) and the untainted restraint (*anāsrava-samvara*), excluding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), may also be associated with only one [of the three types of restraint] if it is not subsumed under restraint.
If a person, with a different state of mind, undertakes one part of seclusion (*viveka*), they may also be endowed with five or eight [factors].
If a person, when a wholesome mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises, simultaneously undertakes two parts of seclusion, or undertakes five parts of seclusion.
Furthermore, in which realms and how many courses of action—whether unwholesome or wholesome—arise simultaneously through both manifestation and acquisition?
The verse says:
Unwholesome speech, harsh speech, and malice [are present] in two ways in the hells.
The commentary states:
These three types of karmic paths exist in hell by way of two meanings:
first, by way of presence (*sammukhībhāva*); second, by way of possession (*prāpti*).
From weeping arises improper speech; from mutual abuse arises harsh speech; and from the continuity of affliction and mutual hatred arises ill-will.
The verse says:
From the attainment [of objects] arise covetousness and wrong view.
The commentary states:

If one possesses craving and false views by virtue of their possession (*prāpti*), they do not exist by virtue of being present, because there are no desirable objects and because the relationship between karma and its fruit has been realized.
Because death occurs only through the exhaustion of karma, there is no killing; because they do not possess property or wives, there is no stealing or sexual misconduct.
Because there is no purpose for it, there is no lying; and because they never engage in social discord themselves, there is no divisive speech.
The verse says:
"Three in the Northern Continent.
The commentary says:
By virtue of the context concerning "attainment" (*prāpti*),

greed, malice, and false views do not exist in the present state, because there is no sense of "mine" and nothing to be grasped, because the mental continuum is supple, because there is no object belonging to the category of malice, and because there is no malicious intent.
The verse says:
"The seventh belongs to them themselves.
The commentary says:
Inappropriate speech does not exist in their presence. Why is this?

Because those beings sometimes sing with a defiled mind, yet they lack malicious intent; because they do not kill living beings and so forth; because their lifespan is fixed; because they do not possess wealth or wives; and because there is no purpose [for such speech].
How does that person engage in unchaste conduct?
If that person desires to unite in amorous play with this woman, he takes her hand and they go together beneath a tree.
If this woman was fit for union, the tree would immediately close over them, and they would then engage in intercourse;
if she was not fit for union, the tree would not close, and they would immediately turn away from one another and depart.
The verse says:
"In other [realms], the ten unwholesome actions of the desire realm.
The commentary says:
Since the beginning of speech,

with the exception of the hells and the northern continent (Uttarakuru), the ten paths of unwholesome action exist in other places both by way of actual manifestation and as non-restraint (*avirati*).
Among animals, hungry ghosts, and gods, there are paths of action that are not [of the nature of] non-restraint.
Within the human realm, there are also courses of action (karmapatha) subsumed under non-restraint.
Although gods cannot kill other gods, they can kill beings of other realms.
If the heads or waists of gods are severed, they immediately lose their lives.
Having explained the paths of unwholesome action,
the verse says:
"The last three exist in all [realms], because they are present and attained."
The commentary states:
Within the five destinies and the three realms, in all places, non-attachment, non-hatred, and right view exist both through actual manifestation and through possession.
The verse says:
"In the formless realm and among the non-percipient gods, there are seven by way of possession.
The commentary explains:
"The seven virtuous courses of action of body and speech exist in the formless realm and among the non-percipient gods solely by way of possession."
Because an Ārya who has been born into the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu) is endowed with the acquisition (prāpti) of past and future untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara).

The beings in the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva) are endowed with the acquisition of meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara), according to the stage (bhūmi) upon which they rely; this includes the untainted restraint that an Ārya has produced or relinquished.
If one is born in the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), one is endowed with this past restraint (saṃvara) and also endowed with the future restraint based on the five stages (bhūmi).
The verse says:
"The rest [are] also present, except for those in the hells and the northern continent (uttarakuru)."
The commentary states:
"The remainder" refers to other realms and other paths.
Within those other realms and paths, these seven types of wholesome courses of action exist by way of manifestation as well, with the exception of the hells and the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru).
As for "the rest," this refers to animals and hungry ghosts (*preta*); among them, there is only that which is not governed by restraint (*asaṃvara*).
In the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), there is only that which is comprised within restraint (*saṃvara*); in all other places, both types are present.
Furthermore, regarding these ten paths of unwholesome action and the paths of wholesome action, the verse says:
"All are capable of yielding the fruit of superior outflow and retribution.
The commentary explains:
Now, let us first discuss the unwholesome.
Because one has habitually practiced and frequently engaged in all ten types of unwholesome actions, one is born in the hells; this is called the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).

Once the retribution of the hells has been fully experienced, one obtains a corresponding category, namely the homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) of human beings and so forth; because of the taking of life, one’s lifespan is short.
Due to stealing, there will be obstacles regarding one's wealth and possessions;
due to sexual misconduct, one will have many enemies and hatred, and face obstacles regarding one's wife and concubines;
due to lying, one will frequently be subjected to slander.
Due to divisive speech, one's friends and relatives will not be harmonious;
due to harsh speech, one will constantly hear unpleasant sounds;
and due to idle chatter, people will not accept one's words even when they are logical and true.
Due to desire, one becomes excessively full of desire;
due to hatred, one becomes excessively full of hatred;
and due to wrong views, one becomes dull-witted and full of delusion.
Because this view is largely characterized by ignorance, it is called the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the ten unwholesome paths of action.
Furthermore, even a short lifespan within the human realm is itself the fruit of wholesome karma.
In what sense is this the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) of killing?
It is not said that human lifespan is an outflowing fruit. Why is that?
Through evil karma, one's lifespan is diminished.
It should be understood that killing is the cause for obstructing the lifespan in the human realm.
As for the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), it arises through the repeated practice and frequent performance of killing.
All external requisites for life lose their power and flavor due to stealing; there is much lightning and dust due to theft;
much grime and filth due to sexual misconduct;
and much foul stench due to lying.
Due to divisive speech, the external vessel-world possesses elevations and depressions;
due to harsh speech, the earth has a foul taste, and its high and dry regions are mutually contradictory and unsuitable for all things;
due to idle chatter, the seasons are not harmonious, and the four great elements undergo transformations that are unbalanced.
Due to covetousness, all fruits that are sown will be meager and weak;
due to malice, all that is produced will be bitter and acrid;
due to wrong views, all means of subsistence will yield either little fruit or no fruit at all—these are called the dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) of the ten unwholesome actions.
Is it because of this very karma that one's lifespan is short in this life, or because of another karma?
Other masters say:
it is indeed this very karma.
Why is this? Because in the past, the fruit of ripening (*vipākaphala*) of this karma was already established, whereas at present it is its fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*).
Other masters say:
In the past, it was by way of the preliminary stage (*pūrvāṅga*); now, it is by way of the fundamental act (*maula*), because it is taught as being accompanied by its associated factors (*sahabhū*).

Regarding the outflow fruit (*niṣyandaphala*) of killing and so forth: although they do not constitute a homogeneous outflow (*nisyanda-jāti*), they are described in this way because of their similarity in specific differentiation.
Furthermore, how do the ten paths of action produce three kinds of results?
When a person commits the act of killing, they produce suffering for the victim, they terminate that life, and they deprive them of their vitality and vigor.
Therefore, the verse says:
"By causing suffering and removing life, one destroys the three: power, flavor, and fruit.
The commentary explains: because one causes suffering to others, there is a ripening fruit (*vipākaphala*); consequently, one undergoes suffering and harm in hell.
Because of committing killing, there is a result concordant with the cause (*niṣyanda-phala*): in this life, one's desirable lifespan is short.
Because of diminishing the power and flavor of others, there is a dominant result (*adhipati-phala*): external medicinal herbs and the like lack power and flavor, or their power and flavor are weak.
It should be understood that the three fruits of the remaining paths of action are likewise so.
It should be understood that the three fruits of the wholesome paths of action are also thus.
As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said:
There are wrong speech, wrong action, and wrong livelihood.
What wrong livelihood is there that differs from these two?
There is none that differs from these two.
The verse says:
Bodily and vocal actions arising from greed are established separately as wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
The commentary says:

If, with respect to sentient beings, one generates two types of karma—bodily and vocal—arising from hatred and delusion, these are termed wrong speech and wrong action; distinct from these two, wrong livelihood is established separately.
The verse says:
"Difficult to cure."
The commentary states:

The dharma of sensual desire universally draws in sentient beings; therefore, the karma arising from it is difficult to restrain and protect within the mind, and for this reason, right livelihood is not easily rectified.
In this context, because it is intended to inspire a sense of earnestness in others, these two are now established as the third [category].
Here, a verse is spoken:
"The householder is seen to be difficult to cure, Constantly clinging to various views."
"A bhikṣu’s life is difficult to sustain, for his livelihood depends upon others.
The verse says:
"Life arises from craving; if one clings [to it], [it is difficult to maintain]."
The commentary states:
If someone maintains that the two types of bodily and vocal karma arising from craving for the requisites of life are called "wrong livelihood" (mithyājīva) and nothing else, why is this so?
Engaging in dance, song, and so forth for one's own amusement is not established as a requisite for sustaining life.
The verse says:
Because it is not [taught] in the Sūtras.
The commentary states:
This interpretation is not correct. Why is this so?
As it is said in the Sūtra:
In the *Śīlaskandha-sūtra*, the Blessed One established activities such as watching elephant fights within wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*). Why is this so?
The point that [this occurs] due to the improper enjoyment of sense objects is now concluded.
Regarding the five kinds of fruits previously mentioned, which karma possesses fruit through how many of those fruits?
The verse says:
Regarding cessation and the path, there are defilements; karma has its fruit by way of five [factors].
The commentary says:

This path is cultivated for the sake of attaining cessation; furthermore, because delusions are extinguished by means of this path, it is called the "path to cessation," specifically the sequential path (*ānantarya-mārga*).
If this path is with outflows (*sāsrava*), then any karma contained within it has five kinds of results as its fruit.
Why is this? The desirable fruit obtained within its own level by this karma is called the *vipākaphala* (fruition of maturation).
Subsequently, a phenomenon that is either equal to or superior to it and resembles it is the *niṣyandaphala* (fruit of outflow).
The fruit of separation (*visamyoga-phala*) refers to the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), which is the mind’s freedom from all fetters (*saṃyojana*).

The fruit of effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) consists of those dharmas produced by the power of the Path, namely the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and the dharmas arising simultaneously with it, as well as other dharmas to be attained in the future and this very cessation through deliberation.
The dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*) consists of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) other than its own nature, excluding those that have already arisen.
The verse says:
"In the case of the stainless, by four."
The commentary says:
Within the untainted (anāsrava) cessation and the path, karma possesses four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (vipākaphala).
The verse says:
"Other wholesome and unwholesome [actions] are with outflows.
The commentary explains:

If a wholesome action is with outflows—distinct from the paths of cessation and the path itself, as well as unwholesome actions—these two have fruits by way of four fruits, excluding the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*).
The verse says:
"The remaining outflow-free karma [is exhausted] by three; the indeterminate is likewise.
The commentary says:
All uncontaminated karma, as well as other types of cessation, the Path, and neutral karma, possess results by way of three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation and the fruit of disjunction.
The verse says:
Four, two, and the remaining three are the results of wholesome karma, whether wholesome and so forth.
The commentary says:
This meaning should be understood according to its sequence, which will be explained later.
Sometimes wholesome karma has wholesome dharmas as its fruit; in such cases, there are four fruits, excluding the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).
If unwholesome dharmas are taken as the fruit, there are two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
If neutral (*avyākṛta*) dharmas are taken as the fruit, there are three fruits, excluding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the dissociated fruit (*visamyoga-phala*).
The verse says:
"If there are two, such as the unwholesome and the wholesome, there are three and four respectively.
The commentary says:
This meaning should be understood according to its sequence:
if unwholesome karma has wholesome dharmas as its fruit, there are two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
If unwholesome dharmas are taken as the fruit, there are three fruits, excluding the fruit of retribution and the fruit of dissociation.
If neutral dharmas are taken as the fruit, there are four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation.
What is the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*)?

It refers to the neutral views of self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*) and extreme views (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*); these are the outflowing fruits of the unwholesome universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) that are abandoned through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
The verse says:
"The indeterminate has two or three; the three, in turn, [apply] to the wholesome and so forth.
The commentary says:
If an indeterminate action has wholesome dharmas as its fruit, it has two fruits: namely, the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāra-phala) and the dominant fruit (adhipati-phala).
If it has unwholesome dharmas as its fruit, it has three fruits, excluding the retributive fruit (vipāka-phala) and the fruit of disjunction (visamyoga-phala).
Why is this so? The unwholesome afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of suffering are the outflow-results (*niṣyanda-phala*) of the two neutral views.
If one takes neutral dharmas as their result, then there are three results.
The verse says:
"All past [dharmas] are four.
The commentary says:
"All" refers to the dharmas of the three periods of time.
If these dharmas are the fruits of past karma, each has four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
The verse says:
"Intermediate karma brings such results.
The commentary states:
If karma of the present life takes dharmas of the future as its result, there are four results, as previously explained.
The verse says:
"In the middle, there are two fruits.
The commentary explains:
If a present dharma is the fruit of a present karma, there are only two fruits: namely, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
The verse says:
For future karma, there are three future fruits.
The commentary states:
If future karma takes future dharmas as its fruit, then there are three fruits, excluding the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the disjunct fruit (*visamyoga-phala*).
The verse says:
There are four dharmas of the same stage (*sabhūmika*).
The commentary states:
with the exception of the fruit of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*), all [the other fruits] are present.
The verse says:
"Three or two, if they belong to different stages.
The commentary says:

If the karma of a different stage is outflow-free (*anāsrava*), it has three fruits—excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of dissociation (*visamyogaphala*)—because it does not fall within the realms (*dhātu*).
If it is with-outflow (*sāsrava*), it has two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāraphala*) and the dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*).
The verse says:
"The learner possesses the three trainings, etc.
The commentary explains:
If there is a training path that takes the dharmas of one in training as its fruit, it has three fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation and the fruit of disjunction.
It is the same if it takes the dharmas of one beyond training as its fruit.
If one takes dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner as the fruit, there are three fruits, excluding the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*) and the fruit of outflow (*niṣyandaphala*).
The verse says:
"Learner's karma with respect to learner dharmas and so forth has only one fruit, or else three fruits and two."
The commentary states:
If the karma of one beyond training (aśaikṣa) has the dharmas of one still in training (śaikṣa) as its fruit, there is then one fruit, namely the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
If it has the dharmas of one beyond training as its fruit, there are then three fruits, excluding the retributive fruit (vipākaphala) and the fruit of disjunction (visamyogaphala).
If one takes dharmas that are neither-learner-nor-non-learner as the fruit, there are two fruits: namely, the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
The verse says:
"Other than these two, for the learner and so forth, there are two, two, and five fruits."
The commentary states:

"The karma of neither-trainee-nor-non-trainee" refers to karma that is neither of the trainee (śaikṣa) nor the non-trainee (aśaikṣa). If one takes the dharmas of a trainee as its fruit, there are two fruits: namely, the fruit of human effort (puruṣakāraphala) and the dominant fruit (adhipatiphala).
The same applies when taking the dharmas of one beyond training (aśaikṣadharma) as the fruit.
If one takes dharmas that are neither of training nor beyond training (naivaśaikṣanāśaikṣadharma) as the fruit, there are five fruits.
The verse says:
"Three, four, and one; for those [actions] abandoned by seeing, [the results] are those [same categories].
The commentary explains:

If an action abandoned by seeing has as its result phenomena abandoned by seeing, it possesses three results—excluding the ripening result (*vipākaphala*) and the disconnection result (*visamyogaphala*).
If one takes the dharmas to be abandoned by the path of cultivation as the fruit, there are four fruits, excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*).
If one takes the dharmas not to be abandoned as the fruit, there is one fruit, namely the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
The verse says:
Two fruits, four, and three [fruits] are for karma to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
The commentary says:

If karma to be abandoned by the path of cultivation takes as its fruit a dharma to be abandoned by the vision of the truths, then it has two fruits, namely: the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the sovereign fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
If one takes the dharmas abandoned through the path of cultivation as the fruit, there are four fruits, excluding the fruit of disjunction.
If one takes the dharmas not to be abandoned as the fruit, there are three fruits, excluding the fruit of retribution and the fruit of outflow.
The verse says:
"Not for the karma that is being extinguished; for those [other karmas], there is one, two, or four fruits, respectively.
The commentary explains:

Regarding karma that is not to be abandoned by seeing (*na-darśana-heya*): if it takes as its fruit phenomena to be abandoned by seeing, there is one fruit, namely the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*).
If it takes as its fruit phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), there are two fruits, namely the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) and the dominant fruit.
If that which is not a dharma to be extinguished is taken as the fruit, there are four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).

Regarding the further explanation of the sequence, one should know that within the preceding, middle, and subsequent [sections], various meanings are restated to clarify cause and effect, because of the analysis of the meaning of the correspondence with karma.
The essential nature and characteristics of this karma should also be investigated.

In the Abhidharma-piṭaka, it is taught that there are three types of karma: namely, unwholesome action (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), wholesome action (*yoniśo-manasikāra*), and action that is neither unwholesome nor wholesome.
What are the characteristics of this karma?
The verse says:
It is unwholesome action performed with defilement; others say it is that which lacks the proper method or sequence.
The commentary states:
If karma is defiled, it is called "unreasonable action" (*ayoniśomanasikāra-ja*), because it arises from improper reflection; such is the view of some teachers.
Other teachers, however, say:
Losing the sequence of skillful means is called improper action (*ayoniśomanasikāra*).
If a person should act in such a way, should dwell in such a way, should eat in such a way, or should dress in such a way, yet performs these matters incorrectly, this is called improper action.
Because this karma is performed in an improper manner, it is entirely termed "unreasonably performed.
All wholesome karma is termed "reasonably performed," as is that which does not lose its sequential order of skillful means.
Apart from these two, there is action that is neither rational nor irrational.
Does a single karma project a single birth, or does a single karma project many births?
Furthermore, do many karmas project a single birth, or does a single karma project a single birth?
If one speaks according to this *siddhānta*, it should be stated thus.
The verse says:
"A single karma projects a single birth."
The commentary states:
Only a single karma of one lifetime can project [a birth], but it cannot project multiple lifetimes.
"Birth" (janman) is a name for the homogeneous group (nikāya-sabhāga); when one attains that, it is called "birth."
If that is so, Venerable Ānanda, why did you say:

"By the fruit of the gift of a single meal given by me in the past, I was born seven times among the Trāyastriṃśa gods and seven times as a universal monarch (cakravartin); even until now, I am still born into a wealthy Śākya family"?
By the retribution of this karma, one obtains the fruit of great wealth and the ability to remember past lives; furthermore, another distinct karma is produced.
This statement is made to manifest its functional efficacy.
For example, suppose there is a person who, through effort applied to a single gold coin, acquires a thousand gold coins, and then says these words:
"It is because of this one gold coin that I have now attained great wealth."
Furthermore, it is said that for this person, by relying on the giving of food at this time, a most extensive continuity of volitional intentions arises.
Among these volitional intentions, there are those capable of drawing forth and encompassing karmic fruition.

Multiple karmas cannot produce a single lifetime; nor can multiple [karmas] each individually project the homogeneous character (*nikāyasabhāga*) that constitutes this lifetime. It is accepted that while one karma projects [the existence], other karmas [contribute to its completion].
The verse says:
"Many karmas can bring it to completion.
The commentary says:
For example, it is like a painter who uses a single color to sketch the outline of a human figure, which is then brought to completion with many colors. Why is this?

Because among sentient beings in the world who belong to the same human category and share the same commonality (*nikāya-sabhāga*), there are those whose bodies and limbs are complete, and who possess the perfection of such characteristics as complexion, form, stature, strength, and physical beauty; therefore, they are the most distinct and lovely within the human community.
There are others who do not possess all parts therein; it is not karma alone that can project rebirth.
What are the remaining dharmas that have retribution as their fruit?
If one considers them in every respect, the verse says:
"The two meditative attainments are not projectors; they are mindless and possess acquisitions.
The commentary states:
The two mindless attainments also have retribution (*vipāka*), yet they cannot project a homogeneous life-span (*nikāya-sabhāga*), because they do not arise simultaneously with karma.
The same applies to "attainment" (*prāpti*), as it does not share the same fruit as the karma itself.
The Blessed One said:
"There are three kinds of obstructions: namely, the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and the obstruction of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*)."
What is the essential nature of these three obstructions?
The verse says:

Karmas that are grave, such as those involving the immediate [retributions], Defiled persistence, afflictions, and the evil destinies, The northern continent and the heaven of non-perception— These are declared to be the three obstructions.
The commentary states:
There are five types of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and so forth, which are termed "obstructions of karma" (*karmāvaraṇa*).

These are: killing one's mother, killing one's father, killing an arhat, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and with malicious intent drawing blood from the body of a Tathāgata; these are termed "obstructions of karma."
The state of being defiled and abiding in delusion is called the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
There are two kinds of delusion:
first, that which is defiled and abiding, meaning that which functions constantly; [the second is that which arises occasionally].
The second is "strong and sharp," which refers to those of the heavy grade.

Among these, the defilements that persist are called the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); for example, in the case of eunuchs and the like, although their afflictions are strong and sharp, the afflictions themselves do not constitute an obstacle.
Why is this? If a defilement is strong and sharp because it belongs to the heavy category, then because this defilement arises only occasionally and not constantly, it can at times be extinguished.
Defilements of the light category do not arise constantly.

Why is this? If the afflictions were to arise constantly, there would be no time for human effort to bring about their cessation; for these afflictions develop from the weak grade to the medium grade, and from the medium grade to the superior grade.
This affliction is the direct obstacle.

The three types of evil destinies are called obstacles of retribution; the same applies to one portion of the good destinies, namely, the people of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Heaven of Non-conception.
What phenomena do these three obstacles obstruct?
They obstruct the Noble Path and the roots of goodness that serve as the preparatory application for the Noble Path.

Furthermore, there are other karmas whose retribution in the evil destinies and so forth is fixed—namely, those fixed in birth from an egg or moisture, birth in a female body, and birth in an eighth existence—which should also be described as karmic obstacles.
If an action can be understood and described by way of five causes, that action is established as an obstruction.
What are these five? First, by way of basis; second, by way of fruit; third, by way of path; fourth, by way of birth; and fifth, by way of person; therefore, only five are mentioned.
Among these, the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is the coarsest, and the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) is the next coarsest. Why is this?
Because due to these two, a person cannot be cured in their second birth.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
They are taught in this sequence because each subsequent one serves as a vehicle for the next.
What is the meaning of "immediate" (*anantara*)?
Within the production of karmic fruition, there is no other karma or separate arising of fruition capable of obstructing it.
Furthermore, if the person who committed this karma relinquishes their life, there is no phenomenon that can hinder the immediate arising of the fruit of hell.

Because this person is associated with these dharmas and is born into the Avīci hell due to them, it is called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*), just as, for example, one is called a "śramaṇa" [based on their practice].
Furthermore, it should be understood in which realms these three kinds of obstacles exist.
If it is certain, the verse says:
"In the three continents, [it occurs] immediately.
The commentary says:
This does not exist in the Northern Continent (Uttarakuru), nor in other realms of existence, much less in other world-systems.
Within the human realm, only men and women are capable of performing this karma.
The verse says:
The eunuchs and others did not permit it.
The commentary asks:
For what reason is this non-existent for them?
The cause of protection is this very cause.
Furthermore, there is another cause, as the verse says:
"Scant kindness and scant shame."
The commentary states:
Regarding the sequence, [the relationship] is such that for a certain person there are parents, and for parents there is a certain person.
Parents have less debt of gratitude toward their child because they do not possess the full complement of bodily parts as the predominant factor, and because their affection is less.
I do not give rise to a profound sense of shame and modesty toward my parents; because I have violated this shame and modesty, I am touched by the karma of an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
For this reason, it is not permitted for the karma of immediate retribution to exist among animals or in the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
The Venerable One says:
If wisdom is clear and lucid, there are five types of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), just as with a clever and intelligent horse.
If a person kills a non-human parent, there is no immediate karmic offense.
Having explained the karmic obstructions,
the verse says:
"The remaining obstructions exist within the five destinies."
The commentary states:
What are the "others"? They are the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle of karmic retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*).

Regarding the obstruction of karmic fruition (*vipākāvaraṇa*): among human beings, it refers to those of the Northern Continent (*Uttarakuru*); among devas, it refers to the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*).
What is the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of these deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*)?

Four have bodily action as their substance; one has vocal action as its substance. Three have the taking of life as their intrinsic nature; one has false speech as its intrinsic nature; and one has the preliminary stage of taking life as its intrinsic nature.

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are by nature incapable of being killed; however, because the name of the effect is established upon its cause, it is said that the schism of the Saṃgha constitutes an ānantarya (immediate) karma.
Since the Saṃgha is split by means of this cause, the cause itself receives the name of "schism."
How is its meaning refuted?
The verse says:
The schism of the Saṃgha is not a state of harmony; by nature it is not an associated dharma; it is a non-defiled, indeterminate dharma.
The commentary states:
"Reconciliation" refers to the non-obscured, neutral mental dissociated formations (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*); the same applies to the restoration of a schism in the Saṅgha.
How, then, does this constitute an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*)?
Why is it that those capable of causing schism do not possess this [quality]?
The verse says:
"The assembly possesses this."
The commentary says:
Why is this? Because this refutation belongs to that which is to be refuted; it does not belong to the refuter.
If that is so, with what factors is the schismatic associated?
The verse says:
Through this offense of lying, the schismatic is associated [with it].
The commentary states:
The schismatic is associated with the offense of causing a schism in the Saṃgha; this offense is defined as false speech.

Furthermore, this false speech arises simultaneously with the schism in the Saṃgha, consisting of both informative (vijñapti) and non-informative (avijñapti) action, and the schismatic is associated with this offense.
The verse says:
"In the Vīci hell, one matures for an eon.
The commentary says:

One [instance] of the karma of immediate retribution ripens in the Avīci Great Hell during one intermediate kalpa; as for the remaining karmas of immediate retribution, their ripening in the Avīci Great Hell is not certain.
If a person commits many deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*), all these many deeds ripen immediately. What does this person obtain by virtue of these deeds?
The verse says:
"As the suffering increases, so too does the experience [of it] increase."
The commentary states:

Because this person has ripened many acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), they obtain in the Avīci hell a physical basis that is greatest, thickest, and most supple; thus, the matters of suffering there are of the most numerous kinds and most difficult to endure.
Due to these two causes, the feelings experienced increase by two, three, four, or five parts.
Who is capable of breaking the harmony of the Saṃgha?
The verse says:
The bhikṣu sees good conduct and breaks [it].
The commentary says:
A householder cannot break a bhikṣu; neither can nuns and others break him.
This bhikṣu practices what is seen much, not what is driven by craving; he abides in right practice, and because his practice cannot be censured, wrong practice cannot destroy it. Why is this?
Because this person's teaching is not to be trusted or accepted.
Where is it refuted?
The verse says:
Elsewhere, the commentary states:
If the Blessed One were in this place, then because it is different from this place, [the assembly] could be split.
One must not confront the World-Honored One directly, for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are not to be lightly provoked, and their teachings are most worthy of trust and acceptance.
Whom, then, would one refute?
The verse says:
"Ordinary persons.
The commentary says:

It is only the concord of the assembly of ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) that can be disrupted, not that of the noble ones (*ārya*), because the latter have personally realized and seen the Dharma of the true principle.
This is the view of other masters regarding those ordinary persons who have not yet attained *kṣānti*.
By how many members of the Saṃgha is a schism brought about?
The verse says:
When they tolerate a different teacher and a different path, it is already split.
The commentary states:

At that time, when those monks tolerate a teacher other than the Tathāgata and accept a path other than the true path taught by the Tathāgata, by this measure it should be said that the Saṃgha has already been split.
Once destroyed, for how long does it remain?
For this night.
The verse says:
"Not remaining overnight.
The commentary explains:
Once the Saṃgha has been split, it does not remain divided past this night; it will certainly be reconciled again. This is what is meant by the "reconciliation of a split Saṃgha" as described.
The verse says:
This is called the breaking of the wheel.
The commentary says:

Why is this? At that time, the Wheel of Dharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has already been shattered; because it can obstruct the arising of the Noble Path, it is called a "shattered wheel" (*cakrabheda*), or alternatively, a "schism of the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*).
At which location is this wheel broken so that it can be formed?
The verse says:
Jambudvīpa.
The commentary states:
It is broken only on Jambudvīpa; it does not occur elsewhere.
By how many people is it broken?
The verse says:
"Ninefold, etc.
The commentary says:
It is determined that nine [monks] constitute a schism; beyond this number, there is no fixed limit.
Eight bhikṣus are called the Saṃgha, while the ninth is the one capable of causing the schism. Why is this so?
The Saṃgha must necessarily abide within two groups and two factions; if it does so, schism occurs.
There is a distinct form of Saṃgha-bheda (schism), which is established through the breaking of the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual).
If one performs a *karman* separately in a different residence without acting in concert, this is called a breach of the *karman*.
Regarding this schism, the verse says:
"The karma for schism exists in the three continents.
The commentary explains:
In the three continents and so forth, wherever there is the true teaching of a Tathāgata,
by how many bhikṣus is it established?
The verse says:
"This is due to eight and the rest.
The commentary states:
Since only the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) is performed here and the fourteen categories of schismatic laws are not established, the number eight is fixed as the standard.
This schism of the wheel cannot be accomplished during six periods.
The verse says:

At the beginning or the end, before the Ābhāsvara heaven, before the pair [of disciples], at the time the Teacher passes away, and when the separate residence has not yet been established—the schism of the wheel cannot be accomplished.
The commentary states:

"The former refers to when not long after the Wheel of Dharma was turned; the latter refers to when the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa. During these two periods, the great assembly was respectful and practiced with a single flavor, and therefore there was no schism."
In the interim, prior to the Ābhāsvara heaven, the Saṃgha was not split.

Within the True Dharma, as long as the Ābhāsvara of precepts and the Ābhāsvara of view had not yet arisen, it was also not split even before the pair [of disciples] appeared; this continued until the two disciples had not yet produced the pair of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. This is because once split, it does not endure for a night, and because the two [sides] may reunite.
If the Great Teacher has already entered parinirvāṇa, there is no schism because there is no one to stand in opposition.
Furthermore, as long as the formal separation [of the community] has not yet been enacted, there is likewise no schism. Why is this?
If two assistants are established separately while sharing the same residence, it is called a schism of the Saṃgha.
At these six times, the breaking of the Wheel is not accomplished.
Not all Buddhas have this breaking of the Wheel, for this matter is established based on karma.
Why is it that acts such as killing one’s mother constitute an immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) in certain cases, but not in others?
The verse says:
Because of the field of gratitude and the field of merit, through abandonment, separation, and eradication.
The commentary states:
Regarding the killing of one's father and mother, it is due to abandoning those who have been kind.
In what way are they kind?
Because this is the very source from which one's own body arises,
how could one abandon it?
It means to relinquish that life-faculty (jīvitendriya).
The field of merit refers to the Arhat.

Because the body of an Arhat is the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the afflictions of the three realms and serves as the vessel for the aggregates such as ethical discipline (*śīla*), it is called the field of merit.
Because one deprives this body [of life], one commits an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karma*).
If the parents undergo a change of gender, within that same physical basis (*āśraya*), the verse says:
"There is also an obstruction regarding a different gender."
The commentary states: Therefore, it is said in the Sūtra:

"Is there such a case where one does not deprive a man of his life-force, yet he is neither his father nor an Arhat, and is nonetheless touched by the karma of an immediate transgression (ānantarya-karma)?"
Is there a case where, if a mother’s gender changes,
one causes a woman to lose her life-force, yet she is neither one's mother nor an Arhat, and one is nonetheless touched by the offense of immediate retribution?
There is such a case: if the father undergoes a change of gender (becomes female).

Or, suppose an embryo (*kalala*) of one woman is miscarried, and another woman takes it up and places it within her own birth canal; with which of these women would this person consider herself to be the mother?
If one kills which woman does it constitute an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) karma?
The verse says:
"She who gave birth from blood is the mother."
The commentary states:
If this human body is formed from the blood of this woman, she is one's biological mother.
Regarding the second woman, one should seek her permission and consult her in all matters.
Why is this? Because this woman can suckle this child and can nurture and instruct him regarding right and wrong.
If a person employs the means to kill his mother but mistakenly kills another person instead, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).
If one does not employ the means of killing against one's own mother, but kills her by mistake, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).

However, if the father intends to kill his son and employs the means for that purpose, and the mother dies because she was hidden beneath the bed while the father fled elsewhere, this person incurs the immediate retribution.

If a person performs two harmful acts—killing his mother and killing another person—two non-informative (avijñapti) karmas arise simultaneously; however, the informative (vijñapti) karma is only that of the immediate retribution (ānantarya), because the power of this immediate retribution karma is superior.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
Because it is composed of atoms, informative action (vijñapti) is also of two kinds.

If one does not perceive someone as an Arhat, yet kills an Arhat, there is an immediate retribution (ānantarya) karma; this is because the intention is fixed upon that basis, thinking, "I must kill him now."
If a person kills his father, and that father is an Arhat, this person incurs only one immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), because the basis [of the act] is one.
If that is so, how is one to interpret this *Avadāna-sūtra*?
The Sūtra says:
"Go and tell Śikhaṇḍin that you have now committed two acts of immediate retribution (ānantarya-karma):
because you caused your father to lose his life-force, and you also caused an Arhat to lose his life-force."
This statement is made because it is shown that this immediate karma (ānantarya-karma) is established by two causes and conditions;
furthermore, this statement is made to reprove that person by means of these two gateways.
Is there an immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) for definitively giving rise to an evil mind toward a Tathāgata and drawing blood?
If it is by way of the intent to kill, then there is an immediate retribution.
The verse says:
There is no intention to strike the Buddha.
The commentary says:
If a person merely has the intention to strike [the Buddha] and thereby causes him to bleed, there is no immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*).
If a person commits an act of killing against one who is not an Arhat, but that person becomes an Arhat after being harmed, does the perpetrator incur the karma of immediate retribution?
The verse says:
After [the attainment of] Arhatship, there is no longer [the possibility of] harming.
The commentary says:
In this person, there is no immediate retributive karma (ānantarya-karma). Why?
Because the preparatory effort for this killing was not directed toward an Arhat.

If a person has already performed the preliminary effort for an *ānantarya* [karma], but has not yet turned back from that effort, can they first attain freedom from desire (*vairāgya*) or the fruits of the noble path (*āryaphala*)?
The verse says:
For one who proceeds toward an *ānantarya* [karma], there is no freedom from desire or fruit.
The commentary states:
If a person commits an act of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), the preparatory effort (*prayoga*) must necessarily be accomplished.

During the period of this preparatory effort, there can be no detachment from desire (*vairāgya*) nor the attainment of the fruits of holiness (*ārya-phala*); were it otherwise, the effort would not be definitive.

If a person, while performing the preliminary stages (*prayoga*) for other courses of action (*karmapatha*), attains freedom from desire (*vairāgya*) or the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*), those subsequent courses of action will not arise. Why is this?
Because this present basis is entirely contrary to that karma,
among the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*), which one is the most grave?
The verse says:
The false speech that divides the Sangha is permitted to be the gravest of all offenses.
The commentary explains:

When one who understands the Dharma speaks falsely regarding what is not the Dharma, this constitutes the division of the harmonious Sangha; because it manifests a perversion of the truth, it is the gravest offense among all forms of misconduct.
Why is this? Because it can harm the Dharma-body of all Tathāgatas, and because it can obstruct the path to the heavenly realms and the path to Nirvāṇa in the world. Why is this?

When the Great Assembly is in the midst of schism, all worldly entry into the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), the realization of the fruits [of the path], the abandonment of desire, and the exhaustion of the outflows are entirely obstructed; all practices such as meditative cultivation, recitation, and correct reflection cannot arise. All the world, including humans and devas, becomes agitated, giving rise to grief, affliction, and distracted minds; this state persists until the Sangha has once again reached reconciliation.
Furthermore, because the retribution for this karma ripens fully for one entire kalpa in the Avīci Hell, it is called "greatly heavy.
One should understand that the remaining actions of immediate retribution follow in this same order.
The fifth, third, and first [offenses] are the most serious, while among all of them, the second is the lightest.
If that is so, why did the Blessed One say:
"Among the three types of punishment, mental punishment is the most serious"?
Furthermore, it is said:
among all sins, false view is the most grave.
Among the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), the schism of the Sangha is definitively judged to be the heaviest offense.
What does this mean?
If one considers the retribution for a single uninterrupted eon, no falsehood other than that which causes a schism in the Saṃgha is superior.
If one definitively judges the three types of karma, mental punishment is the most severe, because the punishments for the other two follow from it.
If one were to definitively judge among the various views, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) is the most grave, because it involves the total denial of its object.

Furthermore, this statement should be understood as being made in sequence based on its great retribution, its killing of many sentient beings, and its severing of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Among virtuous actions, which one yields the greatest karmic fruit?
The verse says:
The volition directed toward the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) yields the greatest fruit among all virtues.
The commentary states:
Among wholesome karmas, the volitional intention (*cetanā*) of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) yields the greatest retribution. Why is this?
Because its retribution is the subtle and tranquil state lasting for eighty thousand great eons,
this statement is made in reference to the fruit of retribution (*vipākaphala*).

If, however, one speaks in terms of the fruit of separation (*visamyogaphala*), the volition associated with the Vajra-samādhi is the greatest fruit among all, because the total extinction of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) constitutes its fruit.
Therefore, it is said that in this world, one attains immediate rebirth in hell both by means of the immediate karmas (*ānantarya-karma*) and also by means of those similar to the immediate karmas;
it is by both types.
Other masters say:
"Only through an immediate transgression (*ānantarya-karman*) does one necessarily attain birth in the intermediate state (*antara-bhava*); through its counterparts (*sabhāga*), it is not certain.
What are the counterparts of the immediate transgressions?
The verse says:

To defile one’s mother who is an Arhat, to kill a Bodhisattva established in the stage of certainty, to kill a noble person on the path of training (śaikṣa), to deprive the Saṃgha of its cause for harmony, and to destroy a stūpa of the Buddha—these are the five actions similar to the immediate (ānantarya) offenses.
The commentary states:
One should understand that these five karmas correspond in sequence to the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*).
This is the case when a person defiles his own mother who is an Arhat by engaging in unchaste conduct.

If one kills a bodhisattva who has reached the stage of certainty (*niyata-bhūmi*), or kills a noble one (*ārya*) still in training (*śaikṣa*), or destroys the causes and conditions for the harmony of the great assembly, or, conceiving the thought that it is a *caitya* of the Buddha, destroys a *stūpa* of the Buddha—such karma is called "similar to the immediate" (*ānantarya-sabhāga*).
There are other karmas that, if they possess a retribution, create an obstruction most urgently during three periods.
What are these three periods?
The verse says:
"Patience (kṣānti), the stage of Non-returner (anāgāmin), and Arhatship: in these stages, karma arises as an obstacle.
The commentary explains:

If a person progresses from the Summit (mūrdhan) thought-moment toward Patience, at that time all karma that would lead to the retribution of the evil realms arises as an obstacle, because they must transcend the ground of such retribution.
For example, when a person must depart from their own country, all their creditors rise up; so too it is with karmic actions.
If a person is destined to attain the fruit of Anāgāmin, all mixed karmas of the desire realm arise as obstacles, with the sole exception of karma to be experienced in the present life.

If a person is destined to attain the fruit of arhatship, all karma pertaining to the form realm and the formless realm will arise to act as an obstruction; this has already been explained previously.
Regarding the case of one who kills a bodhisattva of fixed destiny, the verse asks:
From what stage does a bodhisattva [become fixed]?
The commentary asks:
At what stage should one say that this is a bodhisattva?
The verse says:
Regarding the phrase "from the time of performing the karma of the marks," the commentary explains:
it refers to the time of practicing the karma that brings about the retribution of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor marks.
Why is this? Because at this time, this person has already entered the stage of the bodhisattva’s correct determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*). How is it so?
From this time forth, for this person, it shall always be so.
The verse says:
Born in a good realm, of noble family and faculties, male, remembering past lives, and non-retrogressive.
The commentary states:
As for "the good paths," they are called the good paths because they are most excellent and praiseworthy, as one is born therein among the realms of humans and gods.
Furthermore, within those good paths, one is born into the kṣatriya caste, the brāhmaṇa caste, or the great householder caste.
Among them, one is born into a mahābrāhmaṇa family; such a person has already been born into a noble family.
Among those born into noble families, some possess their faculties while others do not.
These faculties are of two kinds: namely, the physical faculties (rūpendriya) and the mental faculties (dharmendriya).
If one does not possess these, one goes from light toward darkness;
if one possesses these, one goes from light toward light.
One will constantly obtain the body of a man, never the body of a woman, let alone that of a eunuch or the like.
This person recollects all matters of their former existences throughout all lifetimes, due to the perfection of both the wisdom arising from hearing and the wisdom arising from reflection.

Regarding the activities that bring peace, happiness, and benefit to sentient beings, they never grow weary or exhausted by any category of suffering or by any adverse and evil actions committed by others.
This is what is said in the world: one should know that it is not merely by purchasing a *dāsa* that one becomes such;
rather, it is a Bodhisattva.

Why is this? Because these Great Beings have already reached the supreme stage of all excellent qualities (*guṇa*), and for no other reason than their connection with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), they establish themselves among all sentient beings as if they were their servants.
Because they are free from pride, they are able to endure all that is most difficult to seek for the sake of all sentient beings, and they constantly desire to shoulder all tasks involving suffering.
Because it obstructs others, one cannot accomplish one's own purpose; therefore, it is said that what is being discussed is not obtained by direct purchase.
Regarding the karma that brings about the fruit of the marks, the verse says:
"In Jambudvīpa, a male human, facing the Buddha with the Buddha’s intention, through the category of wisdom born of reflection for a hundred kalpas, can induce this in others."
The commentary states:
Only in Jambudvīpa do Bodhisattvas cultivate the karma that draws forth the marks of a Great Man, not in other continents. Why is this?
Because the people of Jambudvīpa possess the sharpest faculties of wisdom,
it is practiced only by men and not by women, as they have transcended the female state.
At what time is this cultivated?
When the Great Master is present before one, because the volition has the Buddha as its intentional object,
this karma consists of the category of wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), not of wisdom born of hearing (*śrutamayī*) or cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī*).
This occurs during the remaining period, namely the duration of one hundred great eons, and not during any other longer period.

All Buddhas are likewise; however, because the World-Honored One Śākyamuni’s right effort was most intense, he was able to transcend nine *kalpas* and project the remaining marks of merit over ninety-one *kalpas*.
Therefore, the Tathāgata said:
"O Lord of the Earth!

Since my birth from this life back through ninety-one kalpas, I do not recall nor do I see a time when, in a single lifetime, I caused even a slight interruption or harm by giving a single cooked meal; how much less so for great deeds? From that time on, I have possessed the natural recollection of past lives."
The ancient masters have said that a bodhisattva who has already emerged from the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa eliminates four kinds of faults and constantly attains two kinds of supreme virtues.
Regarding the various marks of a bodhisattva, the verse says: "Each arises from one hundred merits.
The commentary asks: What is the measure of this merit?

Other masters say that its measure is the karma capable of producing wealth and happiness among all sentient beings throughout the ten directions, excluding those bodhisattvas who are near to [the state of] practice.
Just as the predominant condition of the karma of sentient beings is able to bring about the arising of a trichiliocosm of such magnitude, so it is said by the Vaibhāṣika masters.
Other masters say:
"Only the Buddhas are able to know the quantity of this karma.
Furthermore, when the present Blessed One was formerly in the stage of a bodhisattva, how many Buddhas did he serve?

During the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-five thousand Buddhas; during the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-six thousand Buddhas; and during the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa, he served seventy-seven thousand Buddhas.
During the final period of each asaṃkhyeya kalpa, which Buddha, World-Honored One, appeared?
This should be understood according to the sequence of the reverse order.
The verse says:
He appeared after three asaṃkhyeyas [of kalpas], during the times of Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, and Ratnaprabha.
The commentary states:
Under the World-Honored One Ratnaśikhin, the first asaṃkhyeya was completed.
Under the World-Honored One Dīpaṃkara, the second asaṃkhyeya was brought to completion.
Under the World-Honored One Vipaśyin, the third asaṃkhyeya was brought to completion.
Regarding all Buddhas, the verse says:
"First Śākyamuni.
The commentary says:
There was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Śākyamuni, who had already appeared in the world in the past.
Under this World-Honored One, the present Buddha sought to cultivate the bodhisattva practices and first made the vow for enlightenment:
"May I, when I attain Buddhahood, possess all these same characteristics."
In the past, when the World-Honored One appeared during the final age, and his True Dharma remained for only one thousand years,
in what stage was the Bodhisattva situated and which *pāramitā* did he fulfill?
The verse says:
"Giving universally to all, through great compassion, the giving is fulfilled.
The commentary says:

At that time, one is impartial toward all sentient beings regarding all things worthy of giving: whether it be material wealth, even up to one's eyes and marrow; or the gift of Dharma, which is free from the secrecy of a teacher; or the gift of fearlessness, providing relief for both the present and future lives.
Only through great compassion, which seeks nothing for itself, is the perfection of giving fulfilled by this measure.
The verse says:
Though his body is cut into pieces, he feels no resentment; thus, his desire is perfected through morality and patience.
The commentary states:

If at that time a bodhisattva has not yet attained the state of being free from desire, yet when their body is cut and severed limb by limb, they harbor neither love nor hatred toward themselves or others, and do not give rise to even the slightest sense of resentment; at that moment, both the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) and the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) are simultaneously fulfilled.
The verse says:
"Praise of Tiṣya’s diligence.
The commentary says:
In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Tiṣya who had entered the fire-element samādhi within a rocky cave on a jewel mountain.
