When the present Buddha, the World-Honored One, was formerly in the stage of a Bodhisattva, he encountered this Tathāgata while traveling with a specific purpose; at that time, one foot was planted upon the ground while the other had not yet been lowered.
For seven days and seven nights, he sat only after reciting a single verse of praise.
The verse says:
"Neither on earth, nor in heaven, nor in the Brahma realm, nor in any place of stillness, Has such a thing ever existed throughout the three times and the ten directions."
"Searching throughout these lands, mountains, and forests, who is there equal to the Honored One in the three virtues?
At that time, the perfection of diligence was already fulfilled, and nine great eons had been transcended to their ultimate end.
The verse says:
"Concentration and wisdom awaken without interval.
The commentary says:
Having first perfected the dhyānapāramitā and prajñāpāramitā for the sake of unsurpassed bodhi, [he abides] in the state of vajrasamādhi.
Why are these six called *pāramitās*?
Because they reach the limit of one's own perfected virtue (*ātma-puṇya-pariniṣpatti*).
Furthermore, "parama" refers to the supreme grade of the Bodhisattva; the correct practice of that is called *pāramī*. (Note: *pāramī* is the Pali form corresponding to the Sanskrit *pāramitā*.)
This collection of right practice is called *pāramitā* because its members are mutually inseparable.
As stated in the Sūtra:

"There are three types of meritorious action: first, the class of meritorious action consisting of giving; second, the class of meritorious action consisting of ethical discipline; and third, the class of meritorious action consisting of cultivation."
How are these three called "categories of meritorious action"?
The verse says:
Meritorious action, categories of meritorious action—these three are like the paths of action.
The commentary states:
These three, beginning with giving, are merit, action, and category, respectively, as appropriate.
Just as with the paths of action (*karmapatha*), they are both action and path.
However, because the paths of action are not themselves karma, they are called "paths of karma.
These three [roots] are likewise so designated.
Within the category of meritorious actions consisting of giving, bodily and vocal karma are of three kinds, as they are capable of initiating [the action].
Volition (*cetanā*) is twofold: it is both merit (*puṇya*) and action (*karman*). Other dharmas that arise simultaneously with it are merely merit and not action; they do not belong to this category.
Within the nature of morality (*śīla*), because there are only bodily and vocal actions, there are only three types.

Within the nature of cultivation, the cultivation of the immeasurable of loving-kindness (*maitrī-apramāṇa*) is both merit and a category of meritorious action (*puṇya-kriyā-vastu*). This is because the volition associated with it arises through the gateway of loving-kindness and co-arises together with this contemplation.
The mind and morality are both merit and karma;
the remaining associated factors, such as faith and so forth, are merit alone and nothing else.
Furthermore, that which constructs merit is called "meritorious karma," namely the preliminary stage of merit; these three are the types of bases for the preliminary stage.
In order to accomplish these three, one performs meritorious deeds; thus, true meritorious action consists solely of volition (*cetanā*).
Other masters say that these three are types of meritorious action that have volition as their object (*ālambana*).
What is the phenomenon that constitutes the giver?
Some say that the object given is called "giving.
Regarding these three, the verse says:
"By this, it is giving.
The commentary explains:
If, by means of a certain cause, the act of giving is accomplished, that cause is designated as "giving."

Since the act of giving is also accomplished through seeking out objects of desire out of fear, that [fear] is not permitted here as a cause of giving; this statement is made in order to distinguish it from such cases.
The verse says:
"With the intention to offer and benefit.
The commentary says:
One gives to others out of a desire to perform an act of worship or for the sake of their benefit; therefore, these two are the causes of giving.
If that were so, then giving would be merely a cause and not an action (*karman*).
Nevertheless, since it is precisely by means of this factor that giving arises and thus becomes perfected, this is indeed what constitutes giving.
What are the characteristics of this factor?
The verse says:
"Body, speech, and dependent origination.
The commentary asks:
What dharma is dependent origination?
This collection of dharmas is able to give rise to bodily and vocal karma; this is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"When a wise person, through a virtuous mind, Gives wealth to another,"
"This wholesome aggregate of a single moment is called the act of giving.
The verse says:
"This has great wealth as its fruit."
The commentary states:
This category of meritorious action consisting of giving can obtain the retribution of great wealth and happiness.
Furthermore, for what purpose is this giving performed?
The verse says:
One gives for the benefit of both self and others, not for the sake of either one alone.
The commentary says:

In this regard, when a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire, or an ordinary person who has not yet abandoned desire, gives material goods to a caitya, this gift benefits only oneself and does not benefit others, because others derive no benefit from it.

If an noble one who has already abandoned desire gives material things to other sentient beings—excluding karma that ripens in the present life—this giving is solely for the benefit of others, because others obtain benefit thereby;
it is not for their own sake, because they have forever transcended the level where the retribution of such karma would ripen.

If a noble one who has not yet abandoned desire, or an ordinary person who has not yet abandoned desire, gives material things to other sentient beings, this giving serves a twofold benefit, namely for oneself and for others.

If a noble one who has already abandoned desire gives material goods to a caitya—excluding karma that ripens in the present life—this karma does not serve the dual benefit of self and others; rather, this giving is performed solely out of reverence and gratitude.
If explained according to the general meaning, this giving has great wealth and happiness as its fruit.
The verse says:
"The distinction of excellence arises from the ability to give; for among the types of giving, it is superior."
The commentary states:
Regarding those who are superior in the act of giving, the verse says:
"By virtue of faith and so forth, persons are superior."
The commentary states:
Because they are endowed with virtues such as faith, ethical discipline, and learning, they are superior.
The gift bestowed by such a person is the most excellent in terms of its yielding of results, due to the superior qualities of the donor.
If a donor possesses such virtues, the verse says:
"One gives with reverence and so forth.
The commentary explains:
If one practices giving with a mind of reverence, gives with one's own hands, gives at the proper time, and gives without causing harm or distress, for this reason the verse says:
"One obtains great honor and great happiness, [resources] that are timely and difficult to seize."
The commentary states:
If a donor is able to practice the fourfold virtuous giving, they will successively obtain four kinds of desirable and superior fruits;
namely, they will receive honor and respect from others, and they will give rise to a mental disposition of enjoyment toward great, superior, and desirable objects.
When it is time to enjoy them, one obtains wealth and resources, and does not miss the proper time for enjoyment;
furthermore, the wealth and resources obtained cannot be seized or plundered by enemies, relatives, water, fire, or other such forces.
Having explained the meaning of the donor’s superior qualities,
because the donor possesses superior qualities, the gift possesses a superior category.
Furthermore, the object given possesses superior qualities.
How so? The verse says:
"Form and other qualities are superior to material objects."
The commentary states:

If the object to be given possesses any one of the qualities such as color, fragrance, taste, or tangibility, that object is superior by virtue of those qualities; if one gives such a virtuous object, [it is a gift of excellence].
What constitutes this giving?
It should be understood according to the following sequence.
The verse says:
"Exquisite form, a good reputation, lovely features, and softness; at all times, the body experiences pleasant touch.
The commentary states:
If one gives material objects possessing virtuous qualities, one obtains the retribution of an upright and lovely physical form.
If one gives things possessing the quality of fragrance, one will obtain a great and excellent reputation, just as the fragrance of incense pervades and covers all four directions.
If one gives things possessing the quality of flavor, one will obtain a reward like that of delicious food, becoming beloved by all the world.

If one gives objects possessing the quality of touch, one obtains a body that is soft and smooth, and furthermore, one obtains a body whose touch is pleasant and comfortable at all times, like the physical field of a precious woman.
What virtues constitute excellence?
The verse says:
Through the path, suffering, kindness, and virtue, the field of giving possesses superior merit.
The commentary states:
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one gives a gift to an animal, one shall receive a hundredfold karmic retribution."
If one gives material gifts to sentient beings who have broken the precepts within the human realm, one should receive a thousandfold fruit of retribution.
This is because the field [of merit] possesses superior qualities due to the distinctions of suffering, as stated in the section on "Categories of Meritorious Action with Accumulation":
first, giving to the sick; second, giving to those who nurse and treat the sick; and third, giving during the cold season—such acts of giving are thus described.
Furthermore, it is said:
If a faithful son or daughter of good family is endowed with these seven types of meritorious actions that involve acquisition, the merit they obtain is beyond measure.
A field possesses superior merit by virtue of the distinction of gratitude, as in the case of one's parents and other benefactors, as explained in the *Ṛkṣamṛga-jātaka*.
A field possesses superior merit by virtue of the distinction of qualities, as the Sūtra states:
"If one gives material gifts to a person of moral discipline, one shall receive a hundred-thousandfold karmic fruit."
Regarding all such forms of giving, the verse says:
"Giving liberation to those who are not liberated is supreme."
The commentary states:
If a person free from desire gives material goods to another person free from desire, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, declares this gift to be the most supreme among all gifts of material wealth.
The verse says:
"Bodhisattva.
The commentary says:

The giving practiced by a bodhisattva is the cause for the peace, happiness, and benefit of all sentient beings; therefore, if this giving is performed by one who is not free from desire, or given to one who is not free from desire, it is the most excellent among all forms of giving, with the exception of the giving of a bodhisattva.
Regarding these eight kinds of giving taught by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the verse says:
"And the eighth.
The commentary explains:
Most excellent.
What are the eight?
First, giving that has already been reached;
Second, giving out of fear;
third, giving what has already been given to me;
fourth, giving what will be given to me.
Fifth, giving as one has done in the past, namely to one's father, deceased ancestors, and so forth;
sixth, giving for the sake of attaining the heavenly realms;
seventh, giving for the sake of obtaining a good reputation.
The eighth is the gift for the adornment of the mind, the gift as a provision for the mind, the gift that accords with principle, and the gift for attaining the supreme benefit for oneself.
Regarding the "gift to those who have arrived," the former masters explain it as the practice of giving toward those who have arrived and those who are intimate.

Regarding giving out of fear: this person perceives that wealth and possessions are currently tending toward destruction; they give because it is better for them to destroy [the wealth] through giving than to let it perish on its own, acting out of such a motivation.
The remainder is easy to understand and thus is not analyzed in detail.
If one gives material gifts to a person who is a candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattipratipannaka), the retribution of this gift is immeasurable.
If one gives material gifts to one who has attained stream-entry (srotāpanna), it is a hundred times more immeasurable.
This has been explained at length; it should be understood as it appears in the sūtra.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Preaching the Dharma to one's parents when they are ill causes a person to be reborn later as a bodhisattva; even though the gift was given among ordinary people, its karmic fruit is immeasurable."
The commentary states:
If these five types of persons are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), giving to them yields fruit that is incalculable and immeasurable.
Among them, as for the Bodhisattva in his final birth who is a teacher of the Dharma—in which of the four kinds of superior fields (*viśiṣṭakṣetra*) is he established?
They are included within the field of gratitude. Why is this?

Such persons are spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); they can bestow the eye of wisdom upon those blinded by the ignorance of the world, they can reveal what is equal and what is unequal, and they can give rise to the untainted *dharmakāya*.
To speak briefly, such a person is able to perform the deeds that a Buddha should perform.
If one wishes to know the characteristics of the lightness and heaviness of various karmas, it should be known that, in brief, there are six kinds of causes.

The verse says: "The subsequent part consists of the field and the basis; the preceding part consists of the intention and the vow. Because these are of inferior or superior grades, karma is likewise inferior or superior. The commentary explains: [The subsequent part refers to the field and the basis; the preceding part refers to the intention and the vow. Because these factors are of inferior or superior grades, karma is accordingly classified as inferior or superior.
The "subsequent part" refers to when, after having performed this action, one continues to perform it repeatedly.
The "field" refers to the locus where harm or benefit is inflicted.
The "basis" refers to the path of action (*karmapatha*).

The preliminary stage (*pūrvāṅga*) consists of the volitions of body, speech, and mind directed toward attaining the path of action (*karmapatha*), by which that path of action is brought to completion.
Volition (*cetanā*) is the thought: "In such and such a way I shall do it; in such and such a way I am doing it."
"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to seeking a future application.
There are those who, by virtue of belonging to a subsequent portion [of time], perform an action of a heavy grade, because the retribution is fixed and established.

Furthermore, there are those for whom an action becomes of a heavy grade by virtue of belonging to a field (*kṣetra*); regarding the field, it is by virtue of belonging to the basis (*āśraya*) that this action becomes of a heavy grade, not through any other cause.
The basis refers to the path of action, such as parents or other sentient beings.
Because killing is grave by virtue of its basis, it is not so because of stealing and the like; the same should be understood for the remaining cases.
If a person performs an action and all six of these causes are of the superior grade, one should know that this action is of the most heavy grade.
If a person performs an action and all six of these causes are of the inferior grade, one should know that this action is of the lightest grade.
The Sūtra states:
"Karma is of two kinds: that which is performed and that which is accumulated.
What is karma that is accumulated?
Due to five causes.
The verse says:
Through intentional performance, completion, absence of regret or antidote, by way of associates and retribution, it is said that karma increases.
The commentary says:
What does it mean to act intentionally?
This karma is performed with intention; it is not preceded by a lack of intention, nor is it performed impulsively. Rather, one acts only after thorough investigation, examination, and discernment.
How is it by way of completion?
Some fall into the evil destinies through a single misdeed, while others do so through as many as three.
Some fall into the evil destinies through a single course of action (*karmapatha*), while others do so through as many as ten.

In this context, if a person is destined to fall into an evil realm due to a certain measure of karma, and that measure is not yet complete, then this karma is merely "done" (kṛta) but not yet "accumulated" (upacita); only when it is complete does it become "accumulated."
What is meant by "by way of the antidote to remorse"?
If a person performs an action without a mind of remorse, they do not undergo the experience of wholesome conduct as an antidote.
What is meant by "by way of its accompaniment"?
Deluded, they commit evil, taking evil as their companions and kindred.
How is it by way of retribution?
This karma, once determined, is able to yield its retribution.
One should also consider wholesome karma in this same way.
If one performs an action that differs from these characteristics, it is merely a performance and not a long-term cultivation.
As previously stated, when a person who has not yet abandoned desire gives material goods to a caitya, this gift serves only their own benefit and does not benefit others.
In this regard, if there were no one to enjoy the gift, how could this action constitute merit?
There are two types of meritorious action:
first, that which has relinquishment as its nature, which arises through the act of giving away an object; [and second, that which has enjoyment as its nature].
The second is merit by way of enjoyment; that is, when this meritorious action arises through the enjoyment of the object given.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"Merit by way of relinquishment toward a caitya."
The commentary states:
Among these, there is no category of merit consisting of enjoyment.
If one does not enjoy it, how can there be merit?
What is the reason for this proof?
If there is one who can receive [the gift], there must be merit; if there is no one who can receive it, then there is no merit, because in either case there is no benefit.
This reason does not constitute a valid proof.

Why is this? If merit were to arise solely from benefiting others, then the cultivation of the immeasurables such as loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and right view would not constitute merit; therefore, one must accept this principle: that in the case of a *caitya*, merit consists exclusively of the act of relinquishment (*tyāga*).
The verse says:
"Just as loving-kindness, though it is not received.
The commentary says:

For example, within meditations such as loving-kindness and compassion, although there is no recipient nor any actual act of benefiting others, immeasurable merit arises originating from one's own mind.
In the same way, when a virtuous person has passed away, the merit arising from one's own mind produced by the thought of honoring and serving them likewise comes into being.
If that were so, then acts such as giving and showing respect would result in being fruitless.
This is not the case. Why?
Karmic action arises from the object of veneration because the mind is paramount.

For example, suppose a person wishes to kill an enemy, but the enemy has already died; even though this person still perceives the enemy and gives rise to a volitional intention (*saṃcetanā*), they produce much non-merit through bodily and verbal actions—not merely by the initial intent to kill.

Now that such a Great Teacher has passed away, if a person performs acts such as respectful offerings out of a mind of veneration, they generate the greatest merit—not merely by virtue of the mind of veneration alone.
If one practices giving toward a virtuous field and performs seeds of action such as showing reverence, one obtains desirable retribution.
If one acts toward a non-virtuous field, one should obtain undesirable retribution.
The verse says:
Even in a field of evil there may be good fruit, because the seeds of the fruit were not inverted.
The commentary says:
Seeing fruit in a bad field does not contradict the non-erroneous nature of the seed;
that is to say, from a grape seed, only a grape fruit is produced, and its taste is sweet and delicious.
From a *vibhītaka* seed, only a *vibhītaka* tree grows, and its fruit is bitter.
In the same way, from the seed of a gift born of the intention to bring happiness and benefit to others, even when sown in a bad field, only a desirable retribution arises, not an undesirable one.
The same applies to unwholesome actions: due to defects in the field, this seed may yield little fruit or no fruit at all.
Having explained the category of meritorious action consisting of giving, along with its establishment and refutation, the category consisting of morality shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
"Wrong discipline refers to unwholesome form; right discipline is the departure from these two.
The commentary says:
Regarding unwholesome form: bodily and vocal actions are termed "unwholesome discipline" (*duḥśīla*); the abstention from these actions is termed "wholesome discipline" (*suśīla*).
This discipline of abstention is of two kinds: there is the informative (*vijñapti*) bodily and vocal action that is capable of avoiding evil, which is termed "informative discipline."
However, it is the nature of abstention itself that is designated as "unmanifest precept" (avijñapti-śīla).
It is not merely the abstention from unwholesome precepts that is called "wholesome precept. Why is this?
The verse says:
"And this is prohibited by the Buddha.
The commentary says:

Although this karma is not inherently an evil precept (*dauḥśīlya*), the Buddha, the World-Honored One, established prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*) for the sake of protecting people and the True Dharma.
Just as with eating at improper times and so forth, to remain far removed from what is prohibited is called virtuous conduct (*kuśala-śīla*).
This morality is of two kinds, namely informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*).
If a person receives this morality, they incur the offense of broken morality through the act of transgression.
Thus, by way of a summary, the nature of morality has been explained.
The verse says:
These are the four virtues of purity.
The commentary says:
If one possesses four virtues, it is called pure morality; if one lacks these four virtues, it is called defiled morality.
What are the four virtues?
The verse says:
"Not defiled by the cause of wrong discipline; it relies on the counteragent and is characterized by tranquility.
The commentary explains:

"Not defiled by wrong discipline" means that, as previously stated, one does not transgress even a single aspect of the precepts, and thus remains untouched by various afflictions such as greed, as well as by defilements such as gain.
This precept relies upon the antidote to breaking the precepts, namely by relying on the foundations of mindfulness and so forth.
This precept arises based on tranquility; it does not arise based on birth in superior realms within the good paths, because it is dedicated toward the attainment of nirvāṇa.

Other masters state that purity is attained through five causes: first, purity of the fundamental paths of action; second, purity of the preliminary stages; third, not being assailed by improper thoughts and reflections; fourth, being sustained by the four foundations of mindfulness; and fifth, dedication toward *nirvāṇa*.
Other masters say that there are four kinds of ethical discipline (*śīla*): first,
the discipline of fear (*bhaya-śīla*), which is acquired through the fear of lacking the necessary provisions, of mental distress, of severe punishment, and of rebirth in the evil realms.

Second is the precept obtained in view of [worldly gain], which refers to that acquired through greed for the requisites of pleasure within saṃsāra, as well as the respect, offerings, and good reputation of others.
Third is the precept conducive to the factors of enlightenment, which refers to that which can lead to liberation.
A person of right view feels weary of birth and death and seeks the attainment of liberation.
The fourfold untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) can counteract all afflictions; they are stainless and pure.
Having explained the nature of precepts, the category of meritorious action consisting of cultivation shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
"Wholesome karma on the stages of tranquility is cultivation."
The commentary states:
What is the dharma that is "quiescent"?
It is the dharma that arises simultaneously with karma and the intrinsic nature of the meditative state.
Why is this dharma called "cultivation" (bhāvanā)?
The verse says:
Because it perfumes the mind.
The commentary states:
What is meant by "perfuming" (*vāsanā*)?

This wholesome karma of the stage of tranquility is supremely capable of perfuming the mind, because it enables the mind to become of one nature with its virtues, and the same applies to the continuum (*saṃtati*).
It is like perfuming sesame seeds with flowers;
as previously stated, this generosity has great wealth and happiness as its fruit.
What of morality and cultivation?
The verse says:
Through superior morality one attains rebirth in the heavens; through cultivation, one attains the fruit of dissociation.
The commentary says:

Generosity can also induce rebirth in the heavenly realms; through its superior capacity, ethical discipline can induce rebirth in the heavenly realms and can also induce the fruit of dissociation; through its superior capacity, cultivation can induce the fruit of dissociation and can also induce rebirth in the heavenly realms and so forth.
The Sūtra states:
"There are four types of persons who can produce merit conducive to Brahmā.
What dharma is called "merit conducive to Brahmā"?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
It is in order to measure the karma that can induce the retribution of the marks (lakṣaṇa) that the "Brahma-merit" (brahma-puṇya) karma is taught.
Any single karma cultivated by a Bodhisattva that is capable of causing him to obtain one of the marks—this measure of karma is called Brahma-merit.
The former masters have said, as the verse states:
"Four types of action are called 'Brahma-merit,' because they result in rebirth in heaven for an eon.
The commentary explains:
According to the measure of its meritorious karma, it can induce birth in the heavenly realms and the retribution of pleasure for one kalpa; this karma is called "Brahma-merit" (brahmapuṇya).
It is said that there are four kinds of this karma. What are the four?
First, if this location has not yet established a *caitya* for the Tathāgata, one should construct a *stūpa* for the Tathāgata therein.
Second, if this location has not yet established a *saṃghārāma*, one should construct a *saṃghārāma* therein.
Fourth, when the assembly of disciples of the World-Honored Ones of the three periods has already been divided, one is able to further attract and lead them back into harmony;
and fifth, one cultivates the contemplation of the four immeasurable minds toward sentient beings in the ten directions.
These four types of persons are born in the heavenly realms with a lifespan equal to that of the Brahmakāyika devas, where they experience the retribution of joy and bliss.
Since the lifespan of the Brahmakāyika devas is one kalpa, the Buddha taught that the karma of these persons is equivalent to their meritorious karma.
In another section, that master speaks this verse:
"A person possessing faith and right view, if they cultivate the ten superior practices,
generates the karma of Brahma-merit, because of the bliss of rebirth in heaven for an eon."
Having explained the gift of material wealth, the gift of the Dharma shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
"The gift of the Dharma consists of teaching the sūtras and so forth, according to the true principle and without defilement."
The commentary states:

To explain the meaning of the texts according to the true principles of the twelvefold collection of the sublime teachings, such as the sūtras, with a mind free from defilement, is called the gift of Dharma (dharmadāna).

Therefore, such a person creates for themselves the greatest transgression; they diminish their own merit and damage the merit of others, if they preach the Dharma with a perverted mind, or with a defiled mind, or for the sake of seeking gain, honor, and fame.
This person is also like that.
Having already explained the distinctions among the types of meritorious action, there are furthermore three types of karmic categories.
The verse says:
Regarding the determination of merit, liberation, and decisive resolution, there are three types capable of inducing wholesome results.
The commentary states:
Furthermore, there are three distinct categories of karmic types.
First is the capacity for the portion of merit (*puṇyabhāga*), which refers to karma that can induce desirable retributions among gods or humans.
Second is the capacity for the portion of liberation (*mokṣabhāga*), which refers to karma that, once arisen, ensures that this person will certainly take nirvāṇa as their dharma at a later time.

If, upon hearing the faults of saṃsāra, the selflessness of all phenomena, the merits of nirvāṇa, and the correct teachings corresponding to the grace of the Buddhas, there arise such reactions as the bristling of body hair, the shedding of tears, and expressions of sorrowful praise, it should be determined that this person already possesses the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).

For example, just as one knows that there were seeds previously within a fissure in the earth by seeing a sprout grow during the summer months, so too the power of the three levels of the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) exists in four ways during the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth; this shall be explained later.
These are what are spoken of in the world as letters, seals, calculation, composition, and numeration. What are the characteristics of these five?
The verse says:
Actions accomplished through correct reasoning, together with the three types of dependent origination, are, in their respective order: letters, seals, calculation, composition, and numeration.
The commentary states:
"That which is accomplished through correct reasoning" means that which is produced by right means.
"There are three" refers to the actions of body, speech, and mind.
Regarding these characters and seals: if produced through superior skillful means and belonging to bodily action (*kāyakarman*), they constitute a common dependent origination (*sahabhū-pratyaya*).

As for calculations, measurements, and scripts, if produced through superior skillful means and belonging to vocal action (*vākkarman*), they likewise constitute a common dependent origination; these have the four or five aggregates (*skandha*) as their nature.

If this enumeration is produced through superior skillful means, it belongs to mental action (*manas-karman*) and arises together with its objects; it has the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) as its nature, and this enumeration is itself the mental faculty (*citta*).
I shall now explain the various names for all phenomena (*dharma*).
The verse says:
There are those characterized by reproach, concealment, and inferior nature; they are defiled.
The commentary explains:
If a phenomenon is defiled, it is sometimes called "blameworthy," or "obscured," or "inferior.
The verse says:
"The wholesome is non-outflowing and sublime."
The commentary states:
If it is wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*), it is called "excellent" (*praṇīta*).
One should know that this term "middling" (*madhya*) refers to those dharmas that differ from both the inferior and the excellent.
The verse says:
Conditioned wholesome [dharmas] are that which should be practiced.
The commentary says:
If conditioned phenomena that are wholesome are called "concordant with practice" (*yogavihita*),
it follows by implication that all others are "not concordant with practice.
Why is the unconditioned not concordant with practice?
Because it cannot be cultivated and increased, and because it lacks a fruit.
All things are for the sake of attaining a fruit, and all other dharmas have something superior; what dharma alone would be unsurpassed?
The verse says:
"Liberation is unsurpassed.
The commentary says:
Nirvana is the departure from all phenomena of birth and death; therefore, it is called liberation.
This dharma is peerless among all dharmas. Why is this?
Because it is virtuous, real, and eternally abiding, even *nirvāṇa*— which is equal to the Dharma— does not exist,
let alone anything superior to it. *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Thirteen.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Fourteen.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.

Chapter Five: Analysis of Afflictions (Kleśavibhāga). It has been stated previously that the many diverse varieties of the world arise from karma; and since all karmas depend upon afflictions, they reach the point of being produced and grow.

If one is separated from the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), the various karmas that produce the various realms of existence no longer possess functional power; therefore, one should know those [afflictions].
The verse says:
Latent afflictions are the root of existence.
The commentary states:
What constitutes the "basis for existence"?
If an affliction is currently arising, it is capable of performing ten kinds of functions:

1. Firmly establishing the root; 2. Establishing the continuity; 3. Repeatedly cultivating one's own field; 4. Producing the outflow; 5. Being able to project the existence of karma (*karmabhava*); 6. Perfecting one's own provisions; 7. Causing delusion regarding objects; 8. Leading the continuity of consciousness; 9. Causing separation from the categories of pure wholesome dharmas; 10. Accomplishing the meaning of bondage, because one cannot transcend one's own realm.
How many kinds of these latent afflictions (anuśaya) are there?
To state it briefly, there are.
The verse says:
Six. The commentary asks:
What are these six?
The verse says:
That is to say, desire, hatred, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
The commentary says:
The phrase "like desire" indicates that other afflictions are similar to desire because they are latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) with respect to their objects; this point shall be explained later.
The verse says:
Furthermore, it is said that those [afflictions] are six, which become seven through the differentiation of desire.
The commentary states:

Regarding the six underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) mentioned in the preceding verse, desire is divided into two; thus, they are further explained as seven: namely, the underlying tendency of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of aversion (*pratighānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of existence (*bhavarāgānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of pride (*mānānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of ignorance (*avidyānuśaya*), the underlying tendency of views (*dṛṣṭyanuśaya*), and the underlying tendency of doubt (*vicikitsānuśaya*).
What is the meaning of this?

One should understand whether the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) is identical to the desire for sensual pleasure (*kāmarāga*), or whether the latent tendency is distinct from the desire for sensual pleasure—
just as, for example, the substance of a pebble is distinct from Devadatta’s garment.
If that were so, what would be the consequence?
If sensual desire itself were the latent tendency (*anuśaya*), it would contradict the Buddha’s sūtra.
The sūtra says:

There are people in the world whose minds are not repeatedly and for a long time defiled by the mental affliction of sensual desire; they see and know, as it truly is, the meaning of renunciation regarding this mental affliction of sensual desire. For such a person, this mental affliction of sensual desire is correctly severed by means of the faculties and powers, and its latent tendencies are forever extinguished and abandoned.

If you maintain that desire (*chanda*) and latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are distinct, and thereby establish that latent dispositions are dissociated from desire, then you contradict the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
That Piṭaka states:
"The latent disposition of sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*) is associated with three faculties."
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"Sensual desire itself is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*), and so on, up to doubt itself is the latent tendency.
Does this not contradict the Sūtra stated previously?
There is no contradiction.

Why? For the Sūtra states, "and having attained the permanent cessation and separation from the latent tendencies (anuśaya)," which refers to the permanent cessation and separation from the associated dharmas (anucara-dharma).

Furthermore, in the sūtras, the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) is a figurative expression, or an expression referring to its acquisition (*prāpti*), just as, for example, the suffering of hell or the bliss of heaven is spoken of, or as fire is said to be suffering.

The words of the Abhidharma-piṭaka all arise based on their direct characteristics; since latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are themselves afflictions, all latent dispositions are associated with feeling (*vedanā*).
How is this known?
Because they defile the mind through their latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), act as obstacles, and are contrary to the wholesome;

because when the mind is defiled by latent afflictions, unarisen wholesome states cannot arise and one falls away from those already arisen—therefore, it is known that latent afflictions are inseparable from the mind.
If this point were established by way of non-association (*viprayoga*),
then wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) would never be found, because they would exist at all times.
Since wholesome phenomena are found only at certain times, it is known that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are associated with the mind (*citta-samprayukta*).
The Sautrāntika masters say:
This argument does not prove the point.

If one maintains that the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are not associated with the mind, then those three points would not be considered the work of the latent dispositions for such a person; rather, they would be the work of the manifest active states (*paryavasthāna*).
If one maintains such a position, there is no fault. It is as the Sautrāntikas maintain:
that which is the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of sensual desire is itself the latent tendency of sensual desire.
This latent tendency is neither associated with the mind nor dissociated from the mind, because it is not a distinct category [of entity].

If a defilement in its dormant state is called a latent tendency (*anuśaya*), and if a defilement in its awakened state is called an active mind (*paryavasthāna*), what are the characteristics of this dormant defilement?
When it does not manifest before one, how does it follow along as a seed? And when it awakens, what are the characteristics of its actual manifestation?
What is the seed of delusion?
It is the functional capacity within the continuity of this body that arises from delusion and is capable of producing delusion; it is designated as a "seed.
For example, just as sprouts and the like arise from a rice grain (*śāli*) and are capable of producing further rice grains.

If one maintains that the seeds of the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are distinct dharmas, meaning that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are dissociated (*viprayukta*), then this person should also establish a distinct dharma as the seed of mindfulness (*smṛti*).
If it is said that the latent tendencies are neither associated (*saṃprayukta*) nor dissociated, how is this interpreted in the *Ṣaṭṣaṭka-sūtra*?
The Sūtra states:
"For this person, this affliction becomes a latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of desire with respect to pleasant feeling.
By such statements as these, it is shown that at this time, the affliction has not yet attained the status of a latent tendency.
If that is so, at what time [do they exist]?
It is at the time of sleep.
Alternatively, the name of the effect is applied to the cause; therefore, they are called "latent dispositions" (anuśaya).
Setting aside this discussion for now, we should further clarify the original meaning.
Regarding the distinctions among desires mentioned in the sūtras— namely, desire for sensory objects (*kāma-cchanda*) and desire for existence (*bhava-cchanda*)—
what is this "desire for existence"?
The verse says:
"There is birth in the two realms for those with desire.
The commentary says:
Those born in the realm of form and the formless realm who give rise to desire are said to "possess desire.
For what reason is this designation used?
The verse says:
"Because it arises through the internal door, it is said that one abandons the notion of liberation from it.
The commentary explains:

Regarding persons in those two realms, they frequently give rise to a desire for meditative attainment (*samāpatti*); because this desire arises by way of the internal door, it is called "having desire."

Furthermore, within these two realms, there are others who conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*; in order to eliminate that notion of *nirvāṇa*, this desire is called "desire for existence" (*bhava-rāga*).
"Existence" (*bhava*) refers to the body, which is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Because one consumes the flavor of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and the flavor of the basis (*āśraya*) regarding those sentient beings, and because one is free from desire for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), this desire is therefore called "desire for existence" (*bhavarāga*).
These six types of latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are further divided into ten within the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
What are these ten?
The verse says:

The five views refer to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*); by means of these, they further constitute ten.
The commentary states:
Originally, six were established as the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*); among them, the views are divided into five, thus making ten.

Among these, five have "view" (*dṛṣṭi*) as their intrinsic nature: namely, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), the esteeming of views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and the esteeming of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
Five have that which is not a view as their nature: namely, desire (*rāga*), hatred (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*).

Furthermore, these ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are further established as ninety-eight in the Abhidharma-piṭaka: there are thirty-six in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), thirty-one in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and thirty-one in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
To speak briefly, these latent proclivities (anuśaya) are called the afflictions of the three realms, or they are said to be the afflictions abandoned through seeing and meditation.
Among them, there are thirty-two [proclivities] in the desire realm that are abandoned through seeing the truths.
What are these thirty-two?
The verse says:

"Those [factors] are seventeen, seven, and eight; they are free from three and two views; they are abandoned sequentially and simultaneously, because of seeing the suffering and so forth of the desire realm."
The commentary states:
Regarding these ten afflictions mentioned, all ten exist in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and are abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).

Among them, seven are abandoned through the vision of origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*), and seven are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana-prahātavya*), because the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāha-dṛṣṭi*), and the adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are excluded.
Eight [afflictions] are abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) have been excluded.
Thus, these thirty-two afflictions of the desire realm are called "abandoned by the vision of the truths" (*satyadarśana-heya*), because they are eliminated solely through the vision of the truths.
The verse says:
The four afflictions are termed "abandoned through cultivation.
The commentary says:
The four afflictions are desire, hatred, pride, and ignorance.
How is it that these are abandoned through cultivation?
If a person has already seen the Four Truths, they are only able to eliminate such a view of a self-body by repeatedly cultivating the Path thereafter.
Among these, only one category is to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*); the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is likewise.

False views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) comprise four categories, being abandoned through the vision of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path; the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) are also like this.
The grasping at precepts has two categories, which are abandoned through the vision of suffering and the path.
Desire, hatred, pride, and ignorance have five categories, which are abandoned through the vision of the four truths and the path of cultivation.
Among these, what characteristics are abandoned by the vision of suffering, and so forth, up to what characteristics are abandoned by the path of cultivation?

Because they are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) and because they take those [truths] as their objects, they are said to be abandoned by the vision of the truths; the remainder are called abandoned by the path of cultivation.
If established in this manner, there are twelve views;
four doubts, five desires, five angers, five prides, and five ignorances. Thus, the afflictions of the desire realm total thirty-six types.
The verse says:
"Combined with that, excluding only hatred and the delusions of form.
The commentary says:
Excluding the five grades of hatred, the afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) are likewise named.
Altogether there are thirty-one, as in the case of the afflictions of the form realm.
The verse says:
The same applies to the formless realm.
The commentary states:
the afflictions of the formless realm are likewise thirty-one.
The verse says:
"Therefore, ninety-eight are established.
The commentary says:

These six underlying tendencies (anuśaya), due to differences in their objective referents (ālambana), their intrinsic characteristics (lakṣaṇa), their antidotes (pratipakṣa), and their realms (dhātu), are established by the Abhidharma masters as ninety-eight underlying tendencies.
Are these latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*) necessarily abandoned solely by seeing the four truths, or not?
It is said: they are not. Why is that?
The verse says:
"That which is to be abandoned by the receptivity [of the path] regarding the Peak of Existence is definitely abandoned through vision.
The commentary says:

These latent defilements (*anuśaya*) are abandoned by the "patience regarding the category of existence" (*bhavāgra-jāti-kṣānti*); they are necessarily abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), not through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The verse says:
"The others are abandoned by both vision and cultivation."
The commentary states:
The phrase "destroyed by patience" (kṣānti) applies here as well.

Regarding the remaining stages, those latent defilements (anuśaya) destroyed by the patience regarding the dharma of reality (dharmajñānakṣānti) and the subsequent patience (anvayajñānakṣānti) are, for noble ones, destroyed by the vision of the truths (satyadarśana), whereas for ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), they are destroyed by the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The verse says:
"That which is not extinguished by patience must necessarily be extinguished by the path.
The commentary says:
Regarding the afflictions in all stages, those which are to be abandoned by knowledge are always abandoned through the path of cultivation by these two types of persons.
Other masters say:
the afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of the truths are not abandoned by ordinary worldlings.
Why is this? In the *Mahā-vibhaṅga-karmavibhāga-sūtra*, it is said:
"Those who speculate about the past assert that [the self] is eternal, or that some [part of it] is eternal, or that it arises without a cause."

Regarding these three types of persons who have become detached from desire, it is said that there is a "path of practice" (pratipad) when they give rise to various views taking the desire realm as their object.

Since the afflictions of the form realm cannot take the phenomena of the desire realm as their objects—due to having abandoned desire for the desire realm—it is therefore known that the various views associated with the desire realm cannot be extinguished [by those practitioners].
When these views arise, one has already fallen away from meditative absorption, just as in the case of Devadatta; so say the Vaibhāṣika masters.
These five views have thus been explained by their names.
It does not arise from intrinsic nature.
What is that intrinsic nature?
The verse says:

The views of self (*ātman*) and what belongs to self (*ātmīya*), permanence and annihilation, the absence of [karmic] inferiority or superiority, and the view that what is not the cause or the path is the cause or the path—these are called the nature of the five views.
The commentary explains:

The view of self and what belongs to self is called the view of a body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). It is called "destruction" (*uccheda*) because it perishes moment by moment; it is called a "body" (*kāya*) because it is an accumulation, with the meaning being the aggregates (*skandha*).
This dharma is both disintegrating and aggregating; therefore, it is called the "destruction of the body," namely the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*).
This is taught in this way in order to eliminate the notion of permanence regarding them, as well as the notion of a single, unified entity regarding their aggregation.
Why is this? Because that view of self regarding the five aggregates is preceded by this notion.
To grasp and assert [the self] in relation to the cessation and the body in an improper manner is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

All views that take tainted phenomena as their objects have the cessation of the body as their object; yet, the view of self and what belongs to self is specifically designated as the "view of the cessation of the body" (satkāyadṛṣṭi) so that one may understand this view arises only with respect to the cessation of the body, and not with respect to a self or what belongs to a self.
As the Sūtra says:
"If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas in the world who give rise to the view that there is a self, all of them do so only with respect to the five aggregates."
When I observe such types [of views], that which they accept as "self" is either clung to as being eternal or clung to as being annihilated;
this is called the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), because of clinging to the extreme of permanence or the extreme of annihilation.
Because one clings to the truly existent truths of suffering and so forth and perceives them as non-existent, it is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

All views arise in contradiction to reason and are thus entirely wrong views; however, only this specific view is designated as "wrong view" because it is the most evil, capable of severing the roots of virtue. Therefore, it is called wrong view.
For example, it is like foul ghee or a wicked *caṇḍāla*;
because these are instances of total negation (*apavāda*), all other views involve only superimposition (*samāropa*).
To grasp inferior phenomena as supreme is called the "view of grasping at views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
What dharma is called "inferior"?
It refers to all contaminated dharmas (*sāsrava-dharma*), which are abandoned by the noble ones (*ārya*). To grasp these dharmas as supreme is called the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
One should speak of the "view of grasping at excellence" (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*) and so forth; here, the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) is excluded.
Viewing what is not a cause as a cause and viewing what is not the path as the path is called the "clinging to rules and rituals" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
For example, Maheśvara is not a cause of the world, yet they perceive him as a cause;
the same applies to other things such as the World-Ruler (Lokapāla) gods.
Entering fire or water is not a cause for rebirth in heaven, yet they perceive it as a cause.
Only those who cling to the views of the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and so forth consider their wisdom to be the path to liberation; they perceive that as the path.
In this context, it should be understood that the term "right view" (samyagdṛṣṭi) is excluded.
One should understand that the nature of these five views is thus.
If this view were not produced from among the causes, why would it not be abandoned by the vision of the origin (*samudaya-darśana-prahātavya*)?
If someone views Īśvara or Prajāpati as the cause, that person must necessarily grasp them as permanent, unitary, a self, and an agent; therefore, this verse says:

"Regarding Īśvara and the like, [the view] arises from the inversion of permanence and self; because its causes are based on false grasping, it is therefore abandoned by the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*)."
The commentary states:
Through the vision of the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), both the grasping at permanence and the grasping at a self regarding [the elements such as] *īśvara* and so forth are extinguished.
Since the grasping at non-causality is produced by these two inversions, it is extinguished together with this view.

If a person, by means of such practices as entering fire or water, gives rise to the attachment that one will be reborn in heaven, or through precepts and such attachments reckons that purity is attained—this attachment is also to be abandoned through the vision of suffering; so it is stated in the words of the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Again he said:

"If there are those who hold such a view, thinking that at this time a son of good family observes the cow-vow, the deer-vow, or the dog-vow, and through these practices attains purification, liberation, and transcendence, surpassing suffering and pleasure to reach the state beyond suffering and pleasure."
If one believes what is not a cause to be a cause, this clinging to precepts and views is abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya*).
As explained at length in that Piṭaka,
why is this clinging abandoned through the vision of suffering?
Because it contradicts suffering, this adherence is an error of excessive over-extension.
All conditioned phenomena that take objects within the realm of outflows (sāsrava) contradict suffering.
Furthermore, what distinction is there between this [view] and the adherence to non-causes as causes?
The clinging to specific precepts is abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Taking phenomena abandoned by the path of seeing as its object, this [clinging] is also contrary to the truth regarding suffering.

If a person gives rise to wrong view or doubt regarding the path—either asserting that there is no path to liberation, or thinking whether this path is the path to liberation or not—how could they, based on these two, distinguish and contemplate it as being pure?

If one maintains that there is a distinct path of liberation and thereby denies this [specific] path of liberation, such a person regards it as purification based on their adherence to that distinct path of liberation, not out of wrong view; therefore, this adherence does not take as its object the afflictions to be abandoned by seeing the path.

If a person regards as purification that wrong view which is abandoned by the vision of the two truths of origin and cessation, why would this clinging to precepts not also be abandoned by the vision of the truths of origin and cessation?
Therefore, the meaning you maintain must be further examined.
Regarding what was previously stated—that there is the inversion of permanence and the inversion of self—is it only these that are called inversions, or are there others as well?

There are four inversions: namely, the inversion of perceiving the impermanent as permanent, the inversion of perceiving suffering as pleasure, the inversion of perceiving the impure as pure, and the inversion of perceiving the non-self as self.
What are the essential characteristics of these four types of inversion?
The verse says:
Four inversions arise from two and a half views.
The commentary states:

From among the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), taking the view of eternalism constitutes the inversion of permanence; from the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the inversions of pleasure (*sukha-viparyāsa*) and purity (*śubha-viparyāsa*) are established; and from the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of a self constitutes the inversion of self (*ātma-viparyāsa*).
Other masters say:
How is it that the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) is an inversion by way of "mine" (*mamakāra*)?
Because that [view] regards the self as sovereign over that object, one gives rise to the view of "mine" (*mamakāradṛṣṭi*) toward that object.
Therefore, all these views are but the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi), arising through two doors.

If you maintain that "I" is the first attachment and "mine" is the second, then if "I" and "that which possesses things" were called "I," these two expressions would have to constitute distinct attachments.
Why are other afflictions not established as inversions?
It is because the meaning of "inversion" is established by means of three reasons. What are these three?
The verse says:
"Because of perversion, and because of conceptual determination and superimposition.
The commentary says:
These two and a half views are exclusively inverted; they are so because they definitively judge their objects and because they involve the superimposition of meaning.
The view of nihilism and false view cannot superimpose meaning, as they arise through the gate of non-existence.
The grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is not exclusively an inversion, because it takes as its object that which is partially pure.
The remaining afflictions lack this capacity for definitive judgment; therefore, they are not established as inversions.
If that is so, it is stated in the Sūtra:
"To apprehend the impermanent as permanent is called a perversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*), a perversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*), and a perversion of view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*).
In this context, why is it said that only the view is a perversion?
The verse says:
"Perception and mind follow from view.
The commentary says:
Because they are subject to the inversion of views and are associated with the inversion of views, perception (*saṃjñā*) and mind (*citta*) are also said to be inverted.
Why are feeling (*vedanā*) and the others not said to be inverted?
Because they are established as such in the world.
In worldly discourse, it is said that this person possesses perverted perception and a perverted mind.
This meaning is clear; it does not say they possess perverted feeling.

Such perversions are entirely extinguished in a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), because all views are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), and the other associated mental factors are likewise extinguished.

There are twelve kinds of inversions: to conceive of the impermanent as permanent is an inversion of perception, thought, and view; likewise, up to conceiving of the non-self as self, these are inversions of perception, thought, and view.

Among these, eight inversions are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), while four inversions are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya*). That is to say, regarding suffering as pleasure constitutes an inversion of perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) and an inversion of mind (*citta-viparyāsa*); regarding the impure as pure likewise constitutes an inversion of perception and an inversion of mind. Other schools (*nikāya*) explain it in this manner.

If this were not the case, how could sensual desire arise in noble ones who have not yet abandoned desire, given that they have already abandoned the inversion of perceiving pleasure and the inversion of perceiving purity?
The Vaibhāṣika masters do not accept this position.
Why is this? He says:
"If these two arise from a mind characterized by the perceptions of pleasure and purity, they are established as inversions for the noble ones."
Since the mind arises through the perception of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*), why are these two not established as the inversion of self?
For what reason?
Because, with respect to a woman and one’s own body, if the perception of a sentient being were absent, the desire for sexual intercourse would not arise.
Furthermore, it is stated in the Sūtra:

"By means of the much-heard noble disciple who has, as they truly are, seen and known this Noble Truth of Suffering... until: at this time, for this noble disciple, the perversion of perception, the perversion of mind, and the perversion of view that conceive the impermanent to be permanent are all forever extinguished," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Therefore, if perception and thought arise from [false] views, they constitute a perversion and nothing else, because the mind is temporarily deranged.
This is, for example, like the mental derangement regarding a fire-wheel or the mental derangement regarding a yakṣa.
If that is so, how do you explain the Venerable Ānanda’s statement based on what the Venerable Vāgīśa said:
"Because you have given rise to a perversion of perception, your mind is consumed by feverish distress"?
What does this statement mean?
For this reason, all eight inversions of perception and inversion of mind have not yet been extinguished in the noble ones; thus say the other schools.
If that is so, how does this not contradict the Buddha’s sūtras?

These eight [defilements] are ultimately extinguished only through the correct seeing and knowing of the Four Truths; there is no possibility of attaining their extinction apart from the contemplation of the Four Truths. Since [the sūtra] speaks of the means for their extinction, there is thus no contradiction.
Is it only the inversion of view that has distinctions, or do other afflictions as well?
Pride also has them.
How does it have distinctions?
The verse says:
The seven types of pride.
The commentary says:
What are the seven? First, pride;
second, excessive pride; third, pride beyond pride; fourth, the pride of "I am"; fifth, overweening pride; sixth, inferiority pride; and seventh, false pride.
If one does not make such distinctions, pride is simply the loftiness of mind.

This loftiness of mind becomes sevenfold due to the differences in its arising: when one considers oneself superior to those who are inferior, or considers oneself equal to those who are one's equals, if a person gives rise to such a loftiness of mind through discrimination, it is called pride (*māna*).
To consider oneself equal to those who are actually superior is called *adhimāna* (exaggerated pride).
To consider oneself superior to those who are actually superior is called *atimāna* (excessive pride).
To conceptually discriminate among the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) and reckon them as "I" and "mine" is called *asmimāna* (the pride of "I am").
To reckon oneself as having attained superior qualities when one has not yet attained them is called *adhimāna* (conceit).
To reckon oneself as possessing only a small measure of inferiority when one actually possesses a great measure of superiority is called *ūnamāna* (inferiority-conceit).
To reckon oneself as possessing qualities when one actually lacks them is called *mithyāmāna* (false conceit).
If that is so, the Abhidharma-piṭaka states that there are nine types of conceit (*māna*): first, the conceit "I am superior"; second, the conceit "I am equal";

third, the conceit "I am inferior"; fourth, the conceit "There is someone superior to me"; fifth, the conceit "There is someone equal to me"; sixth, the conceit "There is someone inferior to me"; seventh, the conceit "There is no one superior to me"; eighth, the conceit "There is no one equal to me"; and ninth, the conceit "There is no one inferior to me."
What is the meaning of this?
These nine arise from the preceding seven types of pride.
The verse says:
The nine types of pride arise from three.
The commentary asks:
what are these three?

That is to say, from overestimation (*adhimāna*), pride (*māna*), and inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*); among these, the first three types of pride arise based on views, namely: overestimation, pride, and inferiority-pride.
Inferior pride (*ūnamāna*), pride (*māna*), and excessive pride (*adhimāna*) constitute the second triad of prides.
Pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*adhimāna*), and inferior pride (*ūnamāna*) constitute the third triad of prides.

This meaning corresponds to the following: to consider oneself superior on the basis of many qualities while considering others inferior on the basis of few is established as pride (*māna*), because it possesses a state of loftiness.
When one considers that no other is inferior to oneself, what in this case constitutes the state of loftiness?
Being at such a high station, one recognizes oneself as being most inferior among the assembly of sentient beings whom one holds dear, and thus gives rise to a sense of self-respect.
Furthermore, this matter is clearly explained in the *Paññāprabhāsa-śāstra*.
As it says: "I am King Caṇḍāla."

According to the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, this pride that conceives of oneself as superior is either *māna* (pride), *atimāna* (excessive pride), or *mānātimāna* (excessive-excessive pride), depending on whether one regards those who are inferior, equal, or superior.
Furthermore, by what means are these seven types of pride extinguished?
Therefore, a verse says:
"They are extinguished by [the paths of] vision and cultivation."
The commentary states:
They are said to be extinguished by means of both vision and cultivation.
All seven are to be abandoned through the path of seeing and the path of cultivation; those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation have not yet been extinguished in the noble ones.
Do these necessarily arise in the presence of a Noble One (ārya), or do they not?
They are not fixed; as the verse says:
"The afflictions of the manifest mind, such as killing and so forth, are abandoned through cultivation just like those [afflictions abandoned by seeing]."
The commentary states:

There are higher mental afflictions capable of giving rise to volitional intent for the commission of acts ranging from killing to speaking falsehoods; these are all abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because they take as their objective domain those phenomena that are themselves abandoned through the path of cultivation.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The noble ones do not give rise to craving for existence.
The commentary explains:
Non-existence-thirst (*vibhava-tṛṣṇā*) is also to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
What dharma is this "non-existence"?
It refers to the lack of existence within the three realms; the arising of attachment and delight toward that non-existence is called non-existence-thirst.
The statement "such as" indicates a portion of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), namely that wish: "May I be reborn as the elephant king Airāvaṇa," and so forth.
The verse says:
"The types of pride (*māna*)," etc.
The commentary states:
Among the nine types of pride (*māna*), there are types of pride that are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); the pride of self (*asmimāna*) is likewise.
Such [types of pride] do not manifest in noble ones (*ārya*).
The nine types of pride are not the pride of "I" (asmimāna); by the word "etcetera," even non-existence-craving (vibhavatṛṣṇā) is included.
For what reason do such factors as these remain unextinguished and fail to arise manifestly?
The verse says:
Because it is perfected by the absence of views.
The commentary says:
Because they are fulfilled by the vision [of the truths], those [defilements] do not arise.
What is the meaning of this?
The nine types of pride and the pride of "I am" (asmimāna) are fulfilled by the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi); because these have been broken and overturned, they can no longer arise.

The higher-level afflictions such as killing and so forth are fulfilled by wrong view; craving for non-existence is fulfilled by the view of annihilationism; and one portion of craving for existence is fulfilled by the view of eternalism.
The verse says:
"In one of evil nature, there is also no sorrow.
The commentary explains:
If the mind of remorse were of a defiled nature, it too would be abandoned through the path of cultivation and could not manifest even in an Ārya, for it is perfected by doubt.
Furthermore, among the ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*), how many are universal (*sarvatraga*) and how many are non-universal?
The verse says:

The universal [afflictions] are those views that arise regarding suffering and its origin, the doubts associated with them, the ignorance (*avidyā*) that accompanies them, and the independent ignorance.
The commentary states:

Those views and doubts that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as the ignorance associated with them and the independent ignorance, are all to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin.
These eleven afflictions are termed "universal" (*sarvatraga*) within their own respective categories and realms.

Because they consist of seven views, two doubts, and two types of ignorance, they total eleven; they are so called because they arise by taking as their objects everything that exists within their own realm.
What kind of person, possessing [defilements] of the desire realm, conceives them as purification and conceives what is not a causal condition to be a causal condition?
It is said that these do not arise simultaneously with the possession of those conditions or within their own realm.
Although this is not the case, because they can take all five categories of their own realm as objects, it is said that they "take the entirety of their own realm as objects.
If that were so, one could not establish only eleven [defilements] as universal (sarvatraga) afflictions.

Wherever there is the view of a self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), there must necessarily be attachment to a self (*ātmasneha*); wherever there is the view of superiority (*viśeṣadṛṣṭi*) or the view of purity (*śuddhidṛṣṭi*), there must necessarily be the attainment of pleasure therein, from which pride (*māna*) arises. Therefore, craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and pride (*māna*) should be established as universal afflictions (*sarvatragakleśa*).
If that is so, these two afflictions take as their objects the cessation through seeing and the cessation through cultivation; by which path are they abandoned?
They are abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), because their objects are mixed.
Furthermore, some maintain that [these two] are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*), because they are established by being produced through the power of vision.

These two are specific-characteristic afflictions (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa-kleśa*) and not general-characteristic afflictions (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-kleśa*); therefore, they are not universal (*sarvatraga*). The Vaibhāṣika masters speak thus.
Regarding the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) taught as existing within the realms of dissimilar categories, there are eleven types.
Among these, the verse says:
Nine afflictions have the higher stages as their object; from among them, two views are excluded.
The commentary states:

Among the eleven [afflictions], excluding the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), the remaining nine afflictions are called "universal" (*sarvatraga*).
Unlike those belonging to different realms (*visabhāga-dhātu*), these universal afflictions can sometimes take one different realm as their object, or even two realms.
As stated in the Abhidharma-piṭaka:
"These afflictions associated with the desire realm sometimes take phenomena associated with the form realm as their object;
these afflictions associated with the desire realm sometimes take phenomena associated with the formless realm as their object."
These afflictions associated with the desire realm can sometimes take phenomena associated with the form realm or the formless realm as their objects.

From this passage, one should understand this meaning: if a person is born in the desire realm, they may give rise to the view of a living being (*sattvadṛṣṭi*) and the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) toward Brahmā.
Why do the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) not establish a basis by taking the dissimilar higher realms as their objects?
Because one does not grasp them as "self" or "belonging to self," and because these views arise from such grasping.
What kind of view is this?
These two types of grasping are not views, but are merely false wisdom (*mithyājñāna*).
Are all pervasive mental factors (*sarvatraga*) necessarily afflictions (*kleśa*)?
This is incorrect.
The verse says:
Apart from acquisition (*prāpti*), they arise simultaneously with that [mind] and are also universal (*sarvatraga*).
The commentary states:
All other dharmas that arise simultaneously with the universal afflictions (sarvatraga-kleśa) are themselves universal, up to and including their acquisition (prāpti).
This is not the case for others, because their fruits are not identical; therefore, four alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) are set forth.
There are pervasive afflictions that do not become causes by way of being pervasive causes; regarding this, four permutations (catuṣkoṭi) should be established.
The first permutation refers to pervasive afflictions of the future.
The second phrase refers to other dharmas that arise together with past and present [dharmas].
The third and fourth phrases should be established by one’s own reflection.
Among the ninety-eight afflictions (*kleśa*), how many take contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas as their object, and how many take uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dharmas as their object?
The verse says:

False view, doubt, and the two [types of] attachment should be understood as ignorance that proceeds alone; they are abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, and have the six untainted [factors] as their objects.
The commentary says:

The three afflictions abandoned through the vision of cessation—namely, false view, doubt, and the ignorance associated with these two as well as independent ignorance—and likewise the same three abandoned through the vision of the path, take uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*) as their objects; all remaining afflictions take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as their objects. This principle is established by itself.
Furthermore, a verse in this regard states:
"The cessation and the path of one's own level, as well as those of the six levels and the nine levels, serve as the objects of non-outflow delusions; by way of the path, they act as mutual causes."
The commentary states:

Defilements such as wrong view can take the truth of cessation as their object; the cessation of their own respective level is their object. Thus, if one is active in the desire realm, the cessation of the desire realm is the object, and so on, up to the cessation of the Peak of Existence for one active at the Peak of Existence.
Taking the Path as its object, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) are active;
all six levels of the Path categorized as Dharma-knowledge (*dharmajñāna-pakṣya*) serve as its objects.
If it is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the Form and Formless Realms, taking the Path as its object, the afflictions of the eight levels of the Form and Formless Realms are active.
All nine stages take the subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) and the subsequent path as their objects. Why is this?
Because paths serve as mutual causes for one another.

Although dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) serve as mutual causes for one another, because subsequent knowledge is not the antidote to the desire realm, when it takes the Path as its object, the afflictions of the desire realm cannot take subsequent knowledge or the subsequent path as their object.

If that were so, since dharma-knowledge is the antidote to the form and formless realms and takes the path as its object, the defilements belonging to the form and formless realms would necessarily become its objective referents (*ālambana*).

This category of dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) regarding the path is not a complete antidote; because the dharma-knowledges of suffering and origin are not antidotes for the form and formless realms, and furthermore, they do not serve as complete antidotes for the afflictions of the form and formless realms due to the absence of such [afflictions] prior to them, it is therefore not their object.

Furthermore, why is it that desire (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), pride (*māna*), adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and adherence to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) are not admitted to take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object?
The verse says:
Because they are not to be abandoned by means of desire.
The commentary states:

Desire must necessarily be abandoned; however, if this [desire] takes uncontaminated phenomena as its object, it should not be abandonable, just as one’s longing for wholesome dharmas is not to be abandoned.
The verse says:
"Because it is neither anger nor a fault.
The commentary explains:
