When hatred arises, it does so by taking the faults of others as its object; since the Truths of Cessation and the Path are not faults, hatred does not arise by taking them as its object.
The verse says:
It is not pride, nor are the two types of grasping, because they possess the nature of tranquility, purity, and excellence.
The commentary states:
Because the two truths of cessation and the path have tranquility as their nature, one certainly does not give rise to a conceited mind on account of them.
Since these two constitute one's own true purity, clinging to their purity does not constitute the grasping of precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
These two dharmas are the most supreme among all dharmas; to give rise to an attachment to superiority regarding inferior dharmas is called the "view of attachment to views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa).
Therefore, such afflictions as these should not take uncontaminated (anāsrava) dharmas as their objects.

Among the ninety-eight latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), how many function as latent dispositions by way of their objects (*ālambana-anuśaya*), and how many function as latent dispositions by way of association (*samprayoga-anuśaya*)?
The verse says:
The universal latent dispositions (*sarvatraga-anuśaya*) possess the latent dispositions of their own level solely by way of taking them as objects.
The commentary states:
Universal afflictions, within their own level, take as their objects both their own category and other categories, thereby attaining arising and growth.
The verse says:
"Not universal within their own category.
The commentary explains:
the remaining non-universal afflictions, within their own level, function as latent tendencies (anuśaya) by taking only their own category as an object.

For example, the latent dispositions (anuśaya) that take as their object the category of afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of suffering (duḥkha-darśana-prahātavya) do not take other categories as their object; this extends up to the latent dispositions that take as their object the category of afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga-prahātavya), which likewise do not take other categories as their object.
Having provided this general explanation, we now offer a specific distinction.
The verse says:
"It is not the case that the uncontaminated [dharmas] have higher objects."
The commentary states:

If these afflictions take the untainted (*anāsrava*) as their object, they do not function as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) by virtue of that objective support; the same applies to those that take a higher stage as their object.
For what reason is this so?
These are the dharmas that serve as its objects.
The verse says:
Because it does not take itself as an object.
The commentary states:

If a certain category of phenomena is grasped by the view of self and the craving for self as one's own support, then other afflictions are also able to adhere as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within those phenomena, just as dust settles on a damp cloth or seeds take root in a moist field.
The untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas are not like this, nor are those of the higher stages; therefore, when taking them as objects, there is no sense of latent proclivity (*anuśaya*) toward them.
If a person in a lower realm seeks to attain a higher stage, this is a wholesome desire for the Dharma (*dharmecchā*), not an affliction (*kleśa*).

Nirvana and the Path are the antidotes to the afflictions of the higher stages that they take as objects, and they are also the antidotes to the afflictions of the lower stages; therefore, those afflictions cannot find a foothold within these three objects, just as a foot cannot remain upon a hot stone.
The term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*) means "to grow along with.
Although it may have an object, there is no growth within that [object], just as a person suffering from a wind disorder (*vāta-roga*) does not benefit from taking coarse and astringent medicine.
If it has already been explained that an affliction becomes a latent tendency (anuśaya) by way of its object,
the verse says:
"If it is associated with that [affliction], it [becomes a latent tendency] therein by way of association."
The commentary states:

The term "proclivity" (anuśaya) signifies a flow. If an affliction is associated with this dharma, that affliction becomes a proclivity toward this dharma by virtue of such association, persisting until it is extinguished.
There are certain afflictions that do not take uncontaminated phenomena as their objects, nor are they universal or of a different realm; these afflictions are acquired solely through association.
Are these latent dispositions (anuśaya) not also acquired by way of taking an object?
There are [such defilements], namely the universal defilements that do not belong to the same level (*bhūmi*).
Among the ninety-eight defilements, how many are of an evil nature (*akuśala*) and how many are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*)?
The verse says:
"The afflictions of the upper realms are neutral (*avyākṛta*).
The commentary states:
All afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) have neutrality as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Why is this? All evil natures are defiled and have the retribution of painful sensations as their fruit; such painful retribution does not exist for them, because they are not the cause of affliction by others.
The verse says:
In the desire realm, the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, together with ignorance.
The commentary says:

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with these two—these three are by nature indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
For what reason is this so?
Because they do not contradict [wholesome acts] such as giving (*dāna*).
Thinking, "I shall certainly experience happiness in future lives," one now practices virtue, observes the precepts, and cultivates meditative concentration.

Since this extreme view is conducive to liberation, the World-Honored One said that among the five external views, this view is the most excellent: namely, "I do not exist; what belongs to me does not exist; I shall not exist; and what belongs to me shall likewise not exist."
These two attachments do not have the retribution of suffering because they are delusions regarding one's own nature and because they arise without afflicting others.

If that is so, then craving for the celestial realms and the conceit of "I am" should likewise follow this principle; the innate view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
"If [afflictions] exist in animals and the like, they would constitute evil if they were discriminative; this is what the former masters have taught.
The verse says:
"The remaining afflictions are of an evil nature."
The commentary states:
In the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all afflictions other than these two are unwholesome (*akuśala*).
How many afflictions are not roots of the wholesome, and how many are not non-roots of the wholesome?
The verse says:
Among the unwholesome roots of the desire realm, they are greed, hatred, and ignorance.
The commentary says:

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), all forms of greed, all forms of hatred, and all forms of ignorance—excluding those associated with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—are sequentially designated as the three unwholesome roots (*akuśalamūla*): namely, the unwholesome root of greed (*lobha*), the unwholesome root of hatred (*dveṣa*), and the unwholesome root of ignorance (*moha*).
If an affliction is non-virtuous and also serves as the root of non-virtuous phenomena, it is accepted that this phenomenon constitutes a root of unwholesomeness (akuśalamūla).
It follows as a matter of course that all other afflictions are not roots of unwholesomeness.
How many dharmas constitute the roots of the indeterminate (avyākṛta), and how many do not?
The verse says:
There are three roots of the indeterminate.
The commentary asks:
What are these three?
The verse says:
"Craving, ignorance, and wisdom.
The commentary explains:
Whatever indeterminate craving, ignorance, and wisdom born of maturation exist—all such things are indeterminate roots; so say the masters of Kaśmīra.
The verse says:
Because it arises from two conditions and from height, the others are not [so].
The commentary says:
That which is called doubt arises from two conditions and should not be established as a faculty (*indriya*), because it is characterized by instability.
Pride has the characteristic of arising through loftiness; because it arises through loftiness, it is not a faculty, as its nature differs from that of a faculty.

Why is this? The meaning of a "root" (indriya) is that it is firmly attached and grows downward; this is a well-known fact in the world. Since doubt (vicikitsā) and pride (māna) do not possess these characteristics, they are not established as roots.
The verse says:
The external teachers say there are four.
The commentary says:
The masters outside the land of Kaśmīra say that there are four neutral roots (*avyākṛtamūla*).
The verse says:
They are craving (*tṛṣṇā*), views (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and delusion (*moha*).
The commentary states:
These four are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), namely: indeterminate craving, indeterminate views, indeterminate pride, and indeterminate ignorance.
For what reason do these four constitute the indeterminate roots?
The verse says:
"The three types of persons [arise] from delusion.
The commentary says:

There are three types of persons who cultivate meditative concentration, namely those who cultivate higher contemplative practices through craving, views, or pride; these three types of persons are established as such by virtue of relying upon ignorance.

Regarding what is taught in the sūtras, there are fourteen types of the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Are they called "indeterminate" because they are [intrinsically] indeterminate, or for some other reason?
It is not so.
What is it? If a question is to be set aside and not answered, it is called "unanswered" (avyākṛta).
There are four kinds of questions:

First, that which should be answered categorically; second, that which should be answered analytically; third, that which should be answered with a counter-question; and fourth, that which should be set aside—these should be understood in their proper sequence herein.
The verse says:
"Categorical, analytical, counter-interrogative, and setting aside; for example, regarding death and birth, superiority, and whether the self is different or not.
The commentary says:
If one asks, "Must all sentient beings die?
one should give a categorical answer: "They must certainly all die.
If one asks, "Will all who have died be born again? [one should not give a categorical answer].
One should answer by means of analysis: if there is delusion, one will be born again; if there is no delusion, one will not be born.
If one asks whether the human realm is superior or inferior, one should answer with a counter-question: "Upon what basis do you now ask this?"
If he answers based on the gods, one should declare that humans are inferior.
If he answers based on the evil realms, one should declare that humans are superior.
If it is asked whether sentient beings and the five aggregates are identical or distinct?
This should be set aside as an undeclared matter (*avyākṛta*), because sentient beings do not exist substantially, just like the black or white color of the son of a barren woman.
How is this "setting aside" itself established as a declaration?
It is so established because there is this very declaration that it cannot be declared.
Furthermore, other masters say:
this matter should also be answered categorically—namely, that not all [beings] are destined to be born.
If someone were to ask: "If a sentient being is about to die, will they be born again? [the answer would be categorical].

This should be answered with a distinction: within the human realm there are two kinds, namely the inferior and the superior; since each of these two has its own respective object of observation, both must be answered categorically. This is, for example, like consciousness, which is both cause and effect.
If a person asks a question that requires a categorical answer, yet one does not answer categorically, it should be a case of answering by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*).
Is a sentient being different from the five aggregates?
To say "this is not something to be answered" is itself not an answer; it should not constitute an answer. This is a question that should be set aside (*sthāpanīya-praśna*).
Since it should be answered by setting aside [the question] in this manner, why does this not constitute an answer?
The Abhidharma masters say:

"Tathāgata, Bhagavat, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha"—this is the correct teaching of the Dharma; "the community of disciples practices correctly"; "form is impermanent, up to consciousness"; "it is suffering, up to the path"—these are matters that should be answered categorically, because they are conducive to the benefit of others.
Regarding those who ask for clarification: if someone says,
"Please, Venerable One, teach the Dharma," that person should be asked:
Those phenomena are many—whether past, present, or future.
Which phenomenon should I explain? If they say:
One should speak of past phenomena.
One should ask them:
"Past phenomena are many, namely from form up to consciousness."
If they say, "It should be stated as 'form,'" one should ask them:
Form is of many kinds, namely: wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
If they say: "Wholesome form should be explained."
One should ask him:
"There are seven kinds of wholesome bodily conduct, namely, abstaining from taking life up to abstaining from idle chatter. If he says:
One should explain abstaining from taking life.
One should ask them:
"Abstaining from taking life is of three kinds; namely, that which arises from non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion."
If they say, "It should be stated as non-greed," one should ask them:
That which arises from non-greed is of two kinds, namely, the distinction between informative (*vijñapti*) and non-informative (*avijñapti*).
This is called an analytical answer (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*).
If a person with a deceitful mind asks such a question, one should provide an analytical answer in this manner.
One should say to him:
"The dharmas are manifold; you should not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding them," until he remains silent or provides his own answer.
These two individuals asked nothing; they simply requested one another to speak, and neither of them gave a formal answer (*vyākaraṇa*).
Since they merely questioned each other reciprocally, how can it be said that the former constitutes a question and the latter constitutes an answer?
In this regard, both meanings are established. Why is this?
If someone says:
Please explain this for me:
Is it that this person did not ask a question?
It is because he asked that [the Buddha] gave a response to his inquiry.
If that is so, why is this not a case of answering with a counter-question?
As for "setting aside" (sthāpanīya), it refers to such matters as whether the world is finite or infinite.
Furthermore, according to the sūtras, one should see that there are four modes of answering questions.
The Mahāsāṃghika Bhadanta says in the Sūtra:
"Bhikṣus!
There are four ways of answering questions."
What are the four? Bhikṣus!
There are questions that should be answered categorically, up to and including questions that should be set aside.
"Monks! What kind of question should be answered categorically?
That 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent' is such a question."
"Monks! What kind of question should be answered by way of analysis?
If someone asks: 'If one intentionally performs an action, what kind of fruit and retribution does one receive?'"
This question should be answered by way of analysis.
Bhikṣus! What kind of question should be answered by counter-questioning?
If someone asks whether perception is identical to the self or whether perception is different from the self,
one should respond to that question by asking them in return:
"Venerable sir!"
Based on what kind of self do you ask such a question?
If you answer regarding a coarse self, then one should declare: "The self is different from perception.
O Bhikṣu!
This is called answering by counter-question. Bhikṣus!
What kind of question should be set aside?

That is to say, there are fourteen types of non-explanatory propositions (*avyākṛta-vastu*): whether the world is eternal, non-eternal, both eternal and non-eternal, or neither eternal nor non-eternal; whether the world has an end, is infinite, both finite and infinite, or neither finite nor infinite; whether the Tathāgata exists after death, does not exist after death, both exists and does not exist after death, or neither exists nor does not exist after death; and whether the life-principle is identical to the body or the life-principle is distinct from the body.
If a person’s latent defilements (*anuśaya*) arise with respect to an object, that person is associated with that object by virtue of those defilements.
This point must be explained: by virtue of past defilements, with what object is one associated? And so on, up to: by virtue of present defilements, with what object is one associated?
Briefly stated, there are two kinds of afflictions:
first, those with specific characteristics, namely desire, hatred, and pride;
second, those with universal characteristics, namely views, doubt, and ignorance.
Regarding this, a verse says:
"Due to desire, hatred, and pride, in the past and the present, wherever they arise and have not yet been extinguished, one is associated with that category.
The commentary states:

Regarding past and present desire, hatred, and pride: as long as these have arisen in a given state and have not yet been extinguished, within that state, these three are associated with those sentient beings.
Why is this? These three are afflictions of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-kleśa*); they do not necessarily arise in all cases or in all places.
The verse says:
"Among all [factors], it is by way of the mind that is to arise.
The commentary states:
"The phrase 'already arisen but not yet ceased' carries over here."
Because desire, hatred, and pride of the future arise based on the mental ground, they are associated with all categories throughout the three time periods.
The verse says:
"The others [are associated] with their own period."
The commentary states:
Desire, hatred, and pride are afflictions distinct from those of the mental ground; when they exist in the future, they are associated only with future objects. What are the others?
Because it arises in dependence upon the five consciousnesses, it is established as a dharma born of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).
Due to those afflictions, the verse says:
"It does not arise within any [of the five consciousnesses]."
The commentary states:
If these three afflictions are of a nature that does not arise, yet they arise based on the five consciousnesses, they still correspond with all categories, namely the three periods of time.
The verse says:
"Appropriate among all others.
The commentary asks: What are these "others"?
These are view, doubt, and ignorance.
If these three pertain to all three time periods, they are associated with all objects and across all times, because they are universal defilements (*sarvatraga-kleśa*).
The phrase "until it is extinguished" applies throughout this discussion.
Are the past and the future substantially existent entities (*dravyasat*), or are they nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*)?
If they were substantially existent, they would exist at all times; consequently, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) would become eternal.
If [the entity] does not exist, then since there is nothing within non-existence, how can there be conjunction or liberation?
The Vaibhāṣika masters establish that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are impermanent because they are associated with the characteristics of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*).
He establishes this point clearly, stating in verse:
"The three time periods exist.
The commentary says:
What is the reason for this proof?
The verse says:
Because it is taught.
The commentary says:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"O Bhikṣus!"
If past form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be one who regards past form with detachment and without regret.
Because past form exists, the learned noble disciple is one who regards past form with detachment and without regret.
If future form did not exist, the learned noble disciple would not be one who has no longing for future form.
Because future form exists, the learned noble disciple is one who has no longing for future form.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"By means of two.
The commentary explains:
It arises in dependence upon two consciousnesses;
this meaning is what is taught in the Sūtra. What are these two?
This refers to the eye and visible forms, up to the mind and mental phenomena.
That sutra states:
"If the past and future did not exist, the consciousness that takes them as objects would not arise from two [causes]."
Thus, based on the testimony of the *Āgamas*, it is known that the past and future exist.
If one seeks proof through reasoning, the verse says:
"The object exists."
The commentary states:
If there is an object (*viṣaya*), consciousness arises; it does not arise in the absence of an object.
If past and future objects did not exist, there would have to be a consciousness that takes non-existence as its objective condition (*ālambana*).
Therefore, by this reasoning, consciousness also ought not to exist, because its objective referent is non-existent.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The effect."
The commentary states:
If past phenomena do not exist, how could the two types of karma—wholesome and unwholesome—have results in the future? Why is this so?
When the retribution arises, the cause of retribution necessarily does not exist; therefore, it is known that the past and future exist.
Thus do the Vaibhāṣika masters maintain.
If a person says of themselves, "I am a fellow student of the Sarvāstivāda school," this meaning must necessarily be accepted as true. Why?
The verse says:
"Because they maintain that everything exists, they are called Sarvāstivādins.
The commentary explains:
If a person asserts that everything exists—namely, the past, the future, the present, space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation—they are accepted as being of the Sarvāstivāda school.
Furthermore, others say:
phenomena of the present world necessarily exist; likewise, past karma that has not yet yielded its fruit exists.
However, past karma that has already yielded its fruit, as well as future [karma] that has not yet yielded its fruit, are both non-existent.

If one asserts that the three time periods exist based on such conceptual distinctions, this person is not included within the Sarvāstivāda school, but is rather included within the Vibhajyavāda school.
How many types of people are there within the Sarvāstivāda school?
The verse says:
Those four kinds;
those masters have positions regarding their characteristics and states, distinguished by various different names.
The commentary states:
The Venerable Dharmatrāta establishes the three time periods based on differences in state (*avasthā*).
He asserts that when a dharma moves through the time periods, there is only a difference in its state, not a difference in its essential nature (*dravya*).

For example, when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into another ornamental object, there is a difference because of the difference in its distinct form; it is not different because of a difference in the substance itself, for the color and other qualities remain the same.
Furthermore, it is like milk transforming into curd: while it abandons its taste, potency, and maturation, it does not abandon its color-dharma; so it is here as well.
When [a dharma] proceeds from the future world into the present, it abandons its characteristic of being future, yet does not abandon its own substantial category.
From the present state of correct practice, one passes into the past; there, the characteristics of the present existence are abandoned, yet its own essential nature is not abandoned.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
"The three time periods are established on the basis of the difference in their characteristics."

He says: If a dharma proceeds through the time periods, if it is associated with the characteristics of the past, it is likewise not dissociated from the characteristics of the future and the present.
If the future is associated with the characteristics of the future, it is not dissociated from the characteristics of the past and the present either.
If the present is associated with the characteristics of the present, it is not dissociated from the characteristics of the past and the future either.
For example, it is like a man who is attached to one woman, yet does not cease to have desire for others; all phenomena are likewise.
The Venerable Vasumitra says:
"The three time periods are established by way of differences in state."
They say: if a dharma proceeds through the time periods, it is said to be different at each successive stage.
It is different because of the difference in stages, not because of a difference in the substance itself.

For example, a single stroke, when placed in one position, is called "one"; if placed in ten positions, it is called "ten"; if placed in a hundred positions, it is called "a hundred"; and if placed in a thousand positions, it is called "a thousand. The nature of phenomena across the three periods of time is likewise so.
The Venerable Buddhadeva says:
"The three time periods are established by way of difference.
He explains:
If a dharma functions within the world, it is described as different when viewed from the perspective of what precedes it and what follows it.
For example, a single woman may be called a daughter or a mother; likewise, a dharma is so designated across the three periods of time.
Among the masters of the Sarvāstivāda school, the first is placed among the followers of the Sāṃkhya because he establishes the existence of time through transformation (*pariṇāma*).
As for the second, his doctrine of the three times is confused, since he maintains that every moment of time is associated with all characteristics.
He establishes the analogy of a person who gives rise to desire for one woman, while toward other women there is only the possession (*prāpti*).
In this context, what is the point of similarity?

Regarding the fourth [point], within a single world-age, all three time periods are simultaneously present: within the past world-age, the preceding and succeeding moments are called the past and the future, while the intermediate moment is called the present; the same applies to the other world-ages as well.
Therefore, among the four teachers, the verse says:
"The third is acceptable.
The commentary says:
If the Master establishes the time periods based on differences in functional capacity,
then for this person, the verse says:
"The various time periods are established by way of functional capacity."
The commentary states:

When dharmas have not yet performed their function, they are called "future"; when they are currently performing their function, they are called "present"; and when they have already ceased performing their function, they are called "past."
This master maintains that while the functional capacity (*śakti*) is superior, the substantial nature (*svabhāva*) of the phenomenon is the same as that [of the future].
His position does not go beyond this meaning; you must now explain this point:
if a phenomenon has already passed away, it exists substantially by virtue of its generic category (*jāti*), and the same applies to the future.
How can they be called "past" and "future"?
Has this not already been explained?
It is said that the [various] time periods are established by way of functional capacity (*sāmarthya*).
If that were so, what capacity would the non-homogeneous (*asabhāga*) eye-faculty of the present possess for projecting or yielding fruit?

Furthermore, since these future causes of the same kind (*sabhāga-hetu*) are already established as having either full or partial capacity due to their actual projection of fruit, the characteristics of the time-periods (*adhvan-lakṣaṇa*) would thus become intermingled.
Furthermore, this point must be explained:
since this phenomenon exists eternally by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it should eternally exercise its functional capacity (*kāritra*).
The verse says:
"What is the obstruction?
The commentary says:
What dharma acts as the obstruction?
Due to this obstruction, these dharmas sometimes exercise their functional capacity and sometimes do not.
The verse says:
Because conditions are incomplete, they are not eternal.
The commentary states:
If you argue that it is because the causes and conditions are not complete,
this reasoning is incorrect, because you maintain that its essence exists eternally.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"How is this so? The commentary explains:
Because functional capacity (*śakti*) serves as the cause, these phenomena are described as past, future, or present.
Regarding this functional capacity, what is your position?
Does it exist as something distinct [from the phenomenon itself], or does it not exist at all?
The verse says:
Because it destroys the principle of the established tenet (*siddhānta*).
The commentary says:
If you say that this capacity does not exist in the past, future, or present, then,
because this capacity would not be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it follows by implication that it must be eternal.

Therefore, one should not say this: that at the time when dharmas have not yet performed their function they are called "future," at the time when they are currently performing their function they are called "present," and at the time when their performance of function has already ceased they are called "past."
The verse says:
Because capacity and [the possessor] are not different.
The commentary says:
There is no such fault.
If the capacity were different from the phenomenon, this fault would occur;
however, because the capacity is not different from the phenomenon, there is no such fault.
If that were so, you would ultimately fail to avoid the original fault.
As the verse says:
"The meaning of the world would then not be established."
The commentary states:
If you claim that a dharma is simply its functional capacity, and this dharma exists eternally by way of its essence, why is it sometimes described as past and sometimes as future?
Therefore, the establishment of the three time periods is untenable.
In this context, which meaning of "time" is untenable?

If a phenomenon has not yet arisen, it is called the future time; if a phenomenon has already arisen but not yet ceased, it is called the present time; if a phenomenon has already passed away and ceased, it is called the past time.
Regarding this point, you must certainly explain it:
if past and future dharmas exist as real entities just like present dharmas, the verse asks:
"How can there be that which has not yet arisen and that which has ceased?"
The commentary states:
If a phenomenon were to exist substantially by way of its own essence, how could these statements be established:
namely, "this phenomenon has not yet arisen" and "this phenomenon has already ceased"?
Regarding past lives, what phenomenon did not previously exist such that it is said this phenomenon has not yet arisen?
Furthermore, due to the non-existence of what phenomenon subsequently, is it said that this phenomenon has already ceased?
Therefore, the doctrine of the three times is not established in any way whatsoever.

If you do not accept this principle—that what has not yet existed comes into being and subsequently ceases—it is because of your claim that [existence] arises through the correspondence of causal characteristics (*ākāra*).
This dharma ought not to be established as permanent; this statement is merely empty words, for it is inconsistent with arising and ceasing.
To say that this dharma exists eternally yet is not permanent is something never before seen in either word or reason.
In this regard, a verse is spoken:
"The nature of phenomena exists eternally, yet you do not admit that phenomena are permanent;
that phenomena are not distinct from their nature—this is the work of the True Sovereign."
"What you have said— that because the Buddha has so taught, the three times exist—
and that we also maintain that the past and future exist:
as for the past, it refers to those phenomena that previously existed."
Regarding the future: if there is a cause for a phenomenon, it shall exist.
If one establishes the thesis in this way, one may say that it "exists," but this is not said because of its substantial existence.
Who says such a thing?
As it exists in the present, so it is in the past and the future.
If it were otherwise, how could it exist?
The verse says:
"By virtue of the nature of the past and future.
The commentary states:
This statement is made because of the existence of the past and future natures.
Now that it has come again, how can it be called "past" or "future"?
Therefore, there must have been a cause in the past, and there shall be a fruit in the future.
This is stated in order to enable others to understand and to eliminate their false views that deny cause and effect.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"There is the past; there is the future.
This is as when it is said that a lamp exists, yet it did not exist before [being lit] and will not exist after [being extinguished].
In the world there is such a saying;
furthermore, there is a worldly expression, as when one says:
"The lamp has already been extinguished; it was not extinguished by me."
The statement that the past and future exist is also like this.
If it were not so, the meaning of the past and future could not be established.
As for what you said—that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke to the ascetic Śīlavant:
If an action has already passed away, been extinguished, ceased, and perished, this action nonetheless exists.
This is because it is not admitted that this action existed previously;
rather, its existence is asserted on the grounds that it has already been admitted [to exist as a latent potential].
If that is so, why did the Buddha further state that they exist?

In this context, the Blessed One spoke these words based on the fact that within his own mental continuum there exists the functional capacity of past karma, which is able to bestow the retributive fruits of the two periods—past and future.
If it were not so, this karma would exist by way of its own intrinsic nature and thus could not be established as past.
You must certainly accept this point,
for the Blessed One stated in the *Tattva-śūnyatā-sūtra*:
When the eye-faculty arises, it comes from nowhere; when it ceases, it does not accumulate anywhere. Bhikṣus!
Thus, this eye-faculty did not exist previously, and having existed, it later ceases to be.
If the future eye-faculty were already existent, then this statement—that "what has not yet come into being comes into being," and so forth—would not be made.
If you maintain that this statement refers to what has not yet come into being within the present, that interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this? Because the meaning of "time" (*adhvan*) is not different from the meaning of "phenomenon" (*dharma*).

If you maintain that existence arises where there was previously no self-nature, this point is established of itself: namely, that you assert the future eye-faculty does not exist, because consciousness arises in dependence upon two conditions.
This statement should now be considered:
regarding the mental consciousness that arises based on the faculty of mind (manas) and taking mental objects (dharmas) as its condition—
is the faculty of mind a generative condition for this consciousness in the same way that mental objects are, or do they merely serve as its objective referent?
If all dharmas serve as the generative conditions for consciousness, then those future dharmas ought to exist throughout the coming thousand kalpas.
Or, if those dharmas do not exist, how could they produce the present consciousness?
Furthermore, since nirvāṇa can oppose all arising, how can it be established as a condition for the arising of mental consciousness?
If you maintain that all phenomena are merely objects of cognition (*ālambana*), we also say that future phenomena are exclusively objects of cognition.
If it does not exist, how can it function as an object? To this I say:
it exists in the same manner that it constitutes an object.
How is it that they constitute an objective sphere?
They are both what has already come to be and what is yet to come to be. Why is this so?
No one recollects past form, sensation, and so forth while perceiving them as existing.
How could they exist [now]?
It is like a person currently experiencing present form.
If the recollection of the past is likewise, then just as those [dharmas] ought to exist in the present, so too do the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, perceive them.
If those dharmas existed now, they would have to be of the present.
If it does not exist as it does now, then it must follow that there is a cognition whose object is a non-existent dharma; this point would be established.
If you maintain that this dharma has already ceased, that argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because that which has already been dispersed cannot be known.
If you maintain that those forms are dispersed by means of atoms (*paramāṇu*), [then...]
If that were so, atoms would have to be eternal, for there would be nothing other than the conjunction and disjunction of atoms, and no single entity capable of arising or ceasing.
You would thus be accepting the tenets of the naked ascetics (Nirgranthas) while abandoning the Buddha’s scriptures.
The Sūtra says:
"This eye-faculty, when it arises, comes from nowhere," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Since feeling and the other [aggregates] are not composed of a collection of atoms (*paramāṇu*), how could they be dispersed?
One recollects that object exactly as it was when it arose;
if that object existed just as it did in the past, it would logically follow that it must be eternal.
If, however, there is no object, then the fact that cognition takes a non-existent thing as its objective support is established of itself.
If even "non-existence" (abhāva) is an object of consciousness, then a thirteenth base (āyatana) should be established to include this object.
If there is no thirteenth base, by what base would this consciousness take its object?
Thus, the name itself is the object.
If that were so, this cognition would take the name as its object and fail to understand the meaning within that name.
For one who takes a sound that previously did not exist as an object, what dharma serves as the object for that person?
Sound is the object.
If that were so, then whenever a person has not yet obtained sound, that person would necessarily have to produce it.
If you say that this object exists in a future state, that argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because this exists;
how could one therein conceive of it as non-existent?
If you maintain that the future does not exist in the present, this argument is incorrect.
Why is this? Because this object is a single entity.

Furthermore, these future objects are differentiated; that which was non-existent comes into being, and thus the objective sphere of consciousness is established as being of two kinds: namely, existence and non-existence.
If that is so, how should one interpret the *Bodhisattvabhāṣita-sūtra*, which says:
"That there should be a phenomenon that does not exist in the world, yet which I should know or should see—such a thing is impossible"?
This proof is not valid, for it does not accord with the intent of the sūtra.

The sūtra states that various non-Buddhists give rise to overweening pride (*adhimāna*); although the characteristics of meditative absorption do not actually exist, they perceive them as already present.
I am not like that; if there were truly a determinate characteristic of a self, then one would perceive it—this is the intended meaning of the Sūtra.
Otherwise, since omniscience takes truly existent phenomena as its objects, how could doubt and discernment be established?
Furthermore, what is the distinction?
Moreover, this meaning is established by this proof; it must necessarily be so.
For in another sutra, the Blessed One, the World-Honored One, said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu; be my disciple.
If I instruct you in the morning, you shall attain the supreme realization by evening.
If I instruct you in the evening, you shall attain the supreme realization by morning."
If something exists, you should know that it exists;
if it does not exist, you should know that it does not exist.
If there is something superior, you should know that there is something superior.
If it is unsurpassed, you should know it to be unsurpassed.
Therefore, this statement—that because consciousness must necessarily have an object—is not a proof.
As for what you said, that there is fruition because of karma: [this is not established].
Regarding the fact that the past is not non-existent, we shall now discuss this together. Why is this?
The Sautrāntikas do not assert that the fruit of retribution arises from past karma; how then can it arise from a superior transformation within the continuity of the past?
This point shall be demonstrated in the chapter refuting the doctrine of a self (*pudgala-viniścaya*).
For one who maintains that the past and future exist as real entities, for such a person, the fruit of retribution exists eternally.
Regarding this retribution, what capacity does karma possess?
If you say it has the capacity to produce existence (*bhava*),
then since "production" (*jāti*) carries the sense of bringing into being what was previously non-existent, the principle that "what was originally non-existent now exists" is established by itself.
If everything exists exactly as you maintain, then with respect to what dharma and in what place could there be any functional capacity?
If you hold such a view, it merely conforms to the position of the Vātsīputrīyas.

He said: "If it exists, it must exist; if it does not exist, it must not exist. If it does not exist, it is not produced; if it exists, it does not perish. This causes it to become manifest in the present, for the cause possesses functional efficacy."
What dharma causes [the result] to manifest in the present, and what dharma leads it to another location?
If that were so, this dharma would have to be permanent.
Furthermore, if there is no form within it, how could it possess the functional capacity to lead [the result]?
Even before this [effect] exists, this principle is established by itself.
If you maintain that the specific nature (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) is the causal capacity, then even before this [effect] exists, this principle is likewise established naturally.
Therefore, within the doctrine of the Sarvāstivāda school, this position—that everything past and future exists—is not logical.
If one were to grasp the meaning of "all exists" (*sarvam asti*) as it is taught in the sūtras, such an adherence would be the most excellent.
How is it that the sūtras speak of "all exists"?
As the sūtra says:
"O Brahmin!"
If one asserts that all exists, it must exist only as the twelve bases (*āyatana*) or only as the three time periods.
If something exists according to its logical necessity, it must exist in that very way.
If the past and future lacked substantial reality (*dravya*), how could sentient beings, by virtue of these [dharmas], be associated with them or arise from them?
Because afflictions arise with that as their cause, and because latent afflictions arise taking that as their object, it is said that these two time periods are associated by way of their nature.
Therefore, the Vaibhāṣika masters state:
"The past and future time periods truly exist."
If a meaning can be understood through inference or authoritative scripture, a person who cherishes themselves must certainly accept it.
If this is not the case, such a person should understand it thus:
"This Dharma is exceedingly profound; it cannot necessarily be comprehended through one's own mere deliberation, and therefore it should not be rejected."
There is another sense in which arising itself is ceasing, namely, the arising of form is the ceasing of form.
There is another sense in which there is a distinct arising and a distinct ceasing, namely, future arising is present ceasing.
There is another sense in which there is "arising from the world," because it is subsumed under the actual arising within the world.

There is also "arising from the world" in the sense that the future world is not of a single moment; thus, the future world must possess that which is "yet to be" (*bhavya*), proceeding from the state of being yet to be to the state of being presently existent (*pratyutpanna*).
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Fourteen (Fascicle Fifteen) Composed by Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha of Central India during the Chen Dynasty.
This concludes the second part of the "Chapter on the Analysis of Delusions" (*Madhyavibhāga*). Having already explained the meaning of the world, [the discussion] proceeds now by way of association.
One should now reflect upon this meaning:
Once this category has ceased, do sentient beings attain separation from it?
Furthermore, when sentient beings have already attained separation from this category, has this category already ceased?
Among these, if one has already become dissociated from a particular category, that category has necessarily already ceased for that person.
If a category has already ceased, sentient beings may have either become dissociated from it or not yet become dissociated from it.
For example, as the verse says:

"When suffering and the lower-level afflictions have been extinguished, one is bound by the remaining universal [afflictions]; when those of the preceding category have already been extinguished, one is bound by the remaining afflictions of the same object."
The commentary states:

When the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of origin (*samudaya-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, all categories of defilements to be abandoned by the vision of suffering have been completely extinguished.

However, regarding those categories to be abandoned by the vision of the truth of origin—which take that [suffering] as their object—the remaining universal afflictions (*sarvatraga-kleśa*) remain associated with them. Furthermore, within the categories to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), there are nine grades of afflictions.

Regarding the category [of afflictions] already previously extinguished, it should be understood that this refers to other afflictions which take that [extinguished category] as their object and are associated with it.
Within which categories can how many afflictions arise by taking those categories as their objects?
If one were to answer this question sentence by sentence, one would have to explain countless dharmas; therefore, the former masters composed the *Abhidharmavibhāṣā-saṃgraha*. They said:
"How may we, by means of little effort, cross over the vast current of questions?"
Briefly stated, there are sixteen types of dharmas: namely, five categories each corresponding to the desire, form, and formless realms, plus the untainted mind;
there are likewise sixteen of a similar kind.
Among these, which phenomena serve as the objects of which minds?
Only when a person has understood this can one then consider the meaning of how many delusions arise in relation to those objects.

The verse here says: "Those associated with desire that are seen through the truths of suffering and origin, and those to be abandoned through cultivation and cessation—these, along with one [type] from their own realm and the material, are the objects of the stainless consciousness. The commentary explains: "Those associated with desire" refers to the phenomena belonging to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). "Seen through the truths of suffering and origin" means those [phenomena] to be abandoned by seeing the truths of suffering and its origin. "And those to be abandoned through cultivation and cessation" refers to the phenomena to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and those to be abandoned by cessation (*nirodha-heya*). "Along with one [type] from their own realm" refers to the phenomena of the desire realm itself that are to be abandoned by seeing the truth of cessation. "And the material" refers to the phenomena of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) that are to be abandoned by seeing the truth of cessation. These are the objects of the "stainless consciousness," which is the supramundane wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). Thus, it is established that these nine categories of phenomena constitute the objective domain of the stainless consciousness.
This dharma belongs to its own realm (*svadhātu*); because it comprises three categories, it is said to be "three of its own realm.
This dharma comprises one category of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); therefore, it is said to be "one of the form realm."

Regarding the phenomena associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that are to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya-darśana-heya*) as well as those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), all are objects of the five consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).

Within their own realm, there are three types of consciousness: namely, the aforementioned three [desire-realm consciousnesses], one consciousness of the form realm (*rūpadhātu-citta*), which is that to be abandoned through the path of cultivation, and the untainted consciousness (*anāsrava-citta*).
The verse says:
Three [realms] of its own level and the lower levels, and one pure consciousness of the higher level, are the objects of [the latter].
The commentary says:

Regarding the mental concomitants associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as in the three categories of dharmas previously mentioned, these are the objects of eight types of mind: namely, the three types of mind of its own realm as before, the three types of mind of the lower realms as before, and one type of mind of the upper realm—namely, the mind to be abandoned by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) and the outflow-free mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
The verse says:
The formless [realms] are the objects of three consciousnesses of the three realms and of the untainted consciousness.
The commentary says:

Regarding the three categories of factors associated with the formless realm, these are the objects of ten types of consciousness: namely, three for each of the three realms of consciousness as previously stated, and one for the untainted (anāsrava) consciousness.
Having explained that [the afflictions] of the three realms are abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin, as well as through the path of cultivation,
the verse says:
Those abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path all have their own [respective] and higher stages as their objects.
The commentary states:
Among those dharmas to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, "one's own mind" refers to the mind to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path;
it should be understood that this mind is the dominant [condition], and those dharmas are the objects of this mind.

Why is this so? The phenomena associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned by the vision of cessation are the objects of only six consciousnesses; namely, the five previously mentioned consciousnesses and its own extended consciousness.

The same applies to the factors abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga-prahātavya-dharma*); that is to say, the five consciousnesses previously mentioned and their corresponding mental consciousnesses (*sva-viprayukta-vijñāna*).

Thus, because these factors abandoned by the path of seeing cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) in the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpya-dhātu*) are the objects of the mental consciousnesses abandoned by the path of seeing cessation and the path respectively, they constitute the objects of nine consciousnesses and eleven consciousnesses.
Having explained the dharmas of the three realms and five categories, the verse says:
"After the [dharmas] of the three realms, the uncontaminated [dharmas]; these three are the objects of the uncontaminated mind."
The commentary states:

If untainted (*anāsrava*) dharmas serve as the objects of ten types of mind—namely, the three final categories of mind from each of the three realms, which are the minds abandoned through the vision of cessation and the path, as well as those abandoned through cultivation, and the untainted mind itself—then [the following applies].
Furthermore, in order to summarize this meaning, one and a half verses are composed:
"Seeing suffering and its origin, and cultivating cessation, In the three realms, there are outflow-free [knowledges] With five, eight, and ten consciousnesses;
The objects perceived by these ten consciousnesses..."
"Those abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path, / All have their own extended spheres as objects.
Having thus understood the establishment of these sixteen moments of mind,
how should one contemplate the actual state of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) with respect to the sixteen objects?
In order to establish this meaning, we shall clarify the specific method:
among those consciousnesses that take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) can arise based upon it?
If such a question should arise, one should reflect for oneself:

there are seven types of the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*); within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is to be abandoned only by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), it belongs to the five categories [of afflictions] as well as the untainted (*anāsrava*).
Briefly stated, this faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) is the object of twelve types of consciousness:
four types of consciousness belonging to the desire realm— excluding that which is abandoned by the vision of cessation—
and five types of consciousness belonging to the form realm.
In the formless realm, there are two types of consciousness: those to be abandoned by the path of vision and the path of cultivation, as well as untainted consciousness.
These twelve types of consciousness can take the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as their object.

Within this, according to the principle of reality, the afflictions belonging to the categories of the desire realm and the form realm that take conditioned objects as their conditions, as well as the two categories of the formless realm and all pervasive afflictions, give rise to latent tendencies therein.
It should be understood in this way:
within the mind that takes the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*) as its object, how many underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) can arise based upon it?
This refers to what was previously described as taking the faculty of pleasure as its object.
Furthermore, of what consciousnesses do these twelve consciousnesses constitute the objects?
They are precisely the twelve classes of consciousness previously mentioned.

Moreover, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) there are two categories, namely the minds to be abandoned through the vision of suffering (*duḥkha-darśana-heya*) and the vision of origination (*samudaya-darśana-heya*). It should be understood that these fourteen minds take as their objects the consciousnesses that perceive feeling (*vedanā*). Within this context, the minds of the formless realm to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and origination are further added.
In the desire realm, there are four types of consciousness that take conditioned objects as their domain.
In the form realm, there are five types of consciousness that take conditioned objects as their domain.
Based on these fourteen types of consciousness, the latent proclivities (anuśaya) arise.
This meaning should be understood; by this method, the remainder should also be understood.
If the mind is bound by a certain defilement, do all those defilements exist as latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) within that mind?

An underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) is present when a defilement is associated with the mind and has not been extinguished, and its object, which it takes as its focal point, has also not been extinguished.
It is not an underlying tendency when a defilement associated with the mind has already been extinguished.
If this is the meaning, the verse says:
"The bound mind is of two kinds; it is defiled or undefiled by virtue of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*).
The commentary explains:
If the mind is defiled, it is bound by the afflictions (*kleśa*) because those afflictions can lie latent (*anuśaya*) within it;

furthermore, because they are associated with the mind and take it as their object, the afflictions cannot fail to lie latent therein, for the afflictions and that mind are mutually associated and have not yet been extinguished.

If there is no defiled mind, yet one is bound by the fact that the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) remain unextinguished simply because they are capable of taking those [objects] as their objective conditions;
furthermore, how do the ten types of afflictions arise?
Regarding "from the beginning": because of association with ignorance (*moha*), one is deluded and obscured regarding the objects of the truths (*satya*).
Such a person does not contemplate the characteristic of suffering-as-suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); it does not manifest to that person, and this applies likewise even up to the Path (*mārga*).
Therefore, the verse says:
"From delusion and doubt.
The commentary explains:
If a person is already deluded and hears two conflicting meanings, they give rise to doubt, thinking, "Is this suffering, or is this not suffering? and so on, up to the Path.
The verse says:
"Wrong view."
The commentary states:
From doubt arises false view.
If a person possesses a doubting mind, due to improper hearing and improper reflection, a definitive false cognition arises, extending even to the denial of suffering and so forth.
The verse says:
"From the view of a self-identity.
The commentary says:

That [view] is said to arise from false view and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), because of the grasping at "I" and "mine" which persists even when the five aggregates have been eliminated through [the realization of] suffering.
The verse says:
"The view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)."
The commentary states:
[These views] arise from the view of a self-identity and the view of extremes, because they grasp at the two extremes of permanence and annihilation regarding the self.
The verse says:
"From this, there is the grasping at precepts and observances.
The commentary explains:
from the view of extremes, the grasping at precepts and observances arises.
Why is this? Because if a person adheres to one extreme, they will, by virtue of that adherence, conceive of purification through that extreme.
The verse says:
Next is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
The commentary states:
from the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), the adherence to views arises.
Why is this? If one conceives of purification through a particular dharma, one will necessarily grasp that dharma as supreme.
Since grasping what is inferior as superior constitutes the view of dogmatic attachment (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), the verse says:
"Self-view, desire, and pride.
The commentary states:
Because a mind of attachment arises toward self-view, and because a mind of haughtiness arises by means of self-view, therefore from self-view, desire and pride arise.
The verse says:
Hatred arises toward others upon seeing them.
The commentary says:
If a person is attached to their own view and encounters another view that serves as an antidote to it, they give rise to hatred.
Other masters say:
one gives rise to hatred toward one's own view at the moment it has already been grasped and then abandoned.
The verse says:
"In successive order.
The commentary explains:

The various afflictions such as desire, which are to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*), arise in this sequential order because they originate based on views that take their own continuum as their object.
When an affliction is about to arise, it necessarily arises due to three causes and conditions.
Regarding that which can give rise to the causal conditions, the verse says:
From unabated latent dispositions (*anuśaya*), and from the presence of objects before the sense faculties, through improper mental attention (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), the afflictions arise.
The commentary states:

Regarding "affliction," it is, for example, like the latent tendency of desire (*kāma-anuśaya*). When this has not yet been extinguished and not yet permanently abandoned, it is associated with the affliction of desire; when an object appears before the sense faculty, [the affliction arises].
Within that state, improper mental attention arises; through the presence of these three factors, the afflictions of desire are able to arise.
These three follow a specific sequence: namely, the power of the cause, the power of the condition, and the power of the preparatory application.
The verse says:
"Possessing causes and conditions.
The commentary says:
If other afflictions arise possessing their causes, it should be understood that they are likewise.

It is said that at times afflictions also arise through the power of the object (*viṣaya*), without arising from the power of a cause, such as in the case of an Arhat of the "regressive" type (*parihāṇadharman*).

Regarding these latent afflictions (*anuśaya*), the Blessed One has spoken of them in the sūtras as the three floods (*ogha*): namely, the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*), the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*), and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*).

Alternatively, they are spoken of as the four violent torrents (*vr̥kṣa*): namely, the torrent of desire, the torrent of existence, the torrent of views (*dṛṣṭi-vr̥kṣa*), and the torrent of ignorance.
Some describe them as the four fetters, which are the four rivers;
others describe them as the four graspings, namely: grasping at sense-desires, grasping at views, grasping at rules and observances, and grasping at a doctrine of self.
Regarding this, a verse says:
"In the desire realm, the afflictions that arise together with the perversions, excluding delusion, are called the 'desire-flood' (*kāma-ogha*).
The commentary explains:

Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), the remaining afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) together with all the outbursts of delusion (*paryavasthāna*) should be known as the "flood of desire" (*kāma-ogha*).
It consists of forty-one entities:
thirty-one underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)—excluding the five types of ignorance and the ten outbursts of delusion—which are merely afflictions and not underlying tendencies.
The verse says:
Only the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) constitute the outflows of form and formlessness (*rūpārūpya-bhava-āsrava*).
The commentary says:
Excluding the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), all latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) associated with the formations of the form and formless realms are called the "outflow of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*).
It consists of fifty-two entities:
twenty-six afflictions of the form realm, excluding the five categories of ignorance; the same applies to the formless realm.
Is it not the case that in the higher realms (*ūrdhvadhātu*), the two types of perversely arisen afflictions—namely, lethargy (*styāna*) and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—do not exist?
As stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"What constitutes the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*)?"

Excluding ignorance (*avidyā*), what of the remaining afflictions associated with the form and formless realms—namely, the fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and outbursts of delusion (*paryavasthāna*)? Why are these not included here?
The Master of Kaśmīra said:
"Because they lack self-mastery.
Furthermore, for what reason are the realms of form and formlessness combined and spoken of as a single "existence-taint" (*bhava-āsrava*)?
The verse says:
Because they are indeterminate, arise through the internal door, and are produced by depending on the tranquil stages, they are combined into one.
The commentary says:

The afflictions of these two realms are identical in being of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*), arise based on the internal door, and are produced within the stages of meditative concentration (*samāpatti-bhūmi*); because these three factors are equal, they are established together as one.
Based on this cause, the meaning of "desire" (kāma) is established; furthermore, based on this same cause, the meaning of "outflow" (āsrava) is established.
Now, the ignorance within the three realms is established as the "outflow of ignorance" (avidyā-āsrava), and this principle is thereby self-evident.
There are fifteen entities; why is this ignorance established separately as a *āsrava* (outflow)?
Regarding all *āsravas*, the verse says:
"Because it is the root, ignorance is established as a separate *āsrava*."
The commentary states:
All outflows (āsrava) have ignorance as their root; therefore, ignorance is established separately as an outflow.
As it has been explained regarding the outflows, one should know that the same applies to the others.
The verse says:
"The same applies to the 'floods' and 'bonds,' because views are established separately for clarity.
The commentary says:
That which is called the outflow of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) is itself the flood of desire (*kāma-ogha*) and the fetter of desire (*kāma-bandhana*).

That which is called the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*) is itself the flood of existence (*bhava-ogha*) and the fetter of existence (*bhava-bandhana*), with the exception of the various views (*dṛṣṭi*).
He says that because of their distinct discernment (*vijñapti*), views (*dṛṣṭi*) are established as separate categories within the floods (*ogha*) and the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The verse states:
"It is not because they lack companions in the stream, for they do not flow with it."
The commentary states:
Because they cause [beings] to flow, they are called "flows" (āsrava).
The meanings of "flows" and so forth shall be explained later.

He says that if one sees [the outflows] alone and without companions, they do not conform to the flow because they are clearly manifest; therefore, they are not established as a separate category from the flow, but are established together as the category of the flow.

This river of the flood of desire consists of twenty-nine entities: namely, fifteen consisting of desire, hatred, and pride; four consisting of doubt; and ten consisting of the afflictions that arise from perversions.
The flood of the afflictions (*ogha*) consists of twenty-eight factors: namely, twenty consisting of desire (*kāma*) and pride (*māna*), and eight consisting of doubt (*vicikitsā*).
The flood of views (*dṛṣṭi*) consists of thirty-six factors, and the flood of ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of fifteen factors.
Just as with the violent river, one should know that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are likewise.
The verse says:
As it was stated, those associated with delusion (*moha*) are called "grasping" (*upādāna*) because they consist of two parts of views (*dṛṣṭi*).
The commentary states:

This "grasping of desire" (*kāma-upādāna*) is established based on the fetters of desire together with ignorance; it consists of thirty-four entities. Specifically, there are twenty consisting of desire, hatred, pride, and ignorance; four consisting of doubt; and ten consisting of the afflictions arising from perversions (*paryavasthāna*).

This "clinging to the doctrine of self" (ātmavādopādāna), established as being associated with ignorance (avidyā) and bound by existence (bhava), consists of thirty-eight entities: namely, thirty consisting of desire (rāga), pride (māna), and ignorance (avidyā), and eight consisting of doubt (vicikitsā).
These are the fetters of views; excluding the clinging to precepts and rituals, they are established as the clinging to views, which consists of thirty entities.
The clinging to precepts and rituals consists of six entities.
Why is it that, among the various views, the clinging to precepts and rituals is separated and established as a distinct clinging?
Because it opposes the noble path and because it deceives both groups:
the householders are deceived by this affliction, as they falsely conceive self-starvation to be the way to heaven.

The "renunciant division" (pravrajyā-varga) arises from abandoning desirable objects and practicing what is bitter and harsh as the path, calculating that one will thereby attain liberation; thus, it is established.

As for the "grasping at desire" (kāma-upādāna) and the "grasping at views" (dṛṣṭi-upādāna), these are established as two types of grasping because they are the causes of strife between the two divisions of householders and renunciants.
Householders engage in strife with other householders because they grasp at the five sensory objects;
renunciants engage in strife with other renunciants because they grasp at various differing views.

These two categories grasp both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and its fruit, as well as the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) and its fruit; therefore, the afflictions of the two realms are established as "grasping at self-views" (*ātma-vādopādāna*).
Why is ignorance (*avidyā*) combined with these and not designated as a separate form of grasping?
They are established as "grasping" (upādāna) because they are capable of grasping at birth and death.
The verse says:
Because ignorance is not capable of grasping, it is combined [with the others].
The commentary states:

Because ignorance has non-comprehension as its characteristic and is dull and obtuse, it cannot grasp [objects] on its own; therefore, it is combined with the other afflictions to constitute "grasping" (*upādāna*).
In the sūtras, the Blessed One said:
What is the bond of desire?
It is explained at length as in the Sūtra.

Regarding the objects of desire, when sentient beings are defiled by desire, seek after desire, love desire, delight in desire, crave desire, are distracted by desire, are attached to desire, are thoroughly attached to desire, take pleasure in desire, become fixed upon desire, and greedily covet desire—this desire causes the minds of sentient beings to undergo transformation and remain therein; this is called the bond of desire.
This applies likewise to the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth.
In another sutra it is said:
"Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is also called grasping (*upādāna*)."
Therefore, it is known that among desire and the rest, it is specifically craving (*tṛṣṇā*) that constitutes "clinging" (*upādāna*); this point has already been explained.
In the Sūtras, only the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) are designated as "floods" (*ogha*), "torrents" (*vega*), "bonds" (*bandhana*), and "clinging."
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the term "latent tendency" (*anuśaya*),
and what is the meaning of the term "grasping" (*upādāna*)?
The verse says:
Because they are subtle and persistent, because they are of two kinds, and because they are constant without effort, they are called "latent tendencies" (*anuśaya*).
The commentary states:
Here, "subtle" means that their mode of activity (*ākāra*) is extremely fine; therefore, they cannot be known by others.
"Following along" means that they are constantly present by virtue of their acquisition (*prāpti*).

As for the "two kinds of latent dispositions" (*anuśaya*), they function as two types of fetters within the continuum of sentient beings as they flow along: namely, the fetter of the object (*ālambana-bandhana*) and the fetter of association (*samprayoga-bandhana*).

Regarding the phrase "because it is constant without effort": if one does not apply effort to produce [the affliction], or if one applies an antidote to suppress it, it nevertheless manifests repeatedly.
For these three reasons, those afflictions are called *anuśaya* (latent tendencies).
The verse says:

Because they cause [beings] to abide and cause them to flow, because they can pull [them along] and can join [them together], and because they can grasp, they are called *āsrava*, *ogha*, and so forth.
The commentary states:
They are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) because they cause one to dwell within non-restraint and leak through the six sense-gates, flowing from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci Hell.
They are called "floods" (*ogha*) because they are able to drag sentient beings and cause them to enter the ocean of suffering.
Because it binds sentient beings so that they cannot be separated from suffering, it is called "bondage" (saṃyojana).
Because sentient beings, by means of this, grasp at desire and so forth, as well as the requisites for birth, it is therefore called "clinging" (upādāna).
Furthermore, this interpretation is the most excellent.
Because the continuum flows toward the six sense objects by means of that [craving], it is called "flow" (*āsrava*).
As the Sūtra says:
"Elder! It is like a boat that must be pulled against the current with great effort;
yet if one relinquishes that effort, the boat will flow with the current without further difficulty."
The various afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise.
According to the wording of the sūtra, one should understand that because their flow is excessive, violent, and rapid, these afflictions are called "fierce rivers" (*ogha*). Why is this so?
Because of these afflictions, sentient beings drift along, being able only to follow them and unable to resist them.

If an action is excessive, it is called "bondage" (*bandhana*), because it causes one to be joined with various sufferings, or because it repeatedly associates [with the defilements], or because it grasps at desire and so forth, or because it is produced by grasping and can produce grasping; therefore, it is called "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Based on this meaning, it is said that they are called "outflows" (*āsrava*) and so forth, up to "grasping" (*upādāna*).
The verse says:
"Due to the distinctions of fetters (*saṃyojana*) and so forth, they are further said to be of five kinds."
The commentary states:

These latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) are further explained as being of five types based on the distinctions of fetters (*saṃyojana*), bonds (*bandhana*), latent proclivities (*anuśaya*), defilements (*kleśa*), and perversely arisen [afflictions] (*paryavasthāna*).

Among these, there are nine kinds of fetters, namely: the fetter of compliance (*anunaya-saṃyojana*), the fetter of aversion (*pratigha-saṃyojana*), the fetter of pride (*māna-saṃyojana*), the fetter of ignorance (*avidyā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*), the fetter of doubt (*vicikitsā-saṃyojana*), the fetter of envy (*īrṣyā-saṃyojana*), and the fetter of avarice (*mātsarya-saṃyojana*).
Among these, the fetter of compliance refers to the desires of the three realms; the remaining fetters should be understood accordingly.
The fetter of views refers to the three views, and the fetter of grasping refers to two views; therefore, this statement was made.

Is this not the case? Among those factors associated with views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-dharma*), there is association with the fetter of conformity (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) alone, and not with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); yet, within that [state], the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of the fetter of views is not non-latent.

Regarding the existence [of these fetters]: when the knowledge of origination has arisen but the knowledge of cessation has not yet arisen, one is associated with the view of grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) and the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) with respect to those phenomena to be abandoned by the vision of cessation and the path.

Why is this? Because those dharmas are associated with the fetter of compliance (*anunaya-saṃyojana*) but are not associated with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*); for while the universal [factors] have already been extinguished, the non-universal [factors] take them as their object, and there is no associated fetter of views present.

Regarding how the view-predispositions (dṛṣṭi-anuśaya) underlie those [other factors], it refers to the two types of grasping views (*parāmarśa-dṛṣṭi*), which do so solely by way of association (*saṃprayoga*).
Furthermore, for what reason are three of these views combined within the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and established as a distinct "view-fetter" (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
Furthermore, why are the two views established separately as the fetter of grasping (*parāmarśa-saṃyojana*)?
The verse says:
Because they are equal in their grasping of objects, the views are established as a separate fetter.
The commentary states:

The three views consist of only eighteen entities, and the two graspings likewise consist of only eighteen entities. Therefore, it is said that because they are equal in terms of their entities, the two graspings are established as separate fetters apart from the views.

These two views have the nature of the grasper (*grāhaka*), whereas the remaining ones are not so; they are merely the grasped (*grāhya*). Because of this distinction between the grasper and the grasped, they are established as two fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Why are envy (*īrṣyā*) and avarice (*mātsarya*) established as two distinct fetters (*saṃyojana*) among all the fetters, while other secondary afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are not?
The verse says:
Because they are exclusively unwholesome, and because both are independent, Envy and avarice are established separately as two fetters.
The commentary states:
There is no other category of afflictions that arise without inversion which, when these two are present in a particular state, renders that state exclusively unwholesome.
Furthermore, these two arise independently and do not depend on anything else.
If one maintains that only eight are manifest outbursts (*paryavasthāna*), for such a person this answer may be given.
However, for one who establishes ten as manifest outbursts, both resentment (*pratigha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) also possess these two natures.
Therefore, this "rescue" does not constitute a rescue from difficulty.
The verse says:
