Because it lacks the value of wealth and property, because it is a pervasive characteristic, and because it can impair both groups, envy and avarice are established as distinct fetters.
The commentary states:

Other masters say that within the arising of perversions, envy and avarice involve threefold losses; through jealousy one receives the retribution of being despised, and through avarice one receives the retribution of poverty.
As a verse says:
"One who lacks wealth is not honored by those dear to oneself.
Because they arise from the characteristics of sorrow and joy, they are able to manifest the characteristics of the various afflictions.

Envy (*īrṣyā*) can harm the faction of others, while stinginess (*mātsarya*) can harm one's own faction; because one cannot endure the gains and benefits obtained by others, and because one cannot provide benefit to others oneself, envy and stinginess are established as two separate fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Furthermore, in another place, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, spoke of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The verse says:
"There are five kinds of lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)."
The commentary says:
What are these five?
They are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), sensual desire (*rāga*), and ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Why are they called the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)?
Because they are favorable to the lower realm.
The "lower realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); these five afflictions are favorable because they accord with the affairs of the desire realm.
What constitutes excellence?
The verse says:
By two [factors], one does not transcend desire; by three, one returns to the lower realms.
The commentary states:
Due to sensual desire and ill-will, sentient beings are unable to transcend the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

Due to the three [defilements] beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), even if they have already transcended it, they return again to the realm of desire, just like a gatekeeper or a deserter who seeks to rebel.
Furthermore, for three reasons one cannot transcend the lower class of sentient beings, namely, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
For two reasons one cannot transcend the lower realm, namely, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Therefore, these five are called the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
If a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), by virtue of the total extinction of three fetters, has already extinguished six afflictions,
for what reason are three views excluded and only the extinction of three fetters mentioned?

That is to say: the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the clinging to precepts and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and doubt (*vicikitsā*). If one were to speak exhaustively, one should mention all of them.
Why, then, [mention only these]?
The verse says:
"By means of grasping the three: doors, faculties, and [objects].
The commentary states:
There are three categories of afflictions, namely those of one type, two types, and four types; these three are able to grasp all the doors of affliction.

Furthermore, extreme views arise from the view of a self-entity; the grasping of views arises from the attachment to precepts and observances; and false views arise from doubt. Therefore, these are the roots of grasping.
Other masters say: A verse states:

"The desire not to go, confusion regarding the path, and doubt regarding the path—these three matters are obstacles to the practice of liberation; therefore, it is said that the three fetters are extinguished."
The commentary states:
If a person wishes to travel to another place, there are three kinds of obstacles:
first, the lack of desire to go;
Second is the path of delusion, due to taking a divergent path;
third is doubt regarding the path.
For one who wishes to travel in order to seek liberation, there are these three obstacles.
In this context, due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one gives rise to a mind of fear toward liberation and thus does not wish to depart.
Due to the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), one abandons the Noble Path and adopts other paths, thereby becoming confused regarding the path.
Due to doubt, one gives rise to two conflicting paths regarding the mundane and supramundane ways, and thus cannot progress.
By eliminating the obstacles to the practice of the three gates of liberation, one is able to advance to the path of liberation and become a *srotāpanna*.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, in order to manifest the virtues of a *srotāpanna*, spoke of the extinction of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Just as the World-Honored One has already spoken of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), he further speaks in this manner.
The verse says:
There are five higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The commentary says:
Furthermore, there are five fetters pertaining to the higher realms.
What are these five?
The verse says:
"Two are desire for the form and formless realms, along with restlessness, pride, and ignorance.
The commentary explains:

It should be understood that these five are the fetters conducive to the higher realms (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), namely: desire for the realm of form (*rūpārāga*), desire for the formless realm (*ārūpyārāga*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), pride (*māna*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because one cannot attain liberation from the higher realms as long as these five have not been extinguished, these five are taught.
Having thus explained the meaning of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) regarding the higher realms,
what are the bonds (*bandhana*)?
There are three fetters:
first, the fetter of desire, which refers to all desires;
second, the fetter of hatred; [and third, the fetter of ignorance].
The three bonds of ignorance refer to all ignorance.
Why are these three called "bonds"?
The verse says:
"Because of feeling, three bonds are taught.
The commentary states:
Because they are subject to the three types of feeling, three bonds are taught.
Why is this? Because the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of desire is bound to pleasant feeling through both objective conditions (*ālambana*) and association (*samprayoga*);
hatred is bound to painful feeling; and ignorance is the latent tendency bound to neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Desire and hatred are not so.
Furthermore, because they take one’s own continuum as their object, it is necessarily thus.
The meaning of the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) has already been explained previously; the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) shall now be discussed.
These are the major afflictions (*kleśa*) which should be called "afflictions" because they can defile the mind;
the minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) are likewise so named. What are the minor afflictions?
The verse says:
"Other afflicted mental factors are called the aggregate of formations; regarding a small portion of the afflictions, they are said not to be afflictions.
The commentary says:

There are other defiled dharmas distinct from the great afflictions that are subsumed under the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) and are associated with the mind; these are called "minor secondary afflictions" (*upakleśa*), not "great afflictions."
That which was explained regarding the coarse categories has now been addressed;
herein, I shall now explain those [defilements] comprised within the outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and the stains (*upakleśa*).
What phenomena constitute these outbursts?
Afflictions are also called "uprisings of inversion" (*paryavasthāna*), as stated in the Sūtras;
regarding the mind transformed by the uprising of sensual desire (*kāmarāga-paryavasthāna*), it is explained in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*.
The verse says:
Lack of shame and lack of dread, envy and avarice, restlessness and excitement, remorse, languor, and sleep—these eight are the upakleśas (secondary afflictions), along with anger and concealment.
The commentary states:

According to the principles of the *Vibhāṣā*, there are ten types of outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). Eight are as previously mentioned, with the addition of anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*) to make ten.
Among these, lack of shame (*ahrī*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*) have already been explained previously.
The state of mind that finds no joy or satisfaction in the perfect virtues of others is called envy (*īrṣyā*).
The mental fixation that is contrary to the clear understanding [resulting from] the giving of Dharma and material wealth is called stinginess (*mātsarya*).
A mind that is scattered and not tranquil is called *uddhacca* (restlessness).
Sorrow, regret, and lethargy have already been explained previously.
An inability to maintain the body and a subtle dullness of mind is called *middha* (torpor).
It is established that these [mental states] must necessarily be defiled; the same applies to remorse (*kaukṛtya*), with the exception of ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and distress (*paritāpana*).
Hostility toward sentient beings or non-sentient things is termed resentment (*krodha*) and indignation (*upanāha*).
To conceal that which is censurable is called *mrakṣa* (concealment).
These are the ten types of defilements arising from inversion.
The verse says:
Desire-to-be-born (*icchā-utpāda*), lack of shame (*ahrīkya*), agitation (*auddhatya*), and stinginess (*mātsarya*).
The commentary states:
these three secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) of craving (*rāga*).
The verse says:
"Regarding concealment and dispute.
The commentary says:
Other masters say that concealment (*mrakṣa*) is the outflow (*niṣyanda*) of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Other masters say it is the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Still other masters say it is the outflow of both desire and delusion (*rāga* and *moha*).
The sequence has already been explained.
As for those not yet explained, the verse says:
From delusion arise lethargy, sleep, and lack of shame.
The commentary states:
These three secondary afflictions are the outflows of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The verse says:
"Regret arises from doubt.
The commentary states:
If a person lacks understanding regarding a matter, they will inevitably give rise to a mind of regret and anxiety.
The verse says:
Anger and enmity belong to the outflow of hatred (*dveṣa-niḥsaraṇa*).
The commentary says:
These two secondary afflictions arise from hatred.
These ten types, being outflows of the primary afflictions, are therefore called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are six other defilements of affliction (*kleśamala*).
The commentary states:
There are another six types of minor afflictions which are designated as "defilements of affliction. As the verse says:

Deceit (*śāṭhya*), guile (*māyā*), and intoxication (*mada*) are as previously described; [the remaining afflictions are] non-abandonment (*apratinihsarga*), the fault of bondage (*saṃyojana-doṣa*), and oppression (*paritāpana*).
The commentary states:
herein, the feigning of falsehood toward others is termed a deceitful mind (*śāṭhya-citta*).
Deviousness and crookedness are termed *śāṭhya* (deceit).

This affliction prevents one from expressing one's own intentions as they truly are; it employs expedient means to avoid being clearly understood and to cause others to accept things without clear discernment. This has already been explained above.
"Intoxication" is explained as before.
What kind of firm adherence is termed "non-relinquishment"?
Because of this affliction, one does not accept the correct teaching as it has been truly taught; repeatedly contemplating the object of the mind of anger is termed "hostility."
The intention to harm or insult others is called *pradāśa* (maliciousness).
Due to this affliction, one performs acts such as beating or reviling to cause suffering and distress to others.
Among these six types of afflictive stains (*kleśamala*), the verse says:
"From desire arise deceit and intoxication.
The commentary states:
These two minor afflictions arise from self-love; because one deceives and because one disregards others, they are the stains that are outflows of desire.
The verse says:
Hatred gives rise to fetters, faults, and affliction.
The commentary says:
Since these two minor afflictions arise from a mind intent on harming others, they are stains that are outflows of *pratigha* (hostility).
The verse says:
From *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* (clinging to views) comes non-relinquishment; from *dṛṣṭi* (view) arises *śāṭhya* (deceit).
The commentary states:

If a person gives rise to the view of dogmatic attachment (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) regarding the grasping at precepts (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), this person possesses two types of perverse attachments that must be abandoned through reasoned instruction.
Because these two views are unable to abandon such perverse attachments, they are the outflows (*niṣyanda*) and stains of those two views.
As a verse says:
"What dharma is called crookedness?
It refers to views such as wrong view."
Therefore, deceitfulness (*śāṭhya*) is a defilement that is a natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the various views.
Among these, which afflictions are abandoned by which paths?
Regarding the ten afflictions of manifest emergence (*paryavasthāna*) previously mentioned, the verse says:
Among these, there is no distinction regarding shame (*hrī*); as for languor (*styāna*), sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and arousal (*pragraha*), there are two types.
The commentary states:

These five factors are of two kinds—either abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*) or abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*)—because they are associated with the afflictions of both categories.
These afflictions are abandoned through the vision of the truths with which they are associated; that is, they are abandoned by seeing those very truths.
The verse says:
"The others are abandoned through cultivation."
The commentary states:

Other manifest afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) distinct from these five are necessarily abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); namely, envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), regret (*kaukṛtya*), anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), and concealment (*mrakṣa*).
The verse says:
"And the afflictions and stains of mastery.
The commentary says:

These five minor afflictions (upakleśas) are associated exclusively with ignorance; therefore, like the five [other] minor afflictions such as envy (īrṣyā) and so forth, they are abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
The same applies to the autonomous afflictions (svatantra-kleśa) and the stains (mala).
These six types of defilements of affliction are abandoned through the path of cultivation because they are independent, as previously explained.
Regarding all minor afflictions, the verse says: "In the desire realm, those that are unwholesome."
The commentary says:
If they exist within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), they are all entirely unwholesome (*akuśala*).
The verse says:
3.2. The commentary states:
Lethargy, restlessness, and sleep are either unwholesome or neutral.
The verse says:
"In the higher realms, they are indeterminate.
The commentary says:
From the Desire Realm upward, all minor defilements (upakleśa) that exist are indeterminate (avyākṛta).
Among these, how many defilements exist in which realm?
It should be understood as stated in the verse:
Deceit and guile exist from the desire realm up to the first dhyāna.
The commentary states:
these two afflictions exist in the desire realm and the first dhyāna.
How is it known that there is deception regarding the Brahma realm?
The verse says:
Because Brahmā deceives.
The commentary states:
Regarding the Great Brahmā King in the realm of form, it has already been explained previously that he deceived the Venerable Āśvajit by misrepresenting his own nature.
Deceit (*śāṭhya*) is associated with its meaning; this shall now be further explained.
Within that [context], it is also said that there is deceit because it reaches through association (*saṃprayoga*).
The verse says:
Lassitude, restlessness, and intoxication belong to the three realms.
The commentary states:
these three minor afflictions exist throughout all three realms.
The verse says:
"The remaining afflictions exist only in the Desire Realm.
The commentary says:
Among the sixteen [secondary afflictions], excluding the five primary afflictions, the remaining eleven secondary afflictions (upakleśa) function only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Having explained the primary and secondary afflictions, one may ask:
among them, how many arise based on the level of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna-bhūmi*), and how many arise based on the level of the six consciousnesses?
To state it briefly, the verse says:
"The view of extinction, as well as pride and torpor, arise based on the level of the mental consciousness.
The commentary explains:
All afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths arise based on the mental level (*manobhūmi*), and the same applies to pride (*māna*) and torpor (*middha*).
If these two are abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), why is that?
This [set] arises fully within the mind-ground.
The verse says:
"The minor secondary afflictions are autonomous."
The commentary states:

Whenever a minor defilement arises independently, if it is to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one should know that it likewise arises based on the mental ground (*manobhūmi*).
The verse says:
"The others arise based on the six consciousnesses.
The commentary explains:
It should be understood that the remaining major afflictions (*kleśa*) and minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise based on the level of the six consciousnesses.
What are the remaining [afflictions]?

They are desire, hatred, ignorance, and other minor derivative afflictions (*upakleśa*) to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), which are associated with desire and so forth;

furthermore, they include lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and others mentioned among the universal afflictive ground (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*). These are what was previously described.
Regarding the five faculties beginning with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*), which faculty is associated with which affliction (*kleśa*) or secondary affliction (*upakleśa*) therein?
The verse says:
"In the desire realm, [the faculties] are associated with joy (*saumanasya*) and pleasure (*sukha*)."
The commentary states:
It should be understood according to principle that desire is associated with both the faculty of pleasure and the faculty of joy.
The verse says:
"Hatred is associated with sorrow and suffering.
The commentary explains:
Hatred is associated with the two faculties of suffering and sorrow.
Why is this? Because these two afflictions arise from the characteristics of joy and distress, and because they take the six consciousnesses as their basis.
The verse says:
"Ignorance is associated with all.
The commentary states:
Because ignorance is associated with all afflictions, it is therefore associated with the five faculties.
The verse says:
Wrong view is associated with grief and joy.
The commentary says:
Because false view arises based on the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), it is associated with both sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and joy (*saumanasya*).
Accordingly, for those who have performed meritorious deeds and those who have not, the verse states:
"Doubt is associated with sorrow."
The commentary states:
If a person possesses a doubting mind and seeks definitive knowledge, sorrow arises from that doubt.
The verse says:
"The remaining afflictions correspond with joy.
The commentary explains:
"The other various afflictions are associated with joy."
What are the remaining factors?
They are the four views and pride, because they are characterized by joy.
Having thus made this distinction.
With which realms are the various afflictions associated?
The verse says:
They arise in the desire realm.
The commentary states:
The arising of various afflictions (*kleśa*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) should be determined in this manner.
Having explained the afflictions associated with fixed [wrong views], those associated with commonality shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
"All [mental factors] are associated with equanimity.
The commentary says:
All latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) are associated with the faculty of equanimity (*upekṣendriya*).
When the continuum is severed, it is said that those afflictions necessarily arise based on the feeling of equanimity.
If this is so, how are the afflictions of the higher realms to be categorized?
The verse says:
"In accordance with its own stage and those above it, it is associated with the afflictions of the higher stages.
The commentary says:

The various afflictions (*kleśa*) of the higher stages are associated with the feelings (*vedanā*) of their own respective stages; as for the quantity of those feelings according to the faculties (*indriya*) in those stages, it is just as it is in those stages.

If an affliction arises based on the four levels of consciousness (*vijñāna-bhūmi*), one should understand, according to reason, that it is associated with the feelings of the four levels of consciousness.
Having explained that the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) are associated with the faculties, the association of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
The faculty of mental grief (*daurmanasyendriya*) is associated with sorrow, regret, envy, jealousy, anger, vexation, the fetter of resentment, and the stubbornness of not relinquishing.
The commentary states:

Such afflictions as these are associated with the faculty of mental distress (*daurmanasyendriya*), because they arise by taking the aspect of sorrow and affliction as their object and because they arise based on the level of the mental consciousness (*manobhūmi*).
The verse says:
Avarice (*mātsarya*) is the opposite of this meaning.
The commentary states:
This affliction is associated with the faculty of joy (*saumanasyendriya*), because it belongs to the category of craving and attachment, and because it arises conditioned by the appearance of joy.
The verse says:
Deceit, guile, concealment, and sleep—these three types.
The commentary says:
These four afflictions are associated with the two faculties of joy (*saumanasya*) and sorrow (*daurmanasya*). Why is this?
At times one deceives others with a joyful mind, and at times with a mind of sorrow and distress; even sleep is likewise.
The verse says:
"Intoxication, joy, and pleasure.
The commentary says:
If one is intoxicated while in the third dhyāna, it is associated with the faculty of pleasure (sukhendriya).
If in a lower stage, it is associated with the faculty of joy (saumanasyendriya).
If in a higher stage, it is associated with the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya).
Why is this? The verse says:
"Equanimity is universal."
The commentary states:
All secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) are associated with the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*). Why is this?
The faculty of equanimity has no place of obstruction, just as ignorance does not.
The verse says:
The remaining four or five faculties correspond accordingly.
The commentary states:

Lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), lethargy (*styāna*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)—these four afflictions are associated with the five faculties, because they belong to the category of the universal unwholesome (*akuśala-mahābhūmika*) and the category of the universal afflictive (*kleśa-mahābhūmika*).
Regarding the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) taught in the sūtras— namely, sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt—
is it intended that these include sloth, torpor, restlessness, and doubt as they are subsumed under all three realms, or are they taken only as they are subsumed under the desire realm?
This unadulterated, complete accumulation of evil constitutes the five hindrances (*pañca nīvaraṇāni*), because the sūtras state that they are exclusively unwholesome.
The verse says:
"The five hindrances exist within the desire realm."
The commentary states:
Since the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are not established in other realms, they exist only within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Furthermore, for what reason are the two minor afflictions (*upakleśa*) of torpor (*middha*) and lethargy (*styāna*) established as a single hindrance?
The same applies to restlessness and remorse.
The verse says:
Regarding the objects of their respective antidotes, two are combined into one.
The commentary states:
These two pairs are combined into one because they share the same antidote, the same nutriment, and the same function.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
Regarding sloth and torpor, there is one nutriment and one non-nutriment.
What dharma is the nutriment for the hindrance of sloth and torpor?
There are five kinds of dharmas: namely, languor, unease, yawning, lack of moderation in eating, and mental depression.
What is the nutriment for the hindrance of torpor and languor?
It is the perception of light.
Their objective basis is also one: namely, that these two minor afflictions cause the mind to sink.
The two minor afflictions of restlessness and remorse are also said to have the same nutriment and the same non-nutriment.
What phenomena constitute the nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse?
There are four: thoughts of relatives, thoughts of one's country, thoughts of immortality, and frequently recollecting past experiences—namely, play, pleasure, and service.
What dharma is not the nutriment for the hindrance of restlessness and remorse? It is śamatha.
These two also share the same objective.

Why is this? Because these two are alike in their ability to prevent the mind from becoming tranquil; therefore, they are combined into one hindrance (*nīvaraṇa*) as a single antidote to the same object of nourishment.
If all afflictions (*kleśa*) were hindrances, why are only five designated as such?
The verse says:
Because doubt arises regarding the collection of phenomena that can be destroyed.
The commentary says:
By the hindrance of sensual desire and ill will, the aggregate of virtue is destroyed.
By the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the aggregate of wisdom is destroyed.
By the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the aggregate of concentration is destroyed.
If concentration and wisdom are absent, one gives rise to doubt and confusion regarding the Four Noble Truths; consequently, liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation are destroyed.
For this reason, the five [hindrances] are called "obstructions" (nīvaraṇa).

Within this interpretation, since it contradicts the collection of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), the hindrance of restlessness-and-regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa*) ought to appear before the obstacle to wisdom (*prajñā-āvaraṇa*).
Therefore, other masters say:
"They respectively destroy the collection of meditative concentration and the collection of wisdom."
Why is this? For it is said in the sūtras:
"If a person practices meditative concentration, they should fear drowsiness and lethargy."
If a person practices the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), they fear restlessness and remorse (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*).
Other masters offer a different interpretation of the meaning of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*);
how do they interpret it?

If a person is in the state of the six consciousnesses operating, then due to grasping at signs within objects that are either attractive or repulsive, if they are in a state of abiding, the hindrances of sensual desire and ill-will arise with those [signs] as their primary cause.

First, when the mind is about to enter the state of meditative concentration; second, once it has entered concentration, because one practices śamatha and vipaśyanā in an improper manner, there arise lethargy-and-drowsiness, restlessness-and-regret, and doubt. These respectively obstruct śamatha and vipaśyanā; therefore, liberation and the knowledge and vision of liberation cannot be accomplished.
Therefore, it is said that there are five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

Now, one should reflect upon this meaning: these are universal afflictions (*kleśa*) belonging to a different realm (*visabhāga-dhātu*), which are abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodha-darśana*) and the path (*mārga-darśana*); they take contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) as their objects. When one examines those objects at such a time, those afflictions are not abandoned.
At the time of their cessation, those objects cannot be observed.
For this reason, how could they be ceased?
It is not necessarily the case that all afflictions are ceased merely by discerning their objects.
Why is this? Because the various afflictions are extinguished by means of four causes. What are these four?
If one considers the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-heya*), they are abandoned by way of three causes.
The verse says:
"By discerning their objects, by the cessation of the cognitive subject that takes those objects as its focus, and by the cessation of the afflictions regarding those objects."
The commentary states:

Herein, "by means of discerning those objects" refers to the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of suffering and its origin; these are able to arise taking their own level as an object, as well as taking uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) as their objects.
"Because that which takes it as an object ceases" refers to the universal afflictions (*sarvatraga*) belonging to a different realm.
Why? Because the universal afflictions belonging to one's own realm are the objects of those [afflictions].
If that which is taken as an object is extinguished, the affliction that takes it as its cognitive support is likewise extinguished, because the affliction regarding that object has ceased.
That "extinction" refers to the cessation through seeing.
As for the afflictions to be abandoned by the path, they arise taking contaminated objects as their cognitive support.
Why is this? The afflictions that arise conditioned by uncontaminated objects constitute their domain; if these afflictions are extinguished, those [objects] are likewise extinguished.
How, then, can the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation be extinguished?
The verse says:
"Because the antidote arises, [the afflictions] are exhausted.
The commentary explains:
If this category of afflictions arises when the path of antidote is produced, these afflictions are immediately extinguished.
Which affliction is that which is to be countered?
Which path is that which is capable of countering it?
The most superior and highest grade of afflictions (*kleśa*) is that which is to be counteracted, while the most inferior and lowest grade of the Path is the counteragent.
This point shall be explained in detail later.
How many types of such counteragents are there?
The verse says:
Cessation, maintenance, distancing, and aversion—these four are the antidotes; their sequence is explained differently.
The commentary says:
First is the counteractive of cessation (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Second is the counteractive of maintenance (*dhāraṇa-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path subsequent to that; by means of this path, one is able to maintain the cessation attained by the preceding path.

Third is the counteractive of distancing (*dūrībhāva-pratipakṣa*), which refers to all paths subsequent to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); for they cause the possession (*prāpti*) of the afflictions already abandoned to become distantly separated.
Other masters say:
"This is itself liberation; this path causes the possession of the afflictions to become most distantly separated."

The fourth is the antidote of revulsion, which means that by means of this path one contemplates the defects inherent in all the elements (*dhātu*) and thereby gives rise to a mind of weary detachment (*nirveda*).
Furthermore, the four antidotes should follow this sequence.

First, the antidote of aversion (*vidūṣaṇā-pratipakṣa*), which refers to the path of expedient means (*prayoga-mārga*) cultivated by taking suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) as objects.
Second, the antidote of abandonment (*prahāṇa-pratipakṣa*), which is the aforementioned path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Third, the antidote of maintenance (*ādhāra-pratipakṣa*), which is the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The fourth is the antidote of distancing, which refers to the path of excellence.
When a defilement is in the process of being extinguished, where can it be extinguished?
The verse says:
"One should eliminate delusion regarding one's own objective sphere.
The commentary asks: Why is this so?

When the various afflictions (*kleśa*) are in the process of being extinguished, they cannot be made to disengage from or associate with the mental continuum (*saṃtati*), because their location is unknowable.
However, they can be made to disengage from their objects (*ālambana*), whereby those afflictions are unable to arise again by taking that object as a condition.
If that were so, future afflictions could be separated from their objects;
but as for those that have already passed, how can they be separated from their objects?
If you say that by discerning the object, these afflictions can be separated from it—
This point is not necessarily fixed; therefore, this meaning should be explained.
To what extent should it be said that these afflictions have been extinguished?
If the afflictions arise based on one's own continuum, they are severed by the cessation of their acquisition (*prāpti*).

If afflictions arise in dependence upon the continuum of another, then all forms and all non-defiled phenomena that can take them as objects are said to be "permanently abandoned" by that person, because the afflictions within their own continuum have been extinguished.
If that is so, how many kinds of "remoteness" (dūratā) are there?
The verse says:

Because of difference in characteristics and because of antidotes; because of different locations and different times; the four great elements, the precepts, and location; and the two [kinds of] time—these are the meanings of remoteness.
The commentary states:
Regarding "distance by way of characteristics," it is like the four great elements; because their characteristics differ, they are said to be mutually distant even though they arise together.

Regarding "distance by way of opposition," it is like the case of ethical discipline (*śīla*) in relation to the violation of discipline, and the violation of discipline in relation to ethical discipline is likewise.

Regarding distance in terms of location: this refers to phenomena that are most distant from one another; they are said to be "distant" because their locations are separate, such as the eastern and western oceans.
Regarding distance in terms of time: for example, the past and the future are described as being distant.
In what period are these two distant?
They are distant in the present period.
If [the past] has already ceased without interval and [the future] is about to arise, how can they be distant in relation to the present?
It is distant due to the difference in world-systems (*lokadhātu*), not because it has long since ceased or will only arise after a long time.
If that were so, one would also have to establish the present as being distant.
It is not so; it is called "distant" by way of its functional capacity (*kāritra*).
If that is so, how is the sense of "proximity" established for unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)?
Because they possess acquisition (*prāpti*) throughout all times.
If that is so, it should likewise apply to the past and the future; what then of space (*ākāśa*)?

If that is so, then the past and the future are mutually distant because they are separated by the present; the present is near to both of them because it is proximate to them, and unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) are near because they are not separated by anything.
If that were so, since the past and future are proximate to the present, they should possess both meanings.
If one holds this position, the argument may be valid;
however, regarding the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, the future is distant because it has not yet arrived.
Because the past has already ceased and perished, it is distant.
Since one practices with urgency and constancy, the afflictions are extinguished as one advances toward the superior path; do they not likewise become progressively more refined?
This is not so. Why? The verse says:
"All afflictions are extinguished by the same [path].
The commentary explains:
If those afflictions are to be extinguished, and if this path is the path for their extinction, then by means of this path, they are extinguished by the same [path].
The verse says:
"One acquires again that permanent separation.
The commentary says:
During how many periods is it said that one may receive [the precepts] again?
What are these six?
The verse says:
"During the six moments of the arising of the antidote, the attainment of the fruit, and the refinement of the faculties.
The commentary states:
"The arising of the antidote" refers here to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).
"Attaining the fruits" refers to the four fruits of śrāmaṇya.
"Refining the faculties" refers to cultivating the path of superior faculties.
During these six occasions, one repeatedly attains permanent separation from the various afflictions.
This attainment should be understood according to reason:

while some individuals attain it during six periods, others attain this permanent liberation even during as few as two periods; thus, within these various distinct stages, one attains what is termed the "knowledge of permanent abandonment."

There are two kinds of permanent abandonment (*atyanta-prahāṇa*): first, permanent abandonment by means of knowledge (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), and second, permanent abandonment by means of cessation (*nirodha-prahāṇa*).

Permanent abandonment by means of knowledge refers to untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*); permanent abandonment by means of cessation refers solely to cessation (*nirodha*). These combined are termed "knowledge of permanent abandonment" (*prahāṇa-jñāna*), because the cause is predicated here of the effect.
Is every cessation necessarily the knowledge of permanent abandonment?
How is this explained?
The verse says:
"Nine are permanently severed.
The commentary says:
What are these nine?
The verse here says:
"In the desire realm, the cessation of the first two categories of afflictions constitutes one [fruit].
The commentary explains:

Regarding the abandonment of the first two categories of afflictions within the desire realm—namely, the afflictions to be abandoned through the vision of the truths of suffering and origin—this constitutes one knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*).
The verse states:
"The latter two abandonments consist of two."
The commentary states:

Within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are two types of abandonment consisting of the cessation and dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through the vision of cessation (*nirodhadarśana*); and there is a third consisting of the cessation and dissociation from the afflictions abandoned through the vision of the path (*mārgadarśana*).
Thus, for the afflictions associated with the desire realm that are abandoned through the vision of the truths, there are three knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*).
The verse says:
"The same applies to the three above.
The commentary says:

The establishment of the three types of knowledge of perpetual abandonment (*parijñā*) regarding the cessation and separation from the defilements associated with the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned by the vision of the truths is likewise as follows:

the cessation and separation from the defilements to be abandoned by the vision of suffering and its origin constitute one; the cessation and separation from the defilements to be abandoned by the vision of cessation constitute two; and the cessation and separation from the defilements to be abandoned by the vision of the path constitute three.
Thus, through the abandonment of the defilements to be eliminated by the vision of the truths within these three realms, six knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) are established.
The verse says:

"The remaining [defilements] of the lower realm, the form realm, and all [defilements] of the formless realm, when completely extinguished, constitute three further knowledges of permanent abandonment."
The commentary states:

The abandonment of the lower-tier fetters constitutes the first; the abandonment of the flow toward the form realm constitutes the second, meaning the permanent severance of desire for the form realm;
and the abandonment of all flows constitutes the third, meaning the total exhaustion and permanent severance of all fetters.

Why is the abandonment of the defilements to be eliminated through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) in the form and formless realms established as a distinct "knowledge of permanent abandonment" (*atyantaprahāṇajñāna*), whereas those to be eliminated through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) are not?
This is because the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*) for the defilements eliminated through the path of cultivation are not uniform.
Regarding these nine knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*), the preceding verse states:
"Six are the fruits of patience" (*ṣaḍ kṣāntiphala*).
The commentary explains:
Its nature is the abandonment of the afflictions to be eliminated by the vision of the truths; it is the fruit of the eight patiences.
The verse says:
"The other [fruits] are those of the knowledges."
The commentary states:

The three types of knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*), such as the abandonment of the lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-kleśa-prahāṇa*), are fruits of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*); therefore, they are called "fruits of knowledge" (*jñāna-phala*).
If this is so, why are they also said to be "fruits of patience" (*kṣānti-phala*)?

Because patience (*kṣānti*) is of the same category as wisdom (*jñāna*), the activity of wisdom is described in terms of patience; this is like describing the activities of a king by means of his retinue.
Furthermore, it is because [patience] shares the same fruit as wisdom.
The verse says:
"All [results] are not attained by the *anāgamya*; the original dhyānas have five or eight.
The commentary says:
If judged according to the intention of the *Vibhāṣā*, all nine grades of knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) are the fruits of the *anāgamya* concentration. Why is this?
Because by relying on this stage, one is able to eradicate the two categories of afflictions—those abandoned through seeing and those abandoned through cultivation—belonging to the three realms.

If one discusses the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas, there are five; that is, they have the nature of the abandonment of the afflictions associated with the form and formless realms, because the abandonment of all afflictions of the desire realm is not the fruit of the *anāgamya* (preliminary) concentration.
The Venerable Ghoṣaka maintains that the eight knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) are the fruits of the fundamental dhyānas. Why is this?

The intention of this master is to clarify that if a person who has already abandoned desire enters the contemplation of the Four Truths, all afflictions of the desire realm pertaining to the truths are extinguished and abandoned; this is the fruit of the path of seeing.

Because this meditative absorption serves as the cause for its attainment and results in the fruit of stainless disjunction (*visamyoga*), this knowledge of permanent abandonment belongs to the fruit of that specific stage.

The cessation and disjunction from the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-kleśa*) are, however, solely the fruit of the threshold concentration (*anāgamya*). It should be understood that the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*) is analogous to the [fundamental] concentrations.
Regarding the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the verse says:
"The fruit of the formless attainments is one.
The commentary says:
The path and fruit of the sphere of infinite space constitute one knowledge of permanent abandonment—namely, the knowledge of permanent abandonment regarding the detachment from the realm of form.
The verse says:
"The three fundamental [attainments] and one of the formless."
The commentary states:
The three fundamental formless absorptions have only one knowledge of permanent abandonment as their fruit; that is, the extinction of all fetters is their fruit.
The verse says:
"All [are] the fruits of the noble path.
The commentary states:
All nine knowledges of permanent abandonment are fruits of the noble path.
The verse says:
"The worldly path is twofold.
The commentary says:

If discussed in terms of the mundane path (*laukikamārga*), the abandonment of the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya*) and the abandonment of the defilements of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*)—these two types of knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) are solely the fruits of the mundane path.
The verse says:
"The same applies to the [other] categories."
The commentary states:
The fruit of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) also has two [results], namely the last two.
The verse says:
"Three are the dharma-knowledges.
The commentary states:

Because the dharma-knowledge, by its general capacity, serves as the antidote to the afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) within the three realms, it takes the final three knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) as its fruit.
The verse says:
"Two types; six and five are the knowledges of permanent abandonment.
The commentary says:

The path belonging to the category of dharma-knowledge has six knowledges of permanent abandonment as its fruit, namely, the fruits of the dharma-patience and dharma-knowledge. The path belonging to the category of subsequent knowledge has five as its fruit, namely, the fruits of the subsequent patience and subsequent knowledge.
Because it is spoken of as a "type" (*jāti*), it comprehensively includes both patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
Why is a single abandonment (*prahāṇa*) not established as the "knowledge of permanent severance"?
Because the fruit of patience is established as "cessation" (*nirodha*).
Therefore, the verse says:

"Because it attains the separation from the outflows (*āsrava*), because it diminishes the portion of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), and because it uproots the two causes, it is the knowledge of abandonment (*prahāṇajñāna*).
The commentary states:
If cessation possesses all three causes, it may be called "knowledge of permanent abandonment" (*parijñā*).

Ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) lack cessation through uncontaminated attainment (*anāsrava-prāpti*), nor do they diminish any portion of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*); therefore, the cessation attained by ordinary beings is not termed "knowledge of permanent abandonment."

If a Noble One has the cessation that is the fruit of patience, within this cessation—and even while abiding in the patience of the subsequent knowledge of suffering (duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti)—there is the acquisition of the untainted permanent detachment; yet, there has not yet been any impairment of the factors pertaining to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

The subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhe ’nvaya-jñāna*) possesses these two meanings, but lacks the meaning of having extracted the two causes, because the pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*) to be abandoned by the vision of the origin has not yet been eliminated. In all other subsequent knowledges (*dharma-anvaya-jñāna*), all three meanings are present; therefore, the attainment of cessation and detachment within this stage is designated by the name "knowledge of permanent abandonment" (*parijñā*).
This cessation is the fruit of knowledge; by virtue of the first three causes and the fourth cause, it is termed "knowledge of permanent abandonment.
The verse says:
"Because it transcends the realms."
The commentary states:

If a person is one who has departed from the realms (*dhātu*), because they have become free from desire for all realms, they attain separation from the two fetters (*saṃyojana*); that is said to be the fifth cause.
If it were the case that one is separated from the specific afflictions that take those [realms] as their objects, this point would be acceptable.

However, since this "realm of renunciation" (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*) does not differ from the uprooting of the two causes, there is no need to establish the meaning of the "realm of renunciation" as a fifth cause.
Which person possesses how many knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*)?
The verse says:
From none up to five are associated with those in the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
The commentary states:
Ordinary persons do not possess association with the knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*).

Even if a noble one is within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), up until the stage of the acceptance of the dharma regarding origination (*samudaye dharmakṣānti*), they likewise do not possess association with this.

Regarding the dharma-knowledge of origination (*samudaya-dharmajñāna*), it is associated with one; regarding the subsequent knowledge of origination (*samudaya-anvayajñāna*), it is associated with two; regarding the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharmajñāna*), it is associated with three; regarding the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvayajñāna*), it is associated with four; regarding the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharmajñāna*), it is associated with five; and regarding the subsequent patience toward the path (*mārga-anvayakṣānti*), it is also associated with five, because one has not yet left the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*).
The verse says:
"Abiding in cultivation, one is further associated with six, up to being associated with one or two.
The commentary says:

If a noble person is in the stage of cultivation—that is, when in possession of the knowledge of the path (*mārgānvaya-jñāna*) and so forth, associated with six [knowledges]—until they have either not yet abandoned desire for the desire realm or have already regressed; subsequently, from this stage, when they reach the state of having abandoned desire for the desire realm, whether before or after, they become associated with one knowledge: the knowledge of the permanent abandonment through dissociation from the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇa-parijñā*).

If one attains the fruit of arhatship, one further possesses one additional application, namely, the application of the knowledge of the permanent abandonment of all fetters (*sarvasaṃyojana-prahāṇajñāna*).

If one regresses due to the active afflictions of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one possesses only one application, namely, the application of the knowledge of the permanent abandonment of the lower-tier afflictions (*avarabhāgīya-prahāṇajñāna*).

If one reaches the stage of detachment from the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one is associated with two [knowledges]: namely, the knowledge of the permanent abandonment of the lower-tier afflictions (*avarabhāgīya-kleśa*) and the knowledge of the permanent abandonment of the afflictions of the form realm.
If one regresses due to the active afflictions of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), one is likewise associated only with these two.

For what reason are only the Anāgāmin and the Arhat established as being associated with each individual knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*), rather than being established as associated with many?
It is for this reason.
The verse says:
"Their calculation is based on the separation from the realms, up to the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The commentary says:
The knowledge of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*) is established as a single unit based on two causes. What are these two?

Because both of these stages—the detachment from the various realms and the attainment of the fruits of śrāmaṇya—possess these two causes, all cessations and abandonments are combined and established as each individual knowledge of permanent abandonment.
Furthermore, which person abandons how many knowledges of permanent abandonment (*parijñā*), and likewise acquires how many?
The verse says:
"Some abandon one, two, five, or six; none acquire five."
The commentary states:
"Abandoning one" refers to when one falls back from the fruit of arhatship, or falls back from the state of being free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*).

"Abandoning two" refers to an anāgāmin who, having already become free from desire for the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), subsequently falls back from the state of being free from desire for the realm of desire.

Regarding the "abandonment of five": this refers to a person who has already previously become detached from the desires of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and subsequently abides in the stage of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*). Why is this?
Because at the moment this person attains the abandonment of the lower-tier fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), they abandon the first five knowledges of permanent eradication (*parijñā*).
Regarding the "abandonment of six": if a person practices in successive stages, by becoming free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), the abandonment is as it is with the acquisition.
There is also the case of "attaining one," which occurs when a person attains what has not been attained before.
There are those who obtain two, namely, when a person falls away from detachment from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
There are those who obtain six, namely, when a person falls away from the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
There is no falling away from six; one may regain five.
The Treatise on the Knowledge of Permanent Abandonment is concluded.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Fifteen; *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Sixteen.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.

Chapter Six: Distinguishing the Persons of the Noble Path and its Fruits, Part One. This meaning has already been explained: namely, that as it is called "cessation," it is termed "knowledge of permanent abandonment."
Furthermore, regarding this point, the verse says:
"The cessation of afflictions has been explained as occurring through the vision and cultivation of the four truths.
The commentary states:
The various afflictions are of two kinds: first, those to be abandoned through the vision of the truths; second, those to be abandoned through the path of cultivation.
This meaning has already been explained in detail previously, and their abandonment is likewise so.
The two paths—those of seeing and cultivation—are now to be explained.
Are these two paths with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
It is for this reason that the following statement is made.
The verse says:
There are two kinds of the path of cultivation; the path of seeing is exclusively outflow-free (*anāsrava*).
The commentary says:
Why is it that there are two kinds of cultivation of the path?
Because there is cultivation based on the mundane and cultivation based on the supramundane.
The path of seeing is exclusively supramundane, as it is able to counteract the afflictions of the three realms.
Furthermore, it is able to simultaneously eliminate the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned by the vision of the truths.
Why is this? Because the mundane path lacks such capacity; this is due to the strength of the afflictions and the weakness of the mundane path.
It was previously stated that [liberation] is attained by seeing the four truths. What phenomena are designated as the "four truths"?
The verse says:
It has already been stated that there are four truths.
The commentary says:
Where is this stated?
It is stated within the analysis of contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena.
How is it explained?
As the verse says:
"The untainted phenomena are the Noble Path"; this is stated according to their own names.
The Truth of Cessation has also been explained, as the verse says:
"Cessation through deliberation is defined as eternal separation, corresponding respectively to each of the fetters.
The Truth of Suffering and the Truth of Origination have also been explained, as the verse says:
The truth of suffering, the truth of origination, the world, the locus of views, and the three realms of existence—does the sequence of these four truths correspond to what was previously stated?
It is said: no.
Nevertheless, there is another meaning.
The verse says:
"That is, the truth of suffering and the truth of origination; the truths of cessation and the path are likewise."
The commentary states:
Herein, this sequence is as previously explained.
The essential nature of the Four Noble Truths is likewise explained here.
To clarify this meaning, these words are provided; they need not be explained further.
The verse says:
"In accordance with the sequence of correct contemplation."
The commentary states:

If one observes that this truth arises first based on prior conditions, then by virtue of that observation, this truth is established as being "prior"; the same applies to the subsequent three truths.
Otherwise, one should have first explained the cause and subsequently explained the result.
Why is this? There are some dharmas whose sequence is established according to their arising, such as the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*).
There are other dharmas whose sequence is explained according to the manifestation of their characteristics, such as the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Why is there no such definition?
It is because first one generates the desire to extinguish what has already arisen, and subsequently one generates the desire to prevent what has not yet arisen from arising.
There are other dharmas that establish their sequence in accordance with their correct explanation, such as, for example, the Eightfold Noble Path.
Now, the Four Noble Truths are taught according to the sequence of correct contemplation during practice.
Furthermore, what is the reason that the cultivation of contemplation follows such a sequence?
It is because this craving, which resides in various places, is capable of binding; through the liberation from both the binder and the bound, one seeks liberation on this basis.
In the stage of observation, the initial sequence for developing contemplation is as follows: therefore, one first discerns suffering (*duḥkha*).
Since one asks what phenomena constitute the cause of this suffering, one next discerns the origin (*samudaya*).
By what dharma is this suffering extinguished?
Therefore, next, one discriminates cessation (*nirodha*).
By what dharma is this cessation realized?
Therefore, next comes the investigation of the path.
For example, just as one first observes an illness, then seeks out its causes and conditions, its cessation, and the medicine for it;
so too are the Four Noble Truths revealed by the Blessed One, the Buddha, in the sūtras.
In which sutra? In the *Cikitsā-sūtra*.
The sutra says:
If a physician possesses the fourfold qualities, he is able to extract and treat the thorns of others.
What are these fourfold qualities? First, knowing the disease;
second, knowing the causes and conditions of the disease; third, knowing the cessation of the disease; and fourth, knowing the medicine that treats the disease, as explained at length in the sutra.

Just as one sequentially discerns the Four Noble Truths during the stage of investigation, the sequence of seeing the Four Noble Truths during the stage of meditative cultivation is likewise; this is due to the proficiency gained through prior practice, just as, for example, one lets a horse run unimpeded over ground it has already traversed.
For one who possesses right contemplation, what is the meaning of this phrase?
Its meaning is "to proceed toward perfect awakening.
Why is this exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) and not tainted (*sāsrava*)?

By means of this, one proceeds toward nirvāṇa; it is called "right" (*samyak*) because it arises by taking the true object as its condition, and it is called "awakening" (*bodha*) because it is the knowing of what was previously unknown, for it is able to penetrate the pure object as it truly is.

In this context, the appropriated aggregates that are the fruit are called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), and the appropriated aggregates that are the cause are called the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), because suffering arises from the accumulation of these [aggregates].
Therefore, these two truths differ by virtue of the distinction between the meanings of fruit and cause; they do not differ by way of being distinct entities.
The two truths of cessation and the path differ not only by name but also by substance.
It is stated in the Sūtras that there are four noble truths.
What is the meaning of this statement?
This dharma is exclusively the truth for the noble ones; therefore, the Sūtra calls them the "Noble Truths" (*āryasatya*).
If that is so, are these four false for other people?
They are truths for all people, because they are free from inversion.
In this context, because other persons cannot perceive in the manner that the noble ones do, these are said to be truths only for the noble ones;
they are not so for those who are not noble, due to their inverted perception.
As a verse says:
"What the noble ones call happiness, others call suffering;
what others call purity, the noble ones call suffering."
There are two truths that are exclusively noble truths (*āryasatya*), and there are three truths that are both noble and non-noble truths; such is the explanation of other masters.

If feeling (*vedanā*) were only a portion of the intrinsic nature of suffering (*duḥkha-svabhāva*), how could it be said that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) associated with outflows (*sāsrava*) are called the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*)?

The verse says: Suffering corresponds to the three types of suffering; as is appropriate, it exists without exception in what is desirable, what is undesirable, and all other conditioned phenomena. The commentary says: [Suffering] corresponds to the three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). As is appropriate, these exist without exception in all things—whether they are desirable, undesirable, or otherwise—all conditioned phenomena that flow on.

There are three types of suffering: first, the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); second, the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); and third, the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*). Because they correspond, in accordance with reality, to these two types of suffering without exception, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) that are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*) are suffering.

Among these, that which is pleasant is suffering by virtue of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*); that which is unpleasant is suffering by virtue of the suffering of suffering itself (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); and that which is other than these two is suffering by virtue of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
What are the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is neither?
They are the three feelings (vedanā), in their respective order, because they are associated with the three feelings.
All conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta) that are subject to outflows (sāsrava) receive the designations "agreeable," "disagreeable," and so forth.
Why is this? Because this transformation of pleasant feeling is itself suffering.
As the Sūtra says:
Pleasant feeling is pleasant when it arises and pleasant while it persists, but painful when it ceases.
Painful feeling is painful by its very nature; that is to say, it is painful when it arises and painful while it persists.
Neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is suffering by way of its conditioned nature (*saṃskāra*), because it arises dependent upon causes and conditions.
As the Sūtra says:
"That which is impermanent is suffering."
The same should be said for feelings and the conditioned phenomena associated with them.
Other masters say:
"Painful feeling is suffering solely by virtue of its nature as suffering; pleasant feeling is suffering solely by virtue of its change; and even the suffering of conditioned formations is likewise."
Because the pleasant and the unpleasant are not universal, these two are called "partial suffering.

Since all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the former two types of sensation are also suffering by virtue of the suffering inherent in formations, this one is called "complete suffering."
This suffering can be seen only by the Noble Ones.
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"For example, a single eyelash, when placed upon the palm of the hand, is not perceived by a person; [but when it enters the eye, it causes great pain]."
If this were to fall into the eye, it would cause injury and distress.
Ordinary beings are like the palm of the hand; they do not perceive the eyelash of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).
Noble ones are like the eye itself; because of this, they give rise to revulsion and fear.

Why is this? Ordinary beings give rise to a sense of suffering and fear toward the five aggregates of the Avīci hell, yet they do not even equal the sense of suffering and fear that noble ones give rise to toward the aggregates of the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra).

If that were so, then the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) should also be established as having the nature of suffering due to conditioned existence (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*), because it is conditioned. This is not correct. Why?
Suffering has the characteristic of being contrary to the mind; therefore, the Path is not suffering.
Why is this? Because when this Path arises, it does not contradict the intention of the Noble Ones, and because it is capable of leading to the complete extinction of all suffering.

If a noble one observes nirvāṇa through its characteristic of tranquility, then that phenomenon which the noble one observes as suffering through its characteristic of suffering—it is only the cessation of this phenomenon that the noble one observes as tranquility.
If there is pleasant feeling among all phenomena, why is it said that there is only the Noble Truth of Suffering?
It is because pleasure is so slight; for example, even though there are mung beans within a heap of black beans, it is still called a "heap of black beans."
Other masters say this.
Why? For what wise person, by means of the slight pleasure produced when an abscess is gradually moistened with cold water, would consider that abscess itself to be pleasure?
Regarding this, the masters of other schools state a verse:
"Because it is a cause of suffering, because it is mixed with manifold sufferings,
and because it is craved by those who suffer— therefore, pleasure is said to be suffering."

All that exists, whether accompanied by suffering or pleasure, the Noble Ones perceive as suffering because it has the single flavor of the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*); therefore, suffering is established as a Noble Truth, while pleasure is not.
How is it that one contemplates feelings whose intrinsic nature is pleasure as suffering through the aspect of suffering?
Because they are tainted (*sāsrava*) and impermanent, they are contrary to the mind and are therefore suffering.
For example, just as one contemplates form, perception, and so forth through the aspect of suffering, although form and the rest are not themselves suffering in the same way that painful feeling is.
As for what you have said—that it is suffering because it has suffering as its cause—this meaning is not correct.
Why? Because this grasping possesses the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*), not the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*).
How do the noble ones (ārya) conceive of suffering within births in the form and formless realms?
For what reason?
Because for those beings, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are no longer the cause of suffering.
Furthermore, it is said in the Sūtras:
"What is the use of the suffering of conditioned existence (saṃskāra-duḥkhatā)? If noble ones perceive pleasure as suffering because of its impermanence."
What is the distinction between the characteristic of impermanence and the characteristic of suffering?
It is impermanent because its nature is to arise and perish;
it is suffering because, being subject to the outflows, it is contrary to the mind.
If one perceives impermanence, that which is perceived will contradict one's expectations; therefore, the perception of impermanence can induce the perception of suffering.
Other schools maintain that there is no such thing as pleasant feeling at all, and that all feelings are exclusively suffering.
How is this known?
By means of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
How is it known by means of scripture?
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said:
"Whatever feeling there may be, all are synonyms for suffering.
Furthermore, there is another teaching: one should contemplate pleasant feelings through the characteristic of suffering.
There is another specific explanation: to conceive and cling to the notion of pleasure within suffering is called a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
This is established by the authority of the *Āgama*.
How is it established by reasoning?
Because the causes of pleasure are not fixed. Why is this?
Whatever food, drink, cold, heat, and so forth sentient beings possess, they conceive of as the cause of pleasure.
If used in excess or at an improper time, these causes further become causes of suffering.

This interpretation is not tenable; for it would imply that due to the increase of a cause of pleasure, or through its equilibrium, suffering arises at all times. Therefore, from the very beginning, they are all causes of suffering and not causes of pleasure.
At a later time, this suffering gradually increases until it finally becomes manifest.
The distinctions in postures should be understood in the same way regarding the remedies for suffering and the variations of suffering, because one gives rise to the perception of pleasure therein.

Why is this? Because with respect to all worldly requisites for life, such as food and drink, as long as one has not yet been oppressed by distinct forms of suffering, if they are experienced, they are not permitted to be classified as pleasure.
Separate suffering refers to the suffering born of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, fatigue, and sensual desire.
Therefore, fools give rise to the perception of pleasure toward the remedies for suffering, rather than toward pleasure itself;
the same applies to the various forms of suffering, wherein all ordinary worldlings give rise to the perception of pleasure, just as one shifts a heavy burden from one shoulder to the other.
Therefore, by this reasoning, it is certain that pleasure does not exist.
The Abhidharma masters maintain that pleasure definitely exists; this position is logical.
How is this known?
In this regard, one should question those who deny the existence of pleasure:
"What phenomenon is called suffering? If you say:
That which has the nature of oppression and affliction is called suffering.
How, then, can this pleasure be oppressive? If you say:
Harm is suffering.
Since pleasure is capable of increasing [well-being], how can it be harmful? If you say:
That which is not beloved is suffering. Since this very thing is what is beloved, how can it be suffering?

That which is beloved later becomes no longer beloved for the Noble One—namely, at the time of detachment from desire. Therefore, this pleasure is not established; because it is not established, it is not beloved, and not for any other reason.
Why is this? If feeling were by its very nature something desirable, then that feeling, by its very nature, could never at any time or through any cause become undesirable.
This principle must be so.
Why? Because the Noble Ones loathe this feeling by means of its distinct characteristic of fault.
He contemplates this feeling as a basis for negligence, something accomplished through great effort, subject to change, and impermanent.
For these reasons, it is not beloved, nor does it possess a desirable intrinsic nature.
If this feeling were inherently unattractive by its very nature, no one would ever give rise to desire for it, and there would be no need to cultivate detachment from it.
Since one observes its faults through a different principle, we know that pleasant feeling definitely exists by virtue of its own essential characteristic.
Regarding what you have said— that the Blessed One, the World-Honored One,
stated that whatever sensation there may be is merely another name for suffering—
the World-Honored One himself has clarified the meaning of this sutra.
The Sūtra says:

"Ānanda! It is based on the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and the transformation of the conditioned that I have taught: whatever feeling there may be, all of it is a synonym for suffering."
Therefore, it is known that this sutra was not spoken with reference to the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); this meaning is established by itself.
Furthermore, if all sensations (*vedanā*) were suffering by their very nature (*svabhāva*), for what purpose would the Venerable Ānanda have asked the Buddha this question:
"How is it, Blessed One, that you say there are three kinds of sensation, namely: pleasure, pain, and neither-pain-nor-pleasure?"
The Blessed One further stated that whatever sensation there may be, all of it is a synonym for suffering.
On what basis did the Blessed One say this—that whatever sensation there may be, all of it is a synonym for suffering?
If your interpretation were logical, the Venerable Ānanda should have asked the Buddha this:
"Blessed One, with what meaning did you say that there are three kinds of feeling?"
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, should have replied to Ānanda: "Ānanda!
This statement was spoken with a specific intention, namely that there are three kinds of feeling."
Since the Buddha, the World-Honored One, did not speak in such a manner, there must therefore be three feelings that exist substantially by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Thus, we know that this sūtra was spoken with a specific intention (*abhiprāya*); that is to say, it refers to all feelings whatsoever as being synonyms for suffering (*duḥkha*).
As for what you have said— that one should contemplate pleasant sensation with the characteristic of suffering—
that meaning is not so. Why is this?
Within this sensation there are two natures:
first, the nature of pleasure, because it is by its very essence something desirable;
second, the nature of suffering, because by another principle it is a phenomenon subject to transformation and impermanence.
If one contemplates this sensation through the aspect of pleasure, it gives rise to further bondage, because sentient beings possessed of desire delight in savoring its flavor.
If one contemplates this sensation through the aspect of suffering, one is able to attain liberation, because sentient beings bound by fetters thereby achieve detachment from desire.

What is seen through correct reasoning leads to liberation; the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in accordance with this principle, skillfully instruct sentient beings to cultivate and study this contemplation.
How can it be known that this sensation is pleasant by its very nature?
As this verse says:
"Having already known that formations are impermanent, And further observing their transformation,
The Perfectly Awakened One, the Knower, Therefore spoke of all sufferings."
Regarding what you have said— that the conceptualization of pleasure within suffering is called a perversion, and therefore one knows that pleasure does not exist—
this is not correct. Why is this so?
This statement is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
In the world, there is the perception of pleasure regarding the experience of sensual objects and regarding places of rebirth;
however, within this context, pleasant sensation (*sukhavedanā*) is actually suffering by another principle.
If one perceives these as being exclusively pleasurable, that perception is called a perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Since sensual objects involve little pleasure and much suffering, to view them as having exclusive pleasure is a perversion.
The same applies to the realms of rebirth; therefore, this very fact serves as proof for the denial of pleasure.
This argument is not established. If all feelings are suffering by their very nature, what purpose is served by further stating that there are three types of feeling?
If you say: "It is said so in conformity with worldly convention," [we reply:]...
This interpretation is not correct.
Why? Because the statement that "all sensations are suffering" was spoken with a specific underlying intention.
Furthermore, by means of speaking according to reality, as it is said in the Sūtra:
"This is the faculty of pleasure; this is the faculty of joy.
One should see that these names refer to pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*).
"This is the faculty of pain (duḥkhendriya), this is the faculty of grief (daurmanasyendriya); one should see these as the feeling of suffering (duḥkhavedanā).

Having explained this in detail, if a person thus observes the five faculties with such accordance with reality and correct knowledge (yathābhūta-samyakjñāna), that person will then abandon the three fetters (trisaṃyojana) and so forth.
How is it that worldly discrimination regarding painful sensations has three grades?
If you say that, among the inferior, superior, and middling grades, the world sequentially gives rise to the mental states of pleasant sensation and so forth; [then this is the case].
This argument is not tenable, because pleasure also has three grades; thus, when one experiences a minor grade of suffering, one ought to give rise to a perception of the highest grade of pleasure.
When a person correctly experiences the pleasure produced by superior types of odors, tastes, and tangibles, what kind of suffering is being experienced at that time?
One correctly experiences slight suffering and gives rise to a perception of pleasure within that slight suffering.
