If this were so, then at the time when this slight painful feeling has not yet arisen and at the time when it has ceased, there should arise a mental state of the highest degree of pleasure, because the suffering would have been extinguished without remainder.
This should be stated likewise when the pleasure of sensual objects is present before one.
Furthermore, how is this adherence consistent with reason?
That is to say, why is it that within a mild sensation of suffering, one experiences it as most intense and distinct, yet within a moderate sensation of suffering, it is not so clear?
Furthermore, in the three dhyānas, pleasant feeling is a subtle suffering; from the fourth dhyāna upward, neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is moderate suffering.
How can this position be considered consistent with reason?
That is to say, one discriminates feelings of pleasure and so forth within mild suffering and the like.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said: "Mahānāma!"
If form were merely suffering and not pleasure, and were not accompanied by pleasure— as explained at length in the Sūtra—
then one would know that there is a feeling of pleasure, yet it is simply not established.
It is impossible for the meaning of the existence of pleasant feeling to be established on the basis of the absence of such a Sūtra as you have cited.
As for what you have said—that because the causes of pleasure are not determinate, there is no pleasure—this meaning is not correct;
you speak these words because you do not understand the meaning of "cause. Why is this so?
The various objects (*viṣaya*) become causes of pleasure or causes of suffering depending on the distinctions of their respective bases (*āśraya*), and not merely by the objects themselves.

When these objects reach such a distinction of base, they necessarily become causes of pleasure; there is no time when they reach this state and do not become causes of pleasure. Therefore, it is possible to establish that the cause of pleasure is determinate.

For example, the heat of fire becomes the cause for the beautiful ripening of food and drink when it reaches a particular state of ripeness; this very heat of fire is the cause of that beautiful ripening.

If it reaches such a state of ripeness, it will necessarily become the cause of beautiful ripening, and there is no time when, having reached that state, it would not become the cause of beautiful ripening.
How can the cause of pleasure within meditative concentration be indeterminate?
As for your claim that the perception of pleasure arises from the counteraction of suffering, this is not the case; this position has already been refuted previously.

If, at that time, a person is experiencing a pleasant sensation produced by the application of superior perfumes and other such distinctions, that person will conceive the notion of pleasure regarding the remedy.
This notion of pleasure should arise most clearly when this suffering has not yet arisen or has already ceased.
If one conceives the notion of pleasure within the bliss of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), what is its antidote?
When shifting a heavy burden from one shoulder to another, there is necessarily a feeling of pleasure arising in that distinct state, as long as such a bodily position has not ceased.
If it were not so, the perception of pleasure at the very end should arise as the most intense.
One should know that the same applies when a person who is utterly exhausted changes their posture.
As for what you asked: how can there be an arising of the perception of suffering at a later time?

If suffering were not produced gradually from the beginning, this would be untenable; for it arises through specific transformations of the body, just as wine and the like are sweet in taste at first but sour in taste later.

Therefore, it must be established that pleasant feeling definitely exists; for if all contaminated phenomena were suffering due to their association with the three types of suffering, then what was stated as the Truth of Origination would be identical to the Truth of Suffering, which contradicts the Sūtras.
Why is this? Because it is stated in the sūtras that craving alone is the origin (*samudaya*), due to the preeminence of craving.
When the sūtras describe it as the origin, they do not deny that other phenomena are also origins.
How can this meaning be known?
Because it is stated elsewhere that distinct phenomena are also the origin (*samudaya*).
The Blessed One spoke this verse:
"Karma, craving, and ignorance— these three serve as the causes for all forms of existence in the future.
Furthermore, another sutra states:

The five kinds of seeds are a specific designation for the consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-vijñāna*), and the earth element is a specific designation for the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*).
Therefore, this statement in the Sūtra was spoken with a particular intention; thus, it is of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*).
In the Abhidharma teachings, it is stated that one relies on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, because the Blessed One wished to explain the cause for the continuous existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), he taught that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the origin (*samudaya*).

Because the Buddha wishes to explain that birth has a cause and that existence (*bhava*) has a cause, he speaks of other factors in the verse, namely karma, craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and ignorance (*avidyā*).
As the Sūtra says:
"Karma is the cause of birth; craving is the cause of existence."

Furthermore, because the sūtras contain causes, conditions, and sequential initiations, the Blessed One established seeds and fields, teaching that consciousness and the other [factors] also function as causes.
What dharma is called "birth" (*jāti*)?
What dharma is called "existence" (*bhava*)?

Because of the distinctions in categories such as realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and types of birth (*upapatti*), the appropriation of this body is called "birth"; the uninterrupted succession into a future existence without such distinctions is called "existence."
These two sequences have karma and craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) as their respective causes.

For example, seeds such as śāli rice and barley, due to their distinct specific natures (*prakāra*), can serve as the causes for the production of specific sprouts; whereas water and other such conditions, being non-distinct, universally serve as the causes for the production of all sprouts.
Karma and craving are illustrated by this analogy; craving is the cause of existence (*bhava*).
What reasoning serves as proof for this?
It is because those without craving do not undergo rebirth.

Why is this? When two people—one with craving and one without craving—both die, we see only the one with craving being reborn, while we do not see the one without craving being reborn. Since there is no rebirth for one who is free from craving, we know that craving is the cause of existence.

Furthermore, due to the transformation of the continuum, wherever there is a mind characterized by craving and views that continues, it undergoes repeated transformations therein; therefore, one should know through inference that it is likewise in the future.

Furthermore, there is no other affliction capable of grasping this body as intensely as craving; it is like the dry *māṣūra* powder used for bathing and rubbing. There is no other cause that adheres so firmly as this love for a self; this is the logical principle.

In some places, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, taught that there are four truths; in other places, he taught that there are two truths, namely conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). What are the characteristics of these two truths?

The verse says: "If it is destroyed, that cognition no longer exists; by means of cognition, the rest are likewise removed. Conventional truth is like a jar or water; that which differs from this is called ultimate truth. The commentary explains: When a jar is broken, the cognition of "jar" no longer arises. Similarly, when one realizes the true nature of things through wisdom (*jñāna*), all other conventional designations are eliminated. Just as a jar or the water within it exists only conventionally, that which is distinct from such conventional constructs is termed ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If an object is broken down part by part, the cognition of that object no longer arises; such an object is called conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), like a jar and so forth.
If this jar is broken into shards, the cognition of a "jar" no longer arises based on those shards; therefore, objects such as jars exist only nominally (*prajñaptisat*) by virtue of their form.

Furthermore, when other phenomena are analytically excluded from this entity by means of wisdom, and the cognition of that entity no longer arises, this entity is called conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), such as water and so forth.

If this water is analyzed away from its constituent factors such as color and the great elements by means of wisdom, the cognition of "water" no longer arises; therefore, things such as water exist only as conventional designations based on aggregation.

The true meaning is revealed through the gates of names, phrases, and syllables; one gives rise to knowledge of the true meaning by taking names, phrases, and syllables as its object. If, upon entering meditative equipoise, one could not take names and so forth as objects, or if, upon emerging from equipoise, one could not take the true meaning as an object, then names and so forth, as well as this knowledge, would exist merely as conventional designations. Therefore, because they reveal [the truth], names and so forth, along with this knowledge, exist as conventionalities.
Regarding these three dharmas, by what dharma is the conventional (saṃvṛti) established?
That which is merely a name and lacks an intrinsic essence is the conventional.

Because it accords with worldly convention, such things as saying "there is a jar" or "there is water," and so forth, are called true speech and are not said to be false; therefore, this is established as conventional truth (saṃvṛtisatya).
Apart from these three, all else is called ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
If an object is broken down part by part, the cognition of that object does not change;
likewise, if other phenomena are analytically excluded by means of cognition, the cognition of that object remains unchanged.
If, apart from names and so forth, the cognition of an object does not differ [from the object itself], this phenomenon is called "real," just as in the case of form (*rūpa*) and other such things.

If one analyzes this form down to its atoms, or if one removes other factors such as taste through cognition, the cognition that takes form as its object arises without difference; as it is with form, so it should be understood for sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest. This is called worldly truth (*loka-satya*).
Because such phenomena exist substantially in the world, they are established as true realities (*satya*).
Furthermore, other masters say:

if a phenomenon is an object of supramundane knowledge (*lokottara-jñāna*), or an object of the subsequent knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) attained after supramundane knowledge, it is likewise called a true reality—namely, the true object (*viṣaya-satya*), the true fruit (*phala-satya*), and the true path (*mārga-satya*).
If other phenomena differ from these three, they are called conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Having briefly explained the truths, it should be understood that if explained in detail, they are as taught in the *Ṣaḍabhiññā-śāstra*.
By what means can one cultivate the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths?
This matter should now be explained; therefore, the sequence of the initial undertaking of practice shall now be set forth.
The verse says:
"Abiding in virtuous conduct, one possesses learning; after reflection, one studies and cultivates wisdom. The commentary explains:

If a person desires to contemplate the Four Noble Truths, they first study and uphold the precepts. Next, they take up the textual passages that accord with the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths. Then, they listen to the correct meaning of those passages. Having heard them, they reflect upon the meaning correctly and in accordance with reality. After reflecting without error, they subsequently practice contemplative cultivation to bring about the development of wisdom through meditation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
This person, relying on the wisdom born of hearing, gives rise to the wisdom born of reflection; relying on the wisdom born of reflection, they give rise to the wisdom born of cultivation.
What are the characteristics of these three types of wisdom?
The verse says:
"Name and meaning are the objects of the three wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The commentary states:
"That which is called the wisdom of hearing takes name as its object."
The wisdom born of reflection takes both names and meanings as its object; sometimes it is led by the phrasing to the meaning, and sometimes it is led by the meaning to the phrasing.
The wisdom born of cultivation takes only the meaning as its object.
Why is this? Because this wisdom has already been perfected; it does not contemplate words and letters, but arises solely by taking meaning as its object.
It is like a person who has never learned to swim and cannot let go of a flotation device.
If one has studied but not yet mastered [the skill], one must either cling to or grasp at something;
if the study is already complete, one can cross by oneself without relying on any floating object.
The three types of wisdom are analogous to this; so say the Vaibhāṣika masters.
Within this process of conceptual discrimination, the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) is not established.
If reflection arises by taking names as its object, it constitutes the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
if it arises by taking meanings as its object, it constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*).
If one establishes the characteristics of the three types of wisdom in this manner, there will be no fault:

the definitive knowledge arising from authoritative testimony (āptavacana) is called the wisdom of hearing (śrutamayī-prajñā); the definitive knowledge arising from the discernment of principles based on the sacred teachings is called the wisdom of reflection (cintamayī-prajñā); and the knowledge arising from samādhi is called the wisdom of cultivation (bhāvanāmayī-prajñā).

These three types of wisdom all derive their names from their causes: that which arises from hearing is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (śrutamayī-prajñā); the same applies to the wisdoms derived from reflection (cintāmayī) and cultivation (bhāvanāmayī). This is, for example, like referring to food as "life" or grass as "oxen."
If a person, being courageous, seeks to attain the cultivation of meditation (*vipaśyanā*), how can this cultivation of meditation be accomplished?
Therefore, the sequence of this meaning should be explained.
The verse says:
There are two types of persons who are secluded.
The commentary states:

If a person is able to dwell in seclusion through both body and mind—namely, by being distant from social crowds as well as unwholesome factors such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
For what kind of person can these two forms of seclusion be easily accomplished?
For one who possesses contentment and few desires.
The verse says:
"There is no lack of contentment for one with great desire.
The commentary explains:
If a person lacks contentment and possesses great desire, these two [qualities] will be difficult for such a person to achieve; even if they were achieved, they would not be pure.
What are the distinct characteristics of this lack of contentment and great desire?
The verse says:
Seeking much for what has already been obtained, and seeking to obtain what has not yet been obtained.
The commentary states:
When one has already obtained favorable conditions such as clothing and so forth, yet seeks to obtain more of them, this is called "lack of contentment" (*asantuṣṭi*).
To seek what has not yet been obtained is called "great desire" (*mahecchatā*).
The Abhidharma masters say this. Is it not so?
This seeking for much gain pertains to what has not yet been attained, not to what has already been attained.
If that is so, what is the difference between these two?
You should explain this; for if you hold such a view, the meaning would be tenable.

When one has already obtained clothing and other requisites that are neither desirable nor abundant, and the mind becomes distressed and uneasy because of this, it is called "lack of contentment" (*asamtuṣṭi*).
Not obtaining what is desirable and seeking much more than one has obtained is called "great desire.
The verse says:
The antidotes to these two are their opposites.
The commentary states:
One should understand that these two qualities—contentment and fewness of desires—are the remedies for the aforementioned lack of contentment and great desire.
The verse says:
"Either belonging to the three realms or to the outflow-free realm.
The commentary states:
These two types of antidotes either belong to the three realms or belong to the outflow-free realm.
Lack of contentment and great desire belong exclusively to the Desire Realm.
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of this contentment and fewness of desires?
The verse says:
"Of the nature of non-attachment.
The commentary states:
"Its intrinsic nature is the wholesome root of non-attachment."
The verse says:
"The noble lineages.
The commentary says:
Because these—contentment and fewness of desires—have non-greed as their intrinsic nature, they are included within the noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), since the noble ones arise from them.
They are called "noble lineages" because, once established as such, they have non-greed as their intrinsic nature.
The verse says:
"The first three constitute the essence of contentment.
The commentary says:
The first three refer to contentment with whatever clothing, food and drink, and dwelling one happens to obtain.
These three forms of contentment constitute the essence of the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*).
The fourth noble lineage refers to the delight in cultivation and cessation.
What is the nature of this fourth [noble lineage]?
Its nature is non-attachment, because it arises from turning away from the desire for existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, what meaning does the Blessed Buddha intend to demonstrate by means of the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*)?
The verse says:
"The subsequent [section] reveals the three lifetimes of karma.
The commentary says:

Since the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the Lord of Dharma, his disciples renounce the requisites of life and the basis of action to leave the household life and seek liberation by relying upon the Buddha.
The Lord of Dharma establishes two primary matters:

first, the requisites of life; second, the basis of action. By means of the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*), the requisites of life are established; by means of the fourth noble lineage, the basis of action is established.
"Relying upon these requisites for life, you have established such a foundation of karma; before long, you shall attain liberation.
How did the Lord of Dharma establish such requisites for life and such a foundation of karma?"
The verse says:
Because it is the antidote to the arising of craving.
The commentary says:
In the Sūtras it is taught that there are four ways in which craving arises.
As the Sūtra says:
"O Bhikṣus, due to craving for robes, desire arises, desire persists, and desire is grasped; due to craving for food, drink, and dwellings, desire arises, desire persists, and desire is grasped."
For a bhikṣu, craving for existence and non-existence arises in this manner, as explained at length in the sūtra.
To counteract these four types of craving, the four noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) are taught.
The verse says:
"In order to temporarily and permanently eliminate craving for 'mine' and for what belongs to the self.
The commentary says:
The meaning previously explained has another further intention, and therefore it must be stated again.
The category of "mine" refers to the three things such as clothing;
the category of "self" refers to one's own body.
Regarding these two, craving arises; herein, the first three noble lineages are established for the sake of temporarily extinguishing craving for the category of "mine" (mamakāra-tṛṣṇā).

The fourth noble lineage is established for the sake of eternally extinguishing the four types of craving, namely: craving for the category of "mine" and craving for the category of "self" (ātmakāra-tṛṣṇā).
This meaning has already been explained.
By means of this meaning, the practitioner attains thorough self-mastery, whereby subsequent cultivation of insight reaches fulfillment.
If a person is thus mastered, they become a fit vessel for the Path.
Regarding the cultivation [of meditation], by focusing on which dharma-gate does one enter into the practice of contemplation?
The verse says:
Entry into cultivation arises from two causes: the contemplation of impurity and mindfulness of breathing.
The commentary asks:
Who enters into cultivation by means of the contemplation of impurity?
And who enters into the stages of cultivation by means of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānasmṛti*)?
The verse says:
"Abounding in desire and abounding in vitarka and vicāra.
The commentary says:
If a person’s desire to practice arises constantly or intensely, that person enters into cultivation by means of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

If a person’s mind becomes distracted due to excessive discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), that person enters into cultivation by means of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*).
Why is this? Because this mindfulness does not take multiple objects as its focus, it is able to give rise to the cessation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*);
whereas the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), by taking various differentiated forms and shapes as its objects, is capable of inducing applied and sustained thought.
Other masters say this.
Furthermore, other masters say:
because they do not arise by taking external objects as their focal point, vitarka and vicāra are not produced.

The contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), because it arises by taking external objects as its condition—just like visual consciousness—induces vitarka and vicāra through the observation of those objects.
Within this context, there are four kinds of desire:
first, desire for form (rūpa-rāga); second, desire for physical appearance (saṃsthāna-rāga); third, desire for touch (sparśa-rāga); and fourth, desire for deportment (īryāpatha-rāga).
The various masters say:

To counteract the first kind of desire, the practitioner of meditation should take as their object the colors of decay, such as blackness, and perform the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
To counteract the second kind of desire, they should take as their object a bloated corpse, one being devoured, or one that is dismembered, and perform the contemplation of impurity.
To counteract the third desire, one should practice the contemplation of impurity by taking as the object a skeleton with red tendons still connecting the bones.
To counteract the fourth desire, one should practice the contemplation of impurity by taking as the object an unmoving corpse.
The various masters say:
If one wishes to cultivate the universal antidote, the verse states:
"The contemplation of bones is the universal antidote for desire."
The commentary states:

Within this interconnected mass of bones, none of the four categories of sensual objects exist. If one takes this skeletal mass as the object and cultivates the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), it is universally capable of counteracting the four types of desire.

Because the contemplation of impurity consists entirely of conceptual constructs, taking as its essence the deliberation upon a single object, it cannot permanently eradicate the afflictions; it can only suppress them.
There are three stages in which a practitioner cultivates the contemplation of impurity:

first, the initial development of the practice; second, the stage where the practice has been repeatedly cultivated and established; and third, the stage where one has transcended the stage of deliberate reflection.
The verse here says:
"The visualization of the quantity of bones extending to the ocean, increasing and decreasing, is called the first stage.
The commentary explains:

If a practitioner wishes to cultivate the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), they should initially place the mind upon a part of their own body, whether it be the toes of the feet or the forehead, whichever location they prefer.

Once the mind has followed the object, one subsequently forms a mental image of the body; having removed the skin, flesh, blood, and so forth, one gradually purifies the bones until the mind perceives them as a complete collection of skeletal remains.

Just as one visualizes a heap of bones through imaginative perception, so too does one visualize a second; in this manner, the visualization gradually increases until it fills the rooms, temples, monasteries, and the kingdom, eventually pervading the entire earth with the oceans as its boundary.
One visualizes in this way that the heap of bones fills [the entire space] in order to increase one's resolve.
Thereafter, one further contracts the previous visualization until one visualizes only the heap of bones of one's own body, in order to gradually narrow the coarse and expansive mind.
When the mind has reached this extent and mastery in the meditation on impurity (*aśubhā-bhāvanā*) is attained, at this stage the person is said to have "first initiated the practice.
The verse says:
"Excluding half of the skull from the feet, it is called 'perfected through cultivation' (*parijita*)."
The commentary states:

Furthermore, in order to gradually simplify the distinctions in the scope of the mind, one removes the bones of the feet from within the collection of bones and contemplates the remaining bones; this is called "inferior simplification" (adhamā saṃkṣepa).

Proceeding in this sequence until one removes half the body and removes half the skull bone, contemplating the remaining half of the skull bone—this is called the two intermediate and superior abridgments.
Because mastery is attained through this brief [instruction], in this stage the person is said to have already perfected their practice through repeated cultivation.
The verse says:
"Settling the mind between the eyebrows is called transcending deliberation."
The commentary states:

This practitioner of meditation removes the remaining half of the skull and fixes the mind solely upon the space between his own eyebrows; or, by taking the bone or another object as a focal point, he dwells with one-pointed concentration. In this state, this person is said to have "transcended the stage of applied thought."
There is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) which is "small" because its object is small, not because its mastery is small.

Regarding this, there are four permutations: contemplating what is already matured but not yet matured, and contemplating what is not yet matured but already matured; for these take as their objects the range from one's own body up to a heap of bones by the seashore.
Furthermore, regarding this contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*): what is its intrinsic nature?
To how many stages (*bhūmi*) does it belong? What is its object (*ālambana*)?
And in what place can it arise?
The sequence of this meaning should be understood as follows.
The verse says:
Its nature is non-attachment; it exists in ten stages; its object is the realm of desire; and it arises in persons.
The commentary states:
This contemplation has non-attachment as its intrinsic nature.
There are ten stages, namely: the four dhyānas, the four preparatory concentrations (sāmantaka), the intermediate dhyāna, and the desire realm.

Taking the phenomena perceived in the desire realm as its object—where "perceived" refers to color and shape—this concentration therefore takes meaning (*artha*) as its object; this interpretation is plausible.
This contemplation arises only within the human realm and not in other realms; how much less so in other worlds.
Within the human realm, it excludes the northern continent of Kuru.
For these reasons, this contemplation is called the "contemplation of impurity" (aśubha-bhāvanā).
The observation of the objects of the world is likewise.

If they have non-arising as their nature and take the three periods of time as their objects, this is due to conceptual mental construction; thus, they are exclusively with outflows (*sāsrava*). They may be acquired through detachment (*vairāgya-lābhika*) or acquired through effort (*prāyogika-lābhika*), depending on whether they were previously attained or not.
Having explained the characteristics and classifications of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*) shall now be discussed.
The verse says:
Mindfulness of breathing is wisdom; it belongs to five stages, has wind as its object, and relies upon the body of the desire realm.
The commentary states:

If the wind enters toward the body, it is called *āna*; if the wind exits away from the body, it is called *apāna*. To maintain mindfulness by taking these two as its object is called *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing).

This mindfulness has wisdom as its intrinsic nature; yet it is called "mindfulness" because, for example, as in the case of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), this wisdom is established by the power of mindfulness, and is therefore designated as "mindfulness."
This mindfulness arises based on five stages: namely, the three preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*), the intermediate stage of the first dhyāna, and the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Because it is said to be associated with equanimity (*upekṣā*), and because suffering and pleasure arise in accordance with applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*);
and since this concentration is the antidote to applied and sustained thought, it is not associated with suffering or pleasure.

Furthermore, because suffering and pleasure are fixed adversaries of the concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), and because this contemplation is accomplished by means of the concentrated mind, it is not associated with suffering or pleasure.
Other masters maintain that for a practitioner of contemplation,
there is only the feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) upon entering the four meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
According to that master, this contemplation exists in eight stages; beyond these, it does not exist in other stages because those are not stages for inhalation and exhalation.

This meditative concentration takes wind as its object and arises based on the desire realm among humans and devas; it is acquired either through detachment from desire or through preparatory application.
This contemplation is genuine reflection, belonging to the practitioner of inner observation within the True Dharma.
A verse says:
It does not exist among the non-Buddhists.
The commentary states:
This contemplation does not exist within the teachings of outsiders, for because they lack the correct teaching, they are unable to realize the subtle, sublime Dharma themselves.
Regarding this contemplation, the verse says:
Sixth, by way of enumeration and so forth.
The commentary states:
If this contemplation is complete, it must correspond with six causes in order to be perfected.
The six causes are:
first, counting; second, following; third, settling; fourth, characteristics; fifth, transformation; and sixth, purification.

Among these, regarding the two breaths of inhalation and exhalation, one does not apply effort, but rather relinquishes the characteristics of body and mind along with the mind, counting from one and two up to ten solely by means of mindfulness.
Because one fears that the mind may become either too brief or distracted, the count is neither too few nor too many.
Within this counting, there are three faults:
first, undercounting, which means counting one for two;
Second is counting too many, which means counting two as one.
Third is confused counting, which means counting the inhalation while exhaling, or counting the exhalation while inhaling.
To be free from these three faults is called correct counting.
If the mind becomes distracted in the interim, one should count again from the beginning until concentration is attained.
"Following" means that without applying effort, one follows the movement of the inhalation and exhalation.
Whether this breath enters deeply or exits far, the mind likewise follows the course of the breath as it moves.
Does this breath circulate throughout the entire body, or does it circulate through only one part of the body? Just as the breath moves, the mind follows its movement.

If the breath enters and moves, reaching the throat, the heart, the navel, below the navel, the thighs, and the shins—following these locations in succession down to the feet—the mind also follows its movement.
If the breath goes out, whether for the distance of one span or one fathom, even as far as the wind-circle and the Vairambha winds, the mind also follows it.
This is because one contemplates and reflects upon reality through this observation.
This interpretation is not correct.

As for "peaceful abiding" (*ānāpāna*), one should fix the mind firmly upon a point—whether it be between the eyebrows, at the tip of the nose, or anywhere from there down to the toes—according to one's preference, remaining there like a mani jewel strung upon a thread.
The practitioner observes this breath to determine whether it is beneficial or harmful, cold or hot, and so forth.

This contemplation does not take only the wind element as its object; rather, with the four great elements and the derived matter, as well as the mind and mental factors—which possess those elements as their support—as its basis, it takes the five aggregates as its objective field.

"Transformation" refers to the wisdom that transforms the wind-object as its condition, establishing this mindfulness within the stages of the most superior wholesome roots, up to the "supreme mundane dharma.
"Purification" refers to this mindfulness having already entered the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
Other masters say:

that which begins with the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and ends with the diamond-like mind (*vajropama-citta*) is called "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*); the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are called "purification" (*viśuddhi*).
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"First is counting, second is following; third is settling, fourth is observing signs;
fifth is transforming, and sixth is purification—these are called the contemplation of mindfulness of breathing.
Within this, one should understand the method of inhalation and exhalation.
The verse says:
Inhalation and exhalation follow the body.
The commentary says:
The level of the earth upon which one relies for the body is the same as that of the inhalation and exhalation, because the breath is a part of the body.
This breath arises based on the distinction between body and mind; it does not exist among beings born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) nor during stages such as the *kalala* (embryonic phase).
Because these [breaths] do not exist in one who has entered the mindless attainments (*acittaka-samāpatti*) or is in the fourth dhyāna. Why is this?

If the element of space already exists within the body and a mind belonging to the level of inhalation and exhalation (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa-bhūmika*) is present before one, these breaths will necessarily arise.
If a person emerges from the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna, they will first enter [the state of] death.
If they enter the meditative attainment of the fourth dhyāna, there is only emergence and no entry.
The verse says:
"Sentient beings" (sattva).
The commentary states:
Because it is a provisional designation for a portion within the collection of phenomena (dharma-skandha) that constitutes sentient beings.
The verse says:
Not grasping.
The commentary says:
Because it is dissociated from the faculties, it is not that which is grasped by mind and mental factors as their support.
The verse says:
"It is a result of outflow."
The commentary states:
It is neither an increase nor a retribution.
If the body increases, this [state] does not increase; therefore, it is not an increase. Because it is a reconnection after having been severed, it is not a retribution.
Why is this? Because there is no matter of retribution that possesses such characteristics; therefore, these are outflows.
The verse says:
It is not an object for an inferior mind, nor is it an object for any other [inferior] mind.
The commentary explains:

These two breaths can be taken as objects by minds of the same level or by minds of a higher level; they cannot be taken as objects by minds of a lower level, nor can they be taken as objects by minds such as those of deportment (*airyāpathika*) or transformation (*nairmāṇika*).
Having explained the two dharma-gates for entering cultivation,
if one has already attained samādhi by means of these two gates, the verse says:
"Once the practice of contemplation is perfected, one then cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness."
The commentary states:
In order to accomplish the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness is explained next. Why is this?
Because the four foundations of mindfulness comprehensively encompass all phenomena and can counteract the four inversions,
how does one practice the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness?
The verse says:
"The body, sensation, and mental factors [are analyzed] by means of discerning their two characteristics.
The commentary explains:
First, one discerns the body through its specific and general characteristics; subsequently, one discerns sensation, mind, and mental factors.
The specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the individual intrinsic nature of each [phenomenon].

The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is, for example, that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) have impermanence as their characteristic; all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) have suffering as their characteristic; and all phenomena (*dharma*) have selflessness and emptiness as their characteristic.
Furthermore, what are the specific characteristics of the body?
Its characteristics are the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements; these are distinct from the previous three and are termed "dharmas.
Furthermore, it is said:

If a person correctly enters into meditative cultivation and contemplates the body, through the correct vision of its division into atoms and its momentary cessation, the application of mindfulness to the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) is thus accomplished; the same applies to the other applications of mindfulness.
Furthermore, what is the nature of the foundations of mindfulness?
There are three foundations of mindfulness:

namely, the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*), the foundation of mindfulness as association (*saṃprayoga-smṛtyupasthāna*), and the foundation of mindfulness as object (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding the application of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*), the verse says:
"The nature is wisdom.
The commentary explains:
What is this wisdom?
The verse says:
It consists of hearing, reflection, and cultivation.
The commentary states:
Since the three types of wisdom— those arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation— are themselves the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) by nature,
the foundations of mindfulness are established as three in accordance with these wisdoms.
The verse says:
"Because they have other associated objects.
The commentary says:

As for the remaining dharmas that arise simultaneously with wisdom, they are called "associated foundations of mindfulness" (saṃprayukta-smṛtyupasthāna), because they are associated with the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna) and because they take the objects of focus as the foundation of mindfulness (ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna).
These two foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) regarding their objects are called the "foundations of mindfulness as objects.
Since the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna) is wisdom (prajñā), how is this to be known?
When one contemplates the body within the body, discerning both the specific and general characteristics of the body, it is called the "foundation of mindfulness on the body" (kāya-smṛtyupasthāna).
Based on the statement in this sutra, what dharma is called "contemplative wisdom" (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*)? Why is this so?
Because if a person possesses wisdom regarding their internal body, they are able to contemplate both the general and specific characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa* and *viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
How is it that wisdom is said to be the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
because mindfulness is predominant therein, they are called foundations of mindfulness.
The *Yibian* states:
"Because it is established through the power of mindfulness, it is like a wedge firmly held within split wood.
If one maintains this view, the meaning is tenable."
Because one abides by means of wisdom and mindfulness, wisdom is called "application of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*), for it does not forget what has been seen.
As the Venerable Āniruddha said:

"If this practitioner of meditation abides in contemplation, observing the body through both its specific and general characteristics, and if mindfulness takes the body as its object, then [that mindfulness] arises, abides, and increases."
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, himself said:
"If a practitioner of meditation abides in contemplation, they observe the body through two distinct and universal characteristics, maintaining mindfulness without forgetfulness.
Based on this sutra, it is known that wisdom is the essential nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
In this context, the following meaning is taught: "Monks!
Regarding these four foundations of mindfulness, how do they arise and originate?"
What is their cessation and relinquishment?
The arising and accumulation of this nutriment is itself the arising and accumulation of the body.
The cessation and relinquishment of this nutriment is itself the cessation and relinquishment of the body.
This sutra speaks only of the foundations of mindfulness as objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*), because mindfulness dwells within them.
As it is with the objects, so it is with their names, since they take as their objects the continuums of oneself, others, and both.
Each of the four foundations of mindfulness has three types.
The verse says:
"Their sequence is according to their arising."
The commentary says:
They arise in successive order.
How is it that their arising occurs in this manner?
Because one first observes that which is coarse:
since the body is coarse and is the basis for sensual desire, this [desire] arises from feeling;
this [feeling] arises because the mind is not subdued, and this [lack of subduing] arises because the afflictions have not been extinguished; thus, the sequence is established.
The verse says:
"Four, because they counteract perversions and so forth.
The commentary says:

Because they serve as antidotes to [the misconceptions of] purity, pleasure, permanence, and self, it is said that there are four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) in sequence, neither more nor less.
Among these four applications of mindfulness, the objects of the first three are unmixed; the fourth has two types:
if one perceives only the object of dharmas, they are unmixed, just as with the body and so forth.
If one contemplates the two, three, or four [foundations of mindfulness] together as having the same principle and the same object, they become intermingled.
Having thus repeatedly practiced the four foundations of mindfulness with the body and so forth as their objects, the verse says:
"This person dwells in the total synthesis of the objects within the mindfulness of dharmas, because they contemplate the characteristics of dharmas as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self."
The commentary states:

This practitioner of meditation dwells upon a mixed object; within the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), they take all four factors—body and so forth—collectively as a single object and examine them by way of four characteristics: namely, the characteristic of impermanence (*anityatā-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of suffering (*duḥkha-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of non-self (*anātma-lakṣaṇa*).
The verse says:
From this, the "Heat" practice arises.
The commentary says:

From this foundation of mindfulness of dharmas, by practicing in this sequence repeatedly until reaching the highest of the high degrees, there arises a root of goodness called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*); because it is like heat, it is named "Heat."
Because it is the precursor to the fire of the Four Noble Paths that can burn the fuel of the afflictions, it is called "Heat" (*uṣmagata*).
The verse says:
It takes the Four Truths as its object and possesses sixteen aspects.
The commentary states:
Because this root of goodness, "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), is extensive in its stages, it takes the four truths as its objects and possesses sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
It contemplates suffering through four characteristics, namely: impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
One contemplates origination through four aspects: cause, origination, production, and condition.
One contemplates cessation through four aspects: cessation, tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
One contemplates the Path through four aspects: namely, as the path, as suchness, as practice, and as departure.
The distinctions among these sixteen aspects will be explained later.
As it was with the stage of "Heat," so it is here as well.
The verse says:
"From Heat (ūṣmagata) and Peak (mūrdhan), it is likewise.
The commentary says:

This "Heat" (*ūṣmagata*) increases through the stages of weak, medium, and superior; from the superior stage of Heat, there arises a root of goodness called "Summit" (*mūrdhan*). This root of goodness should be understood as being like Heat: it takes the Four Truths as its objects and possesses sixteen aspects (*ākāra*).
Because this is the most superior grade and excels those [preceding stages], it is established with a distinct name.
Because it is the pinnacle (*mūrdhan*) of wholesome dharmas, it is called "Summit. Why is this so?
Because there is falling away from this and because there are faults,
the verse says:
"Regarding the two, one establishes the signs through mindfulness of the Dharma."
The commentary states:

Within the two roots of goodness, namely *uṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), one establishes the signs (*nimitta*) by means of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
What dharma is called "establishing the signs"?
Regarding the four truths, sixteen aspects are first established.
The verse says:
"The long [duration] arises from the remainder."
The commentary states:
Once these two roots of goodness have arisen, they further cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and thereby achieve growth.
However, once they have grown, what was previously attained no longer manifests before them, due to a lack of reverence.
The verse says:
"From that, patience.
The commentary says:

Increasing sequentially from the soft, medium, and superior [levels], the roots of goodness of the "summit" (mūrdhan) and the "patience" (kṣānti) arise; for these are capable of withstanding the principles of the Four Noble Truths to the utmost degree and are free from falling back.
This patience also has three types, namely: weak, medium, and superior.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"The two patiences are the same as those."
The commentary states:

As previously explained for the "summits" (mūrdhan) in their soft and medium degrees, the same applies to the two types of "patience" (kṣānti); because they are characterized by stability, all [these stages] are termed "patience.
The verse says:
"Mindfulness of dharmas increases.
The commentary states:
These three grades of patience all take mindfulness of dharmas as their means of growth, and not by means of the other foundations of mindfulness.
The verse says:
"Taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object, it is of the highest degree.
The commentary says:

This is the supreme grade of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*), because it serves to induce the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*); therefore, it arises taking the suffering of the desire realm as its object.

Consequently, it is established by implication that the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) take the suffering and other [truths] of the three realms as their objects, since no restrictive definition has been stated.

At this time, one is able to extinguish the [perceptions] of the form realm and the formless realm, and to counteract the objects of each individual truth; even down to contemplating the suffering of the desire realm with two moments of mind—this entire process is called "intermediate patience" (madhyā-kṣānti).
If, for a single moment, one takes the suffering of the desire realm as an object, this is called "superior patience" (adhimātra-kṣānti).
The verse says:
"In a single thought-moment."
The commentary states:
This supreme patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) lasts for only a single moment and does not endure for a long time.
The verse says:
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is also like this.
The commentary states:

Just as the highest degree of patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*) takes the suffering of the desire realm as its object, possessing a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) for a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), so too does the Supreme Mundane Dharma take the suffering of the desire realm as its object, possessing a single characteristic for a single moment.
This dharma is a mundane dharma because it is associated with outflows (*sāsrava*).

Because it is the most excellent among mundane dharmas, it is called the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). It is devoid of a homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*), for by its own power it is able to induce the Noble Path.
Therefore, because the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth have the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as their intrinsic nature, they share the same nature as wisdom (*prajñā*).
The verse says:
"The five aggregates are dissociated from [the outflows] up to..."
The commentary states:
All of these have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their nature, because they include their associated categories; however, they are merely excluded from "possession" (*prāpti*).
Possession is not included within the levels such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and so forth.

Why is this? It is so that an Ārya, by virtue of having already attained [the roots of goodness] through their manifestation, does not need to manifest the roots of goodness such as *uṣmagata* (heat) again.

Within this context, taking the three truths as objects, one cultivates the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding the establishment of characteristics during the stage of *uṣmagata*; there are four present applications of mindfulness of the same type.
If one takes the Truth of Cessation as an object, there are two types:

among all similar categories of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), if one cultivates any one of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) in the present within the context of increase, one will possess all four in the future.

If one takes cessation (*nirodha*) as the object, during the stage of increase (*vṛddhi*), one cultivates only the last *smṛtyupasthāna* (mindfulness) of its corresponding type, and further cultivates all four *smṛtyupasthānas* and all modes of activity (*sarva-ākāra*).

Because these have already been attained by nature, if one establishes the signs within the "summit" (*mūrdhan*), although one cultivates the last *smṛtyupasthāna* while taking the Four Noble Truths as objects, during the stage of increase when taking the truth of cessation as the object, one cultivates only the last *smṛtyupasthāna*; however, in the future, all four and all modes of activity will be fully present.

If one takes the three truths as objects, the four foundations of mindfulness increase; in the present life, one cultivates any one of them, while in the future, all four and all modes of practice are cultivated.

If one establishes the marks within the stage of Patience (kṣānti), one cultivates the final foundation of mindfulness throughout all stages; in the future, all four and all modes of practice are cultivated.

If one establishes the aspects within the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), one cultivates only the final application of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna); however, in the future, all four applications of mindfulness will be cultivated with all four aspects, because there is no subsequent stage and because it resembles the Path of Seeing (darśanamārga).
The verse says:
"Thus, the aids to penetration (nirvedhabhāgīya) are fourfold.
The commentary says:

Thus, there are four kinds of roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), namely: heat (*uṣmagata*), summits (*mūrdhan*), patience (*kṣānti*), and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Among these four, the first two are of weak grade because they are subject to regression.
Because there is the possibility of falling back, patience (*kṣānti*) is of medium grade;
the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is of superior grade.
What is the meaning of the "capacities for penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
"Decisive determination" (*nirṇaya*) has the meaning of being free from doubt; "discrimination" (*viniścaya*) has the meaning of discerning the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

These two constitute the meaning of the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), because the Noble Path is able to extinguish all doubts and is able to discern the characteristics of the Four Noble Truths—namely, that "this phenomenon is suffering," up to "this phenomenon is the path. Therefore, all of the Noble Path is termed "decisive determination" (*viniścaya*).
Regarding "stages" (*bhāga*): within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), they are called "stages" because they correspond to each respective path.
If a dharma can induce this [path] to arise, it is called a "root of merit conducive to penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).
The verse says:
"The category of wisdom cultivated through meditation.
The commentary explains:
These four all belong to the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā), as they do not belong to the stages of hearing or reflection (śruta-cintā).
The verse says:
"In the future and the intermediate dhyāna stages."
The commentary states:
The future dhyāna, the intermediate dhyāna, and the four fundamental dhyānas are the stages upon which these roots of goodness depend, as they are subsumed within these six stages.
They do not exist in the lower stages because there is no meditative concentration (dhyāna) therein.
They do not exist in the higher stages because they are of the same category as the companions of the path of seeing; therefore, they are absent there.

Furthermore, they do not take the desire realm as their object, because this desire realm must first be known and then abandoned. Consequently, these two stages do not mutually possess both śamatha and vipaśyanā.

These two are of the same category as the aids to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); because they do not exist in the [first] two stages, those two stages are not the basis for the roots of goodness that constitute the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*).

These four roots of goodness take the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) as their retribution; however, they can only bring them to completion and cannot project them, because they arise from turning one's back on and loathing birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
The verse says:
"It is said that there are two in the lower stages.
The commentary explains:
The Venerable Ghoṣaka says:
The first two roots of merit conducive to penetration take seven stages as their basis, or they arise based on the stage of the desire realm; these are all four roots of merit, beginning with "Heat."
The verse says:
Desire relies on three.
The commentary says:
The first three arise among human beings in the three continents;
if they have already arisen previously, they may also manifest in the heavenly realms.
The fourth may also arise in the heavens.
The first three [attainments] are acquired by both men and women, arising in dependence upon the bodies of men and women.
The verse says:
"The first is acquired by a woman through two bases."
The commentary states:
If a woman attains the "highest worldly dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), she necessarily attains it by means of two bases.
If a man attains it, he does so solely by means of the male base.
Why is this? Because she has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the female state.
How, then, does she abandon the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
The verse says:
"By abandoning the stage, the noble ones abandon it.
The commentary says:
The Noble Ones attain these four roots of goodness according to the stage upon which they rely.
If a Noble One abandons that stage, they immediately abandon these roots of goodness; they do not abandon them through any other cause.
How so? Because of attaining the superior stages, and not due to any other cause.
The verse says:
The non-noble relinquishment occurs through death.
The commentary says:

If an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) necessarily relinquishes [the roots of goodness] by relinquishing the homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga), whether they attain a superior stage or not, the verse says:
"The first two are abandoned through falling away.
The commentary explains:

The two roots of goodness, namely *ūṣmagata* (Heat) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), are abandoned by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) either through falling away or through death; however, noble ones (*ārya*) do not abandon these two through falling away.
From the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) up to the highest mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), even ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) do not fall back.
The verse says:
"Because of seeing the truths within the fundamental [stages]."
The commentary states:

If a person gives rise to the roots of goodness such as "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) based on the fundamental meditative absorptions, they will necessarily perceive the Four Truths in this very life if they have not already done so, because their mind of revulsion [toward suffering] is extremely intense.
The verse says:
"Having fallen away, one obtains what was not previously possessed.
The commentary says:

If a person regresses from the first two [levels] and subsequently reacquires them, this is the acquisition of what was never previously acquired; it is not the re-acquisition of what was previously abandoned.
This is analogous to the *prātimokṣa* restraint, which is not something already habitually cultivated, as it is accomplished through deliberate effort.
If there are remaining [factors] within each stage, one further cultivates and connects them from those remainders;
if there are none, one cultivates from the root.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 16.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Seventeen.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.

Analysis of the Chapter on the Persons Who Have Attained the Fruits of the Noble Path, Part Two. Furthermore, regarding these two types of retrogression—retrogression from what has been attained and retrogression from what has not yet been attained—what is their essential nature?
The verse says:
The two types of retrogression consist in the non-attainment [of the fruit].
The commentary states:
These two types of falling back (*parihāṇi*) have non-attainment (*aprāpti*) as their intrinsic nature.
Falling back due to opposition necessarily arises from transgressions, whereas falling back through relinquishment (*tyāga*) is not fixed.
If one who has already attained "warmth" (ūṣmagata) subsequently falls away, they will certainly take nirvāṇa as their dharma.
If this is so, what is the difference between this warmth and the roots of merit conducive to liberation (mokṣabhāgīya kuśalamūla)?
Because the stage of seeing the Four Truths is proximate,
provided there are no obstacles, the verse further states:
"In the 'Heat' stage, one does not accept false teachings."
The commentary states:
If one who has already attained "Heat" (ūṣmagata) subsequently regresses, they will not be susceptible to false teachings at this stage.
If they are not susceptible to false teachings, how does this differ from "Summit" (mūrdhan)?
The verse says:
At the stage of the Peak, one does not sever the roots of goodness.
The commentary says:

If a person who has attained the "summit" (mūrdhan) subsequently regresses, they cannot sever their roots of goodness at this stage; however, there is the possibility of entering the evil realms, and they may also give rise to an immediate retributive karma (ānantarya-karma).
The verse says:
Through patience, one does not fall into the evil realms.
The commentary says:

If one falls away from patience (*kṣānti*) through equanimity (*upekṣā*), there is no possibility of re-entering the evil destinies (*durgati*), because one has already distanced oneself from the afflictions and karma that lead to the evil destinies.

Why is this? Because upon attaining the stage of patience, regarding the various types of rebirth within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) based on the persistence of afflictions—all such categories have already attained the state of non-arising (*anutpāda*). These include: rebirth in the evil destinies; birth from eggs, moisture, or as a womb-born being; birth in the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*); birth in Uttarakuru; birth in the Heaven of Great Brahmā (*mahābrahman*); being a eunuch (*paṇḍaka*); acting as a eunuch; possessing both sexual organs (*ubhayavyañjana*); and the eighth existence (*aṣṭama-bhava*). Since these states of non-arising apply even at the level of the "mild" (*mṛdu*) stage, how much more so for the higher stages! Furthermore, regarding the afflictions to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they too are non-arising. How much more so for those above!
Because that non-arising is attained as it truly is, there is therefore no possibility of entering the evil realms.
The verse says:
"The Supreme Worldly Dharma transcends the ordinary."
The commentary states:
It is impossible for one who has attained the mundane supreme roots of goodness (*laukikāgradharma*) to lose them through either retrogression or death.

This is because such a person, within this stage, has already attained the non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); thus, there is no possibility of falling back into the state of an ordinary person.
Why is this? Because, being free from effortful application, one will necessarily realize the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*) in the second moment.

These four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), beginning with "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), each have three grades—mild, medium, and superior—which constitute three natures (*tridhātu*) due to the distinctions in the natures of the Śrāvakas and others.
In this regard, the verse says:
"The two natures of the disciple are transformed to become Buddhahood.
The commentary explains:
There is the sense that by transforming these two roots of goodness—*uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan*—one arises from the lineage of a śrāvaka and attains great perfect enlightenment;
however, once one has attained *kṣānti*, this possibility no longer exists.
For what reason is it not obtained?
It is said that this is because they have already transcended birth in the various evil realms (*durgati*).
Since Bodhisattvas regard the transformation of others for their benefit as their own supreme task, they intentionally go to the various evil destinies to undergo rebirth.
This nature cannot be altered; therefore, this [other] meaning does not exist.
The verse says:
"The three transform, the rest remain."
The commentary states:

From the śrāvaka lineage, one may turn toward the three roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and attain a distinct great perfect enlightenment, namely, that of a pratyekabuddha.
However, the pratyekabuddha lineage itself cannot be turned back.
Why is this? The verse says:
Because there is no seeking of the benefit of others, the nature of other transformations is not obstructed.
The commentary states:

If a practitioner has originally made the vow for solitary awakening (pratyekabuddha) and subsequently enters meditative cultivation to attain the two roots of goodness—Heat and Summits—these roots of goodness cannot be transformed into the roots of goodness of a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because they have not made vows or cultivated contemplation for the sake of benefiting others.
Although these two stages can still be altered, there is no possibility of alteration in that case, because their mental resolve is firm.
If one turns to become a śrāvaka, this principle is not obstructed.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"Upon attaining awakening, they reach it in a single sitting; thereafter, they are fixed as either Buddhas or pratyekabuddhas."
The commentary states:

Regarding the Great Teacher, the Buddha Bhagavān, and the rhinoceros-like Buddha—these two, while remaining in a single sitting and relying upon the fourth dhyāna, by virtue of their lucid and immovable samādhi, initiate from the very beginning the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and continue until awakening; thus, they attain ultimate awakening in that single sitting alone, namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
This meaning shall be explained later.
Other masters say:
from the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity up to enlightenment, one attains the ultimate goal in a single sitting.

If someone maintains that there is a distinct Pratyekabuddha different from the rhinoceros-like Pratyekabuddha, and that for such a person the two roots of goodness transform into those of a Bodhisattva,
this point is not refuted.

Is it the case that one has not cultivated the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) in past lives, but produces the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) through exertion in this very life; is such a possibility certain, or is it not?
This is not the case. Why?
The verse says:
Regarding the phrase "preceded by those factors conducive to liberation" (*pūrvaṃ tad-vimokṣabhāgīya*), the commentary states:

This meaning should be understood as certain: having first produced the roots of merit that are factors conducive to liberation (*vimokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) in a previous birth, one only now, in this present life, attains the roots of merit that are factors conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*).

If a person practices with urgency, through how many lifetimes must they practice to attain the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) and the roots of merit conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*)?
The verse says:
"Swift liberation occurs in three lifetimes."
The commentary states:

In the first birth, one first produces the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*); in the second birth, one subsequently cultivates the roots of goodness conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*); and in the third birth, one attains the Noble Path (*āryamārga*). This is like the sequence of sowing seeds, the growth of sprouts, and the formation of fruit.
Why is the sequence as it is?
Within this Dharma—the truth and the teaching—one should cause one’s own continuum to enter, abide, mature, and be liberated.
Regarding the roots of virtue conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*), the masters say: [The verse says:]
"Of the nature of hearing and reflection.
The commentary explains:
"This karma belongs solely to the category of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection, not to the category of wisdom derived from cultivation."
How many types of karma are there?
The verse says:
three types of karma.
The commentary states:
If one speaks of what is most excellent, it is solely mental action (manas-karma), as it is embraced by aspiration (praṇidhāna).
However, the two actions of body and speech also constitute the capacity for the factors conducive to liberation (mokṣa-bhāgīya).

Why is this? Because there are those who, by giving a single meal or by delighting in observing a single precept, are led by the power of liberation; through this karma, they produce the roots of goodness conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*).
Where does this karma project [rebirth]?
The verse says:
It projects birth in the human realm.
The commentary states:
Within the human realm, this karma can be projected and produced in three continents, but not elsewhere.
This is because the two factors of wisdom (*prajñā*) and renunciation (*nirveda*) are respectively absent in those other places.

Having explained the capacity for the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) through their correspondence with the meaning, the sequence of entering the contemplation of the Four Truths is now to be explained.
Within this context, everything up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) has already been discussed; what remains is now being explained, and thus these words are spoken.
The verse says:
Immediately following the Supreme Mundane Dharma, there is the stainless Dharma-knowledge-acceptance (anāsrava-dharmajñāna-kṣānti).
The commentary says:
Immediately following the "supreme mundane roots of goodness" (*laukikāgradharma*), the "patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) arises without interval.
What is its object?
The verse says:
"Suffering of the desire realm.
The commentary states:

The suffering of the desire realm is its object; this patience is called "the patience of the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). To indicate that it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it is distinguished by means of its outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Because this patience (*kṣānti*) can attain the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), it is called "patience for the knowledge of phenomena" (*dharmajñānakṣānti*), just as one refers to a tree by its flowers or fruit.
This patience is said to be the entry into the stage of those rightly settled (*samyaktvaniyāma*). Why is this?
Because through this patience, the practitioner of contemplation is able to enter right concentration.
What, then, is this very dharma?
It is said in the Sūtra:
Nirvāṇa is called "correct.
To be "fixed" therein means to be unswerving and non-different [from it]; because one has attained this certainty, it is called "entry.
If this patience (*kṣānti*) has already arisen, such a person is called a "path-walker" (*mārgajina*).

At the moment immediately preceding the arising of this dharma, the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) has already been transformed and ceased; this is the future functional capacity of this *kṣānti*.
This interpretation is plausible.
There is no remainder, just as when a lamp is lit.

Other masters say that the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (laukikāgradharma) extinguishes the nature of an ordinary person (pṛthagjanatva), but this interpretation is incorrect because it would be identical to other mundane phenomena.
This interpretation is without fault, because this and that are mutually contradictory; it is like killing an enemy by mounting upon the shoulders of one's superior enemy.
Other masters say:
extinction occurs by means of two [paths], for these two resemble the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
The verse says:
"Next, the dharma-knowledge of suffering.

The commentary explains: Immediately following the receptivity to the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna-kṣānti*), the dharma-knowledge regarding the suffering of the desire realm arises; this is called the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*).
One should know that "non-outflow" (anāsrava) flows to all places.
Just as the Dharma-knowledge-acceptance (dharma-jñāna-kṣānti) and Dharma-knowledge (dharma-jñāna) arise regarding suffering in the desire realm, the verse says:
"In the same way, [the subsequent] acceptance and knowledge arise regarding the remaining categories of suffering."
The commentary states:

Immediately after the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*), there arises a subsequent patience of subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) which takes the suffering of the form and formless realms collectively as its single object; this is called the subsequent patience of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*).
Immediately following this, subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*) arises; this is called the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*).
Because one realizes the true principle of phenomena (*dharma-tattva*) upon first entering contemplation, this principle remains indestructible.
Whether a Buddha appears in the world or does not appear, this principle remains constant; therefore, it is called "Dharma.

Consequently, because the subsequent observation is of the same category as the preceding observation, and the subsequent object of focus is of the same category as the preceding object, the subsequent is designated by the name "category" (anvaya) because it conforms to the preceding.
Just as four patiences and knowledges arise regarding suffering, the verse says:
"The same for the three truths.
The commentary says:

Immediately after the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*), the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) arises regarding the desire realm; immediately thereafter, the dharma-knowledge of origin (*samudaya-dharma-jñāna*) arises. In this same immediate succession, the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of origin (*samudaya-anvaya-jñāna*) arise for the remaining [realms].

Regarding the desire realm, the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-dharma-jñāna*) arise; subsequently, the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-anvaya-jñāna*) arise for the remaining [realms].

Regarding the desire realm, the receptivity to the dharma-knowledge of the path that counteracts suffering (*mārga-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the dharma-knowledge of the path (*mārga-dharma-jñāna*) arise; subsequently, the receptivity to the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*) and the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) arise for the remaining [realms].
The verse says:
These sixteen moments of mind contemplate the four truths.
The commentary says:
According to this sequence, the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths consists of sixteen moments of mind.
Other schools, however,
maintain that the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths consists of only a single moment of mind.
One should understand that this contemplation regarding that [sūtra] is of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*). Why?
Because in that sūtra, the contemplation of the Four Truths is taught without distinguishing their respective categories.
Regarding this contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, the verse says:
"There are three: seeing the object and the entity.
The commentary explains:
Contemplation by way of seeing refers to the discernment of the characteristics of the truths through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Contemplation by way of objective domain refers to being associated with untainted wisdom while sharing its same objective domain.
As for the contemplation of phenomena (*vastu-vipaśyanā*), it arises from dissociated factors (*viprayukta-dharma*), namely the arising of ethical discipline and so forth.
Once suffering has been seen, these three contemplations are thereby established.
Regarding the remaining truths, such as origin (*samudaya*) and so on, there is contemplation of phenomena by way of abandonment, realization, and cultivation.

If they claim that these are established as a single contemplation based on viewing them through the lens of insight (*darśana*), this is incorrect, because the characteristics of the four truths are distinct.
Furthermore, their claim that one perceives all truths through the characteristic of selflessness (*anātman*) is also untenable.
Why is this? Because this contemplation is not established by beginning with the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
If that were so, it would contradict the Sūtra.
The Sūtra says:

"The noble disciple discerns suffering by way of the characteristic of suffering; he discerns origination by way of the characteristic of origination; he discerns cessation by way of the characteristic of cessation; and he discerns the path by way of the characteristic of the path."
The wisdom associated with untainted reflection is called the awakening factor of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga).
If you say: "This statement in the sutra was spoken in order to reveal the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga)," [we reply:]...
This interpretation is not correct, because [the truths] are seen and cultivated [successively].
If you argue that one speaks of "contemplating the truths simultaneously" because, by seeing one truth, one gains mastery over the others; [we reply: no.
This interpretation is without fault.
Within the contemplation of the Four Truths, some say one emerges from contemplation, while others say one does not emerge; this point should be considered.
