If it is explained in this way, then at that time, suffering is correctly seen and thus ceases, while the origin is eliminated, leading to the attainment of cessation through the cultivation of the path.

If one maintains that the truths are observed simultaneously in this manner, there is no fault; for while one truth is observed through a single vision, the other truths are said to be observed through the observation of their respective objects.
If one considers them in terms of the sequence of vision,
it is stated in the sūtras that the four truths are contemplated in a fixed order;
this teaching is evident.
The Sūtra says:
"O Householder!
One does not contemplate the truths all at once."
How does one contemplate?
One contemplates in successive order.
As explained at length, there are three sūtras, each containing a simile.
If you say:
"If a person has no doubt and no lack of firm resolve regarding the Truth of Suffering, they likewise have no doubt and no lack of firm resolve regarding the Buddha," then based on this sutra,
one knows that there is a simultaneous contemplation of the Four Noble Truths.
This interpretation is not correct; it is said that because [the mind] relies on what does not arise again and must necessarily cease, this statement was made.
Regarding the sixteen moments of mind that were mentioned, the verse says:
"The Supreme Mundane Dharma shares the same stage."
The commentary states:
Following the stage upon which the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) relies, the sixteen moments of mind (*ṣoḍaśa-citta*) of the contemplation likewise rely upon that same stage.
There are six stages upon which the Supreme Mundane Dharma relies, as has already been explained previously.
Why must this principle— that patience comes first and wisdom follows— be necessarily accepted?
For this reason,
the verse says:
"Patience (kṣānti) and knowledge (jñāna) constitute the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), respectively.
The commentary explains:

"Patience" refers to the path of uninterrupted transition; because the severance of the acquisition (prāpti) of the afflictions cannot be interrupted, it is called the path of uninterrupted transition.

"Knowledge" refers to the path of liberation; because it is the attainment of the state of having already been liberated from afflictions regarding persons and phenomena, and because it arises simultaneously with the attainment of cessation and dissociation, it is called the path of liberation.
Therefore, these two must necessarily exist together, just as when one pulls back the bolt while opening a door.

If it were said that the second path of liberation arises simultaneously with the attainment of dissociation from defilements, then the knowledge that discerns dissociation from doubt could not arise regarding this object, because it is through *kṣānti* (receptivity) that the defilements are extinguished.
This objection is not valid. If you say:
"The nine clusters of fetters are abandoned by patience (*kṣānti*), not by knowledge (*jñāna*)."
This would contradict the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
This interpretation is not correct, because patience (*kṣānti*) is a concomitant category of knowledge (*jñāna*).
Just as the affairs of a minister are spoken of as the affairs of the king, so it is with patience in relation to knowledge.
Are all sixteen moments of mind considered the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) because they involve the vision of the truths, or is it not so?
Nevertheless, the verse says:
"Because one sees what was never seen before, the path of seeing consists of fifteen moments of mind."
The commentary states:

Beginning with the patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) up to the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*), these fifteen moments of mind are called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
For what reason is it named the Path of Seeing?

Because one sees truths never before seen, at the sixteenth moment of mind there is nothing previously unseen that is now being seen for the first time; rather, because one repeatedly practices what has already been seen, it constitutes the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
Is it not otherwise?
This mind also perceives truths that were not previously perceived by the patience regarding the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñānakṣānti*).
This interpretation is incorrect.
Why is this? Because the present reflection concerns the truths (*satya*) and not the moments (*kṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it is not by means of the eighth moment that the truth is not seen.
For example, if there is a single field where only one stalk remains unharvested, it is called an "unharvested field.
This principle does not apply here, because [the path of subsequent knowledge] is subsumed under the category of the fruit (*phala*).

Furthermore, because it consists of the cultivation of the eight knowledges and sixteen aspects, because the path has already been previously extinguished, and because the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is its continuity, the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*) is therefore established as belonging to the path of cultivation.
This meaning of non-retrogression arises from the firm maintenance of the abandonment and separation from the afflictions of those who have seen the truths (*dṛṣṭisatyakleśa*). If you say:
"Therefore, this belongs to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*)."
This interpretation is not correct, because it entails the fault of excessive over-extension.
How can the seven knowledges be categorized as belonging to the path of seeing?
Because the vision has not yet reached its culmination.

In this context, because the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana*) is not yet complete, these seven knowledges (*jñāna*) exist within the interval of vision; therefore, they are enumerated as the path of vision (*darśanamārga*).
Having thus explained this point—that which determines the arising and the distinctions between the paths of vision and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Furthermore, the distinctions among those who have already entered the path of the noble ones shall now be explained in detail.
It should be understood that within this context—referring to the fifteen moments whose nature is the previously described path of vision (darśanamārga)—there are two types of persons.
The verse says:
"The two types of persons with dull and sharp faculties are those who practice through faith and through the Dharma among the [nine] types.
The commentary says:
If a person of dull faculties practices therein, they are said to be "one who follows by faith" (śraddhānusārin).
If a person of sharp faculties practices therein, they are said to be "one who follows by the Dharma" (dharmānusārin).
Because such a person follows by means of faith and because they follow the meaning [of the teachings], they are called "one who follows by faith."

Furthermore, because one follows by means of the faculty of faith, this constitutes the "person following through faith"; thus, it is called "following through faith," as one first investigates the meaning by relying on others.
It is the same for "following through the Dharma," as one first investigates the meaning by oneself through the true Dharma, such as the sūtras and so forth.
For this purpose, four authorities are taught:

the Dharma is the authority, not the person; the meaning is the authority, not the words and phrases; the definitive meaning is the authority, not the non-definitive meaning; and wisdom is the authority, not consciousness.

How are these four distinguished? They are distinguished by way of four types of persons: first, by way of the person who is arrogant; second, by way of the person who is a Lokāyatika; third, by way of the person who abides in the grasping of their own views; and fourth, by way of the person who excels in learning.

In this regard, for those who are arrogant, the Dharma is the authority and not the person, because it is through common discourse and deliberation that something is determined to be obtained by wisdom, rather than merely by differences in physical demeanor.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has said that while there are persons who teach the Dharma, herein it is the Dharma that is the authority, not the person.
This Dharma is of two kinds:
words and phrases, and their meaning.
In this context, the meaning is the authority, not the words, because one does not become attached to the verbal expressions of a particular land. Why is this?
One should not establish the grasping of words as the supreme certainty; rather, one should contemplate and discern the meaning.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that there are two kinds of sūtras: those of definitive meaning (nītārtha) and those of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
If one discriminates the meaning, one should take the sūtras of definitive meaning as the authority, and not those of non-definitive meaning.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that consciousness arises in the wholesome realms through meritorious and immovable formations; he has taught that the knowledge of the Four Noble Truths leads to the attainment of Nirvana.
If a person practices the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma, they take wisdom as the measure, not consciousness.
Furthermore, because there is loss or non-loss during four periods, four measures are established in relation to four types of persons:
first, the period of recitation; second, the period of memorization; third, the period of discernment; and fourth, the period of practice.
Regarding these two persons, the verse says:
"If one has already abandoned the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation, they are candidates for the first fruit.
The commentary explains:

The "first fruit of the śramaṇa" refers to the fruit of srotāpanna; it is so called because it is the foremost among all fruits to be attained, and because this fruit has not yet been attained [prior to its realization].
If it were by way of actual existence, then those who merely follow through faith or follow through the Dharma—
whether they have already abandoned the afflictions of the realm of cultivation via the mundane path or are still bound by all fetters— are said to be "candidates for the fruit of stream-entry."
The verse says:
"Up until the destruction of the five categories.
The commentary says:

If this person has previously, by means of the mundane path, eliminated the afflictions of the desire realm to the extent of exhausting up to five categories, such a person is said to be "heading toward the first fruit.
The verse says:
"Heading toward the second, before the destruction of the ninth."
The commentary states:

If these two types of persons, from the fifth stage onward, first eliminate six, seven, or eight categories [of afflictions] before entering the path of seeing, they are said to be "candidates for the second fruit," namely, *sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returners).
The verse says:
Having become free from desire for the realms of desire and form, one then proceeds toward the third fruit.
The commentary says:

If this person has already eliminated the ninth grade [of defilement] and is free from the afflictions of the desire realm, and further eliminates the afflictions of the higher realms up to the sphere of nothingness, these two types of persons are said to be "heading toward the third fruit," namely, the Anāgāmin.
The verse says:
The sixteen [moments] are the fruits of the two abidings; they correspond to the three types of persons according to their respective inclinations.
The commentary says:
If the sixteenth moment of mind arises, one cannot further say that this person is a follower by faith or a follower by dharma, nor can one say they are "heading toward the fruit.
How, then, can it be described?
Regarding those who abide in the fruits:
in which fruit do they abide?

If they were previously directed toward a particular fruit, they now abide in that very fruit—whether it be the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), or the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*).
The fruit of arhatship differs from the preceding three; it cannot be attained from the beginning in the same manner as they are, by means of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*). Why is this?

Because the path of seeing is capable of eliminating those afflictions to be eliminated by the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and it is logically impossible to first eliminate the afflictions of the truths (*satya*) and then become free from desire for the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*).
The verse says:
At that time, one attains the state of faith and joy, or the state of seeing; these correspond to those of dull and sharp faculties.
The commentary says:
At this time, those of dull faculties who previously followed by means of faith are now called "attainers through faith" (śraddhādhimukta).
Those of sharp faculties who previously followed by means of the Dharma are now called "attainers through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
Because one has attained the highest degree of faith and wisdom, it is therefore manifested by faith, aspiration, and vision.

Furthermore, for what reason is a person who has already abandoned five categories of afflictions through cultivation designated as a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) specifically at the sixteenth moment of mind?
They are said to be "candidates for the fruit of once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin) for this reason.
The verse says:
Because they have not yet attained the path superior to the fruit, and because they have not yet practiced that superior path, they abide in the fruit and are not candidates.
The commentary states:
It is a settled principle that when a person has correctly attained a fruit, they do not simultaneously attain a path superior to that fruit.

Therefore, as long as a person abides in a fruit and has not yet practiced the path superior to that fruit in order to attain a distinct fruit, at that time they cannot be said to be "heading toward" (*pratipannaka*) that distinct fruit.
The same applies to other fruits.
If a person who has become detached from the third dhyāna enters right concentration again by relying on a lower stage, that person will necessarily manifest the path of superior fruit.

If it were not so, then one born from a lower realm into a higher realm would not be associated with the faculty of pleasure (*sukhendriya*). This is the meaning [of the teaching] regarding the establishment of those who have attained multiple cessations (*nirodha*) and those who have abandoned desire (*vītarāga*) as entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktvaniyāma*).
The systematic establishment of persons shall now be explained; therefore, this point will first be established.

Just as it was stated regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) that they consist of nine grades, so too does the verse say:
"The faults have nine grades, and the virtues (*guṇa*) of each stage (*bhūmi*) are likewise."
The commentary states:

Just as it has been explained that there are nine grades of afflictions in the desire realm, one should know that in each stage of the form and formless realms, up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are likewise nine grades of afflictions.
As it is with afflictions, so it is with virtues.
To counteract these faults, they are called the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
In each stage (*bhūmi*), there are nine times nine grades; why is this so?
The verse says:
There are three grades—mild, medium, and superior—with further distinctions such as "even milder" and so forth.
The commentary says:

The fundamental [distinctions] are divided into three grades—mild, medium, and superior—and because each grade is further differentiated into mild, medium, and superior sub-grades, they are established as nine grades in total.
What is this? There are the weak-weak grade, the weak-medium grade, and the weak-strong grade.
There are the medium-weak grade, the medium-medium grade, and the medium-strong grade.
There are superior-weak, superior-middle, and superior-superior grades.

Among these, the superior-superior grade of afflictions is extinguished by the weak-weak grade of the path, and so on, until the weak-weak grade of afflictions is extinguished by the superior-superior grade of the path.

Why is this? Because the path-factors of the highest-superior grade cannot arise [from them], and because within the mental continuum of one who has already produced the highest-superior grade of the path, the defilements of the highest-superior grade no longer exist.
It is like washing clothes: first one removes coarse dust and grime, and only afterward does one remove the fine.
Again, it is like coarse darkness being dispelled by subtle light, and subtle darkness being dispelled by great light.
The delusions of the path are likewise. Why is this?

Because the power of the white dharmas is strong and the power of the black dharmas is weak; therefore, by the arising of even a single moment of the mild-mild noble path, all the afflictions of the highest-of-the-high (adhimātra-adhimātra) grade—which have been reinforced through the beginningless cycle of birth and death—are entirely extinguished and abandoned.

For example, three diseases that have been aggravated over a long period can be eradicated by a single *liang* of *trikuṭa* powder; likewise, a small lamp for a single moment can destroy a great darkness that has persisted for a long time.
Thus, regarding all nine grades of afflictions, the verse says:
"As long as the grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have not been extinguished, one who abides in the fruit completes seven births.
The commentary explains:

If a person has already entered the fruit [of stream-entry] but has not yet eliminated even one grade of the afflictions to be abandoned by the path of cultivation, such a person is called a *srotāpanna*.
Because they can undergo at most seven more births, they are said to be "seven-births," which is superior to all subsequent [categories].
Why is this? Because not everyone undergoes seven births; therefore, the sūtra speaks of seven births as being preeminent.
To undergo birth seven times is the completion of those births.
Why is this? The word "superior" (viśeṣa) has the sense of being "extreme.
A "path" (mārga) refers to the stream leading toward nirvāṇa, for by traveling along this path, one reaches nirvāṇa.
Because this person has already reached this stream, they are called a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer).
What does it mean to "reach the stream"?
If reaching the stream were defined by the attainment of the first path, then the eighth [candidate] would also have to be considered a *srotāpanna*.

If one were called a "Stream-enterer" (srotāpanna) merely by attaining the first fruit, then those who have extinguished many of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), as well as those who have already extinguished all nine grades of such afflictions, would also have to be established as Stream-enterers.
However, with respect to those who have attained all the fruits, it is by virtue of attaining the first fruit that one is established as a Stream-enterer.
For what reason is one who attains the first fruit designated as a *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer), yet not designated as an "eighth person"?

It is because they have attained the path leading toward the fruit, because they have attained both the paths of seeing and cultivation, and because they have realized the complete flow [of the noble stream].
Within the subsequent knowledge of the path (mārgānvaya-jñāna), this person therefore attains the name of Srotāpanna, whereas one who is merely "heading toward" it does not.
This person undergoes seven existences and seven intermediate states within the human realm, and likewise in the celestial realm; thus, this person undergoes twenty-eight births in total.
Why is it said that seven births are superior?
It is because of the equality of the number seven; thus, seven births are said to be superior.
For example, as with the "sevenfold supreme knowledge" (*saptasthāna-kauśalya*) and the "seven-leaf tree" (*saptaparṇa*); so say the Vaibhāṣikas.
If that is so, how does the Sūtra state:
"It is impossible for one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta) to undergo an eighth existence"?

The intention of this Sūtra refers only to a single path; if one were to analyze it according to the literal text, even the intermediate state (antarābhava) would not exist, just as it is likewise for those who ascend to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) as their supreme attainment.
The eighth birth should not exist; however, since this is stated in reference to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no fault.
What is the proof for this?
There are both sūtras and reasoning.
By what means is it established that there are seven returns each for humans and devas, rather than the two combined having seven returns?
The Sūtra states that there are only seven returns within the realms of humans and devas.
How is this meaning to be understood: that there are seven returns to the human realm and seven returns to the celestial realm?
It is because the Sūtra states:
"Seven times among humans and seven times among devas."
The Kāśyapīyas state:
There are distinct teachings which say that one undergoes seven rebirths among humans and seven among devas; this should be understood in the same sense.
If a person attains the fruit of *srotāpanna* within the human realm, they will subsequently necessarily attain the fruit of *arhat* within the human realm.
It is the same regarding the heavenly realms.
Furthermore, what is the cause that a *srotāpanna* does not undergo an eighth existence?

It is because the continuity [of their karma] matures within such a limited duration; the nature of the path is likewise. This is, for example, like the venom of a seven-step snake, or like a quartan fever.

Furthermore, because seven fetters (saṃyojana) remain as a residue—two lower fetters remaining and five upper fetters complete—one does not attain parinirvāṇa even though the Noble Path manifests during the intermediate state; this is because one must undergo seven more births, being sustained by the force of karma and impelled by the two types of karma belonging to the lower and upper realms.
If no Buddhas appear in the world, one may attain the fruit of Arhatship while remaining at home.
Once the fruit of Arhatship has been attained, one will certainly not remain at home; by the very nature of things, one will necessarily assume the deportment of a bhikṣu.
Other masters say:
"Or he may adopt the deportment of a person on a different path.
How is it that such a person does not fall away from the wholesome path?"

Because karma for proceeding along evil paths does not increase; because karma that has already increased and is capable of producing retribution no longer possesses the functional power to do so once retribution has been produced; because the continuum is suppressed by exceptionally powerful roots of goodness; and because both conduct and intention are pure.
If there is karma that inevitably leads to rebirth in the evil realms, one cannot even attain the roots of goodness of patience, let alone the stage of a *srotāpanna*.
Regarding this, a verse says:
"The fool, by committing a small offense, is born in the evil realms; The wise, though committing a great offense, avoid the evil realms."
"Just as a small piece of round iron will surely sink in water, yet when that same iron is fashioned into a bowl, it can float.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"Seven births are considered the maximum; one shall bring an end to suffering."
What is the end of suffering?
It is that which, having transcended these seven [stages], there is no further suffering, such that suffering does not continue in succession.
Furthermore, nirvana is called the final limit of suffering.
How is it that one "produces" nirvāṇa?
It is because, by being able to eliminate obstacles, one attains nirvāṇa; for example, people say, "I am producing emptiness.

There are others for whom seven births are considered supreme, yet this is not fixed. Therefore, those who have not yet extinguished the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) while abiding in a fruit are not described as being "supreme with seven births."
The verse says:
"If one has extinguished three or four categories [of afflictions], one is a 'family-to-family' (kulaṃkula) practitioner after two or three births.
The commentary says:
This stream-enterer becomes a "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner through three causes and conditions:
first, by the destruction of afflictions, specifically because three or four categories of afflictions have been eliminated;
second, by attaining the untainted faculties that serve as the antidotes to those afflictions.
Thirdly, because two births remain as the remainder after [the first] two.

In the verse, only two causes are explicitly shown; however, when a *srotāpanna* subsequently attains cessation, they acquire the meaning of untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) which serve as the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*). Since this is not established by mere verbal explanation, it is the minimum possible occurrence at the time of birth, and since such [a state] ought not to arise [otherwise], only "birth" (*jāti*) is mentioned.
Why is it not established that [the defilements] are extinguished by means of the extinction of the fifth category?
Because when the five categories are extinguished, the sixth category is necessarily extinguished as well. Why is this so?

A single category of affliction cannot obstruct the fruit that a practitioner of insight (vipaśyanā) ought to attain, just as in the case of the "one-interval" person (*ekavīcika*), who does not cross over the realms.
Regarding those who go from family to family (*kulād-kulaga*), there are two types:

first, the "deva-family-to-family" (*devakulād-kulaga*), which refers to one born among the gods who attains parinirvāṇa after going through two or three families, whether in this heaven or in that heaven.
The same applies to those of the "two-household" (dvivārṣika) family within the human realm, whether in this continent or that continent.
Furthermore, regarding the person who has attained the first fruit, the verse says:
"Having extinguished up to five categories [of afflictions], one is a candidate for the second fruit."
The commentary states:

If a person, having attained the fruit, has already abandoned from one up to five grades of the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and their mind is currently engaged with the sixth grade, it should be known that this person is "heading toward" the second fruit.
The verse says:
Having already extinguished the sixth category, one becomes a Sakṛdāgāmin.
The commentary says:

When this person who has attained the fruit has already abandoned the sixth category [of afflictions] and their mind is currently engaged with the seventh category, they are said to have reached the second fruit.

Because they will be reborn once more in the heavens and then return once more to the human realm, they are called a *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner). Beyond this, there is no further birth; for the three categories of delusion—desire, hatred, and ignorance—have become attenuated, and now only the weak grade remains.
Regarding this person who has attained the fruit, the verse says:
"Having already extinguished seven or eight categories [of afflictions], being in one more birth is called 'One-Interval' (ekavīcika), and thus they are heading toward the third fruit.
The commentary says:
Due to three causes and conditions, a Sakṛdāgāmin becomes an Ekavīcika:

first, because of the extinction of seven or eight grades of afflictions; second, because of the attainment of the untainted faculties that serve as the antidote to those afflictions; and third, because only one more birth remains.
How can a single category of affliction obstruct this person from attaining the fruit of *anāgāmin*?
It is because this person ought to transcend the lower realm (*adhobhūmi*).
As previously stated, within the three stages, three types of karma arise as obstructions.
Just as karma can act as an obstruction, one should know that afflictions (*kleśa*) do likewise.

Because they obstruct the stages of the retributive fruit (*vipākaphala*), the fruit of maturation (*niṣyandaphala*), and the fruit of outflow (*puruṣakāraphala*) that are to be traversed, both afflictions and karma constitute obstructions.
The "single interval" (ekavicika) refers to an obstruction to the Dharma; this obstruction is unique, occurring in a single lifetime, because it obstructs this person from attaining parinirvāṇa.
Because this single delusion obstructs this person from attaining the fruit of anāgāmin, they are called "one-interval."
The meaning of "extinguishing seven or eight categories" is as follows:

if one has already extinguished the third, fourth, seventh, or eighth category of afflictions prior to entering the contemplation of the Four Truths, and only later realizes the fruit, one does not become a *kulaṅkula* (one who goes from family to family), nor is one an *ekavīcika* (one with one interval). This continues until the superior path resulting from that fruit manifests before one.
The verse says:
Nine types of Anāgāmins are extinguished.
The commentary says:

One who has attained the fruit [of the path] by extinguishing the ninth grade of afflictions should be known as an Anāgāmin, because they will not return again to the desire realm due to the complete extinction of the five lower fetters.
These five cessations are spoken of by way of their numerical combination. Why is this?
Because, having necessarily already ceased three previously, one subsequently ceases two.
The verse says:
Among these, there are those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, upon rebirth, with exertion, without exertion, or as those who go upstream.
The commentary says:
Because this person attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, they are called one who "extinguishes in the interval.

Likewise, because they attain parinirvāṇa immediately upon being born, they are called one who "extinguishes upon birth," rather than one who attains parinirvāṇa through application (*sābhisaṃskāra*).
Through parinirvāṇa by way of practice, this meaning should be understood: there are five types of these non-returners (anāgāmin).
One who attains extinction in the intermediate state (antarāparinirvāyin) attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate existence (antarābhava).

Regarding those who undergo birth and cessation: they are those who, having already been born, will soon enter parinirvāṇa because they have fully cultivated the path of transport; their cessation occurs through nirvāṇa with remainder.
Other masters say that they possess both types of nirvāṇa.
This interpretation is not correct, because such a person lacks mastery over the relinquishing of life.

As for those who speak of "extinction with exertion" (*sābhisaṃskāra-parinirvāyin*), it refers to one who, having taken birth, does not cease their application in cultivation and attains parinirvāṇa through great effort, owing to their constant practice of the path that carries them forward.

Regarding those who attain extinction through non-exertion (*anabhisamskāra-parinirvāyin*): they do not do so by means of great effort, but rather because they have cultivated with reverence the path that carries one across.
Other masters say:
it is because they attain parinirvāṇa by means of both conditioned and unconditioned paths.
This interpretation is not correct, because it entails the fault of excessive over-extension.
In the sūtra, the non-cessation of formations is taught first, followed by the cessation of formations; such a sequence accords with reason.
The path that carries [one] and the path that does not carry [one] are established by means of cultivation and non-cultivation; therefore, cessation is not attained through effort.
That which is attained through effort and is subject to arising and ceasing refers to the most capable path of carrying and the supreme path.
Those whose afflictions are of the weakest grade are "those who go upstream" (ūrdhvasrotas), meaning they ascend to be reborn in higher realms.
Regarding these places of rebirth, they do not attain parinirvāṇa therein.
The term "stream" (srotas) carries the sense of "flowing" or "proceeding."
The verse says:
"In this regard, regarding meditative concentration, there is mixed cultivation and no inferiority.
The commentary says:
These persons who go upstream (ūrdhvasrotas) are of two kinds by way of cause and effect; that is, by way of cause and by way of effect.
By way of cause, it is because they have either practiced meditative concentration with intermingling or practiced meditative concentration without intermingling as their cause.
Regarding the result: Akaniṣṭha is supreme because it is the highest of the heavens, and the Peak of Existence (Bhavāgra) is supreme.
In this regard, if a person takes the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration as the cause, they will be reborn in Akaniṣṭha and attain parinirvāṇa there.
The verse says:
"Transcending, partially transcending, and universal retrogression.
The commentary explains:
Akaniṣṭha is the supreme [destination].
There are three types of those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), distinguished by their modes of transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*) and so forth.

Among these, the "transcender" is one who, having practiced the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) in a mixed manner within the desire realm, falls back from the three higher absorptions; yet, by relishing the flavor of the first absorption, he dies and is reborn in the Brahmakāyika heaven. Due to the habitual cultivation of his past lives, he further practices the fourth absorption in a mixed manner therein; dying from that state, he is reborn in Akaniṣṭha.
This person dies in the intermediate state and emerges above; this is called "emergence.
As for "half-emergence," after arising in the Pure Abodes from the First Dhyāna, one bypasses one distinct location until finally arising in Akaniṣṭha.
A noble one will certainly not be born in the realm of Mahābrahmā, because that is a place of biased views and because [the noble one] has transcended all [such states] in a single lifetime.
As for those who regress universally: if a person practices in all stages, they will eventually enter Akaniṣṭha.
An Anāgāmin of the "never-returning" type does not undergo a second birth in the place where he was born, because his practice has become superior.
If this is so, then the meaning of "Anāgāmin" (Non-returner) is fully realized for such a person, as they never again return to the place where they were already born.
One who thus practices the mixed meditative absorption (vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna) should be known as one who proceeds to Akaniṣṭha.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"The others proceed to the Peak (mūrdhan)."
The commentary states:
For those who ascend through the stages by means of non-mixed cultivation (aśubhā-vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna), the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is considered supreme. Why is this?
This person, following their meditative absorption, gives rise to a mind that relishes its flavor; having been born in all [other] places, they enter only the five Pure Abodes.
By successively taking birth in the three formless realms, they eventually take birth in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) and attain parinirvāṇa.
This refers to one who practices *śamatha*, while the former refers to one who practices *vipaśyanā*.

Regarding those who proceed upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*) and attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state, I see this meaning as not contradicting reason when I speak of the Akaniṣṭha and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as superior; for beyond these, there is no further place of practice. It is, for example, like saying that the *srotāpanna* is "superior" by virtue of seven births.
These five persons are all those who practice the *anāgāmin* stage of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).
The verse says:
"The remaining four practice the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)."
The commentary states:
There is another type of non-returner who proceeds to the formless realm.
Having already become detached from the desire realm, they relinquish birth in the form realm and undergo birth in the formless realm.
These persons are further of four kinds, due to distinctions such as those of birth and cessation.
Thus, these non-returners (anāgāmin) constitute six types in total.
The verse says:
The cessation in the desire realm is further distinguished.
The commentary states:
there are other non-returners who attain parinirvāṇa in this very life; this is called "parinirvāṇa in the present life" (dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāṇa), and it is designated as the seventh.
The verse says:
"When these three types of persons are further divided into three each, one should know there are nine modes of colored action.
The commentary says:
Furthermore, because there are three types of *anāgāmins*, each with its own three distinctions, there are nine types of *anāgāmins* who proceed to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). The three types are:
those who attain cessation in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), those who attain cessation upon rebirth (*upapadyaparinirvāyin*), and those who flow upwards (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
What are the three distinctions for each?

Regarding those who attain parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), they are distinguished by three analogies of iron sparks: because they attain parinirvāṇa swiftly, not swiftly, or after a long time.

Regarding "those who attain parinirvāṇa upon birth" (upapadyaparinirvāyin): this refers to those who attain parinirvāṇa after being born, whether they have no further application of effort or do have such application. Why is this?
Because these three types alike attain parinirvāṇa after having been born; therefore, all three are equally designated as "attaining parinirvāṇa upon birth."
Regarding those who go upstream (*ūrdhvasrotas*), because they differ in their transcendence and other such distinctions, there are three types of persons.
All three are further differentiated from one another by whether their parinirvāṇa occurs swiftly, not swiftly, or after a long period of time.
The verse says:
Furthermore, there are distinctions among those persons, due to differences in karma, afflictions, and faculties.
The commentary says:
These three types and nine kinds of *anāgāmin*s differ from one another due to distinctions in their karma, afflictions (*kleśa*), and faculties (*indriya*).

These three types of persons possess distinctions in their karma regarding retribution in the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharma-vedanīya*), retribution in the next life (*upapadya-vedanīya*), and retribution in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
Furthermore, it is because there are distinctions in the frequency with which the weak, medium, and superior afflictions operate within their respective continuums.
Moreover, it is because each of these three types of persons possesses distinctions among superior, medium, and weak faculties.
Therefore, these three types of persons each have their distinctions according to principle.
The former two and the third differ due to distinctions in their afflictions and their faculties; the latter three differ due to distinctions in their subsequent karmic retribution.
Because these nine persons possess nine types of karma, afflictions, and faculties, there are thus nine kinds of Anāgāmins.
If this is so, why does the Sūtra speak of seven types of noble persons?
The verse says:
"The upward-streamer is not differentiated; thus seven noble beings are taught.
The commentary says:
The "Upstreamer" (ūrdhva-srotas) is so named because their nature is to flow upwards.
Since it is taught that this person is free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*), the Sūtra speaks of seven types of noble practitioners (*ārya-pudgala*).
Why is it that, based on such an upstreamer, the Sūtra describes seven noble practices, rather than describing the practices of other learners (*śaikṣa*)?
Only this person practices [this path] in other stages, whereas others do not.
This person performs only wholesome karma and does not perform unwholesome karma.
If a person practices this conduct, they go there once and do not return.
The three meanings thus described are absent in all other noble ones; therefore, the verse says:
"Because they have gone and will not return, they practice wholesome deeds and do not practice unwholesome ones."
The commentary says:
Therefore, the seven noble practices are established for those who proceed upward (ūrdhvasrotas), but not for others.
If that is so, why does the Sūtra state:
Who are the noble persons (*āryapudgala*)?
They are those in training (*śaikṣa*) who are endowed with right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Furthermore, the sense of being "noble" also applies to other persons.

This is stated as "existing" with a specific intention in mind: namely, that one has attained the permanent non-performance of the five kinds of evil and is protected [thereby], and furthermore, because one has already largely extinguished the afflictions of an evil nature.
If the term "noble person" (*ārya*) were not established according to this specific intention, then such a person would be what is described in this treatise.
Furthermore, regarding those who have already been reborn as non-returners (*anāgāmin*), is there such a distinction?
There is not, for this reason.
The verse says:
Regarding "a noble one who has been reborn in the desire realm does not go to another realm," the commentary explains:
A noble person who has already undergone a subsequent birth within the desire realm will certainly not be reborn in any other realm.
Why is this? Because if one attains the stage of Anāgāmin, one will certainly attain parinirvāṇa in this very life.
Among those in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), if a noble one (ārya) is reborn there, they may at times enter the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu).
If one is an "up-streamer" (ūrdhvasrotas), the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) is the supreme [destination].
If that is so, why did Śakra, Lord of the Devas, say:
"The deva named Akaniṣṭha whom I have heard of was a disciple of the Blessed One; having passed away from my presence, he went there to be reborn"?
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
This statement was made because of a failure to understand the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Why did the Blessed One, the Buddha, not refute this statement?
In order to conform to the joyful mind of Śakra, he did not prevent it.
The verse says:
"Both these [beings] and those born in the higher realms have neither the refinement of faculties nor retrogression."
The commentary states:
These are the noble ones (*ārya*) born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), as well as certain other noble ones, who take rebirth in the higher realms.
Such individuals do not practice the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), nor do they possess the causes and conditions for falling away from their state.

Why is it not permitted that those who have been reborn as humans in the desire realm, or those who have gone to the form or formless realms, undergo the refinement of their faculties (*indriya*) or experience retrogression?
This is because, by transitioning through different births and dwelling in them, their faculties gradually mature and they attain a superior basis (*āśraya*).
Due to these two meanings, there is neither the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) nor the occurrence of falling away (*parihāṇi*).
Furthermore, why does a learner (*śaikṣa*) who has not yet attained freedom from desire not undergo "extinction in the intermediate state" (*antarā-parinirvāṇa*)?

The Vaibhāṣika masters explain it thus: because the path is not yet matured; because the thought [of that state] does not immediately manifest; because the latent afflictions (*anuśaya*) are not of an inferior grade; and because the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) is difficult to escape.

The tasks this person must perform are many: first, they must eliminate the afflictions of an evil or neutral nature; second, they must attain the second and third fruits of śrāmaṇya; and third, they must achieve liberation from the three realms.
If one is in the intermediate state (antarābhava), it has already been stated previously that such a feat cannot be accomplished.
If one cultivates mixed concentration (miśra-samādhi), this person will certainly be reborn in the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
Among these, which meditative concentration (*samādhi*) should be practiced as a preliminary mixed cultivation?
The verse says:
"The subsequent concentration is to be mixed first."
The commentary states:
If a person wishes to practice the meditative absorptions in a mixed manner, they must first practice the fourth dhyāna in a mixed manner. Why is this?
Because this concentration is the most excellent among all matters and all pleasant practices, if one is to practice mixed cultivation, it must necessarily proceed by means of such a method:

either an Arhat or an Anāgāmin first cultivates the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) fourth dhyāna associated with many successions; having emerged from this meditative absorption, they next cultivate the contaminated (*sāsrava*) fourth dhyāna associated with many successions; and having emerged from this meditative absorption, they enter once more into the uncontaminated fourth dhyāna.

Through this sequence, the untainted and tainted continuities are gradually diminished until one enters the untainted contemplation for two moments, the tainted contemplation for two moments, and again the untainted contemplation for two moments; this is called the preparatory stage of the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā-samādhi*).
The verse says:
"It is accomplished by a single thought-moment of mixture.
The commentary says:

If a person, immediately following a moment of the untainted (*anāsrava*), manifests and cultivates a moment of the tainted (*sāsrava*), and immediately following a moment of the tainted, manifests and cultivates a moment of the untainted— then,
because this moment of the tainted is intermingled with two moments of the untainted, this mixed cultivation (*miśra-bhāvanā*) is accomplished.

The first two moments resemble the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the third moment resembles the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*); by such means, one attains the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna.
Once the fourth dhyāna has been thus mixed, through this functional capacity, all remaining meditative absorptions can likewise be mixed.
In what place is this mixed cultivation accomplished?

It is accomplished in the three continents of the desire realm; having previously mastered mixed cultivation and subsequently fallen away from it, one again practices mixed cultivation in the form realm.
Furthermore, what is the function of the mixed cultivation of the four dhyānas?
The verse says:
It is for the sake of rebirth, for sport, and for the fear of falling away through afflictions.
The commentary states:
For three reasons, noble ones practice the meditative absorptions in a mixed manner.
If a person of sharp faculties who is an anāgāmin seeks birth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens, it is for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life.

If an Anāgāmin of dull faculties, out of fear of the afflictions, desires to attain a state of ultimate transcendence regarding the meditative absorptions associated with relishing, so as not to fall back again.
If an Arhat possesses sharp faculties, they cultivate this concentration for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life;
if they possess dull faculties, they cultivate it out of fear of the afflictions and a desire not to fall back again.
Furthermore, why are there exactly five gods born in the Śuddhāvāsa (Pure Abode) heavens?
It is because they are those who have practiced the mixed cultivation of the fourth dhyāna.
The verse says:
"Due to the five grades of mixed cultivation, there are five births in the Pure Abodes.
The commentary explains:
This mixed cultivation consists of only five grades, namely, the distinctions of weak, medium, strong, strong-medium, and strongest.
In the first round, one cultivates three minds to bring them into manifestation: namely, the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), the with-outflows (*sāsrava*), and the outflow-free;
in the second round, six minds;
and in the third round, nine minds.
The fourth set consists of twelve minds;
the fifth set consists of fifteen minds.

These fifteen modes of cultivation take the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens as their fruit. Within this context, one is born there by following all that is with-outflow (sāsrava), whereas by following that which is without-outflow (anāsrava), one does not descend to lower realms.
Other masters say:
"By means of the successive predominance of the faculties such as faith (*śraddhā*) and so forth, one attains birth in the five heavens.
The verse says:
An Anāgāmin who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is called a "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin).
The commentary explains:
because the attainment of cessation exists in this person, or because it constitutes this person, he is said to have "attained cessation."

If an Anāgāmin attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they are called "one who has realized through the body" (*kāyasākṣin*), because they have realized through the body a state resembling *nirvāṇa*.
How is it that they realize it through the body?
Because the mind does not exist [in that state], and because it arises in dependence upon the body.
In other sūtras, eighteen types of persons in training (śaikṣa) are mentioned; why is the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin) not mentioned therein?
Because causes and conditions do not exist.
What causes and conditions do not exist?
There are three types of untainted training and the fruits of untainted training; it is by virtue of these two distinctions that the distinctions among those in training (śaikṣa) are established.
The same applies to the cessation of the mind (*nirodhasamāpatti*), which is neither the fruit of one in training (*śaikṣa*) nor of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Therefore, by virtue of attaining this meditative attainment, one cannot be established as a specific category of person in training.
If categorized according to coarse distinctions, the classifications of the *anāgāmin* should be distinguished as previously explained.
However, if categorized according to subtle distinctions, when divided individually, their number becomes many thousands.
What is the meaning of this?

There are three types of persons who attain extinction in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*), distinguished by their faculties as weak, medium, or superior; they become fourfold through the distinction of stages (*bhūmi*); they become sixfold through the distinction of their natures, such as those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*) and so forth; they become sixteenfold through the distinction of different locations; and they become thirty-sixfold through the distinction of detachment from each stage.

Regarding noble beings who are still bound by all fetters in the desire realm, up to those who have attained the eighth stage of detachment from the fourth dhyāna—calculated by way of distinctions in place, lineage, detachment, and faculties—there are two thousand five hundred and ninety-two types.

Why is this so? Within a single category there are six natures; within each nature there are nine types of persons, ranging from those bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*) up to those who have abandoned eight grades of afflictions (*kleśa*).
From the meditative attainments obtained by oneself, six times nine makes fifty-four.
Sixteen times fifty-four makes eight hundred and sixty-four.
Next, due to the distinctions of the faculties (indriya), this is further tripled.

If one calculates in this manner, it follows that those who have attained the nine grades of detachment from the lower realms must be considered "fully bound" (sakalabandhana) regarding the higher stages.
If one calculates according to the principle of equality, this applies equally to those who attain cessation in the intermediate state up to those who proceed to the highest realm (ūrdhvasrotas).
If one were to include all such persons, there would be forty thousand three hundred and ten non-returners (anāgāmin).
The verse says:
Having abandoned eight categories [of afflictions] in the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra), one becomes a candidate for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka).
The commentary states:
The meaning of *anāgāmin* extends here as well.

When a person who is an *anāgāmin* becomes free from desire for even one grade of affliction in the first dhyāna, up until they have extinguished eight grades of afflictions in the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), that person becomes a candidate for Arhatship (*arhattva-pratipannaka*).
The verse says:
"The ninth path of immediate succession.
The commentary explains:

One who is able to extinguish the ninth grade of afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is also an "Arhat-candidate" (*arhattvapratipannaka*) during the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*).
The verse says:
This is called the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*).
The commentary states:

This refers to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*) that can extinguish the ninth grade of afflictions; it is called "vajra" because it is a meditative concentration (*samādhi*) capable of shattering all afflictions, such that no affliction remains capable of shattering it.
This path does not destroy all afflictions because they have already been destroyed;
it is able to destroy all afflictions because it is the most superior of all the supreme grades among the paths of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Other masters say:

There are many varieties of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which is subsumed under the "not-yet-reached" concentration (*anāgamya*). It takes the suffering and origin of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as its object.

There are eight [moments] associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of suffering and origin; there are eight associated with the aspects of the dharma-knowledge of cessation and the path; and there are four associated with the aspects of the subsequent knowledge of cessation that take the cessation of the first dhyāna as their object, up to four that take the cessation of the Peak of Existence as their object.
There are four [moments] associated with the aspect of the subsequent knowledge of the path (*mārgānvayajñāna*), because they collectively take all categories of subsequent knowledge as their object.
Due to these distinctions in wisdom, aspects, and objects, these vajra-samādhis constitute fifty-two vajra-samādhis.
As it is for those comprised within the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), so it is for those comprised within up to the fourth dhyāna.

Regarding those comprised within the spheres of infinite space, infinite consciousness, nothingness, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one should know accordingly that there are twenty, eight, two, fourteen, and twenty [types of suffering] respectively.

In the formless realm, there is no dharma-knowledge that takes the cessation of lower stages as its object, nor is there any subsequent knowledge (anvaya-jñāna) that takes the path which serves as the antidote to lower stages as its object,
because these two types of knowledge mutually serve as causes for one another.
Other masters maintain that the antidotes for each individual stage (*bhūmi*) within the Knowledge of the Path (*mārga-anvaya-jñāna*) are also objects of this samādhi.
According to those masters, because twenty-eight additional [antidotes] are added to the Vajra Samādhi included within the *anāgamya* concentration, there are eighty Vajra Samādhis in total.
The same applies up to those included in the fourth dhyāna.
In the bases such as the sphere of infinite space (ākāśānantyāyatana), there are, in sequence, forty, thirty, twenty-two, and fourteen samādhis.
Furthermore, due to the distinctions of lineage (*gotra*) and faculties (*indriya*), this samādhi further becomes manifold.
As for the aforementioned ninth category of afflictions at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), these are eliminated by the vajra-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).
The verse says:
Through the attainment of the ninth cessation, there is the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
The commentary says:
The knowledge that arises simultaneously with the attainment (*prāpti*) of the abandonment of the afflictions of the ninth category is called the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣayajñāna*).

It is precisely the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) produced immediately after the vajra-samādhi; therefore, it is named the knowledge of exhaustion because it arises together with the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Regarding this wisdom, the first verse states:
"It is the state of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The commentary explains:

This person was previously a candidate for arhatship; when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) arises, they immediately become one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) and are named an arhat, by virtue of attaining the fruit of arhatship.
Because there is no further training to be practiced in order to attain a distinct fruit, they are called "those beyond training" (aśaikṣa).
Therefore, because they are engaged in performing deeds for the benefit of others, they are called Arhats.
Because they are worthy of veneration by all those who possess desire, they are called Arhats.
Therefore, this point is established: that which was stated—that these seven types of persons are "those in training" (śaikṣa)—is self-evident.
What is meant by "one in training" (śaikṣa)?

It refers to one who, for the sake of attaining the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya), constantly trains in the three trainings as their practice—namely, the training in higher ethics (adhiśīla-śikṣā), the training in higher mind (adhicitta-śikṣā), and the training in higher wisdom (adhiprajñā-śikṣā). These three trainings have ethical discipline, concentration, and wisdom as their essential nature.
If that were so, ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) would also have to be considered those in training (*śaikṣa*).
This is not the case, because they have not yet seen and known the principle of the Four Truths as it truly is, and because they subsequently engage in false training.
Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, stated emphatically in a sutra:
"Śivaka! He trains in the three trainings."
Because they train in the three trainings, they are called "those in training" (śaikṣa).
What is the meaning of this repetition?
It means that if a person is training correctly, they are not training erroneously.
If a person trains as previously described, they shall likewise train thereafter.
If this is so, how can an *ārya* abiding in their natural state (*prakṛtistha*) be considered "one in training" (*śaikṣa*)?

It is by virtue of their intention (*āśaya*) that they are "in training," just as a traveler who has briefly rested is still considered a traveler; for their training remains inseparable from them until its attainment.
Furthermore, what are the dharmas of those in training (śaikṣa)?
They are all the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas of persons in training.
What are the dharmas of those beyond training (aśaikṣa)?
All dharmas without outflows belonging to those beyond training (aśaikṣa) and nirvāṇa—
why are these not considered "belonging to training" (śaikṣa)?
Because those beyond training and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are associated with them.
Why are they not "beyond training" (aśaikṣa)?
Because those who are still in training (śaikṣa) and ordinary worldlings (pṛthagjana) are associated with them.

When all those in training and those beyond training are combined, they constitute eight types of persons: four are those on the path directed toward the fruits, and four are those who have attained the fruits.

First, practicing the path to realize the fruit of stream-entry; second, realizing the fruit of stream-entry; continuing in this manner up to seventh, practicing the path to realize the fruit of arhatship; and eighth, realizing the fruit of arhatship.
These individuals are established as eight by way of their designations, but as only five by way of substantial entities.

The first one is a person on the path toward the fruit, while the latter four are persons abiding in the fruits; since no other persons on the paths toward the fruits are established outside of these three fruits, they are subsumed under the three fruits.
This meaning can be explained according to the sequence [of attainment].

Furthermore, there are three types of persons who have previously extensively extinguished [defilements] and attained detachment from the desire realm; they establish themselves in the stage of the candidate for *sakṛdāgāmin* and the candidate for *anāgāmin* within the path of vision (*darśanamārga*). These are not included among the *srotāpanna* or the *sakṛdāgāmin*.
Why is this? It has already been stated previously that there are two kinds of the path of cultivation:
first, the mundane path; second, the supramundane path.
By which path does a person in training (śaikṣa) attain detachment?
From which realm do they attain detachment?
The verse says:
"By means of supramundane detachment from the Peak of Existence.
The commentary explains:
If one attains detachment from the Peak of Existence, one is necessarily a learner (*śaikṣa*), and this occurs by means of the supramundane path, not by the mundane path.
Why is this so? Because above the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is no further world; thus, the path of its own level cannot serve as an antidote.
Why is it that the path of one's own level cannot act as an antidote?

Because it is underlain by the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of the afflictions belonging to its own level, if an affliction is latently disposed toward a particular category of the path, that category of the path cannot be established as capable of destroying that affliction.

If a path were the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to a certain affliction, that affliction could not be latently disposed toward that path; therefore, a path belonging to its own level cannot serve as the antidote for the afflictions of its own level.
The verse says:
"The other two types.
The commentary says:
Excluding the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there are two kinds of detachment from desire across all stages, achieved through both mundane and supramundane paths.
Both ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) can attain this detachment. Regarding this, the verse says:
"Through the mundane path, the noble ones (*ārya*) attain two types of acquisition upon becoming detached from desire."
The commentary states:
By means of the mundane path, when a noble one attains the state of being free from desire, two kinds of attainment of cessation arise:
first, the mundane attainment; second, the supramundane attainment.
The verse says:
Others say it is by means of the supramundane.
The commentary says:
According to the supramundane path, when a noble one attains freedom from desire, there are likewise two kinds of acquisition of cessation.
Other masters say this. Why is that?
The verse says:
Because it is improper to abandon the afflictions.
The commentary says:
If a noble one attains freedom from desire by means of the noble path, or if a worldling attains non-arising [attainment], within this context,

if a person becomes free from desire through the noble path, they may further cultivate the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*) based on the higher meditative absorptions, such as the sphere of nothingness and the sphere of infinite space.

Because this person has abandoned the previous path by means of equanimity (*upekṣā*), and because the path of the fruit is entirely absent [therein], they would not be dissociated from the defilements (*kleśa*) of the higher stages.
If they were to abandon these, they would again become associated with those defilements.
The verse says:
"In the Peak of Existence, there is partial liberation; as above, birth [therein] would be untenable.
The commentary explains:
Although this person lacks the worldly attainment of cessation (*laukika-vairāgya-prāpti*), they likewise cannot be associated with those afflictions.
For example, when a learner (*śaikṣa*) has attained partial liberation from the afflictions of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), there is necessarily no worldly attainment of cessation therein.

Because of the cultivation of the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), one has already abandoned the acquisitions (*prāpti*) of supramundane states and is no longer associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*) of those stages.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Seventeen; *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle Eighteen.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.

Part Three of the Chapter on the Analysis of the Persons Who Attain the Fruits of the Noble Path. Furthermore, just as when an ordinary person is born in a stage from the First Dhyāna upwards, through the abandonment, cessation, and attainment of detachment from the afflictions of the Desire Realm, they no longer become associated with those afflictions.
It is the same in that case as well; therefore, this position does not constitute proof.
Furthermore, by means of which stage?
From which stage is one liberated from desire?
The verse says:
"By means of the untainted *anāgamya*, one becomes free from desire for all stages.
The commentary says:
If one cultivates the untainted path based on the stage of the threshold concentration (anāgamya), one is able to become free from desire for all stages up to the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra);
if a person relies on an access concentration (sāmantaka), they attain freedom from desire for the lower stages.
Is it the case that all paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), just like the uninterrupted paths (ānantarya-mārga), also arise from the preparatory concentrations (sāmantaka)? No. Why is this?
The verse says:
Following the preparatory stage (*sāmantaka*) of a meditative absorption, the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) is superior in three stages.
The commentary says:

There are nine stages of birth for all sentient beings, namely: the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).
Among these, the process from the abandonment of desire in the desire realm up to the abandonment of desire in the second dhyāna is called the excellence of the three stages.
Within these three stages, the final path of liberation arises either from an access concentration (*sāmantaka*) or from a fundamental meditative absorption (*mauladhyāna*).
The verse states:
"Not from an upper access concentration."
The commentary states:

From the third stage of excellence upward, all final paths of liberation arise from the fundamental dhyānas; none arise from the preparatory stages (sāmantaka), because the faculty of equanimity (upekṣendriya) is uniform therein.

Within the three dhyānas, both the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental states (*maula*) differ in terms of their faculty of feeling (*vedanendriya*); consequently, some individuals are unable to enter the fundamental states because it is difficult for them to accomplish the cultivation of the necessary faculties.
Therefore, regarding the three stages of detachment from desire, the final path of liberation may also arise from a preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka*).
It has already been explained that one attains detachment from all stages by means of the untainted non-attainment concentration (*anāsravānāgamya*).
Since it has not yet been explained for the remaining stages, it should now be stated.
The verse says:
"The Noble One [attains] extinction through eight [paths] from his own stage and above."
The commentary states:

If one attains detachment through the eight kinds of untainted meditative absorptions—namely, the form-sphere absorptions (*rūpadhyāna*), the intermediate absorption (*dhyānāntara*), and the formless-sphere absorptions (*ārūpyadhyāna*)—one attains detachment from both one’s own level and the levels above, but not from the levels below, because one has already attained detachment from them previously.

In this context, because the supramundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take the four truths as their objects, they arise with the sixteen aspects according to those truths; this point is established by itself.
The verse says:

The paths of liberation and uninterrupted transition, being mundane, respectively [take] the lower and upper stages as their objects through the notions of "calm" (*śānta*), "coarse" (*audārika*), and so forth.
The commentary states:
When the path of liberation arises, it has characteristics such as tranquility; when the uninterrupted path arises, it has characteristics such as coarseness and heaviness.
These two paths arise respectively by taking the higher stage as their object and the lower stage as their object.
If the path of liberation contemplates a higher stage, it takes as its object any one of the characteristics of tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
If the uninterrupted path contemplates a lower stage, it takes as its object any one of the characteristics of coarseness, affliction, and thick walls.
Because it is not tranquil, it is called "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).
Because it is accomplished through great effort and is not sublime, it is called "affliction" (*paritāpana*).
Because its many faults act as obstacles, one cannot attain deliverance from this stage; therefore, it is called a "thick wall."
For example, just as a criminal cannot leave prison due to heavy obstructions,
by reversing this correspondence, one understands the meaning of the characteristics of tranquility, excellence, and renunciation.
Having explained the remaining meanings according to their respective origins, next:
what knowledge arises immediately after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*)?
The verse says:

If one does not destroy the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), there is no subsequent knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*); [rather], either the knowledge of exhaustion or the right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi*) arises.
The commentary explains:

If a person becomes an Arhat of the "unshakable" type (*akopyadharman*), immediately following the knowledge of exhaustion, the knowledge of non-arising necessarily arises; it is not the case that the knowledge of exhaustion or the right view of one beyond training arises.

If one is not a person of non-retrogressive nature (avinipātadharman), from the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) there arises either further knowledge of exhaustion or the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi); it is not the case that there is retrogression from the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna).
Furthermore, regarding this right view of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), is it necessarily non-arising for an Arhat of the "unshakable" type?
The verse says:
This applies to all.
The commentary states:

For an Arhat of the "unshakable dharma" type, after the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna), sometimes further knowledge of non-arising arises, and sometimes the right view of one beyond training (aśaikṣasamyagdṛṣṭi) arises.
Why is this? This right view is common to all arhats without distinction.
Regarding the four fruits previously mentioned, to what dharma do these fruits belong?
If this is the fruit of śrāmaṇya,
what dharma is called śrāmaṇya?
The verse says:
"The path of the stainless śramaṇa.
The commentary states:
If the path is untainted (anāsrava), it is called the state of a śramaṇa.
By what means does this practitioner become a śramaṇa?
By virtue of being able to pacify the afflictions (kleśa).
As the Sūtra says:

This person is able to pacify many kinds of unwholesome dharmas, unwise dharmas, and defiled dharmas that accord with birth and death and lead to future existence, even unto old age and death; therefore, he is called a śramaṇa.
Because ordinary persons are not necessarily able to pacify all evils, they are not true śramaṇas.
Furthermore, for such a śramaṇa, what dharma constitutes the fruit?
The verse says:
"Conditioned and unconditioned fruits.
The commentary says:
Conditioned and unconditioned dharmas constitute the fruits of the śramaṇa.
These fruits have already been explained previously; they are of four kinds, namely: srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat.
As the Sūtra says:
"O Bhikṣus!
There are four fruits of the śramaṇa," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Furthermore, how many kinds of these fruits are there?
The verse says:
"They are one less than ninety."
The commentary states:
These śrāmaṇya and the fruits of śrāmaṇya consist of eighty-nine factors each, categorized as both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
What dharma is this?
The verse says:
"The path of liberation and cessation.
The commentary explains:
To eliminate the afflictions of view, there are eight paths of uninterrupted transition and eight paths of liberation.
To eliminate the afflictions of cultivation, for each of the nine stages, there are nine grades of paths of uninterrupted transition.
Each [stage] extinguishes the nine grades of afflictions, and each has nine grades of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

Among these, all paths of uninterrupted continuity (*ānantarya-mārga*) are called "śramaṇya" (the state of a śramaṇa), and all paths of liberation are called "conditioned fruits of śramaṇya" (*saṃskṛta-śrāmaṇyaphala*), because they are the outflow fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*) and the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) of those paths of uninterrupted continuity.
The extinction and separation from all afflictions is called the unconditioned fruit of the śramaṇa.
According to this principle, there are ninety-nine conditioned and ninety-nine unconditioned fruits respectively, each being reduced by one.
If that is so, this point ought to be analyzed with respect to the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
It cannot be distinguished, for if the fruits were many, it would be so.
The verse says:
The establishment of four kinds of fruits is due to the possession of five causes.
The commentary states:
Within the stages of cessation and the path, if five causes are present, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, establishes the fruits of śrāmaṇya within these stages.
What are these five causes?
The verse says:

"By abandoning the former and attaining a distinct path, one acquires the supernormal powers, the fruits of cessation, and the fruits of fruition; furthermore, upon attaining the eight knowledges, one cultivates the sixteen aspects.
The commentary explains:
First, one abandons the preceding path;
second, one attains the hitherto unattained path, because through abandonment and attainment one proceeds toward the path and its fruit;
third, one counts the attainment of cessation, because by means of a single attainment, one attains all cessations.
Fourth, because one simultaneously attains the eight knowledges (*jñāna*).

Fifth, because one cultivates the sixteen aspects of the four truths (*satya*) through both the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*) and subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), namely the aspects of impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth.
Based on these five causes, each and every fruit possesses these five causes; however, they cannot be established within the fruit of Buddhahood.

If only the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) is called "śramaṇya" (the state of being a śramaṇa), how can the two kinds of fruits obtained through the worldly path (*laukika-mārga*) be called "fruits of śramaṇya"?
The verse says:
Because detachment is attained through the worldly path, one obtains the fruit maintained by the untainted [path].
The commentary states:
Among the two fruits, it is not only through extinction by the mundane path that they constitute a fruit—namely, the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin and the fruit of the Anāgāmin. How so?

The fruits of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) are extinguished therein with mutual separation, yet they share a single attainment (*prāpti*), because all cessations (*nirodha*) are subsumed as individual fruits.
Therefore, it is said in the Sūtra:
"What is the fruit of the once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmiphala*)?"
It refers to the abandonment of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the attenuation of desire, hatred, and delusion.
What is the fruit of *anāgāmin*?
It is the abandonment of the five lower fetters (*avarabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), attained through the path free from outflows (*anāsrava-mārga*).
Therefore, this path is sustained; by the power of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*), it is not lost until death.
Consequently, this cessation should rightly be established as the fruit of śramaṇaship (*śrāmaṇyaphala*); this is what was previously described as the fruit of śramaṇaship.
Furthermore, this verse says:
"The Brahmin’s Brahma-wheel," because he is said to turn the Brahma-wheel.
The commentary explains:

Because they are able to dispel and wash away all afflictions, they are called *brāhmaṇas*; or they are called the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahmacakra*), because it is turned by Brahmā and because it accords with the unsurpassed Dharma of Brahmā.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is called Brahmā; as it is said in the sūtra:
"The World-Honored One is Brahmā; he is thus tranquil, thus cool," and so forth, as extensively explained in the sūtra.
Therefore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is named Brahmā.
This wheel is the wheel of the Buddha, the World-Honored One; thus it is called the "Brahma-wheel" (*brahmacakra*), for it is turned solely by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The verse says:
"The Wheel of Dharma is named the Path of Seeing.
The commentary says:
What is the meaning of "wheel" (*cakra*)?
Because one proceeds by means of it, it is called a wheel.
Since the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) resembles a wheel, this dharma is designated as a wheel.
What constitutes similarity?
The verse says:
"Swift motion, and so forth; spokes, and so forth."

The commentary states: It is called "wheel-like" because of its rapid movement; because it abandons this [place] and proceeds to that; because it subdues what has not yet been subdued and firmly maintains what has already been subdued so as not to lose it; and because it moves from below to above and from above to below. It is said to be "wheel-like" due to these meanings, such as rapid movement and so forth.
