Regarding the meaning of the spokes and so forth: this refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
Because it resembles a wheel by virtue of the meaning of the spokes and other parts, the Venerable Ghoṣaka calls this a "wheel.
Right View, Right Resolve, Right Effort, and Right Mindfulness—these four factors resemble the spokes.
Right speech, right action, and right livelihood—these three factors resemble the hub;
right concentration—this single factor resembles the rim.
Therefore, the path of seeing is called the Wheel of Dharma.
On what basis is this Path of Seeing established as the Wheel of Dharma?
It is proven by the fact that when the Path of Seeing arose in the noble Kauṇḍinya, it was declared: "The Blessed One has turned the Wheel of Dharma."
What are the three turnings and twelve aspects?
"This phenomenon is the noble truth of suffering; this truth must be known; this phenomenon has been known.
Through these three turnings, in each and every turning, the eye of dharma is accomplished, knowledge is accomplished, clarity is accomplished, and wisdom is accomplished.
These three turnings and four aspects exist for each of the truths, because they are identical in being threefold and twelvefold respectively.
Thus, one speaks of "three turnings and twelve aspects," just as one might speak of someone being wise in two respects or seven respects.
Through this turning, the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning are manifested in their respective order; thus say the Vaibhāṣika masters.
If one maintains this view, not only does the path of seeing consist of three turnings and twelve aspects, but how then is this established as the Wheel of Dharma?
This Dharma-gate is originally named the Wheel of Dharma (dharmacakra), and herein it also possesses the three turnings and twelve aspects.
If so, what are the three turnings?
It is because within this [teaching], the Four Noble Truths are turned three times.
What are the twelve aspects?

They consist of three rounds of reflection upon the Four Noble Truths: namely, that this phenomenon is called the Noble Truth of Suffering, as well as the Noble Truths of Origin, Cessation, and the Path; that this phenomenon must be fully known, must be abandoned, must be realized, and must be cultivated; and that this phenomenon has been fully known, has been abandoned, has been realized, and has been cultivated.
Why is it called "turning"?
Because by means of practice, it causes the mental continuum of another to cross over and enables them to understand this meaning.
Furthermore, the entire Noble Path is the Wheel of Dharma, because it is able to cause the mental continuum of disciples to cross over through practice.
This dharma is said to have been "turned" when it is correctly transmitted and taught because it gives rise to the Path of Seeing within the mental continuum of another.
Furthermore, in which realms are how many fruits of śrāmaṇya attained?
The verse says:
"The three [types of craving] belong to the desire realm; the last belongs to all three realms.
The commentary says:
Only within the desire realm (kāmadhātu) are the first three fruits attained; they are not attained elsewhere.
As for the final fruit of the śramaṇa—namely, arhatship—this fruit is attainable throughout all three realms.
Since the first two fruits are attained by those who have not yet abandoned desire, they cannot be attained in the higher realms;
this principle is logical.
But why should the third fruit not be attainable in the higher realms?
The verse says:
There is no path of seeing in the higher realms.
The commentary explains:
Above the desire realm, there is no path of vision.
If one were to abandon this path, it would be impossible for a person who has already attained freedom from desire to reach the fruit of an Anāgāmin.
By this reasoning, there are therefore only three fruits in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
For what reason is there no path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) in the higher realms?

Because there is no correct hearing [of the Dharma] in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), and because it cannot take the objects of the lower realms as its cognitive domain, there is no path of seeing there.
Regarding the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), the verse says:
"Because there is no weariness, this is performed; because that is the ultimate according to the sūtra.
The commentary explains:

Ordinary beings in the realm of form (rūpadhātu), due to their attachment to the bliss of meditative absorption (samāpatti) and because they lack the sensation of suffering, do not give rise to a mind of revulsion.
Without revulsion, there is no other principle capable of inducing the Noble Path (āryamārga).
Such as these are called logical principles (*yukti*), and there is also scriptural authority (*āgama*) to corroborate them.
A sutra states:
"There are five types of persons who perform the action here and reach its consummation there."
What are these five? They are those who attain cessation in the intermediate state, up to those who ascend to the highest realm (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
"The practitioner" refers to one who has first initiated the cultivation of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), because this is the direct means for attaining nirvāṇa.
"Ultimate" refers to the attainment of the fruit of arhatship.
According to this sūtra, one knows that the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) does not exist in the higher realms.

This point was already explained previously: for an arhat of the "unshakable dharma" (*akopyadharman*) type, the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) necessarily arises after the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
Are there distinctions among arhats?
It is said that there are.
The verse says:
There are six types of arhats.
The commentary states:
In the sūtras it is taught that there are six natures among arhats.

1. The dharma of falling back; 2. The dharma of self-harm; 3. The dharma of guarding; 4. The dharma of abiding immovably; 5. The dharma of that which should be thoroughly realized; 6. The dharma of non-retrogression.
The verse says:
The first five are of the nature of faith and inclination.
The commentary says:
Excluding the one person of immovable dharma, the remaining five first attain through faith and joy.
The verse says:
Their liberation depends on time and affection.
The commentary states:

It should be understood that for these five types of persons, their liberation is attained in dependence upon time; furthermore, because they must constantly guard what is most cherished, they are said to possess "liberation at times," as they attain liberation by observing the proper occasion.
Because the syllable "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) has been removed, it is called "liberation by time" (*samaya-vimukta*), like a jar of ghee.
Why is this? Because that person must necessarily wait for the right time for their cultivation of samādhi to be accomplished before it manifests.
"Time" refers to the conditions of life, freedom from illness, a suitable dwelling, the right season, and so forth.
By observing these times, both types of liberation are accomplished.
The verse says:
"The unbreakable dharma is indestructible.
The commentary explains:
If the liberation attained by an Arhat of the unbreakable type is not subject to breaking, then it is eternally established as indestructible, because there is no falling away from it.
The verse says:
"Therefore, [is it] non-timely liberation?
The commentary says:
Therefore, it is said that this person does not rely on timely liberation.
Why is this? Because this person does not wait for the right time; they are constantly liberated at will, being able to bring the cultivation of samādhi into manifestation.

Furthermore, they are established as "occasionally liberated" (sāmayikī-vimukti) and "unconditionally liberated" (asamayikī-vimukti) based on liberation for a temporary period versus liberation for eternity, and based on the sense of being subject to regression versus not being subject to regression.
The verse says:
This is of the same category as the previously mentioned "attainment through vision" (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
The commentary says:
Regarding this Arhat of immovable dharma, it should be understood that among those in the stage of training (śaikṣa), he was of the nature of one who has attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
As for these six types of Arhats, do they possess their six natures from the very beginning, or do they acquire them later?
The verse says:
Some are obtained by nature; others are obtained through the refinement of the faculties (*indriya*).
The commentary says:

Some individuals, from the very beginning, have the nature of falling back (parihāṇadharman); some, from the very beginning, have the nature of self-harm (anurakṣaṇādharman); and the same applies to the remaining natures.

Furthermore, there may be one who initially has the nature of falling back, but later, through the practice of refining the faculties (indriyasaṃcāra), further advances to attain the nature of self-harm, and so on, up to advancing to attain the nature of being unshakable (akopyadharman); it should be understood that this is likewise the case for all.
Among these, those subject to falling away (parihāṇa-dharma) are persons who will certainly fall away from the dharmas they have attained, yet are not of a nature capable of committing self-harm.
Those subject to self-harm (ātma-ghāta-dharma) are persons who will certainly kill themselves.
Regarding those who protect the Dharma (*dharmapāla*): if a person, according to what they have attained, must necessarily protect it, they are so designated.

Regarding those who abide in the immovable Dharma (*akopyadharman*): if a person is free from the strongest causes and conditions for falling back, although they do not constantly guard [their attainment], they must necessarily abide in the immovability of what they have attained; because they do not fall back and are free from [further] application (*prayoga*), they cannot achieve further progress.
One who has attained mastery of the Dharma is a person whose nature is such that they will certainly attain the state of the "unbreakable dharma" at a later time.
One of the unbreakable dharma is a person who will certainly not fall back or decline as previous persons do.
Regarding the first two individuals within the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), they lack constant cultivation and reverential cultivation; they differ only in their faculties (*indriya*).
The third person constantly cultivates the preparatory application (*prayoga*) but has dull faculties;
the fourth person reverentially cultivates the preparatory application and has sharp faculties.
The fifth person possesses both types of cultivation but has dull faculties;
the sixth person possesses both virtues and cultivations and has the sharpest faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

It is not necessarily the case that the first person, who is subject to falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), must actually fall back, nor is it necessarily the case that even the person who has attained penetration (*prativedhadharman*) must actually achieve penetration.
The "non-declining dharma" (avinipātadharman) is designated by this name solely on account of its existence;
thus, if one maintains this view, it is not contradictory to hold that all six types of arhats exist within the three realms.

If one maintains that there are necessarily such matters as falling back (*parihāṇi*) and so forth, up until the point of full penetration (*prativedha*), then for such a person, there are six types of Arhats in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). In the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*), there are only two: namely, those who abide in the immovable dharma (*akopyadharman*) and those of unbreakable dharma (*anepaṇīyadharman*). This is because these two types of persons do not undergo falling back, self-harm, or the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*); such matters do not exist for them.
Among these six types of persons, which one undergoes retrogression?
From what dharma does this retrogression occur?
Is it from the fruit, or is it from the lineage?
The verse says:
There are four types of persons characterized by falling away; there are five fruits from which one may fall away.
The commentary says:
The four types of persons, beginning with those who harm themselves, fall away from their nature.
Why is this? For one who is subject to falling away from the Dharma does not further fall away from their own original nature.
The five types of persons, such as those subject to falling back (*parihāṇadharman*), all fall away from their fruits.
Although these five may fall away, the verse says:
"Not previously."
The commentary states:

If a person has previously attained a certain nature, that person does not fall away from it, because it has been made firm and solid through the accomplishment of the paths of both those still in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
If there is a nature acquired through training (*śaikṣa*), which is accomplished by means of either the mundane or supramundane paths, there is no falling away from it.
However, regarding the nature subsequently attained through the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), this nature is subject to falling away.
If a person attains the first fruit, that person does not fall away from the first fruit, though they may fall away from the other fruits.
Therefore, there is no falling away from the fruit of srotāpanna.
If one maintains such a position, there are three types of those subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*):

first, those who attain parinirvāṇa while remaining within the state of being subject to falling away; second, those who fall away from the nature obtained through the cultivation of the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*); and third, those who fall away from the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).
There are four types of those who harm themselves; three are as previously described, and the fourth is one whose nature reverts to regression.

In this manner, by adding one grade at a time to each of the other three, one should understand that there are five, six, and seven persons respectively, according to the sequence, who constitute the natures originally attained.
If one falls back and becomes a person in training (śaikṣa), one abides within that state and does not abide in any other nature.
Were it otherwise, through the acquisition and increase of that nature, one would only advance further and never fall back.
Furthermore, what is the cause for not falling back from the first fruit?
The verse says:
Because the afflictions of the path of seeing have no [substantial] category.
The commentary states:
Why are they without a [substantial] category?
Because all afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths arise based upon the self, and because those [afflictions] take the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) as their root.
This self, which serves as the basis [for such notions], is necessarily and eternally non-existent; therefore, it is said to be "without a category" (*anālambana*).
If that were so, it would follow that it takes a non-existent thing as its object.

It does not take a non-existent thing as its object, because it takes the Truths (*satya*) as its object; however, within those Truths, it does not take them as its object in accordance with how they are conceptually discriminated.
If that is so, why are other afflictions not likewise [the cause]?
There is a distinction. Why is this?

Regarding the perception of categories such as form, because one discriminates them through the notions of an agent, an experiencer, or a sovereign, an unreal self-nature is superimposed and arises; with the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) as its basis, the remaining afflictions such as the extreme views arise. Therefore, it is said that there are no [real] categories.

The afflictions to be abandoned through the path of cultivation—namely desire, hatred, pride, and ignorance—arise with craving as their predominant factor toward categories such as form; they arise because of a failure to understand [the nature of things] as their intrinsic nature. For this reason, it is said that they "possess categories" (*sānvaya*).
Why is this? Because they possess subtle, pure objects and the like;
since they arise by taking these as their objects, our [notions of] "I" and so forth lack even a semblance of such existence.
Furthermore, regarding the afflictions (*kleśa*) abandoned through the path, there are corresponding categories of objects for each, such as the agreeable and the disagreeable.

However, all afflictions abandoned by seeing the truths (*darśana-heya*) take the characteristic of a self (*ātman*) and so forth as their common object; therefore, they have no mutually corresponding categories of objects.

Furthermore, regarding the objects of focus of the Path of Seeing—namely impermanence, suffering, non-self, and emptiness—they truly exist; they are not objects of the mundane path, and because they have never previously been realized or seen throughout beginningless saṃsāra, there is no possibility of falling back from the first fruit.

Furthermore, for a noble one (ārya), if they do not observe with a focused mind, the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-kleśa) will arise due to the loss of mindfulness; however, if they observe with a focused mind, they will not arise.

For example, just as the notion of a snake arises with respect to a vine, if one does not examine [the object] with thorough attention, afflictions such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) cannot arise; for various views are produced through clear and decisive conceptual determination.
Therefore, for a noble one, there is no possibility of falling away from the afflictions abandoned through the vision of the truths.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
there is no possibility of falling away from the fruit of arhatship.
This meaning is truly plausible.
How is this to be known?
By means of scripture (*āgama*) and reasoning (*yukti*).
What is this? The *Āgama* states:
"O Bhikṣus!"
This is true cessation, which is that which is extinguished by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Furthermore, the verse says:
"It is taught as the matter of heedfulness."
The commentary states:
The Sūtra says, "Regarding those in training (*śaikṣa*), I declare that within their state of vigilance (*apramāda*), there must necessarily be acts of vigilance;
however, I do not say this regarding Arhats."
If you say:
"There are also matters of non-heedlessness even in the case of an Arhat," as the Sūtra says:
“Ānanda! Regarding matters such as gain and praise, I have said that they can also act as obstacles for an Arhat. This is not the case;

what this sutra refers to as ‘retrogression’ speaks only of retrogressing from dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). As for the unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*) which has been personally realized by the body, I say that there is no other cause or condition by which an Arhat could fall away from it.”
If you say: "There is falling away from the one liberated by occasion (samayavimukta)," this point may well be granted, for we also maintain this view.
Regarding this meaning of "liberation through time," one must deliberate:
does it refer to the fruit of arhatship, or to the nine meditative absorptions (dhyāna)—that is, the fundamental dhyānas and fundamental samādhis?
How is it that, because it manifests in dependence on specific times, it is called "liberation dependent on time" (*samaya-vimukti*)?
And why is it called "beloved" (*priya*) because one repeatedly seeks and cultivates it for the sake of dwelling in happiness in the present life?
Other masters say:
Because it is that which is to be savored and relished, it is called "beloved" (*priya*).
Since the liberation of an Arhat is constantly accompanied [by the body], it cannot be established as being dependent on time.
Since it is no longer something that is loved, it cannot be established as "beloved.
If there is the possibility of falling back from the fruit of Arhatship, how so?

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has taught that only the dwelling in happiness in the present life based on training in the mind may be subject to decline; therefore, one should understand this meaning: that the liberation of all Arhats is necessarily an indestructible dharma.

Regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life, there is falling away from arhatship due to the distraction of the mind by gain, praise, and the like; due to the loss of mastery; and due to dull faculties.
There are also those who do not fall back, namely those of sharp faculties.
Among these, if there is falling back, they are called Arhats of the nature of falling back (*parihāṇadharman*);
if there is no falling back, they are called Arhats of the nature of non-falling back (*aparihāṇadharman*).
The principles regarding self-harm and so forth should be considered in this way.

What is the difference between these three types of persons: those of non-retrogressive nature (*aparihāṇadharman*), those who abide in the immovable nature (*akopyadharman*), and those of unbreakable nature (*anurakṣaṇādharman*)?

The one of non-retrogressive nature (*avinipātadharman*) does not reach this state through the refinement of faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*); the one of unshakeable nature (*akopyadharman*) reaches it by means of refining the faculties.
These two individuals do not fall away from the specific attainments (*samāpatti*) they have acquired through their respective practices.

One who dwells in immovability abides within whatever merit has been attained; from this merit, he certainly does not fall back, nor does he further advance to produce other merits, for if other merits were produced, he would be moved from this state.
In this way, one should understand the distinction between these three types of persons.
The verse says:
"The one liberated by time and Gautika."
The commentary states:

While still in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), the Venerable Godhika, because he repeatedly relished the flavor of meditative absorption and because his faculties were dull, fell away from occasional liberation (*sāmayikī vimukti*). Giving rise to a mind of regret, he desired to relinquish his life and took up a weapon to kill himself.
At the time of his death, he attained arhatship and entered parinirvāṇa immediately; therefore, Godhika did not fall away from the fruit of arhatship.
This is stated in the *Daśottara-sūtra*:
"There is one dharma that must inevitably arise, namely, the deliverance through loving-attentiveness (maitrī-vimukti) attained in dependence on the proper occasion."
Furthermore, there is one dharma that must certainly be realized, namely, the unshakable liberation of mind (*akopyā cetovimukti*).
If the beloved liberation of mind dependent on time (*sāmayikī kāntā cetovimukti*) is the fruit of arhatship, why are these two explained separately within the ten [types of arhats]?
Since it has never been heard stated elsewhere that an Arhat must be reborn after death, how can this textual passage be taken as definitive proof?
If you say that an Arhat who is of dull faculties must necessarily be reborn, what meaning does this scriptural passage intend to establish?
If you say: "Because one wishes to demonstrate that there is capacity for producing a fruit,
this passage is cited as proof," then it could also be used as proof for other fruits.
If you say: "Because this fruit ought to arise, it is said that it ought to arise;
other fruits ought to arise even more so; therefore, time-liberation is not the fruit of arhatship."
If that is so, why is it said that an Arhat is "liberated by occasion" (samaya-vimukta)?
If an Arhat, due to having dull faculties, achieves [liberation] only when practicing samādhi and contemplation at the appropriate time, he is said to be liberated by occasion;
the opposite of this is called non-occasional liberation (asamaya-vimukta).
The Abhidharma-piṭaka states:
There are three bases by which the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm give rise to active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
What are these three?

First, the latent tendencies (anuśaya) of the desire realm have not yet been extinguished or abandoned; second, the mental states of desire belonging to the desire realm arise in relation to sense objects that are present before the faculties; third, one engages in improper reflection (ayoniśomanasikāra) regarding these.
You say that this passage is taught because afflictions arise based on complete causes.
What affliction could possibly arise from incomplete causes?
Such is the proof for the meaning of non-retrogression according to the *Āgama*.
How so by way of reasoning?
If an Arhat has already attained such an antidote, by virtue of which all afflictions have become subject to the law of never arising again, how could he ever fall away?
If this antidote has not yet arisen, how can the outflows (āsrava) be exhausted?
Since the seeds of the afflictions have not been permanently uprooted, they will arise again as phenomena.
If the outflows are not yet exhausted, how can one be called an Arhat?
The proof of the meaning of non-retrogression based on reasoning is as follows.
The verse says:
"By means of the simile of the mass of fire, there is retrogression."
The commentary states:
If that is so, you ought to defend the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra*.
This sūtra says:

A learned noble disciple who practices in this way and dwells in this manner may, at some time and in some place, due to the loss of mindfulness, again give rise to unwholesome and unwise vitarka-vicāra.
This interpretation is not correct. Why?
Because in this passage, the arhat is not definitively manifested.
How is this known?
From the words of this sūtra:
"The mind of an arhat has for a long time been inclined toward emptiness and stillness, even to the point of being on the verge of falling into nirvāṇa."
By virtue of these words, it is known that the preceding [argument] is not a proof.
Furthermore, another sūtra states:
"An arhat possesses such power that, by means of all dharmas within the sphere of the outflows (*āsrava*), the arhat is at all times cool and at all times tranquil."
Because of these words, the previous [argument] is not a proof.
There is such a statement:
"until one has abandoned the formations."
If that were so, then this same principle would apply to those in training (śaikṣa) while they are in the process of acting.
However, because the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra* speaks with reference to the stage of one in training, such a fault does not apply to the Arhat.
The Vaibhāṣika masters say:
"Do all Arhats fall away from their fruit?
Is it only Arhats who possess the six types of spiritual lineage (*gotra*), or do other persons also possess them?"
The verse says:
"There are six types of ordinary practitioners.
The commentary says:
Not only do Arhats possess the six dispositions; ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those in training (*śaikṣa*) all likewise possess the six dispositions. Why is this?
It is because these six dispositions of the Arhat take those [dispositions] as their preceding stages.
Furthermore, the verse says:
"There is no refinement of the faculties on the path of vision.
The commentary explains:
The cultivation of the faculties (*indriya*) occurs at a location distinct from the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
it does not occur within the path of seeing itself, because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) is insufficient for such cultivation.

Some cultivate the transformation of the remaining faculties while still in the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), while others cultivate the practice of refining the faculties while in the stage of those who have attained through faith and aspiration (*śraddhādhimukta*).
The Sūtra states:
"Regarding the four kinds of abidings in happiness in the present life based on the mind that this person has attained, I say that there is the possibility of falling away from any one of them."
This is the unshakable liberation of mind, realized by the original body of a single Arhat; I say that there is no other cause or condition capable of causing an Arhat to fall away from this state.
How does an Arhat of the "unshakable dharma" type fall away from the dwelling in happiness in the present life?
The verse says:
There are three kinds of falling away: regarding what has been attained, what has not yet been attained, and [the loss of] enjoyment.
The commentary states:
"One who has fallen away from what was attained" refers to a person who falls away from qualities already acquired.
"One who has fallen away from what was not yet attained" refers to a person who is unable to attain the qualities they ought to have attained.
Regarding "retrogression from enjoyment," it refers to when a person does not cause the merits they have attained to manifest.
Among these three types of retrogression, the verse says:
"The last is indestructible for the Buddha; the middle one has three remaining."
The commentary states:
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses only *parihāṇi* of enjoyment (*upabhoga-parihāṇi*) and no others, because the Tathāgata exclusively practices deeds for the benefit of others.

An Arhat of the "unshakable dharma" (*akopya-dharman*) may possess both *parihāṇi* of enjoyment and *parihāṇi* of non-attainment (*aprāpti-parihāṇi*), because they have not yet attained the distinctions of the superior qualities of a person.
Other arhats also experience decline regarding what has already been attained, decline regarding what has not yet been attained, and decline regarding enjoyment.
These two [types of decline] can be understood from the sūtras, which speak of decline based on decline regarding enjoyment.
The fact that an Arhat established in the dharma of non-retrogression does not fall back does not contradict the Sūtras.
Therefore, all untainted (anāsrava) liberations are indestructible.

As for the meaning of the Arhat established in the dharma of non-retrogression as it has been set forth, this meaning is neither otherwise than it is nor not otherwise; thus, this meaning cannot be challenged.
This means that all Arhats possess the quality of being "unbreakable" (*abhedyadharman*); this name manifests the sense of being indestructible.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Vibhāṣā*:
"If there is an Arhat who falls away from the fruit of Arhatship, will this Arhat undergo rebirth again?"
One will not undergo further rebirth.
How is this known?
The verse says:
"Because one does not die while in the state of regression.
The commentary explains:
There is no person who, having regressed from a noble fruit, would pass away while remaining in that state of regression.
Why is this? As it is said in the Sūtra:
"O Bhikṣus!"
If a noble disciple should lose mindfulness, it is entirely slow to do so;
nevertheless, once this loss of mindfulness has ceased, it is swiftly extinguished.
According to the statement in this sutra, for this reason, there is no such thing as death.
If it were not so, this true holy life would not be a state of rest.
If a person were to fall away from this fruit, would they have to perform again that which was already accomplished while dwelling in their former fruit?
The verse says:
One does not perform what is not to be done.
The commentary explains:
If a person has already fallen away from a stage but does not again perform actions contrary to their original fruit— just as a strong man may stumble but does not fall—
how many paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are there when such a person cultivates the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃvara*)?
The verse says:
"The nine [attainments] of the uninterrupted path and the path of liberation are unshakable.
The commentary explains:

If a person seeks to penetrate the indestructible nature of phenomena (dharmatā), this is the practice of one who penetrates the nature of phenomena; there are nine paths of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) and nine paths of liberation (vimukti-mārga), just as when a person seeks to attain the fruit of arhatship, there are paths of uninterrupted transition and liberation.
Why is this so? Because it is of a nature characterized by dull faculties (*mṛdv-indriya*).
The verse says:
"By long-standing practice.
The commentary explains:

This person has repeatedly cultivated the nature of weak faculties over a long period; these faculties cannot be turned back by even a slight effort, because they have been rendered firm and solid by the paths of both those still in training and those beyond training.
The verse says:
"In each of the *dṛṣṭiprāpta* [attainments], there is one.
The commentary says:

If a person wishes to penetrate the nature of one who has attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), there is only one uninterrupted path (ānantaryamārga) to be cultivated, as well as one path of liberation (vimuktimārga), and within that, there is also one path of skillful means (prayogamārga).
These are all the paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). The verse says:
"They are untainted (*anāsrava*).
The commentary explains:

Why is this? It is because it is impossible for one to cultivate the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya*) by means of a path associated with outflows (*sāsrava*), since the faculties are themselves without outflows (*anāsrava*) and the objects of focus (*ālambana*) of the path are all suchness (*tathatā*).
In which realm can the faculties be cultivated so as to increase?
The verse says:
They increase in the human realm.
The commentary states:
The cultivation of the faculties (*indriya*) through refinement can be attained within the human realm, but not in other places, because there is no falling away [from the fruit] there.
Furthermore, which person, relying upon which stage (*bhūmi*), is able to cultivate the refinement of the faculties?
The verse says:
Those beyond training rely on nine stages; those still in training rely on only six.
The commentary says:

If an adept (aśaikṣa) relies upon nine stages to cultivate the practice of refining the faculties—namely, the threshold stage (anāgamya), the intermediate dhyāna, the four form-dhyānas, and the three formless attainments.
If there is a practitioner in training who, relying on the six stages, cultivates the practice of refining the faculties, they are excluded from the three formless realms. Why?
Because of this principle.
The verse says:
One abandons the differentiated fruits and attains the increase of the path of superior fruits.
The commentary says:

If a person cultivates the practice of refining the faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*), they abandon the fruit and the path of the inferior faculties that surpasses the fruit, and immediately attain the fruit and the path of the superior faculties.

Since the fruit of Anāgāmin is not included within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), for this reason, those in training (*śaikṣa*) do not perform the refinement of faculties within the formless realm.
Therefore, there are only nine types of Arhats based on the distinctions of their faculties.
Why is this so? The verse says:
"The two Buddhas and seven śrāvakas; there are nine because of the nine faculties.
The commentary says:
Which are the seven śrāvakas?

There are five types of persons subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), and two types of persons whose nature is indestructible (*akopyadharman*): first, those who have attained it through the refinement of their faculties (*indriya-saṃcāra*); second, those who are of an indestructible nature from the very beginning.
Within the nature of non-destruction from the beginning, there are distinctions, namely two types of Buddhas:
first, the Pratyekabuddha; second, the Mahāsambuddha.
Because these nine persons possess distinctions in their faculties—such as the "soft-soft," "medium-soft," and "superior-soft"—they constitute nine types of Arhats.

There are only seven types of noble persons: those who follow by faith, those who follow by dharma, those who are devoted through faith, those who have attained vision, those who are body-witnesses, those liberated by wisdom, and those liberated both ways.
Regarding these seven types of persons, the verse says:
"Due to preparatory application, faculties, the attainment of cessation, and the two types of liberation, there are seven persons.
The commentary explains:
If they are established as two persons by way of their application (*prayoga*), these are: the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*).
This is because, prior [to the path of seeing], the former accepted the teachings of others through faith, while the latter practiced according to the dharma by applying themselves to the meaning.

If two persons are distinguished by their faculties, they are called the "one who delights in faith" (śraddhādhimukta) and the "one who has attained vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta); this is because of the difference between dull and sharp faculties, being respectively superior in terms of faith and superior in terms of wisdom.

If categorized by way of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), there is one type of person, namely the "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*), because he has personally realized the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) with his body.

If categorized by way of liberation (*vimukti*), there are two types of persons, namely those liberated by wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and those doubly liberated (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*), because they are liberated from the hindrance of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the hindrance to meditative concentration (*samāpattyāvaraṇa*) through wisdom and meditative concentration, respectively.
This person becomes seven by way of name.
The verse says:
"Or six persons, because the three types of noble ones (āryapudgala) occur in pairs."
The commentary states:
If, according to the ultimate sense, there are only six types of persons, why is this so?
In the path of seeing (darśanamārga), there are two types of persons: namely, those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin) and those who follow by dharma (dharmānusārin).

If these two persons, during the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga), become distinct individuals, they are called those who have attained through devotion (śraddhādhimukta) and those who have attained through vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta).

If these two types of persons are further distinguished within the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga), they are called those liberated by time (samayavimukta) and those liberated at any time (asamayavimukta).

Within this context, if distinguished by their faculties (indriya), there are three types based on those who follow through faith (śraddhānusārin); if distinguished by their nature (gotra), there are five types; and if distinguished by the path (mārga), there are fifteen types, because they abide in the eight patiences (kṣānti) and the seven knowledges (jñāna).
If one counts seventy-three persons based on their freedom from desire (*vairāgya*), there is first the person bound by all fetters (*sakalabandhana*).

Regarding those who have become free from desire for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), there are nine types; likewise, there are nine types for each stage up to the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). These are distinguished by their bases (*āśraya*), namely, those born in the three continents and the six heavens of the desire realm.

Based on the categories of faculties (*indriya*), lineages (*gotra*), paths (*mārga*), detachment (*vairāgya*), and bases (*āśraya*), the total number amounts to one hundred thousand, forty-seven thousand, eight hundred, and twenty-five persons.
As for the remaining noble ones (*ārya*), they should be enumerated in this same manner according to their respective meanings and principles.
Regarding what was called "liberation through both parts," who is this person?
And who is the one liberated by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukta*)?
The verse says:
One who attains the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is "liberated in both ways" (ubhayatobhāgavimukta); others are "liberated by wisdom" (prajñāvimukta).
The commentary explains:

If a person first attains the meditative absorption of the cessation of mind and subsequently reaches the stage of one beyond training (aśaikṣa), they are called "liberated in both parts," because through both wisdom (prajñā) and meditative concentration (samādhi), they are liberated from the obstacles of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa) and the obstacles to the eight liberations (vimokṣāvaraṇa).
The remainder [of the trainees] do so solely by the power of wisdom (*prajñā*), because they are exclusively liberated from the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
As the Blessed One said in a verse:
"If one abandons these five fetters, One is a learner endowed with the quality of non-retrogression."
To what extent does such a person become a "fully endowed learner" (śaikṣa)?
The verse says:
"By virtue of concentration, faculties, and fruit, one is said to be a fully perfected learner."
The commentary states:

A person in training (śaikṣa) is said to be "fully trained" for three reasons: first, by way of the fruit; second, by way of the faculties (indriya); and third, by way of meditative attainment (samāpatti).
Regarding those who possess the fruit alone: this refers to a person who has attained the state of non-returner (anāgāmin) through faith and aspiration, but is not yet a bodily witness (kāyasākṣin).
"By means of the faculties alone" refers to those who have attained vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*) but have not yet abandoned desire.
"By means of both the fruit and the faculties" refers to those who have attained vision and are *anāgāmins* who have not yet attained bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*).
"By means of both the fruit and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*)" refers to those *anāgāmins* who have attained through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*) and have already attained bodily realization.
Regarding those who possess the fruit, the faculties, and meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), these refer to the *dṛṣṭiprāpta*, the *kāyasākṣin*, and the *anāgāmin*.

It is impossible for there to be a learner (*śaikṣa*) who possesses the status of a learner solely by virtue of meditative attainment, or solely by virtue of both faculties and meditative attainment, without possessing the fruit.
The verse says:
"The perfection of the qualities of one beyond training is due to two.
The commentary says:
Those who have attained perfection as an Aśaikṣa do so by means of two factors: first, by way of their faculties (indriya), and second, by way of meditative attainment (samāpatti).
It is impossible for one to become an Aśaikṣa if the fruit has not been fully perfected; therefore, regarding the fruit, whether it is perfected or not is irrelevant.
One who is perfected by the faculties alone, but not by meditative attainment (*samāpatti*), refers to one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*).
One who is liberated through wisdom (*prajñāvimukta*) and is perfected by meditative attainment alone, but not by the faculties, refers to one liberated by occasion (*samayavimukta*).

Regarding the person liberated in both ways who is perfected in terms of faculties (*indriya*) and meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), this refers to the one liberated at any time (*asamayavimukta*).

There are many distinctions among the paths described for such a person liberated in both ways, namely: the mundane path and the supramundane path; the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*); or alternatively, the path of preparation (*prayogamārga*), the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*), the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), and the path of advancement (*viśeṣamārga*).
Briefly stated, how many kinds of this path are there?
The verse says:
Briefly stated, the path consists of the four paths of preparation, the uninterrupted path, the path of liberation, and the path of advancement.
The commentary states:
Regarding the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), it is that path from which the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises without interval.
Regarding the path of uninterrupted transition, it is that path by means of which one is able to eliminate the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

The path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) is the first path that arises immediately after the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), following the cessation of the afflictive obscurations.

The path of advancement (*viśeṣa-mārga*) refers to the remaining paths arising subsequent to the path of liberation, namely the paths of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the refinement of the faculties (*indriya-saṃskāra*).
Why are these four called the "path"?
Because this dharma is the road to parinirvāṇa, it is called the path;
for if a person sets out upon this road, they will certainly reach nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, because practitioners seek nirvāṇa by means of this dharma, it is called the "path.
How is it that the advancement toward liberation is called the path?

Because it belongs to the same category as the preceding paths, because it is of the highest degree, and because it enables one to reach the subsequent state, the preceding is designated as the path for the subsequent.
Because these serve as the means for entering *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, all four are the Path (*mārga*).
Furthermore, this Path is sometimes called "practice" (*pratipat*), because one proceeds to *nirvāṇa* by means of this practice.
This practice is of four kinds, as the Sūtra says:

there is practice that is difficult and slow in wisdom; there is practice that is difficult and quick in wisdom; there is practice that is pleasant and slow in wisdom; and there is practice that is pleasant and quick in wisdom.
The verse here says:
"Based on meditative concentration, it is a pleasant practice on the path.
The commentary explains:
Among the four dhyānas, these four types of paths are called "pleasant practice" (sukha-pratipad) because they include the [dhyāna] factors and because śamatha and vipaśyanā arise in equilibrium;
since this path is accomplished without effort, it is called pleasant practice.
The verse says:
"In other stages, there is ascetic practice.
The commentary says:

In other stages—namely, the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*), the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*), and the formless concentrations (*ārūpya*)—this path is called "ascetic practice" (*duṣkara*). Because it does not include the [meditative] factors, because śamatha and vipaśyanā are not fully developed, and because it is accomplished through great effort, it is designated as ascetic practice.

Why is this? Because the preparatory concentration (*anāgamya*) and the intermediate concentration (*dhyānāntara*) lack the perfection of *śamatha*, as they have not yet reached the first or second dhyānas.
The formless attainments lack *vipaśyanā* because thought and reflection are subtle.
Furthermore, this asceticism of pleasure has two types.
The verse says:
"Slow wisdom" refers to those with dull faculties; "swift wisdom" pertains to those with sharp faculties.
The commentary explains:
if a person has dull faculties, whether they practice with ease or through hardship, this practice is termed "slow wisdom."
If a person possesses sharp faculties, this practice is called "swift knowledge" (*kṣiprajñā*).
Furthermore, because wisdom is slow within this practice, it is termed "slow knowledge" (*dhandhajñā*);
the same applies to swift knowledge.
Furthermore, because this practice is for those who proceed slowly, it is called "slow knowledge" (*dhandhābhijñā*);
the same applies to "swift knowledge" (*kṣiprābhijñā*).

Furthermore, this path is also called the "aids to enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*), and there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*), namely: the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).
The verse here says:
"The two knowledges of exhaustion and non-arising are enlightenment.
The commentary explains:
These—the knowledge of exhaustion and the knowledge of non-arising—become three types of enlightenment due to the distinction between persons:
first, the enlightenment of the śrāvaka; second, the enlightenment of the pratyekabuddha; and third, the unsurpassed perfect and complete enlightenment.

Because of the extinction of ignorance without remainder, one has already realized as it truly is and is capable of awakening; since that which was to be done has been accomplished, there is nothing further to be done.
The verse says:
"In accordance with this, there are thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
The commentary states:
Because those factors serve as the means for the arising, abiding, and enjoyment of the birth of enlightenment (bodhi), the thirty-seven are given the name "aids to awakening" (bodhipakṣa).
The verse says:
"By name and by actual meaning, there are ten.
The commentary states:
These factors that assist awakening are thirty-seven when explained by way of their names.
If considered by way of substantial entities, all the factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) are only ten. What are these ten?
The verse says:
Faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, wisdom, joy, equanimity, as well as pliancy, ethical discipline, and awakening.
The commentary states:
faith is the clarity and purity of the mind with respect to seven points.
Vigor (*vīrya*) is the mind’s courage regarding its objects.
Mindfulness (*smṛti*) is the mind’s clarity and non-forgetfulness regarding the focal object.
Concentration (*samādhi*) is the mind’s one-pointed tranquility regarding its objects.
Wisdom is understanding according to reality;
joy is the mind’s peace and happiness;
equanimity is the mind being free from effortful application.
Pliancy (praśrabdhi) means that body and mind follow their respective functions.
Precept (śīla) means being able to bring body and speech to equilibrium.
Awakening (bodha) means being able to exercise deliberation.
How are these ten entities established within the seven bases?
The verse says:
Wisdom is the foundation of mindfulness; diligence is called right effort; and the bases of psychic power are called concentration.
The commentary states:
Among these, the four foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of power have wisdom, diligence, and concentration as their intrinsic natures.
Next, the five faculties are explained; as with the faculties, so it is with the powers.
They differ because they are grasped as distinct entities. Why is this?
The five entities—faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom—are both faculties (*indriya*) and powers (*bala*).
Among these, the foundation of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, and right view are wisdom.
Right effort, the factor of enlightenment of energy, and right exertion are diligence.
The bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), the factor of enlightenment of concentration (*samādhisambodhyaṅga*), and right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) are simply concentration.

The factors of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicayasambodhyaṅga*), energy (*vīryasambodhyaṅga*), joy (*prītisambodhyaṅga*), tranquility (*praśrabdhisambodhyaṅga*), equanimity (*upekṣāsambodhyaṅga*), and right mindfulness (*samyaksmṛti*) are simply mindfulness. What dharma remains?
The factors of enlightenment consisting of joy, tranquility, equanimity, right view, and the factor of morality—these five are the remainder.
Thus, these factors conducive to enlightenment consist of only ten entities.

According to the Vaibhāṣika masters, there are eleven entities based on the nature of suffering; since the two types of karma—bodily and vocal—are not mutually inclusive, the constituent parts of ethical discipline (*śīla*) are divided into two distinct entities. These aforementioned foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth have wisdom (*prajñā*), diligence (*vīrya*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).
In this regard, it should be understood that the verse says:
"Names are established according to their predominant [characteristic]; all are acquired through application.
The commentary explains:
Among these, they are designated by such names according to their predominant characteristics.
All dharmas acquired through application are, in fact, the foundations of mindfulness, the right efforts, and the bases of psychic power.
Why is diligence called "right effort"?
Because it is able to establish the actions of body, speech, and mind so that they become superior.
Why is samādhi called a "basis of psychic power" (ṛddhipāda)?
Because all supreme virtues rely upon them as their basis.
If someone were to say that only samādhi is called the bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda), namely desire and so forth;
In that [realm], the factors of enlightenment consist of thirteen entities because of the increase of the mind of desire.
If one maintains this view, it contradicts the Sūtra.
The Sūtra says:
"Monks! I shall now explain to you the *ṛddhi* (supernormal power) and the bases of *ṛddhi*, up to the point where it is asked: 'What is *ṛddhi*?
Within this True Dharma, there is a monk who realizes various spheres of *ṛddhi*: namely, being originally one, he becomes many; as explained at length in the Sūtra."
Why are those previously mentioned called "faculties" (*indriya*) and those subsequently mentioned called "powers" (*bala*)?
It is because of the distinction between the weak and the superior, and because of being susceptible to being overcome or not being susceptible to being overcome.

Although the faculties are predominant during the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*), they are not yet "powers" because, while in a state of inferiority, they can still be overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*) which are their opposites. Thus, they are faculties but not powers.

Regarding "power" (*bala*): within the cultivation of insight (*vipaśyanā*), it exists at the stage of supreme excellence because the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be countered cannot overcome it; therefore, it is a power and not a faculty (*indriya*).
How is the sequence established?
If a person believes that this practice has a superior fruit, they will cultivate right effort in order to attain that fruit.
If a person constantly cultivates right effort, mindfulness becomes established.
If a person focuses their attention on the object of meditation, because the mind does not become distracted, they immediately attain concentration (*samādhi*).
Once the mind has attained concentration, one then perceives and knows reality as it truly is (*yathābhūtam*).
For this reason, the sequence is established.
Furthermore, in which stages are which factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) to be manifested?
The verse says:

"Those distinguished in the initial generation of the resolve and in the stages of penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) are to be known in their sevenfold sequence throughout the stages of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and vision (*darśana*)."
The commentary states:
Within the stage of initial practice, one first cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) in order to maintain awareness of objects such as the body.
Because one seeks to attain superior growth and increase of diligence (vīrya), one cultivates the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa) at the stage of "heat" (uṣmagata).
Because one is able to enter the roots of goodness from which there is no regression, one cultivates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) at the stage of the "Summit" (*mūrdhan*).
Because there is no further regression, one reaches the stage of "Increased Progress" (*adhimātra*); therefore, one cultivates the five faculties (*indriya*) at the stage of "Patience" (*kṣānti*).
Because it cannot be overcome by delusions, one cultivates the five powers during the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Furthermore, no other worldly dharmas can overcome it.
Because it is proximate to the state of enlightenment (*bodhi*), one cultivates the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*) within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Because they are manifested through their issuance, one cultivates the Noble Path within the Path of Vision (darśanamārga).
Since these [eight] follow from that [sevenfold set], and in order to conform to the numerical sequence, the seven are mentioned first and the eight are mentioned afterward.
If one follows the sequence of cultivation, one first cultivates eight [factors] and subsequently cultivates seven.

Regarding this, the Vaibhāṣika masters state that the factor of awakening consisting of the investigation of phenomena (dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga) is both awakening and a factor of awakening, and right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) is both the path and a factor of the path.
Other masters, without breaking this sequence, explain the order of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
For a beginner, in order to subdue the various forms of distracted and distorted cognitions regarding manifold objects, one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

The four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) are the locus where the practitioner binds and records the mind; they serve to eliminate all conceptualizations based on craving and recollection.
Because of this scriptural statement, it is known that the four foundations of mindfulness constitute the beginning of the practice.

By the power of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one is able to generate diligence in order to accomplish four tasks, and because it can correctly establish the mind so that it becomes superior.

Following the four foundations of mindfulness, one cultivates the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*); through these right efforts, the mind is free from sorrow and regret, and the mind is governed to achieve meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Next, one cultivates the four right efforts and the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), because by relying on meditative concentration, faith, and the other faculties, these serve as the predominant conditions for the arising of supramundane dharmas.

Next, one cultivates the five faculties (*indriya*); these faculties are most capable of subduing their respective opposing factors, and in initiating practice through their own functional power, they are able to produce supramundane dharmas independently of similar causes (*sabhāgahetu*).

Next, one cultivates the five faculties and the five powers; within the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), one cultivates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*); and within both the paths of seeing and cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), one cultivates the factors of the noble path (*āryamārgāṅga*). Why is this so?
The Sūtra states this:

"Within the Noble Eightfold Path, everything should be cultivated until cultivation is perfected—namely, from the four foundations of mindfulness until cultivation is perfected, up to and including the seven factors of enlightenment until cultivation is perfected."
Furthermore, another sutra states:
"When a bhikṣu proclaims words according to reality, it refers to the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths, which is like a path one has personally traveled.
To proceed further along such a path is the analogy for cultivating the Eightfold Noble Path."
Therefore, one should know that within these two stages, the eightfold noble path is cultivated, and all these [stages] are accomplished in their proper sequence.
Having explained the sequence, this meaning shall now be discussed:
among the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), how many are with outflows (*sāsrava*) and how many are without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
The verse says:
"The untainted factors of enlightenment and the path.
The commentary says:

Because they are established within the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) and the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are all untainted (*anāsrava*).
Although there are also factors such as right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) in the mundane realm, these do not receive the name of the noble path (*āryamārga*).
The verse says:
"Other dharmas are of two kinds.
The commentary says:
The remaining factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipākṣikadharma) are both with outflows (sāsrava) and without outflows (anāsrava).
Furthermore, in which stages (bhūmi) do how many factors conducive to enlightenment exist?
The verse says:
"Complete in the first dhyāna.
The commentary explains:
Within the stage of the first dhyāna, all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharmas) are fully present.
The verse says:
In the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*), joy (*prīti*) is excluded.
The commentary says:
What is the absence of joy?
Because one is led by the power of the preparatory concentrations (*sāmantaka*), and because doubt and fear regarding the lower stages have not yet subsided.
The verse says:
"Second dhyāna is free from vitarka.
The commentary states:
In the second dhyāna, that which is abandoned by correct awakening consists of only thirty-six [factors], because vitarka and vicāra do not exist therein.
The verse says:
"In two [cases], they are free from two.
The commentary says:
In the third and fourth dhyānas, the factors that assist awakening (bodhipākṣika-dharma) are devoid of both joy (prīti) and applied thought (vitarka); there are thus only thirty-five.
The verse says:
"And in the intermediate dhyāna."
The commentary states:
In the intermediate dhyāna as well, there are two [factors] to be abandoned, totaling thirty-five.
The verse says:
"Excluding the precepts, the first two, and the formless [factors].
The commentary explains:
In the three formless realms (*ārūpyadhātu*), right speech, right action, right livelihood, and right mindfulness are excluded; thus, there are only thirty-two [factors] present.
The verse says:
In the desire realm and at the peak of existence, they are dissociated from the factors of the noble path.
The commentary says:
In these two stages, there are only twenty-two factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma). Why is this?
Because these two stages are not vessels for the untainted path (anāsravamārga).

If a person is currently in the stage of contemplation on the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣikadharma*), at which stage should it be known that they attain right understanding and pure faith?
The verse says:

Upon seeing the three truths, one attains the precepts as well as right understanding and faith in the Dharma; upon seeing the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one attains faith in the Buddha and faith in the assembly of disciples.
The commentary states:

If a person correctly perceives the noble truths of suffering, its origin, and its cessation, they attain correct understanding and pure faith in the Dharma, as well as the precepts cherished by the noble ones.
By means of perceiving the noble truth of the path, they attain correct understanding and pure faith in the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the community of his noble disciples.

Why is this? It is because these two types of correct understanding and pure faith consist of generating correct understanding and pure faith toward the unlearned (*aśaikṣa*) qualities uniquely attained by one who can become a Buddha;

generating correct understanding and pure faith toward the learned (*śaikṣa*) and unlearned qualities that constitute the Saṅgha; and further attaining the precepts as well as correct understanding and pure faith toward the Dharma.
The verse says:
"Dharma refers to the three truths, as well as the paths of bodhisattvas and pratyekabuddhas.
The commentary explains:

Therefore, when a person correctly contemplates the Four Noble Truths and attains right understanding and pure faith regarding the Dharma, this Dharma—due to the distinctions in its bases of faith and its designations—is described as the fourfold right understanding and pure faith.
The verse says:
If categorized by substance, there are only two: faith and ethical discipline.
The commentary says:

Regarding the right understanding and pure faith in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha: faith is their intrinsic nature, which is one dharma beloved by the noble ones; and ethical discipline is the single dharma of morality. Therefore, in terms of substantial entities, they consist of only two things.
Are these two with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*)?
All correct understanding and pure faith are exclusively— according to the verse—
without outflows.
The commentary states:
What is the meaning of "pure faith through right understanding"?
Having realized the Four Truths as they truly are, one attains untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) regarding these four points; this is called pure faith through right understanding.
This faith is accomplished through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) and applies to both types of individuals.
When such a person correctly emerges from meditative absorption, the four types of faith arise as they do in the present, following this sequence.
How does one emerge from meditative absorption and manifest its arising?

One knows that the Blessed One is the Perfectly Awakened One and the All-Knowing; that the Blessed One’s True Dharma and Right Teaching are foremost among all correct teachings; and that the Blessed One’s community of noble disciples is peerless in right practice—resembling, respectively, a physician, a medical formula, and a nurse who sustains a patient.
The purification of faith produced by this mental clarity is called "purity of ethical discipline through faith" (*śīla-śraddhā-viśuddhi*).

Alternatively, it is said that the fourth [type] is as follows: when a person has attained purity of faith, such right practice is called "purity of ethical discipline through faith," because it resembles the state of being free from illness.
Alternatively, it is said that these four are like a guide, like the path, like a caravan companion, and like a vehicle.
As stated in the Sūtra:
"A person in training (śaikṣa) is endowed with eight factors, while a person beyond training (aśaikṣa) is endowed with ten."
Why is it not said that those in training (śaikṣa) possess right liberation and the knowledge and vision of right liberation?
The verse says:
Liberation is not a factor of training; because they are still bound, there are two kinds.
The commentary states:
For those in the stage of training (*śaikṣa*), there is currently bondage, because they have not yet been able to escape the fetters of affliction (*kleśa*).
If they are currently bound, how can they be established as being liberated?
If one is liberated from only a portion of the bonds, one cannot be said to be "already liberated.
If there were no liberation, how could the knowledge and vision of liberation (vimukti-jñāna-darśana) be established?

Because those beyond training (aśaikṣa) have eternally been liberated from all bonds of affliction, it can be said that they possess liberation; this is because it is manifested by their own two types of realized wisdom (pratyātma-jñāna).
These words are logical.
What dharma is called liberation?
This liberation is of two kinds:
There are two: the conditioned and the unconditioned.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"The cessation of afflictions is the unconditioned; the purification of the mind realizes the conditioned."
The commentary states:
Unconditioned liberation refers to the total extinction of all afflictions.
Conditioned liberation refers to the pure realization of the mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The verse says:
"This division.
The commentary says:
This conditioned liberation is called a factor of the state beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), because its constituent factors are conditioned.
The verse says:
"That is to say, the two liberations."
The commentary states:
This conditioned liberation is described in the sūtras as two kinds of liberation, namely, liberation of mind (*citta-vimukti*) and liberation by wisdom (*prajñā-vimukti*).
It should be understood that these two constitute the factors of liberation for one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
If that is so, how is this statement explained in another sutra:
"Viyaghra! What is liberation?"
This refers to the mind being eternally perfected and pure.
In this regard, there is a bhikṣu who, regarding the mind of desire, is free from desire and liberated; regarding the minds of hatred and delusion, he is free from desire and liberated.

In this way, if the aggregate of liberation (*vimuktipakṣa*) is not yet perfected, one brings it to perfection; if it is already perfected, one maintains it through desire, diligence, and so forth, as explained at length in the Sūtra.
Therefore, one should not consider liberation to be merely the mind’s state of being understood.
What is this true wisdom?
It is when all afflictions such as desire have been eliminated, and the mind is exclusively stainless; other masters describe this as liberation.
Having explained right liberation,
what kind of thing is the knowledge and vision of right liberation, which is distinct from right view?
The verse says:
"Wisdom is as described regarding bodhi.
The commentary states:
This refers to what was previously called "bodhi."

This dharma should now be understood as being called the "knowledge and vision of right liberation," namely, the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*).
Furthermore, by which mind is there liberation?
Is it a past, present, or future mind?
The verse says:
Liberation arises from the mind that is currently being produced; the one beyond training [is liberated] from the obstacle of afflictions.
The commentary says:

The future mind is termed "presently arising"; this mind belongs to one who is beyond training (aśaikṣa), and from it, one attains liberation from the hindrances of affliction—thus says the Abhidharma.
What dharma acts as an obstacle to this mind?
The acquisition (*prāpti*) of the afflictions (*kleśa*) acts as the obstacle, because it is able to hinder its arising. Why is this so?

At the time of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), this acquisition (*prāpti*) is extinguished; at the moment it is extinguished, this mind of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-citta*) arises. This arising is itself liberation.
When this acquisition has already ceased and this mind of one beyond training has already arisen, it is said to be "already liberated."
If that were so, then the mind that has not yet arisen and the worldly mind would also be liberated; why, then, do you speak only of the "presently arising" and the "beyond-training" (aśaikṣa) minds?
If it is the case that whatever arises is necessarily liberated, then it is precisely this [presently arising] mind that is what we are discussing here.
From what delusion is the worldly mind liberated?
It is liberated from its obstructions.
If a person has not yet attained liberation, does it mean that the mind of liberation does not arise?
Is it born?
It is not like the liberated mind discussed here.
What is this mind like?
Because it is associated with the acquisition of the afflictions (*kleśaprāpti*),
at what stage does this path exist such that it can eliminate its own arising obstacles?
The verse says:
The path currently ceasing can extinguish those afflictions that obstruct the path.
The commentary states:
If the path is present in the current moment, it can diminish prior afflictions and serves as the *samanantarapratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) for future afflictions.

The power [of the path] draws forth the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) regarding future afflictions, so as to permanently obstruct them and prevent their further arising. Therefore, while the Path itself is present in the current moment, it damages the present and obstructs that which is about to arise in the future; this is what was previously described as unconditioned liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti*).

The sūtras speak of three kinds of realms (*dhātu*): namely, the realm of cessation (*nirodha-dhātu*), the realm of detachment (*virāga-dhātu*), and the realm of permanent elimination (*prahāṇa-dhātu*).
What is the distinction between these dharmas?
The verse says:
The unconditioned realm of liberation (*asaṃskṛta-vimukti-dhātu*).
The commentary states:
This unconditioned liberation is itself the three realms.
A verse here says:
"Detachment from desire means the cessation of desire.
The commentary explains:
The cessation of the afflictions of desire is called the "sphere of detachment from the realm of desire.
The verse says:
The sphere of cessation is the cessation of the remaining delusions.
The commentary says:
The cessation of craving and other afflictions is called the "element of cessation" (nirodhadhātu).
The verse says:
"Permanent elimination is the cessation of other categories.
The commentary explains:
"The cessation of all phenomena other than those belonging to the category of afflictions is termed the realm of permanent elimination (*atyantanirodhadhātu*)."
These three realms are themselves unconditioned liberation.
If one gives rise to revulsion toward these types of states by means of this kind of mind, can one attain detachment from them by means of this same kind of mind?
Regarding this, there are four permutations.
How are the four propositions formulated?
The verse says:
"Disenchantment arises from [the truths of] suffering and its origin, by means of patience and knowledge."
The commentary states:
Through the mind of receptivity and knowledge regarding suffering and its origin, one merely gives rise to revulsion, and not through any other dharma. Why is this?
Because these two belong to the category of objects that cause distress and affliction.
The verse says:
"Free from desire."
The commentary states:
It is by means of the minds of patience (*kṣānti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) regarding cessation and the path that one attains detachment from desire, and not by any other dharmas. Why is this so?
These two belong to the category of the objects of joy and bliss.
The verse says:
"The two [are abandoned] by the cessation of all."
The commentary states:

These patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*) regarding the origin, cessation, and path of all suffering are able to extinguish all afflictions; by means of them, the mind attains revulsion and also achieves detachment.
It is not by other factors that these two [types of knowledge] function.

If they were unable to eliminate the afflictions, then even if a person who has already attained detachment from desire were to repeatedly contemplate the Four Truths, the *dharmajñānakṣānti* would still be unable to eliminate those afflictions.
If wisdom is comprised within the paths of preparation, liberation, or advancement, this wisdom likewise cannot extinguish the afflictions.
The verse says:
"In this regard, four alternatives are established."
The commentary states:
Therefore, one should understand that the meaning of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) is as follows.
*Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, Fascicle 18.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Nineteen.
Composed by Vasubandhu;
translated by the Chen Dynasty Indian Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha.

Chapter Seven: Analysis of Wisdom (Prajñā-vibhaṅga), Part One. Having already explained the various patiences (kṣānti) and the various knowledges (jñāna), [the author] now explains right view (samyagdṛṣṭi) and right knowledge (samyagjñāna).
Are all patiences (kṣānti) not wisdom (jñāna), and is right knowledge (samyag-jñāna) not right view (samyag-dṛṣṭi)?
The verse says:
"Immaculate patience is not wisdom."
The commentary states:

These eight kinds of untainted patience (*anāsrava-kṣānti*) previously mentioned are not cognitions (*jñāna*), because the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) and doubts that ought to be abandoned have not yet been eliminated; therefore, they may be called "views" (*dṛṣṭi*), as their essential nature consists of decisive determination and investigative seeking.
Just as with patience (*kṣānti*), it is merely the seeing of the nature [of phenomena] and not wisdom (*jñāna*).
As the verse says:
"Exhaustion and non-arising are not seeing."
The commentary says:

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are not views (*darśana*), because their nature is not that of decisive judgment, investigation, or seeking.
The verse says:
"Distinct from those two noble wisdoms.
The commentary explains:

distinct from patience (*kṣānti*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*), the remaining untainted (*anāsrava*) prajñā is both vision (*darśana*) and knowledge (*jñāna*).
The verse says:
"Other wisdoms.
The commentary says:
All worldly *prajñā* is entirely wisdom (*jñāna*).
The verse says:
There are six types of seeing.
The commentary states:
The five views and mundane right view—these six types of mundane prajñā are called both "views" and "wisdom. All others are not views but are merely wisdom.
By how many knowledges (*jñāna*) are all knowledges subsumed?
By ten knowledges.
If subsumed briefly, the ten knowledges consist of only two knowledges.
The verse says:
"There is knowledge of the outflowing and the non-outflowing.
The commentary says:
All-knowledge does not transcend two natures, namely: mundane knowledge and supramundane knowledge.
Regarding these two, the verse says:
"The first is called conventional knowledge."
The commentary states:
Knowledge associated with outflows (sāsrava-jñāna) is called conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna). Why is this?
Because this knowledge takes as its object many conventional categories such as jars, clothing, men, and women, the verse says:
"Untainted knowledge is of two kinds: dharma-knowledge and subsequent knowledge."
The commentary states:
The untainted [wisdom] is divided into two types of knowledge, namely, dharma-knowledge (dharmajñāna) and subsequent knowledge (anvayajñāna).

When these two types of knowledge are combined with the preceding one, they constitute three types of knowledge, namely: conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna), dharma-knowledge, and subsequent knowledge.
The verse here says:
"Conventional knowledge has all things as its object.
The commentary explains:
All conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are the objects of conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The verse says:
"Taking desire, suffering, and so forth as its objects is the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*)."
The commentary states:
