This bodily power should be understood as having the sphere of tangibility (*spraṣṭavyāyatana*) as its intrinsic nature.
It is derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by a superior category of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), distinct from the seven types of tangibles; so say other masters.
The verse says:
There are four kinds of fearlessness.
The commentary says:
According to the scriptural text, there are four kinds of fearlessness.
The verse says:
"The first two correspond to the first ten powers; the latter two correspond to the second seven."
The commentary states:
The power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible is like the first fearlessness.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"I have now become a Tathāgata, a Samyaksaṃbuddha," as explained at length in the sūtra;
this should be known as the first fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
The power of knowledge regarding the exhaustion of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*) is like the second fearlessness.
As the Sūtra says:
"I have now exhausted all outflows," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
One should know that this is the second fearlessness.
The power of knowledge regarding the results of actions (*karmavipāka-jñānabala*) is like the third fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*).
As the Sūtra says:
"That which I have taught to my disciples as dharmas associated with obstacles," as explained at length in the Sūtra.
One should know that this is the third fearlessness.
The power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*) is like the fourth fearlessness.
As the Sūtra says:
This is what I have taught: for the assembly of disciples, it is the path of all pure qualities for the transcendence of birth and death, as explained at length in the sūtras.
This should be known as the fourth fearlessness.
These four dharmas should be understood as the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*).
Fearlessness has the nature of being without dread.
Why, then, is wisdom said to be fearlessness?
Because of these four dharmas, the Buddhas have no further doubt within the great assemblies; therefore, they are called "fearless.
Since this absence of doubt is accomplished through wisdom, it is said that fearlessness resides in wisdom, not that wisdom itself is fearlessness.
What meaning do these four reveal?
They reveal the meanings of self-benefit and benefit for others; the former two are self-benefit, and the latter two are benefit for others.
Furthermore, these four are solely matters of benefiting others, because they can eliminate the defilements of the speaker as well as the defilements of that which is spoken.
Having explained the four fearlessnesses,
regarding the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), there are three types based on the distinctions among the assemblies of disciples, as stated in the Sūtra.
Regarding these applications of mindfulness, the verse says:
"Third, the nature of mindfulness and wisdom.
The commentary states:
These three foundations of mindfulness have mindfulness and wisdom as their nature.

At that time, among the assembly of disciples, there were those who listened and practiced with a mind of reverence, those who listened and practiced without a mind of reverence, and others who possessed both.
Toward them all, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was without a mind of attachment, without a mind of anger, and without a mind of defilement.
Why are these three described as the unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) of a Buddha?
These three manifest the complete exhaustion of the Tathāgata’s habitual tendencies (vāsanā).

Furthermore, whether his own disciples respectfully practice the Teacher’s instructions, do not respectfully practice them, or engage in both, feelings such as joy or sorrow regarding these matters never arise in him in any way whatsoever, just as they do not arise in a Buddha; this is not the case for others.
These three non-arising [knowledges] are marvelous qualities for a Buddha that do not exist in others; therefore, these dharmas are established as the "unshared" (āveṇika) attainments.
Great Compassion shall now be explained.
The verse says:
Great Compassion is conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The commentary says:
Great compassion has conventional wisdom (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*) as its intrinsic nature.

If it were otherwise, it would not be able to take all sentient beings as its object, nor could it have the three types of suffering as its cognitive aspect (*ākāra*), just like the compassion of a śrāvaka.
What is called "great compassion"?
The verse says:
By way of its provisions, its mode of activity, its object, its equality, and its supremacy.
The commentary states:
First, it is great by way of its provisions (*sambhāra*), because it is able to produce the great provisions of merit and wisdom.
Second, it is great by way of its mode of activity (*ākāra*), because it takes the three types of suffering as its mode of activity and arises in relation to sentient beings.
Third, it is great by virtue of its object, because it universally takes the sentient beings of the three realms as its object.
Fourth, it is great by virtue of its impartiality, because it impartially brings about the welfare of all sentient beings.
Fifth, it is superior by way of being supreme, for there is no other compassion superior to this.
What is the distinction between great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and compassion (*karuṇā*)?
The verse says:
There are eight kinds of distinctions.
The commentary states:
First, the distinction of nature, because its nature consists of non-hatred and non-delusion.
Second is the distinction of their modes of activity (*ākāra*), because they take one suffering and three sufferings as their respective modes of activity.
Third is the distinction of their objects (*viṣaya*), because they arise by taking one realm and the three realms as their respective objects.
There is a distinction of four stages, because it relies upon the four dhyānas, with the fourth dhyāna serving as its stage.
There is a distinction of five continuums, because it arises within the continuums of śrāvakas and so forth, as well as the continuum of a Buddha.
Sixth is the distinction of attainment, because it is attained by means of detachment from the desire realm and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Seventh is the distinction of rescue, because those who seek rescue are brought to actual rescue.
There are eight distinctions of compassion, because they differ from [ordinary] compassion.
It has already been explained that the Buddhas possess eighteen qualities not shared with others.
Are these qualities exclusively shared with all Buddhas?
There are common and uncommon [qualities] shared with all Buddhas.
How is this so? The verse says:
"By reason of the accumulations, the Dharma-body, and the performance of the benefit of others, all Buddhas are equal; they are not equal in terms of lifespan, caste, or physical dimensions.
The commentary states:
By virtue of these three causes and conditions, all Buddhas are entirely equal.
First is the equality of the perfection of causes, because the accumulations of merit and wisdom practiced in the past have been equally fulfilled.
Second is the equality of the perfection of results, because the attained dharmakāya has been equally and fully accomplished.
Third is equality in benefiting others, because the activities of benefiting others, which arise from turning away from [self-centered] realization, are identical until the ultimate end.
By virtue of these three meanings, all Buddhas are equal.
"Non-common" refers to differentiation by way of lifespan, lineage, physical stature, and so forth.
The lifespans thus established vary in length because there are differences between births in previous lives and subsequent lives.
Because the castes of Brahmins and Kṣatriyas are different;
because the clans of Kāśyapa, Gautama, and others are different;
and because the stature and radiance of their bodies vary in magnitude.
The word "etc. refers to the fact that the dharmas abide whether the body is destroyed or not destroyed, and so forth.
Thus, there are distinctions based on their arising according to time.

If a wise person contemplates the three kinds of supreme perfections of the Buddhas, they will certainly be able to develop a heart of extreme affection and veneration toward the Buddha Bhagavān; namely, the perfection of the excellence of causes, the perfection of the excellence of results, and the perfection of the excellence of benefits.
Among these, the excellence of the causes for fulfillment is fourfold:
first, the repeated practice of all merit and wisdom; second, practice over a long period of time; third, uninterrupted practice; and fourth, practice performed with reverence.
The supreme qualities of the perfected fruit are fourfold:
first, the supreme quality of wisdom; second, the supreme quality of abandonment; third, the supreme quality of power; and fourth, the supreme quality of the form body.

The excellence of the fulfillment of kindness has four aspects: namely, the kindness of permanently liberating [beings] from the three evil realms and the cycle of birth and death, or establishing them in the good realms, as well as the kindness of the three vehicles.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of supreme qualities of wisdom:
first, untaught wisdom; second, all-encompassing wisdom; third, wisdom of all modes; and fourth, effortless wisdom.
The excellence of abandonment (*prahāṇa-viśeṣa*) also has four types:

first, the cessation of all obstacles to liberation; second, the cessation of all obstacles to meditative concentration; third, the cessation of all obstacles to omniscience; and fourth, eternal cessation.
The sovereign power of superior qualities also consists of four kinds:
first, the sovereign power of mastery over external objects regarding their emanation, transformation, fulfillment through aspiration, and their aggregation or dispersal;
second, the sovereign power of mastery over the relinquishing and assuming of the lifespan.
Third, the sovereign power of moving most swiftly and to the furthest reaches through obstructions and space, and the mastery of causing the many to enter into the few;
fourth, the sovereign power of the excellence of the marvelous qualities of various intrinsic natures.
Furthermore, there are four kinds of superior power and virtue:

first, the ability to transform those who are difficult to transform; second, the certainty of severing doubts when answering difficult questions; third, the establishment of a teaching that leads definitively to liberation; and fourth, the capacity to subdue evil Māras, non-Buddhists, and others.
The supreme qualities of the form body (*rūpakāya*) are fourfold:

first, the supreme quality of the major marks; second, the supreme quality of the minor marks; third, the supreme quality of the powers; and fourth, the supreme quality of the adamantine, true bone-body.
The supreme virtues of all Buddhas, if described in general, are as such; yet if one were to differentiate these supreme virtues according to their particulars, they would be limitless.

These supreme virtues can only be fully known and fully expounded by the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas themselves; even if the Tathāgatas were to sustain their life-span for countless *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they could only then exhaustively describe them.
Such Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are pools of great jewels consisting of boundless and marvelous qualities—the virtues of wisdom, the virtues of abandonment, and the virtues of grace.

Yet ordinary beings, due to their own poverty of virtue and the impairment of their faith and aspiration, fail to give rise to a mind of reverence toward the Buddha even when they have realized or heard of such perfect and supreme qualities; they act likewise toward the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.

If an intelligent person hears of these merits and gives rise to a heart of refuge that penetrates to the very marrow of their bones—and does likewise toward the Buddha’s True Dharma—then by means of this single-minded pure faith, they have already subdued the accumulation of evil karma with indeterminate retribution. Such a person will receive the auspicious and blissful rewards of the human and celestial realms, and ultimately attain the excellence of Parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, the appearance of the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, in the world serves as the unsurpassed field of merit for all sentient beings, because they are able to produce subsequent fruits that are non-empty, desirable, supreme, swift, and wholesome.
How is this known?
The Blessed One himself spoke a verse to clarify this meaning.
The verse says:
"If a person in a future age performs even a small amount of goodness toward the Buddha,
having been reborn among the devas, they will surely attain the state of deathlessness.
Having thus spoken of such unique qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) of the Buddhas, [he continued:]
The verse says:
There are other Buddha-dharmas shared with disciples and ordinary beings.
The commentary says:
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, possess merits that are shared with their disciples or shared with ordinary worldlings.
What are these merits?
They are as follows, in order.
The verse says:
The qualities of non-contention, the knowledge resulting from prayer, the analytical knowledges, and so forth.
The commentary says:

The various virtues consist of the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the concentrations of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-samādhi*), the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*).

Regarding the *araṇā-samādhi* herein: there are certain Arhat bhikṣus who, having already understood that the manifold sufferings of sentient beings arise from delusion, desire to become a supreme field of merit for others; they wish to suppress the arising of afflictions within themselves that are triggered by others, and thus they give rise to a cognition characterized in this way.
By means of this wisdom, others cannot give rise to any kind of dispute.
By means of this wisdom, no other person can, upon observing the practitioner, give rise to a mind of desire, a mind of hatred, or a mind of pride, and so forth.
Because of this correct practice, one will certainly not arouse any affliction that might arise in another person; therefore, it is called "non-contention" (araṇā).
What is the essential nature and characteristic of this samādhi?
The verse says:
"Conventional knowledge is non-contentious.
The commentary says:
This is the intrinsic nature of samādhi, namely conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*).
The verse says:
"The subsequent concentration."
The commentary states:

"The subsequent concentration" refers to the final stage of the fourth dhyāna. Although this concentration generally takes the fourth dhyāna as its basis, it is characterized by bliss and swift wisdom.
The verse says:
"Those of immovable nature.
The commentary says:
It arises only within the mental continuum of an Arhat of the "unbreakable" (akopya) type, and not in that of other Arhats. Why is this?
Because other Arhats, at times, are unable to prevent the arising of further disputes within their own mental continua.
The verse says:
"Born in the human realm.
The commentary says:
This meditative absorption is attained through cultivation while in the human realm, specifically within the three continents.
With what object does this absorption arise?
The verse says:
"Those not yet arisen, which are of the nature of desire-realm existence or its objects.
The commentary explains:

Future phenomena belonging to the desire realm, whether they are of the nature of existence (*bhava*) or its objects (*viṣaya*), serve as the objects of this meditative absorption; for one vows that the various afflictions of others shall not arise, and it is by means of this gateway that [the absorption] is produced.

For one who is not deluded regarding the categories [of existence], it is impossible to prevent the abandonment of the universal defilements (*sarvatraga-kleśa*), because they arise when their conditions are complete within their respective realms and stages.
As it is said regarding the "absence of contention" (*araṇā*), the verse states:
"The Knowledge of Vows (*praṇidhijñāna*) is likewise."
The commentary states:

This also has conventional knowledge as its nature; it takes the subsequent dhyāna as its stage; it arises in a continuous succession based on the unshakable dharma (avinipātadharman); and it is cultivated and attained within the human realm.
If that is so, what is the distinction?
The verse says:
It takes all objects as its cognitive domain.
The commentary states:
Because the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*) arises by taking all phenomena as its object, it differs from that [knowledge].
Phenomena belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) cannot be realized through the knowledge resulting from aspiration.
Nevertheless, it can be inferred from the distinctions among similar instances.
The Vaibhāṣikas say:
"In this context, the farmer serves as the analogy."
What is the dharma-gate of the knowledge resulting from aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*)?

It is when one desires to know various matters sought by oneself; for this purpose, one enters the fourth *samādhi* of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika*), making the aspiration: "May I certainly know this matter."
One knows this very matter as it truly is.
According to the power of the range—whether near or far—of that meditative concentration, one knows the near and the far in the same way.
The verse says:
Regarding the dharma, its meaning, and regional dialects, there is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

The commentary states: There are four kinds of analytical knowledges: first, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*); second, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*); third, the analytical knowledge of regional dialects (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*); and fourth, the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
These analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) should be understood as being like the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*). How so?
Just as it arises in dependence upon an unimpaired continuity of the Dharma, they are cultivated and attained within the human realm.
These two share the same objective sphere and stage as those [other analytical knowledges], yet they are said to differ from them due to differences in their intrinsic nature.
The verse says:
The first three are called by name and meaning; they are, in order, the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
The commentary states:

The non-reversing wisdom regarding the collections of names, phrases, and syllables, regarding meanings, and regarding languages is, respectively, to be understood as the analytical knowledges of phenomena (*dharma*), meaning (*artha*), and language (*nirukti*).
The verse says:
"In the fourth [dhyāna], one is liberated through principle and possesses mastery over the path of speech.
The commentary says:
The phrase "irreversible wisdom" continues [from the previous context].

Within the discourse on the middle way that is free from the faults of obscuration, and within the manifestation of mastery over meditative concentration and the path, this irreversible wisdom is termed the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
The verse says:
This has as its object the path and the truths.
The commentary says:
Correct teaching and the Path are the objective spheres of this knowledge.
The verse says:
Nine knowledges.
The commentary states:
This analytical knowledge (pratisaṃvid) has nine knowledges as its nature; that is, the analytical knowledge of eloquence regarding the path, excluding the knowledge of cessation.
The verse says:
"All stages" (sarvabhūmi).
The commentary explains:
This understanding arises based on all stages, from the desire realm up to the peak of existence (bhavāgra), because it takes as its object any one of the paths or the teachings regarding the path.
The verse says:
Ten, or six, meanings are explained.
The commentary says:
Regarding the analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*): if "meaning" refers to all phenomena (*sarva-dharma*), this knowledge has ten knowledges as its nature.

If "meaning" refers exclusively to *nirvāṇa*, it has only six knowledges as its nature, namely: the knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-jñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of cessation (*nirodha-jñāna*), the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), and conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*).
The verse says:
"The spheres of totality.
The commentary says:
This analytical knowledge of meaning arises based on all stages.
The verse says:
"The others are conventional knowledge."
The commentary states:

The remaining two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), namely those of phenomena (*dharma*) and language (*nirukti*), have conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛtijñāna*) as their nature, because they take names, phrases, and so forth—the linguistic expressions—as their objects.
The verse says:
"The factors of the desire realm are explained.
The commentary says:

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) comprises five stages, as it is subsumed within the desire realm and the four dhyānas; above these, there is no collection of names and so forth.
The verse says:
"Regarding speech, [it exists] in the desire realm and the first dhyāna."
The commentary states:

Regarding the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), it takes the desire realm and the first dhyāna as its basis, because there is no applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*) in the stages above.
In the *Prajñapti-śāstra*, the four analytical knowledges are analyzed as follows:

Regarding names, phrases, and syllables; regarding the meanings they signify; regarding the distinct explanations of those meanings—such as singular, dual, plural, number three, time, gender, and so forth; and regarding the absence of obstruction or error in such explanations—the non-reversible knowledge therein is called the analytical knowledges of dharma, meaning, and eloquence; therefore, these are attained in that successive order.
Dialectic (vāda) consists of explaining words based on principles, such as calling something "form" (rūpa) because it possesses resistance.
Eloquence (pratibhāna) refers to superior verbal expression regarding the establishment of positions and the refutation of others.
Other masters say:
These four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) correspond respectively to arithmetic, the words of the Buddha, phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), and the theory of causes and conditions (*hetu-vidyā*).
First is the dharma-gate of preparatory application. Why is this?
If a person has not cultivated clear and distinct preparatory application regarding the four bases, they cannot give rise to this understanding.
Other masters say:
Within the True Dharma of the Buddha Bhagavān, all those preparatory applications are fully perfected.
If a person attains one, that person necessarily possesses all four.
Why is this? The verse says:
"If not complete, it is not yet attained."
The commentary states:
If one has not attained those [qualities] in their full measure, it cannot be said that this person has attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Regarding the aforementioned qualities such as the absence of conflict (*araṇā*), the verse says:
"Six are obtained through the concentration of the ultimate limit (*prāntakoṭika-samādhi*).
The commentary explains:
Because these six are obtained by means of the power of the concentration of the ultimate limit, they are called "the concentrations of the ultimate limit."
The verse says:
These six.
The commentary says:

This fourth concentration is named "the Far-Reaching Limit" (dūramgamā), and its essence consists of six factors: namely, the concentration of non-contention (araṇā-samādhi), the knowledge resulting from resolve (praṇidhijñāna), the three analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid), and the concentration of the far-reaching limit itself.

Regarding the unimpeded analytical knowledge of languages (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), although it is obtained through the power of the "limit of the distant" (*dūre-anta*) concentration, it does not arise by taking the fourth dhyāna as its basis; therefore, it is not included here.
What dharma is called the "concentration of the limit of the distant" (*dūre-anta-samādhi*)?
The verse says:
The final concentration accords with all stages; this reaches the ultimate limit of increase.
The commentary says:
This concentration takes only the fourth dhyāna as its basis.
How, then, does it accord with all stages?

First, one enters the first dhyāna from a wholesome volitional mind of the desire realm; from the first dhyāna, one enters the second dhyāna; proceeding in this sequence, one eventually enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one practices in reverse order down to the mind of the desire realm.
Furthermore, from the mind of the desire realm, one again practices in forward order up to the fourth dhyāna.
Thus one cultivates in accordance with all stages.
How is it called "reaching the ultimate of increase"?
One cultivates the fourth dhyāna in this way: from the weak stage one cultivates the medium, and from the medium stage one cultivates the superior.

Each of these three stages is further divided into three, thus forming nine grades; the final grade is named "Ultimate Culmination of the Peak" (*yūṣmad-vardhana-paryanta*), and this concentration is thus called the "Concentration Reaching the Farthest Limit" (*dūraṅgama-samādhi*).
The term *koṭi* (limit) may signify differentiation, or it may signify the ultimate limit, as in the cases of the "four limits" (*catur-koṭi*) and the "limit of reality" (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Regarding these six qualities, the verse says:
"They belong to the Buddha alone; they are not acquired through practice."
The commentary states:
For all persons other than the Buddha, [these qualities] must be attained through cultivation and are not attained through the abandonment of desire.
Only for the World-Honored Buddha are there qualities that are not attained through cultivation; rather, all his qualities are attained through the abandonment of desire.

Why is this? Because the World-Honored One alone is the Dharma King who has attained mastery over all phenomena; therefore, all merits manifest before him in accordance with the Tathāgata’s intentions.
All such virtues as these are attained in common with disciples.
Furthermore, qualities such as the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are also attained in common with ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
What dharma is designated as "supernormal knowledge"?
The verse says:

The realization of the knowledge of the supernormal power of will, of supernormal powers, of the divine ear, of the mind, of past lives, and of death and rebirth—these six types are called the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
The commentary says:

The supernormal knowledge of the realization of the power of will, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the divine ear, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the distinction of others' minds, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of recollection of past lives, the supernormal knowledge of the realization of death and rebirth, and the supernormal knowledge of the realization of the exhaustion of the outflows—these six are called supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*).
Among these, the first five are attained in common with ordinary beings.
Regarding all six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the verse says:
"the knowledge of liberation."
The commentary states:
Its nature is the knowledge of the path of liberation, just like the fruits of śrāmaṇya.
The verse says:
Regarding these four conventional knowledges (*saṃvṛtijñāna*),
the commentary states:

with the exception of the supernormal knowledge of discerning the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*) and the supernormal knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñāna*), the remaining four all have conventional knowledge as their essential nature.
The verse says:
"The wisdom of others' minds consists of five knowledges.
The commentary says:

The supernormal knowledge of others' minds has five types of wisdom as its essence, namely: dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, path-knowledge, conventional knowledge, and knowledge of others' minds.
The verse says:
"The supernormal knowledge of exhaustion is like the [ten] powers."
The commentary states:

As previously explained regarding the power of knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*), it should be understood that this supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) is likewise; its essence consists of either six knowledges or ten knowledges.
Just as that [power] takes all stages (*bhūmi*) as its basis, it should be understood that this is also the case here.
The verse says:
"The other five are in the four dhyānas.
The commentary says:
The remaining five rely upon the stages of the four dhyānas as their basis.
Why do these not rely upon the stages of the formless attainments?
Because three of them involve the wisdom of thorough knowledge which takes form as its object; therefore, they cannot arise by relying on the stages of the formless attainments.
The supernormal knowledge of the discernment of others' minds arises through the gateway of form; therefore, it does not take the stages of the formless attainments as its support.

The supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives arises from the sequential order of maintaining the distinctions of states; therefore, it also does not take the stages of the formless attainments as its support, because it takes as its objects place, name, lineage, dwelling, and so forth.

If a person wishes to know the minds of others, they should first observe the two characteristics of body and mind within their own continuum, thinking: "The characteristic of my body is such, and the characteristic of my mind is such."

Just as one contemplates the characteristics of one's own body and mind, one likewise gives rise to such contemplation regarding the mental continuums of others; by means of this, one knows the minds of others, and thus supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) is produced.
If this supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) has been perfected, one knows the minds of others without observing physical forms (*rūpa*).

If a person wishes to recollect past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*), they first observe the successive stages of the cessation of their own consciousness; having thus reflected in reverse order upon the distinctions of the various states up to the mind at the moment of conception (*garbhāvakrānti*), they subsequently achieve this supernormal knowledge by recollecting a single moment of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Just as one recollects one's own past lives, so too does one recollect the past lives of others.
Once this supernormal power is perfected, one can also give rise to the recollection of past lives.
If a particular matter was previously experienced, that matter is what is recollected; otherwise, it is not.
If that is so, how is it that the same applies to the matters of others?
If that is so, how does one recollect the past lives in the five Śuddhāvāsa heavens?
It is because one has attained the ability to recollect them through having heard of them previously.

If a person falls from the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and is reborn in this realm, they can attain the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsābhijñā*) by relying on the mental continuum of another; the remaining types of such knowledge are attained by relying on one's own mental continuum.
The supernormal powers (abhijñā) such as the power of success at will (rddhi-vidhi-jñāna) have the observation of lightness, sound, and light as their preparatory applications (prayoga).
Furthermore, regarding these five supernormal powers, the verse says:
"They have as their objects the realms of their own level and lower levels."
The commentary states:

According to the level upon which it relies, the nature of the supernormal power of *ṛddhi* (psychic power) allows one to travel to that level and manifest various things such as transformed bodies; this applies to lower levels, but not to higher levels.
Thus, by means of the supernormal knowledge of the divine ear, one can hear sounds of one's own level and those of lower levels, but cannot hear sounds of higher levels.
By means of the supernormal knowledge of discerning the minds of others, one cannot know the minds of others belonging to higher levels.
By means of the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*), one cannot recollect the past lives of those in higher stages.
By means of the supernormal knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādābhijñā*), one cannot perceive the death and rebirth of those in higher stages.

Therefore, by relying on a mind belonging to the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), neither the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) nor the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives can apprehend [objects], because they belong to the higher stages.
How are these various supernormal knowledges (abhijñā) attained?
If they have not been attained before, they are all acquired through practice.
The verse says:
"Once fully detached from, one attains them.
The commentary states:
These five supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), if they were practiced repeatedly in other lifetimes, are attained through detachment from desire (vairāgya).
If they are distinct and superior, they are obtained through cultivation; all [of these] arise through cultivation.
The verse says:
The third consists of the three foundations of mindfulness.
The commentary states:

The supernormal knowledge of discerning the minds of others is subsumed under three applications of mindfulness—namely, the applications of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena—because its objects of focus are the mind and mental factors.
The verse says:
"The ear and eye of the mind-made [body] are primary.
The commentary says:

The supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of the divine ear and divine eye are subsumed under the first foundation of mindfulness, namely the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), because they take form (*rūpa*) as their object.
The supernormal knowledge of the power of transformation (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*) takes the four external sense bases (*āyatana*)—excluding sound—as its object.
The supernormal wisdoms of the divine ear and the divine eye take sound and form as their respective objects.
If this is so, how can the supernormal wisdom of knowledge of death and rebirth know things in this way?
As the Sūtra says:

Those sentient beings, being associated with misconduct of body, speech, and mind, reviling the noble ones and giving rise to wrong views, and because they have accepted the dharma and karma of wrong views, upon the relinquishing of this body and life, they will inevitably undergo birth in the non-conducive evil realms, falling into the dark places of defeat.
The remainder is explained at length as in the Sūtra.

It cannot be known by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); rather, there is a distinct knowledge that is a concomitant of the supernormal wisdom of the divine eye, which arises within the continuum of an Ārya and is able to know such things.
Because it is not determinate, it follows as a matter of course that the remaining supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) have the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) as their nature.
The verse says:
The divine ear and eye are neutral (*avyākṛta*); all other supernormal knowledges are wholesome (*kuśala*).
The commentary states:

The supernormal wisdoms of the divine ear and the divine eye are indeterminate (avyākṛta) in nature; these supernormal wisdoms have as their essence the cognitions associated with the auditory consciousness and the visual consciousness.
If that is so, how can these two be established when they take the four dhyāna stages as their basis?
They do not contradict [the rule], because they are designated as belonging to those stages according to the stage upon which they depend.

The eye and ear faculties are the supports for this consciousness, which takes the four dhyānas as its stage; furthermore, those stages are established according to the uninterrupted paths (*ānantarya-mārga*).
The remaining four [faculties] are all of a wholesome nature.
If that is so, how is it stated in the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*:
"What is supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*)?
It is wholesome wisdom (*kuśalā prajñā*)."
This text is spoken either from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) or from the perspective of multiple meanings.
Regarding the six supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), the verse says:
"The three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*) are attained."
The commentary states:

The supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*), of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda*), and of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*)—these three are said to be the attainment of the "lights" (*vidyā*) of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Why are only these three called the attainment of the lights, while the others are not?
The verse says:
“Regarding the prior limit, it is the antidote to ignorance and so forth.
The commentary says:
Because these three can successively eliminate the ignorance regarding the past, the future, and the middle [present], only these three are designated as "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*).
Among these three, that which is truly without further training (*aśaikṣa*) is stated in the verse:
"The last is without training."
The commentary states:
The knowledge that realizes the exhaustion of the outflows (āsravakṣaya-jñāna) is necessarily that of one beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The verse says:
Second, they are called "arising in that same continuum.
The commentary states:

Because the remaining two types of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) arise within the continuum of one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they are designated as "beyond training"; however, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is neither that of one in training (*śaikṣa*) nor that of one beyond training.
If that is so, why do you not admit that these two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) are called "of one in training" (*śaikṣa*)?
The verse says:
Because ignorance (*avidyā*) continues to exist, they are not said to belong to those in training.
The commentary states:
Because the Buddha did not declare these two supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) to be factors of one in training (*śaikṣadharma*).
How did he not so declare them?
If ignorance (avidyā) persists within the continuum, it would be unreasonable for the attainment of clarity (vidyā) to be established therein, because it would still be suppressed by ignorance.
Regarding the six supernormal knowledges (abhijñā), the verse says:
"One, three, and six are guides."
The commentary states:

The supernormal power of psychic transformation (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna*), the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracitta-vijñāna*), and the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-abhijñā*)—these three, in their respective order, constitute the three guides (*nirdeśa*). Namely, the guide of psychic transformation, the guide of reading minds, and the guide of correct instruction. These three are each called "guides" because, from the very beginning, they are most capable of attracting those whose minds are to be converted.

There are minds that are obstructed by increase, minds lacking faith, and minds unwilling to practice; because those beings to be converted give rise to a mind of devotion, a mind of faithful acceptance, and a mind of practice due to these three [teachings], these three are said to be the guides.
The verse says:
Among the three, the authentic teaching is supreme.
The commentary says:
Among the three types of guidance, correct instruction is the most excellent. Why is this?
The verse says:
Because they are not indeterminate and because they produce wholesome and desirable fruits.
The commentary states:
The guidance of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*) and the guidance of reading minds (*ādeśanā-vidhi*) can be performed through clear knowledge (*vidyā*).
There is a field of knowledge called *gāndhārī*; by reciting this mantra, one is able to fly through the air.
Furthermore, there is a field of knowledge called *aikṣaṇikā*; mastery of this field of knowledge enables one to know the minds of others.
The authentic, correct teaching cannot be produced by any other expedient means.
Because it is not indeterminate, it is superior to the previous two.
While the guidance of the former two can only turn back the accomplishment of worldly affairs;
Through correct instruction, it is able to produce both virtuous fruits and desirable fruits; because it can thereby manifest the correct means, it is superior to the previous two.
The supernormal power of success (ṛddhi) has already been explained; what is this phenomenon?
According to the principles of the *Vibhāṣā*, the verse says:
it is the meditative concentration of success (ṛddhi-samādhi).
The commentary states:
Because those matters are accomplished according to one's will, the meditative concentration is named "the accomplishment of what is wished for" (*ṛddhi*).
By what means are they accomplished?
This matter should be explained.
The verse says:
In the intermediate state, one practices emptiness and undergoes miraculous birth.
The commentary states:
Within this, there are three types of movement through emptiness: first, movement by leading the body; second, movement by the power of aspiration; and third, movement with the speed of mind.
Regarding this, the verse says:
"The mind travels swiftly; only the Buddha [possesses such movement].
The commentary states:
This movement is as rapid as the mind; only the World-Honored One, the Buddha, possesses such movement, while others do not.
Because one reaches even the most distant place by generating a single moment of focused mind,
the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"The realm of the Buddhas is inconceivable."
The remaining two are not [attained] because they are established as being attained through the Buddha.
The verse says:
"The others are accomplished through mastery over the body and vows."
The commentary states:
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas possess a mode of bodily movement that draws the body along in succession, like a bird drawing its body along step by step.
For those who have accomplished their vows, even the most distant places are made as if nearest through the power of their resolve; it is by this means that they travel swiftly.
There are two types of transformation-born (upapāduka) success (ṛddhi):
first, that associated with the desire realm; second, that associated with the form realm.
Regarding this, the verse says:
Regarding the external sense bases (*bāhyāyatana*) manifested in the desire realm, they consist of four sense bases and are of two types.
The commentary states:

Those born by transformation (*upapāduka*) in the desire realm have the sense bases of visible form, odor, taste, and tangibility as their substance; these are of two kinds: either corresponding to one's own body or corresponding to another's body.
The verse says:
"Form is twofold.
The commentary says:

The transformation-born beings associated with the realm of form (rūpadhātu) have only two bases (āyatana) as their substance, namely the base of form (rūpāyatana) and the base of tangibles (spraṣṭavyāyatana), because fragrance and taste do not exist there.
These are also of two types, as previously described.

Just as there are four types of beings born by transformation (*upapāduka*) in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), so it is in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); therefore, briefly stated, there are eight types of beings born by transformation.

If a person born in the form realm transforms and produces objects of the desire realm, why do those objects not reach [the senses] and thus fail to provide the attainment of odors (*gandha*) and tastes (*rasa*)?
For example, just as garments and ornaments have no [inherent] attainment (*prāpti*), so too it is with the beings produced by transformation.
Other masters say:
"The beings produced therein consist of only two bases (*āyatana*)."
Is it that one produces various objects through the supernormal power of miraculous transformation (*nirmāṇa-abhijñā*), or is it not so? It is not. Why is this?
Regarding the fruit of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-phala*): what dharma is this?
The verse says:
By means of the transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*), this mind consists of fourteen types.
The commentary states:
there are fruits of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñāphala*) which are transformative minds capable of producing all manner of created objects.
This mind has fourteen [types].
The verse says:
As the fruits of the successive meditative attainments (dhyāna), they range from two to five.
The commentary states:

There are two types of minds that are the fruits of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) belonging to the first dhyāna stage: first, those of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and second, those of the first dhyāna stage.

There are three types of minds that are the fruits of supernormal knowledge belonging to the second dhyāna stage: namely, those of the desire realm, the first dhyāna, and the second dhyāna stages; it is thus for each [subsequent stage].
Regarding the minds that are the fruits of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā*) in the third and fourth dhyāna stages, one should understand that there are four or five types.
One should know that these transformation-minds (*nirmāṇacitta*) are the fruits of those meditative concentrations and belong to their own stage as well as lower stages.
The verse says:
Not above.
The commentary says:
There is no transformation mind of a higher stage that serves as the fruit of a lower stage concentration.
Regarding the transformation mind of the desire realm that is the fruit of the second dhyāna, it originates from the first dhyāna stage; its fruit is superior by virtue of the path.
The verse says:
"Attainment is like meditative absorption.
The commentary says:
This transformative mind (nirmāṇacitta) is acquired in the same manner as the acquisition of meditative absorption (samādhi).
Is it the case that one emerges from contemplation immediately upon the arising of this transformative mind, or not?
There is no such principle.
Therefore, this meaning is stated.
The verse says:
"Pure concentration arises spontaneously; two [types] arise from it."
The commentary states:

From a pure meditative concentration (*śuddha-samādhi*), the supernormal power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-abhijñā*) arises in succession; from the supernormal power of transformation, the mind that produces transformations (*nirmāṇa-phala-citta*) arises in succession; and from the mind that produces transformations, immeasurable minds that produce transformations arise, but they do not arise from any other type of mind.

Next, from the mind that is the fruit of transformation, the supernormal power of transformation arises; from the supernormal power of transformation, pure concentration arises, or the mind that is the fruit of transformation arises. Why is this?

If a person abides in the fruit of concentration and does not re-enter the fundamental concentration, there is no principle by which they could emerge from contemplation directly from that fruit of concentration.
Regarding all created objects, the verse says:
"They arise through transformation from their own stage."
The commentary states:
According to the level of the beings to be transformed, the level of the mind that performs the transformation is the same as theirs. Why is this?
A transformation-mind (*nirmāṇa-citta*) belonging to one stage cannot produce objects belonging to another stage.
As the verse says:
"Speech [is produced] by means of [a mind] from another stage."
The commentary states:
Speech can also be produced by means of a mind belonging to the same level (*bhūmi*).
If the person to be converted resides in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) or the first dhyāna level, speech may be induced by means of a mind belonging to that same level.

If the person being transformed resides in a higher stage, they can only engage in speech by means of a mind belonging to the first dhyāna, because in the higher stages there is no mind that initiates informative action (*vijñapti-karman*).
If one causes many persons being transformed to speak, do they speak simultaneously or not?
The verse says:
"The emanator is not the Buddha.
The commentary explains:
Apart from those emanated by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, all other emanated persons speak in the same manner as their emanator.
If the emanator speaks, he does so together with many emanated persons.
As the verse says:
"When one person speaks correctly, all those who are manifested speak together;
if one person remains silent, all those who are manifested do likewise."

"Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, may act according to his will, whether placing himself first or last; among those he transforms, either they question the Buddha and he answers, or the Buddha questions them and they answer."

At that time, if a mind of speech arises, at that very moment there would be no mind of transformation; thus, there would be nothing to be transformed. How, then, could one transform a person so that the transformed being speaks?
The verse says:
Having established the vow, one acts separately.
The commentary says:

Because he desires that those to be converted remain for a long time, he first forms the aspiration for emanation and then enters meditative absorption; subsequently, by means of a distinct mind, he initiates informative action (*vijñapti-karman*), thereby causing them to possess speech as well.
"Does that which one desires for the sake of life all succeed according to one's wish, or does it also succeed after death?
The verse says:
"The success of one's wishes occurs even after death."
The commentary states:

Because of the power of the vow made by the noble and great Kāśyapa, his skeletal body remains undecayed; thus, one knows that even after death, the matters of one's vows can likewise be accomplished.
The verse says:
"It is not non-existent; other things are said to be non-existent.
The commentary says:

If a thing is not solid and its continuity does not endure, one's aspiration regarding it will not be fulfilled; for this reason, the noble Mahākāśyapa did not aspire to leave behind his physical parts, such as skin and flesh.
Other masters say:
"If a person has already died, there can be no further aspiration.
If that were so, how could the skeletal remains of the noble Mahākāśyapa persist?
It remains because it is sustained by the power and protection of the Great Virtuous Disciples and the various devas.
Is one object produced from a single mind, or is one object produced from multiple minds?
The verse says:
"The first [type] arises from many minds; once established, it possesses the capacity to reverse this.
The commentary says:
When first practicing, one must give rise to multiple transformative minds (*nirmāṇa-citta*) for each object to be transformed before the act of transformation is accomplished.
Once the supernormal power of transformation has been perfected, however, one can transform many objects with a single transformative mind, according to the extent of what one wishes to manifest.
Are all minds of transformation (nirmāṇa-citta) indeterminate (avyākṛta)?
The verse says:
Those acquired through cultivation are indeterminate.
The commentary states:
If the mind of transformation is the fruit obtained through cultivation, it is necessarily indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
The verse says:
If there are three types obtained by birth.
The commentary states:
If the mind of transformation is obtained by birth, then it may be wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.

This refers to that produced by the mind of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*) acquired at birth by devas, nāgas, spirits, and so forth—whether manifesting as a transformation within one's own body or as a transformation within another's body. It has the nine bases (*āyatana*) as its nature; it possesses the base of form (*rūpāyatana*), excluding sound, because it does not arise independently of the sense faculties, just like the *kīṭikā* insect or the *iṣikā* grass.
There are two kinds of the attainment of mastery (vaśitā): first, that acquired through cultivation; second, that acquired at birth.
These, in turn, are of two kinds.
The verse says:
"Mentally produced, produced by spells and medicines, and produced by karma—thus there are five kinds.
The commentary explains:
To speak briefly, there are five types of beings produced by mind (manomaya): [those produced by mind, by spells, by medicines, by karma, and those born from eggs].

First, that produced as a fruit of cultivation; second, that acquired at birth; third, that accomplished through mantras; fourth, that accomplished through medicinal substances; and fifth, that accomplished through karma.
Regarding that accomplished through karma, examples include King Māndhātṛ and other such beings, as well as sentient beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Regarding the divine ear and divine eye that have been described: are these called "divine" because they belong to the same category as the gods, or are they called "divine" because they are like those of the gods?
This point should be considered:
if the divine ear and divine eye refer to those of Bodhisattvas, Cakravartins, and the Great Treasures (ratna), then if these ears and eyes belonged to the same category as the gods, the verse says:
The divine ear and the divine eye are pure matter belonging to the stage of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bhūmi*).
The commentary states:
This is because when a person enters the four dhyānas, they take sound and light as their objects and cultivate preparatory practices (*prayoga*) as the means.

Based on the stages of the four dhyānas, the four great elements are of two kinds; from them arise pure forms that extend to the edges of the ears and eyes, serving as the supports for hearing sounds and seeing forms. Because they are produced by relying on the stages of meditative concentration, these ears and eyes belong to the celestial category.
Furthermore, regarding these two, the verse says:
"Because they are equal, complete, and constant, their objects are distant, subtle, and so forth.
The commentary explains:
The divine ear and divine eye are never non-homogeneous (aprakṛtastha), because they are always associated with consciousness.
They are never deficient in their faculties, as they are free from defects such as blindness or confusion.
For example, for beings in the form realm, all forms and sounds—whether superior, subtle, obstructed, or distant—are within their sensory range.
Regarding the fleshly eye, as stated in the verse:
"Distant, obstructed, or subtle forms, as well as colors in all directions, are not seen by the fleshly eye;
it sees only those forms directly before it. The divine eye, however, is the reverse of this."
If one sees forms with the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), how far are the forms seen?
They are near or far according to the person and the eye; the forms seen are likewise near or far.

Whether it be a Śrāvaka, a Pratyekabuddha, or the Buddha, the World-Honored One, if they do not apply deliberate effort (*manasikāra*), they are able to see one thousand, two thousand, or three thousand world-systems (*lokadhātu*) as they wish.
If one applies effort with the desire to see [the Buddhas], the verse says:
"Two thousand, three thousand, and countless [Buddhas]—the Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas.
The commentary says:
If a great śrāvaka, desiring to see with the divine eye, applies great effort of mind, he can see a medium two-thousandfold world system.
If a rhinoceros-horn-like pratyekabuddha, desiring to see with the divine eye, applies great effort of mind, he can see a great three-thousandfold world system.
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wishes to see with his divine eye, he can see incalculable worlds (*asaṃkhyeya-loka-dhātu*), according to his desire to see. Why is this?
Just as wisdom functions with respect to phenomena (*dharma*), so too does the divine eye function with respect to forms (*rūpa*).
Is it only the supernormal power of success (ṛddhi) that is acquired by birth, or are others also acquired by birth?
The verse says:
Others are also acquired by birth.
The commentary states:
The four [supernormal powers], such as the divine eye, are also obtained by birth.
However, whatever is obtained merely through birth cannot be designated as "supernormal knowledge" (abhijñā).
The verse says:
"The eye; the intermediate state is not its object.
The commentary says:
This refers to one who has acquired the divine eye through birth, yet cannot see the forms of beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Why is this?
Such forms are visible only to the eye of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-cakṣus*), not to the divine eye acquired at birth, except for those of the same kind.
The verse says:
The knowledge of others' minds is threefold.
The commentary says:
The term "innate" (upapatti-lābhika) continues to apply here.
If it is innate, one should know that it is of three kinds: namely, wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate.
The verse says:
Regarding "produced by the power of vidyā-mantras," the commentary explains:

Not only are there three types of knowledge acquired at birth, but there is also the knowledge of others' minds obtained by those who study the *Icchanika-śāstra* and are able to discern physical characteristics; this is accomplished through the analytical reflection of thought, or it is produced by the power of vidyā-mantras.
This should be understood as being of three kinds—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—and is not exclusively wholesome like that which is acquired through cultivation.
Regarding the knowledge of others' minds and the knowledge of past lives acquired by birth, the verse says:
"In hell, one can know for the first time."
The commentary states:

From the moment beings in the hells first take birth until they are as yet not oppressed by painful sensations, they are able to discern the minds of others and to recollect their past lives within that interval.
If one is born and abides in another realm, one always knows [this] by means of these two.
The verse says:
Among humans, it is not acquired at birth.
The commentary states:
Only among human beings, as previously described, are the five [attainments] such as *ṛddhi* (supernatural power) acquired through non-arising (*anutpāda*).
If that is so, how can there be those who possess the natural recollection of past lives?
This arises from the distinctions made by karma. Why is this so?

For in that regard, there are also three kinds of knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*): that which is obtained through cultivation, that which is obtained by birth, and that which is produced by karma.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty;
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty-one.
Composed by Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha from Central India.

Chapter Eight: The Analysis of Samāpatti. Having already analyzed and explained the various categories of merit that depend upon wisdom—namely, those belonging to the class of wisdom—I shall now analyze and explain the merits belonging to distinct classes.
Therefore, one should first provide a detailed explanation based on the meditative concentrations (dhyāna), because all virtuous qualities depend upon them.
The verse says:
"The four concentrations are of two kinds."
The commentary states:

Briefly stated, there are two types of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), distinguished by the categories of concentration acquired through birth (*upapatti-lābhika*) and concentration acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-lābhika*).
Furthermore, this concentration consists of only four types, namely: the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
Among these, the meditative attainments acquired at birth need not be discussed further here.
In the "Chapter on the Analysis of the World," the verse states:
"The meditative attainments acquired at birth have already been explained."
The commentary says: How is this explained?
Each dhyāna is fixed to three stages; there are eight stages across the four dhyānas.
Since it must necessarily be stated that one who cultivates meditative concentration (samādhi) attains it, these words are spoken.
The verse says:
"Cultivating concentration is a single category of the wholesome."
The commentary states:
If there is no conceptual differentiation, the mind alone being of a single, virtuous type is called concentration (*samādhi*), because it is the nature of meditative absorption (*samāpatti*).
The verse says:
"Accompanied by the five aggregates as its associates.
The commentary explains:
If one analyzes the various meditative absorptions along with their accompanying and associated factors, one should know that their nature consists of the five aggregates.
What dharma is called "one-pointedness"?
It refers to one object and so forth.

If that were the case, then only the mind being one-pointed would constitute concentration (*samādhi*), rather than a distinct category of mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) constituting concentration.
It is not said that all minds are concentration; rather, because those factors cause all minds to become of one kind, those factors are called concentration.
Those factors are termed "one-kind. Is it not so?
Because all states of mind perish moment by moment, they are all of one category.
If you argue that the second moment of mind is of one category because it does not scatter from this same object, [we reply:]...

This interpretation is incorrect; within associated mental states (*samprayukta-dharma*), the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*) would then be rendered useless. Since this [state] is indeed samādhi, all minds must therefore share a single object of focus.
Why do you not accept this principle?

If you say that all minds become of one category because they share the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*), then it would follow that all minds must be established as being of one category; this too constitutes a logical fallacy.
This interpretation is not correct, because the power of this concentration is weak.
The Sautrāntika masters say:
"It is called concentration because this mind is of a single type."
Why is this? Samādhi refers to training based on the mind; with the purification of the mind as its excellence, it is termed the "four dhyānas" in the sūtras.
Other masters say:
This kind of concentration is called *dhyāna*.
What is the meaning of *dhyāna*?
It is called *dhyāna* because by means of it, one knows and sees.
Why is this? If the mind attains concentration, one is then able to know and see things as they truly are.
This is defined by the meaning of "deliberation" (cintā); "deliberation" (cintā) is precisely *prajñā*.
This is the teaching of this *siddhānta*.
If that were so, all forms of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) should be called *dhyāna*, because they are all of a nature capable of bringing about knowledge and vision according to reality.
This interpretation is not correct, because that name is established based on its association with a superior category; for example, light is named after its function.
With which superior category of phenomena is it associated?
If a meditative concentration is associated with its constituent parts, this concentration is then associated with superior qualities.
Why is this? Because it arises simultaneously with both śamatha and vipaśyanā, it is described as a dwelling in happiness in the present life and as a practice that is pleasant whether slow or swift.
Because it involves the most clear and distinct deliberation, it is therefore of a superior category.
If a single type of wholesome state is called *dhyāna*, how can that which is defiled also be called *dhyāna*?
Because of wrong reflection (*mithyā-manasikāra*), if that were so, there would be the fault of a great error.

This meaning is not [correct], because in the case of what is similar, it is merely established as a name; for example, like a rotten seed. Therefore, the Blessed Buddha also spoke of unwholesome dharmas (*akuśala-dharma*) as being *dhyāna*.
Furthermore, regarding this category of wholesome [states], what characteristics define the first dhyāna?
And so on, up to: what characteristics define the fourth dhyāna?
The verse says:
“There is applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*).
The commentary explains:
that which is wholesome, of a single type, and associated with applied thought, sustained thought, joy, and bliss is called the first dhyāna.
By the mention of "observation" (*vitarka*), "investigation" (*vicāra*) is also thereby mentioned, because they function in association like fire and smoke.
Since there is no state of non-separation [between them], there is no observation that is separated from joy and bliss.
Regarding the remaining three meditative attainments, the verse says:
"The lower levels are abandoned by each preceding one.
The commentary explains:
The term "a single class" (ekajātīya) applies here as well.
That which is free from applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), yet possesses only joy (*prīti*) and bliss (*sukha*), is the second dhyāna.
That which is free from applied thought, sustained thought, and joy, yet possesses only bliss, is the third dhyāna.
The fourth dhyāna is that which is free from applied thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and bliss (*sukha*), and consists solely of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
As it was said regarding the four dhyānas, the verse states:
"The same applies to the formless [attainments]."
The commentary states:
How many kinds of formless realms are there?
Their meaning is the same as that of the meditative absorptions.
That [attainment] is also of two kinds, because it is acquired through cultivation (*bhāvanā-labdha*) or acquired by birth (*upapatti-labdha*).
It is also of four kinds, due to the reduction of the perception of form (*saṃjñā-hrāsa*).
Its acquisition by birth has already been explained previously; that is to say, there is no specific location within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Birth is of four kinds: the acquisition of the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) and life-force (*jīvita*). Based upon these, the mental continuum proceeds; through cultivation, one attains the formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
If not further differentiated, they are simply of the nature of a single category of wholesome states.
By this principle, the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are the same as the four dhyānas.
The verse says:
"The four aggregates."
The commentary states:

If one analyzes the various meditative absorptions along with their accompanying and associated factors, they should be understood as having the four aggregates (*skandha*) as their nature, because there is no accompanying form (*rūpa*).
The verse says:
"Tranquility arises from detachment from the lower stages.
The commentary explains:

the sphere of infinite space arises from detachment from the fourth dhyāna; the sphere of infinite consciousness arises from detachment from the sphere of infinite space; the sphere of nothingness arises from detachment from the sphere of infinite consciousness; and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception arises from detachment from the sphere of nothingness.
For this reason, the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti) are established as four.
What dharma is called "tranquility" (śānta-viveka)?

Because one is liberated from other stages by means of this path, this path is termed "tranquility"; for through it, that meditative absorption (samādhi) attains the state of being free from desire (vairāgya).
Regarding these four formless absorptions (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), the verse says:
"The suppression of the perception of form is called the three types of preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*).
The commentary explains:

Because the preparatory concentration (*sāmantaka*) of the sphere of infinite space takes the fourth dhyāna as its object, it has not yet attained the name "subduing the perception of form" (*rūpasaṃjñā*).
Why is this? Because within that state, the subduing of the perception of form is not yet complete; it has not yet been extinguished or abandoned.
As previously stated, that the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) consists of only four aggregates (*skandha*) is not established;
it is said that there is no form (*rūpa*) in the formless realm.
If there were form in the formless realm, how could it be called the "formless realm"?
Because the form is subtle, it is like Abhigraha grasping all the forms that exist.
What are its characteristics?
It is simply the form consisting of the protection of body and speech.
Since body and speech do not exist, how could there be the matter that constitutes the protection of body and speech?
If the four great elements do not exist, it is illogical to claim that there is matter derived from the four great elements.
If you say: "It is like the untainted restraint (anāsrava-saṃvara)," this argument is not tenable,
because the four great elements (mahābhūta) are tainted (sāsrava).
In the explanation of those meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), there is even a denial, namely the statement that "there is no perception of form" (*arūpa-saṃjñā*) and so forth.
If they possess a body, they must necessarily possess material sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*); how, then, can it be admitted that they possess subtle matter?
If you maintain that they are called "formless" because their bodily dimensions are extremely subtle, then water-insects, whose forms are invisible, should also be considered formless.

If you maintain that they are called "formless" because their form is extremely pure, then the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) should likewise be established as formless.

If you maintain that they are called "formless" (ārūpya) because they lack a pure form superior to that [of the form realm], then only the Peak of Existence (bhavāgra) would constitute the formless realm, while the others should not; why is this?
Just as with the cultivation of samāpatti, so too is the differentiation of the arising of samāpatti.
The matter produced by that meditative absorption is not apprehended by the faculties of lower stages.
What is the distinction between them?
If you say that the names of the first two realms are established according to their meaning, while the name of the third realm is not established according to its meaning,
what principle serves as proof for this?
Because it is taught that life-force (*āyus*) is associated with heat (*uṣman*) and tactile contact (*sparśa*), they are like two bundles of reeds supporting one another.

Likewise, because name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are taught to be mutually dependent, within the twelvefold dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), it is said that name-and-form arises depending on consciousness, and consciousness arises depending on name-and-form.

Furthermore, there is another proof: because one denies the coming and going of consciousness even when separated from form up to mental formations (*saṃskāra*), it follows that the existence of form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is established.
This interpretation is not correct, for it must be further deliberated upon.

This matter certainly requires joint reflection: when explaining the meaning of the association between life-force (*āyus*) and warmth (*uṣman*), does this statement refer specifically to the life-force of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), or does it refer to all forms of life-force?

Regarding the statement that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are mutually dependent: is this said with reference to the consciousness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), or is it said with reference to all consciousness?

When it is stated that name-and-form arises dependent on consciousness, and that consciousness arises dependent on name-and-form, does this mean that all consciousness takes name-and-form as its support, and all name-and-form takes consciousness as its support?
Is it not the case that all [of them] are thus?

In this context, when it is said that one denies the coming and going of consciousness by means of excluding form and so forth, does this mean denying the coming and going of consciousness by excluding *all* form and so forth, or by excluding *any one* of them?

If you say: "Because the Buddha does not engage in conceptual discrimination, it cannot be conceptually discriminated or deliberated upon by oneself"—this argument is incorrect, for it entails the fault of a great logical error;
namely, that external warmth would then logically fail to be inseparable from life-force (*jīvitendriya*).
Furthermore, external matter should depend upon name, because it is taught without making such distinctions.

Since the Buddha taught the four stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*) and the four nutriments (*āhāra*), there would have to be edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*) and the station of consciousness consisting of matter (*rūpavijñānasthiti*) within the form and formless realms.
If you say: "It refers to those gods who subsist on morsel food and those gods who subsist on joy;
because of this statement, there is no fault of a major error."
The same should apply to the formless realms (*ārūpya*); one should not establish them as having form, because the Buddha stated that the formless is the transcendence of all form.
As the Sūtra says:
"This is the peaceful liberation; transcending all form, it is the formless."
Furthermore, some say that there are sentient beings who are formless.
Others say that because one has transcended all perceptions of form and perceptions of resistance, it is known that there is no form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
Why is this? If that [formless realm] truly possessed form, it would necessarily give rise to the conceptualization of its own form.
If you maintain that it is called "formless" because one contemplates the coarse form of the lower stages, [then the following applies].
This argument is not tenable. Why?

Because this same principle should apply to edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*): since the four dhyānas involve transcendence from the lower stages, the formless realm (*ārūpya*) should likewise be established therein.
Why is it not said that those [formless attainments] are the transcendence of feeling and so forth?
Because they are the transcendence of feeling and so forth belonging to the lower stages.

Since they have transcended every category of form, yet have not transcended every category of feeling and so forth, it is therefore said that they are merely the transcendence of form, and not of feeling and so forth.

Regarding the statement that "existence does not lead to the transcendence of existence": because existence cannot bring about the transcendence of existence, one is unable to transcend all forms of existence and achieve permanent liberation from existence.

Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, stated regarding the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*): "In the formless concentrations, there may be categories of feeling up to categories of consciousness.
He likewise stated regarding the form concentrations (*rūpa-samādhi*): "In the form concentrations, there may be categories of form up to categories of consciousness."
If there were any category of form within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), why would one not say "if there is a category of form"?
Therefore, the verse states:
"In the formless [realm], there is certainly no form."
The commentary states:
By these two proofs, one should know that there is definitely no form in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
To say that there is form there is a false statement, for it contradicts reason.
If that is so, since the continuity of form has been severed for immeasurable eons within those realms, how can form arise again when one subsequently falls back from there?
The verse says:
Form arises again from the mind.
The commentary states:
Form arises again from the mind.
Because it has been perfumed by the causes for the retribution of form in the past, this mind possesses the capacity to produce the present form.
If it does not rely upon form, how could the mind arise?
And how could it not arise?
For this has never been observed to occur.
If that were so, birth in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) would not be possible apart from edible food (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). Why?
Because such a thing has never been observed to occur there.
This has already been explained previously: this basis causes that mental continuum to arise.
Having explained this point, the following meaning shall now be discussed.
Is it because the sphere of infinite space and so forth necessarily take space and so forth as their objects that they are designated by those names, or is it not so?
It is not [the case that they do not]. Why is this?
Regarding the first three, the verse says:

"Infinite Space, Infinite Consciousness, and Nothingness; these names are established by way of their preparatory application (*prayoga*). The commentary explains: [These names are designated based on the specific meditative focus cultivated during the preliminary stages.]
Infinite space, infinite consciousness, and nothingness— by forming such reflections,
one attains the cultivation of meditative practice through this preparatory application.
Therefore, these three names are obtained by him in successive order.
The verse says:
"Because it is obscure, it is neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
The commentary says:
Because their perception is subtle and faint, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception. Why is this?
Their perception is not clear, yet it is not entirely without perception.

If one cultivates such contemplative practice therein, perceiving that perception itself is a disease, perception itself is an abscess, and perception itself is a thorn, while non-perception is delusion and darkness; [one perceives] that this is tranquility, this is sublime—namely, the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Nevertheless, the name is not established on the basis of this preparatory application (*prayoga*). Why?
Because they maintain that such a mode of contemplation must be explained as having subtle characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-sūkṣmatvāt*).
This meaning has already been explained previously.
