or through the power of karma, namely because the fruit of maturation of a karma belonging to a higher realm is about to manifest as a subsequent retribution (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*).
Why is this? If a person does not produce desire for the lower realm, they cannot attain birth in the higher realm.
As the verse says:
Regarding the meditative attainments of form within the realm of form, they are acquired through two types of natural law (*dharmatā*).
The commentary states:

Among those born in the realm of form, the attainment of specific meditative concentrations necessarily depends on two powers—namely, the power of causes and the power of karma—or alternatively, the power of natural law.

When the world is about to be destroyed, all sentient beings descend from their respective levels and are born into the four dhyānas of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because at that time wholesome dharmas arise most perfectly and abundantly.
"How much longer shall this True Dharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, remain?
Within it, such various categories of dharmas as these shall be clearly understood, known, and perceived."
The verse says:
"The Blessed One’s True Dharma is twofold; its essence consists of teaching, cultivation, and realization.
The commentary explains:
Among these, "right teaching" (*saddharma*) refers to the various *Āgamas*, namely the *Sūtra*, *Vinaya*, and *Abhidharma*.

"Attained through right practice" (*samyak-pratipatti-labdha*) refers to *adhigama* (realization); this consists of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) practiced by those of the three vehicles, as well as the fruits of the three vehicles.
Thus are the two kinds of True Dharma named.
How many persons are there herein?
The verse says:
"Among them, there are those who can uphold, those who can explain, and those who can practice.
The commentary states:
Regarding the *Āgamas*, there are two types of persons: first, those who can correctly uphold [the teachings], and second, those who can correctly explain them.
Regarding the stage of "attainment" (adhigama), there is only one type of person: namely, one who is able to practice correctly and attain [the fruit].
As long as these three types of persons continue to abide in succession, the True Dharma likewise continues to abide for that duration.
Why is this? There are two causes and conditions that enable the True Dharma to endure for a long time, namely, correct exposition and correct reception.
Other masters say:
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma will remain for one thousand years.
This statement refers to its preservation through correct practice, not to the *Āgamas*.
If it were according to the *Āgamas*, it would remain for a much longer period.
Why is this? In the final age, there are two kinds of people who are able to uphold this True Dharma:

first, those who gain faith through hearing; second, those who gain faith through correct understanding. All devas will protect such persons, ensuring that the Āgamas and the practice of the True Path do not quickly vanish from the world.
Therefore, within this [treatise], one should diligently cultivate correct practice according to the words and according to the meaning.
In this treatise, the Abhidharma of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is what I have expounded.
Is it as revealed in the Sautrāntika school, or as revealed in the Vibhāṣā?
The verse says:
"The principles of the Kaśmīra Vibhāṣā are established; for the most part, I follow them in composing this treatise."
"It is my own fault that I have been biased toward the True Dharma; the Buddha alone is the authority for judging the correct principles of the Dharma.
The commentary states:
"This Abhidharma is established by the two proofs of the Vaibhāṣika masters of Kaśmīra; I now mostly explain its meaning in accordance with their doctrine."
If there is any partiality or dogmatic attachment therein, that is my own fault.
To correctly discern and judge the True Dharma apart from direct realization, only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is the supreme authority. Why is this so?
Because of having realized and seen all phenomena,
if a noble disciple of the Buddha were to set aside the *āgamas* and the principles of reasoning to determine the True Dharma, that too would not constitute valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty-one and Fascicle Twenty-two,
composed by Vasubandhu.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Paramārtha from Central India:
The Great Master, the Eye of the World, has closed his eyes; Furthermore, those who realize and teach [the Dharma] are gradually perishing and dispersing.
Failing to see the true meaning, people lacking self-restraint Disturb the Dharma through improper reflection.
Having realized for himself that he has entered the most wondrous stillness, he carries the burden of teaching others as they follow him into extinction;
the world is now without a master, its merit destroyed, and delusion moves at will, unrestrained by any hook.

If you know that the life-span of the Buddha’s Dharma is nearly exhausted, having reached the very throat, this is a time when the power of delusion is at its peak; seek liberation and do not be heedless.
Is it possible to attain liberation through a teaching other than this Dharma? No.
No. Why is this so? Because it does not deceive the mind in the manner that the view of a self does.
Why is this? Because that person does not establish the conventional designation of "self" within the continuity of the five aggregates.
For what purpose?

Because of that conceptualization, there exists a distinct, real entity called the "self" and "all," or because the grasping at a self is the root of birth, there is no possibility of liberation regarding other phenomena.
How is it known to be thus?

It is because the designation "self" is applied only to the continuity of the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) and not to any other referent, since a self is not known through either direct perception (pratyakṣa) or inference (anumāna).
Other phenomena, whether they actually exist or are unobstructed, must necessarily be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as the six sense objects and the mind;
or they may be known through inference (*anumāna*), such as the five sense faculties.

In this regard, one may infer as follows: if a particular cause and condition exists, yet other causes and conditions are absent, the arising of an entity is not observed; however, when they do exist, the arising of the entity is observed.

If the conditions such as visual objects are fully present and obstructing factors are entirely absent, yet visual consciousness and other such cognitions do not arise in those who are blind or deaf, as well as in those who are neither blind nor deaf, one may infer by means of *anumāna* (inference) that no distinct cause exists [to account for this difference].
There is another interpretation: the specific causes are precisely the sense faculties, such as the eye.
Since neither direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) nor inference (*anumāna*) exists with respect to a self (*ātman*), it is therefore said that there is definitively no self.
This is what the Vātsīputrīya school asserts:
that there must necessarily exist a self which is neither identical to nor different from the five aggregates.
This statement ought to be subjected to careful analysis.
Is it held by them that [things] exist as substantial entities (*dravyataḥ*) or exist as designations (*prajñaptitaḥ*)?
What are the characteristics of substantial existence,
and what are the characteristics of designation-based existence?
If it exists as a distinct entity like form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it is called a "substantially existent thing" (*dravyasat*).
If it exists merely as an aggregation like milk and so forth, it is called a "nominal existence" (*prajñaptisat*).
If it were to exist as a substantial entity, then because its nature would be distinct from the aggregates (*skandha*), one should say that it is different from the aggregates.
For example, regarding each of the individual aggregates (skandhas), one must necessarily speak of this as their cause.
If there were no cause, it would be unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), which would be identical to the assertions of the non-Buddhist teachers (tīrthika), and it would likewise lack any distinct function.
If you maintain that existence is due to existence by way of designation (*prajñapti*), this is the most excellent explanation;
we also speak in this manner.
We establish the existence of the self (*ātman*) not by asserting existence through substantial reality (*dravyasat*), nor by asserting existence through designation.
What is the meaning of this?
It refers to the grasping at the present internal appropriated aggregates as a self.
Now, this specific statement does not further clarify the meaning and is not something we can understand.
What meaning does this statement clarify?
If the meaning is as follows— that is, that the self is conventionally designated in dependence upon the aggregates (skandhas) among those very aggregates—
then this meaning must be established, just as milk is conventionally designated in dependence upon substances such as color and so forth.
Furthermore, if the meaning were such that the statement "the self exists" is established because of the aggregates— that is, because the aggregates are the cause for the statement "self"—
then this position would likewise share the same fault as the previous one, since it takes the statement "self" as its cause.
We do not say that the self is like this. If it were not so, how would it be?
Just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel, so too is the person designated in dependence upon the aggregates (*skandha*).
How can fire be designated in dependence upon fuel?
If fire were separate from fuel, it could not be designated; nor can it be established that fire is either different from or non-different from fuel.
If fire were different from fuel, the fuel would not be hot.
If fire were not different from fuel, that which is burned would be identical to that which burns.

Likewise, apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), one cannot maintain or speak of a "person" (*pudgala*); nor can it be said that the person is different from the aggregates, because that would entail the fault of [the person] being permanent.
Nor can it be said that the person is not different from the aggregates, for that would entail the fault of [the person's] annihilation.
Good friend, I pray that you explain to me: what is the fuel?
What is fire? Later, I shall come to understand the meaning of fire as it is designated in dependence upon fuel.
What, then, should be said in this context?
That which is burned is the fuel; that which burns is the fire.
If there is something to be said, it must necessarily be stated in this way.
In this regard, you must further clarify: what is the thing that is burned?
What is it that burns? In the world, combustible material is called "fuel" (indhana) and is also termed "the burned.
If it burns, that which possesses the light and the highest heat is called "fire" (agni).
Why is this? Because these substances can ignite that [other substance] and burn it, by virtue of being able to transform its continuum so that it is no longer as it was before.
Each of these two consists of eight substances.

Fire arises dependent upon fuel, just as curd arises dependent upon milk or vinegar arises dependent upon *mātuḷuṅga* fruit; therefore, it is said that fire is spoken of in terms of its heat relative to the fuel.
If this is so, then one knows that fire is distinct from the fuel, because they do not exist simultaneously.
If fire were like a person, it would necessarily arise dependent upon the aggregates (*skandha*); if it were distinct from the aggregates, it would be impermanent.

Furthermore, if that which is the sensation of heat within burning fuel is called "fire," then the remaining three great elements (*mahābhūta*) that arise simultaneously with it are admitted to be the "fuel."
The distinction between these two is clear and easy to understand, as their characteristics differ.
You must now explain how fire exists in relation to fuel:
in what sense is fire said to exist in relation to the heat of the fuel?
Why is this? This fuel is not the cause of fire, nor is heat said to be the cause of fire. Why is this?
Fire alone is hot; this is what is called the cause of fire.
If you say that the term "in relation to" (*apekṣya*) has the meaning of "dependence" or "coexistence":
If that were so, the aggregates would constitute the support for the person and would arise simultaneously with it; furthermore, their mutual distinction would be clearly and easily discernible.
Moreover, if the aggregates were to cease, the person would immediately cease, just as when the fuel is extinguished, the fire is extinguished.
Regarding what you have said: "If fire were different from fuel, the fuel would not be hot.
In this case, what thing is called "hot"? If you say:
That which is hot is called "heat.
Consequently, fuel should not be hot, because it possesses a distinct nature from fire.
Furthermore, if you say:
If there is the nature of heat, it is called "hot.

Although this object is distinct from the fire that possesses the nature of heat, it nevertheless becomes hot because it is associated with that nature of heat; therefore, there is no fault in their being distinct.
Furthermore, if you say that the very object currently burning is called both "fuel" and "fire," then you must now explain this according to its meaning.
If the aggregates were identical to the person, this would mean they are not distinct; such a conclusion would be unavoidable, and therefore this analogy is invalid.
As previously stated, just as fire is designated in dependence upon fuel, so too is the person designated in dependence upon the aggregates.

Furthermore, if it cannot be said that the person is different from the aggregates, then among the five kinds of knowable objects—namely, the past, the future, the present, the unconditioned, and the ineffable—it would follow that this [person] must also be ineffable.
Why is this? Because regarding the objects of knowledge in the past and so forth, it cannot be said that the person is the fifth [aggregate] or not the fifth.

At that time, you must consider: when one speaks of a "person," is it based on observing the aggregates that one speaks of a "person," or is it based on observing the person itself that one speaks of a "person"?

If one observes the aggregates (*skandha*) and speaks of a person by way of grasping them, it is only by relying upon the aggregates that one speaks of a person, because a "person" cannot be found [as a separate entity].
If one observes the person and speaks of a person, how can you say that one speaks of a person by relying upon the aggregates?

Why is this? Because this clinging asserts that only the person (*pudgala*) is the object of cognition. If you say that the aggregates (*skandha*) can be known only if there is a person, and therefore one speaks of clinging to a person with reference to the aggregates; [we reply: so be it. However, since the person is not established as a real entity, this clinging is merely a false conceptualization. Furthermore, because such clinging arises based on the aggregates, it is said to be "clinging to the aggregates. If the person were truly existent, it would follow that it must be perceived independently of the aggregates, just as the aggregates themselves are perceived. Since this is not the case, the person is not established. Therefore, clinging to a person is merely a false conceptualization arising from the aggregates. For this reason, it is said that clinging to a person is clinging to the aggregates. Moreover, if the person were distinct from the aggregates, it would follow that it is permanent, just like space. If it were identical to the aggregates, it would follow that it is impermanent, just like the aggregates. Since it is neither distinct nor identical, the person is not established. Thus, clinging to a person is merely a false conceptualization. Furthermore, if the person were substantially existent, it would follow that it is either different from or identical to the aggregates. If it were identical, it would follow that it is impermanent, just as the aggregates are. Since it is neither different nor identical, the person is not established.
