If that were so, then at the time when the eye-faculty attends to light and other conditions such that this visible form can be known, one should likewise maintain that the visible form is designated in dependence upon the eye-faculty and so forth.
This point is indeed established.
You should explain: among the six consciousnesses, by which consciousness is the person known?
They say it is known by all six consciousnesses.
What is the meaning of this?

If one conceptually observes a person by taking as an object the forms known through the eye, one should say that this person is "known through the eye"; it cannot be said that the person is identical to the forms, nor that they are not identical to the forms.

Furthermore, if one takes the phenomena known by the mind as an object and conceptually observes them as a person, one should say that this person is "known by the mind"; it cannot be said that they are either identical to those phenomena or not identical to them.
If that were so, this person would be identical to milk and the like.

If one conceptually observes milk or water by taking as an object a visible form known by the eye, one should say that the milk or water is what is known by the eye; it cannot be said that it is either identical to or different from the visible form.
It should be explained in this manner.
The same applies to what is known by the nose, tongue, and body, up to the point that it cannot be said whether the tangible is identical to touch or not identical to touch.
Otherwise, milk, water, and so forth would not be composed of the four primary elements, which is a conclusion we do not accept.

Therefore, just as substances such as color and so forth are metaphorically designated as "milk" or "water," so too should the person be metaphorically designated as a "person" based upon the possession of the various aggregates; this principle must be established.
Regarding what you have said— that one observes a person by means of the conceptualization of forms known through the eye—
what is the meaning of this statement?
Is form the cause for the cognition that observes the person, or is it that by directly cognizing form, one simultaneously cognizes the person?
If form is the cause for the cognition of a person, one cannot say that the person is different from it.

If that were so, then form, light, the eye faculty, and applied and sustained thought should likewise not be said to be different [from the person], because they too are causes for the cognition of form.
If one directly realizes form, one simultaneously realizes the person. Is it by means of the very cognition that realizes form that one realizes the person, or by means of a distinct cognition?

If it is by means of the very cognition that realizes form that one realizes the person, then the person and form should not be of different natures; or else, "person" would be merely a conventional designation applied to form.
If it were not so, and if they were both cognized by a single cognition, how could one distinguish between these two—that "this person is not matter" and "this matter is not the person"?
If one cannot make such a distinction, how can one insistently establish this statement, namely, that "form exists" and "the person also exists"?
Why? Because it can be said that they exist based on their being cognized through direct experience.
The same should be said for everything from form (*rūpa*) up to mental phenomena (*dharma*).
If these two were distinguished by separate cognitions because they are apprehended at different times, then the person would be distinct from form, just as yellow is distinct from blue and so forth.
Furthermore, just as with preceding and succeeding moments, this should also be said regarding phenomena (*dharma*).
If you say: "Just as in the case of form (*rūpa*) and the person (*pudgala*), their identity or difference cannot be stated, yet they can be cognized."

It is likewise impossible to say whether these two knowledges are identical or distinct; therefore, it is also impossible to say that this knowledge is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), for that would contradict one’s own established tenet (*siddhānta*).
If you claim that the person exists, yet can only be said to be neither identical to nor different from form (*rūpa*), why did the Blessed One say:
"Form is non-self, and so on up to consciousness is also non-self"?
Regarding what you have said—
that visual consciousness can perceive a person—
does this consciousness arise conditioned by visible forms?
Does it arise conditioned by one person?
Or does it arise conditioned by two?
If that were so, what would be the consequence?
If it arises conditioned by form, it cannot arise conditioned by a person, just as in the case of sound and so forth. Why is this?
If a consciousness arises conditioned by a particular object, only that object is the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for that consciousness.
If [consciousness] were to take a person (*pudgala*) or both as its object, this adherence would be inconsistent with the Sūtras and thus contradicted by the Buddha’s teachings. Why is this?
Because the meaning has already been definitively established in the Sūtras: consciousness arises only in dependence upon two types of phenomena (*dharma*).
Furthermore, there is another sutra that also contradicts this tenet.
The sutra says:
"O Bhikṣus:"
The eye is the cause and visible form is the condition that can produce visual consciousness.
Why is this? Because all visual consciousness whatsoever arises solely with the eye as its cause and visible form as its condition.
If it were as you maintain, this person would necessarily be impermanent. Why?
Because the causes and conditions that produce visual consciousness are all impermanent.
Because of this scriptural statement, if you maintain that the person is not the object of visual consciousness, then the person is not known by visual consciousness.
Furthermore, if you establish the thesis that the person is known by all six consciousnesses, then this person must be known by auditory consciousness as well.
It would follow that it is distinct from color; for example, because it is known by visual consciousness, it would follow that it is distinct from sound, just as color is.
One should understand that this applies to other objects as well.
Furthermore, the words of this sutra contradict what you maintain.
The sutra says:
"O Brahmin!"

These five faculties each have their own distinct range of activity and their own distinct objective sphere; they experience these respective ranges and spheres through their own functioning. It is not the case that one faculty can experience the range of activity or the objective sphere of another faculty—namely, the eye-faculty, ear-faculty, nose-faculty, tongue-faculty, and body-faculty.
The mind is able to experience the spheres and objects of the five sense faculties; therefore, the mind is that upon which they depend.
A person is not an object; if it were not an object, it should not be cognizable by the six consciousnesses.
If that were so, the mental faculty (*manas*) would have to be distinct [from the other faculties], yet it does not apply [to them].
As the Sūtra says:
"There are six faculties, each with its own respective range and its own respective object; they each desire their own respective range and object."

This statement is made within the context of the six metaphors for the self among sentient beings; however, this interpretation is incorrect. In this sutra, it is not definitively stated that the six sense-faculties (indriya) function as faculties (indriya), because the five [physical] faculties lack the capacity for such activities as desiring to see, and their corresponding consciousnesses are likewise devoid of such qualities.
The mental consciousness induced by that predominant basis is established as having this [basis] as its faculty; therefore, it is called a "faculty.

Since this mental consciousness is induced by the predominant condition of a mind belonging to a specific category, and this consciousness is not capable of desiring to experience the spheres of activity or objects of other faculties, there is no fault.
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
"O bhikṣus!
I shall now for you expound the Dharma-gate of all that should be known and all that should be cognized."
The eye faculty is that which should be known and that which should be cognized, as are forms, eye-consciousness, and eye-contact.
With eye-contact as a causal condition, feelings arise internally—namely, suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Even down to the internal feelings—namely, suffering, pleasure, and neither-suffering-nor-pleasure—that arise conditioned by mental contact;
this is called the Dharma-door of all that should be known and all that should be cognized.
According to this sūtra, whatever is to be known (*jñeya*) and whatever is to be cognized (*vijñeya*) is definitively limited to this extent and does not exceed it.

Since the person (*pudgala*) is not mentioned therein, the person is certainly not something to be known, because its cognitive domain would be identical to that of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Those who grasp at a self say:
"We see persons with our own eyes; since we see a self where there is no 'mine,' [a self must exist].
They thus fall into the deep pit of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
In the sūtras, the Blessed One himself spoke of definitive meaning, saying:
"It is only with respect to the five aggregates that one speaks of a 'person' as a conventional designation.
This is stated in the *Pudgala-sūtra*:

Dependent upon the eye and conditioned by visible forms, visual consciousness arises; from the conjunction of these three, contact arises, which in turn gives rise to feeling, perception, attention, and so forth.
These four formless aggregates, together with the eye-faculty and visible forms—precisely this much is designated as a "person."
Based upon this, various names are established, namely: sattva, nara, mānuṣa, manuja, pudgala, jīva, and poṣa.
Regarding this, it is stated: "I see forms with the eye.
Concerning this, there is a traditional account which says:
"This living being has such a name, such a clan, such a caste, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, such longevity, such a duration of stay, and such a limit to its lifespan."
"Monks! Such matters are to be accepted by name alone, to be accepted by word alone, and to be accepted by tradition alone.
All such phenomena are impermanent, conditioned, volitionally produced, and arisen from causes and conditions."

Regarding such sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), the Blessed Buddha has declared them to be the reliance and the authority within this context; these sūtras are not to be further scrutinized or reconsidered.
Furthermore, another sūtra states:
"O Brahmin!"
If one speaks of "all that exists," it refers exclusively to the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
If a person were not subsumed within these, such a person would certainly not exist.
This principle is established: if something is subsumed within the bases, it is not the case that it cannot be spoken of.
In that school, there is a sūtra which says:
"O Bhikṣus!"
Whatever eye there is, whatever forms there are— explained at length as in the Sūtra— it is by this measure alone,
O Bhikṣus, that the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, declare all that exists to be finite and reveal the full extent of all teachings.
Furthermore, the *Bimbisāra-sūtra* states:
"O Bhikṣus!

An infant, an unlearned worldling, follows after the conventional designation of 'self. Yet herein there is no self and nothing belonging to a self; it is only suffering that, seeking birth, comes to be born," as explained at length in the sūtra.
There was an Arhat bhikṣuṇī named Śailā who spoke this verse to Māra:
"Just as from a collection of parts, The name 'chariot' is spoken therein, So too,
depending upon the aggregates (skandhas), A 'sentient being' is spoken by way of designation."
In a certain portion of the Āgamas, this verse was spoken for the sake of the brahmin Pācari:
“Pācari, listen: the Dharma that can untie all fetters—by means of this mind there is defilement, and again by means of this mind there is purification.”
The "self" has no essence of self; it is discriminated through inversion.
There is no self and no sentient beings; there are only dharmas, namely cause and effect.
The constituents of existence are only twelve; there are only the aggregates, bases, and elements.
Reflecting deeply upon this Dharma, one truly cannot find a person.
Just as one observes that the internal is empty, so too is the external;
these two cannot be found, nor can the practitioner or the meaning of emptiness.
Furthermore, another sutra states: There are five kinds of faults within the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*):

namely, giving rise to the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*); falling into the sphere of views; being no different from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); having a mind that follows deviant paths and perverse practices; failing to enter the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and failing to give rise to pure faith; the mind not abiding therein; and for such a person, the noble Dharma (*ārya-dharma*) does not become purified.
He does not accept this passage as an authoritative source. Why?
Because this passage is not recited or taught within our own school.
Is it the school that serves as the authoritative standard, or is it the word of the Buddha?
If one takes the school as the authoritative standard, then the Blessed One, the Buddha, would not be the true teacher for them, and they would not be the offspring of Śākyamuni.
If one takes the Buddha’s words as the authoritative standard (*pramāṇa*), why not take such passages as authoritative?
They reply:
"Such passages are not the Buddha’s words."
Why is it not the word of the Buddha?
Because it was not recited by our school in the past, and because an irrational matter has arisen now.
What is irrational about this?
"This textual passage is recited by all other schools; this textual passage does not contradict the Buddha’s sūtras or the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Because we do not recite it, it is not the word of the Buddha."
This statement is entirely without proper reflection and is merely a forced fabrication.
Is there not this sūtra for them as well?
Namely: "All phenomena are without self."
If you say: "We do not say that the person is the same as the dharmas,
nor do we say that the person is different from the dharmas," then it follows that this person would not be cognizable by mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Consciousness arises conditioned by two [factors], as determined by the scriptural text.
Regarding this passage, how do you analyze it to resolve the objection?
The Sūtra says:
To grasp at a self where there is no self constitutes a perversion of perception, a perversion of mind, and a perversion of view.
This grasping at a self where there is no self is a perversion; it is not [a grasping] of an actual self.
What, then, is not the self?
Regarding the aggregates, bases, and elements,
you previously stated:
"It cannot be said that the self is form or is not form."
These words are utterly intolerable. Why is this?
For it is stated in another sutra:
"Monks! If there are any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who contemplate and cling to the notion of a self, they all do so solely based upon the five aggregates of clinging.
Therefore, none of them conceive the notion of 'I' with respect to a [real] self."
Furthermore, another sutra states:

"If there are persons who can recollect various past lives—whether they have already recollected them, are currently recollecting them, or will recollect them in the future—all of them do so solely by depending upon the five aggregates."
If that is so, how is one to understand this statement in the Sūtra:
"I had such a form, etc., in a previous life"?
This statement is intended to reveal that the person capable of recollecting past lives can recollect many different types of past lives.
If one perceives that a person possesses form, one would fall into the fault of the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi).
Since [the Buddha] does not speak of a "self," it is said that all forms and so forth have no locus of belonging.
These words are not intended to reveal a self; therefore, the person exists as a conventional designation (prajñaptisat), like a collection or a stream.
If that were so, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, would not be omniscient. Why?
Because there is no mind or mental factor capable of knowing all phenomena as they arise and perish moment by moment; therefore, it is the person who knows.
If that were so, since you maintain that the person does not cease when the mind ceases, you have already admitted that the person is eternal.
We do not say that the Blessed Buddha is omniscient because his knowledge manifests simultaneously with respect to all objects.

If it were not so, how would this be? It is the continuum [of consciousness] that is designated as "Buddha. Possessing such a superior capacity, because he generates non-erroneous knowledge regarding any object he wishes to know simply by turning his mind toward it, he is called "Omniscient" (sarvajña).
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
"Because of the capacity within the continuum, Fire is said to consume everything;
So too is it said for the Omniscient One, Not because of simultaneous knowledge of all things."
How can this meaning be known?
It is known by the teaching of the past and other time periods.
As the verse says:
"These are the Buddhas of the past, these are the Buddhas of the future, and these are the Buddhas of the present world; they are able to remove the sorrows of sentient beings.
You all merely admit that the five aggregates exist across the three times, but you do not admit the existence of a person (pudgala).
If it were only the five aggregates that constitute a person, why would this sutra be taught?
The sutra says:
"I shall now, for your sake, speak of the heavy burden, the taking up of the heavy burden, the laying down of the heavy burden, and the bearing of the heavy burden."
Why is this statement inexpressible?
Because a burden cannot itself carry its own burden.
Why is it unable to do so?
Because it has never been seen before, it cannot be described; nor can it be said that this matter has not been seen before.
Furthermore, one must establish that the taking up of the burden is not included within the aggregates (*skandha*), in order to prove this point.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, distinguishes those who bear the heavy burden: such a person, with such a name and such a clan, even down to such a duration of stay and such a limit of lifespan.
One should understand that this is what is called "bearing a heavy burden"; do not conceive of it as some other entity, nor grasp it as being eternal, nor grasp it as being inexpressible.

It is the aggregates themselves that can extinguish the aggregates—meaning the preceding aggregates [extinguish] the subsequent ones. To clarify the meaning of bearing a heavy burden, this passage was spoken; there must certainly be a person.
Why is this? Because this sutra states:
"There are no spontaneously born sentient beings; such a tenet is a false view."
Who says that there are spontaneously born sentient beings?
Just as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, distinguishes sentient beings, so do I.

Therefore, if someone denies the continuity of the five aggregates that arise spontaneously in other births—referring to what the world designates as "spontaneously born sentient beings"—that person is said to have given rise to false views.

This means that there are no spontaneously born sentient beings, because it is the aggregates (*skandhas*) that are spontaneously born. Thus, what you have stated is a false view that denies the person (*pudgala*).
By the vision of which truth (*satya*) is it abandoned?
This wrong view should not be abandoned through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya), nor should it be abandoned through the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga). Why is this?
Because persons are not included within the four truths.
If you say: "There is another sutra that serves as proof, showing that the person is not the aggregates," as the sutra says:
"One person is born in the world for the benefit and happiness of many people," as explained at length in the sūtra.
Based on these words of the sūtra, it follows that the person is not the aggregates (skandhas).
This interpretation is not correct, because the designation "one" is applied metaphorically to a collection, just as one speaks of "a single sesame seed" or "a single grain of rice";
or it refers to a single aggregate, as when one speaks of "a single mountain" or "a single house."

One should say that the person (*pudgala*) is indeed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), because you admit that it has arising, just as the aggregates (*skandha*) do not exist previously and come into existence later.
But the birth of the person is not like this. Why is it not so?

Birth occurs because one takes up a distinct aggregate; for example, when a person is born as a Yājñika or a Vaiyākaraṇa, they are said to be "born" by virtue of taking up a specific field of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*).
Furthermore, it is like a bhikṣu or a person on the path who is "born"; they are said to be born by virtue of grasping at signs.
It is also like an old person who has already been born or a sick person who has already been born; they are said to be born by virtue of assuming a distinct state.
This interpretation is incorrect, because it has been rejected.
The Blessed One, the Buddha, has already rejected this meaning in the sūtras.
Which sūtra?
In the *Tattvaśūnyatā-sūtra*,
the sūtra says:
"O bhikṣus!"
Thus, there is karma and there is its retribution, yet an agent cannot be found because such a thing does not truly exist.
It is this [karma] that abandons these aggregates and takes up those aggregates, except for the "person" (pudgala) established by conventional worldly parlance regarding phenomena.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Phalguna-sūtra*:
"I do not say that a sentient being can grasp the aggregates; rather, it is only the continuity of dharmas that arises.
From this sūtra, one therefore knows that there is no person whatsoever who can grasp the aggregates or who can abandon the aggregates.
What do you now believe and maintain as the basis for your analogy of a person—whether it be the birth of a physician, a teacher, or even a patient?
If you maintain that it is the "self," this is not established, because such a self does not exist.
If one maintains that the mind and mental factors exist moment by moment as something previously non-existent, this cannot serve as an analogy.

If one maintains that the body is also like the mind, then, just as with the characteristics of the body's luminosity, there would have to be a distinction between the aggregates (*skandha*) and the person (*pudgala*).
Old age and sickness—these two are distinct states of the body; this is the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*) established by the Sāṃkhyas, which has already been refuted above.
Therefore, the examples cited by the teacher Yaśas and others are not valid.
If you maintain that while the aggregates (skandhas) possess the sense of "not having existed" coming into existence,
the person (pudgala) does not, then it follows that the person must be distinct from the aggregates and likewise eternal.
This meaning is clearly demonstrated.
You state that the aggregates (skandhas) are five and the person (pudgala) is one; why then do you not say that the person is different from the aggregates?
How can you say that the four great elements (mahābhūtas) and form (rūpa) are one?
Since form is not different from the four great elements, such is the fault in your thesis.
What is the proposition?
The proposition is that there is only the Great [Elements].
Nevertheless, just as only the four great elements constitute form (*rūpa*), so too it is accepted that only the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) constitute a person (*pudgala*).
If the person were merely the aggregates, why did the Blessed One, the Buddha, not declare that the life-principle is identical to the body or that the life-principle is distinct from the body?
It was because he took into account the intention of the questioner that he did not provide such a declaration.
This questioner maintains the view that there exists a distinct, real entity called the "life-principle" (jīva) which acts as the agent within; it is based on this that he asks his question.
Since such an entity certainly does not exist in reality, how could it be declared to be either identical to or different from [the body]?
It is like the tortoise’s hair being either coarse and rough or soft and smooth;
this knot has already been explained by the ancient masters of old.
There was a venerable Arhat named Nāgasena, to whom King Milinda went and said:
I now wish to question the Venerable One; for śramaṇas often speak at length.
If the Venerable One answers directly according to my questions, I shall then question the Venerable One.
The Venerable One said:
"O King, ask whatever you wish.
The King then asked:
"Is the life-principle (jīva) identical to the body?
Or is the life-principle different from the body?
The Venerable One replied:
"This matter is not something that can be definitively declared.
The King said,
"Venerable Sir!"
Did I not previously cause the Venerable One to take an oath that he should not speak further words?
I have further words; this matter is not something that can be spoken of.
The Venerable One said:
"I now wish to question the Great King; yet many kings speak with much verbiage.
If you answer my questions directly, I shall then proceed to question you."
The king said:
"Venerable sir, ask whatever you wish.
The venerable one then asked:
"Regarding the mango tree in Your Majesty's inner palace— is its fruit sour or sweet?
The King replied,
"There is no mango tree in my inner palace."
The Venerable One said:
"Great King!
Did I not previously cause you to take an oath?"
This means that one should not speak differently.
The King asked:
"What different words am I speaking?"
"In my inner garden there is no mango tree; since the tree does not exist, how could I describe the taste of its fruit as sour or sweet?
Great King!
In the same way, since this 'life-principle' (jīva) does not exist, how could I declare it to be either different from or identical to the body?"
Why did the Buddha, the World-Honored One, not directly declare "no-self"?
It was because the Buddha took into account the disposition of the questioner's mind, and therefore did not provide a direct answer. Why is this so?
This continuity of the aggregates is designated by the name "living being.
Lest people, by grasping at this, fall into wrong views, it is therefore not spoken of.
Because they have not thoroughly realized the principle of dependent origination consisting of twelve links, they are not vessels for receiving this correct teaching.
Furthermore, by means of this reasoning, one should resolve this point.
It was for this reason that the Blessed One spoke these words:
"Ānanda! The non-Buddhist ascetic of the Vatsa clan questioned me:"
"Am I existent, or am I non-existent?
I do not answer this.
Would it not be inappropriate to speak such words?"
It means that all phenomena are without self. Ānanda!
If I were to answer the question of the Vatsagotra outsider by saying that all phenomena are without self, [he would not understand].
Furthermore, these non-Buddhists were already immersed in the darkness of delusion; will they not now enter even deeper into that darkness than before?
Previously there was "I" and "mine," but now there is forever no "I."
If one clings to a self, one falls into the view of eternalism; if one clings to non-self, one falls into the view of nihilism. This is explained at length as in the sūtra.
Herein, a verse says:
"Observing the body wounded by tusks, And the abandonment of wholesome karma,"
The Buddhas preach the True Dharma like a tigress carrying her cub in her mouth:
if one believes that a self exists as spoken, one will be wounded through and through by its fangs;
yet if one abandons the conventionally designated self, the good child will fall.
He further spoke in verse:
"Because the person does not truly exist, the Buddha did not declare them to be either identical to or different from [the aggregates].
Nor can it be said that they do not exist; do not cling to the notion of a non-existent conventional self."
Within this continuity of the aggregates, there exists the principle of the fruits of good and evil;
yet some deny the existence of a "life-principle" (jīva) because they assert that no such life-principle exists.
Such persons are not yet capable of receiving the correct teaching on the principle of true emptiness.
When asked whether a self exists or does not exist, he did not answer that it either exists or does not exist.
If one considers the intent of the question, why did he not record [an answer] regarding its existence?
Because it would lead to the same difficulty as the previous case regarding non-existence after death, he did not record [an answer].
Regarding questions such as whether the world is eternal, the Buddha likewise did not provide a categorical answer (*avyākṛta*), because he took into account the intention of the questioner.
If that person conceives of a self (*ātman*) as being the world, then since such a self does not exist, none of the four possible answers would be logically tenable.
If they maintain that all of birth and death is called the "world," this response is likewise unreasonable. Why?
Because if the world were eternal, not a single person could attain parinirvāṇa.
If it were not permanent, then everything would be subject to total annihilation and would naturally enter parinirvāṇa.
If both [permanence and impermanence] were present, then necessarily one part would fail to attain nirvāṇa while another part would attain it.
If it were neither of the two, it would follow that there is neither the attainment of nirvāṇa nor the non-attainment of nirvāṇa;

for the attainment of nirvāṇa is contingent upon the Path. Therefore, it cannot be definitively answered as one of four alternatives, just as, for example, the Buddha did not declare whether the sparrow held in the hand of a Nirgrantha disciple was dead or alive.
For this reason, the Buddha did not provide a definitive answer to the four questions concerning whether the world is finite and so forth.
This is because these four questions share the same underlying meaning as the previous four points.
How is this known?
There was a non-Buddhist named Uktika who asked the Buddha these four questions.
He further asked:
"Does the entire world attain liberation through this path, or only a portion of the world?"
The Venerable Ānanda said:
"Uttika! You have already asked the Blessed One about this matter at the outset; for what reason do you now ask about this same matter again by means of a different approach?"

Regarding the Tathāgata’s four questions concerning death after passing away and so forth, the Buddha likewise did not provide a definitive answer because he took into account the intention of the questioner. Why was this?
That person held that a self already liberated is what is called the "Tathāgata," and thus posed these questions.
To those who maintain that there is a self, one should pose this question:
"Why does the Blessed One declare that a living person exists, yet does not declare that a person exists after death?"
In order to avoid the fault of falling into the extreme of eternalism,
how should this matter be explained?
The Buddha said:
"Maṇḍalika! Indeed, you shall in the future become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Furthermore, how can a śrāvaka who has passed away and died in the past be reborn later, and yet be prophesied [by another]?"
If it were said that "a certain person was born in such-and-such a place," this would likewise entail the fault of eternalism.

If the Blessed One did not predict [the future] because he previously saw sentient beings existing but no longer sees them after they have entered parinirvāṇa, then his failure to predict would be due to ignorance; this would thereby deny the Master’s quality of omniscience.
You should perhaps accept this point: because the self does not exist, the Buddha did not provide a definitive teaching [on its existence].
If the Buddha saw a person and did not teach regarding them, then even though he did not teach that this person exists, it follows as a matter of course that they are eternally abiding.
If you say that this meaning— that the Buddha both sees and does not see—
is likewise inexpressible, then you must gradually establish this principle so that everything becomes inexpressible.

The Buddha, the World-Honored One, is omniscient; it cannot be said that he is not omniscient, nor can it be said that "I definitely exist. It is on the basis of this statement, relying on reality and abiding therein, [that he speaks].

To negate the self and assert "no-self" is called a *dṛṣṭisthāna* (a basis for views); to assert that [the self] exists is likewise a *dṛṣṭisthāna*. Therefore, this statement cannot be taken as authoritative proof.
The Abhidharma masters say:
both of these are *antagrāhadṛṣṭi* (extreme views), as they are subsumed under the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
This statement is logical,
as it is said in the *Bāṣya-sūtra*:
"Ānanda!..."
If one says there is a self, that person falls into the view of eternalism.
If one says there is no self, that person falls into the view of nihilism.
If you say that there is no person, then what is it that transmigrates through birth and death?
Why is this? Because birth and death proceed and return of their own accord; this principle cannot be expressed in words.
Thus the Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
All sentient beings, with ignorance as their veil and craving as their bond, wander back and forth between this world and that, whether in the realms of hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, or gods.
Thus, throughout the long night, they undergo manifold sufferings, increasing their craving and constantly accumulating drops of blood.
If this is so, how can such a person traverse the cycle of birth and death?
By abandoning these aggregates, one undergoes those other aggregates.
Your current thesis has already been refuted previously.
If that were so, how could there be coming and going apart from a person?
Just as fire perishes moment by moment, yet is said to "move" by virtue of its continuity,
so too this collection of aggregates is called a "sentient being.
With craving as the fuel for grasping, it is designated as "coming and going" with reference to that continuity.
If the world were merely an aggregation of the aggregates (skandhas), why did the Blessed One say:
"In the past, I was once a teacher of the world named Sunetra"?
Why should it not be said in this way?
Because the aggregates (skandhas) are distinct.
If that is so, what is this "person" (pudgala)?
If the person of the past were identical to the person of the present, then the person would be permanent; therefore, "I am now the teacher of that past life.
These words reveal a single continuum (*saṃtāna*).
It is like saying, "This fire that was burning there has reached here."
If a self truly existed, only the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, would be able to perceive it clearly.
Having perceived it, the World-Honored One would then establish the grasping at a self, causing it to become firm and substantial.
Since the "self" exists, the "mine" is also established.

It is for the sake of clarifying this meaning that the Buddha taught the sūtras: when sentient beings give rise to the grasping of "mine" toward the five aggregates, it becomes solidified and substantial.
Thus, when they have established the view of a self and the view of "mine" regarding the five aggregates, their attachment to that which is "mine" becomes further solidified.
Bound by this solidified attachment to "mine," they become increasingly remote from liberation.
If you say: "I do not give rise to self-love toward a self," how can this statement be consistent with reason?

That is to say, one gives rise to self-love toward a non-self by means of the conviction that a self exists, yet does not give rise to self-love toward a real self; therefore, within the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, there is no cause or condition for the arising of the tumor-like views of those who deny the self while giving rise to the grasping at a self.

Furthermore, there are those who deny existence and cling to the notion that everything is non-existent; these are the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who falsely imagine that the self (*ātman*) is a distinct, substantially existent entity.

Within the True Dharma, there are those who give rise to the clinging to a self (*ātmagrāha*) as well as the clinging to universal non-existence. Such people alike fail to attain liberation, because there is no distinction between them.
If a self does not exist in any way whatsoever, and since the mind arises and perishes moment by moment, how can one remember events experienced over a long period of time now?
How is this further known?

From the recollection of the characteristics of an object, a mind characterized by a specific category arises; from this mind characterized by a specific category, an immediate subsequent recollection is produced.
What are its characteristics?
Does it possess association, perception, and so forth, identical to those of the mental application of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-manasikāra*),
and does it lack any distinction in its basis?
Sorrow, lamentation, distraction, and other such factors impair its power. Why is this?
This mind, which is a specific type of conceptualization, cannot produce this mindfulness if it shares the same object but belongs to a different category.
If they are of the same kind but not the same object, this cognition cannot arise.
If both are the same but exist for only a single moment, this cognition also cannot arise.
Only when they differ from these three conditions can this cognition arise.
If the arising of memory necessarily occurs by means of this [mind], for no other entity is seen to possess efficacy regarding memory,
how can it be that one mind perceives an object while another mind subsequently recollects it?
Why is this? That which is seen by Devadatta’s mind should not be remembered by Yajñadatta’s mind.
This argument is incorrect, because they are not associated.
The mind associated with heaven and the mind associated with sacrifice—these two are not concomitant, because they do not stand in a cause-and-effect relationship.
It is not as in the case of a single continuous stream of mind, where there is concomitance; that is not so here.
We do not say that one mind sees and another mind remembers. How is this so?
From the mind that saw, a distinct mind of recollection arises due to the transformation of the continuum, as previously explained.
If that were so, what fault would there be?
From a mind of recollection, another mind arises that knows [the object].
If there were no self, who could remember?
What is the meaning of "being able to recollect"?
It is because through mindfulness one can apprehend an object; this apprehension of the object is not distinct from mindfulness itself.
Since it is precisely this mindfulness that performs the act of apprehension, this is what I have stated previously.
The causal conditions that can produce this mindfulness are what are called the various types of conceptualization within the mind.
Furthermore, regarding what you have stated—that from this continuity there arise designations and numerous instances of recollection—this is termed "recollection."
If there is no self, whose thought is this thought?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the distinct term "sixth"?
Its meaning is "master."
It is, for example, like someone asking:
"What is the primary factor here?
It is like the case of the Brahmin's cow.
How so? Because the Brahmin is the owner of this cow, as it is subject to him through acts such as riding, driving, and employing it.
If that is the case, where can this mindfulness be employed?
On this basis, the self is regarded as their master.
Within the context of objects that ought to be remembered, what purpose does [the self] serve therein?
It serves to cause those [mental states] to become objects of memory.
It is rare indeed that one who possesses mastery over pleasure would speak thus, saying: "This is made to arise by this.
How can this be made to act?
Does "making to act" (niyojana) mean causing [something] to arise, or does it mean sending away [something]?
Because there is no activity due to mindfulness, the latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) are said to arise based upon it.
If that were so, the master would become the cause of the wealth, and the wealth would become the result of the master. Why is this?

Because the cause exercises sovereignty over the fruit through its presence in the fruit, and because the cause is apprehended by means of the fruit; since this cause is capable of producing mindfulness, and this mindfulness belongs to this cause, "sovereignty" (adhipati) thus has the sense of "cause" (hetu).
The collection of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that continues in a series and is gathered into one place is designated by the name "Devadatta" or "Gośālīputra.

This person, who is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti-pudgala*), is called "Gośālīputra" because he is conceived as the causal condition for the transformation and arising of cattle in other places.
Within this [collection], there is not a single person named Devadatta, nor is there a single thing called "cow.
Therefore, within this [collection], if one were to exclude the sense of being a cause, it could not be established as the primary [referent].
What is it that cognizes?
Whose cognition is this? It should be explained in the same manner as [the analysis of] mindfulness.

The causes and conditions for this consciousness are the sense faculties, objects, applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*); one should understand its specific distinctions according to the principle.
If someone says, "I exist," it is because there is an observer who perceives existence.
All existent things (*bhāva*) and so forth must necessarily be observed in relation to an existent agent (*bhavitr*) and so forth;
for example, as in the case of Devadatta walking. Herein, the action (*bhāva*) is called "walking," which must necessarily be observed in relation to the walker, Devadatta.
The case of consciousness is likewise: that which is capable of cognizing must necessarily arise in dependence upon its object.
One should ask this person:
"What is this 'Devadatta' of whom you speak?"
If it is said:
"I am given by the gods," this self has already been refuted previously and cannot be established.
If you say: "It is that which is manifested by worldly convention," then this person does not constitute a single entity;
rather, it is a collection of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) that receives such a name.
In this context, just as it was explained regarding Devadatta and the formations (*saṃskāra*), so too is it with Devadatta and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How is it explained regarding Devadatta and the formations?
The formations arise and perish moment by moment in a continuous succession without any difference; this is what is called "Devadatta."
Ordinary worldlings cling to that [continuum] and accept it as a single sentient being; it acts as the cause for its own continuum in other locations.
Regarding this, the world speaks of "Devadatta walking," and when it arises in another location, they speak of "walking."
For example, when a continuity of light or sound arises in a different location, it is termed "motion.
That very [continuity] acts as the cause for consciousness; thus, one says "Devadatta’s consciousness.
The Noble Ones also employ such designations in accordance with worldly convention, in order to conform to common linguistic usage.
In the sūtras it is said that consciousness cognizes its object; what, then, does consciousness do in this regard?
It does nothing at all.
Just as the fruit of consciousness resembles its cause yet performs no action, it is only because it attains a nature similar [to its object] that it is described in such a way.
The same applies to the statement that consciousness cognizes its object: it performs no action whatsoever, but merely acquires a semblance of the object.
What is the meaning of this "semblance"?

It is that the essence [of the consciousness] arises as resembling that [object]; therefore, although this consciousness arises from the sense organ, it is said to cognize the object and not the organ.
Furthermore, in this context, because the subsequent consciousness serves as the cause for the continuity of consciousness, it is said that "consciousness cognizes the object.
This statement is not erroneous, as the designation of an "agent" is applied to the cause, just as one says, "the bell is ringing."
Furthermore, for example, just as a lamp moves, so too does consciousness cognize its object.
What is meant by "the lamp moves"?
It is a conventional designation applied to the continuity of light that we call a "lamp."
When this continuum arises in another location, it is said that the lamp moves to another location.
In the same way, regarding the continuum of the mind, "consciousness" is used as a conventional designation.
When this mental continuum produces consciousness with respect to another object, that consciousness is said to belong to that object.
Furthermore, for example, as it is said in the world: "form exists, form arises, and form abides.
In this context, there are two modes of expression: that which possesses existence (*sattā*) and so forth, and that which is not different from existence (*sattā*) and so forth.
The same applies to the two statements regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If consciousness arises from consciousness and not from a self (*ātman*), why is it that its arising is not always similar to its predecessor?
Furthermore, why does it not arise according to a fixed sequence?

For example, just as sprouts, nodes, leaves, and so forth, exist through the characteristic of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) called "alteration while abiding," the nature of all conditioned dharmas is likewise such that their continuity is necessarily distinct.
If it were not so, then upon entering a meditative absorption attained at will (*kāmacāra-samādhi*), one would observe that the person’s body and mind arise as identical [to their prior state].
Since the entire continuum would not differ from the first moment, one should not emerge from the absorption spontaneously at a later time.

Furthermore, there is a definite sequence in the arising of the mind; for if a particular mind ought to arise from this [preceding] mind, then that [subsequent] mind necessarily arises from it, and thus there exists a distinct mind.
A mental state of a similar type has the capacity to produce another mental state of a similar type due to its specific nature.
For example, from a woman's mind, there may sequentially arise a mind associated with physical impurity, or a mind directed toward her husband, son, or others.
Furthermore, at a later time, due to a transformation in the continuum (*saṃtati-pariṇāma*), the mind of a woman arises once more.

This mind possesses the functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) to produce a defiled body and mind, or to produce a mind directed toward this husband, son, and so forth, because they belong to the same genus (*jāti*).
If it were otherwise, there would be no functional efficacy.
Furthermore, from this mind of the woman, immeasurable distinct minds arise due to various causes and conditions.
Among these many minds, whichever arises most frequently, arises with greater clarity, or arises most recently will arise first in succession, because the power of its cultivation is strongest.
Apart from the differences in external conditions for the present body, this mind possesses a powerful force of cultivation.
Why, then, does it not constantly receive its fruit?
It is because this mind possesses the characteristics of duration and transformation (*sthity-anyathātva*).
This characteristic of change (sthity-anyathātva-lakṣaṇa) possesses the merit of being conducive to the arising of distinct fruits of cultivation.
Regarding this characteristic of phenomena within all categories of mind, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess mastery over the knowledge of the immediate cause (anantara-hetu).
Regarding this, a verse is spoken:
“In a single tail-feather of a peacock, All causal characteristics are complete;
That others cannot know this— Such wisdom is the power of the Buddha.”
"How much less could we know the various distinctions among formless minds?
Furthermore, other non-Buddhists maintain that [the mind] arises from the self.
These two difficulties are most clearly established for those non-Buddhists."
Why is it that the mind does not arise perpetually with a single identical characteristic?
Why is it that it does not arise in a fixed sequence, as is the case,
for example, with the sprout, the node, and the leaf?
If you maintain that they differ due to the distinctions in the conjunctions of the observing minds, this is not correct;
for distinct conjunctions are not established, and because the objects of the two conjunctions are limited in number.

Regarding that which they describe as the characteristic of conjunction (*saṃyoga*): it is the state of not having arrived [at a location] that is prior, and arriving [there] subsequently that is designated as conjunction.

According to the characteristic of conjunction as they maintain it, one must then establish that the self (*ātman*) has a limited dimension; thus, the meaning of its omnipresence (*vibhu*) would not be established.
Therefore, since the mind undergoes movement, one should also say that the self undergoes movement and its cessation.
If you maintain that this is because of a partial conjunction,
that argument is incorrect, for a single entity cannot possess parts.
I also grant you that there is conjunction;
nevertheless, if the mind is eternally non-different, how can there be distinctions in conjunction? If you say:
The claim that because there are distinctions in observational knowledge (*jñāna*), there must therefore be distinctions in the mind (*citta*), is incorrect;
for the same difficulty applies to both knowledge and the mind.
Since the self (*ātman*) is without distinction, how could knowledge possess distinction?
If you maintain that, by observing the differentiation of effort (*prayatna*), the differentiation of cognition arises from its conjunction with a self (*ātman*),
this argument is not tenable.
Why do you not simply maintain that the differentiation of associated mental cognition arises solely from the differentiation of effort?
Why is this? Because herein no capacity of a self can be perceived or found in any respect whatsoever.
It is like when a medicinal preparation has been completed, a deceitful physician utters the words "svāhā."
If you say: "By means of me,
these two are established," this position is merely words.
If you say: "This self is that which serves as the basis," then,
in that case, what among these things is the supported?
What is that which is supported? Why is this so?
Because these two are not that which is held, just like painting colors and the seeds of the *bādara* tree.
Nor can it be that which supports, like a wall or a jar, because there would be the dual fault of mutual obstruction.
If the self were the support for those [aggregates] in this manner, it would not be so; if it were not thus, how could the earth element be the support for fragrance and the other qualities?

I am now greatly delighted that this analogy confirms my position: namely, that there is no earth-element (pṛthivī-mahābhūta) existing apart from fragrance and so forth that can be apprehended; rather, the "earth-element" is a mere conventional designation (prajñapti-saṃvṛti) applied to fragrance and the like.
In this way, there is no distinct self apart from the functional activity and the mind; it is merely to these two that the designation "self" is applied.
Who could definitively discern that earth exists as something distinct from its fragrance and other qualities?
You should now understand this: for example, it is like an independent person having a second head or distinct colors and so forth among the five sense objects.
If there were no separate earth-element apart from fragrance and the other qualities, how could one say that the earth possesses four attributes?
In order to distinguish them individually and to cause others to understand, odors and so forth receive the names "earth" and so on, yet there is no separate entity such as "earth.
For example, when one speaks of a wooden statue, although it has the form of a body, the cognition of it differs depending on the distinction of its perceived functions.
Why do all cognitions of omniscience not arise simultaneously?
If a particular causal efficacy (*kāritra*) is the strongest, that efficacy would obstruct other efficacies.
If this were so, why does this strongest efficacy not constantly produce its fruit?
This is that reasoning;
this very reasoning constitutes that analytical cultivation, so that I have no further need for it.
One must certainly accept the existence of self-notion (*ātman-saṃjñā*) and so forth, because they possess the nature of *guṇa*.
Since these qualities (*guṇa*) must necessarily depend upon a substratum (*dravya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*) therefore depends upon the self (*ātman*).
It is a quality of the self; if one were to maintain that it depends upon another substance, that would be inconsistent, because there is no cognition apart from the self and other substances.
This argument is not tenable, because that nature of *guṇa* (quality) is not established.
That which you have posited—namely, that mindfulness and so forth are of the nature of *guṇa*—is not established for me.
We maintain that everything that exists is designated as *dravya* (substance), because the Sūtra states:
"The fruits of śrāmaṇya consist of only six things.
Therefore, it is not established that those [fruits] have the *āśraya* (basis) as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Why is this? Because the meaning of "dependence" has already been analyzed previously and found to be untenable;
therefore, these words are merely idle talk.
If the self truly does not exist, what is the purpose of performing karma?
It is for the sake of thinking, "I shall experience pleasure" and "I shall experience suffering," that one performs karma. What, then, is this "I"?
I grasp at objects as "self.
What phenomena do I grasp at as objects?
The aggregates are the objects.
How do you know this?
Because affection arises toward it, and because it serves as the same basis for cognitions such as "white" or "black.

As it is said, "I am white," "I am black," "I am fat," "I am thin," "I am old," or "I am young"—one perceives that these conceptual attachments to "I" and the cognitions of "white," "black," and so forth, all share the same basis.

Since you do not admit that such distinctions exist within me, this "I" which I grasp must arise merely in relation to the aggregates; because they are beneficial to me, the term "I" is used as a conventional designation for the body.
For example, as it is said in the world:
"That minister is myself.
This is a metaphorical designation of the term "self" with respect to one who has been beneficial to oneself.
My own reckoning and adherence is not thus.
If [the self] takes only the body as its object, why does it not take another's body as its object?
This argument is incorrect, for it is inconsistent.

This grasping at a self occurs in conjunction with whatever phenomena—whether physical or mental—are present; it does not occur elsewhere, because it has been habitually practiced throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
What constitutes correspondence?
It refers to the principle of cause and effect.
If there is no self, then whose is this clinging to a self? Whose is this conceptualization?
Furthermore, what is the meaning of the term "distinct" (prthak) in the sixth [category]?
This question has already been addressed previously, yet it arises again now; the answer is likewise as before.
Up to this point: if a phenomenon (dharma) is the object of such conceptual construction (parikalpa), then by virtue of that conceptual construction, it belongs to that phenomenon.
If that is so, what dharma constitutes the act of grasping?
It is a defiled mind that, having been perfumed by past acts of grasping at a self, takes its own continuum as its objective sphere.
If there were no self, who would experience suffering and who would experience pleasure?
It is within this basis that either suffering or pleasure arises, just as a tree has flowers and a forest has fruit.
Upon what do this suffering and pleasure depend?
It should be understood that they depend on any one of the six internal sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), as previously explained.
If one maintains that there is no self (*ātman*), who is it that performs actions and who is it that experiences their results?
What is the meaning of the terms "karmic formation" (*abhisamskāra*) and "experience" (*upabhoga*)?
That which previously did not exist but causes something to come into being is called "formation"; the actual acquisition of the fruit of prior karma is called "experience."
This is a different designation for what has already been said; it does not reveal a distinct meaning.
The masters who analyze the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇavādin) state:
"One who possesses mastery over an object is called an agent (kartṛ)."
We observe that there are people in the world who possess sovereign power over certain matters, such as Devadatta.
Regarding activities such as staying, eating, and walking, what dharma do you now designate as "Devadatta"?
If you say that the "self" is named Devadatta, this has already been refuted by me; such a self does not exist as a real entity.
If you say that the five aggregates (skandhas) are the agent, then there would be no autonomy.
There are three kinds of karma, namely those of body, speech, and mind.
Among these, regarding bodily karma: this body, in its performance of actions, is necessarily bound to the mind; likewise, the mental action is also bound to the body.

It is the same for the mind that arises from its own causes and conditions regarding its own activity; therefore, there is no autonomy in any single thing. Since all existing phenomena are bound to causes and conditions, their arising is entirely devoid of autonomy.
In your doctrine, this grasped self is not admitted to be the agent unless other causes and conditions are observed; therefore, this Īśvara is not established.
Because these characteristics are absent, it is therefore impossible for any [of the elements] to be established as the agent.
Within the context of causal activity, that which possesses superior functional capacity is conventionally designated as the "agent."
Since no functional capacity of a self is perceived in other matters, it is untenable to establish the self as an agent. Why is this so?
Volition arises from recollection;
applied and sustained thought arise from volition; effort arises from applied and sustained thought; and wind arises from effort.
Since karma arises from wind, what function do I perform therein?
What are the characteristics of the experience of the fruit?
If I am truly employing this matter, then I am called the experiencer; such is the characteristic of experiencing the fruit.
What is the meaning of this statement?
If you claim that cognition (*buddhi*) constitutes sensation (*vedanā*), this is not correct;
for I have no functional capacity regarding cognition, since my functional capacity in relation to consciousness (*vijñāna*) has already been refuted.
If the self does not exist, why do wholesome and unwholesome karmas not arise without depending on what is not a sentient being?
This is because they depend upon the aggregates such as feeling (*vedanā*) and so forth.
Upon what does it depend?
It depends upon the six sense bases.
That this is not the self has already been explained previously.
If the self does not exist, how can a fruit arise in the future from an action that has already ceased?
If the self does exist, how can a fruit arise in the future from an action that has already ceased?
They arise from that which can depend upon them, whether dharma or non-dharma.
As you have stated, what is there that depends and what is the basis?
This argument has already been refuted; therefore, dharma and non-dharma have no basis of dependence.
Furthermore, we do not say that from a karma already ceased and extinguished, a retribution arises in the future. If that is so,
how then does a fruit arise from a specific excellence produced by the transformation of the continuum of karma?
It is like the case of a seed and its fruit.
As it is said in the world that fruit arises from a seed, this fruit does not arise from a seed that has already perished, nor does it arise without an interval.
What is arising?
It arises from a specific excellence in the transformation of the continuity of the seed.
That is to say, it refers to the flower produced in succession by the sprout, node, leaf, and so forth, as well as the fruit that follows the flower.
Since it arises from the flower, why is it called the fruit of the seed?
Because the capacity to produce the fruit within the flower is transmitted through successive stages, and this is the work performed by the seed.
This is the functional capacity of the final flower; if it were not preceded by the functional capacity of the seed, this flower would lack the capacity to produce such a concordant fruit.
Thus, regarding the arising of retribution from this karma, the meaning is no different from what has been stated.
Retribution does not arise from karma that has already perished, nor does it arise immediately thereafter.
If that is so, how can a fruit arise from a specific transformation of the continuity of karma?
In this context, what is this "continuity" (saṃtati)?
What is this "transformation" (anyathātva)?
What is this phenomenon called "superiority"?
It refers to the arising of successive moments of mind preceded by karma; this is termed a "continuum.
When this continuum becomes different from its preceding states in each subsequent moment, it is termed "transformation."

Within this process of transformation, that specific transformation which is immediately followed by the production of a fruit is called a "superior state" (*viśeṣa*), because it is the most excellent among all other transformations.

For example, the dying consciousness accompanied by grasping (*sopādāna-citta*) possesses the capacity for future rebirth; although various karmas may precede it, the capacity produced by whichever karma is most heavy, most proximate, or most habitually practiced manifests clearly therein, and not that of other karmas.
As the verse says:
"If karma is heavy, proximate, frequently practiced, Or was performed in the past—
These ripen in order from first to last, As the continuity of cyclic existence proceeds."
Among these, the capacity established by the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) ceases immediately after it has produced its fruit, namely the retribution (*vipāka-phala*).

As for the capacity established by the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) within the outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*): if it pertains to defiled phenomena, it ceases as soon as their antidote (*pratipakṣa*) arises; if it pertains to non-defiled phenomena, this capacity ceases through the permanent cessation of the mental continuum, which occurs at the time of parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, why is it that from a retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*), another retributive fruit does not arise?
For example, from a seed-fruit, another seed-fruit arises.
In this context, the meaning established by all these propositions need not be identical to the meaning of the analogy; here, another distinct fruit does not arise from a fruit.
If that is so, how does it arise?
It arises from a specific transformation of the moist swelling.
Herein, it is the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that can produce sprouts and the like; this is the seed of the fruit, and nothing else.
Furthermore, this preceding continuum is designated as a "seed" by virtue of its future name, because it is similar [to that which follows].

Here, too, it is the same: from this retribution, there arise—due to the differentiation of conditions such as hearing the two types of teachings, correct and false—either outflowing wholesome or unwholesome minds.
If transformation were to arise as birth, then from this [transformation] another distinct retribution would further arise, because it does not proceed by way of a different principle.
This analogy is identical to the thesis being established.
Furthermore, by means of this analogy, one should further understand this meaning.

For example, when a *mātuluṅga* flower is stained with the juice of *leha*, a transformation occurs within the continuum that gives rise to a red-colored pulp inside the fruit; it does not arise from anything else.
In this way, from the retribution produced by karma, no other distinct retribution can arise.

If it were to arise according to the principle previously explained, then—just as I have understood through my own wisdom—it has been demonstrated that, due to various superior capacities and distinctions, the continuum perfumed by various karmas reaches such a state that it is able to produce such and such a retribution.
This meaning is the domain of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones alone.
Herein, a verse is spoken:
"The superior category of karmic perfuming, The state of retribution, and purity."
By every kind of reasoning, none but a Buddha knows this;
the Buddha’s teachings and principles correspond with one another. Understanding the true meaning is the supreme authority (*pramāṇa*);
there is no harm in relying on these two modes of explanation. Why, then, do you resort to such fallacious arguments?
Thus well-established and pure in reasoning, having seen that such is the nature of all the Buddhas' teachings,
may those who act through various blind and dark false views abandon their external attachments and attain clear practice.
This single vast path to the land of nirvāṇa is illuminated by the light of the words of the Buddhas, the suns;
though the principle of non-self has been matured through the practices of the multitudes of sages, those with clouded eyes do not see it even when it is opened.
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, addressed Pūrṇa:
"You all should diligently uphold this Dharma. If anyone relies upon it to practice contemplation, they will certainly all attain the fivefold virtues."
Having thus revealed the method of the correct meaning, to open for wise people the gateway to the poison of [false] knowledge,
may they abandon external and erroneous attachments, so that both themselves and others may attain the true goal.
Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, Fascicle Twenty-Two
